If you play Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines for a short while, even a half hour, and odds are you'll see immediatly why this game is such a cult classic.  It is one of those rare titles where the writing, gameplay, and atmosphere come together perfectly to create a game that is pure, unmitigated fun.
The game starts with you choosing your Vampire clan (there are seven), each one with their own unique stats and skillsets.  Some clans are better as brawlers, whilest others are better at sneaking, and some are better at the social aspect of the game. Whichever way, the player can upgrade their character accordingly in order to fit their playing style. However, as many others have noted, it is probably better to save the Malkavians and Nosferatu for a 2nd run through, simply because they offer very different traits that makes gameplay much more unique compared to the other clans (Malk's have special dialog and encounter situations that only happen to them, while Nosferatu must rely on sewers to travel and are incapable of Seduction.)
One of the best parts of the game is, as noted, the atmosphere.  You play through four main areas of Los Angeles; each hub offers their own specific feel that reflects the progression of the story up to that point.  Although the game isn't open world, there is plenty of sidequests to keep you busy outside of the main story, and you'll need them:  upgrading your character requires Expierence Points, and those only come from completing quests (not, repleat: NOT in defeating enemies).  Upgrading stats gets fairly expensive quickly, so you truly have to sit back and think how you want to spend them.
The characters you encounter, from Smiling Jack to Jeanette (the "cold finger running down your spine"), are some of the more memorable in gaming, period.  They have some depth to them, and don't come across as your typical NPC.  Not to mention, some of the lines they say, and the lines you can say back, are pure gold.  Plus, they really fit with the whole idea of your character being the "new kid on the block".   Love them or hate them, you still need them.  They of course know this too, so don't expect to get anything for free.  In fact, one running theme in the game is to be careful who you trust.
Wise, wise words.
Bloodlines is widely regarded as a "flawed masterpiece", and as such there are a few features that are lackluster.  Long story short, the publishers forced the game on the market before the developers, Troika Games, could finish it: the result was an unplayable mess that hardly sold.  Even now, you NEED to download the unofficial patch (see the forums) to play this game.  Repeat: NEED THE UNOFFICAL PATCH TO EVEN RUN THE GAME.  STEAM SELLS THE UNFIXED, BUG FILLED GAME WHICH IS PRETTY MUCH UNPLAYABLE.  GET THE UNOFFICAL PATCH BEFORE PLAYING.
The rushed release also effected it in other ways.  In my opinion, the story really fizzles around 3/4 of the way through.  The rich atmosphere of the game kind of falls away, instead replaced by linear missions that simply rush you to the end.  The ending (there are a few) itself is a letdown for many: love it or hate it, I feel it has an anticlimatic feel to it.  It's almost as if Troika had some more story to tell that would have made the end feel more natural.  Instead the last part of the game is kinda thrust upon you suddenly.
Speaking of the end, another complaint many have is the combat.  Personally, I don't mind it, but I'd be kidding if I said it wasn't clunky as heck.  Earlier parts of the game allow you to bypass this somewhat (depending if you like sneaking or talking as an alternative), but that option is gone in the end stages.  In fact, the final act is pretty much 2 hours of endless brawls, after brawls, after brawls.  The sudden shift to an all combat intensive game-type can be either wearisome, or a total nightmare if you haven't really invested in combat skills throughout the story.  Tip: invest in combat skills.
Despite what is, in my opinion, a kinda weak finish, Bloodlines still is a great buy.  In no way is Bloodlines like Twilight or other recent supernatural franchises:  is a unique, one of a kind game.  Theres a meme online that saids all you need to know about Bloodlines: as soon as you mention it, someone will reinstall it.  Nuff said.

In a way this game (when you manage to run it with the unofficial patch) reminds me about Bathesda's Elder Scrolls series. It has small, more compact world because of the source engine I presume, but lots of content. I am mentioning Elder Scrolls for the solo purpose of saying that just like TES, VTM:B must be loved with all its flaws, bugs, errors and imperfections.
I honestly believe that Troika Games just had horrible luck as if universe screwed them up while they were creating the game.
Starting with engine itself, Troika used an unfinished Source Engine and had to work with it, adding their own code. Troika worked on the same engine that Half-Life 2 were even before the engine was shown publicly. In fact they had an agreement that they can't sell the game before the Half-Life 2 release.
After the engine came Activision. Even though Troika employers kept on working overtime on the game, Activision still rushed the release and cut off sponsorship of the game. So in the end we got ourselves a rushed, unpolished product that in fact was fixed and updated by fans for more than 11 years now.
And you might think thats it? Troika Games sold too little copies of the game to keep up afloat and ended up being closed. How did that happen if the game is so good as I keep on saying?
Bad luck.
Release date of the game is November 2004. What else happened in 2004 prior the November?
Unreal Tournament 2004, Far Cry, Sacred, Painkiller, Hitman: Contracts, Manhunt, Thief: Deadly Shadows,  Doom 3, Silent Hill 4: The Room, Sims 2, Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War, Star Wars: Battlefront, Myst IV: Revelation, Rome: Total War and many other awesome games. Year 2004 was an amazing year in the industry.
And you may think that with all that competition on the market VTM:B were safe since they released in November, while other games were earlier? Well, still bad luck Troika Games.
What happened in November in the PC game industry? (I am not mentioning games such as MGS3 and other console games since I am talking about PC)
CS:Source, Half Life 2, NFS: Underground 2, World Of Warcraft, Prince Of Persia: Warrior Within and so on. With all respect to Troika Games, they had no chance of wining a competition.
Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines is probably one of my favorite games of all time. With all it's imperfections and glitches it delivers an amazing lore, story, humor and experience. Gameplay itself (fighting) is done horribly and sloppy though so don't expect to be blown away with it, dialoges is what makes it so special. Depending on the vampire clan you chose it can take you 3 or more walkthroughs to experience all the game aspects such as different approaches (stealth, fighting with magic or brute force, persuation/intimidation/seduction) and even a special, Malkavian clan walkthorugh. You see, Malkavians are insane vampires. And by insane I mean totally sick. When you play as a Malkavian character literally every dialogue line for you is changed in a mad/insane way. In fact you can have a dialog with a news reporter on your TV if you are playing as a Malkavian.
All and all, when playing this game keep in mind that it was released in 2004 and it has lots of flaws that modern games don't, but thats simply because people are always becoming better at what they do and creating videogames is not an exception.

The game's plot like is basically a mixture of the Godfather, and Goodfellas, you're a war hero, come back from the war and fall into a life of crime with your friend. The open world nature of this game is not the same as GTA, which to me is a good thing, there aren't a million half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥mini-games to play. Each section of the city feels different, China-town feels different than Little Italy. I'm not going to list any spoilers but I do feel like this plot is decent, the voice acting is pretty good for the most part, the in-car conversations are pretty humorous a lot of the time. The driving is a HUGE improvement over the first game, the cars feel like real cars would from the 40s that is spongey suspension and sluggish acceleration, this is not bad design, it's how the actual cars behaved back then. The map is actually displayed in the radar instead of the lame "map" that's in the first game.
The guns are all fun, though the pistols pretty much all seem the same power, even the magnum (and the magnum sound a little goofy, like a cartoon gun). There is an actual cover system in the game, and overall the fights are much improved over the first game. This is a great game, it's heavy on graphics card, so I recommend looking into mods on how to disable the physics of the clothing in the game.
Overall I've really enjoyed this game and don't understand why people are criticizing it for NOT being just a GTA clone, it's a game I honestly find more fun than GTA.

I'll start this review by saying: this is the third (or fourth, can't remember) time I've edited this review. Every single time I've given it a thumbs up. The reason I keep coming back to it is because I almost every time I play (coming from a guy who's 700+ hours on this) I find something new I love about it. The gameplay is one of a kind, the skill ceiling is as high as you can imagine, I've been playing for almost 2 years and I'm still getting better, still learning new things. I know some people say this game has a bad community, honestly, I disagree. So many of the people I've talked to and played with in KAG are fun, positive people, while there are, obviously, some instances of less-than-stellar community, they are, in my experience, few and far between. One thing to keep in mind is there is an undeniably steep learning curve. If you're the type of person who can't play a game where you have to get rekt a few times to be any good, this isn't the game for you. However, it's not a punishing game, I had fun playing when I was god-awful, and I have (a bit more) fun now that I'm, at least in my opinion, not bad. I've never gotten tired of KAG. I've played this game for countless hours, yet I can really only claim to be good at one of the three classes, knight; I'm trying to get better at archer and I'm an abysmal builder. While the playerbase is smaller than it used to be, it's far from dead, I still see new players all the time (especially with the sale on) and I often play with people I've enjoyed getting rekt by for 2 years. In conclusion, BUY THIS GAME. Especially with the sale on, this is MORE than worth the money; I can honestly say I would have trouble thinking of a better 10$ I've spent. Buy it, play it, have an amazing time.

As venerable as this game's graphics look, many hail it as the progenitor of the 6DoF genre of games.  Much like the original Elite game's fame as the first to bring 3D vector models and sandbox gameplay to the personal computer, Descent was a pioneer in its own right on several levels.
For starters, the only game that rivaled its level of controls complexity at the time of its release, it can be argued, was Mechwarrior 2.  Pretty much every game before 1995 that involved first-person flight or movement were restricted to three axes (turn up-down, turn left-right, and move forward-back).  The occasional lateral movement was included (slide left-right), and was far less common, but games such as Quake and Duke Nuke'Em come to mind.  They might or might not include jumping, and crouching started getting introduced, but the physics of the world they took place in also limited their control schemes.  Most space flight games of the age had no lateral movement either.  The original Elite had no slide left-right, but had roll instead.  Each scheme had its own challenges, but never gave you all the options in a single package.
Then along comes Descent, a game with no gravity and no limits.  You could turn up-down-left-right, you could slide up-down-left-right, you could move forward-back, you could roll, you could look behind you, and you could afterburner for short boosts.  Not only that, but you could move in as many as three directions at once, and the speed benefits were additive, allowing you to perform what was then dubbed 'chording' for the greatest velocities.  Triple-chording was tricky, took skill to get right, and was sometimes dangerous (running into walls or lava), especially in the middle of dogfighting.  In the sense that EVE Online is the hardest MMO ever created by at least a couple orders of magnitude, Descent was harder than other first-person shooters by an equivalent amount.
It was also, along with Quake and Duke, one of the first few shooters you could play against other players.  All three originally supported only IPX protocols instead of TCP for network play, which meant you could only play against others on the same LAN, but services later started to appear (such as KaliDOS, Kali95, and Khan) that would do IPX-to-TCP translation and allow you to play against others across the internet through dial-up connections, ISDN, or eventually cable modems.  I have countless memories of LANfests and ladder matches in the early days of Descent and Descent 2 that, even to this day, have no equal because of Descent's no-direction-is-safe design.
6DoF games have traditionally been a niche for the hardcore gamer, with very few other games in the genre released.  The original Descent had two more games released, of course, and there was also a direct competitor launched later called Forsaken which received decent support on its own (see ProjectX for details).  Much later, Jumpgate Evolution had aspirations of becoming the king's successor (and would have succeeded) before it was cancelled.  Not long ago, Miner Wars was released as an homage to this genre, but it fell short and was riddled with bugs.  The most recent inheritor of the throne, though moreso in control scheme than setting, has become Elite: Dangerous, and this makes me a happy camper.
Regardless, Descent deserves a place in the history books as the grandfather to this playstyle all by itself.  Even if you discount the control scheme and ridiculously tricky and hilariously awesome multiplayer in its heyday, other aspects shine that were uncommon as well.  All of the original game takes place in the confined spaces of off-world mining facilities, with the layout of most of them painfully unfriendly to two-dimensional thinking.  Since there was no gravity and the mine traversed deep into the structure of the asteroid or planetoid it was carved into, there was also no reason to limit the level's layout to traditional gravity-based constraints.  It was a great deal easier to get lost if you weren't paying attention to all the options in all directions.
Lastly (at least among the aspects of the game that deserve special mention) was the lack of blood and gore.  In an age where the amount of violence against living antagonists (whether NPCs or other players) was increasing exponentially, Descent was a nice alternative that gave parents a choice they could get behind instead of turning a blind eye to the scary biologicals of Quake or sexism and bloodied aliens of Duke.
Having typed this giant wall of text, you'd think acquiring a classic like Descent is a decision without flaws.  What's worthy of mention here is that this version is the original, and runs inside a DOSbox emulator.  Because of this and the fact that the game was coded from the ground up for much older hardware, before even the first 3DFX Voodoo cards came out, the original verison of Descent suffers from having some of its routines tied directly to the speed of the machine.  The ability for certain missiles to track you, in particular, are greatly augmented by faster clock speeds.  Whereas someone playing the game on a 486/33 machine back in 1995 could easily dodge deadly missiles with just a little practice, it's much harder now.
Leveraging DOSbox in order to play this game today also brings other problems which can be avoided.  Two of the most well-known community efforts to resolve issues like those stated above are D1X-Rebirth (which endeavors to provide a fairly faithful recreation of the original) and D2X-XL (which has several features the original game doesn't, and lets you play both Descent 1 and Descent 2 inside the same engine), both of which are more than passing improvements to the DOSbox method.  If they're better than this Steam product, then why purchase the Steam version, you might ask?  Because they contain none of the copyrighted files necessary to play the original games.  There are what's called .PIG and .HOG files located in the original game's installation directory which contain all the data for the game, such as textures, creature models, and level designs, that can legally only be obtained except through purchase of the game created by Interplay.
So I strongly encourage you to try this game as it was originally crafted, through the DOSbox method provided here, and if some part of the DOSbox experience or the performance or behaviors of the robots and weapons frustrates you, try leveraging the results of the community and follow the installation instructions of D1X-Rebirth or D2X-XL to give it another spin.  One way or another, you'll get far more than your money's worth.

Remember that one DLC mission in Saints the Third where you drink the irradiated Saint's Flow, and gain superpowers?  Then you spend the next half hour sprinting super fast, punching brutes to death, and blasting police cars with hadokens.  That was great, wasn't it?  Imagine if the whole game had been nothing but that.  How quickly would it have gotten too easy, and too repetetive?  That's basically Saints IV.
I really tried hard to like this game.  I'd give it a neutral review if that were an option.  The things it does well, it does spectacularly well.  Every gameplay mechanic from Saints the Third has been noticeably improved.  Cooler cars, a better arsenal of guns, and little or no reason to use them, because everything is all about the new superpowers.
Overall, I felt like it delivered about eight hours of the best action and storytelling of the series in the story missions and homie loyalty missions.  What ruined it for me is that that's watered down with another twenty hours of repetetive speedrunning activities, and searching for over 1,000 collectables in a city that just feels lifeless. This really would have been perfect as a DLC for Saints the Third.
It really had it's moments where it shined, but in the end, I felt like I had to force myself to finish it just to see how the story turned out, and I have no interest in finishing the DLC or getting Gat out of Hell.

An extremely user-friendly interface, charming graphics, a solid base gameplay (with lots of variations and different levels of challenge) and entertaining, even if not mindblowing, story and dialogue.
The base game doesn't last very long, but that also means that it doesn't overstay its welcome and that each level has at least a little something that makes it unique and prevents the player from always using the same strategy. The fact that each level has two optional challenges and that there's a New Game+ mean that there are a lot of potential challenges for the players who want them.
Most importantly, the user interface never hides any information. You always know exactly what your characters can do and what the enemies will do if you let them. If you lose in this game it's because you did something wrong or your characters weren't strong enough, not because of some obscure "gotcha" mechanic or random chance.
My only problem with the game is the fact that interesting and important story content (a personal sidequest for each one of the major characters) is only available in New Game + mode. When you're replaying the game, you're probably fast-forwarding past the story so you're probably going to see these scenes in a vacuum. On the other hand when you're playing the first time, which is the only time you're actually paying attention to the story, the characters will feel underdeveloped because their development is hidden in their personal sidequests. I think the game would be better if all story content were available during your first "run", and the New Game+ mode was just about gameplay and challenge.
That said, this is an interesting and charming little game that succeeds in fusing RPG progression and tower defense gameplay, and is more than worth the money.

So after playing this game for a bit, I thought I should post a review.
Quick pro/con
Pros:
No bugs (I've seen)
Runs smooth
Graphics are ok
Relaxing/Casual gameplay
Play 2 win
Cons:
Repetative
Limited Content
Missing Content
Now for the more detailed summary of my opinions on the game.
First note, I love this game, it's very enjoyable for me, and my negative opinions do not mean, "Don't get the game".
So when you first start, you should be able to feel that the game is smooth. I bet the lowest, or low laptops can handle this game with "Fantastic" settings on. When you press play and start the game, you will be given a ship and a base (Spoiler, sorry) and a tutorial. My first negative view point is the trade system. It's fun at first, pick up the green items, and give them to a port that has that item in red, simple trade. Yet.... you do it all yourself. It's fun, don't get me wrong, but it would be so much more efficent if you could make a fleet, order them to pick up _ and then sell that item to another port that wants it. Then you could have multiple fleets, going around. Or, maybe even have a building in your base/port that automatically has ships trade goods that your port/base makes. Something on the lines of those two thoughts. For now though, you are very dependent on trading yourself, going from port to port across the map. Which leads me to my other negative opionion.
Now I have no idea if this game has a difficulty setting based on the ship your sail, or the level you are, or the size of your fleet. But half way through the game, you will be attacked over, and over and over and over an- Annoying right? Every port you go to along the way you will be attacked by pirates, nothing big either, just annying little ships, that damage your ships and make you pay fee's to repair and re crew them. Now, there's a way to kinda, side step this, press ESC and click restart, you will pop up to the port you were just at before you sailed to the other port you clicked. Now..... a bug or a glitch, I don't know what to call it, but if you pick up (Oh lets just say) Sugar at a port to sell at another port, when you get attacked and restart, the sugar you just bought is now needed at that port. So you don't even need to make a journy anywhere to sell that sugar, meaning, you don't have to pay your crew their wages. I use it, I won't lie, making 30k in less then 10 minutes, damn right I will use that, Haha.
Now, another problem with this game is the AI/enviroment your surrounded in. To me, it's very lonely, unless you do open world and sail from port to port, taking hours in real life, to get anywhere. And then.... when you do that.... EVERYTHING ATTACKS YOU. Even if you sail for the Spainish armada, Spain attacks you. IT's not enjoyable to move 5 feet and get attacked by 6 ships. My advice and opinion to the dev's are to make it less hostile, add conveys in there that you can trade with, or offer to join. There are little missions where you can do this, but eh..... I would love to see this world be much more alive. As well as the ports. "Very big port" is actually like.. 20 buildings with a few dock tiers. With no people. AGain, it's lonely. I would think if you go to a dock, it would be full of people and other ships docking and sailing off, but it's just your ship/ships and... nothing else. Not even a bird. So I would love to see animals, merchant ships in open world, and just.... life! added into the game.
And the story, this game has pretty much no story to it. It's a very largely based free roam/arcade style to it. Like Mount and Blade Warband, it.... a little less Ragdoll and a little more ships.
And my last thought is the content. After 10 hours, I'd say... it's the same thing.... over and over and over and over. You sail and trade and fight. And the fighting, what most people look for, it's not the best, and I will warn you, if you want a napoleon total war naval battle, you aren't getting it. The ships have about 10 people, even though you have 800+ in the stats. And these people don't move...... very poor graphics models that just sit there. I was very excited to board a ship.... till I saw how it was done. A little message showing you, "You fire and kill _" "They fire and kill _" That's it... no ropes being shot over to the other ship, men with guns and swords shooting and fighting... no animations. And it makes combat.... just boring. Don't play the game for combat.
So, it's a fun game to play if you have nothing else to do, it's relaxing, and I enjoy it for an hour or two, but hey... it's free to play, play to win game. And it's about 7/10 in my eyes. This is my first review, so... I might suck at it, but there is my opinions on the game.

There are contorted, monstrous bodies in the wasteland. There are drugs that take away all of your pain. There are gangs that violate and murder whoever they want. But, there are no women, and there is no hope in this world. Until a drug addicted loser finds Buddy, a baby girl. The wasteland is unforgiving.
I think this game is best played with nothing but a brief description in mind, so after reading this paragraph, I recommend you stop reading. Comparisons can easily be drawn to Earthbound: the music and aesthetics of Lisa certainly recall Earthbound, but moreso than that, Lisa is willing to be bold with its gameplay. Where other games will treat death or a dark setting seriously in a cutscene but then have the game just rely on killing and ignore its setting, LIsa does not. There is some humor, mostly dark, but more than that Lisa is warped and sinister. It is easily one of my favorite games. It's a different kind of RPG experience that offers something both refreshing and depressing. Lisa has a rich setting and story, with great aesthetics, and solid gameplay (in the style of JRPGs with agility deciding turns).
There are lots of colorful characters, some nice humor, and fun music. But, above else, Lisa is a miserable game, that is engrossing and moving.
Lisa follows the rather doleful story of Brad and his attempt to save his "daughter" Buddy. Grief haunts Brad, with repeated images of death, and menacing figures from his past challenging his sanity. It's a tragic story set in a terrible world.
The gameplay and story bleed over into eachother, and this game does not let you forget that its world is terrible. You will be forced to choose who of your party gets executed and is lost forever. You will have to decide between mutilating your own body, making yourself weaker and forcing you to use drugs more, or leaving your party to die. Sleeping out in the wasteland is free, but you might wake up to find your party has been kidnapped by a gang. It's a lovely synthesis between form and content that most games don't dare to approach.
The one complaintI have had someone express to me regarding the game is the humor that pops up in the game. Most of it is dark and some of it is wacky. The humor and dark setting are mixed beautifully, like a little Bong Joon-Ho or Harold and Maude, but it might not be for everyone.
Throughout the game you have to question if there is anything morally right in the world of Lisa: what life is she supposed to have? Do you get to decide her fate? are you the hero? Questions are left unanswered, and that's for the better. Lisa is enticing until the very end.

I have been an avid fan of every CoH Title that has ever hit the market.
Until this.     This game has the worst AI I've ever seen in a modern Video Game.
Easy Difficulty : AI Rushes you at first, making light contact and small engagements for the more important Strategic Points near your base. Then the AI seemingly calms....before launching a massive combined arms assault aimed at routing the player from his frontline. Once you've survived this onslaught... you've won the match. The AI is an absolute pushover from hereon forward.
Standard-Expert Difficulties. The AI plays no smarter, no more efficient, no more strategic, and even blatantly worse then the AI on easy... the catch is.... the AI has no resource limits... No Offmap Support Timers... No Special Ability Timers...and No Fog of War.   The Enemy knows exactly where you are, where you're moving, and when you're doing it. Then Proceeds to Spam the everloving♥♥♥♥♥♥out of Grenades, Offmap Artillery and Air Support, Flamethrowers (AI is Especially fond of these), Mortars... Pretty much anything that is limited or restricted from the player in Early and Mid game.    I LOVE this game playing against Humans and scripted Campaign missions with Scripted AI... but the Dynamic AI found in skirmishes and online CPU matches, as well as the AI featured in the Non-Linear Campaign in Ardennes Assault is utter garbage.
Rule of thumb : If you've liked COH titles in the past, DO NOT BUY THIS GAME. It is an absurd contradiction of the franchise, and will only sour your experience. Save yourself.... Don't buy it.

I've put hundreds of hours into this game and thought it was time that I write a review for it. While I do like the game as a whole, there are several annoyances that I have encountered within this game that I feel the developers (or whoever monitors the game after its release) have failed to address. The war spoil system is done completely wrong. I'm sure many have had this same issue from getting duplicate bulletins to the random bulletin that applies to a doctrine or faction that you don't even have access to. I understand they may have wanted to randomize what you get but to give me duplicates and bulletins I can't even use is unreasonable. Within in that is what those bulletins actually do for you and I would have liked to seen more out of them. A 2% faster reload time on infantry? Does that even help me? How can I even view these faster reload times to make sure its working and its not just something to make me feel like my infantry are reloading faster? My point is, that a lot of people are not going to use a bulletin that says 2% increase on whatever because that is such a small percentage. And if you are hardcore into COH2 and that 2% helps you win a battle, then great, but I highly doubt that 2% helped and it was more micromanaging your troops than any one bulletin.
Another complaint that I have is the level of difficulty that the theater of war provided. Now I understand the AI can cheat and will most likely have to if you really want to challenge yourself but there's a point where it goes from challenging to just down right unfair. If I have to make 50 bunkers and upgrade them all with MGs just to get through a mission then thats just a waste of time at that point. I'd rather be challenge in a way that makes me utilize my troops to the best of their abilities rather than fortify the hell out of my base (or go to ridiculous ends to make sure I have a fair chance) so much so that I just get to sit there are watch all the enemies die. And if you enjoy that then I'm certain you enjoyed the theater of war a lot. The campaign had a decent storyline and gameplay. Ardennes Assault was similar to what I said about the theater of war but brought in a interesting way of doing a campaign with being able to reinforce companies and attacking certain territories which I thought was a fresh look of COH2. Computer skirmishes were as you expect them; not too hard but punishing of small mistakes, and the online play was fairly balanced. I know a lot of people complained about the newer factions being to overpowered but in reality if you were good enough, you knew how to counter their foward outposts. Was it worth my money? I'd say yes because of how many hours I have played and it is still a nice tactical game. I put in about 40 dollars into this game (got both original and ardennes on sale), so 40 dollars for hundreds of hours seems like well spent money to me. I would have really liked to see them patched and improved the flaws with the game (especially the rewards system) and there is a beta out right now to fix it but I feel it is just too late and they would do better to just develop COH3 rather than waste their time on this one.

In a way this game (when you manage to run it with the unofficial patch) reminds me about Bathesda's Elder Scrolls series. It has small, more compact world because of the source engine I presume, but lots of content. I am mentioning Elder Scrolls for the solo purpose of saying that just like TES, VTM:B must be loved with all its flaws, bugs, errors and imperfections.
I honestly believe that Troika Games just had horrible luck as if universe screwed them up while they were creating the game.
Starting with engine itself, Troika used an unfinished Source Engine and had to work with it, adding their own code. Troika worked on the same engine that Half-Life 2 were even before the engine was shown publicly. In fact they had an agreement that they can't sell the game before the Half-Life 2 release.
After the engine came Activision. Even though Troika employers kept on working overtime on the game, Activision still rushed the release and cut off sponsorship of the game. So in the end we got ourselves a rushed, unpolished product that in fact was fixed and updated by fans for more than 11 years now.
And you might think thats it? Troika Games sold too little copies of the game to keep up afloat and ended up being closed. How did that happen if the game is so good as I keep on saying?
Bad luck.
Release date of the game is November 2004. What else happened in 2004 prior the November?
Unreal Tournament 2004, Far Cry, Sacred, Painkiller, Hitman: Contracts, Manhunt, Thief: Deadly Shadows,  Doom 3, Silent Hill 4: The Room, Sims 2, Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War, Star Wars: Battlefront, Myst IV: Revelation, Rome: Total War and many other awesome games. Year 2004 was an amazing year in the industry.
And you may think that with all that competition on the market VTM:B were safe since they released in November, while other games were earlier? Well, still bad luck Troika Games.
What happened in November in the PC game industry? (I am not mentioning games such as MGS3 and other console games since I am talking about PC)
CS:Source, Half Life 2, NFS: Underground 2, World Of Warcraft, Prince Of Persia: Warrior Within and so on. With all respect to Troika Games, they had no chance of wining a competition.
Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines is probably one of my favorite games of all time. With all it's imperfections and glitches it delivers an amazing lore, story, humor and experience. Gameplay itself (fighting) is done horribly and sloppy though so don't expect to be blown away with it, dialoges is what makes it so special. Depending on the vampire clan you chose it can take you 3 or more walkthroughs to experience all the game aspects such as different approaches (stealth, fighting with magic or brute force, persuation/intimidation/seduction) and even a special, Malkavian clan walkthorugh. You see, Malkavians are insane vampires. And by insane I mean totally sick. When you play as a Malkavian character literally every dialogue line for you is changed in a mad/insane way. In fact you can have a dialog with a news reporter on your TV if you are playing as a Malkavian.
All and all, when playing this game keep in mind that it was released in 2004 and it has lots of flaws that modern games don't, but thats simply because people are always becoming better at what they do and creating videogames is not an exception.

Metro 2033 Redux.. Is actually ♥♥♥♥ing great!
After I played the original Metro 2033 and reading the first Metro book I was pleasantly surprised to find out months after completing the original they made a Redux version! I was quite late to the train already but I quickly picked up the game and went through it, and to my surprise it was absolutely stunning, even though I played the original and already knew everything.. this game still shocked me, it looked beautiful and the npc dialogue sounded MUCH MUCH more cleaner and clearer. The game uses Metro Last Lights mechanics which are basically the same as the original metro but much more cleaner and finely tweaked. This game excells at making you feel anxious, scared and immersed, throughout the two playthroughs I had I felt like I was completely in Artyom's shoes. for example, when you make it to the Library and you encounter your first Librarian face to face alone.. you feel anxious and scared because you don't know what it might do or what may or may not happen, and anything can happen which is something that I like alot, the few flaws that this game have are just small flaws like lack of Ammo, filters and un-damaged gas masks on higher difficulties (not really a flaw but its something to note), and that you cant equip grenades, throwing knives, ect like you could in the original metro 2033 which really helped with stealthy parts instead of accidentally pressing the bind and realizing you threw a fire bomb because you didnt have it set up correctly, Some of the puzzles are hard to complete because there aren't really any big hints, and the game is quite linear, you follow an npc, do something for an npc rinse and repeat. The times you don't have a npc by your side are the best in my opinion like near the end or in the library.
While I'm already on the topic the ending is magnificent and gets your brain going because its basically a big puzzle that involves a decent ammount of patients.
To wrap it all up, this game is quite an amazing experience that I think every serious Gamer should enjoy, it's scary, fun and exciting, I definitely reccomend this version over the original though for a few main reasons, like the graphics are alot better and there are 10x less bugs

I have played tons of games, and this is the ONLY game in which I actually sat through the credits. This game is absolutely amazing, and I would easily be able to call it the best I've ever touched. I won't lie, it has it's issues. Gas masks are super ♥♥♥♥ing annoying, and don't add much to the immersion. They would have been fine if they didn't cause nearly a quarter of my deaths. Artyom heavily breathes when he needs air, and it's super goddamn annoying. There's nothing more unsastifying than to die to something as stupid as not having on a non cracked long filter gas mask. The beasts are bullet sponges, and humans have godlike accuracy (and this is only on Survival Normal). This is by far the most frustrating experience I've ever had, but despite the issues I had this game is still the best I've played. I recommend playing on Spartan, because Survival is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ I've never dropped a game because I was having a hard time, but I was so serious about quitting this game at one point and I actually just ended up jumping into Last Light, not expecting to come back.
The Redux is beautifully done and looks like a 2017 release. The game runs well @60FPS (VSync Limit), and I only recall having one or two hiccups. TURN OFF SMAA, It will murder your framerate signficantly, you don't need it either, game looks no different. The facial animations and whatnot are still bad, and still very creepy since this Redux didn't fix all the facial animations, but it's nothing that breaks immersion. Speaking of immersion, this is the most immersive game ever. There is no HUD, throw in a super creepy and mysterious world to go through and you have yourself one of the most immersive titles out right now. There is HUD, but it's rarely shown. When you swap a weapon, reload, use a medkit, etc. the hud for those specific items will show. If you're taking damage, your screen will get darker with blood at the edges. Survival can be a huge pain in the♥♥♥♥♥but does also help the immersion, as you truly feel as if you're a human fighting against something greater. This game is also one of the few games I regret buying on sale, as I would have gladly paid $60 for Metro 2033 Redux alone.
As for game length, I beat it in 10 hours (those two other hours was simply having the game paused). At least one hour total was a combination of me trying to get past a level, trying to find filters as fast as possible because I keep dying to no oxygen, etc. Even though this game was 10 hours, it felt much longer, and in this case that's a good thing. It's jam packed with awesome and memorable moments. The story is truly phenomonal.
If you couldn't tell, this game is ♥♥♥♥ing amazing. You will not regret playing it.

I wasn't expecting a lot from FTL from the get go. At first glance it doesn't have much to hold your attention. What this game lacks in graphical intrigue it makes up for in game play elements. You start your journey in a basic ship with a few members of a motly crew, trying to reach the other end of the galaxy to empart a message of doom and death that follows you after every turn based move. A story that is as compelling as why did the chicken cross the road. Despite the basic story it does offer an enjoyable gaming experience. Moving your crew around your ship to defend the various races boarding parties, fix broken subsystems and gain boosts from operating key systems on board they gain skill points for repeating each of these tasks. All this happens while making limited tactical choices about where to fire each of your weapons on an attacking ship as each cooldown bar slowly recharges.
At the core of the game is a random number generation that can grant you great fortune or bitter dismay as you face random challenges picked out from a hat. This and other ships and ship upgrades provides the games replay value.
Worth every penny of the full asking price.

This game explores some serious life issues: Abuse. The pain of childhood, and of parenthood. Manhood and womanhood. Strength. Loss.
This game had me near crying at several points. The story is freaking powerful. It's also remarkably well written, and downright hilarious at times.
And the gameplay?
It's fun enough that I want to play through it again right after beating it. This turn-based RPG is sometimes brutally difficult, in part because it slaps many old-school conventions in the face (e.g., sleeping can be dangerous). Battles are challenging. Tactical thinking is essential since many enemies are VERY dangerous and you're frequently outnumbered. I really applaud the AI as it keeps you on your toes.
The game doesn't hold your hand. There is no map, compass, or any attempt to make navigation easier. You just have to remember your way around, though there are plenty of memorable environments.
Characters will force you to make decisions with lasting consequences. There are dozens of hard choices to make along the journey, which brings me to another topic the game explores: decision. Will you save your friends, or your stuff? I got very attached to the buddies I picked up, only to have them devoured by a mutant, or bail on me when I least expected it. You just never know what you'll face, nor what to choose. Thinking back to many of those times, I don't know what I should have done. All the options sucked.
But I can't help asking myself, "Did I make the right choice?"
Highly recommended.

This game may not have cutting-edge graphics, but it sure has a lot of heart.  Defender's Quest is a strange combination of the tower defense and RPG genres, and it's one of my very favorite games in either genre.  Through the game's substantial and satisfying campaign, you'll assemble a motley crew of heroes who serve as your "towers" in this tower defense game.  Unlike towers, however, your heroes will level up as they gain experience, and you can assign various skills and pieces of equipment to them.  It's fun stuff.
The developers for this game are fantastic, and their continued work on Defender's Quest highlights their "long tail" philosophy.  Rather than abandoning their game after release, Level Up Labs have diligently improved upon their work, adding content, improving the graphics, and rebuilding the engine.  Defender's Quest is far more refined now than it was upon release, and its developers ought to be proud.
Defender's Quest is an excellent game with a committed development team, and I very much look forward to its in-development sequel.

Remember that one DLC mission in Saints the Third where you drink the irradiated Saint's Flow, and gain superpowers?  Then you spend the next half hour sprinting super fast, punching brutes to death, and blasting police cars with hadokens.  That was great, wasn't it?  Imagine if the whole game had been nothing but that.  How quickly would it have gotten too easy, and too repetetive?  That's basically Saints IV.
I really tried hard to like this game.  I'd give it a neutral review if that were an option.  The things it does well, it does spectacularly well.  Every gameplay mechanic from Saints the Third has been noticeably improved.  Cooler cars, a better arsenal of guns, and little or no reason to use them, because everything is all about the new superpowers.
Overall, I felt like it delivered about eight hours of the best action and storytelling of the series in the story missions and homie loyalty missions.  What ruined it for me is that that's watered down with another twenty hours of repetetive speedrunning activities, and searching for over 1,000 collectables in a city that just feels lifeless. This really would have been perfect as a DLC for Saints the Third.
It really had it's moments where it shined, but in the end, I felt like I had to force myself to finish it just to see how the story turned out, and I have no interest in finishing the DLC or getting Gat out of Hell.

Metro 2033 Redux is a mediocre game in almost every aspect. Don't get me wrong, it's still quite nice visually, considering this is a remaster of a 7 year old game. But in every other category it's either bad or mediocre.
My two main complaints with the game have to do with sound and graphics options. Pretty much any time a character is talking, you will barely be able to hear them unless you are looking directly at them. This is an issue I would have expected to be resolved a long time ago. How it is still present years later baffles me. Definitely make sure to turn on subtitles before you start playing. As for graphics options, well, they're mostly nonexistent. On my i5 4690k/GTX 970 system I was able to tweak enough settings to get it running at 60fps or above. However, many of the options you would expect in a modern-ish title on PC simply aren't there.
Everything else about the game is, as I said earlier, completely mediocre and unoriginal. The monsters are nothing special, neither unique nor especially intimidating. Fighting them is usually boring but can become frustrating when several of them gang up on you or cheaply attack you from behind. I found the gunfights against other humans to be more entertaining, though they won't put up much of a struggle against you, even on hardore difficulty.
The story is a run-of-the-mill post apocalyptic dystopian affair. The surface of the earth has become uninhabitable so everyone now lives underground in the subway system where they have to defend themselves from mutants and hostile human groups including Red Communists and Nazis. Some of the characters you encounter are interesting... if you can actually manage to hear them, that is. Others will probably just♥♥♥♥♥♥you off, like this little boy you have to carry on your back with your ability to aim severely impaired and his infuriating voice constantly in your ears.
Thankfully I got this game on sale and so my disappointment is somewhat minimized by that fact. However, after years of hearing so much praised heaped upon this game, I was expecting a much better experience than the one I got. Hopefully Last Light will be better, if I ever get around to playing it.

Love this game!
...but you know what to expect. This is not the giant, neverending, loud and rude GTA. It is something different. More ... european in style.
There are no side/sub-missions. There are not minigames. There is just the (slightly short) story and a town which is smaller that Liberty City or San Andreas cities, BUT... everything in this game is just gorgeous and lovely. The town is much more "squeezed" as the GTA towns. There a no city-highways and no giant airports, but the city is much warmer and much more inviting. There are no popculture-jokes and there is no unnecessary rudeness. All in all, it Mafia II is grown-up - a Mafia-themed movie with you in an active role and some lovely ideas, if you just look around for them. This is not a game to rush through and to hunt records and achievements, it is more like a time travel to the 40´s/50´s that is ment to be enjoyed PLUS, for those who enjoyed Mafia I, with one or two surprising and VERY decent links to the that game.
The only big problem I have with this game is the lack of a free ride mode like in the 1st part: Of course you can drive around town between the missions, but I really miss driving a taxi around town - or maybe even a police car, a security truck a race car in a race or something like that.
So, in short:
Graphics: 8/10 (not too good in the distance, blurry sometimes. Probably  ´Morbus Console´)
Atmosphere: 10/10
Gameplay/"Size": 8/10 (lack of Free Ride Mode / kind of a short story)
Story: 8/10 (sometimes a bit ... gangster-generic and not as good as Mafia I´s story, but still totally okay in my opinion)
Music: 9/10 (only 3 radio stations, but they are filled with authentic music, good radio hosts and actually some bits of a history lesson)
Value for money: 8/10 (€29 is a bit much, but if there is an offer, grab it with your hands, teeth and whatever you got)

Descent is one of the all-time greats, a first person shooter with complete freedom of movement, satisfying weaponry, interesting level designs and great soundtrack (though the Mac and PlayStation versions had even better renditions of the music). It features a lenghty single player component, support for user created maps (sadly, the map editor isn't included in the Steam release, nor is there Steam Workshop support, but DLE is available for free on the net, so are plenty of new maps), as well as plenty of competitive and cooperative multiplayer modes for up to 8 players.
The Steam release is the original DOS version bundled with the DosBox DOS emulator, which isn't the easiest (albeit not impossible) to set up for online play. I strongly suggest looking into the Steam community hub for guides on how to set up one of the source ports, such as DXX Rebirth or D2X-XL for easier online matches and generally better support for modern hardware and screen resolutions, as well as controller support. At least until Interplay and Olde Sküül update the official release with their own enhanced port they're reportedly working on.

LISA is ruthlessly gut-wrenching down to its story, setting, characters, and gameplay design. The game thrusts the player into Brad's tormented world as he sets out into a bizzare and hellish wasteland on a rescue mission.
The player is forced to make exceedingly difficult choices throughout the game. The turn-based combat, as well as artistic design, takes heavy inspiration from Earthbound. LISA distinctly carves out its own niche, however. It's difficult to explain the range of emotions the player will experience when playing through this game.
The game suffers from some very minor performance issues at times, though it doesn't detract from the game very much at all. The difficult choices all feel compelling save for one unfortunate event around the middle of the game. To be clear, this one particular event  just feels cheap. You'll know it when you see it. However, I'd argue it's a very much forgivable misstep.
LISA is absolutely unashamed and relentless in its delivery of heavy, mature, and disturbing themes. This only makes it all the more essential to play in my opinion.

What can I say about LISA? First off, it's a solid Earthbound tribute, albeit being way more sadistic and messed up. If you're a Mother fan, you'll see definitely catch the similarities.
Overall, I really enjoyed the game. The graphics were simple yet expressive, and the sprite work was fantastic. The soundtrack really set the mood too as well, and it helped immensely with immersion. The combat was pretty fun as it reminded me of Xenogears, one of my favorite RPGs. The story draws you in quickly and from then on it's a crazy rollercoaster of laughs, frustration, feels, and tears. The game attaches you to Brad, the protagonist, in such a way that it really makes you feel for him later on. However, as much as I enjoyed this game, there are some flaws.
I'm not a fan of the Joy gameplay element. Having to potentially manage a whole party of joy addicts is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ More should've been done with the addiciton mechanic, like being able to become clean or at least increasing the amount of joy there is in the game to compensate. Perhaps include more of Buzzo's goons as merchants? It just seems like the devs didn't really think that through. Nothing is worse than trying to do a joyless playthrough and battles take forever because Brad and frends do 0 damage.
My next con is that for a game with tons of party members it seems rather difficult to grind the others up to speed if you lose some and need new ones. It sucks to lose your best party members and have to use much weaker ones when you're at a point in the game where they'll get owned quickly.
A map would've also been useful. I eventually memorized the areas but some of the ones in the beginning are very samey. This gets better in Areas 2 and 3 though.
Despite the game's flaws, this is a fantastic game and is a must-play if you like oldschool RPGs and good stories. This one will rip your heart out and♥♥♥♥♥♥on it.

What to say about this game, man. First don't let the 1.1 hours mislead you, I've put around ten hours so far into this game. The Unofficial patch functions outside of steam so the counters not gonna work. I reccomend the patch by the way it has a list of improvements that make the game more enjoyable.
The Pro's:
-Lore. There's a lot of it and it is fairly easy to understand most of it.
-Graphics. Top notch for it's time, early 2000's, it has aged pretty well to my eyes.
-Audio/Voice Acting. The background music is pretty atmospheric and in tense situtions got my heart quickening a bit. The VO is well acted and cast, Each important and even supporting characters feel very distinct.
-Gameplay. It's an rpg so you'll have to manage stats and what not but I found keeping track of your "Humanity" interesting as well as "The Masquerade". Falling to zero in either of those is game over. Also don't die, that's a game over too...
-You Are a Vampire Baby! Bloody act like it!!!!!
The Cons:
-Some small bugs are still present even with the patch but that's to be expected. Nothing is perfect.

This is a fun top-down shooter with a heavy emphasis on co-operative gameplay.
You can play by yourself but the harder missions will be much easier with friends. Up to four people can play together and teamwork is encouraged. For example, one player can carry a heavy anti-tank gun while another can carry the gun's ammunition, allowing for much faster reloads. You can play with random strangers but I strongly recommend playing with friends and using voice chat to get the best experience.
Also, this game has full friendly fire so you need to be careful. At first I was annoyed by the friendly fire, but after some hilarious experiences I can safely say I've had more fun getting accidentally teamkilled in this game than any other.
The levels are all procedurally generated so no mission map or objectives will ever be the same. There's a large variety of weapons and special abilities that you can earn, and three different alien races to fight. A weapon or tactic that's useful against one race may not be useful against another - this encourages experimentation and use of tactics. Many times I've failed a mission only to say to myself or my team, "That plan (or loadout) didn't work. Let's try this plan (or loadout) instead." Seeing your plans pay off this way is really neat.
The firefights can be incredibly intense. If you've called for evac, and there's a horde of aliens bearing down on you, and you're down to your last few bullets, it can lead to some adrenaline-pumping close calls or last stands!
The graphics are adequate. The music is suitably epic during large battles, with alien ambience for the quieter moments. I particularly liked the "Bugs Hard" soundtrack.
The story is sort of a spoof of the movie "Starship Troopers." On the surface the plot is about how the soldiers of Super Earth fight to make the galaxy safe for managed democracy. But there are subtle doses of humor that I liked a lot.
If you like cooperative top-down shooters then check out Helldivers!

Helldivers is  a great 'hang-out' game, and one of the better local co-op games on pc.  It's fun to play fast and loose the with over-the-top weapons.  It's equally fun to play with stealth and scouting.

Helldivers combines intense action gameplay with the meta of a galactic conquest. A twinstick with plenty of flavor and content for hours on end. Seamless multiplayer makes every mission feel like a part of something bigger, and the ease of finding company is admirable.
Each mission pits the players against against one of three distinct races, each with their own ways of fighting. Selecting a mission, preparing and deploying all flow together with ease. Weapon variety is deceptive, as they all fill the same role: killing weak enemies. The actual variety of loadouts comes from a set of special abilities, or "Stratagems". They range from simple artillery strikes and special weapons to deployable cars with seats for the whole team.
The actual gameplay consists mainly of complering a variety of objectives(enought to keep the game fresh) and defending against endless hordes of enemies. Completing missions has "rewarding" written all over it, as every mission brings the players closer to unlocking a new toy, as well as progressing the entire playerbase towards their common goal.
While not as abundant as in their previous game, Arrowhead has incorporated plenty of references that a sci-fi fan is sure to get a chuckle out of.
Be wary of the DLC, as it varies in usefullness and quality.

Hundreds of hours on the console, nearly maximum of the prestige rank. Game is still just as fun now to play.
Essentially it does everything right.
The controls are tight and feel very fleshed out. Accommodating for every type of action a player can perform without being complicated. The game even having a system for pressing buttons in a code entering fashion to activate objectives and call in support, which feels very nice to use yet it doesn't feel obtuse or confusing at all.
The combat is relatively simple twin stick shooting, with a variety of enemy types and enemy abilities however once again remaining basic enough that it's easy to remember what each enemy can do without them losing their individuality. There's three different enemy factions, which also helps a lot for variety.
The gameplay itself is the games strongest point. The maps are totally randomized and are composed of very nondescript geography to the point where even after hundreds of hours it is rare to actually notice two maps that have the same features. The objectives are each unique, randomly generated and placed around the map, and are very understandable to complete. It just doesn't get boring, although the escort objective is obnoxious.
There is a variety of outfits, weapons, passive perks and equipment that players can choose from and gradually unlock. Which is the low point of the game is that there are certain things that are distinctly underpowered and have never been buffed, and thus they might as well not exist which makes the customization smaller then it could be.
The game does have a lot of purchasable content, and for twenty dollars for the base game it does feel like a lot of that content should have been in the game to begin with to flesh it out more. Especially with all the underpowered things in the vanilla game that aren't ever used. It still doesn't feel however like the game has less content then it should, and the main emphasis of play is just on shooting things anyways. The game has also recieved multiple free expansions and pieces of content so it's not like the developers were ransoming content away. The purchasable content has a few powerful weapons in it, but it isn't required to have them to be able to play effectively so players aren't majorly at a disadvantage if they don't buy it.
Although the game does have a low playerbase by now, it's still no problem to find multiplayer so long as you turn off the region filter in the search filters; and there's really no problem with lag at all. The game is very social in its matchmaking system and so it really doesn't require many players to be ingame for there to be options for drop in cooperation.
Other then the imbalance of certain items, the biggest problem with the game is that the progression of the games world wide online system is very bad. Certain online events lock players out of going on any other kinds of missions for that faction of enemies, which means less diversity and no access to earning certain rewards; for the duration of that event. When an enemy faction is defeated, it can't be fought for the duration of that online cycle which means it literally isn't playable content anymore until the world wide playerbase has completed that war. Beyond that, the Retaliatory Strike and Boss mission types are ridiculously overpowered.
The game is totally worth playing even if twin stick shooters, or even shooters, aren't your main thing. It's just that well designed, fun and replayable. And honestly, fourty dollars for the Deluxe addition with all the purchasable content is still worth the cash because of how replayable the game is.

NOTICE 1
**I’m a total newcomer to this game**
NOTICE 2
** Don’t buy DESCENT 1 on Steam unless it’s on a really low sale. When I say “recommended” I really just mean the game itself, not buying it on Steam. You can get this game and DESCENT 2 on
for $10. **
DESCENT is basically classic DOOM in zero gravity. The space ship you fly and missiles you launch at robots might lead you to believe it’s a space flight game, but it’s really a straight-up mid 90’s first person shooter in space (or rather underground on worlds all over the solar system). You explore labyrinthine levels collecting blue, yellow, and red keys to eventually reach the exit. The zero-g factor as well as a few other things though make DESCENT unlike most shooters released before or since.
If you’ve ever played that game FORSAKEN from Acclaim, the levels are kind of like that. You progress trough them similarly to how you would in DOOM, but they are much more three-dimensional here, which makes navigating them a task in itself. Luckily, DESCENT gives you a 3D automap and a great deal of control over it compared to DOOM’s automap, which you’ll need to use if you don’t want to get lost.
Not only do you have to navigate DESCENT’s mazes, but also plan what you do in them. Every level has hostages to rescue for extra points, but they die if you lose a life while carrying them. Also, after destroying the mainframe at the end of each level you have 45 seconds to find and escape through the exit, so it’s usually best to grab the hostages right before facing the mainframe. This navigation and planning can make DESCENT surprisingly cerebral for an action game.
Ultimately what makes DESCENT challenging though is its large and unique gallery of enemies. The problem is with how the developers decided to place them in the levels, making DESCENT an unnecessarily hard game in some parts, even compared to DOOM.
You’ve got your different varieties of enemy ships that shoot different weapons at you, but there are also enemies with interesting behaviors. One type does a pretty good job of flanking you if you let it; another simply watches you and enhances the AI of enemies around it. Eventually you discover different methods and maneuvers to use against each one. Thinking on your feet in DESCENT becomes intense in a new way when you’re doing it in zero-g.
Where it get’s annoying is when DESCENT sets up its many unfair ambushes. You’ll enter rooms from the only entrance only to be immediately surrounded. Enemies sit behind doors ready to attack in ways that are unavoidable unless you know it’s coming ahead of time from having reloaded the game. Worst of all is probably one particular enemy that, as soon as it becomes aware of you, almost instantly slices down your health with a chain gun while giving off a high-pitched pig-like scream.
Some of this might actually be affected by the source ports that have been released for DESCENT and are pretty necessary for playing the game in modern resolutions and at high framerates. I used DXX Rebirth but I think there are others. The issue is that some parts of the enemy AI are tied to framerate, the biggest issue being homing missiles. On the DXX Rebirth, once fired they’re almost impossible to dodge because they can turn on a dime.
Lastly, if you have a PC flightstick, DESCENT is supposed to be best played with them. I worked out a fine keyboard and mouse scheme. You might also want to try mapping out an Xbox 360 configuration too, which the source ports make possible.
Overall, there really have been few games like DESCENT made before or since, other than its sequels. If you’re into FPSs of its era it offers almost 30 levels of some of the most difficult FPS action this side of super-hardcore DOOM WADs.

Love this game!
...but you know what to expect. This is not the giant, neverending, loud and rude GTA. It is something different. More ... european in style.
There are no side/sub-missions. There are not minigames. There is just the (slightly short) story and a town which is smaller that Liberty City or San Andreas cities, BUT... everything in this game is just gorgeous and lovely. The town is much more "squeezed" as the GTA towns. There a no city-highways and no giant airports, but the city is much warmer and much more inviting. There are no popculture-jokes and there is no unnecessary rudeness. All in all, it Mafia II is grown-up - a Mafia-themed movie with you in an active role and some lovely ideas, if you just look around for them. This is not a game to rush through and to hunt records and achievements, it is more like a time travel to the 40´s/50´s that is ment to be enjoyed PLUS, for those who enjoyed Mafia I, with one or two surprising and VERY decent links to the that game.
The only big problem I have with this game is the lack of a free ride mode like in the 1st part: Of course you can drive around town between the missions, but I really miss driving a taxi around town - or maybe even a police car, a security truck a race car in a race or something like that.
So, in short:
Graphics: 8/10 (not too good in the distance, blurry sometimes. Probably  ´Morbus Console´)
Atmosphere: 10/10
Gameplay/"Size": 8/10 (lack of Free Ride Mode / kind of a short story)
Story: 8/10 (sometimes a bit ... gangster-generic and not as good as Mafia I´s story, but still totally okay in my opinion)
Music: 9/10 (only 3 radio stations, but they are filled with authentic music, good radio hosts and actually some bits of a history lesson)
Value for money: 8/10 (€29 is a bit much, but if there is an offer, grab it with your hands, teeth and whatever you got)

Star Wars is cool and all. But why bother with regular Star Wars when you can have Star Wars with gangs and superpowers, with the US President as protagonist and Johnny ♥♥♥♥ing Gat as ancillary?
Because that's what the Saints Row 4 campaign feels like - an epic sci-fi movie, a wacky comedy, and Grand Theft Auto all rolled into one. It never quite feels too easy, but it's not particularly difficult. The charm is in feeling like a badass.
It's rare that video games can fully capture the choreographed action scenes of movies, all those precise moves and dramatic sequences one after another. But Saints Row manages it. It's like fifteen hours of the coolest, most adrenaline-filled action scenes, with none of the boring filler that you have to sit through when watching a movie. And when it's all over, you can casually have sex with whomever you want, while cheesy Sex Music™ plays in the background.
It is true that the sandbox gameplay here is lacking. The map is small and is recycled from the third game. The collectibles are tedious. The 20fps cutscene lock is weird. But I never play Saints Row games for their sandbox gameplay. Once I finish the side missions, I'll probably mess around for an hour or two and then uninstall. Until I play it again, of course.

It's Civ 5. What more is there to say? This game has it all. Grand strategy, depth, immersion, and a modding community that will can change your game entirely. Very few strategy games manage to captivate the player so much, let alone have them stay up all night creating the perfect empire.
Balance-wise, yes, some civs are greatly overpowered/underpowered. But is this such a bad thing? With so many civs provided, it would be unrealistic to expect them to be perfectly balanced. I for one, think that this serves to diversify one's games, so that no game is like the last.
To nitpick a little, there is the issue of the learning curve. I believe there are two learning curves for this game, one for new players and one for experienced ones. As it is with all grand strategy games, it takes some time for one to get used to the mechanics and victory conditions of the game. However, the advisors and well-organised Civilopedia do a good job walking a player through the game. One gaming session should be enough to grasp how to play.
As for the learning curve for experienced players, there are so many mechanics and strategies in the game that it will take a while for any player to fully master how to play. This is not necessarily a bad thing, as it serves as testimony to how much depth this game has. But if I had to criticize something, there you go.
To sum things up, if you're a fan of strategy games, buy this game! If you're stuggling to decide whether you'll like grand strategy, then watch some playthroughs on Youtube to see if this is your cup of tea. I'd recommend that you wait until the game's on sale, though. Civ 5 is no longer a new game, as Civ 6 already came out a while ago. Add this to your wishlist and wait until a good deal pops up. Although the game is worth the full price (in my opinion) there's nothing wrong with trying to save a few bucks!

What can I say about LISA? First off, it's a solid Earthbound tribute, albeit being way more sadistic and messed up. If you're a Mother fan, you'll see definitely catch the similarities.
Overall, I really enjoyed the game. The graphics were simple yet expressive, and the sprite work was fantastic. The soundtrack really set the mood too as well, and it helped immensely with immersion. The combat was pretty fun as it reminded me of Xenogears, one of my favorite RPGs. The story draws you in quickly and from then on it's a crazy rollercoaster of laughs, frustration, feels, and tears. The game attaches you to Brad, the protagonist, in such a way that it really makes you feel for him later on. However, as much as I enjoyed this game, there are some flaws.
I'm not a fan of the Joy gameplay element. Having to potentially manage a whole party of joy addicts is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ More should've been done with the addiciton mechanic, like being able to become clean or at least increasing the amount of joy there is in the game to compensate. Perhaps include more of Buzzo's goons as merchants? It just seems like the devs didn't really think that through. Nothing is worse than trying to do a joyless playthrough and battles take forever because Brad and frends do 0 damage.
My next con is that for a game with tons of party members it seems rather difficult to grind the others up to speed if you lose some and need new ones. It sucks to lose your best party members and have to use much weaker ones when you're at a point in the game where they'll get owned quickly.
A map would've also been useful. I eventually memorized the areas but some of the ones in the beginning are very samey. This gets better in Areas 2 and 3 though.
Despite the game's flaws, this is a fantastic game and is a must-play if you like oldschool RPGs and good stories. This one will rip your heart out and♥♥♥♥♥♥on it.
It's a memorable experience.

LISA is like a lot of RPGs. It has a plot, recruitable characters, some sidequests, and even a hidden superboss. However, not very many RPGs can claim to be like LISA. Not many RPGs can claim to have choices that carry the weight they do in LISA. Not many RPGs can successfully replicate quirky MOTHER-esque humor, AND blend it with a grim post-apocalyptic setting to create an entirely unique atmophere that actually WORKS. Not many RPGs can invoke deep emotional responses in its players that carry on, not only throughout the game, but also after the game is completed.
LISA is a game of morals, choices, and consequences. It's a game where the only decision you will be confident is right, is the decision to play it.

A charming retro style 2D rogue-like platform game.
PROS
-100% Free to Play
-Good Controls
-Customizable Graphics & CRT Simulation
-Neat Retro Style Graphics
-Free Roam Metroidvania Style Platforming
CONS
-No Music
-No Map
FEATURES
The game's objective is to simply beat it, but it's not that simple now is it?  How you beat it involves collecting everything in the game & getting 100%.  What happens after that, well you have to beat the game to find out!
The game has 3 different game modes.  Normal mode gives you infinite lives & respawns you at checkpoints every time you die.  YOLO mode gives you one life & when you die it's game over.  Cat mode gives you 9 lives total.  These modes are meant to simulate a more retro or arcade style of game play with a limited amount of continues.  If you're new you should definitely play on Normal mode as this game's difficulty scales pretty quick & you will die often.  You will always die in one hit as well & there are several areas that are almost impossible to pass without at least one death so unless you're a pro MLG you probably won't be playing the 1 life mode that much.
GRAPHICS
The games graphics are very nice looking for a retro style game.  You can also swap between 2 different modes which make it look more/less retro by increasing the color pallet limitations.  Both look very nice but I prefer the additional colors so it's 16 color mode for me.  There's also some nice CRT simulation effects that give the game a nice nostalgic feel for us older folks.  You'll feel like it's Saturday morning all over again!
GAMEPLAY
The controls are very fluid & pitch perfect for a 2D platform game.  You won't have any problems just jumping in & playing with a controller or keyboard.  I'd still recommend you get a controller to play since it feels more natural with 2D platformers to use one.  The controls are very simple as you just move & jump from platform to platform while avoiding hazards in your path.
There are also upgrades to collect that help you progress through the game such as Double Jump & Wall Cling.  It's pretty neat seeing Metroidvania style upgrades in a game like this.
CONS
The only really bad part about this game is that there is no map system so you will probably get lost a lot.  The game involves a lot of back tracking as well so you can pick up items you missed while you try to figure out where you need to go but even then it's still a trial just to remember where you've been.  It would have been nice if they implemented some sort of Metroid style map system to keep you on the right path.
The game also has no audio tracks so you'll be hearing basic Boops & Beeps from sound effects for the majority of your play time unless you just play something of your own in the background.
OVERALL
Overall the game is a very good retro 2D platform game with collectibles all throughout & I highly recommend it to anyone who's a fan of the genre.  It's hard to not recommend it when it's free now isn't it?  Give it a try!
