This was my introduction to the Saints Row franchise, and after dissecting every single game this one is probably my favorite next to SR2.
My Steam hours (coupled with the 500+ hours i have on this game on ps3) were all well worth it and full of nonstop action, despite many things that could and deserved to be criticized this game is fantastic. I've never really written a review before but I'll try to detail the GOOD and BAD of sriv as best I can. I may also SPOIL some of the storyline so please read at your own risk.
Let's start with the pros:
Saints Row IV is action packed and fast paced, while still maintaining a fun (albeit strange) storyline and hours worth of gameplay, along with DLC that I've almost had more fun playing than the actual game, I wont spoil anything but since the game is cheap (the whole franchise goes on sale for like 8 dollars total) I think they're definitely worth the price. I replay How the Saints Save Christmas every year. It leaves room to develop every character a little bit in their own way and was always a joy to come back to.
It's a lot of fun to use all the superpowers you get (and the upgrades you can get along the game are definitely worth collecting!) and I think I spent a lot of my time just jumping up and over buildings, and running into♥♥♥♥♥♥ If creating a lot of chaos in a small space is your thing, this will appeal to you. Fighting the police in-game for a long time will actually get a miniboss to show up eventually.
There's tons of collectibles (3 audio logs per each character, pieces of text adventures and letters to Santa, to name a few!) that I found very rewarding, and it gives you a good insight to the characters you're interacting with. It helps to play the previous games, but this was new to the Saints Row franchise and I think portrayed the characters extremely well.
The character customization is creative and leaves you with a lot of freedom, it's by no means the best CC in the world but it was good for its time, you're also able to go and recreate your character however you want at almost any point in the game, and there's tons of clothing and accessories available to you. With the introduction of the workshop for IV, I'm sure the amount of things you can do with your character will triple.
The game itself isn't very difficult to play and leaves itself open for players of all skill levels while still feeling rewarding to the more experienced, there's plenty of things to do outside of the main story of varying difficulties and I personally found that some of the diversions (like the races) helped me develop my video game skills.
This game also has its criticisms:
Out of all the Saints Row games (excluding Gat out of Hell, which is a standalone expansion to this one) this one feels the most out of place. As much fun as i had with it, comparing it to the 3 games preceding it it kind of feels like a joke. Saints Row as a franchise started out as kind of a response to GTA and this game simply does not fit that genre at all. There's an ability to romance characters but it's a one-time thing and for the most part was just a joke. I thought it was fun but when I found out there was romancing and it just turned out to be that I was kind of disappointed. The only romance option with any real depth is with Johnny and it doesn't actually get you anywhere afterwards, there's one scene per character and that's it.
It's also objectively the easiest, as much as I love the idea of leaving the game open to newer players (comparing this to MGS, another game I like which I'd argue has a fairly high skill floor even at easier difficulties. i know these aren't the same genre of game but bear with me) this game was extremely easy even on the highest difficulty.  There was very little I really had difficulty with and I don't consider myself an expert at video games at all.
This game is rife with bugs, the cars don't work very well and as much as you're not going to use cars it's still really irritating, I find my car jammed in walls constantly. The AI for most enemies isn't great and the powers are glitchy. Homies shoot at random♥♥♥♥♥♥and can raise your notoriety very quickly while also being pretty useless. I actually got trapped in a car because Shaundi started to drive it and I could not get her out of it, nor could I get her to drive us to the location in the mission.
This game's multiplayer is lacking, there's not a lot to do once you've completed the game and all you can really do is shoot things until a Warden shows up. Once you're done in the game Wardens aren't that difficult, and they don't reward you with anything. You can't replay missions and there's no multiplayer-specific things you can do. There's also really no online community for this game, it's all friend-based and most people I see don't have any interest in going on multiplayer for more than a little bit because of the reasons i listed above.
There's also no details to this game. Virtual Steelport is just.. uninteresting. Saints Row 2's Stilwater had a lot of things to do, a lot of interesting people to look at and it just felt more like a town, just by looking at it you could feel the city around you had personality. Different parts of Stilwater felt different, but still connected to the rest of the city, and the people were the same. Everything in Virtual Steelport looks identical. You can't interact with any of the buildings in the game that aren't stores or Image As Designed, and the people running around are boring. They have funny outfits but they have nothing to them other than that, they barely interact with you and don't give you a good feel of the town you're in. You are supposed to be in a simulation but it's just so bland to look at, Virtual Steelport doesn't even feel like a city despite what it's trying to represent.
There's a radio in SRIV, and where the music is actually pretty good, there's no incentive to listen to it. Cars become obsolete almost immediately in the game, and to listen to the radio outside of a vehicle you have to enable it in your menu, just for it to be shut off anyway by a mission or something, I think this game really missed a detail that could've helped it. Video game radios can drastically change how you feel playing a game.
There's no meat to the characters. Where you do get to see into their brains as you're saving them (especially with ones like Shaundi and Johnny) it doesn't go anywhere other than that. The development is minimal and doesn't actually add anything to the story outside of their missions, they all feel like they're in their own little bubble and it's kind of boring. It's the worst with Asha who's talked about like she's an important character, but nothing ever happens with her outside of her rescue missions (and side mission afterwards) and has little to no development IN those missions. The game would've felt the same without Asha and to some extent Keith, they didn't actually add anything at all. Keith's only strong point was near the end of the game and they only did that to call back to something from the earlier saints row games that also didn't really make all that much sense. Saints Row was never really noted for developing any characters outside of really just Johnny and even then they didn't do it very well, but they were leaving the door wide open with what we had in this game and decided to ignore it.
While the game is fun to play and I like replaying it, your best bet to actually continue enjoying the game is to just replay it now and then. There's different options you can take with some parts of the game but most of them don't actually change anything and the game becomes really boring once you're done everything. the DLC missions are just fun to play but they're really something you have to come back to every once and awhile.
Overall, I really do like SRIV. It's price tag fairly represents its overall value as a game, but you should also try SR2 and 3.

Alright let me start off by saying I both recommend and don't recommend this game.

The Single player has 4 modes to chose from Tutorial for people who want to learn the game, Challenges which are fun little trials to keep you busy for some time, Save the Princess which is an adventure type, and finally Sand Box for people who love to Build. As for the multiplayer there are again 4 game modes. Take the hill where two teams fight over one control point, Team Deathmatch and well its a deathmatch the two teams kill each other till one of them meet the required number of kills, Capture the Flag the name kind of explains it all the two teams try to steal each others flag, And finally Challenges yes multiplayer challenges.
Now for my thoughts. This game is fun I'll give it that but once you've run though all the modes and completed everything the game has no replay value this is where I don't recommend it. Though if you like spending time storming forts and goofing off with friends the multiplayer is what your looking for. This is where I recommend it.
As for my personal opinion I'm not a fan of the game.

Great RPG, the teams are Red and Blue (the casual). You choose from 3 unique classes that go for their own purpose. Builder, the most important role, builds a base for your flag to be protected in and can make clever traps. Then you have Archer, also known in some cases, the "Scout". The Archers purpose is to hit enemies from far away and move quickly to steal the enemy flag. You also get special arrows to use for certain occasions, such as fire arrows to burn wooden structures. Last, but not least, the Knight. The Knight is a powerhouse fighter that can be very devastating, his special item, BOMBS! Use these bombs to destroy other players or destroy the enemy base. The bombs range from a simple hand grenade, to a large barrel loaded with gunpowder that you carry on your back. I really like this game and I hope you do too.

While the gameplay can be really enjoyable, the game has too much problems, that take the fun away.
I have enjoyed all the fighting, fun special abilities, great emphasis on teamwork (one of the most challenging thing in this game is avoiding friendly fire, which is great!).
However...
- there are not enough maps and mission types - they get boring rather quickly,
- most of the time you cannot obtain any new abilities and weapons, nor can you choose what enemies to fight against. Those choices are blocked by community driven events, that happen quite often. Those event, imho, are not worth taking other choices away. You may get those choices only if you go offline and play the game alone.

It was a desert planet, I think. I don’t recall being slowed down by untouched snow drifts, nor being routinely boiled alive by the gushing magma that volcano worlds like to troll you with, but the actual planet-type itself escapes me. We were there to capture it, and while we certainly weren't attempting that feat on the hardest of the twelve mission difficulty settings available, it was up there in challenge. There were three of us; I’m certain of that much. There were just the two of us at the start of the first mission, but a third jumped in mid-way through and, while we were nothing special, we were competent. We dragged each other through that first invasion with just a few hairy moments and a narrow escape when we finally completed all our objectives, suffering the most when forced to hold ground until a dropship arrived to evacuate us. But we dug in, weathered the last of the storm and then unashamedly ran like frightened girls toward the ship when it finally arrived. Two of us actually made it.
Mission one of three down, we ploughed on. Completing a full set of missions isn’t obligatory, but you soldier on for the prize at the end, be it a fancy new weapon or a fat experience boost. This time, our war was waged against the bug army. There are three distinct enemy races in HellDivers, but the bugs are by far the best. There’s nothing wrong with the robot or cyborg forces, both of which wield superior tech the giant insects don’t possess. Robots teleport in and cyborgs drop from the sky, but bugs come at you from under the ground, burrowing in from anywhere. Should one of their scouts spot you, you’re flooded with snapping claws, acid spit and near-unbreakable carapaces. One second you’re alone with nothing but the swirling sands for company. The next you’re, well... not. It doesn’t take very long at all for a screen to fill with homicidal bugs.
But we were making good pace, confident enough to leave the beaten track to try to hunt down hidden specimens that are used to slowly upgrade you Diver’s arsenal of weapons. We reactivated SAM sites and held off the herd that appeared to destroy it; we nuked insect nests and liberated strategically important sites. Our resource use was slim and slow, saving the big weapons for the eventual end when we called down that shuttle and the entire planet would turn up to try and stop us. But we were all good. Then the fourth character fell from orbit, and everything went to hell.
The new arrival was ten or so levels behind the current team’s average, but that’s usually okay; a decent team can often carry a rookie through harder planets that their default, unleveled equipment shouldn’t allow them to endure. The three of us were battle hardened; our chosen pulse beam rifles, sub machine guns and shotguns all fully researched to their most powerful apex. Even if our new member did minimal damage, it’s better than none at all, right? At worst, it would be a boon to have a new person ordering equipment from the ships in orbit above us. Even if they chipped in now and then with the odd ammo refill or a revive when one us fell, it would make for a better team.
In theory, anyway. Dear, sweet, elusive theory...

Let me say that I really enjoyed this game. It's telling a great mafia story. Here are a few reasons I like this game. 1. It has solid and smooth gameplay. It varies between mainly driving, shooting, and excellent hand to hand combat. Though there are a few glitches that can vary from small bugs, into a glitch that prevents you form completing a mission. This has a nice open world with plenty of places to either shop at, or rob. Which brings me to another point, there are quite a few ways to earn money outside of the main story. The police system in this feels very authentic: if you drive past the speed limit, they fine you. If you get caught with a gun they arrest you, etc. The missions can give some tedious objectives but I didn't mind so much because it was relavent to the story and it felt all the more authentic. There is a large number of cars that you can slightly customize (license plate, paint job, handling, rims). There are also usually a number of collectables to find throughout levels and the world. There is also a good soundtrack that fits the era well and sets a good tone. I just wish that you could explore the world after you complete the story. 2. The Story in this is a memorable mafia story that takes inspiration from films like Goodfellas. It has alot of good characters. The story is presented through good voice acting and interesting cutscenes. The only real problem I have with the story is how nabruptly it ends, of course it is in true mafia movie theme so I can either say the ending was abrupt or brilliant. 3. The graphics may be this game's weakest point, not to say they're god awful, but some parts are just sub-par while other aspects look good and bad. Character models for people like Vito and Joe (the main characters) are pretty good while others look mediocre. I saw a few background characters that almost looked like they were recycled from the first Mafia game. The world looks great, with a decent sized map. Cars look very good as well.
So overall I would recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of mafia movies or action games or period pieces. If you don`t care very much about graphics then you will find that this gets the job done. The gameplay doesnt really add much but it works well and keeps the game above being generic.

The game is a must-have for anyone who romanticises 20th century Italian American mafia. The game provides users with very advanced graphics and little to no frame rate issues. You can try a Demo before purchasing to check it for yourselves. Mafia II really reminds visuals of GTA 4, but has a greater attention to detail and allows interaction with small objects.
I absolutely loved that compared to GTA 4, Mafia II does not blindly follows The Murphy's Law - "if something can go wrong - it will". You may have days when you get simplistic tasks that go smooth and there are days when you are assigned to more challenging missions, which involve many natural unknowns and as you would expect, things often (but not always!) will go wrong.
Another pearl of this game is the radio - while you only have three radio stations, you can observe how the music industry evolved from 1940s to 1950s - from The Chordettes rocking the charts, followed by raise of Frank Sinatra. Equally, radio news keep you updated with all the essential events of the history - fall of Berlin, negative impacts of tobacco, arrival of the TV industry and many more topics that were relevant in the USA during 40s and 50s.
The little things are the ones that make this game so great. If GTA series occupy the best spot of your game shelves, Mafia II must also join the collection.

Initially I would have rated this game as good. Now however I simply can't. There is no feeling of good left to me from this game. Put it this way, in business and other things dealing with money the concept of risk vs reward is very prevalent. This game is no exception to the rule, much as it thinks it is. Now for the purposes of this review let's say that reward is in fun rather than monetary gain. For the average person risk should be relatively low for not having fun. In this game the risk is rather high, especially after a certain point where it's pretty much impossible to unlock new stuff (for me it's the point where I'm at). Compound onto this with the fact that it's nigh on impossible to hit an enemy in the late game for some reason, which would be fine if they didn't have THREE layers of shield, which means that they will eat your health with ease while you sit their wishing you could have a jettison option for the person you have manning weapons. At least in that case your jettisoned person might hit the shield and take a level or two off depending on their velocity.  I enjoyed the game initially, but my goodwill and enjoyment towards the game has dried up like a sponge in the sahara. Until they update the game to nerf the dodge mechanic this game is pretty much unbeatable, and doesn't get my reccomendation.

I'm rewriting my review for KAG because I have so much more to say about it than I previously did.
This game is fantastic. There was a point in time where it was rendered unplayable because of low player count, but it seems the steam summer sale fixed this issue. But be warned, this could happen again.
That aside, this game is frantic, hectic, fun, crazy, and sometimes even frustrating. It's also anything but "Terraria Fortress 2" that my friends like to call it who refuse to buy the game. It's a unique teambuilding experience that involves planning, improvisation, and in some cases a powderkeg or two to completely flatten your enemies. While team deathmatch and capture the flag are not that interesting and end up being rushfests plagued by knights who just jump over everything, Take The Halls is a hilariously fun game that involves strategy in not only base construction but also in unit placement and research trees. And if you get bored of that for some reason, do not worry as the modding community has your back- maps like "Zombies!" scratches your "attempt to survive against the horde of millions undead" itch while "Shipwrecked" is a top down naval battler that is so fun that it almost makes me completely forget about Pixel Piracy. And these are only two mods that I played over the last little bit, this game has amazing replayability and should not be passed up.
The only black spot on this game is the community. People for some reason think it's funny to detonate powder kegs in your base and destroy your ship in "Shipwrecked", but there is an easy to use votekick function that immediately eliminates them from the game and bans them for a short while. But that does not dock any points against the game at all, because it's not the game's flaw but rather the community upon it.

Quick, fun and chaotic!
KAG is a multiplayer game at heart and offers very little for those that prefer to fly solo, but the fun and competitive multiplayer really takes the cake and rises above most other pixel games!
To start out, KAG has three classes to choose from:
The Knight can really push through a crowd if you've got the proper timing for his attacks. His shield makes whatever side is being blocked all but invincible, as a well timed heavy attack can bash through! You can also glide and surf with his shield like Lost Vikings! I'd say the Knight is the easiest class to pick up for beginers. It's very easy to start slicing through baddies with this guy and get in some one-shot kills.
To a knight in the middle of combat though, the Archer is the preferred class and can snipe long distances, really putting the hurt on the enemy team! Their grappling hook helps them get away in a hurry and they can even fake being dead, so watch out!
The final class doesn't get much attention in a standard deathmatch, but really shines in Capture the Flag!
Bring in the Builder class, the real meat behind KAG! This little dude adds an entirely different play-style to the chaotic Knight and Archer classes, though there's just as much depth to the building aspect as the combat.
His role is much more strategic. The Builder can build walls, lay down structures to improve a classes loadout and even throw together some very impressive spike traps and rake in the kills!
The Builder is a bit less exciting than the other classes and has the highest learning curve. You'll have to gather resources for everything you build by digging up stone and gathering wood from fallen trees, so learning the proper amount needed for a specific structure is key!
If you'd like to see some of the basic game mechanics, check out my First Look (it's a lot older than this review)
Overall I'd say KAG is a fantastic game! It's very designed and you can tell a lot of love went into this project. If you're into pixel games and looking for something fast-paced and fun in a chaotic way, this game is perfect for you! And the price can't be beat for the amount of content.

The graphics in this game are GORGEOUS. Whether it's an ice cave or airships and floating islands, every scene is detailed and breath-taking. The movement in the game is also quite unique; closest to anything I've ever played similar to it would be web-slinging with Spider-Man.
That said, there's little sense of free exploration: most caverns or spans appear to have only one way to cross them. Occasionally, when I would find (what SEEMED to be) alternate ways to get across a tricky expanse by landing solidly on an unconventional spot, my grapple and rockets wouldn't recharge because apparently that wasn't the way the developers intended for me to solve that particular problem.
Voice acting (at least for English) is subpar. The narrator is telling a bedtime story to his daughter, and nearly put ME to sleep with his monotonous drone. Also, that was his daughter?! Until he said so near the end, I thought the whiny little quasi-British schoolboy was, well, a BOY. And as beautiful as the music on the menu page is, I was expecting similar scores throughout the game; unfortunately, most of the game was without soundtrack.
But the real frustration with this game is the checkpoint system, as though it's a throwback to early 90s gaming. There's no saving your progress when YOU want to save the game: there are only scattered checkpoints which also serve as somewhat-helpful directional markers. Some sections require crossing two or three tricky spans before reaching the next waypoint, and if you fail, you'll have to go back to the checkpoint and do them all again. And again. And AGAIN.
I tend to try to get all the achievements I can in games, but when I finished my playthrough (less than 8 hours of total gameplay; my "hours played" is artificially inflated by having left the game on pause overnight and through work the next day) and checked the available Achievements, I LOL'd at the thought of counting how many times I used the grapple tool through an entire segment to try to stay under par, then restarting the whole thing again if I went over...
No. Just... no.
Bottom line: Meh. I paid less than $3 for it, so I don't feel cheated, but I'm definitely not going to waste any more time on it.

Let me say that I really enjoyed this game. It's telling a great mafia story. Here are a few reasons I like this game. 1. It has solid and smooth gameplay. It varies between mainly driving, shooting, and excellent hand to hand combat. Though there are a few glitches that can vary from small bugs, into a glitch that prevents you form completing a mission. This has a nice open world with plenty of places to either shop at, or rob. Which brings me to another point, there are quite a few ways to earn money outside of the main story. The police system in this feels very authentic: if you drive past the speed limit, they fine you. If you get caught with a gun they arrest you, etc. The missions can give some tedious objectives but I didn't mind so much because it was relavent to the story and it felt all the more authentic. There is a large number of cars that you can slightly customize (license plate, paint job, handling, rims). There are also usually a number of collectables to find throughout levels and the world. There is also a good soundtrack that fits the era well and sets a good tone. I just wish that you could explore the world after you complete the story. 2. The Story in this is a memorable mafia story that takes inspiration from films like Goodfellas. It has alot of good characters. The story is presented through good voice acting and interesting cutscenes. The only real problem I have with the story is how nabruptly it ends, of course it is in true mafia movie theme so I can either say the ending was abrupt or brilliant. 3. The graphics may be this game's weakest point, not to say they're god awful, but some parts are just sub-par while other aspects look good and bad. Character models for people like Vito and Joe (the main characters) are pretty good while others look mediocre. I saw a few background characters that almost looked like they were recycled from the first Mafia game. The world looks great, with a decent sized map. Cars look very good as well.
So overall I would recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of mafia movies or action games or period pieces. If you don`t care very much about graphics then you will find that this gets the job done. The gameplay doesnt really add much but it works well and keeps the game above being generic.

The game is a must-have for anyone who romanticises 20th century Italian American mafia. The game provides users with very advanced graphics and little to no frame rate issues. You can try a Demo before purchasing to check it for yourselves. Mafia II really reminds visuals of GTA 4, but has a greater attention to detail and allows interaction with small objects.
I absolutely loved that compared to GTA 4, Mafia II does not blindly follows The Murphy's Law - "if something can go wrong - it will". You may have days when you get simplistic tasks that go smooth and there are days when you are assigned to more challenging missions, which involve many natural unknowns and as you would expect, things often (but not always!) will go wrong.
Another pearl of this game is the radio - while you only have three radio stations, you can observe how the music industry evolved from 1940s to 1950s - from The Chordettes rocking the charts, followed by raise of Frank Sinatra. Equally, radio news keep you updated with all the essential events of the history - fall of Berlin, negative impacts of tobacco, arrival of the TV industry and many more topics that were relevant in the USA during 40s and 50s.
The little things are the ones that make this game so great. If GTA series occupy the best spot of your game shelves, Mafia II must also join the collection.

This is a rather cute Visual Novel that's well worth the twenty minutes or so it takes to download and play.  I haven't gotten around to the DLC yet, although I intend to eventually.  While the game is incredibly short, all in all it was enjoyable.
Aside from the length, the one thing that bothers me about Without Within is the decision tree.  (Somewhat spoilers) every decision in the game either leads to the next decision (or the good end) or a bad ending.  If you choose "right", the story continues, and if you choose "wrong", the game proceeds to one of the bad endings almost immediately, with no buildup or other choices.  The story branch that takes you to the good ending is rather enjoyable and quite easy to get, but the bad endings are all dreadful - not because they make you feel bad, but because there's simply no story in them, and the game just ends.  Despite this flaw, the main decision path is quite entertaining, and I am still intent on buying and playing the DLC, as soon as I am able.

Without Within is a short but charming novel brought to us by InvertMouse, a name I had previously not heard but that I will not soon forget. It features soft, well-drawn artwork, a great soundtrack, and a lovable main character that leaves you wanting more. Despite the minimal playtime, I found Without Without thoroughly enjoyable and encourage any visual novel lover to give it a chance.
....
The story follows Vinty, a down-on-her-luck girl trying to become a calligraphy artist. During her journey she’s met nothing but adversity and the story is just a segment of her life as she attempts to conquer her own feelings of hopelessness.
.....
The main menu was the first bit of brilliance that I ran into. The artwork is adorable, the opening theme is soothing, and the interface is very simple and easy to use.  Within only a few seconds of loading the game the novel had grabbed my attention and positioned itself as “not your average indie VN” in my head. The only issue I found with the menu and interface was the stark contrast of the button click soundbyte and calm background music. It was too sharp and loud; a softer sound effect would have fit much better.
....
As I loaded into the game the soundtrack grabbed my attention for a second time, leading me nicely into some simple, yet cute, artwork and starting off the story in a rather amusing fashion. Throughout the entire novel, the soundtrack never disappoints and always fits the mood of each scene perfectly.
....
The soundtrack wasn’t the only thing that made the atmosphere of Without Within, however. The art style was soft, simple, and cute and really lent itself to the story in a way that most generic visual novels don’t often do. When you combine art with music, the result is a wonderful atmosphere that does a great job amplifying the simplicity of the story.
.....
Speaking of the story, the only word I can really use to describe this one is charming. It has a few funny moments, a sad moment here and there, and some great bits that really dig their way into your brain and just make you feel good. I found myself involuntarily smiling many times throughout my first playthrough, connecting with the main character and her melancholy life on a personal level.
.....
InvertMouse really outdid themselves on Without Within, and despite my negative predisposition going into the story, I couldn’t help but love every bit of it. The simple artwork, fitting soundtrack, and heartwarming plot all came together to create a beautiful work of art. I highly encourage anyone who enjoys Visual Novels to give Without Within a chance, because it’s not your average indie novel.

Descent is a classic, and after having logged some time on it in 2014, it holds up after 19 years.  Modern players will probably find the controls and options a bit cumbersome, and will want to reconfigure controls before moving out of the first room.  Modern WASD controls are certainly viable in this game, but some players will find the Mouse Sensitivity to be too low, even when cranked all the way up.
As for this particular adaptation, there are a few shortcomings.  DOSBOX will lag sometimes, and it because very obvious given the often-frantic pace of Descent, especially while escaping the mines.  It is a pity that the game doesn't come with some kind of IPX-to-TCP/IP adapter built-in; FPS Multiplayer was one of Descent's great features in a time when the concept was relatively new, and its absence (to all but the quite technically adept) greatly detracts from this version.
Even for this version's shortcomings, the game is a solid piece of gameplay design, and should find many new players given its release on Steam.

This game is brilliant. Mind-blowing for a 1995 game. You will have tons of fun with this action-packed 360 degree combat game. I recommend this game to anyone who loves classic arcade games, or just a good sci-fi action game. Also, this game kind of reminded me of Metroid at some points.

An era of modern games, good ol' Descent is comparatively simple.  Explore, get keys, kill the boss, escape.  That was enough in the 90s and it's still enough now, as Descent is still fun, aged or not.
One of Descent's big gimmicks when it was released was a fully 3-D world; there's so many ways in which you can (and indeed must) move as to be at times confusing, both then and now.  This adds to the tension of the often close-quarters, twitchy fights you'll find yourself in.  Maps afford a player multiple ways to approach a situation, and a bevy of weapons with which to deal with what you find.
If you didn't grow up with games like Descent or passed it up back in the day, I recommend dropping the paltry sum the Steam distro costs and taking a stroll through gaming history.  I doubt you'll regret it.

Okay, I've played this game for 7 hours. Time to give it it's due.
So when I bought this game during the summer sale I expected a casual game to spend a few hours on. Nothing serious just some mindless fun. This game is nothing like I expected. It's a challenging and complicated endeavour. It requires good team work and intelligent base building. The community I've seen is 50-50 where half the players hate new people and the other half don't seem to care.
You have 3 classes, each have their own innate abilities and mechanics. Builders are required to go out and gather materials as well as build defenses. Knights are your front line troops as well as demolition experts. The Archer is strictly range support but has the best mobility of all 3 classes. Learning the differences and using them effectively matters.
This is one of those games that has turned out to be a wonderful investment. I highly urge anyone with the funds to try it. It might be a little tough getting used to but winning is rewarding. They have 4 game modes, regular TDM, a Battlefield like Conquest mode, CTF and a fourth mode I haven't tried. CTF proves to be the most enjoyable as there are various tactics to use to get to the enemies flag such as drilling under the ground or catapulting your team mates over the enemies defenses.
I highly recommend buying this if you like challenging and rewarding multiplayer experiences.

I cannot recommend this game enough. Since buying and installing it, it's become a sort of obsession to me.
The game itself is a side scroller, but combat is more in the style of Earthbound with a lot of quirky humor and unconventional methods of attack from wrestling moves, to dances, to wuxia martial arts, to magic tricks. There are around 30 recruitable characters in the game, so there's a lot of variety and replayability just because of that.
The storyline is pretty strange, but it's a pretty great post-apocalyptic world with lots of interesting stuff going on, both in the foregound and background. If you're the kind of person who likes to dig through vague details to piece together the lore, this game can scratch that itch. If you like games with eccentric and bizarre characters, this game has that in spades. If you like brutal, heart-wrenching stories about seld-destruction, redemption, and second chances, this game has that too.
An average playthrough will clock in around 10-12 hours, but it's well worth a second play, especially if want to take on the challenge of Pain mode, which gives you limited saves, harder enemies, and even more story tidbits to dig up.
On the downside, it's built in RPG Maker, which does come with some unfortunate quirks which are hard-wired into the game engine. It's not as much of a deal breaker as it may sound like, but it's something that some people overreact too.
Additionally, the game can be frustrating in some ways that you might not be expecting from an RPG. For one, there's fall damage. You can jump off a ledge that's too high and take 500 damage to everyone in your party. Camp sites aren't guaranteed to be safe, meaning you can wake up poisoned, or missing items, or missing party members.  You can get an instant game over from jumping off ledges. Some bosses have attacks that KILL party members (no revive. gone forever)
However! All of that is intentional. Lisa is not a game that's meant to be just another bog-standard RPG. It's supposed to be a game where you make tough decisions and bad♥♥♥♥♥♥happens and you're forced to keep going even though you got dicked over by one wrong step or random chance. The game is SUPPOSED to be painful. If you really want, you can reload your save and just negate some of this, but you'd really be missing the point, then.  You'll still enjoy an engrossing story and some great characters and gameplay, but you'll be robbing yourself of some of the impact the game has to offer.
tl;dr This game is an indie gem that far exceeds it's humble origins and it ends up being something deeper, more meaningful, and enjoyable than anything I've played in the past few years.

This game had me hooked from the very first screen of the very first scene.  It was an emotionally intense experience.  I have seen LISA described as pretentious for daring to reach for its themes, but to me, this was nothing but effective, gripping storytelling the entire way through.  This story is built around a charming, obviously Earthbound-inspired game, packed with humor (sometimes very dark).  The game mechanics are sometimes painful, as advertised, but never tedious.  My only criticism: status ailments are poorly described in-game and require some puzzling to figure out.  Overall, I highly recommend LISA.

One of the my all-time favorite platformers, if not games altogether. LISA is an intense, hilarious, touching, and shocking platformer with an amazing story, surprisingly in-depth combat system, solid controls and gameplay, and basically truckloads of content. It's a very long game for the platformer genre, averaging about 10 hours, but trust me, once you get to the end you'll still feel like it ended too early: I wanted more, though the length is perfect for the storyline.
There are shocking scenes in this game, and I warn that it's not for everyone. Especially those with abusive pasts, or basically anyone young, as many scenes are--at a lack of a better term--♥♥♥♥ed up. But that's exactly why I got this game, I love games that mess with your head and this was advertised as such and let me tell you, it did not disappoint in any manner. When you first start LISA you will be confused, maybe overwhelmed, and probably feel like you can't beat it at points. This game is EXTREMELY unforgiving (assuming you don't reload your last save everytime something bad happens): some enemies possess "fatal" moves, which can one shot any of your party members out of the game for eternity (it's said these are extremely rare, though it happened to me multiple times), resting some places can result in party members being stolen and possibly killed, and you are faced with many very tough decisions, usually involving your party member's lives and all your supplies gathered thus far.
This game accomplishes everything it sets out to do: it's a huge (pretty much open) world, where you can adventure to find hidden secrets and other companions that will help you in battle. The story is engaging and it will have you in tears at the final few scenes (I'll admit I teared up at a few points in this game). LISA is a SOLID experience, and I feel like any story-driven game lover will love the heck out of this game simply because of that fact, if not for the solid combat system and hilarious scenarios.
That was something I did NOT expect: for LISA to be funny. I thought it'd be depressing and shocking the entire time, but some of the scenes in this game made be actually laugh out loud; the writing for this game is beyond brilliant, during the hilarious and dramatic scenes alike. One of my two complaints I have with this game is just how unforgiving it is sometimes: for example, there's an unavoidable event where you could potentially loose your entire party (if you have bad luck), and then the game is unbeatable with no companions. However, it adds a very cool feel to the game; the feeling that each choice really does matter, because it could have fatal consequences. It also lends to the game's foreboding and inevitable mood.
LISA is depressing, so if you're looking for an upbeat adventure, despite the hilarious snippets, you may want to stray away from this game, as it will not necessarily put you in a good mood, but it is an amazing experience and I think most gamers (if not everyone) should experience this story regardless. My only other complaint is the balancing. I feel like the combat--despite the system itself being very solid--is a bit broken given the right team composition. I got a character that could "Oil Up" enemies, and then the other three people in my party could cause fire damage, which will always critical strike on Oiled Up enemies; thus melting many otherwise difficult enemies in no time at all. Also, by late game I had so much money and items that I could easily stockpile healing and "AP/TP" items and last forever in combat. The game starts out with scarce resources, which is a great feeling for an apocalyptic game, but then gets a bit too easy later. And I'm not talking about the final island, which I feel is perfectly balanced and wraps the combat up in an incredibly well-done manner.
Though despite a few cracks like that, the foundation of this game's difficulty is otherwise solid. The curve can be a bit steep but once again, that lends to the overall mood of the game; making you feel hopeless, as you would if you were actually the main character. Brad is his name, and he has an abusive past, he finds a baby girl in a post-apocalyptic world where only men survive, thus vows to raise and protect her from everybody else, but one day she goes missing...
Very engaging story, satisfying gameplay, basically no cons at all, tear-jerking, shocking, hilarious. Pick up LISA today, I even got it on sale for next to nothing, so I paid a couple dollars for a 10 hour long experience that really stuck with me and became one of my all-time favorite games, and that means a lot coming from someone who has played hundreds of games throughout their life.

I think I'm the target audience for retro games.  Back in the day, on an Atari 2600, a Commodore 64 (executive model with the little 16 color screen built in!), and even a little on Intellivision, I spent every moment I could.  I miss a lot of things about playing games back then, like (Non-Super) Mario Bros or Oregon Trail on the Apple II, or Prince of Persia and Street Rod on a 286.  But if I load up those games now, they're just not as much fun as I have locked into my memories.  But at least I'm reliving he glory days with my favorite characters, on maps I've committed to parts of my memory I didn't know still worked.  I think this game covers all the elements of a game I might miss from my early childhood, without that magical attachment to make me want to continue playing.  It's a fun game for a few minutes, then I remember I have a lot of other stuff I'd rather play.  This would be epic without all those other options.  You know, like when this sort of game would have naturally come out.  Like that first ex girlfriend you've moved on from without realizing you did; it's just nice to hold onto those memories without mucking it up by revisiting the situation in your 40's and finding it's not the way you remembered (and she's rendered in 4 colors; I dunno where this metaphor goes, I just rambled).
It's retro, but without a plot or a character attachment to bring me back to my childhood.  Like maybe I'm playing a game from someone else's childhood that I never met.  I didn't hate it, but I'm hard pressed to say I'd recommend it.

I picked this game up on sale because it was 80% off. I'll be honest I wasn't expecting much due to the price tag and that I had never heard of it before but oh boy was I wrong. Visually this game is stunning, the levels all have a tonne of detail and are very well designed. The backgrounds of each level in particular are breath-taking. In the 4th level I found myself dying just to have a look around! Not to mention that the soundtrack compliments this game perfectly, and you find yourself soaring around without a care in the world because of the atmosphere created by this game.
Moving onto the gameplay - it's fun! I've never been a big fan of platfromers, especially 3D platformers, but this game got me hooked and I found myself playing it start to finish from the minute i picked it up. The jumping physics allow you to truly feel free in the air, and the grapelling hook gives you a fine degree of control as you soar from platform to platform.  Certain parts can be frustrating as it is very easy to overshoot a platform or just fall short, but with a little bit of perserverence you should find a way through pretty quickly. I found the waypoint system reasurring and extremely helpful as it can be very easy to lose yourself in the surrounding enviroments.
The voice acting in this game isn't great, and neither are the character models, but then if you pick up this game, chances are you won't be playing it for that. The plot itself is rather simple, esentially just being a hunt. However, the way that the story is told is rather charming and I found myself rather enjoying the narrators commentary as the game progressed.
My only other gripe is that the game is rather short, but then when you consider how much you're spending, then it shouldn't suprise you. What matters is the quality of this game, not the quantity and in that respect I believe it shines.
Definately worth picking up and having a go!

One of the best games ever made.
Good/neutral/evil, stealth, magic ("disiplines"), guns, melee, hand to hand, exploration, different endings and lots and lots of multiple choice, very well-voiced conversations (Fallout 4's female PC for example) make this a true gem of a shooter RPG.
The game still holds up today easily. Use the patch (not plus, at least not on first (few) playthroughs) and enjoy 1920x1080, where the only slight minus are the 10 year old graphics (see screens on store page). Choose FPS or third, or alternate instantly as you like.
It It has truly incredible replay value, as there are multiple ways of building a character AND seven different "classes" (different types of vampire). XP are not given for kills, but for resolving situations (killing everything that moves is one way of resolving pretty much any situation though, but frequently not the only way).
Get it! You won't regret it for a second!

This review will be separated into two appropriate sections. Namly a section for those that have not played the original descent and those that have respectivly.
Overall Game Score: 8/10
-----
If you have never played descent understand that it is a very old game, as of right now the game is 19 years old. For those of you lucky enough to play it as kids or even adults you know how great the original game was. At the time the graphics of descent were extremly advanced and even caused motion sickness in many of its players. The game is a first person ship shooter that takes place in our solar system. After many mining bases have fallen silent you are hired as a mercenary tasked with investigating these mining bases. You learn that the bases have been taken over by an alien AI. In order to stop this virus from spreading you are asked to go deep into the planets and moons of our solar system to destroy the Alien Computer Cores. You pilot an advanced fighter deep into the recesses of this deep beautiful game. You upgrade your ship, find new weapons and eventually destroy the Allien menace over 30 levels of well developed secret filled mines. Whether you are using the stupidly fast firing vulcan or the imobile but very power proximity mines you will find descent to be a solid and very fun game to play.
For those that have played the game, the steam version of descent does perfeectly well in emulating the original title on newer systems. For those of you who have tried to emulate the original descent, you know how problematic that can be. Its easy to remember the framerate issues and terrible crashes that were so common trying to get this game running under a newer operating system. I'll admit I presumptuaosly shut the game down after seeing the dosbox logo pop up, having remembered my frustration attempting to get the game to run in windows XP at the time. I'm glad I reopened it. In short whoever set it up did so masterfully, there are no issues present in running the game. It is exactly as I remember the title when it first came out. The one exception is that multiplayer does not work so keep that in mind. Do yourself a favor and download this gem, it is well worth the money.

HELLDIVERS is a great game that promotes teamwork over skill. though you might be able to clear some of the higher difficulty missions alone a team is pretty much requierd if you wish to grab those sweet rewards available at the hardest difficulties. The friendly-fire mechanic in the game requires you to focus alot on team coordination and not just shoting at the first enemy you see, aswell as causing some rather hilarious situations.
Also no worries about running out of missions sense each mission will have a new set of randomly chosen objectives forcing you to come up with a new plan for every mission.
However the game doesen't come without it's downsides, one of them being the way the in-game campaign works. Sure it's fun working together with the community to gather enough points to conquer a piece of the enemies territory. However the problem lies in the fact that once you defeat and conquer an enemies home planet you will not be able to play against them for the rest of the galactic war (usually lasting for around 2-3 weeks). This leads to for example the "bugs" being defeated within week making it imposible to play against them for another 1-2 weeks which can be quite discouraging at times.
Next is the reasearch point system which honestly is one of my favourite parts of the game. during your missions you have a chance of coming across samples on the ground, gather ten of those and you get a science point. These points are used to uppgrade/unlock weapons and stratagems but they are far to easy to aquire and the uppgrades are way to cheap. This causes higher level players to walk around with tremendous amounts of science points they have no use for. I dont like the fact that the hole idea of running around the map searching for samples is just rendered meaningless once you get far enough into the game.
Still though, no game comes without it's flaws and i think this is an amazing game if you want to team up with some friends and just have a good time.

I tend to find Tower Defense boring, if it doesn't have a gimmick, or mix in other genres the way Orcs Must Die does. Here, the gimmick is RPG elements, and music reminiscent of Final Fantasy IV. That works for me.
There is a ton of content; each map can be replayed on two higher difficulties for increased rewards, after beating it. And then you can replay the whole game in NG+ where enemies have altered behaviors. You can also change the game speed at will, which is something I'd love to see in more Tower Defense, to speed through the parts where I know my towers have things covered and I don't need to watch enemies walk into them and die.

This is a great game within its genre.
It's an atypical tower defense game with a cute story that's interesting enough to keep you playing. Although the gameplay itself does that sufficiently enough, it's a good addition to a genre that usually lacks such features.
Your 'towers' are people and due to it having a story, some of these characters have a personality and that makes it a lot of fun. You can level your towers and have them learn new skills as well as equip them with better weaponry.
The game initially isn't hard, but the option to make it so is available for those longing for a challenge.
All in all, if you enjoy tower defense games but are looking for something new, I'd say you can't go wrong with this game.
If you're not into tower defense games, you might still want to give this game a try as it does certain things common amongst games of its genre differently, and that might just be enough for you.
I had a lot of fun with this game and picked it up rather cheaply, for having put over 20 hours in this game I cannot do anything but recommend it at this point.

First of all, I've been playing this game for the past days on a macbook pro. The graphics (sunset and water) are amazing if you play on maximum quality, everything else is just ok. There are several bad reviews for this game, but all from players that didnt gave much time to actually enjoy the game. My best advice is: GO FOR IT. It's an actually nice game, it works on all your platforms and even have a multiplayer (but I never found anyone there).
Here are some tips for new players:
-- Yes, it's kinda hard to figure out how to move your ship. You have two sails, a front one and a back one (W, S) and you can basically one move if you're turning in the favor of wind. Also there's a rudder that isn't showing off at first, you have to set it on the settings. That will make your ship turn left or right (A, D) and you can do hard turns using the front and back sails. Keep that in mind: You can't move against the wind, so plan your battles well.
-- You can become a merchant or a real pirate. The game is about pirates anyway, so if you don't go for military, you'll end up stuck in the game, because everyone will attack you.
-- There's a reset button (PRESS ESC) so if you die or encounter strong enemies somewhere, you will get back at the last port you visited.
-- To move between locations, you can sail directly anywhere by just clicking on the map OR click "open world" and then actually sail there. On the way to places you find shipwrecks, boxes, blueprints for new ships and treasure maps. My personal advice is: once you get a fast and strong ship, got for open waters all the time, it's worth it.
-- Bigger ships means stronger ships but as well slow ships. Being slow is the worst on this game, since you depend on the wind. Once you get a corvette you can stop getting new ships for a while. Corvette is the fastest ship on the game, except if you pay for the steam version (3 dollars). Use that one to sail everywhere, get all the blueprints and find the hidden ports (there's 20 one them, good luck!). If the enemies are getting much more strong than you, get a galleon, that's the strongest one you can actually buy at the store. Stronger than that, you will need to sail on openseas and capture enemy ships.
-- To make money is easy, buy whatever is at discount "green" and try to sell to a port that the same thing is needed "red". If you find enemies on the way, click restart and you will teleport back to the port, where the same thing that was green is now red. Just sell it and ??? ... PROFIT !!
-- If you think that you messed up the game, go to the settings and there's a hard reset button somewhere. It will take you back to the start of the game. I reseted 7 times before actually enjoying my moves on the game, so many mistakes...
Shiver my timbers! Ahoy.

I can't find anything good to say about this game. Honest. Screenshots look okay, but the game's hardly polished and the interface is terrible (no shift-clicking, crafting/furnace window is not intuitive).
Downfalls:
- Tools have no durability, and the pickaxe tool seems to work on everything, regardless of the material (dirt, stone, wood).
- You also cannot jump and place blocks directly underneath you, so I hope you like digging stairways.
- Trying to build a bridge out from a hill, the game won't let you place blocks unless you hang off the block and place while jumping. (At least in Minecraft you could sneak off a ledge and slap a block on.)
- Physics on this just feel wrong: jumping from block to block you may sometimes miss or just jump up faster than you anticipated.
- The textures are atrocious and hurt my eyes after a while. With no outline of the box you are targeting, things can get disorienting, especially in caves.
Also, many maps are ravaged: trees gone (floating bushes), obscene words spelled out in text, abandoned dirt huts, etc. It just feels like the land has been pillaged for someone's personal cache.
TL;DR - Crappy F2P voxel game with item mall to get you to spend money. Take your hard-earned cash and go buy Minecraft instead. It is a much more satisfying experience.

If you are looking for a great cooperative experience with tons of opportunities for you and your friends to step on eachother's toes this is it. A satisfying shooter with a massive amount of potential viable loadouts and many different kinds of weapons. Great variety of enemies and how to combat them in the three factions. The game takes place over a large meta-war where you fight a three-front war against Cyborgs, Bugs, and the Illuminates (high-tech aliens). The war is divided into three branches for each faction, and you fight within a sector in order to gain enough community points to take over the sector and advance your war. At times the aliens will fight back and may gain territory back depending on if the community fights back hard enough. A small issue appears when two factions are defeated in a meta-war causing the remaining players to be forced to fight the remaining faction without an options to fight the others for variety. Not too big an issue since I believe all three factions are uniquely fun to fight, but can get annoying when you're burnt out on a faction.
You will enjoy firing projectile guns, explosive guns, lasers of many varieties, pilot vehicles, mechs, stationary turrets, call down artillery, bombing runs, FLAMING NAPALM WALLS, you will kill your friends by accidentally landing a drop on them, you will kill yourself by accidentally landing a drop on yourself, you will kill GIGANTIC ALIEN INSECTS BY PURPOSEFULLY LANDING A DROP ON THEM (git gud). You'll unlock pieces of equipment for purely visual customization of your male or female Helldiver (helmet, armor, and cape). Pub games are pretty fun, too! text and voice chat, and a friendly community (tends to happen with cooperatively focused games!). If you enjoy cooperative games with a hard focus on friendly fire, a jovial attitude, and some good ol' democracy, you'll love the hell out of Helldivers.

I picked this game up during the Summer Sale with the leftovers of my Steam wallet. I had read an article about this game some time ago and I thought the premise was interesting enough. I'll be honest, I actually wasn't expecting too much from this game. Indie hasn't really been my thing. It came out and I never really heard anything about it afterwards. Not sure why though. The game is ridiculously good. The developer created a world that is really interesting and its populated whacky characters that had me continuously moving forward. I wanted to see what insane thing was on the next screen and I wasn't disappointed.
Despite all the craziness, the world ties together really nicely. You might meet an npc that gives an offhand comment that you don't get the full implication of until later in the game when you get more context. This kind of attention to detail makes the game great. The world is a blast to traverse through. Maybe a few too many caves but they're short and normally used for transition. They often contain some event that prevents them from being too bad anyways. The mood of all the areas is lended a hand by the music. The music is great and really helps to establish sense of an area. Also that workout song? Beautiful.
This game isn't all whacky though. There are some genuinely creepy elements to the game and a sense of unease is cultivated that often has a rather horrifying pay off. You also are forced into tough choices. I didn't really struggle on the first couple but the later choices are rough and will leave you wondering if you should of done that. I can harp on about the world the game created for a while but how is the gameplay? Its pretty good. A bit standard if I really want to nitpick about it. You pick your attacks/skills and the turn plays out based on who has priority. The combat is helped along by the allies you pick up during your journey. The variety of characters really kept me from getting bored.
They all have their own skill sets that are fun to experiment with. You can find some pretty fun combinations of allies in the game. I will say that the joy addiction system wasn't my favorite thing in the world. It pretty much makes some characters completely worthless due to withdrawals. I ended up avoiding them because, while they CAN be strong, I felt that the withdrawals was a bit too annoying to deal with. Especially considering that the non-addict teammates seemed just as strong to me. I also didn't find much joy in my playthrough but that could of been on me. I really wanted to use Bucket after what I went through to get him, but alas...
In the end, I really enjoyed this game. I would recommend it regardless of price. The ten dollar price tag is more than worth it. If you're a bit leery then do like I did and pick it up during a sale. I managed to beat it after ~11 hours and I can say it was a blast to playthrough. I'm even considering going through it again on the hard difficulty.
TLDR: Great world
Great soundtrack
Good combat
Great story
Great game

A solid successor the one of my favorite RTS games of all time. Developers are constantly fixing and tweaking the game, ever improving it. WWII setting is interesting, but this is not the only game that has it. (Think of Men of War: Assault Squad) Resource collection is passive, meaning that there are no collection units, you just take territory and resources are given to you based on what area you took. Wide variety of units which all serve different purposes to differing degrees of success. Plenty of maps, both community-made and developer-made, which adds to replayability. Many of the commanders are bit mundane, especially the ones which are given to you for free. Some of the best units in the game, (Tiger Ace, Sturmtiger, etc...) are only available to commanders which need to be purchased, so there is a bit of a discrepancy between players who haven't purchased any commanders, and those who have. Additionally, commanders in the store are a little pricy for my taste, ranging from $2 to $4, but they do add a bit of flavor to any player's loadout. Matchmaking is good, but the low amount of players means that you may very well be matched with players from other continents. (I live in the United States and I often see players from Europe and Asia) Overall, a really good game to buy with some friends if it's on sale, or if you're itching for some historical RTS action.

Saints Row 3 was one of my favorite games. Saints Row 4 did everything better. I actually like this game better than GTA5

If you enjoyed Saints Row 3, you should enjoy SR4 is it is by and large more of the same.
SR4 is in my opinion not half as balls-to-the-ball crazy as SR3 was, but it is action packed and very fun to play.
SR4, much like SR3, takes the absolute micky out of things. The first most players would notice would be that you can 'romance' all your homies, as it pokes fun at Mass Effect.
As the theme of the game is an alien invasion, so the bulk of its adoration (or scorn) are directed at more sci-fi sources.
The main antagonost, Zinyak, is an absolute winner writing wise.
One of my personal highlights would be Zinyak and Jane Valderama reading romeo and juliet on the classical radio station.
All the characters have lots of funny moments to shine, but I really don't wana to give any away.
You have a whole arsenal of weird and wonderful weapons, and you can upgrade and customise most of them too.
The upgrades even make some of them act quite differently. eg, The dub-step game that debuts in this game bases the track it plays on its skin.
And with others, you'll change your play style slightly to accomodate, eg, the Disruptor gains a piercing ability, so you'll start trying to line up enemies for multi-kill shots.
There's a whole slew of other weird weapons too, from the inflator (makes body parts extra large until they eventually explode), to the thumper (shoots plungers, forget what their special effect is).
They're fairly creative, and give me an itch to go play Ratchet and Clank again.
I'm not sure of the cause, but as you unlock more super powers and by extension more enemy types, the game seems to misbehave more and more.
The first 10 hours or so I played were rock solid, but then I started to run into weird bugs, eg, all the character models were flickering, and now that I've approached the end game, I'm encountering semi-regular crashes when fighting aliens, particularly those things that travel as round balls.
You could argue this is meta as the game consists largely of you being trapped in a simulation and doing everything you can to crash it with no survivors.
The tank controls are so bad, they need to be criticised harshly. What volition has done is make aiming and movement work co-dependently, so W will always orient the tank to face forward in the direction you're facing. It's weird, but I can get used to it, but W and A work very weirdly, since I usually found that it did a 270 degree rotation to go from forward to left, instead of rotating in a more sensible and direct manner.
I would've much preferred an alternative control scheme where W/S was forward and back on the tank's alignment, and A/D turned the tank, with the aiming of the turret being fully independent.
As much as I enjoyed the game, it feels very rushed.
There's various little bits of polish that are conspicuously missing from SR4 but were in SR3 (eg, car cruise control).
They reused the entire steelport area without any particularly large changes - if we ignore the control nodes and control towers.
There is fairly little in the line of new outfits compared to SR3.
And so on.
I somehow have it in my head 5 years have passed since the last game, and just looking at how my local area changed in that time, I would've expected the steelport to look quite different in numerous areas, but still familliar.
I remember that SR3 had a cruise control option for all vehicles, that basically kept the car at a constant speed, and allowed you to use W and S to change this speed. It would've made for much nicer driving when following people (eg, Matt's loyalty mission).
It doesn't really matter as you'll spend the bulk of the game running around on foot with your super speed.
The problem was a lot worse in SR3 where every bit of DLC was dropped on you right at the start, and you didn't have to earn any of it.
SR4 is similar, but you have to play for a few hours and rescue at least some of your homies before the DLC gets dropped on you.
To use SR3 as an example instead, one of the DLCs give you a reskin of a tank; You don't get access to the original tank until much later in the game, and I would've enjoyed it a lot more if I gained access to the reskin alongside the tank, instead of having access to the reskinned tank from the very start.
This problem is still present in SR4, eg, you get the DLC remix dubstep gun long before you get access to the original dubstep gun.
Some things from the game were censored, so certain regions of the world got a partial version.
To my knowledge, the censorship removed Shaundi's loyalty mission, removed blood, and the alien probe melee weapon.
These are 2 post-processing shaders I absolutely loathe and disable in everything I play.
You cannot turn them off in SR4 at all, thankfully they don't use these too irresponsibly, but I sitll would've preferred to play without it.

The Game

This game is downright brutal when you get to the really difficult (and important) missions.
The easy missions allow you to get a feel for the game. As you move up to more difficult missions, it'll become very clear that you need your fellow Helldivers to accomplish the objectives.
TEAMWORK is very important. As such, it is a MUST to always respect your fellow players to have a great experience. The community is very much alive and helpful, so learning how to survive and spread managed democracy becomes much easier.
FRIENDLY-FIRE is also a very important concern. Always be mindful of your aim and the whereabouts of your team.
The game is pretty simple. Drop in. Accomplish Missions. Extract. That's it. There are many weapons and stratagems (The Helldiver's bread and butter) to upgrade and learn how to use. Once you've upgraded everything, you may choose to wipe your slate clean and start over.
All in all, the game is fun and satisfying when you finish missions and see how hard you've suffered to finish it but without multiplayer, it becomes almost impossible. So going solo is not a very productive option.

This game took me by surprise. The way the game presents the atmosphere in just the first chapter is a pleasant surprise seeing as my first thought of a game taking place mostly in a metro would be the limited world-building, but Metro 2033 easily puts that to rest. The story-telling is incredible, with good pacing between shooting sequences and winding down areas.
On the topic of shooting, I think Metro 2033 really hits the nail head-on with its take on survival shooter. The game offers a Ranger Mode, which among other things hides almost all of the HUD, giving you an immensely immersive experience that I kind of wish more FPS campaigns offered this kind of mode. Ranger mode changes the way you play from a Rambo-style gunning down enemies on sight to a more nuanced style requiring a more stealth-based approach. Ranger Mode definitely provides the more authentic experience, although that's not to say the other mode is any less legitimate (it's a game, play it how you like). The only complaint I have here is that I wish the enemies were more aware on the hardest difficulty, as I sometimes found myself standing right in front of them without them acknowledging me. Other than that, my last point on the shooting is that the guns are feel decidedly satisfying to both shoot, and even to reload even.

Saints Row 3 was one of my favorite games. Saints Row 4 did everything better. I actually like this game better than GTA5

If you enjoyed Saints Row 3, you should enjoy SR4 is it is by and large more of the same.
SR4 is in my opinion not half as balls-to-the-ball crazy as SR3 was, but it is action packed and very fun to play.
SR4, much like SR3, takes the absolute micky out of things. The first most players would notice would be that you can 'romance' all your homies, as it pokes fun at Mass Effect.
As the theme of the game is an alien invasion, so the bulk of its adoration (or scorn) are directed at more sci-fi sources.
The main antagonost, Zinyak, is an absolute winner writing wise.
One of my personal highlights would be Zinyak and Jane Valderama reading romeo and juliet on the classical radio station.
All the characters have lots of funny moments to shine, but I really don't wana to give any away.
You have a whole arsenal of weird and wonderful weapons, and you can upgrade and customise most of them too.
The upgrades even make some of them act quite differently. eg, The dub-step game that debuts in this game bases the track it plays on its skin.
And with others, you'll change your play style slightly to accomodate, eg, the Disruptor gains a piercing ability, so you'll start trying to line up enemies for multi-kill shots.
There's a whole slew of other weird weapons too, from the inflator (makes body parts extra large until they eventually explode), to the thumper (shoots plungers, forget what their special effect is).
They're fairly creative, and give me an itch to go play Ratchet and Clank again.
I'm not sure of the cause, but as you unlock more super powers and by extension more enemy types, the game seems to misbehave more and more.
The first 10 hours or so I played were rock solid, but then I started to run into weird bugs, eg, all the character models were flickering, and now that I've approached the end game, I'm encountering semi-regular crashes when fighting aliens, particularly those things that travel as round balls.
You could argue this is meta as the game consists largely of you being trapped in a simulation and doing everything you can to crash it with no survivors.
The tank controls are so bad, they need to be criticised harshly. What volition has done is make aiming and movement work co-dependently, so W will always orient the tank to face forward in the direction you're facing. It's weird, but I can get used to it, but W and A work very weirdly, since I usually found that it did a 270 degree rotation to go from forward to left, instead of rotating in a more sensible and direct manner.
I would've much preferred an alternative control scheme where W/S was forward and back on the tank's alignment, and A/D turned the tank, with the aiming of the turret being fully independent.
As much as I enjoyed the game, it feels very rushed.
There's various little bits of polish that are conspicuously missing from SR4 but were in SR3 (eg, car cruise control).
They reused the entire steelport area without any particularly large changes - if we ignore the control nodes and control towers.
There is fairly little in the line of new outfits compared to SR3.
And so on.
I somehow have it in my head 5 years have passed since the last game, and just looking at how my local area changed in that time, I would've expected the steelport to look quite different in numerous areas, but still familliar.
I remember that SR3 had a cruise control option for all vehicles, that basically kept the car at a constant speed, and allowed you to use W and S to change this speed. It would've made for much nicer driving when following people (eg, Matt's loyalty mission).
It doesn't really matter as you'll spend the bulk of the game running around on foot with your super speed.
The problem was a lot worse in SR3 where every bit of DLC was dropped on you right at the start, and you didn't have to earn any of it.
SR4 is similar, but you have to play for a few hours and rescue at least some of your homies before the DLC gets dropped on you.
To use SR3 as an example instead, one of the DLCs give you a reskin of a tank; You don't get access to the original tank until much later in the game, and I would've enjoyed it a lot more if I gained access to the reskin alongside the tank, instead of having access to the reskinned tank from the very start.
This problem is still present in SR4, eg, you get the DLC remix dubstep gun long before you get access to the original dubstep gun.
Some things from the game were censored, so certain regions of the world got a partial version.
To my knowledge, the censorship removed Shaundi's loyalty mission, removed blood, and the alien probe melee weapon.
These are 2 post-processing shaders I absolutely loathe and disable in everything I play.
You cannot turn them off in SR4 at all, thankfully they don't use these too irresponsibly, but I sitll would've preferred to play without it.

A solid successor the one of my favorite RTS games of all time. Developers are constantly fixing and tweaking the game, ever improving it. WWII setting is interesting, but this is not the only game that has it. (Think of Men of War: Assault Squad) Resource collection is passive, meaning that there are no collection units, you just take territory and resources are given to you based on what area you took. Wide variety of units which all serve different purposes to differing degrees of success. Plenty of maps, both community-made and developer-made, which adds to replayability. Many of the commanders are bit mundane, especially the ones which are given to you for free. Some of the best units in the game, (Tiger Ace, Sturmtiger, etc...) are only available to commanders which need to be purchased, so there is a bit of a discrepancy between players who haven't purchased any commanders, and those who have. Additionally, commanders in the store are a little pricy for my taste, ranging from $2 to $4, but they do add a bit of flavor to any player's loadout. Matchmaking is good, but the low amount of players means that you may very well be matched with players from other continents. (I live in the United States and I often see players from Europe and Asia) Overall, a really good game to buy with some friends if it's on sale, or if you're itching for some historical RTS action.
