You Have to Win the Game is a short but sweet exploration-based retro platformer seemingly designed with the sole purpose of plunging a bullseye arrow into my nostalgia heart. The game has the look of the early PC games I grew up on, complete with CGA graphics (you play it through an in-game CRT monitor emulated on the screen), but designed with the modern pixel-perfect platforming sensibilities of games like VVVVVV and Super Meat Boy. Thankfully, it's not nearly as hard as those games, and can be easily completed in around an hour or so with a little bit of determination. Checkpoints are liberal, and there is no penalty for dying. And for those who enjoy a tougher challenge, there are harder modes available, along with a collection sidequest for 100% completion.
And the best part? It's absolutely free. Seriously, as in no-strings attached, no microtransaction bull$h%t, 100% free. One might think that may mean the quality probably isn't that great, but I assure you it's rock-solid, and clearly made with love and care by someone who was inspired by those early days of PC gaming as much as I was. If you're a fan of 2D platformers, or games having a retro-style with a bit of challenge to them, check this one out.

IF you love free exploration platformers AND 80s video game stylistics, but don't have countless hours to spare, this is the game for you. Well designed, not too difficult and with a charm of its own, CYHTWTG is a nice introduction before you switch to its even better sequel!

Definetely recommend this game, it's a sometimes challenging platformer but lots of fun and replayability with the time attack feature. Also if you're a completionist there's the challenge of trying to finish it 100%. Cheers!

I heard about this game a few years ago, I bought it the day it came out, and I haven't stopped playing it since. In almost four years, I've never had the same playthrough (Hell, I've only like six victories under my belt), and the number of possible playthroughs and layouts only increased after the Advanced Content update. It's hard and unforgiving, but the raging difficulty is part of the fun. It's what makes me come back, actually! Maybe I'm just masochistic, but I enjoy rogue-type games like this that force you to push ahead, no matter what condition you're in.
For example, there will be some layouts where you will easily beat enemy ships and reach the final level, called "Sectors" in this game, with max shields and high-tier weapons, but there will also be playthroughs were most of the Scrap (money) you make will be spent in basic suplies and in repairing your ship.
Surprisingly enough, at least to me, there is a story! There's a pleasing role change in this game, as you play a Federation ship and you fight against the Rebels, who are trying to destroy your base, and the final fights is against a rebel flagship so overpowered you'll want to cry when you reach it with a single basic laser weapon, a level 2 shield, and less than 5 HP left...
Edit: 10/10

Extremely hard space strategy roguelike, but a great deal of fun once you start getting new weapons and upgrades.
WARNING: You will die repeatedly.
9/10

The thing that FTL does right is that there is a steady stream of new things to try. New ships, new crew, new weapons, new quests and more. This makes it easier to keep going even though you have to start over many many times.

I'm usually not a fan of hard, unforgiving games where you just keep dying, but in FTL it just sort of works. I love the graphics and the UI. Very old-school and yet super intuitive. Its rogue-like gameplay taken to space is just perfectly executed.

This game is, in my opinion, the last of the great AAA pc exclusive games. After Bloodlines, AAA gaming moved almost completely to consoles. They may be making a comeback, with Star Citizen, XCOM 2, some of the stuff released by the better indies, etc - but outside of MMOs, Bloodlines was the biggest PC exclusive game released for a decade or so. Note that it is a 'mature' title - not only for violence, but also adult themes and language. It's not that it's crass game , but it tackled some heavy subjects, and probably had the most mature story in gaming at the time.
Positives:
The story is great. There are multiple sidestories and quests, you'll spend a lot of time just exploring and completing side quests. The atmosphere is great. Dark, gothic, art, brooding music...
Awesome characters. All of the characters you will meet are interesting, have great voice acting, and indepth stories, if you want to take the time to discover what it is.
Really interesting map design: A massive amount of map types. Inner city, sewers, mansions, ships... it goes on and on.
Great gameplay: This game as a RPG FPS hybrid is probably the best of it's kind, rating alongside games like Deus Ex. The rpg stuff is well done, though relatively simplistic, the stealth and conversation system are well developed, and the combat is well done.
Negatives:
Most of the negatives revolve around the fact that the game was released early and somewhat unfinished/unpolished.
Background voice work: Although all the 'name' characters have individual voice actors and are all well done, there seem to be very few 'generic' voice actors. For example, there seems to be only one generic 'bad guy' voice for enemy units. Bad guys only have one or two lines to say, for example which at times can be hilariously inapropriate - For example, you can talk your way into a fight with a Russian gangster who has a heavy Russian accent - but as soon as combat starts, he speaks the same generic American accented lines.
Gunplay: In the vanillar game, using guns is pretty much useless due to low damage, low accuracy, etc. This forces you to generally use melee. This is fixed however in the unoficcial patch.
Fighting: While you can play as a character who talks/stealths their way through situations, there are many situations in which combat is necessary. That's not a huge problem, but it would be nice had the game been a bit more rounded to allow for a non-violent run, but whatevs.
Bugs: The vanilar game is buggy as hell. It has several game breaking bugs in fact, that will make the game impossible to complete. This however is fixed in the unoficial patch.
Make sure you get the 'unoficial patch' - not only does it fix the game breaking bugs, but it also adds features into the game, some of which that were cut (as the game was released early), and even some new stuff.
Final thoughts:
This is one of the better games released on the PC in the 00's. If you haven't played it before, there's no reason not to get it. And remember the unnoficial patch. Seriously. Can't emphasise that enough. Also don't play Malkavian on your first playthrough. Yes they are awesome, yes they are hilarious, but they also spoil their own story which is a lot funnier and less spoiler-y once you know it as well.

This is one of the best action horror games I've ever played, bar none. It was intense, riveting and had a fantastic story based off the novel Metro 2033 by Dmitry Glukhovsky. Unlike other Post-Apocalyptic games, this one takes a very serious and realistic approach to the genre, tossing aside pop-culture gimmicks and jokes and embracing the cold, harsh and horrify reality of life in a land after the bombs.
The graphics are great for the era and run smooth, least for me, 99% of the time. I experienced slow-down only once during the entire game and never crashed or locked-up so that is a bonus indeed.
The music and voice acting was great, fitting the game perfectly and added to the immersion.
Combat was very quick paced and absolutely required a quick eye to often track the fast moving enemies.
The survival elements, even on the easiest settings are a challenge- requiring the player to do at least some resource management or else find yourself without ammo, filters ... and life.
The movement is the game's weakest area, especially climbing and jumping. These two areas could have been done much better and often break immersion with wondering why your character can't get up a 1 foot wall, etc. But, other than this everything works as intended.
This is a great buy ... highly recommended,

Arriving at the bottom of a tower, you discover that a little girl is imprisonned in it, being gifted and pursued by the evil king. Franklin, the one that hide her, can't do anything as magic has taken the tower but he reveals that you can go into worlds created in paintings...
Drawn: The Painted Tower is the first game of a trilogy, where drawings can act as portals to other worlds. The main idea is to use this opportunity to find items that will lead you to Iris. While the main plot is revealed little by little, I'll be honest: it's not really the focus here. You don't have anybody on your tails or pursuing someone, you're just trying to reach a little girl by solving puzzles.
The gameplay is the standard one in this game except for a missing feature: there are no hidden objects scenes. You can say that it's just to find items, use them, combine them and solves riddles and puzzles. However, trust me, it's not boring at all. Objects aren't necessarily easy to find but they're making sense. Everything is making sense, even the actions. Besides, you can find clues thanks to letters or notes scattered around.
The graphics are more close to drawings, however, they're very somber apart for the paintings themselves: a farm in the sunset, a witch doctor in the jungle, a dragon cave, a griffon castle (though it's an ice landscape), a forest during the night (perhaps the only real dark painting) and a giant tree. It"s really changing from the rest of the genre out there.
The soundtrack is also marvellous: very fitting in each scene.
Achievements are also included and ingame, once unlocked, they're for all the profiles.
However, what's the problem here?
I had several crashes. I returned to Windows, with the game closed but the .exe still running. I had to terminate. Once, it was even switching between the game and Windows. I had to do a CTRL-ALT-DELETE to open the task manager to stop this infernal switch.
But despite this, Drawn: The Painted Tower is a fabulous tale. However, you do know what I'll recommend you: to buy it during a sale. Seriously, Big Fish is planning to release the last game of the trilogy and I've to try Dark Flight before. Given the fact that I bought the CE and the SE edition, because I've misread the title, I'll make a comparison of the two versions soon.

If you are looking for a true adventure game, this is not for you. And for this reason, I am not recommending the game.
Some of the blame for my negative feelings about the game falls on me, as I didn't look into the game and purchased it solely on the Steam store page (description, "about this game", screenshots and tags). The tags at the time of purchase were "adventure", "casual", "point & click" and "puzzle". My expectations and hopes were that it would be reminiscent of a LucasArts adventure game.
Steam doesn't give the option of star-ratings or a "maybe" or "neutral" - If any of these were options, my answer wouldn't be a flat "no". If you can get this game on sale in the $2-$3 range, then yes, I recommend it.
TL;DR Pros:
- Pretty artwork.
- Fun concept.
- Short and light.
TL;DR Cons:
- "Adventure game" mechanics are severely dumbed-down.
- Almost entirely games of fetch or hidden items, with a few pattern/number puzzles.
- Crashed multiple times.
The graphics are nice and I enjoyed the concept of the main character's magic.
However, the "adventure game" mechanics are boring and dumbed-down to the point where the majority of the "adventure game" type puzzles involve just finding the inventory items that you need. Go to point A to find ___, then go to point B to use it. In most cases, just *seeing* the item in the scene is the hardest part (don't get me wrong, some "hidden object" games can be fun... but those games aren't the same as adventure games).
The times that you need to combine items to solve a puzzle, and it's not made instantly 100% obvious, are few and far between.
Drawn switches between this item finding mechanic and actual pattern or math puzzles.
The game also ended up crashing multiple times. Fortunately, no progress was lost from any of the crashes.

Does this game have its charms? Yes, its façade is beautiful, but that does not outweigh the many problems with the game’s construction. I have played many puzzle games and most have a beautiful exterior. It is generally the story’s depth, the game’s mechanics, and the variety of engaging puzzles that make for a fun puzzle adventure. This game lacked quality in all of the above.
Problems:
(The Story): This story’s depth runs about as deep as a 3 year old child’s written work. Harsh, but true. The only creativity or beauty seen in this game is visual; that would be fine if this were a pretty painting being sold for 10 dollars and not a puzzle adventure game.
You would be better off grabbing a snack and a movie at your local cinema than playing through this. That would cost the same time and money as Drawn: the Painted Tower, but at least you would have more to say about it than “It’s pretty”.
(Mechanics): As other negative reviewers have said, the game crashes frequently. Also, when you use hints, they come in order of steps needing to be accomplished within a given room. So, if you are at a loss at the end of a room and need a hint, you will have to go through all of the room’s hints to get to the one you are after.
(Puzzles): I don’t know about you, but for me, variety is key in a puzzle game. The variety in Drawn was not so great, but the main problem with some of Drawn’s puzzles is that there are no instructions. So when you do get excited about a hard looking puzzle, your excitement is likely to fade by the time you figure out what exactly you are supposed to do. (In short) Having no instructions was okay a lot of the time, but it was frustrating when a clever looking puzzle was not intuitive.
(Conclusion): Drawn: The Painted Tower is a picture book game for toddlers that frequently crashes, has disappointing puzzles, and will last about as long as a lord of the rings movie.

It's a shame that this game only gets 'Mostly Positive' and even recently 'Mixed' reviews.
I played a fair bit of the original Company of Heroes, and moved over to the second during the early beta. At the time it felt like an incredibly different game, and part of me rejected it outright. However, since playing it for longer I really feel like nothing drastic has changed and the output has been a very fun and engaging RTS.
The gameplay itself is excellent. Unlike some other RTS games like C&C the gameplay is focused much more on micro-play; the way you position your units can win or lose you a game. That's fine, because that's what the majority of the game is focused on. You could have the greatest timings for building up your economy and 'teching' up; but if you leave your big♥♥♥♥♥tank with its♥♥♥♥♥♥hanging out then a couple of AT guns, which aren't all that expensive and quickly available, will leave you wish a massive hole in your army. Cover differentiates between negative, none, medium and heavy. The better the cover, the less damage your unit takes. This made everything feel a little bit more focused on the engagements you had, which were happening almost constantly across the map. Despite this, the game's pace feels very relaxed in comparison to other RTS games like Starcraft. You will feel overwhelmed at first but once you get a build order sorted (many are available online) you can forget about the whole macro strategy and focus more on getting your micromanagement up to speed.
There's a good variety of maps, each of which have their own unique personalities and promote, to a minimal degree, a different approach of play. Some buildings are very open field whereas others are heavily laden with buildings you can jump in and out of. So in an open field map you may want to consider how you're going to advance on the enemy; smoke grenades, mortar fire, artillery, a tank line? You have to think on your feet a lot; so when things go well you are very satisfied.
There is a learning curve, you need to have a quick google and glance at places like
or other wikis that explain the different capabilities of units. This is all part of learning a competitive game, and if you like the WW2 theme and the looks of the gameplay then it's well worth the invested time.
A lot of the negative reviews stem from issues of 'balance'. I think these are entirely nonsense. The balance in Company of Heroes 2 is entirely reasonable with no clear steam-rolling from any one faction. Once the British were released people♥♥♥♥♥♥themselves into thinking they were overpowered because they had no idea how to play. Shortly after, however, players figured out that the Wehrmacht faction's lone sniper unit (an early available unit) could almost negate the British player early on. Everything since has been patched. There will be strategies you find hard to deal with, or some that seem overpowered. However, that is entirely due to the fact that commanders can be used in ways others haven't thought of (even the devs, they're only human) and so rely on the community reporting these worries.
To give an example: Last night I was thrown a curve ball in a 2v2 match where the enemy built nothing but engineers. They attempted to quickly capture the map against the slow-moving British units and rushed for light tanks and vehicles which the British take a little longer to get going. Honestly, I know a lot of players who would have said "♥♥♥♥ it! These Germans are so OP!". But after capturing their territory that connects the others together (and so denies them resources) we quickly caught back up and gave them a run for their money. It was a fairly normal game (around 30 minutes) because as shocking and powerful their strategy appeared they usually have a hole to exploit which was their lack of focus on anti-tank by trying to get the early-game victory.
Don't let the balance/RNG posts fool you! Relic fairly frequently come off feedback from the community and alter balance; something it works, sometimes not - it was no different in CoH1 as notalgic reviewers like to claim. The game is fantastic and a gem. It's a shame that people protested enough to get rid of some exciting features. There used to be a blizzard mechanic that caused the maps to become bitter cold and lack visibility. Getting units to heat was a must, it slowed down the game pace but I felt it offered a unique style of play where you were rewarded for managing to be mobile during this period or using your time wisely to recoup. You could always veto these maps anyway!
All in all. Good game, give it a whirl, ignore bitter players.

Well enough remembering and ranting... here is the review.
This was one of the first true 3d game on the market, together with Quake. Notice how when firing a flare along a corridor lights up the walls as it travels. That was an amazing performance at the time of the original release.
Also this game is one of the few even today that offers true freedom of movement. The original idea was that being in space had to deliver the atmosphere of lack of gravity and allowing you to turn on all axes delivers on that feeling. This also allows for doors to be placed on ceilling and floors.
Another way to get a good feeling is dodging those lasers being fired at you. With enough practice you can be invincible only using your skill alone. Very much like Dark souls.
The AI is good even by todays standards. Some bot types are aggresive when in numbers or retreat if alone or even run to get bigger bots. Playing on higher difficulties takes a lot of caution. This contrast very well with the speedy escape that you need to make after killing the reactors.
The game does not have a tutorial and does not seem to have a steam achievement system and that is just fine, old school games didn't hold your hand or reward you for simple tasks. Man up, jump in your ship, dodge those lasers, rescue the hostages, destroy the reactors and escape in movie fashion with flames following your ship.
One important note that made a huge difference for me: press F3 to remove the cockpit and then the "+" key to maximize the view so you get the feeling of actually being in the game world in person.

Descent originally a DOS game in 1995 was a whole new gaming experience for me back then.
It's basically a first person shooter with the ability to fly. You're equipped with guns, missiles, and other weapons you can use to destroy the alien threat.
Your main objectives are fighting your way through each level by collecting coloured key cards in order to pass through matching doors, each stage ends with a reactor you have to take out, and while these do get progressively harder, they also get repetitive. But it sure does increase your adrenaline as you try and find your way out to the exit in time!
Ahh it does bring back memories!

What can I say? This game was an awesome experience back in the day. It was ahead of its time, as well, being the first 3D game (to my knowledge) to feature polygon entities instead of sprites. I used to play it keyboard only, and became so proficient at it that using a mouse for other games felt wrong. The atmosphere is really gripping, the sense of being alone in a hostile environment, the walls closing in on you, constantly on the alert for the sound of secret doors opening to unleash your foes behind your back... or above you, or below you. Yes, you need to think and act in all directions at once in Descent.
Players today might wonder what all the fuss is about, but they need only look past the dated graphics, have their travel sickness pills handy, and dive in. The gameplay is taut, and very tactical. Running and gunning is not a good idea, you will often need to advance, take cover, watch your back... and watch out for those pesky rockets! It's also a great example of that seemingly lost art, the Hidden Areas (TM)! It's worth your while to really study your environment, as some of the best upgrades and ammo are hidden.
The enemy AI is surprisingly advanced, as robots will try to evade your fire, while keeping you in their sights at all times. You will soon learn to dread certain robots, and to be wary of superficially calm, spacious areas, because these tend to turn into intense battle arenas in the blink of an eye.
Then, after all the rockets and laser blasts have ceased after another blistering fight, you'll breathe a heavy sigh of relief... and then try to get up the nerve to advance to the next area.
This is one of those classics that's dying for a modern version (that keeps the gameplay intact). Until that day (oh happy day!), let's replay this sucker. Thanks, Steam, and here's hoping you'll get Descent 2 and 3 in here as well.

A great combination of combat and exploration on a broad variety of levels with fully free flying, and also the first PC game with textured perspective-vision rendering. Timeless classic. Must be played by every PC gamer.

Descent is one of those classic games everyone should've played. It's one of the earliest proper 3D games, and even today it's an excellent example of a high-octane action oriented shooter. The twist here, of course, is that you can move freely in all directions, which only very few games really do. There's a large arsenal of weapons to acrue, and even upgrade in the case of the laser cannon, which you'll need to fight the huge variety of different foes you'll encounter in Descent.
Mix in incredible tense, skill oriented multiplayer, Descent is everything you could want out of a 3D shooter.
The Steam version on sale as of this writing does feel a bit dated though. There's no support for higher resolutions and the dependency on DosBOX means that performance, even on modern gaming PCs, isn't always top notch. There are a slew of source-ports available for Descent, such as DXX-Rebirth, that do a much better job of providing the classic Descent experience, but updated for the modern age.
All that puts me in a difficult position in recommending this game. I guess I can just say what I've done. I've bought this version on Steam to show that I like this game and I'd support any other in this series coming to Steam, but I won't be playing it on Steam, I'll use one of the excellent source ports instead.
Here's to hoping future updates will allow this version of Descent to compete with those.

I really enjoyed this game. It has a distinct world and art style, and a simple yet moving story that balances the lighthearted innocence of a child's imaginative explorations with deeper, more serious themes at deeper inspection. The end result is a grand adventure with a bit of of sci-fi elements and just a hint of surrealism.
The gameplay is 3D platforming with a heavy emphasis on using a grappling-hook like glove. To me, it evokes parallels to game mechanics like the old classic Bionic Commando, Spider Man games, and more recently, Windlands. But this game fully owns that grappling mechanic and does some very fun things with it. It is deeply satisfying to go flying through the air with enormous leaps, locking on with your energy beam, then flinging yourself up into the sky. It is an action adventure game without any violence or combat. It is a game about acrobatic spacial puzzles that ask you in a hundred ways, "How on earth are you going to get over there?"
The first 90% of the game is not very punishing. Checkpoints are frequent. However, in the last level, the difficulty does spike considerably as you will often be flying blind with little chance to plan your jumps and grapples. But it is doable with dedicated effort. I beat the game in about 8 hours, which felt about right to me.
This is one of the more memorable games I've played in a while, and I highly recommend it. It is charming, imaginitive, fun, and surpassed my expectations in just about every way.

This game is basically a better version of Alien Swarm, and Alien Colonial Marines we never had. You're a special operative designed to make a bright future for your Democracy Motherland, Super Earth, which is under attack by vicious Cyborgs, Zerg-like Bugs, and Protoss-like aliens.
The tips constantly claim this game is difficult when playing alone, however, I must debunk it. It's actually easier if you play everything alone. If you're spotted, just run for your life. When running, try to mow down those sentries on your way before they can sound the alarm to call in more reinforcement.
Also, playing alone is another good thing, since most of time players don't want to spend time looking for samples that can give you research points every 10 sample collected. It doesn't matter what kind of samples you collected, just pick them all up everytime you see them.
Research points is like the backbone of entire game. Don't spend it on just weapons, sometimes, it's fairly important to upgrade your strategams. From calling down ammo supply, to air strikes, they can be a game-chaging potential if you do it right. I suggest you save up all the research points, and don't spend any before lv 10. If you are in need of research points, then just go ahead and collect samples, but that'll be time-consuming and boring.
Now, if you wish to play Co-Op, be careful where you're aiming, since this game is fairly hardcore, that is, you can actually kill your allies even if you really want to help them take out the blasted aliens that are licking their faces. Don't ever do it. Keep in mind, this can happen to you as well, if aliens are very close to you? Just run and reload, so your allies can eliminate the threats.
However, I must say... this game is kind of just "That's it". Really, just that's all the game it can offer you. You're there to do the same things over and over, just RNG give you different objectives. But it's basically like this, Host looks for a proper landing zone, then finish the objectives, then survive about 1 and half minutes for extraction, then hop on aircraft to end the match. That's pretty much it all about.
If you ever want to feel the excitement of being overrun, gun and run, then this game is for you. Double the excitement, or even triple it or maybe quadriple it, if you got friends to play with.
And yes, this games has a tons of meme of Star Troopers. Get ready to filled with puns and fight like hell.

Basically, the game has you deploying into missions from your ship, in which you may browse some lore, enemy info, your stats, weapons, and stratagems. Stratagems are essentially supply drops that can deliver weapons, vehicles, ammunition, reinforcements, airstrikes, or other using D-Pad combinations. Each mission requires you to complete one or more objectives and extract for your next deployment. You select a mission from a map of regions, in which there are planets of varying difficulties, which each contain several missions you must complete in order to conquer said planet and unlock new items. Conquering a planet boosts your community influence in the war. Influence is displayed on a progress bar for each of the three enemy types in the game: the Cyborgs, Bugs, and Illuminate, and enough influence progresses the war front towards the enemy home planet to finish the war, or too little influence can backtrack the war effort towards your capital.

Soon thereafter, HELLDIVERS found a place on my Steam wishlist, and after a rather long break from the game, I purchased it during the Steam Summer Sale and was thoroughly excited to continue establishing managed democracy throughout the galaxy.
Now buy the game.

Gunplay feels ever so satisfying, with guns potentially jamming, and they seem pack a real kick when you fire - especially shotguns. I do regret not keeping the flamethrower however - which was the worst mistake I have ever made in a game.
The story is compelling, if rather basic - but the presentation is pretty fantastic. The supernatural element is what makes it so compelling - and it makes it so much more different then Fallout, which it shares a few but not many similarities. The horror in this game is pretty scary, but not in a Amnesia, or Slenderman sense. It's more in the fact that the world is so cruel to the people of the Metro, with various stations being deserted, overrun by monsters, or even worse. The Dark Ones are rather scary, even if [SPOILER ALERT] I know that they are peaceful [END SPOILER] - I immediately got immersed in the rather claustrophobic and scary last level which certified my decison - 'If it's hostile, you kill it.'
The only thing that I really want for Metro Exodus, is either large levels similar to Deus Ex or even Dishonored, or an open world more in vein of Stalker then Fallout.
Hope you enjoyed, and if so, leave something or other for me.

King Arthur's Gold. Where do we begin?
Let's say you just start in the game. You have no tutorials, you are just thrown into a random game. What do you do? You begin building a fort. You see someone else doing an entirely different thing. Are you doing it wrong? One guy is putting trap blocks over a hole, another is digging a large tunnel with water, another is creating rooms packed with traps and class shops. Who is right and who is wrong?
All of you are right! This game encourages creativity. Using what's around you and turning it against your enemies. A shark in a pit killing soldiers? Turn it into a trap. Enemies built a wall? Launch yourself in a catapult. It is all these different ways to play that make every game so fun.
Assume they are putting heavy siege upon your walls. Off the top of my head, you can:
- Build tunnels for a constant stream of defense.
- Fill a boat with explosives and ram it into them.
- Get a boat full of builders to destroy the small base they built.
- Build walls behind the wall that is under siege
- Dozens of more ways, for you to discover!
To counter these:
- Have builders climb up using ladders to destroy the tunnel.
- Sacrifice yourself by turning the boat back into their wall, toppling it over into their base.
- Knights to stab the builders.
- Put your catapult on a boat for a constant push on each wall.
TL:DR, King Arthurs gold is a fun game that encourages creativity to defeat your enemies.

I'm sure some will disagree, but this is a game that got absolutely everything right back when it first released on DOS, from sound, to graphics, to balance, to gameplay.  It has that X factor that is hard to come by.  It's maddening, addicting, scary, thrilling, and yet deeply rewarding.  Few games back in the early 90's kept me as enthralled as this game did.  The 360 degree movement made the gameplay truly unique at the time, not to mention confusing if you didn't pay attention to where you were.  Combine that with the thrill of uncovering what lay ahead in the mines, the difficult bots that were out to destroy you, a great soundtrack, and action not matched by many at the time.  Descent is an instant classic and it's nice that it lives again so the newer gamers can experience a piece of PC gaming history, and so those of us who were lucky enough to descend into it's depths the first time around, can revisit the mines our corpses littered more then we probably would've liked.

LISA is different from what I'm used to see here on Steam. I bought it during sale, because the trailer remembered me of Earthbound/Mother 3. You are Brad, about 45yrs old, bald, drug-addicted, Karate-Master, suffering from your past and sharing your home with your best friends. One day, you find a baby laying on the ground, which is a bit of a wonder, since women don't exist anymore in the years after the
. Even more of a wonder, it's a girl. Now, what would you do? Give her away? Tell everybody? Throw her on the ground? Take her with you?
Everybody knows what will most likely happen to the only woman left in the world.
So you throw her on the ground.
Well you do. Not on purpose though. You decide to keep and hide her, name her "Buddy", raise her... But still, there is your drug-addiction. And your past. And your friends. And then you come home, just to find everybody dead and Buddy gone.
From here on it gets interesting. Wheres Buddy? What happened? Lisa? Joy! People. They know you. Who are they? Hallucinations. Joy! Decisions, that affect you and your friends. A crazy world full of men. And lots of Joy! You know, the only hope for mankind is your daugther. You know, your daugther is going to get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥by tens, hundreds, thousands... Depression. So much joy! It turns people into monsters! Joy is a hell of a drug!

Besides the comedic entertainment value, the game has some serious moral quandries you are faced with during your quest for your adopted daughter. Answers leave you with permanent consequences and the choices you are presented with are usually all equally troubling. Maybe one or two times was I able to make the choice (after reloading saves haha) that I know was by far the lesser of two evils. To be honest, I don't recommend doing what I did; loading saves to change your initial decision. Stick with your first choice and ride it out. See how the story goes with your initial choices and will leave a lasting impression. (Obviously it still did so for me despite me reloading saves before serious choices were made). Definitely reload during the "Russian Roulette Situation"

FTL: Faster Than Light is an incredible game with great mechanics.
I was skeptical when my first friend first told me about it, even though he mentioned space battles and invasion of ships. I'd seen a bit of footage and the game looked odd and slow-paced.
I couldn't have been more wrong.
As with any roguelike, beginnings are slow, and allow you to get into the pace of the game before you accrue resources and upgrade your ship however you like. Do you like fighting with drones? Try the Engi ship. Do you like stealth? Try the Stealth Cruiser. Do you like flat offense? Upgrade the hell out of your weapons bay on the Kestrel. This game makes it possible to play however you want. The game quickly gets hectic and unrelenting as enemy ships power off your engines, giving you no evasion rate, or pierce your shields with rockets that blow a hole on the hull of your ship. Send your crew to repair this, but be careful of their health! Oxygen quickly depletes and your crew could be in for a bad time.
Do you like being a diplomat? Try to engage your encounters in friendly conversation, and if that doesn't work, blow their ship to space smithereens. Do you hate being a diplomat? Then forget the conversation and blow them up! Show no mercy!
I honestly haven't found a single downside to this game. This game did everything it could do correctly, and the result is a spectacular space-combat roguelike. To anyone who even remotely enjoys roguelikes, this game is a must-buy.
Live, Die, Die, Die, Die, Die, cry tears of joy && || sorrow, Repeat.

This is a very good story-driven linear first person shooter. Assuming you have the hardware to handle it it's also pretty gorgeous. However, worth mentioning that if your graphics device can't render shadows well that it's probably better to hold off on this title-- darkness is very important for stealth, atmosphere, and an important challenge to overcome.
I don't think this is a mechanically-perfect game. Some of the mechanics do make the gameplay a bit more convoluted, as do some of the player-goals. For instance, playing this as a nonlethal stealth game is pretty-much mandatory if you want to get the secret ending, but there's not a lot of options as to how to do that. They introduced a nonlethal takedown to help make that way more easy (i believe this wasn't in the original, which i didn't play), but it feels sort of trivial-- basically you just press e rather than v.
Another mechanical flaw is the save-points, which range from being well-placed to horribly off-target.
Anyway, the game play is otherwise quite good. The guns you start with do feel like they were made by homeless russians living in subway tunnels, but they get more practical as you progress through the game and get new guns or mod your existing ones.
The atmosphere is very detailed, and the game tends to reward you with progress towards the secret ending when you take the time to listen to the world around you.
I definitely recommend this game if you're looking for an immersive, headphones-on sort of game. I don't know how happy fans of the original metro 2033 are with this, but as a newcomer to the series I was deeply satisfied.

I'm not finished playing yet (maybe halfway through), but I have to recommend this game.  It's more difficult than games I typically play (my years of being 'gud' are past); there is no 'easy' setting on this one, just normal and hard.  But even as I fail some levels over and over again, I keep on trying, even if I need to put the game away for a day or two so I can retry with a fresh mind.  The story and the atmosphere pull me onward, when I might normally give up.  It's incredibly immersive, even in normal mode.  If you want even more, you can go to Ranger mode and be rid of the hud completely.  The music is very good - suits the atmosphere without being overwhelming.  Combat is pretty good, though it does have the typical FPS issue.  Apparently in FPS games, we have no feet.  Annoying at times, and infuriating if lurkers are at your feet attacking you and you can't see them to attack in return.  That, and the lack of a save system, are my only gripes.  It does get very aggravating on difficult levels to make it nearly to the end, only to wind up back at the midway point and having to replay the hellish section again.  Especially for people like me, who aren't so great at harder games.  Technically, the game runs very well.  I have had no problems on my Windows 10 laptop, and even managed to sharpen the graphics through my Radeon panel and Reshade.  For an older game, it holds up well, even against many modern games.  If you like FPS games with atmosphere and story, give this one a try!

Let's get one thing out of the way: get this game on a Steam sale - it is NOT worth full price.
And also; I am firmly against blob "tactics" from OKW players; find an actual tactic to use, like an armoured push. Blob-ing deserves to stay firmly in StarCraft.
Right; on to the review.
Pros
-Good (non-DLC) single-player campaign with a variety of types of missions.
-Okay DLC single-player campaigns.
-Excellent multiplayer matches (... when it works).
-Large number of MP maps with community maps also included.
-Mod support is great - new maps, AI, and UI improvements for all.
-Main DLC (like Ardennes Assault) is worth getting, if only for the US forces.
-Different Armies - not just a new paint job on the same models. OKW for all-out attack, Wehrmacht for defensive play, Soviets for infantry pushes, US for armoured warfare, and the Brits for some good old trench warfare/gardening.
-AI is ridiculous.
Cons
-Microtransactions...
-Pathing issues on some maps.
-Lag, crashes, latency issues; you name it, MP has it.
-Steep learning curve with no real tutorials.
-Long MP loading times on par with old LoL loading times.
-No variety with Commanders; the ones that are useful are few and far inbetween.
-Bad progression system based on matchmaking.
-Bad/slow matchmaking.
-Terrible loot system; "War Spoils" is not a proper loot system; it's based on luck, making sure you've prayed to RNGsus / the Devil / Relic (Lelic), and whether you can get put into a balanced game.
-Forums are a poisonous, hate-filled place... Like all other Forums known to man.
You might look at the long list of Cons and say "f**k it; not worth playing" and, you'd be right. I'm recommending this game to those who can ignore the faults of a game and see what lies beneath; CoH2 is, deep down, a good RTS. As much as it tries to hide this beneath bugs/balancing issues, CoH2 can be a hilarious game if played right; I suggest a friend to play with, and I also suggest trying to defeat the Hard AI (good luck; you'll need it).
--6/10 Worth picking up, not worth the full price--

Drawn is full of beautiful artwork, which is a good job because that's the premise of the game: enter magical paintings to gather clues and find ways of advancing up the tower to rescue Iris. It's a mixture of hidden object finding, using the right objects from your inventory in the right places, and solving a number of moderately taxing puzzles. Well ok, the puzzles aren't that hard to complete, but a number of achievements rely on solving them quickly, or within a certain number of moves, or without making any mistakes. That's actually quite difficult for some of the puzzles on your first attempt where you're trying to figure out what to do, but a second playthrough would snag those. Still, it's not the kind of game to play through more than once, it's a linear story, it's not particularly difficult, and it's over in a little over four hours. As for the ending... what just happened? It was all very rushed, a bit confusing, and left all kinds of questions hanging! I guess it was meant to be a cliffhanger for the sequel, but it felt a bit anticlimactic. Thanks for that. Still, great little puzzle game, pretty easy, looks great, nice music, I liked it. Speaking of the sequel, it doesn't appear to be on Steam yet.

LISA is so good. Its got a funny, intresting world to explore with many different directions you can go in and tons of secret areas. Its the best kind of exploration rpg game. One where you are mosthly just exploring and randomly finding cool stuff but at the same time progressing the story.  The sidescrolling mechanic works really well and its a solid 11 hour game.
The game also has hard choices all the time, whether is choosing to give up a limb to save one of your friends or choosing how to spend the very limited amount of money the game gives you.

A lot of indie games try and pull the heartstrings or "make you think," but LISA is one of the only contenders so far that has managed to be both entertaining and thought provoking without being extremely pretentious. The art style is admittedly nostalgic for those of us that played RPGs in the 16-bit generation, but it's also got an extremely appropriate and often creepy style that is less of a cheap sentimental ploy, and more of an endearing framing of its world and setting. The soundtrack is excellent. If I had any complaints about this game, it would be the areas with the large amount of fodder enemies, and the (hopefully one off) "boss fight" that, unceremoniously, can and will kill your party members permanently in one hit.
The choices are rough in this game, as you will run into scenarios where you have to decide between yourself, and the people in your group. Your party members will get kidnapped. They may even run away. It's a harsh world after the apocalypse, and this game never lets you forget that. There's still room for very funny, absurdist situations, dialogue, and even battles. This might be one of the best games I've played in a while for the RPG genre, and definitely my favorite indie title so far. I'm very much looking forward to the follow up.

This game was amazing back when I first got it for cheap cheap from a Steam coupon. I saw it was a tower defense game, and I said to myself, "This is only a few bucks, I'll try it out." Oh my, I didn't know how much I would love this game.
Defender's Quest is a tower defense game with RPG elements, mainly experience points, skill trees, and a good story inbetween the gameplay. It the game has humor, which is rather welcome. The gameplay is where this game really shines.
This is simply the best tower defense game I've ever played. You may have played a tower defense game before, but you haven't played Defender's Quest. It has a lot of depth to its gameplay, it has a very intuitive UI and an unobtrusive tutorial that is very helpful. Tutorial can be turned off entirely in the options, if you really want to. With all the hype around Mafia II, I decided to purchase it a few weeks ago. As you can see, I have 18 hours on record, and I beat the game yesterday. Furthermore, as I was playing on hard several missions proved to be fairly challenging, and I got stuck for up to an hour at a time. This is not my complaint. It was refreshing to play a game that actually challenged me. My complaint is of the content, and the lack thereof. Since you're reading these reviews, you've likely heard the fact that there is basically no free mode. That's false. There is none. Zero. Leaving out free mode in a game like this is like failing to add headshots in a shooter. It's not necessary, you don't need it to beat the game, or to have fun, but seriously, WTF. The game has 15 chapters in it chronicling the criminal activities of Vito Scaletta and his accomplices. The storytelling is superb, alonlg with character development and a powerful ending. However, I felt misled. This game will not put you in the role of a Mafia boss or hitman. It actually has you play as a steet thug who slowly rises to be a street hustler, with loose ties to the actual Families with takes forver to ferment into actual Mafia style badassery, which is very rare. Most missions are very interesting and fun, but with very little actual feeling of an organized, powerful criminal intent. Finally, the police system. As you have likely heard, Mafia II is highly praised for  its advanced system to that governs the police. I have to say, it's pretty good. Unlike GTA's system of amnesiac cops, Mafia II's actually hunt for you after you've shaken them. However, the cops prove to be little more than pesky. GTA's cops compensate for their possible ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ness by being fairly formidable, if not rage-inducing foes. Mafia II's are weak and stupid, easily killed and easy to evade on foot. I've haven't experienced any fun shootouts with the cops in Mafia II.
Ultimately, the game has 0 replay value, other than mindlessly searching for collectibles, of which I've neve cared for in any game. The TOTAL lack of free play (unless you want to shell out money for a DLC that should've been included) is a major disappointment, coupled with the misleadingly short story makes you wonder, "okay, what now?"  I would not recommend purchasing this unless you are prepared for a product that stops having a purpose after a week. Don't get me wrong, I had fun, but I'm not sure if that was worth $15, and it certainly isn't worth $30.

The premise of this game suggested a focus on travel, which I suppose it delivers, but don't expect any freedom to come with that.
is a physics platformer that will have you jumping and swinging from rock to platform over the course of its 3-hour length. However, swinging isn't actually what you'll be doing, despite the game's thumbnail art - rather than tethering to a point, you'll pull yourself directly towards it, hopefully catapaulting yourself to the next platform.
Unfortunately, instead of giving you a sense of freedom, the overwhelming feeling here is restriction. Air control
lasts only a few seconds before you plummet vertically downwards, likely hitting the side of the ledge you were aiming for and sliding off.  The long-jump on the other hand is completely uncontrollable, launching you directly forward with no option to stop or turn, more likely than not throwing you into the abyss. But why jump when you can fly, right?
Well, grappling is a frustrating art to learn - too close and you'll smack into the rock you grappled to, dropping vertically; too far and you won't have enough momentum to reach the next grapple-point. This gets increasingly frustrating as the game progresses, giving you more and more sucessive 'swings' between platforms. The route you need to take is usually pretty obvious, but with the vast majority of acheivements being 'never fall in a level' and 'use fewer grapples than ___', every failure is a punishment. If you don't care about acheivements, that's fine, but you'll have quickly swung your way through the game without much to show for it.
In typical Coffee Stain form, the human(oids) are ugly and the animations are absolutely terrible. When the characters are not looping a short idle pose with their dead, expressionless eyes, they're sliding across the floor at an angle as they run. There is almost no head-tracking, making cutscenes feel staged and impersonal, with NPCs staring straight forward while you can move around freely. They remain on good form with the environments, though.
The mechanics are singular, and frankly I was bored of them within the first half an hour. The standard platforming at the beginning is quite fun, with a good sense of movement, and adding the first grapple to that is fine, but you feel less in control. From this point of the game
, you've seen everything it has to offer. You'll be 'swinging' from floating rock to floating platform over and over, getting up to three changes for your grapple, meaning more rocks between platforms. Later on you get a rocket upgrade, but this is only a mid-air long-jump, and will make you feel even more powerless when you miss your target by an inch.
Frankly the game does not stand up on mechanics alone, despite its short playtime. The story is enough to explain progression and told though the compelling, if unoriginal, method of narration via story-telling. However, with ugly characters, stilted voice acting
, boring and repetative mechanics, short length, and acheivements that are almost exclusively "don't fail once or start again", this game falls very short of the price they are asking.
If a short game about catapulting yourself from rock to rock sounds fun, then you won't be dissapointed. I, unfortunately, was.

Should've reviewed this a long time ago. The game is a fun little tower defense/RPG hybrid with something like six modes of difficulty for each map (with each difficulty mode having different enemies/different enemy abilities, not a simple boost in health), replayability in the form of New Game+ with extra content, and an interesting story with humorous characters.
The base game consists of thirty maps with a story cutscene before/after each and two different endings. There are five challenge maps and two endless maps that can be accessed after completing enough story maps.  I haven't finished NG+ recently, but it adds at least five more.
The game was released on Steam in 2012 and was on Kongregate and other sites before that but the devs have continued to support and update it for free - including adding Steam workshop support, sidequests, a journal for the main character, and most recently this HD update.
The HD update only came out a few days ago, so it's a little buggy (infrequent crashes for me, but since the game autosaves I haven't lost any progress), but the previous version is still accessible and it's possible to port your save file in from the old version. Given the devs' record of support, I'm sure the HD update will be close to bug-free soon.

In this era, there are very, very few games considered "New", or "original", without taking key gameplay elements/codes/graphics/other from a different, more popular game.
Thankfully, King Arthurs Gold (KAG) is one of those few.
In no other game I have played can you
Throw sharks at people
Blow things up
Shoot your enemies bodies back to their base... with a catapult
Build things
Blow said built things with said bombs
Shoot a bow like a shotgun (Screw physics!)
And last but not least-
Tunneling right underneath an enemies castle, and watching in awe as such a magnificient structure comes tumbling down from some stategically placed kegs
As you can see, this game truly is unique- It carries graphic styles and building mechanics from previous games such as Terraria, without actually "Stealing" what those games already have done.
This game has many strong points, but unfortunately many weak points, however small. Like every other multiplayer based game in this era, it is expected that the community is terrible (which is very, very sad), and KAG is no exception- With incompetent allies, moronic chat-spammers, and annoying griefers, this game has its fair share of community troubles.
But that is not something the developers can control.
Some other main complaints about this game are things that the developers CAN control, such as useless kegs (update months ago caused them to be virtually unusable outside of getting shot out of a catapult, but even that can go haywire after a simple arrow can shoot the keg off your back), and weakend ballista bolts- Seriously, 2 shots for 1 bolt? Now that I think of it, though, these really are my only complaints- everything else is generally balanced.
As for the good things, A lot of them I didnt list- For example, you can do things such as launching your best friend straight into enemy territory via catapult, crashing down enemy towers (Just for the awesome physics of this game you should buy it), and taming sharks- thats right. TAMING. SHARKS.
1 last thing before I sign this review off- There is seriously a lack of players in this game right now- What happened to the 5-or-6 full servers ay any given time? now hardly anyone plays Take the Halls, and when someone does it rarely exceeds 10 people.
Rating-
Gameplay: 10/10
Graphics: 10/10
Community: 10/10
Fun-Value/Value for Your Money: 10/10
Uniqueness: 10/10
Total- 50/50
Verdict-
This game is seriously worth the money- You will get every penny you put into this game out in entertainment. There is no reason not to get this game, for it is just a small $10, which is just 2-3 skipped Starbucks coffee. You will seriously enjoy it.

This game is......Decent.
If you are used to playing games such as the Men of War series games......then I would say that this game ISN'T for you. I personally disliked this game for starters it is VERY unrealistic and your tanks can get damaged by machineguns and the like. A smaller problem that I feel like addressing is that tanks like Tigers, panthers, Kingtigers etc can still be destroyed head on by anti-tank weapons that historically couldn't even scratch them. This is really only a problem for people who had gotten into MOW before playing COH or people who are total nerds like me. Another thing I disliked about this game is the whole resource system.......Its horribly flawed, at least in MHO. For example the more units you have the less manpower you gain, which is horrible considering that the amount of units you have doesn't have to be very high before your manpower becomes nothing but a small trickle leaving you totally defensless if you need to quickly create some backup units or build a structure.
The game does have a bright side though. This game is AMAZING when it comes to customization. You can download anything from the steam workshop and swiftly and easily apply it when you play a match. Modding is terrifyingly easy and the steam workshop has a decent amount of content. Don't like that tanks camo? Well then just download and apply a new one that you do like. Its literally that easy. You can change everything from vehicle camo to commanders to a stupid freaking baseplate. You also get custom decals for your vehicles. Maybe its just me but I really liked the customization of this game.
sadly though I don't think the pros overwrite the cons of this game and I'm going to have to give this game a thumbs down. I DON'T recommend this game. I've never played the first COH so I dont know what that one is like. I'm sure its at least slightly better than this one, the first ones usually are the best. But if your looking for a good RTS game then I would suggest looking into the Men of War series games if you haven't gotten to them yet.Or maybe try the Wargame series games such as Red Dragon and those games, which I recommend very much.

This is the game manifestation of utter ridiculousness. To loosely quote Michael Jones from Rooster Teeth “The game is like ‘you want ♥♥♥♥ing super powers, here’s some ♥♥♥♥ing super powers’”. This game has a lot to keep you busy and some great co-op gameplay. Saints Row has always been a GTA clone that doesn’t take itself seriously at all. This is the epitome, constant movie references, game references and outright silliness, this game is just plain fun. With a large open world, constant quests and unlocks to pursue, you can soar, leap and speed through the world as you grow more powerful and undertake a litany of tasks as you struggle against and evil alien foe who has trapped you in a matrix-like simulation which you gain more and more control of as you progress. Do you wanna have fun and feel really god damn bad afterwards when it's all over? Play this.
Combat and party system is more interesting than final fantasy has been for years - Abilities interct well and you can assemble your rag tag group of degenerates and weirdos to set up some devestating combinations, and the "stiff" animation is supplemented and made up for well with combat effects and clever art design.
Exploration can be a little confusing due to the 2D side scrolling nature and multiple maps- But after revisiting a zone or two you'll slowly get the gist of the layouts- Lots of hidden stuff to find and it well rewards nosey and curious gameplay.
The story- I can't really tell much without spoiling it. But this isn't "Press A to say nice thing, Press B to be a jerk." When it says actions have consequences and it isn't grade school "SO DEEP AND MOVING" tripe where you can see a character's death from a mile away- It will mess with your expectations and it will raise your hopes in bursts only so that they can be suplexed down into the dirt even harder, and you will want to know more and see what happens next no matter how rough it gets.
It has it's share of quirky and fun portions and gags are implemented throughout the plot and gameplay itself like the methadone you'll desperately need to ward off the withdrawl and despair in the rest of the game- Not from a bad gameplay perspective, but from how unforgiving and crushing it can be both in plot and difficulty at times.
Summary? If you enjoy turn based RPGs at all you will like this, if you enjoy dark humor you will like this, if you are put off by "permanent" penalties and consequences and like to savescum away your blues and bad decisions you might not enjoy it so much- But you might still enjoy the rest of the game.

So I was thinking that I need a new RPG to play. It should have a nice story, good gameplay and some open choices for the player. After a long time searching I found Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines. I waited for a long time, before grabbing it on sale and what can I say....I love it.
as you may read in other reviews, this game has many bugs. Luckily there is a nice Community that fixes them and brings patches for the game. Before you play it make sure you download the latest patch found here:
.
Now let’s start with
itself, why do I love this game so much? First, it is inspired by the Vampire: The Masquerade Pen and Paper, and the universe of it, a universe that is deep and complex, and instantly took a place in my heart, where Vampires live along mortal people with rules they have to keep, called the Masquerade. In that world, there are 7 playable and some more (Npc only) Clans that all play in a different way and even have a small impact on your story.
are called: Brujah, Gangrel, Malkavian, Nosferatu, Toreador, Tremere and Ventrue. At the beginning you pick 1 of these, decide if you are female or male (sadly no more customization) and then you allocate your "standard skill points" in your character sheet, whilst every clan has his own abilities and different bonuses on some of the attributes.
Then the Story starts. After a pretty, long but well-made intro sequence you can control your character. The controls feel a bit strange at first and you may have to enable mouse look in the options to get a free camera, everything else should feel similar to rpg players/source users.
The graphic is also well designed and fits the dark theme of this game perfectly well, as does the synchronization.
What I liked was the fighting style. You have different melee and ranged weapons that reach from a Tire Iron and a magnum to a katana and a flamethrower. While you fight in 3rd person with your melee weapons, you switch to 1st person while using your ranged firearms. Also nice : most of your attributes increase more than 1 ability, example: 1 point of dexterity will get you +1 lockpicking and +1 sneaking skill, strength will get you +1 unarmed and +1 melee and so on, so there are many different ways to design and actually play your character, which leads to the next point.
has to my knowledge 5 endings, that trigger with your final choice and your positioning to the factions (called sects), which are the Camarilla (the "standard" vampire community) the Anarchs (fighters against the Camarilla) and the Kuei-Jin (eastern vampires that are slightly different). And while you don't actively decide your standing, your actions that you make in the story "speak" for you.
And finally
...... I love it. The Disciplines between the clans are well balanced and with the right combination of Disciplines and weapons, even the hardest bosses turn to ash in seconds (recommandation: Flamethrower)
So what can I say.... I guess the fact I recommended the game and my playtime + this review are showing it is worth playing, but again get the unofficial patch and if you are unsure get it on sale. Now excuse me while I enjoy my 2nd playthrough.

Mafia II casts you as Vito Scaletta, a young Italian who returns from World War II to find his mother and sister on the hook to a loan shark.  Like any gangster in a gangster movie, Vito decides he doesn't want a subpar life of the slums and goes down the organized crime route to make some cash.  You'll be with Vito as he whacks dudes, steals cars and tries on all sorts of snazzy outfits.
All of this is going on in Empire Bay, a New York-esque town packed with people, cops, cars and collectable Playboy magazines.  Now, at first glance, Empire Bay looks like an open world – one teeming with missions and quests for you to take Vito on.  It isn't.  You'll have one mission at any time and it's always one that drives the story forward.  All the icons on the map – clothing stores, gun stores, and so on – are just ways to enhance that mission.  Outgunned and dying a lot?  Buy better weapons after restarting.  Cops on your tail? Go pay to have the license plate changed on your ride.  You're not going to wander around the streets of Mafia II picking up odd jobs and meeting strangers; this is a world built around the missions you're doing.
Is this a bad thing? Of course not – it's just something worth pointing out, seeing as it'd be easy to look at this game and think there are hours of freedom in it.  Problem is, because there's only the task at hand in Empire Bay, the place feels awkwardly empty – it doesn't feel alive.  You cruise the streets and see other people and cars, but it feels like The Truman Show.  Everything is happening because of you. There isn't that "a-ha" moment seen in other games where you realize there's stuff going on in these massive metropolises.  Empire Bay is like an empty play set, and that hurts the believability of being Vito's world.
That's a shame, because what I dig about Mafia II is its story and the way it's told.  I love gangster movies such as Goodfellas and Public Enemies, so watching the exploits of Vito and his best friend, Joe, as they go from job to job, party with the ladies, and put the screws to people is an enjoyable experience.  On top of that, Mafia II uses some cinematic tricks to really up the production value on the cut scenes. There are over-the-shoulder angles you don't normally see and little touches that make the movies visually entertaining.
Trouble is, the story is the most entertaining part of the game.  I felt like everything between the cut scenes, which usually is shooting or punching people, was just something to get through to reach the next story bit.  The mechanics of Mafia II are pretty much those of a basic third-person shooter.  You have a bunch of guns, you take cover, and you kill all the bad guys so that you can move on.  You can try to deviate from this strategy and get creative, but you'll be blow away in a few seconds. Mafia II pretty much demands that you crouch behind boxes, pop out to shoot, and then go back to hiding so you can regain health. The cover system doesn't get sticky, which is nice, but there were plenty of times that I thought I was totally protected but continued taking damage – especially when I ran into a fire-tossing boss.
There are some awesome breaks from this formula, like going undercover as a window washer to whack a main player and having to sneak into a guarded compound unprotected, but these are the exceptions to the rule.  Most of the time, you're just slowly moving forward and gunning down everyone in your path.  It feels stiff – the animations drive that home and the aiming is never natural – and waiting to regenerate health is never a great time.  The gunplay isn't bad, but it's just not that interesting.
When you're not using a Tommy Gun or pistol, you get the job done with your fists.  These are set sections – and there are a ton of them early in the game -- where Vito needs to knock out his opponents.  Again, it sounds cool and is used really well in an unexpected prison section, but the mechanics are nothing special.  You hold the dodge button until the opponent gives you the chance to land a light or heavy attack.  Repeat the stiff animations and curse the camera from there until you win.
Mafia II also struggles with pacing.  There are great moments, like when you're driving a dead body to be buried and your friends are singing in the car, but there are mundane parts where you watch Vito pick up the phone and stare at the wall like a robot.  You'll finish a mission on one side of the town and then have to drive your car all the way home to park it, walk inside your apartment building, walk to your bed, and go to sleep.  Nothing essential happens in this time.  You're just doing menial tasks to close out the chapter.
In a similar vein, police in Mafia II can be interestingly aggressive and annoyingly conscientious.  The game uses a cool mechanic where cops will report your license plate or clothing description, and then it's up to you to make it to a chop shop or clothing store to throw them off the trail.  Other times they'll be stopping you for speeding or fender benders (while they ignore you blowing through red lights).  Most of the time, I dodged these issues without a problem, but during one of the final missions, I ran into the fuzz three separate times on three blind turns and had to get out of the car each time so that I could wait while they wrote me a ticket.
Mafia II is an interesting mobster tale with some great voice acting and cool cut scenes; if you have a “made man” itch, feel free to scratch it here, but be prepared for a pretty standard third-person shooter in the gameplay department. The “take cover, kill everyone, do it again” mechanic didn’t wow me, but it didn’t let me down either.  Mafia II is a solid little game that’ll give you a fun ride – just don’t expect the world.

Fantastic design, solid variety in weapons and upgrades, and that in turn offers an interesting variety in play styles (like using your crew to board the enemy ship, using slugs or sensors to pinpoint and kill enemy crew with beams, locking down the enemy oxygen generator, or else just simply blasting the enemy ship to bits with weapons or droids). The random generation of sectors and long list of unlockable ships make for serious replayability. I'm driven to complete campaigns with ships I don't even necessarily think I'll like that much in hopes of learning a new form of strategy, and am always stoked when I get to try out a ship I've just unlocked that features some of my favorite weapons and systems or crew combinations.  It's not a game in which you invest hours and hours, building up one ship or crew of characters over the course of days or weeks. You upgrade your ship and build your crew very quickly, and either win or lose the campaign in about an hour and a half to two hours (or crash and burn at some point along the way), giving it a bit of an arcade feel. There's also an element of randomness in terms of which weapons and systems become available, so you can't just go to the shop and buy the same loadout every time. The true art in playing this game lies in making adaptive choices as your circumstances in each step of your journey unfolds. Starting out on your first campaigns, I'd personally recommend switching the difficulty to easy and holding off on the advanced edition content until you've got a real grasp of the basics.
The price sits at $10, but I was lucky enough to grab it when it was on sale for $2.50, which for sure makes this the best game I've ever bought in terms of cost vs. hours played and enjoyment had. I'm admittedly a pretty casual gamer and this point in my life, so take my recommendation for what it's worth. I love the game, and I hope that more people give it a try.

The premise of this game suggested a focus on travel, which I suppose it delivers, but don't expect any freedom to come with that.
is a physics platformer that will have you jumping and swinging from rock to platform over the course of its 3-hour length. However, swinging isn't actually what you'll be doing, despite the game's thumbnail art - rather than tethering to a point, you'll pull yourself directly towards it, hopefully catapaulting yourself to the next platform.
Unfortunately, instead of giving you a sense of freedom, the overwhelming feeling here is restriction. Air control
lasts only a few seconds before you plummet vertically downwards, likely hitting the side of the ledge you were aiming for and sliding off.  The long-jump on the other hand is completely uncontrollable, launching you directly forward with no option to stop or turn, more likely than not throwing you into the abyss. But why jump when you can fly, right?
Well, grappling is a frustrating art to learn - too close and you'll smack into the rock you grappled to, dropping vertically; too far and you won't have enough momentum to reach the next grapple-point. This gets increasingly frustrating as the game progresses, giving you more and more sucessive 'swings' between platforms. The route you need to take is usually pretty obvious, but with the vast majority of acheivements being 'never fall in a level' and 'use fewer grapples than ___', every failure is a punishment. If you don't care about acheivements, that's fine, but you'll have quickly swung your way through the game without much to show for it.
In typical Coffee Stain form, the human(oids) are ugly and the animations are absolutely terrible. When the characters are not looping a short idle pose with their dead, expressionless eyes, they're sliding across the floor at an angle as they run. There is almost no head-tracking, making cutscenes feel staged and impersonal, with NPCs staring straight forward while you can move around freely. They remain on good form with the environments, though.
The mechanics are singular, and frankly I was bored of them within the first half an hour. The standard platforming at the beginning is quite fun, with a good sense of movement, and adding the first grapple to that is fine, but you feel less in control. From this point of the game
, you've seen everything it has to offer. You'll be 'swinging' from floating rock to floating platform over and over, getting up to three changes for your grapple, meaning more rocks between platforms. Later on you get a rocket upgrade, but this is only a mid-air long-jump, and will make you feel even more powerless when you miss your target by an inch.
Frankly the game does not stand up on mechanics alone, despite its short playtime. The story is enough to explain progression and told though the compelling, if unoriginal, method of narration via story-telling. However, with ugly characters, stilted voice acting
, boring and repetative mechanics, short length, and acheivements that are almost exclusively "don't fail once or start again", this game falls very short of the price they are asking.
If a short game about catapulting yourself from rock to rock sounds fun, then you won't be dissapointed. I, unfortunately, was.

Defender's Quest: Valley of the Forgotten is perhaps the best tower defense game I ever played. It introduces new enemies and heroes (turrets) at a comfortable and accessible rate, so you never get swamped or overwhelmed, and with 3 difficulty levels for each stage, there is plenty of replayability and opportunity to level up your team.
Every unit and enemy has visible health, damage, range, bonuses and stats readily available for you, such that there is no information or mechanics hidden from the player. You even have complete control over the timing, being able to pause the game to micromanage, or play at various speeds from 0.25x to 16x game speed.
The in-game world has enough charm, and the characters enough personality and depth, to drive the story and the gameplay progression.
I say tower defense, but there are also plenty of RPG elements, such as buying and upgrading weapons and armor, upgrading abilities, and even naming your recruits and heroes, and customising the colour of your recruits' clothing. Naming your knights after King Arthurs' Court of Camelot, for example, or your Mages after your favourite magical girls, lends tremendously to immersion.
The performance is excellence on almost anything. I get around 40fps on an old dual core Thinkpad at 1152x648, thanks to the native C++ engine and the game's 2D nature.
A staple of any tower defense library. I hardly can wait for the sequel.

Combat and party system is more interesting than final fantasy has been for years - Abilities interct well and you can assemble your rag tag group of degenerates and weirdos to set up some devestating combinations, and the "stiff" animation is supplemented and made up for well with combat effects and clever art design.

When it says actions have consequences and it isn't grade school "SO DEEP AND MOVING" tripe where you can see a character's death from a mile away- It will mess with your expectations and it will raise your hopes in bursts only so that they can be suplexed down into the dirt even harder, and you will want to know more and see what happens next no matter how rough it gets.
It has it's share of quirky and fun portions and gags are implemented throughout the plot and gameplay itself like the methadone you'll desperately need to ward off the withdrawl and despair in the rest of the game- Not from a bad gameplay perspective, but from how unforgiving and crushing it can be both in plot and difficulty at times.
Summary? If you enjoy turn based RPGs at all you will like this, if you enjoy dark humor you will like this, if you are put off by "permanent" penalties and consequences and like to savescum away your blues and bad decisions you might not enjoy it so much- But you might still enjoy the rest of the game.

This is more like the game Assassin's Creed IV should have been. Combining the graphics and RPG elements of AC IV with the strategic and management elements of Caribbean Hunt would have resulted in something truly spectacular.
That said, as a PC game this does leave a bit to be desired. For a mobile game, however, it's excellent. Granted, I am far from being a mobile game guru and, I haven't actually played the mobile version, but if it's similar to the PC version, then this is easily the most technically advanced mobile game I have ever seen.
But I'm not reviewing the mobile version. I'm reviewing the Steam version for the PC.
Whatever it is, it been very engaging for me. I have played quite a lot of it - almost nothing else - since I discovered it a couple weeks ago. In the time I've spent so far (66 hours apparently), I have captured all the pirate bases up to the one in Panama that I recently bought the map for. I currently own two fully equipped 2nd-rates, three flutes, two well-equipped man o' wars and several other ships. I've probably bought/caught and sold/scrapped at least that many lesser ships. I have put a fair bit of time in and done several things, but by my estimation I'm still a ways away from completion. Only two days ago, I discovered my first hidden port while sailing around in the open world. Until then, I had no idea such things existed. While it may seem small, I had not expected to find anything new after many hours of play (and I think I'm usually pretty thorough about exploring new places). It is one of the many indicators that the developers spent some time and effort into getting the design up to snuff.
Bottom line: It's more interesting as a PC game than what you might expect from a game that was originally created for mobile devices. It's nowhere close to being mistaken as a AAA title, but I'm addicted anyway.
