This game is actually quite well done. It has everything one could want or expect from a pirate game. Multile means of income, from scavaging shipwrecks for cargo, trading goods between towns, or actually pirracy.
You can sink or capture merchant and military ships to increase the size and power of your fleet, upgrade your ships with things like increased cargo or crew capacity, deadlier cannons, etc.
I also like the actual sailing mechanic. It's intuitive enough to get into fairly easily if you're already familiar with these types of games, but also a bit more complex than most. For instance, the fore and rear sails are raised and lowered independently, and can greatly help turning and manuvering the ship.
Front sails only will point your nose away from the wind, so when you lower the rear sails again you're quickly up to full speed. But if you ever need to turn into the wind, raise the front sails and use only the rear.
Takes a little getting used to, but once you master that, it becomes much easier to get and keep your broadsides on target.
My only real complaints about this game is the UI...the interface is ugly and frankly, quite amature in appearance. But it works, and it isn't that hard to figure out what the different symbols on the menus mean.

Where do I begin with a game that is so adventurious yet repetitive. First off let's start with what most people come to see for the first time with this game, the graphics.
This game is nothing short of beautiful, for it to have been made over two years ago (as of the time this review is being made). The game has aged very well, some triple-a titles can't even look this wonderful, from the gorgeous lighting and shadows to the smooth physics and motion that you receive while grappling, but I'll talk more about the way the game works shortly. This is singlehandedly one of the prettiest indie games I've played and well worth the $5 that my friend spent on it in order to give it to me as a gift (Thank you Ryan c:). Even the landscapes and models are well detailed, from pieces of paper and bottles that you'll find laying around, to the beautiful skybox that inhabits the world, this is a masterpiece of an adventure. The only downfall is the character models, the (lizard?) people that you encounter seem to look a lil cartoonish and have strange ways of walking, it seems like the developers kinda skimped on them entirely, but not on the scenery, which I guess I can forgive since they made such a pretty game.
Now this is one of the best parts of the game, in my opinion. The parkour elements and skills that you need in order to dodge and seemelssly jump from platform to platform, from ice spikes to landing pads, it's wonderful, really! The way that you run and grapple onto platforms isn't clunky or too difficult, the right amount of timing and luck will get you through the levels in no time at all. Overall the gameplay itself has a unique feel, if I could change anything I'd make the height of your character just a tad taller, you seem to be a lil too close to the ground when you're freerunning through caves.
This game starts off so spooky and strange, the atmosphere is dark and omniscent and hell I'd even say it looked like a horror game if it had some depth of field, but it doesn't. You play as a man, telling his daughter a story of his Uncle and the adventure that he undertook in order to find him, and then return back home. During the story of this game you come along a girl by the name of Maddie, she rides on your back for a majority of the time that you'll actually be playing, and she helps you along the way by giving you hints and decoding the texts on the wall in order to reveal where you are and where you're going. The parkour elements that I discussed earlier really do set the stage for the adventurious feeling that this game gives off, you actually get immersed within this short story. As for the ending of the game, well the way that you find your uncle and then leave him within meer seconds of seeing him kinda disappointed me because you only said a few words to him, and then left. He didn't even thank you for finding him, he just left you on your marry way and he stayed behind in the chasm to live out his adventure. After the credits there is an epilogue and you find yourself walking through your uncle's abandoned home, explaining how the adventure you undertook meant a lot to you and your daughter and you are proud you could undertake such a journey in order to find your uncle and bring your soul serenity and peace from the worry of wondering what might have happened to your uncle if you never went after him. I'd be lying if I said I didn't tear up when you let go of the note/picture of you and your daughter and it flies up into the night sky, as you say thank you to your uncle for making all of this happen.
This story is wonderful, although short and sweet. If a game can make me cry, laugh, smile, and feel angry within a playthrough, I'll give it a solid review. And this game, well it did all of those including the first one, which is rare. Overall I'd say this game is a solid 10/10 and you should pick it up if you have the chance, you can find it on sale here and there or cheaper on some third party sites, but it's well worth it. It took me a little over 2 hours to complete the story, and it's a story I'd play again if given the chance.

I recall some time ago I saw this game in my queue and I took a note of it. Put it on my wish list to check later. Later ended up being nearly two years or however long it precisely was. Several large updates for the game and a whole bunch of minor DLC. Hell might be as good place as any to just hop in. This game is when you cross Magicka with Alien Swarm and douse it in Starship Tropers vibe. In short it's a gem.
The game on surface level is extremely simple. This is a twin stick shooter you play with up to four people. On missions you have various objectives you need to do, usually hold area for a little bit, defend objective, interact with objectives and so forth. You pick your weapon, your special perk and four slots for strategems (they function similar to magicks in magicka). Off to the races right? Yes and no. This game is deceptively involved. There is quite a lot of depth, tactics and strategy to this. Different weapons will perform differently against the three enemy factions. The HUGE amount of strategems offered really gives room for some inovative and crazy gameplay. Call down air strikes (of various flavors), drop down vehicles or mechs, call down special weapons, support UAVs and whatnot. There is just so much in here to contemplate that made me really giddy with toys that blow♥♥♥♥♥♥up.
Then you get to the difficulty. On lower difficulties you will stomp everything, on harder difficulties you face different enemy types from the faction forcing you to have specific properties in your gear. Be it anti tank, bug spray, or whatever. Harder difficulties become both tactically challanging and they also become far more hectic...which leads to a lot more of the good ole team killing shenanigans. If you played Magicka or Alien Swarm you will know well how that goes. My first mission ever in multiplayer here I ended up dying in the first 10s by a person joining my game and dropping down on my face. Thankfully just like magicka, reviving a teammate is simple and easy.
The game has a different design than what you expect. At all times there is a galactic campaign ongoing. This means you can end up joining at the end of one where there isn't much to do (or unlock). Still the cycle is pretty quick (few weeks) so you get your chance eventually. Completing any mission earns standing, and standing is used to progress the ongoing campaign.
Unlocking stuff is done two ways (besides the DLC items).Leveling your character and completing planet's set of missions. Completing planets gives you new rewards (usually extra xp, strategems, cosmetics and so forth). If you complete one mission and you still have more to do and you leave, when you come back the sector might be completed from the campaign, however your game will allow you to complete the planet, which is really nice.
The game overall forces you to play in multiplayer if you want to finish all the content . You CAN solo it, but looking stuff up like that ends up pretty crazy. It takes specific gear and really knowing the game inside out. So you are more than encouraged to play with others. If you are looking for a singleplayer game, this isn't really it. You can do it, but game design isn't primarily intended for such. Anyway the reason to complete content originally is to progress your character, get better gear, get research points and upgrade said gear. There is a TON of it and it will take a long♥♥♥♥♥time to max it all out. However don't look at the game that it is the main goal. Main thing here is to play the game, first and foremost. Just doing missions is what this game is about. I find it easy to pick up and put down. I can probably leave this game for however long and just hop back in and have a blast (just like magicka).
This game is worth the price tag, especially on sale. It is far more than a simple twin stick shooter, and there is many of those out there. This game offers a challenge, incentive to get better and satisfaction in doing so. It is tactical, humorous and hectic. Easy to pick up and put down. It's a simple blast with little downsides to what it does. As long as you don't expect it to deliver something outside of its scope this game should give you a laugh, liberty and plenty of freedom.

That said, for all the gimmicks, the templating system and the interactive forms in this product are quite useful for a wide degree of applications, from Game Development to other areas and they're now starting to unlock their potential by toying with formats such as JSON export, and this is the largest draw of the product to me - even with horrid diagramming capabilities (I just want to be able to make some generic boxes and arrows linked together. Articy draft 3 (AD3) is the answer to my prayers as I've been searching high and low for a "narrative-mapping" software. As a game developer, I found AD3 very helpful in many aspects. It can help you with visualizing the flow of your story and narratives, be it linear or non-linear.
AD3 also allows you to store all the details of your characters, items, NPCs etc. On top of that, another very useful feature of AD3 is that you can use it to plan any location/map in your game. For instance, you can overlay a zone / patrol path / landmarks / spots etc. on top of your location/map screenshot.
In conclusion, this is a very good software for developers / storywriters, even at full price.

Whether you're a game designer or developer (or even just a writer,) this program is a very valuable asset. While there are a plethora of cheaper or even free options to do some of the things this program does, the ability to consolidate everything into one well designed and integrated workflow is more than worth the price of admission. I haven't even learned the full potential of this program yet, and despite that, it's saved me the major headache of trying to keep track of branching storylines using Google drive and memory.
Some of the things you can use this program for include branching dialog and storylines, quest design, map design, character design, keeping track of items, jotting notes down to properly integrate later, converting scripts to flowcharts, asset management, and if you need yet more flexibility, you can apply scripting to nodes to make it easier to keep track of things. It can be integrated with Unity too, but I don't use Unity so I can't speak for the usefulness of that. But I can't stress the usefulness and convenience of this program enough.
I could go into more detail about how to use it and whatnot, but the inbuilt documentation does a good enough job of that. However, if you want a more detailed, visual introduction to the program, watch the Nevigo tutorials on
They're old, but still applicable. In addition to this, Nevigo support is very helpful, which is always important when you're dealing with premium tools.
If you need to write a story or plan out a game that is anything other than completely linear, you'd be doing yourself a favor to buy and learn to use articy:draft.

i watched someone else play through the majority of this game a while back, and even without playing it i loved it. and now i'm playing it and i still love it.
so, imagine if Earthbound had a ton of party members like Chrono Cross, except the majority of them are actually useful and interesting. there's like, one member most people would want in their party due to an exclusive debuff + healing, but he isn't absolutely necessary. aside from that, it really feels like i can just pick and choose my favorite gang without worrying i could be using someone better.
of course, that isn't to say this game is easy. while a fair amount of the battles in this game are jokes, a comparable amount of encounters as well as out-of-combat situations will lead to party members either getting knocked out immediately, or even outright permanently killed. several of the latter are mandatory, and they can definitely feel cheap, but at the same time they're spread out enough that the losses never feel like insurmountable setbacks.
not to mention, there are tons of other decisions that can lead to lasting gameplay-affecting consequences like settlements being slaughtered, limbs being cut off, or worse. last but not least, there is a "PAIN MODE" that makes save points only work once. i think PAIN MODE is actually necessary to get an additional ending scene / achievement, but since you can't turn it off i wouldn't recommend it on a first playthrough.
it's hard to put my thoughts on LISA's story into words. the plot of this game is not something i would call unique anymore — "middle-aged man does terrible things for the sake of the person he cares about most" is something similarly done in works as recent as NIER, The Last of Us (i think), and probably more that i'm forgetting right now — and the goofy Earthbound-esque tone somewhat works against the supposed moral dissonance you're supposed to feel when you're doing said terrible things. plot events are rather sparse as well; the bulk of the game can be described as going through quirky environments and interacting with quirky people to get the right materials to proceed to the next area.
at the same time, when those plot events do occur, they hit hard. all of these moments are excellently crafted and executed. they really hammer home how the main character is trying his damnedest to do the right thing, but he's just not good enough a person to be able to do that, and the world doesn't want things to work his way either.
there's one battle near the end of the game that astounded me in not only how much it was able to ♥♥♥♥ with the main character, but also me personally. seriously it was unbelievable.
the fact that this game is made entirely in RPG Maker VX Ace by one guy (save some common RGSS3 scripts) is icing on the cake. you can really tell how much effort and care was put into this game. almost every enemy encounter is unique, and almost every human enemy has a unique name. secret passages, items, and party members are in enough quantity to always keep an eye out for them. the game lasts around 10-12 hours, which is already fairly long for an indie game, but there are also tons of events that can be missed or simply cannot be experienced in a single playthrough. the graphics, while a bit lacking in the animation department, exude a crude but whimsical charm. rigging RPG Maker, a game engine which normally uses a top-down perspective, to do side-scrolling that feels completely natural is an accomplishment in itself. the soundtrack is like the twisted result of putting Earthbound and Silent Hill together and it's incredible.
i should probably mention that i'm fairly certain the kickstarter demo for this game stars party members that end up being killed off at the start of the actual game. i ♥♥♥♥ing love it when creators pull that kind of♥♥♥♥♥♥
perhaps the biggest missed opportunity i can think of is how nearly all of the party members have little-to-no stage presence right after they join, which can be a bit disappointing for those who would enjoy rapport between these characters. on the other hand, i guess i can't really imagine how these misfits would talk amongst themselves without it feeling like forced banter, not to mention the amount of conditional branches it would take to figure out if x party member is around at y point in game to say things that might end up looking contrived amidst the main character's personal affairs.
also text looks weird when its put in a window that's too small to fit all of it. i'm not a fan of that but that's also a default RPG Maker problem.
overall, LISA is one of the most memorable and well-directed RPGs i've seen and then played in a long time. i wouldn't hesitate calling it one of my favorites, right up there with Mother 3 and Live A Live. it's strange, funny, and as miserable as can be.

7/10 the game is really good but has some issues that keep it from being great.
There are many small touches that make the world engaging, like overheard conversations, the fact that many of the weapons are cobbled together from spare parts and that you have to wipe the gore off your gasmask if you encounter an enemy up close.
At the same time, the game is marred by frequent clipping issues and graphical glitches. On one memorable occassion a flying "demon" mutant swooped down to carry off an NPC, but they got stuck in one of the car wrecks littering the ground and froze comically mid-air.
A couple of concepts aren't telegraphed very well. There is one point in the game where your progress is blocked by mysteriously inpenetrable spiderwebs and you're supposed to bring out your lighter to burn them away - something the game never tells you and is never encountered again. Another time a key piece of dialogue failed to play properly leaving me without vital information for dealing with a particular type of bullet-sponge enemy - if you maintain eyecontact they leave you alone. These and other frustrating moments had me Alttabbing our of the game to check guides which is never a point in a game's favor!
And finally, the game has a good ending and a bad ending based on tiiiiiny moral choices you make along the way, which is in no way telegraphed! Unlike many games you can steal everything that isn't nailed down (and let's face it, especially on higher difficulties you'll be scrounging for every piece of equipment and ammo that you can get your hands on), BUT the game counts that against you and can get you the bad ending even if you choose "good" in the obvious moral choices like refusing a reward for saving a child.
TL,DR worth it for the experience, but be prepared to Google for solutions when you get stuck.
Buy this if you want to experience a true post-apocalyptic (2 decade after world war 3) world.

This is the kind of game that makes other high cost, high production gaming companies look bad, once all things are considered. An Excellent game with great gameplay and value. It is well worth playing, did you ever play Sid Meier's Pirates? If you liked that, then you are likely to love this game. Highly recommended.
In Caribbean Hunt you aren’t just a Pirate, you are essentially managing your (income and expenses) of your fleet, men and your day to day business while trying to grow your wealth and power through opportunity, you can become a Merchant/Trader/Tycoon, you can become a smuggler, you can provide transport to people for money, you can hunt treasure maps and use the clues to locate the treasure, you can find Ship Wrecks and plunder them or cause them, you can explore the Caribbean and find new ports and take money for keeping their locations secret, do missions for local Mayors, you can play the game in a variety of different ways and they are all very enjoyable with some surprises mixed in.
At first became a Tycoon, found some very useful spacious cargo ships out in the open world for free and repaired them and provided a minimum crew to man them and use them to make me good income very quickly through trade, learning to trade is its own art and figuring out a way to profit from buying and selling a variety of cargo is very satisfying as a way to grow your wealth and open up new opportunities, like learning about more ports with new maps, or simply upgrading your favourite ship and having more working capital to increase the size of your trades.
But later realized how much fun it was to simply setup my favourite ship the “Corvette”, with some custom modifications like black sails, deck, hull, rim, side, mast and boom. Named it the “Phantom” because at top speeds it goes at over 20 knots recorded over 24 knots with higher winds, no other ships in the Caribbean can match the Phantoms speed so he goes pretty much unseen an untouched. It’s equipped with the fearsome mortar bombs to complement its superior speed and manoeuvrability, it has taken out the game’s biggest and deadliest ships from the “War Galleons” to “Frigates” to “man o war”, “2nd & 1st rate” ships, all among the game’s biggest hitters downed by my tier 3 ship. In time my Outfit has captured our own fleet of these high powered ships and we are now in a position where we can attack and takeover ports across the Caribbean and fight over control of the seas from the many Countries, Confederacies that operate in these waters, and Pirates alike.
There is so much depth to this simple game. On the surface it looks very basic, but there was some really good thought put into features and options and how their value would shine and enrich gameplay.
Pros:
-Being a Pirate in the Caribbean has never been this fun and enjoyable, the game has depth, charm, style and beauty all in one package.
-Great learning curve, the first time you lose a ship or two, you begin to rethink your strategy and how you might overcome the problems you face. This level of tactics and strategy was surprising and did not expect it to be so welcome and add so much more depth. Even now with so many hours in the game there are some things to learn and looking forward to discovering the answers to some questions about things.
-Customizations, upgrades, progression and levelling all feel quite smooth and natural and are greatly satisfying when reaching such goals and you unlock a new perk or thing that allows you to expand your Pirates repertoire.
-Real Money Transactions do exist but are not required to completely enjoy the experience this game provides. Considering that most systems like this are a pain and poorly implemented and ♥♥♥♥ people off, in this game it has been easily tolerable.
-Gameplay diversity and experience is just amazing, sail around the Caribbean in style, dodge or engage in intense strategic battles and encounters, sit back and be a pure business person, be an explorer, satisfy a variety of gaming moods all in one game.
Cons:
-While it is great that the game has a fast forward time button to help you sail faster in open waters, it would have been nice to have more speeds available than just the one x5 speed. Perhaps x3, x5, x10 options would have really helped to pick the right speed for the right situation.
-There are some glitches and bugs, but for the most part you can play the game freely with no problems and it is your choice if you want to cheat yourself out of playing the game the way it was intended or not.
-The ai ships in your own fleet in the heat of battle will do damage to your own ship you are controlling and even sink you by accident, this can leave you really mad that you allowed them to participate in the battle and gave them the order to engage in battle on their own. In many cases you find yourself having to avoid their line of fire as much as the enemies in full scaled naval battles.
-It would be nice if there was a smart trigger to shooting cannons so that they didn’t waste your ammo shooting when clearly there is zero chance that they will hit anything given their position on the ship in relation to the target. It is a minor thing, but it does cause an unnecessary waste of cannon balls that cost valuable gold.
-The Restart button, can be exploited to cheat yourself out of consequences and an authentic and true experience in the learning process. If you want the full experience as a new player I suggest you resist the temptation to use this button, however it is optional.
-lack of multiple save game files really sucks
Bottom line
Cannot recommend this game enough, especially to fans of games like Sid Meier's pirates, pretty sure you will love this game if you liked that game. I am not even the biggest fan of Pirates and Sailing ships theme, but the gameplay in this game is too good, that you get hooked on it regardless of your interest in that theme. And that is a big deal, because most games I like have to have a theme that I enjoy, so for a game to bypass that prejudgement, it is certainly a big deal. It is the sort of game that turns you into a fan of that Pirate theme since the gameplay feels so authentic to what it might be like to run a Pirate/Trading outfit.

According to Steam, I played The Pirate: Caribbean Hunt for 19 hours. I was attracted by the "free too play" option, and hoped it would be a good casual game I could play in downtime, with a multiplayer benefit. The game has great potential, but its business model of nickel-and-diming players all along the way just turns me way off.
The graphics are pretty, good atmosphere, and the game is easy to jump into. I followed the plan, built upo my little base, gained some good skills, and did a fairly good job, mostly trading, and picking on the hapless Danes. Unfortunately, after about ten hours, I began to be pestered incessantly by the Pirate Confederation, who continually plagued me, with superior forces, forcing me to use hit-and-run sail attacks, followed by time-sucking fleeing tactics, staying ahead of their ships during long haul escapes, where I stayed half-a-knot better speed than my pursuers.
I felt like I had no choice, but I actually did: I could have dragged out my credit card, and for about $35, equipped my pirate with the finest base, ships, and superman type skills, to rise through the ranks, defeating anything in my way, using my personal financial might to help my pirate win, even right in the heat of battle! Except of course, other players who spent a little more money than me.
It's a version of Deus Ex Machina, except here, it's Deus Ex Mastercard. And that's just not fun.

I started playing this game a couple of years ago, and then stopped very abruptly.  I didn't walk away from it because it was a bad game; rather, it got under my skin for some reason.  I'm just a bit of a wuss when it comes to creepy noises and tense atmosphere.  When the Redux was released, I resolved to finally grow a proverbial pair and finish the game.  In doing so, I learned two things:
1.  The game doesn't have as much replay value as I'd hoped.  Once you know how the individual stories play out, there's not very much other than visual appeal (and that sense that something is lurking in the shadows).
2.  Two years changes nothing.  I'm still a wuss.
All that aside, the game is still enjoyable.  I applaud its ability to unnerve me.  It is a gorgeous game with a very fitting soundtrack.  As a huge fan of early weird fiction, I appreciate its roots in the works of Lovecraft and Bierce, among others.  The "stories" you find lying around, penned by young Mr. Carter himself, are by far the most interesting part of the game.  The investigative bits are entertaining but don't feel very, well, investigative.  Sort of you're just hoping to stumble upon A) huge obvious bloodstains, or B) random floating text.  Watching the scenes unfold is worth it, though.  Some of it gets a little brutal.  I was, however, not too crazy about the spoken dialogue or the voice acting, but that might just be me.  It wasn't damaging to the overall atmosphere and experience.  Again, I was playing the Redux this time through and had no issues with the way the game ran, and the autosaves appeared ample enough.  Overall, TVoEC is a good gameplay experience if you're into exploration (and since there isn't always a clear path to follow, there is a fair amount) and you feel like being extremely nervous for no apparent reason. Ahhh The Vanishing of Ethan Carter. A “narrative experience that does not hold your hand”. I agree with that sentiment, it does NOT hold your hand, because if it did there would be under two hours of “narrative experience”. I think of this title as an interactive Sixth Sense. There’s a lot of intrigue and I didn’t really understand what was going on until midway through it. Even now I still don’t fully understand what happened, and I believe that was by design. This game requires a particular taste, but for those looking for a unique suspense/thriller experience with hints of crime solving I think you would dig this game.
I’ve played through both the original and the Redux. In my experience, the Redux ran smoother. It also looked better overall, although to the originals credit it still looked amazing if you have a rig capable of cranking up the settings to high. I’d recommend the Redux if you can get a key, but it has been delisted off steam at the time of this review. The original is more than fine if you just want to play though so I’d recommend it regardless.
One gripe I had was there was a lot of senseless running around. I guess it helps build immersion, but when your game is a narrative experience that “doesn’t hold your hand” and you’re trying to refrain from using online guides, but now you must travel half way across the map to solve something you overlooked. Let’s just say that was frustrating. *Spoiler Thankfully they do introduce a quick travel mechanic at the end of the game for cleanup.
Overall the game was quite immersive, from the lush visuals to the amazing soundtrack. I give it a “Recommended” rating for sure. At the time of this review it’s listed at $19.99 on steam. I don’t recall how I got it, but I know I didn’t pay that much. I’d say $10 is a fair price for the entertainment I received, I don’t know if I’d pay $19.99 for it personally. Add it to your Wishlist and wait for a sale, and try to get the Redux if possible.

First person Spider-Man!
I normally have a lot harder time getting into the headspace of a fantasy game than a scifi game, and I'm sure there's a lot of players out there who fall on either side of that fence as far as preferences go.  I snapped it up first sale after it was on my wishlist from just a couple clips of gameplay, not knowing there was a little bit of fantastical nature to the game.  I happened upon A Story About My Uncle after playing Coffee Stain Studios' Goat Simulator and was curious about what else was in their catalog.  Turns out they had published this game for Gone North Games, and now I'm in love with both of these developers.
The majority of the fantasy elements in the story are/are not explained away by the mysteriousness of the world you visit.  What's happened in this land might just be scientific, and your method of travel and equipment are certainly scientific in nature.  So what Gone North Games have done here is successfully blur the lines between a scifi and fantasy aesthetic without making it look like a Thor movie, and I applaud them for that.  This is all made even more enjoyable by just how pretty this game looks on high graphical settings.
For the gameplay side of things, I have not felt such fluid progress in a game since the early levels of Portal or first few tracks of Audiosurf I played.  There is a learning curve as your suit grants and removes abilities throughout the campaign, but I can only think of one actual instance where I got stuck and couldn't figure out what I needed to do immediately.  Even still, there is a difficulty to the game, in that you're running and grappling from platform to platform in the sky like Spider-man, except with a energy lasso instead.  Later in the game there are clear paths for how you should traverse the level, but in several spots there were less obvious paths I was able to successfully traverse, and I appreciate the non-linearity of it all.  ASAMU is not a first person puzzle game or "walking simulator", it is a game highly geared around movement and staying mobile.  The thrill of flying through the level and the close calls of almost missing the timing on some jumps could sell the game alone for some.  The only downside is the length (~3 hours), though I feel the game puts you through its paces just fine before you reach the end.  If you're looking for a fresh experience of flying around like a web slinger be sure to give this a look.

Got this for around 4 euros. I would say for that price, it is okay.
Don't know if I would regret buying this for more, since it only is around 4 hours and I would say that I really spend my time on this game (or messed up parts multiple times ^^).
Graphic is not over the top of course, but still beautiful for such a 'small' game, with an incredible view of field and some epic environments, altough nothing isn't really gonna blow your mind. The graphic really lives from its beautiful lightning, and it has some great details that often make  you want to jump on some more of those floating islands and see what nice little building they made there. Unfortunately, there are also many island that just look the same. Character design is nice as well, but besides the two main characters, they mostly jsut sit somewhere and do noting and react to nothing.
Performance was excellent the entire time, never dropped below of 60 fps for me.
The mechanics are very easy to learn and make this game a lot of fun. You will soon feel like a boss flying through the air and with time goes by, there even will be more useful and unique additional ones.
In the levels, it is not always excactly clear where you have to go, but you mostly find out easely. This could be intentionally, since you can use different  movement methods for most of the level parts which will slightly vary your ways.  However, even when you have quit some freedom on what of the devices you want to use, there is basically always only one path, since you mostly just jump on different rocks or islands. Nonetheless, the level design is great and this way you never wonder for too long where you have to go.
The story is nice and simple, but again, nothing that will flash you away. The game knows how to set up a very friendly atmospehre in the villages and even has quiet a  few parts where some horror feeling comes up. But the villagers are quiet static as I have said before, and also in the spookier parts, you never really get soaked into these emotions. I what I want to say is that the story and atmosphere is nice and with some cool details, but overall, it just does not have much depth.
E.g. you spend the whole game searching for your uncle and don't know what the hell happened to him. But that alreay is all the drama in this game and spoiler alert, at the end he never wasn't in any real trouble. Not that this is such a big deal, but this game could have so much more great tension with just a little bit more dramatic story. There was one single part in the whole game, where you had to get past some scary worm monster thing wihtout it seeing you. But when you made it, that basically is all the game had to offer for a conflict or 'boss fight' as well.
Nice graphics, sweet story and good level desgin. But all in all, the atmosphere/ the story could have been so much better and the game is quiet short. After all, the great movement mechanics are what make this game really fun for some hours.
P.S.: Costum maps could significantly lengthen the hours of fun.

Vampire the Masquerade: Bloodlines Is a longtime RPG favorite that i dutifully dust off and boot up every few years. To this day, I LOVE VTM:B and it remains in my top five RPGs i've ever played, and i've played a LOT of RPGs.
It's a game that was anticipated by fans of the White Wolf pen and paper RPG universe as well as fans of its predecessor, Vampire the Masquerade: Redemption. The game was ahead of its time in many ways when it released back in '04 (actually beating Half-Life 2 to market, making it the 1st game released using the Source engine), but it also released in a fairly unpolished state, had janky first-person shooting mechanics/animations, and had at least one gamebreaking quest bug (Society of Leopold, anyone?) among other problems.
Developer Troika Games managed to patch the major issues out before sadly dissolving shortly after launch, but some things still remained unpolished (the aforementioned off-feeling first-person gunplay being one of them). Fortunately though, even with these issues, the game was still an engaging, atmospheric and fun enough experience to inspire the community to step in and fix up what was left, and even unlock some things that Troika had coded into the game but disabled prior to release. It's definitely stable and playable in its official 1.2 patch state, but i personally would recommend seeking out and applying the latest unofficial fan patch. It has IIRC an option to only apply bugfixes and tweaks without changing the core vanilla gameplay, or choose to apply the fixes along with some gameplay alterations, rebalances and additions. Either way, it's all good. Numerous bloodlines for the player to choose from, each with their own abilities/weaknesses, and several different possible endings depending on the choices you make give VTM:B great replay value. I've owned this game since it came out (This was the 2nd game i ever bought on Steam way back when) and i've still never managed to play through it with every available bloodline.
Just so this review doesn't sound like a total gushing puff piece, i'll say that the graphics are dated and the interface and menus are probably going to seem clunky to those weaned on more modern games.
To sum up, i'll say this: If you love RPGs with all your heart, or even if you just love games with engrossing storylines and dark atmosphere, you should have already long since played Vampire The Masquerade: Bloodlines. Seriously, you're like 11 years late to the party. Get it. Play it. Love it.

Video games have evolved over 30 years, and YHtWtG is an excellent demonstration of this. This game could have been released in 1990 without any alterations, and perfectly blend with other games of that era.
But aside from that (questionable) achievement, the game has little to offer. It has no new mechanics, no interesting features, no exciting gameplay, not even story or graphics or any other means of being special. It's just the experience of old-fashioned maze-like platformers with no map, but rage-inducing jumping sequences that have to be done over and over again (and then you find out that you have to complete that sequence several times more later). Thankfully the game has a lot of checkpoints, so you don't have to restart from the very beginning every time (unless you chose the YOLO mode).
Strangely I don't even feel true nostalgia from playing this game. I'd call this feeling 'fake nostalgia': turns out it's not CGA graphics or story-deprived convoluted platformers I miss, but the feeling of discovery and novelty from playing such games in my youth. This game fails to deliver any of it.
YHtWtG could be a great game in 1990, but today it just doesn't make any sense.

Still early stage of using Articy draft 3 but been using v2 for a while but here's my review.
There are two types of people who may be interested in this, v1/v2 people and new to the program, so I'll speak to both parties.
New users
Articy draft is one of the best programs for writers, designers and developers. It DOES NOT make games but its designed to hold all the information on the narrative of a game or story/novel. If you need a platform to not only write a story but to also formulate plotline and create branching conversations, while keeping track of who is where doing whatever, then this is an excellent resource.
I mostly use it for writing (novel and short stories) and the ability to organize my characters and there traits as well as keep track of everything they have said is a god send. Creating my own templates for my characters makes remembering what a person looks and acts like a Breese. These are just a few of the parts I use and it has too many for a review here.
If you want/are designing a game or story that has a number of characters and plot points then this can easily be a program you will find indispensable. So for all the writers and developers out there I highly recommend.
V1/V2 users
You know how good the program is already so I don't need to sell you there. This is about new features. It looks the same and works the same. The differences between v2 and v3 are fairly small but very useful. Personally I use the documents section a lot and the added features there help a lot. If you use unity game engine though then upgrading to v3 is a very good idea the export feature I would imagine will save a lot of time and effort. My recommendation is that if you are fairly happy with v2 and the new features are not something that shouts "I have to have this" then you may be happy sticking with v2 for a while longer. However if your still using v1 then this is defiantly a recommended upgrade. The number of upgraded and better features makes the expense very much worth it.

Metro 2033 is a very good looking, quite atmospheric corridor shooter with an interesting setting and an OK story.
The game is set in the subways of Moscow some time after the third world war, where people struggle to survive in colonies (subway stations) besieged by mutants and rebels alike.
You are one of these people, who through a series of events is forced to find your way through the metro network in order to deliver some important information on the Dark Ones.
Gameplay in this game is top notch, feeling both responsive and fluid. In one minute, you might find yourself sneaking through the base of a group of nazis with a silenced revolver, while in another, you're gunning down hordes of mutants outside a colony with an machineshotgun; both feeling equally satisfying.
The linux port is... complicated.
On the one hand, it runs great (as long as you stay far away from SSAA) and looks great (it's probably the best looking fps I've played on linux).
On the other, the configuration required to make it playable is atrocious. Expect to have to dive into config files, manually edit them and make them read-only so the game doesn't overwrite your changes. Especially if you have a multi-monitor setup, you're gonna have a bad time.
Once it's working, however, it's great, even on open source (radeonsi) drivers.
Overall recommended.

It's hard to come up with the words to appropriately outline my feelings for this game.
The longer you play video games, the less common it becomes to find a gaming experience that is...transcendant.
There is so much goofy uniqueness to this game that you are constantly blindsided by the horrendous sadism of its characters, the beyond bleak plot, the genuinely disturbing imagery and body horror...
This game disturbed me while I was laughing. And most importantly, I have found myself -never- satisfied with the information I have. There is a lot to discover in terms of the history of this world, and once you have all there is, you will want more. You will likely have some grim ideas about what those answers are, but there will be an insatiable hunger for that knowledge, all the same.
I find I have more fondness in my heart for LISA than I do for much of the nostalgic titles from my childhood, which is an incredible task.
If you want to feel something. REALLY feel something - play this game. Just be aware it is not for the faint of heart. It's going to disturb, depress, and distress the living hell out of you. And it's worth every minute.
Every second spent reading reviews is a second you could be playing LISA. It's really that simple.

I received this game as a gift, but I don't think that should detract from my opinion of it.
First off, I wanted to like this game, I really did.  The premise of the game appealed to me.  It seemed like it should be fun.
Wrong.
The graphics look great (well, in most areas, in the cave areas it's dark as f*** so it's like playing Doom 3 with the monitor off).  The other characters however, looked weird and half-baked. Not that you get to interact with them in any way.  You just pass by them without even registering their attention.  I felt as if I was a ghost travelling through their villages.  All you get in the way of interaction are a few cutscenes at a few places throughout the game.
This could be a blessing though, because the voice acting sounds as if they grabbed people off the street and were only allowed one take while trying to read cue cards from across the room.  Okay, I get the developers are from Sweden, so English might not be their first language, but seriously, try harder next time).
And who tagged this game as story-rich?  It's trite and the ending sucks.
The ambient music is soothing, which is good because you'll need something to calm you down given how many times you'll die.  Oh, that's right.  You will die.  A lot.  And then some more.  I can't tell you how many times I fell to my death.
It doesn't help that the terrain everywhere tries its best to defeat your every attempt at advancement.  Even when jumping straight up to try to get at a higher platform I have been sent flying off sideways because I hit the lip at the edge above, deflecting me to my death.  Jumps I made successfully one time I miss completely because I under or overshoot, even though I did exactly the same thing as before, but I have to keep redoing over and over because the checkpoints are painfully far apart in most places.
Oh yes, checkpoints.  The artificial difficulty enhancer tool that devs throw in to slow you down in order to cover up for the fact their game is so short.  Not being able to save the game anywhere on a PC is inexcusable and lazy.  Sorry devs, if I wanted checkpoints I'd play it on a console.
And I don't mind short games either, if the quality is good.
I've read other reviews saying they only took 3 or 4 hours to finish the game.  Well holy ****, they must be better players than I am!  Steam says I played for a total of 7 hours, and I only did the one playthrough (that's about all I could take).  Honestly it felt like twice that.  If this game was any longer I doubt I'd have the patience to finish it.
All in all, I gave this game a negative review because the frustration involved in getting through the game was just too much.  Others who gave positive reivews have compared this game to Portal, but I will counter with the argument that Portal was incredibly well-balanced, both in game mechanics and difficulty.  Movement in Portal always 'felt' the same.  I never got deflected to my death by seemingly wonky physics or missed a jump because the destination platform was only 2 square feet.  Oh, and there was a quick-save key in Portal too.
At the end of the day, all this frustration just makes this game not FUN. And that's really what makes a game good or bad, isn't it?
Final verdict:  Only for twitch hardcore platformers.  I guess i do not count as one.
On the plus side, never have I seen flailing hands and fatal death plunge speed lines rendered so beautifully.
5/10 Would not flail again.

Gameplay  4.5/5
The  game has an 'intended' solution/path, but you can sometimes create your own with your different abilities (they're just that versatile) without any disadvantage. The quick-restart is a great feature, especially because sometimes you know you'll die 5 to 20 second before respawning (especially mid-game). Late-game is somewhat frustrating, because it needs more precision than your abilities give you, but I played it with a controller so KB+M players might disagree.
Only loading times I saw was loading a game, and transition between levels (maybe 4-5 time). They're really short too (3-4 seconds max). I encountered no gameplay or critical bugs during my playthrough, but YMMV.
Graphics 3/5
Overall, it's good. They do a good job of showing you how alien this world is. Texture quality's not that great but it isn't bad either, and there's no incoherence. Except the NPC.
Oh god, the NPC design/animation is a throwback to mid PS2-era games. Thanksfully, story-important NPC are better developped.
There's a little bug where the camera can clip into the environment when you stand in corners but I'd rather have that     than a blocked camera.
Music 3/5
Fits the game, but there's no 'memorable' track.
Overall 4/5

Before purchasing this game I was apprehensive due to some reviewers claiming that it did not work on modern systems, however I thought I would give it a go after picking it up cheap in a sale. Initially, the game would not even work for me without downloading and installing the unofficial patch, but the process was painless. I was not expecting much from an old, bug-riddled game; instead what I discovered was a rich, atmospheric and immersive world with excellently realised characters and amazing voice acting which puts a lot of modern games to shame. The game also revels in its adult themes of sex, drugs and death without being overly gratuitous.
The story regarding the development of this game is a sad one. The game was rushed out in an unfinished state to compete with the likes of Half Life 2, Halo 2 and Metal Gear Solid 3. The game initially sold only 72,000 copies and marked the end of the developer ‘Troika’. However, over the last 10 years, fans of the game and some talented modders have fixed a lot of the bugs that were present in the initial release, and even restored deleted content. That said, the game is far from being bug-free, but some of them are so hilarious that I almost enjoy them, it certainly doesn’t detract from the overall enjoyment I’m having with this game. I have yet to come across a game-breaking bug.

In regards to gameplay, Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines is very similar to the Deus Ex games, except with Vampires. The play style is varied and is really up to the player how they develop their character. You can choose to level your character up in stealth based skills such as lock picking, hacking, and sneaking, or pure combat based skills for those where subtlety is not an option.  You navigate through 4 hub levels (Santa Monica, Downtown LA, Hollywood, and Chinatown) all of which have many optional side quests.

The game offers a lot of replayability, as there are a wide variety of clans (classes) to play, all of which are quite different to handle and can drastically alter the way you play the game. Although the game itself is rather linear there are multiple ways of completing certain quests, some much more difficult than others. You can also increase stats such as ‘Intimidation’, ‘Persuasion’ and ‘Seduction’ which offer the player some really interesting branching dialogue options.

Well, where do I begin, telling you about this gem? I suppose I'll start with what it is.
Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines is an action-RPG based on the tabletop game of the same name. Gamplay-wise, it plays similarly to the original Deus Ex, leaving multiple options to accomplish your objectives. You could go for the good-old fashioned direct assault, use stealth, or alternatively talk your way out of situations. It's really up to you.
There are numerous vampire clans to choose from, all with their own unique focus. Brujahs and Gangrels focus more on combat, whereas the Tremere make use of powerful blood magic, and the Toreador and Ventrue manipulate their way towards their objectives. There are, however, two more, special clans. The Nosferatu are mutated horribly by their vampiric curse, and must skulk around the sewers and alleys lest they be seen. Needless to say, they're good at stealth. And last, but certainly not least, are the Malkavians. These guys are completely insane, which is reflected in game by your bizarre dialogue choices, hallucinations and voices in your head. They do have some nice powers, though, such as invisibilty and Dementation, which is useful for both dialogue and enemies. You'll also be treated quite differently based on your clan, leaving a lot of replay value.
Really, though, it's the story and atmosphere which make this game truly special. Walking through the streets of a depiction of LA apparently going through it's Goth phase. The hubworlds are small in size but full of detail, and you always feel like you're doing something different. From tracking down and killing a cabal of blood disease-spreading vampires, to exploring a haunted house, to getting your own ghoul (basically someone who has recieved vampire blood and gets some basic vampire abilities from it, but not the whole set), it always feels like you're doing something unique. It feels good to drink blood, and the political intrigue of the secret vampire society you're involved in is extremely engrossing, and all the characters have different personalities, and a good few are quite memorable. The story moves at a good pace, although the story path to a seemingly simple objective often becomes quite convoluted.
Sadly. this game is not without its flaws. First off the bat, there's the bugs and poor optimisation. This game was Christmas rushed (which, as we all know, always ends well), and the game was in an extremely buggy state upon launch, and Troika were unable to fix it on account of going bust shortly after. The game will ouright refuse to work on some modern systems without an unofficial patch, and may be almost unplayable. Even with the patch installed, you will see bugs often. Most won't affect gameplay, but will pull you out of that fantastic atmosphere Troika worked so hard to make. After a certain point close to the end of the game, due to it being rushed out the door, the game forces you into a repetetive series of combat arenas, with no alternative paths. So, if you've not been putting points into combat skills, you're screwed. The final boss (oh, and the boss fights aren't very good throughout the game) is impossible to kill without a gun, when guns are next to useless for a good part of the game. Oh, and even if you have gone the combat route, the game still has a massive unfair difficulty spike near the end. The combat itself is bearable, but very repetetive, and essentially consists of wailing on attack and spamming your most powerful clan Disciplines.
Still, overall, VtM-B is easily one of the best RPGs ever made, and you owe to yourself to get it. Accept the Embrace and find your place in the world of the Kindred...

Metro 2033 is a very good looking, quite atmospheric corridor shooter with an interesting setting and an OK story.
The game is set in the subways of Moscow some time after the third world war, where people struggle to survive in colonies (subway stations) besieged by mutants and rebels alike.
You are one of these people, who through a series of events is forced to find your way through the metro network in order to deliver some important information on the Dark Ones.
Gameplay in this game is top notch, feeling both responsive and fluid. In one minute, you might find yourself sneaking through the base of a group of nazis with a silenced revolver, while in another, you're gunning down hordes of mutants outside a colony with an machineshotgun; both feeling equally satisfying.
The linux port is... complicated.
On the one hand, it runs great (as long as you stay far away from SSAA) and looks great (it's probably the best looking fps I've played on linux).
On the other, the configuration required to make it playable is atrocious. Expect to have to dive into config files, manually edit them and make them read-only so the game doesn't overwrite your changes. Especially if you have a multi-monitor setup, you're gonna have a bad time.
Once it's working, however, it's great, even on open source (radeonsi) drivers.
Overall recommended.

After the first 1,000 or so hours, I realized that I kind of hate it.
Now let me say up front that if you're not looking for a game to take super seriously, you'll probably love it. The main things that ultimately turned me away from Civ 5 were its numerous bugs, game design flaws, etc, but the less deeply you get into the game the less these things are going to bother you.
But, nonetheless, after several years of this game being out, there are still multiple mildly common bugs which can render saved games effectively impossible to continue playing. And when each game generally takes a total of 2 to 20 hours to complete, that can be a lot of time, effort, and emotion down the drain whenever that happens.
And then there's the balance issues, and BOY are there some balance issues. It's a widely known and accepted fact that some randomly dealt starting locations are quite simply better than others - you have "good starts" and you have "bad starts". This, however, is at least kind of okay since the game becomes kind of like poker and you can exploit the other players - AIs or otherwise - in order to pit top dogs against each other or make alliances of convenience with other underdogs.
A more severe balance issue, however, is the unviability of a number of tech and social policy paths. The game presents you with slews of options for how to play it, yet in practice a handful of these are objectively superior to all the other "options" in most if not all situations, and so you either need to play the game very casually with friends or on lower difficulty levels, OR just accept that how you must play the game is pre-dictated by this poor game balance. What this leads to is playing the exact same gameplay styles over and over again, in every single game, and with the games being as long as they are this becomes stale quite fast.
Fortunately, most of these issues can be fixed with mods - at least, up to a point. You see, while Civ 5 has a great modding community that has taken it upon themselves to fix the slews of issues that Firaxis couldn't be bothered to even after several years of game sales, there's this issue in which you can only run one DLL mod at a time without your game crashing. And DLL mods are the ones that do all the really big, cool, and important things, like AI improvements, major gameplay changes/fixes, etc. What this means is that even in the wonderful world of modding, you simply can't have your cake and eat it too.
But it gets worse, because even non-DLL mods have a tendency to be incompatible with each other at times, and not always in immediately apparent ways. Most of the last several hundred hours of my "gameplay" hours actually consisted of me waiting a minute for my game to load, waiting 2+ minutes for my mods to load, spending a few minutes configuring a game, and then realizing that my assortment of virtual mod candy has incompatible flavors that cause the game to crash on startup. I would then spend the next few hours going through the same several minute process over and over again just trying to figure out which mod(s) I needed to make the painstaking decision to remove from my list to get my game to work. Other times the game would work fine, but when I reloaded the save the textures would break.
Bottom line, you can't load up enough mods to fix Civ 5's issues without creating NEW issues that range from yucky to unplayable in nature.
In conclusion, Civ 5 is at its core a good game which has given me several hundred hours of enjoyment and several hundred more hours of pain and frustration. I'd recommend it to anyone looking to enjoy a nice casual adventure in an empire-buliding and world-conquering experience, but even then only with a word of caution. And to everyone else - steer clear, avoid it like the plague.

Great game for 2004. Good graphics, plot, dialogue, and gameplay, despite some tuning issues. If you want to play the game multiple times, start with Toreador, the sort of jack of all trades, or at least don't start with Malkavian, because their dialogue best saved for later. Try to stick with 5-7 skills, any more and they will all start to suck. Stealth is kind of useless when you can just 3 shot people instead. Guns suck early game and you don't really get a lot of ammo until the last few levels. Also, do the entire tutorial, I skipped it and had to beat the game without a lockpick. It's free experience and ammo too. Research is arguably the best skill because you can use it to upgrade other skills if you can be bothered to find skill books.
It's a bit hard to find a guide for builds, so here are my thoughts:
Combat:
Melee > Ranged > Unarmed
Defense is almost necessary
Covert:
Research > Hacking > Lockpicking > Sneaking > Inspection
Mental:
Persuasion > Seduction > Intimidation > Haggle
Discipline:
Thaumaturgy (3 or 4) > Fortitude > Protean > Potence > Celerity > Animalism > Dementation > Presence > Obfuscate > Dominate > Auspex
Also, download the unofficial patch and any mods you want. The game's production was cancelled in beta so it was never really finished, the patch tunes it up a bit.

I'll admit this game gets mahjong itself right (as far as I've seen), but everything else has a lot of problems.
-First off, controls. The puzzles themselves are done with the mouse, and you can work through level selection using only the mouse, but as far as I can tell both neither pausing during a puzzle nor exiting the game from the main menu can be done using the mouse and instead require the ESC key. This isn't impossible for people to figure out, but especially for a game like this with a large casual audience it could stand to be more straightforward by adding clickable buttons for pausing and exiting.
-Secondly there's the timer, or rather the focus on score. Having this is fine, but I feel like there should at least be an option to hide the timer. Having it constantly counting down and flickering in the corner is really distracting, and a lot of people playing this game aren't going to care about getting 3 stars or any stars on a given stage. I feel like there should either be a setting to disable/hide the timer, or else a separate mode where the same puzzles are available but score isn't kept at all.
-Thirdly, I had a weird experience in one level that went completely unexplained by the game. In world 1 level 80 I was approaching the end of the puzzle when suddenly the puzzle disappeared and was replaced by two columns of 4-5 tiles each (they were the same number, but I don't remember which one). I matched these tiles and then the puzzles ended. I've never seen this happen in Mahjong before, and the tutorial didn't say anything about it. If this is intentional behavior then it should probably be explained in the tutorial to stop people from being caught by surprise, and if it's unintentional then it should be fixed.
Finally, the 3D mahjong controls. I think the 3D puzzles are actually super neat, I've never seen them in any other game. Unfortunately the controls are a problem. The tutorial says to click and drag the mouse to rotate the puzzle, and I don't think it's unreasonable to expect the puzzle to follow the mouse movement. Instead, clicking and dragging just sets a direction and a speed, such that if you stop dragging the puzzle will just keep spinning wildly until you release the mouse button. This feels counterintuitive to me, and makes it rather difficult to preform precise rotations.
If these issues were fixed it would be a decent game that I could recommend people to buy. Until then, I would rather suggest people avoid it.

Mahjong Deluxe 3 is a challenge of memory, attention to detail and the ability to differentiate depth perception.  I initially played the basic easy puzzles and found that I’m not quite as quick as required to be a three star winner.  I decided to take on the challenging puzzles and this is when the game took on a different light.  I appreciate a challenge and found these puzzles required time and patience.  My favorite thing with the challenging puzzles occurred when you reached a point of stalemate.  The game shimmers and rearranges the tiles to allow you to find the remaining matching pairs.  This is a great addition and allows for continued game play and limits frustration. The graphics for the tiles are intricate, bright and eye catching, the backgrounds  lend atmosphere to the game play and take you on a journey.  I quite enjoyed the small cute noises made when each tile is selected and the joyous noises made when a selection was correct.  These also differed depending on the genre of tile which is a sweet little touch.  I would recommend this game when you want to activate and challenge your mind and memory potential.

is built around a simple mechanic: each button on your controller maps to a different part of Sam's body (right arm, left arm, right leg, left leg) or bodily function (breathe in, breathe out, blink), and you must guide him through a number of simple tasks by following on-screen prompts.  In co-op, it's more complicated: half of Sam's body is assigned to each player, and even simple tasks like walking require close coordination to pull off.
The game itself is quite funny -- its take on the personification of Death particularly so -- but a lot of the laugh-out-loud moments in the early levels stem from mistimed button presses and lack of familiarity with the controls.  Such failures become less funny and more frustrating as the game progresses, but never enough so that we wanted to stop playing.
's controller support is great, and worthy of an honourable mention.  My wife and I played with one Steam controller and one PS4 controller, and the game was smart enough to show the correct button prompts from different controllers for different players.  This small touch was very much appreciated, and something that I wish more developers took the time to do properly.

TL:DR : This game understands you. (8.75/10)
The graphics aren't the best, but they're as good as they need to be; the soundtrack and effects are pleasant but not particularly obtrusive or overwhelming. The plot itself is as interesting as it needs to be, with dialogue amusing enough to read- but all of it can be readily skipped past or ignored as one pleases.
In terms of gameplay, this is a solid tower defense/tactical RPG. LUL manages to skillfully blend the two, producing a well thought out, fairly original tower defense where one identifies with, develops, and equips one's 'towers' much as one would one's characters in games like FF Tactics or Bahamut's Lagoon. What is particularly striking about this game however, is not the gameplay itself- it's present in the gameplay, to be sure; but what really marks this game as interesting is the attention to detail the studio has given to ALL of the aspects. The graphics aren't the best, but they're every bit as good as they need to be. The plot and dialoge are easily skipped because this is a casual game, where you are not expected to care in the slightest, and yet they are still amusing and substantial enough for if you do happen to care for some reason.
If you need solid proof that LUL clearly understands you, the gamer, just look at the attention they pay to the control scheme. You can play this game without a mouse. Easily. The mouse can help now and then, but these people have dialed in the control system of their game to such an extent that a skilled player could possibly even do better without a mouse than with one, and all the keys are fully mappable, in case their super-intuitive control scheme isn't super-intuitive enough.
To be fair, I've noticed a glitch or two, but they always seem to get corrected fast enough that you would miss them if you blinked at the right moment.
Overall, always good to see this level of attention being given at all levels of development. 8.75/10

Despite this being a slightly controversial view by proportion of positive reviews recieved at the time of writing, I genuinely did not end up enjoying this game.
At the start, the easy-to-use controls mixed with nice graphics and a interesting, supernatural take on murder solving was quite intriguing. However, after my second sitting at the game (and finding via achievements I was over three quarters of the way though it after a total of 2.5 hours) my opinion was quite different, and was only reinforced by the remainder of the game.
I never felt scared or afraid to any significant degree myself so the game failed at any horror aspect it might have been going for. I never had any strong feelings, good or bad, for any of the characters. And most importantly, I never really understood the story. I read every note, listened to every conversation, but never understood why any of this stuff happened. The whole story reveloves around this sleeper thing that you never even find out what it is. All these people being murdered because it's "driving them mad" and they "feel they need to stop Ethan" to make things right but it never got explained. All of the side events that seemed to have little relevance to the rest of the game. Yes you get a small bit of resolution on them at the end that they're a child's stories but that doesn't validate their relevance or inclusion in the game.
Maybe I missed something somewhere along the way and so couldn't piece together the story from there and it all lost meaning, I don't know. But that's as much the game's responsibility as mine, and if I missed it because the game became uninteresting before whenever these things happened, that's the games fault. I can usually get emotional over games and TV etc. quite easily so I don't think it's just me being thick-skinned that stopped me from being engaged with any of the characters.
This game is certainly not worth £15 for three to four hours of lacklustre and, by the end, repetitive gameplay.
FYI I played the Redux version so I don't even have save issues to complain about either but no-one will anymore so thats ok.
ALSO It may say I have only played 0.2hrs of this game this is true, for the fact that the Redux version is counted as a separate game by Steam. You will see many reviews, both positive and negative, of this game have very small recorded game time for this reason.

A lot better than people give it credit for.
Saints Row 1: fun GTA rip off.
Saints Row 2: even better GTA rip off that had a lot going for it
Saints Row The Third: went too whacky while keeping the same basic formula. Not a good mix.
Saints Row IV: dials up the whackiness even more but ditches the old formula. Good combination.
I'll be the first to admit I didn't care for the third Saints Row game because it felt too whacky and I was really surprised to find I still adored Saints Row IV. I later realised my problem wasn't with the tone but the combination of tone and gameplay. Saints Row The Third gave you everything from the start so you had nothing to work towards and this was because whackiness was still tied to the GTA formula which in turn meant giving the player overpowered weapons and planes at the very start. You can't get whackier than that without changing formula and as a result you have nothing to work towards.
Saints Row 4 changes this by turning the game from GTA to a weird mix of GTA and more importantly InFamous or Prototype. That means we can be whacky from the very start yet still have a sense of progression which keeps the game from getting stale. You are now super powered and fighting aliens which sounds bad on paper (I ignored this game for years) but in practice it results in a really fun experience. This is by no means the deepest game ever but if you let yourself get sucked into it you'll have little to complain about.
The campaign is amazing! However after you've completed all side activities, it just gets boring. If you're bored and got nothing to do, get this game!

Overall: The content on offer isn't exactly polished, but on the basis that it works and it's free I'd say it passes the mark needed for a recommendation, or at least a try on your part.
Pros:
Quite a lot of vessels to choose from, ranging from basically a fishing boat with a butt cannon to the well-known man-o-wars and first-rates.
Larger vessels feel like a heavy behemoth, with weight behind their turning. Conversely, smaller ones are sufficiently agile that good use of wind and sails allow experienced players to overcome better-armed AI opponents (but then again, of course you are going to captain a first-rate, so who cares).
You can ram a vessel to death (with a ship upgrade). Ramming is always fun.
Cons
Early-game finance is quite a mess. Trading feels unviable in early game without the associated perks and reputation bonuses (at least I cannot make it work). On the other hand, picking the corsair perk is an absolute must (allows players to board), as boarding allows you to capture a vessel (and its cargo) intact, thus more loot, while expending less in repairs and ammo refill.
Mission rewards are unbalanced. Escort missions' reward is only based on the size of the escort, not the distance needed to travel, making them a waste of time. On the other hand, smuggling missions are hopelessly broken, offering a massive reward for little to no effort involved.
Mission failure states are far too strict. A passenger mission to a neignbouring port not allowing middle stops is understandable, but the same cannot be said about the same mission with a destination halfway across the bloody map, thematically or otherwise. The same problem exists in siege missions, where it makes no sense that players are not allowed to stop by a port nearby the target for resupplies. The fact that this hidden failure state is not explicitly stated is quite aggravating.
Gathering blueprints from shipwrecks is not a very well thought out mechanic. For the time needed to complete an entire blueprint the player could capture said vessel thrice over in the open world. It's really more of a novelty than a viable option.
The UI isn't the most user-friendly, requiring quite some time to get used to. Somewhat related is the controls for the treasure hunts. If there is a help button I've missed it.
Others
There are in-game purchases with real life money. I have yet to feel like the game is skewed towards forcing you to spend real life money at the time of writing, but a heads up for those who care about this sort of thing nonetheless.
Suggestions

This game has hardcore prawn in it!  The really nasty kind, too!  We're talking hardcore prawn that will throw so many balls at your face!  You will be overwhelmed trying to avoid all the balls at the climax!
Hardcore prawn aside, You Have to Win the Game is one of those cool new video games all the kids are playing these days with their backwards baseball caps, CGA graphics, and CRT monitors.  What?  You haven't got a CRT monitor?  That's okay, YHTWTG is such a cool guy, he brought one along for you to play on.
Alright, dialing down the flippancy for a second, this is an 8-bit nostalgia trip, but it gets some points from me for going balls to the wall (literally: see the above mention of prawn) with the style and mimicking the curve and scan lines of a CRT monitor.  The harsh magenta and cyan palette will send you screaming back to the C64/early Macintosh days and every screen has its own title invoking some games of the era like the DIzzy games and a few that escape my mind since you're asking me to remember back to a time when I thought basic multiplication was rocket science that only super old people like third graders could do.
But YHTWTG is not just some kind of Atari game that has beep booped its way into the modern age!  There are actually some pretty contemporary things going on.  Some of them are subtle, like having more frames than are carried in a man's wallet so the platforming is nice and smooth.  Others are part of the game's larger design, like including copious checkpoints and infinite lives on the default mode, so that anybody can win the game, not just masochists.  It's also quite fair, unlike its predecessors who seemed to think you loved to leap of faith into spikes and every unsignposted doom ball from off-screen was an extra quarter for them.  YHTWTG is filled with hard challenges, but all of them are right out there.  Just swinging in the breeze.  In all their naked glory.  Like the hardcore prawn.
You will die.  You will die a lot.  But it will always be your own fault for not being fast, observant, or precise.  This isn't I Wanna Be the Guy.  And that leads nicely into the gameplay: it's a pure platformer.  Your only tools are jumping and reflexes.  The game does have some Metroidy aspects, where you can roam freely between the screens and collect items to expand your ability to jump and open up new areas.  However, your only tool to deal with the obstacles in your path is, and will only ever be, slick evasion.
You'll evolve as you play YHTWTG.  You'll go from struggling to grasp the weight and precision of the platforming, to losing more bodies to flying bullets than all of World War I as you desperately push for the next checkpoint.  But slowly, inevitably, You Have to Win the Game.  And by then, you'll probably feel a little awesome.  Maybe even awesome enough to take on the big guns: cat mode (nine lives) and YOLO mode (one life).  And then you'll be some sort of Neo-esque bullet dodging demigod where you walk through a "boss" room in half a second without breaking stride as if to say, "Hollow King, you ain't nothin' but a ♥♥♥♥♥." There will be moments of utter zen as you move directly through the challenges you've completely dominated, broken by the extreme tension of those that can still wreck your♥♥♥♥♥♥
I freely admit I have not overcome my problem with hardcore prawn (as you can no doubt tell), but man is it satisfying to say that I have even seen the hardcore prawn while YOLO!
So, You Have to Win the Game is a free, fun, full-on nostalgia trip.  There are only a couple reasons I might not recommend it to somebody.  You should probably stay away if you really can't stand the idea of even trying a hardcore platformer.  Though know that it has gone out of its way to be easy enough that you can win by sheer attrition.  It does have one possible design misstep where it confronts you with a cryptogram at the end that you have to get hints for by exploring.   If you're not into cryptograms as I am, I could see that being pretty maddening (though you could always just walkthrough that part).  And, if you're just put off by 8-bit nostalgia, this is not for you.
Otherwise, definitely go and win the game!  You have to.  It said so!  And I am also telling you now!
