It's like Deus Ex with vampires. Perhaps one of my favorite games of all time. I'll try to keep this review friendly to those unfamiliar with the V:TM brand.
+ Very unique subject matter.
+ Incredibly atmospheric. Four sectioned hubs of Los Angeles that are for the most part dirty, dark, grimey, and gothic. A handful of levels take place in specialized locations.
+ Well-written and voice acted cast of characters. Very memorable and all provide their own unique interactions. Plenty of dialogue has been recorded to reflect most every mission.
+ Plot and story for the most part are very intriguing and are strung along at an excellent pace through story and side missions. I would often lose six hours in this game before coming up for air. Multiple endings.
+ Very spooky, but not jump-scare spoopy.
+ Varried clans (a combination of vampiric class and race) that all play differently. Brujah go for brute strength and gain symptathy from their bretheren in the underground. Grossly disfigured Nosferatu are shunned by humans and are forced to navigate towns through sewers and shadows as a trade-off for their stealth proficiency. Crazy Malkavians can initiate conversation with stop signs and discover hidden dialogue options. Lots of lore.
+ Well-assembled skill system that supports combat, navigational, social, physical, and magical attributes.
+ Abundance of options in combat: stealth, melee, firearms, and magic. Stealth handles fairly well, most levels are designed to accomidate it.
+ Excellent original and licensed soundtrack.
- Old and buggy. Download the Unofficial Patch. Only had minor and infrequent gameplay hinderances after downloading this.
- Graphics are dated but serviceable.
- Combat is neither satisfying nor balanced. Melee is boring and hardly nuanced but gets the job done. Firearms are plentiful and seem encouraged but are painfully ineffective even with heavy skill investment. Magic (particularly in the Tremere clan) obliderates foes almost too easily.
- Unavoidable head-on boss confrontations. If you'd like to play a strictly stealthy Nosferatu or charming and persuasive Toreador, you're gonna have a bad time.
- Last few levels of the game were a tad underwhelming, the forth of the four areas in particular and its tied in quests.
- The game advertises itself as "roleplay", but don't expect any customization options outside of stats. Character appearances and armors are pre-set, most of which are fairly repulsive.
In summation, I marathoned this game, compelled to force through the less pleseant levels solely interested in influencing my character's destiny. Many levels were unforgettable, whether that be their creepiness, their utter repulsive enemies or surroundings, or their familiar welcomeness.
You will enjoy this story, exploration, and atmosphere regardless. You MIGHT enjoy the combat based upon which race you choose and your specific talents.

When I bought it I was somewhat sceptical. TDs for me always were gaming fast food. It's easy to digest, a small thing in between and after a few meals I got to have something real. It's somewhat tasty, but not really flashy nor really making me excited for coming back.
That's where DQ is different. It has an actual well thought out story and more importantly it has characters with personality. Thanks to the small trick that your characters are actually towers (which works surprisingly well), they also get connected to gameplay elements. The levels with skill"trees" create the feeling of progression that tds often lack and rare gear is sparse enough to make me actually somewhat hyped for rewards.
It goes one step beyond the usual TD with rpg elements (sanctum, dungeon defenders), it's a full fledged rpg in a lot of ways. And it's actually good rpg.
Considering the pretty low price (it's in sale atm) I see no reason not to recommend it (well, 2d-graphics). It's deep, it is enthralling and most importantly it's fun. And as a cherrytop they just released a big update for free. If you like classic rpgs or tds give the demo a shot.

TL;DR: It's a game with awesome superpowers.  Buy it, if you want to have fun with a friend (or alone)
Saints Row 4 was an amazing experience. Everything is similar to SR3. World, NPCs, gunplay, missions, cars. But to spice it up, they added superpowers. Such as superjump, superspeed, fireballs, iceballs, telekinesis, etc.
These powers make the game so great. They are very well made and spice up the game extremely well.
Storywise SR4 is lousy. Villain appears in the world and you try to stop him, as usual. But in my opinion, game with silly and childish humor and superpowers doesn't need a strong storyline.
You like driving in games? Don't buy Saints Row 4. They are pretty much useless, since you can run and fly faster.
The game gets more fun, when you get more upgrades. When you have reached level 50, you will have a ton of fun with some upgrades (hint: it's the bomb).
Co-Op is enjoyable. I completed it with few people and enjoyed it every time. Using these powers won't tire you, once you get into it.
Although you might have all-beating superpowers, you still have to make your money legit. Do missions and activities to get money and upgrade your guns (which you will need, even though you still have those powers). There are few overpowered weapon choices, which will help you through the game.
You can upgrade your superpowers by collecting these blue clusters around the map. There are around a thousand of them, so you will see a lot of them.
The map is like SR3, but bigger. It doesn't take long to travel through it. It would've been nice to see a bigger map. There is also a fast travel system, which I used frequently during a 100% run.
Character customization is absolutely great (once again). Detailed settings can be applied. I am not the one to customize my character a whole lot, but I know there are tons of people who like to. Shopping for clothes is fun. You can find some funny and cool looking costumes.
Many activities are sometimes a grind, but it doesn't always feel that way, since they take few minutes or less.
Saints Row 4 is a funny and a great game with interesting gameplay mechanic added to it.
I recommend this game to you, if you are into superpowers and relaxing gameplay.
P.S. If you want an open world game with more driving, buy GTA 5. If you want superpowers, buy SR4.
Also, there's Keith David, what else could you possibly want?

It's like Deus Ex with vampires. Perhaps one of my favorite games of all time. I'll try to keep this review friendly to those unfamiliar with the V:TM brand.
+ Very unique subject matter.
+ Incredibly atmospheric. Four sectioned hubs of Los Angeles that are for the most part dirty, dark, grimey, and gothic. A handful of levels take place in specialized locations.
+ Well-written and voice acted cast of characters. Very memorable and all provide their own unique interactions. Plenty of dialogue has been recorded to reflect most every mission.
+ Plot and story for the most part are very intriguing and are strung along at an excellent pace through story and side missions. I would often lose six hours in this game before coming up for air. Multiple endings.
+ Very spooky, but not jump-scare spoopy.
+ Varried clans (a combination of vampiric class and race) that all play differently. Brujah go for brute strength and gain symptathy from their bretheren in the underground. Grossly disfigured Nosferatu are shunned by humans and are forced to navigate towns through sewers and shadows as a trade-off for their stealth proficiency. Crazy Malkavians can initiate conversation with stop signs and discover hidden dialogue options. Lots of lore.
+ Well-assembled skill system that supports combat, navigational, social, physical, and magical attributes.
+ Abundance of options in combat: stealth, melee, firearms, and magic. Stealth handles fairly well, most levels are designed to accomidate it.
+ Excellent original and licensed soundtrack.
- Old and buggy. Download the Unofficial Patch. Only had minor and infrequent gameplay hinderances after downloading this.

You know a game is great, when its community is still putting out mods and patches 10+ years after its release. It's also made me realize how mediocre the writing is in current games. I don't care about Vampires, but man, the story had me on the edge of my seat for 40+ hours. The suspense was killing me! The characters were great, and there's twist after twist, after twist - so try to avoid spoilers. Also, I loved the ending I got.
The game is a bit outdated in terms of gameplay though. It's rather small for an open world game, and lacks "activities"; however it makes up for it with fun sidequests and some surprises. The combat is a bit clunky, but can be more fun depending on what clan you pick. The stealth can be pretty tough if your sneaking skill points are low. So keep em like that if you want some challenge - otherwise stealth will be a breeze. Music fits it well, and voice acting is good but a bit rough around the edges. Replayability is great. Most clans have something different to offer, that make it worth replaying.
Download the Unofficial Patch+. It fixes a lot of game breaking stuff, restores unused content and works on Windows 8.1. It's a bit glitchy, but nothing serious. You're gonna see a lot of clothing going up in the air though. But hell, a AAA game; Batman: Arkham Origins, crashed around fifty times on me, (not kidding, I counted up to 40+ then lost count!) this game only did it like three times. It's extremely easy to patch and mod... seriously, you've gotta be old-man level PC illiterate to find it hard. It won't even take more than two minutes.

All in all this is a truly outstanding and imaginative game. It has everything - politics, character development, action, stealth, upgrades, and an immersive storyline you can influence. There were some silly and frustrating quests (but then, what game doesn't have those?) but this was a rare game where I felt I really 'lived' the story.
If only someone could produce another like this! Would definitely recommend.

I gotta give this game a vote for the thumbs up side because I've been having a lot of fun with it.
Yes it's a mobile port.  That's not bad.  That's awesome!  Your game is saved in the cloud so you can play it anywhere, you can play the daily reward multiple times by switching devices, the mobile version's ads are not mandatory for gameplay (a pretty rare feat), and the game looks pretty darn good considering all my crusty computers can handle it.
It's only the gameplay that I can understand some people having a problem with.  The game has three main modes: cut and dry merch trading, tedious bullet exchanges, and sparce ocean exploring.  I make that sound bad because I can understand most modern gamers not enjoying any of those modes, but I do enjoy it and it comes with great perks.  Do your game chores to build up reputation and you can make money easily.  Money leads to better battle-ready ships.  Then comes, imo, the most satisfying part: picking up that mobile, turning on motion controls, fastforwarding time, and hitting the open ocean for exploration.  There are battles to be had, loot to be found, survivors to be rescued, and even some limited on-land treasure hunting.  You can do any mode right off the back if you have a preference for one or the other, but you're going to face certain difficulties and are likely to get bored a lot faster.  This is definitely one of those games where its whole is more fun than the sum of its parts.
I'll admit that the screenshots of the game over sell the action a bit, but if you've ever enjoyed older trading games, and don't mind the battles being toned down a bit from what's advertised, I definitely recommend this free game.

I picked up CoH2 during the free weekend. I was impressed with the flow of play from Relic's CoH inspired Dawn of War titles (less so Retribution, for reasons that will become clear) and thought i'd take a look.
Wish I hadn't bothered.
First lets address the elephant in the room - the bugs. Stable this game is not. A widely reported game-stopping bug STILL exists in the tutorial mission (encountering a game-stopper within five minutes is surely not a good sign of things to come). due to the way the game processes script triggers and this core issue will come back to bite you many times in the future.
On a high-end PC I experienced all of Relic's greatest hits. Audio bugs are the most frequent - sounds get 'stuck' and loop the same half second over. And over. And over. And over. Your only recourse is to close the program or mute the sound. It intensely dislikes the Steam overlay and god forbid you alt-tab.
On to the actual gameplay. Not much better.
Every mission boils down to: DEFEND AGAINST WAVES!!! which initially receives enough lampshading to be forgivable but even this wears thin and by the sixth mission you're fed up with it.
The AI is impossibly stupid. There is no notion of target priorities - your tank destroyers will cheerfully engage light infantry over heavy vehicles, flamethrowers will stand around playing with themselves while under fire from a unit they could easily wipe out if they just moved a half inch into range, but they will gleefully mow down any number of your own troops if it means getting to hit even one vehicle.
Pathfinding is a nightmare - be prepared to do a lot of micro and button mashing or you'll have tanks doing reverse donuts through hostile bases in no time. In fact the game seems to be more about fighting against the UI than it does the AI.
Unit production is exhausting and badly presented, both infantry and vehicles are spread out across three of the four production buildings with no unifying standard. Icons are not visually dissimilar enough to allow for easy selection of the right unit even if you remember which building it comes from so you're frequently left with the choice between trying to control a combat with the pathfinding and targeting AI fighting you every step of the way or accepting that the units are going to do whatever the hell they want anyway and just focus on making sure you're spamming out the right mix of units to at least make some progress.
If this weren't enough the reinforcement mechanic, by which your recruited units arrive on the battlefield is extremely difficult to manage - its not at all apparent where your forces will appear as they begin the trudge to your waypoint, and the WAVES!!!! design of the missions means you'll often be left wondering where the hell those reinforcements you ordered five minutes ago are, only to find they were wiped out by newly spawned AI units in previously cleared areas.
The game itself is chaotic. There's no opportunity to really implement strategy beyond the basic rock-paper-scissors unit balancing and your role as the player is more to babysit units so they don't empty clips of light arms into armoured tanks and waste anti-tank fire on infantry. Its a chore, taking place faster than you can really respond because of bad UI design that does nothing but get in your way.
If you're a fan of RTS, give this game a miss. Its a mess.

Three words come to mind:

First off, the visuals. This is a very beautiful game. Red Creek Valley may be the site for several "killings," but it sure doesn't look like it. I went into this game blind, and the first things that caught my eye were the breathtaking visuals. On top of that, the soundtrack fit extremely well with each scene.
Of course, this is not always a good thing once the player gets to the "horror" aspects of the game...... but the visuals and audio are definitely things to be appauded.
Next, the story. Playing as Paul Prospero, a psychic detective, the player is able to look into past events and travel to fictional worlds. The whole concept can be disorienting, even disturbing at first, but it serves as a core mechanic for narrating the story. With this ability, the player is able to look into the murders of various characters and figure out exactly what happened. This occult style allows for some interesting puzzles and storytelling methods.
This is probably why the game is so set on not guiding the player.
This brings me to the final point, the only criticism I have for the game, albeit a big one.
For a psychic detective famous for his work, it takes a while for the player to fully understand the extent of Paul's abilities. There is no tutorial whatsoever, and almost all of the hints and items the player must find for themselves. There
a system that helps the player find said items, and it's portrayed with numerous floating words that converge when the player is looking in the correct direction. As one might expect, it's not the most evident of mechanics. I was halfway through the game before I figured this out, and that was only because I
how to play the game. This wouldn't have been such an issue if it was easier to find the missing items, but the option to inspect said items only appears when the mouse is practically on top of the object. I understand why the developers chose this unfriendly approach, as it undeniably fits well with the mysterious mood of the story. Still, a little help on
would've been nice......
To summarize, this is a well thought-out walking simulator story game that holds an interesting plotline. The visuals and audio are works of art, and the storytelling method is not something you'll find every day. The blatant issue is its unfriendliness. The fact that
is a major flaw on game design. Still, I could forgive the developers as they did provide an intriguing story.
I'll recommend this game to anyone in search of a good storyline and not turned off by walking simulators. There are definite "horror" elements to this game, but not so much to be unplayable.
I would wait until the game's on sale, though. Since its an old game, that won't be too difficult. I also highly suggest reading up on how to play. There's a well-written post about this on Steam that's spoiler-free.
Once you know how to play, the game becomes much more enjoyable, and you'll be able to save time that you would've spent floundering around.

“Walking Simulator” isn’t a pejorative to me like it is to some. Honestly I think the term has been mostly reclaimed by a flourishing genre of environmental exploration games that arose in the wake of Dear Esther and Gone Home. I seek out interesting walking sims, ones that promise interesting scenery and clever storytelling, and while they may be rare they do indeed exist. Much of their appeal hinges on their graphics and environment design, and that’s where The Vanishing of Ethan Carter shines the brightest. In fact it might just be the Platonic ideal of the genre, considering how much of its appeal hinges on graphics and story as opposed to actual gameplay.
You play world-weary baritone detective Paul Prospero, a veteran paranormal investigator in search of missing child Ethan Carter. The boy has vanished somewhere in the pastoral fields and forests of Red Creek Valley, and immediately upon arrival it’s clear that the picturesque landscape hides a great evil. Paul’s supernatural attunement allows you to uncover the truth behind a string of gristly murders and the strange events surrounding them, eventually revealing the nature of the place and Ethan’s disappearance. It’s a beautiful and disturbing journey, and one with more than a few surprises in store.
The game is quick to inform you when you begin that it’s a free-form story, one that you’ll need to piece together yourself. This doesn’t mean you need to pore over scattered notes or audio logs, it means you literally need to go out and find pieces of the story. Red Creek Valley is a vast, open place that hides many secrets along the path to your destination. The main story beats are centered around the murders which are usually central to an area but there are other fragments of the story scattered in the far fields and crumbling buildings of the valley. You won’t get the full picture without finding them, and they tend to be far more interesting in nature than the murder investigations.
Those investigations and the additional story fragments are the only breaks in the wandering you’re going to get, and I’d be lying if I said they amounted to much gameplay. The murders require you to locate bits of evidence in and around the scene and then number the sequence of events when presented with their ghostly echoes. There’s no challenge to these sequences, as getting the order wrong does nothing but waste time. For the story fragments every one is different, from pursuing a fleet-footed stranger to rearranging the rooms in a house, but these are still only brief respites from the wandering at the core of the game. The fragments DO reward you with some fantastic scenes though, definitely the creative high points of the title and absolutely worth seeking out.
So yes, the rest of the game is just walking around the valley, and if it weren’t such a lovely valley that might be a bad thing. But my God, even two years out the Redux version looks absolutely incredible in all its vibrant details. Flowering bushes waft in the breeze, leaves flutter down from autumn branches, water splashes over glistening rocks, and the valley itself stretches out to a golden, sun-touched horizon. As far as environments go it’s one of the most immersive around, with convincing flora and realistically-weathered buildings. It does make the characters stand out, though, as their art style doesn’t carry the same masterful touch as the environments and their animations jerk and slide around in unnatural ways. They don’t kill the atmosphere entirely but they certainly do no favors to the otherwise expert presentation.
All that walking will get you through the story in around three hours or so, and between the lovely scenery and simple puzzles you shouldn’t get too bored as long as you’re down with the whole walking sim concept. Some titles like SOMA have enough going on to fully break free of the stigma but The Vanishing lives comfortably in it, challenging you to derive your enjoyment from hours of hiking and sightseeing. There’s very little that happens during your sojourns, limited almost entirely to the optional story fragments. And while some of those include some striking and occasionally terrifying elements, they’re such small, temporary parts of the game that you can’t really expect them to carry the rest.
Then there’s the story, steeped in mysticism and blood. I won’t delve into spoilers but know that right from the outset strange, nigh-inexplicable events will take place alongside the gruesome murders that line your path. It all means something but it won’t be clear until the very end, and that conclusion will take a pretty sharp turn away from what you’ve experienced up to that point. Ultimately it’s a story told heavily through symbolism, and while I appreciate what it represents I also recognize that some will regard it as a bait-and-switch. My advice then would be to proceed with an open mind, and prepare for what you see to not be the whole truth you are chasing.
Put simply, The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is an excellent walking sim but a very thin game. It elevates the genre to one of its ideals, a game so beautiful and meaningful that the act of wandering around in its confines constitutes a complete game. But as complete as it is it may not satisfy, either for lack of depth in its systems or lofty narrative concept that may not have the intended impact. If you have the patience for slow, meandering games then it should not be missed, but its limitations cannot be ignored no matter how good it may sound.

An amazing experience but in my opinion, pain mode is detrimental to the experience as a whole.
I love rpgs and I love good stories and Lisa exceeded at both in the first 20 minutes of gameplay. This game brings to the table a plentitude of funny and original characters, amazing soundtrack and very unique bosses, locations and jokes. The game made me laugh, cry, unnerved and scared and the transition between each emotions was executed with extreme precision and skill. I praise the maker of this magnificent game.
I chose Pain mode as I wanted to extra bits of content as well as the extra challenge with the new bosses and luckily, it wasn't impossible for my first playthrough but caused me a lot of distress as I found myself restarting often because of a silly mistake but I didn't mind that as the pain it caused me was well received. It is the painful rpg after all. What bothered me though is the fact that you don't get a lot of room to test characters and build your dream team, especially if they are under-leveled. The 3 first characters that I got in my game were the same three I kept during the whole game as I could not level up the newer and cooler characters as I knew the lack of save points and the potential game over right around the corner could wipe away hours of gameplay.
In my opinion, if you want to truly enjoy your experience and get to choose the team you want, do not choose Pain Mode unless you want to feel true pain in which case, I invite you to do so. But otherwise, you aren't missing that much without Pain mode as the extra bosses, cutscene and dungeon don't bring much to the story and you can easily get the information online.
I highly recommend this awesome and painful game!

-Unit A is overpowered because of its pinpoint accuracy, so let's change every stats EXCEPT its accuracy to balance it out!
- Unit B is *slightly* overpowered because of its low cost, so lets double/triple nerf it by upping its cost AND reducing its performance.
- Unit C is *slightly* underpowered because of how it performs. So lets up its firepower greatly AND reduce its cost.

It goes without saying that sometime in our lives we attempt to chase dreams that we might or might not have any prospective of reaching. There's ups and downs, and there are lessons to learn along our pursuit. On certain occasions, an impromptu turn of events can teach a lesson that ignites a new spirit, even when one is close to forfeit. We see this idea and scenario applied to almost every tangible entertainment medium possible, and unfortunately most are basically sick of such buyoant tales. Thankfully, InvertMouse takes this unanimously known concept and creates a free, jovial, hour (Or <) long chronicle following a young woman in high hopes of leaving her mark in society, Without Within.
Take the role of Vinty, an aspiring calligrapher that is unfortunately not having things in accord with her ideals as her art, or should I say, "greatness", rarely gets acknowleged by anyone. In addition to that, she has an unfavorable part-time job and a landlady vexing at her to make ends meet to pay for another dull month in the disheveled apartment Vinty has on rent. With the game's very short length in consideration, not much can be said without spoiling the novel for you, so I'll leave off with this, stuff happens and Vinty encounters a relevation. Simple.
Although Without Within stays abstinent from making any unorthodox creation decisions, that doesn't mean it's deplorable by any means. It is evident that the writer(s) for Without Within enjoyed themselves during production, and it is exemplified in the outcome. As conventional as the story might be, nobody can help themselves but to have a handful of chuckles while reading this story as occasional jokes here and there are made and they're funny enough to form a stupid grin on my face most of the time I read. The optimistic themes of self-discovery and inspiration is what the assembles the core of this game, and they are covered rather well as Vinty's change by the end of the novel is believable and to some extent relatable.
An apprehension regarding this game some might have is that it is rather short, clocking in at less than an hour. However, there was no rationale to make this otherwise as the game accomplished in getting it's message across in the time allotted and the game only recalls the events of a day or two. Should you still not be convinced, allow the mention that the game is FREE, damnit. Gratuit pour tous. Doesn't get better than that. Therefore, I cannot denigrate the game for that shortcoming (see Sakura Spirit). My only true issue with this game is with the choice making aspect, which is rather stale. It's as clear as a cloudless morning sky which choices should be made to progress the story, and the alternative choice immediately follows a BAD END. Therefore, no weight is actually on the choices you make as there is only one legitimate end to the game, the others are along the lines of "My carrer has ended.". Lazy to say the least, but it isn't such a massive, game-breaking problem.

And it's free. Do yourself a favor and get it.

To my delight and surprise, this is probably my favorite purchase of the summer sale thus far.  Some important highlights:
1) This is such a great spinoff on the themes of Starship Troopers I’d say it might outshine the series itself, if that wasn’t heresy. The jokes are clever, & the game nails the absurd political/military dynamics. If the gimmicky lines get old, you can simply turn down the voice volume setting.
2) At launch they took a lot of flak for being “DLC: The Game” which was completely fair. Now, however, I can buy the game, and all DLCs, for $20 – a steal, for all that it’s worth. I’m again pleasantly surprised to see the community hasn’t died even after 2+ years. Even outside peaks in the userbase (sales, etc) there are more than enough pubbies to grab a pug game with. Feel free to look up the stats.
3) The progression is rewarding enough without being intrusive. Besides the cosmetic items common to every gorram game these days, there are upgrades for your existing weapons/abilities as well as more to unlock. The DLCs make this a great deal easier – which, again, they deserved a lot of criticism for after launch. Get it on sale, however, and you won’t worry about p2w locked items.
4) The campaign map analog is, personally, highly satisfying. It boosts immersion, & gives you a sense of purpose in slogging towards one of three enemies’ planets. The progress is shared across the entire userbase, whether you’re playing solo, co-op, or matchmaking. I can see how it would feel like a grind, but to be honest, if you’re playing the game to grind/looking for a game to grind in, this probably isn’t it. Helldivers is clearly meant to be taken lightheartedly, & the progression is mostly here as a supporting feature. The DLCs go a long way to reducing your dependency on unlocks/making the game generally more enjoyable. So, again, be sure to pick this up only as a bundle on sale.
5) Servers are stable and co-op is seamlessly integrated – with pugs & among friends. No issues personally, nor have I read of much. The game itself is thoroughly stable, & the graphics are accessible even to low-end PCs.
6) While it is playable solo, most of it is a steep climb if you’re not in a group. This varies depending on mission difficulty and player skill, of course.
7) As a small, personal aside: I immensely appreciate that you’re meant to aim for center-of-mass (headshots aren’t remotely as frequent in reality), and that reloading your magazine doesn’t magically keep any unused rounds from the previous one. This is another unexpected (and at least for me, pleasant) surprise – an immersive detail I haven’t seen in most other shooters I can think of.
So who is this for? I’d say if you liked Magicka (or disliked it for certain stylistic reasons); are a fan of Starship Troopers; enjoy top-down squad-based shooters; cackle gleefully while dismembering enemies of Democracy, Liberty, and Super Earth; are looking for a casual to medium-core co-op game with friends; or some combination thereof.
Well, that’s about all I can think of for now… I hope this recommendation helps. Bottom line: when it’s on sale, I’d give this game a 9/10 must-buy if even any of the features entice you. Go kill things for Super Earth! It’s great for Liberty, Democracy, and  FREEDOM! ...probably.

The community so far has been very helpful when you ask questions, they have a great sense of humor, knows how to have fun, and they don't mind helping you get what you need. In terms of progression it is great, there really is no "best" weapon or perk, it is ALL situational which I think is awesome because it means that you have a reason to unlock EVERYTHING.
The 4-player CoOp is drop in drop out so there's no annoying "host-migration" whenever someone leaves or joins... The matchmaking is really simple to use and even has a filter to adjust parameters, making it easier to find a match you want. Friendly fire is permanent so if you're an elitist, this game is NOT for you because if you aren't killed by the enemy you will die to a teammate and it happens so often that you have no choice but to laugh it off...
If you're looking for an action-packed, insanely fun, mayhem fest of a shooter to play with friends or even alone, give this game a shot.

-Option for Larger Maps and to be able to building higher. (This may also give more options to use Aerial equipment
-Option for Short keys for changing equipment
-More Building material options
-More classes
-More weapons/equipment options (ie. options to jump higher, besides trampoline/catapult)

This game is a true cult classic and deserves your attention if you are into custom-character, story-driven RPG's. Even if you are not a big fan of the Vampire/White Wolf setting, this game's production values are so high I can assure you that for the few dollars this game will cost you, you will be thrilled.
Being an old, pen and paper RPG'er, I can tell you that I never 'got' the World of Darkness setting until I played this game. Like a lot of gamers in the 90's and 00's I had exposure to WoD LARP's in the local gaming community but there was something about them that didn't click for me. With VTMB, you get it. You get the interaction of the feuding clans contrasted against the need to perpetuate the masquerade. You will feel something profound when you explore the haunted hotel. You're going to react strongly to a lot of content in this game, especially when you start to unravel just how much of a pawn your character has become in much larger events.
11 years - This is how long this game has been out. It was released the same year as Halo 2, WOW and Half-Life 2 and like those games, continues to be enjoyed many years later... but without publisher-driven releases. This game was and is a big hit with the modding community, so when you are done your first play through, mod this thing up and go around again!
11/10 - 11 for the number of years this game continues to demonstrate to gamers and developers alike how amazing RPG's should be done. Enjoy!
Update - I had to nominate this for a Write-In Award for Best Undead Undead Game. This game continues to be a popular, critically acclaimed RPG from beyond the grave of most other games.

Vampire: The Masquerade is a game for those who love a good storyline, and as well those who enjoy RPGs, in my opinion. The thing about this game that makes it SO good is the fact it incorporates things such as (scripted) dialogue option and choices that have an impact in the game, even the race of vampire that you choose has an impact on how the dialogue is presented, and as well as how the characters in-game speak to you. Especially what happens to some characters. This game may not look appealing with its graphics, but I gurantee that this is a game worth playing because, despite its graphics everything else makes up for it.
The side quests in the game feels rewarding, especially when its a tough one (and you're lacking a few skill points), but in this game, getting crucial items such as weapons, blood packs and money is scarce--especially when you're trying to be discreet about not being a vampire in society.
The main quest of the game may be a little convoluted at first but that said, once you get to the end everything will make perfect sense. (Hopefully, anyway--if not, this is a game worth re-playing, anyway).
The characters in the game are absolutely wonderful. Each that you interact with has a different personality. There are some characters who you want to help, and there are somewho you don't want to help, and it's usually due to their attitude, tone, look or by how weak/intimidating they are. In some cases though, if you help someone and it goes against the vampire oath (the law basically--the Masquerade--in which your character has agreed to abiding by) then you'll lose a 'Masquerade' point. This feature that's been incorporated in the game is interesting, for the fact that if you help someone for the right reasons (doing something good in regards towards the vampires) you regain that Masquerade point. This adds another thing to look out for when playing the game (your health bar won't just be the only thing you'll have to keep an eye on).
This game is brutal. And when I mean brutal, then I mean--"if you haven't saved your game in a long time, and you're about to go into a fight/fire/lose blood, then you're going to have to play from where you last saved, or the last autosave. And that's just another factor that gives this game character. It's somewhat old school, it has vampires, it's brutal with death (well, it can be if you don't save regularly!), has horror themes, and it's also an RPG.
I definitely recommend this game!

This game needed a bit more... it had potential but ultimately is a bit lacking. I played for 15 minutes, which may seem short, but in this game that is really all you need (see speed run achievement: "beat game in 10 minutes" ... and not in a mario bros warp through secrets kind of way).
I didn't play the game to the point where I acquired all the items needed, but played enough to see where it was going (acquired blue and red orbs). I played until the game glitched and I couldn't jump anymore... a pretty critical part where that's the only thing in the game you can do (left, right, jump, press down to go through platform are the controls). I decided it was enough after giving it a fair chance since it really didn't grab me from the start either.
Although the visual aspect and old retro tv screen were pretty cool, they are gimmicks that will wear off fast as the game itself doesn't hold up... and even if they were trying to mimic one of the old games, just because they are old doesn't make them good, and there are a lot of aspects/mechanics (even in old games even DOS) lacking in this one.
The game has a metroid like environment with a couple of branching paths but ultimately it still doesn't feel expansive. The collectibles are just simple money bags with a couple of items needed to make the map more accessible, which doesn't really end up being fun. There are a couple of interesting "fall through the map" type things but they are over way too fast.
Enemies are extremely simple (crab walking back and forth, or stationary creature firing projectiles for you to avoid). There doesn't need to be a way to defeat the enemies, however, it doesn't hurt.
There is no music (again, just because old games may not have had it, doesn't mean we should take that excuse here, as disabling music in options could be there for real purists).
All in all, the game feels very empty, And it feels like this game is trying to be VVVVVV in spirit. Yes VVVVVV has a unique up down mechanic, and this game has a regular jumping mechanic, but there's another flaw -- this game has no unique mechanic(s), and like I said, it just feels very bland.
However, VVVVVV is superior in almost every way: music, some semblence of story, bigger map, more interesting map challenges/obstacles.
I may try this game again in the future, but first impressions (15 minutes, 35% through the game (?), red/blue orb collected) are not great. The game isn't bad, but really has no striking features that would make me remember it.

“Walking Simulator” isn’t a pejorative to me like it is to some. Honestly I think the term has been mostly reclaimed by a flourishing genre of environmental exploration games that arose in the wake of Dear Esther and Gone Home. I seek out interesting walking sims, ones that promise interesting scenery and clever storytelling, and while they may be rare they do indeed exist. Much of their appeal hinges on their graphics and environment design, and that’s where The Vanishing of Ethan Carter shines the brightest. In fact it might just be the Platonic ideal of the genre, considering how much of its appeal hinges on graphics and story as opposed to actual gameplay.
You play world-weary baritone detective Paul Prospero, a veteran paranormal investigator in search of missing child Ethan Carter. The boy has vanished somewhere in the pastoral fields and forests of Red Creek Valley, and immediately upon arrival it’s clear that the picturesque landscape hides a great evil. Paul’s supernatural attunement allows you to uncover the truth behind a string of gristly murders and the strange events surrounding them, eventually revealing the nature of the place and Ethan’s disappearance. It’s a beautiful and disturbing journey, and one with more than a few surprises in store.
The game is quick to inform you when you begin that it’s a free-form story, one that you’ll need to piece together yourself. This doesn’t mean you need to pore over scattered notes or audio logs, it means you literally need to go out and find pieces of the story. Red Creek Valley is a vast, open place that hides many secrets along the path to your destination. The main story beats are centered around the murders which are usually central to an area but there are other fragments of the story scattered in the far fields and crumbling buildings of the valley. You won’t get the full picture without finding them, and they tend to be far more interesting in nature than the murder investigations.
Those investigations and the additional story fragments are the only breaks in the wandering you’re going to get, and I’d be lying if I said they amounted to much gameplay. The murders require you to locate bits of evidence in and around the scene and then number the sequence of events when presented with their ghostly echoes. There’s no challenge to these sequences, as getting the order wrong does nothing but waste time. For the story fragments every one is different, from pursuing a fleet-footed stranger to rearranging the rooms in a house, but these are still only brief respites from the wandering at the core of the game. The fragments DO reward you with some fantastic scenes though, definitely the creative high points of the title and absolutely worth seeking out.
So yes, the rest of the game is just walking around the valley, and if it weren’t such a lovely valley that might be a bad thing. But my God, even two years out the Redux version looks absolutely incredible in all its vibrant details. Flowering bushes waft in the breeze, leaves flutter down from autumn branches, water splashes over glistening rocks, and the valley itself stretches out to a golden, sun-touched horizon. As far as environments go it’s one of the most immersive around, with convincing flora and realistically-weathered buildings. It does make the characters stand out, though, as their art style doesn’t carry the same masterful touch as the environments and their animations jerk and slide around in unnatural ways. They don’t kill the atmosphere entirely but they certainly do no favors to the otherwise expert presentation.
All that walking will get you through the story in around three hours or so, and between the lovely scenery and simple puzzles you shouldn’t get too bored as long as you’re down with the whole walking sim concept. Some titles like SOMA have enough going on to fully break free of the stigma but The Vanishing lives comfortably in it, challenging you to derive your enjoyment from hours of hiking and sightseeing. There’s very little that happens during your sojourns, limited almost entirely to the optional story fragments. And while some of those include some striking and occasionally terrifying elements, they’re such small, temporary parts of the game that you can’t really expect them to carry the rest.
Then there’s the story, steeped in mysticism and blood. I won’t delve into spoilers but know that right from the outset strange, nigh-inexplicable events will take place alongside the gruesome murders that line your path. It all means something but it won’t be clear until the very end, and that conclusion will take a pretty sharp turn away from what you’ve experienced up to that point. Ultimately it’s a story told heavily through symbolism, and while I appreciate what it represents I also recognize that some will regard it as a bait-and-switch. My advice then would be to proceed with an open mind, and prepare for what you see to not be the whole truth you are chasing.
Put simply, The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is an excellent walking sim but a very thin game. It elevates the genre to one of its ideals, a game so beautiful and meaningful that the act of wandering around in its confines constitutes a complete game. But as complete as it is it may not satisfy, either for lack of depth in its systems or lofty narrative concept that may not have the intended impact. If you have the patience for slow, meandering games then it should not be missed, but its limitations cannot be ignored no matter how good it may sound.

- Unit C is *slightly* underpowered because of how it performs. So lets up its firepower greatly AND reduce its cost.

Despite some of the negative reviews, I decided to try this game because it was free and I have been looking for a game like this for a long time. After playing for 3 hours, I am still enjoying it and plan on playing it a lot longer.
At first, I couldn't figure out how to steer. I went into the options and there was a setting to turn the steering wheel on.
The graphics are nice at 1080p with all the effects turned on. I really like the open world and different missions you can partake in to capture ships, smuggle goods, steal cargo, etc.
There are a LOT of ships you can fight against, capture, or buy. Every ship has a tree with upgrades, and you can purchase these upgrades at a port. Such upgrades include adding guns to the bow or stern, strengthening the hull, or improving the sales. Even your character can be upgraded once you gain enough experience points. You can also start your own pirate town and build buildings to manufacture goods to trade, store goods that you've acquired, or generate money.
The maps required to unlock parts of the map cost in game gold, but to unlock the buildings required to generate currency at your pirate town does cost real money. It's very inexpensive anyway, and I think I only paid a few bucks for the full experience. I haven't, nor do I plan, to purchase gold or ships with real money.
This game is not pay to win, because if you spend real money on the largest "best" ships, your in game gold income will not support crews that large for long. It's best to stay with smaller ships with smaller crews until you build up your income.
I haven't tried the multiplayer part yet, so no review there.
The music gets really repetitive, so I've keep it turned off. I wish there were more animations on the world map. I wish the crew on the ships were animated.
Overall, If you really like games about ships, pirates, smugglers, merchants, etc. definitely give this one a try.
I give it a 4/5

First off, I'm sad that it took me two years to find this gem of a video game. Such a simple game yet somehow you just keep coming back for more because it is SO MUCH DAMN FUN... There's so much to do and unlock and every mission plays out randomly with different difficulties so you never know what you're going to get into.
The community so far has been very helpful when you ask questions, they have a great sense of humor, knows how to have fun, and they don't mind helping you get what you need. In terms of progression it is great, there really is no "best" weapon or perk, it is ALL situational which I think is awesome because it means that you have a reason to unlock EVERYTHING.
The 4-player CoOp is drop in drop out so there's no annoying "host-migration" whenever someone leaves or joins... The matchmaking is really simple to use and even has a filter to adjust parameters, making it easier to find a match you want. Friendly fire is permanent so if you're an elitist, this game is NOT for you because if you aren't killed by the enemy you will die to a teammate and it happens so often that you have no choice but to laugh it off...
If you're looking for an action-packed, insanely fun, mayhem fest of a shooter to play with friends or even alone, give this game a shot.

Before you read this review a few things must be taken into consideration:
Movement in this game is very limited, it can become a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to travel between towns or landmarks sometimes. Somehow I can't help but feel that this is intentional and really adds to the feeling of despair, hopelessness, and even the comedic value of the games atmosphere. The only reason I think this, is because later they give you the means for traveling between areas yet not towns. The long trekking really builds up whatever emotion is supposed to be conveyed at the end. Don't get me wrong though, it's still a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥
Combat in this game is very similar to that of other turn based rpgs. You got your items, skills, hp, mp, exp, etc. The game mixes it up by giving you a combo system that your character can use instead of using skills that take up your power, making it feel very interactive. But what actually makes me enjoy the combat the most in this game as apposed to others is the attack animations of your gang. It never gets old watching your bros ram, shoot, moon, or run over your enemies and making them cry. The dialogue of you posse after battles alone is worth fighting for. You can have 3 other jabronis besides you in a posse at a time. All the other jabronis that you aren't using stay in an inventory that you can access at certain wanted posters. You can heal ya bois by either using items for sleeping at a camp. This game is mostly about making choices and the outcome will mostly be negative in some some way. Even if you feel like you got away unscathed you will have still lost something whether you deemed it valuable or not.
The soundtrack and SFX in LISA really add to the its atmosphere. I really feel a sense of dread when I get into combat with an abomination and hear music that perfectly matches the absolutely horrifying appearance of the thing in front of me. LISA's music (and sometimes even lack there of) exceedingly contributes to how you will feel while playing it. It really plays up what's happening and is easily one of my favorite parts of the game.
The artstyle is like Road Warrior meets Earthbound and it is kept consistently throughout. I personally enjoy the artstyle and color palette of the game but you can determine that for yourself by watching the trailer on the store page.
Everything about this game is so well crafted, from the story and dialogue to the characters and gameplay. I hope some day this hidden indie gem finally gets the attention it deserves. This game will tear your heart out with its tragedy and sew it back together with its wonderfully dark humor. LISA provides players with a suffering that can only be quelled through the
of playing the game.

I know that we've ALL, at least once or twice in our lives, considered how impossible life would be if we had to consciously regulate the autonomous bodily functions that we require to survive in our everyday lives. Manual Samuel takes that idea and runs with. Not just a little bit, but a lot. In fact, Manual Samuel may as well never stop running because this game is one of the most ridiculous and stupid games I have played in such a long time, and I absolutely LOVE it.
The game oozes with both cringe and charm in equal balance, and honestly leaves me in stitches, time and time again. I don't think I've had so many genuine and uncontrollable bouts of laughter from another game since perhaps my early childhood. The corny dad jokes, sarcastic British narrator, beautiful comic artstyle and Beetlejuice hell scene at the beginning of the game won me over immediately, and continues to captivate me the more I play.
The addition of coop, though I've yet to try it, is an amazingly good idea. When playing alone, you need to control Sam's arms, legs, eyelids (yes, eyelids lol), mouth, lungs, peni$ (yes, peni$), EVERYTHING. Imagine sharing those bodily functions with a partner, and having to cooperate with them in order to keep Sam functioning. Lols for days.
This game really is immensely fun and I highly recommend it to anyone that has a good sense of humour and loves a good laugh. Bloody brilliant.

Sid Meyer's Civ 5 is an incredible game. There are so many different civilizations to play as, each with their own unique play style. There are many different strategies to winning the game, some more difficult than others, but each intriguing in its own way. The game also looks ~amazing~ and putting everything on low quality doesn't make the game look bad, I hardly noticed a difference. Single player is incredibly fun and playing quick games(2-3 hours instead of 6-10 normal ones) makes the game much more playable with friends. The game is really fun playing with just one friend, but getting 5 or 6 together makes everything better. The only problem with the game that I have is the warmonger penalty. It doesn't matter that you got pulled into the war with your AI ally because you had a defensive pact and you proceed to take out the aggressor from the game by capturing all of their cities, your AI friend with hate you for the rest of the game because you are a warmonger because you took more than one city from someone else. This is frustrating when you take someone out early on because they settled super close to you and then try to be friends with everyone else and they are still mad at you in 1980 AD about taking out their enemy in 2000 BC. Other than that it is an incredible game.

A Story About My Uncle is a wonderful 3D platformer by indie developer Gone North Games whose main attractions are the mechanics and the visuals.
The main mechanic in this game is based on your electric grapple gun powered by an HEV-like super suit. You have to launch yourself across deep chasms by hooking on to floating rocks and platforms and, my god, is it fun. While the aesthetic and story give off a casual feel, the gameplay itself feels fast and exciting and it never gets old.
While playing the game, it is impossible to note the beauty and astounding level of detail brought into each map. It is absolutely breathtaking. There is a variety of different worlds that you have to explore to find your uncle, ranging from bright ice mountains to dark caves lit only by bioluminescent plants, and they all look amazing. The screenshots provided on this game's Store page are actual screenshots that can merely hint at the beauty to come. Look at the community screenshots to see for yourself. You won't be disappointed.
As I said before, the story itself is pretty casual. I actually found myself only half paying attention to it, as I was too busy enjoying myself and my surroundings.
My verdict: Play this game. It's a wonderful, beautiful little world that will have you... hooked.

I got this game when it was on sale for £4.99 about 3 years after its first release. I thought it would be nice to play but I wasn't expecting to get much from the game having dismissed it when it first came out as something I wouldn't normally play.
How wrong I was was. Within an hour of starting to play this game I had fallen quite dramatically down the rabbit hole and was lost in the wonderfully immersive mafia world of 1940s/50s America. The character acting is absolutely spot on and the appropriate hit music of the day blaring out of the car radio (complete with news reports and adverts) really helps with the atmosphere.
I completed it within a couple of days, though that was mainly because real life went on hold while this took over for the majority of the day and night. Unlike some other games where I would become grumpy at completing the game so quickly, Mafia 2 left me aching for more. So, I played it again almost straight away on the next difficulty setting and enjoyed it just as much (and learned a lot more about how to play the game).
My only gripe would be the lack of open play. The main story is pretty good and you do have the opportunity to go off and do some criminal activity to earn cash, but the game only saves at waypoints when you advance in the main quest storyline, so if you die after earning a load of cash from stealing cars on the side before a save point you lose all that progress. I found this a tad frustrating. It would be awesome if 2K Czech could focus predominantly on open-play (or dare I say it sand-box mmo play :O ) for Mafia 3, if there will be such a thing...

I guess in that respect, it's not exactly the game I was expecting. Even though it's a story from the perspective of a detective, The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is really more about its fantastical ideas than any grounded-in-reality detective story. So I feel as though it's better for consumers to get that picture before they dive in. The story is good in its own right, the visuals are stunning and the presentation is top notch. If you like lovecraftian, sorta unknowable evil type stories then you will almost certainly find something to enjoy here.

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is, in every sense of the word, one of the best games I've had the opportunity of playing.
The game starts off as a narration by the supporting protagonist Paul Prospero and his/our journey through the extremely beautiful Red Creek County. The story is set in Wisconsin but locations are inspired from Poland.
The game employs a creative and unique way of investigating the deaths of various characters in the ghost town. Exploring the town is eerily beautiful and is exemplified by the music backdrop, with each step you take and each location you unlock.
There's enough mystery in the game to keep you spellbound for days to come. The ending is something no one could have expected. I felt surprise, happiness, regret, and shock in a matter of minutes, thanks to the multiple plot twists. The story takes quite an unexpected turn from where it was heading. It's not at all disappointing and it only increases your affection for the game and the lead characters even more.
Some do have a problem with the story leaving many mysteries unsolved. I surely wanted to know how and why things happened the way they did, but nevertheless it's still a game that enraptures you.
You definitely cannot afford to miss this one if you're a fan of visuals, music, and compelling storylines in video games.

I almost never write reviews for games but this one is a worthy exception. This game is absolutely worth your time to play. It is perhaps one of the most brutal games i've played, not in terms of difficulty, but how everything is done within the game itself. For example when you rest you have a chance to have something bad happen to you or your party. It could be anything from losing some money (dirty magazines) to losing a party member permanently. Even in the battles you have to constantly worry because some of the bosses in the later sections of the game do have one-hit kill moves. I don't mean that they're simply out until you rest or revive them, they are just permanently killed without any warning. Normally this would suck but its a natural part of the game. It's happening to both your party members and the people around you. This doesn't matter as much to you however, as there are a large amount of allies, each with their various strengths and weaknesses that all contribute to a fight in some way. Also, the game does a great job of blending both humor and the dark narrative. You'll be laughing one moment and then cursing yourself the next.
All in all, LISA is a great game that is wildly overlooked and if you're intersted in a dark game or RPGs, you should definitely check this game out for the reasonable price of 10 bucks. The length of the game is about 10 hours give or take so you do get your money's worth out of it.

If any of this appeals to you, LISA is a must-play.

Thanks to MikeNnemonic, I was introduced to the original Lisa game a long time ago. Being a huge fan of Yume Nikki, I was in love immediately.  When I heard that Dingaling was making a new game, I was extremely excited. But this game right here... exceeded every expectation I could've ever imagined. It's that good.

Before I begin, I would like to preface this by saying that I am not biased in any way. Though the developer of the game is on my friends list, I added him after learning of and playing LISA. Do not think that I have any ties to the game beyond having played (and greatly enjoyed) it.
LISA is a story about Brad Armstrong, a single father of the last child on Earth. Our hero's quest begins when his daughter is kidnapped. During Brad's journey to save his daughter, he will encounter, battle against, and recruit many denizens of post-apocalyptia. There are over twenty unique followers, and party configuration will change depending on the player. The game allows much freedom in moral choice, survival, and friendship, and no two playthroughs are likely to be the same.
The moral choices in LISA are abrupt, intense, and weighty. Each choice forces the player to question themselves, and just how far he or she is willing to go to survive. Would you hack off an arm to save a friend? How about two arms for your precious supplies? Again and again, the player will be forced into difficult ethical dilemmas, and the proper decision is often subjective.
Party perma-death is also a factor to consider when exploring LISA's vast and open world. Many enemies can instantly kill party members seemingly without warning, and it will take ingenuity and cunning to survive encounters. Scrounging for items and supplies can often be vital, though it isn't wise to stock them up for long periods of time, seeing as they could suddenly be snatched away by an angry biker.
The combat system is original and classic at the same time. Whilst combo moves are available to some characters, and status effects are a force to be reckoned with (unlike many other recent RPGs, I might note), the general feel of combat and the layout of battle is more like a throwback to Earthbound.
In fact, the entire aesthetic of LISA is essentially an unadulterated, mature version of Earthbound's. The humor is similar as well, with many objects and enemies spouting hillarious text that brilliantly juxtaposes against the disturbing, violent art and brutal, intense music.
If this doesn't interest you, than the story will. Whilst its concept is basic (and slightly cliched), the emotions and characters portrayed in the game are relatable and imaginative. When Brad suffers through drug withdrawal and immense pain to save the one he loves and wants to protect most, the player
with him. This is the only game I have played to date where the player shares in the misery of his/her virtual counterpart.
This may all sound rather harsh, but it is made up for completely with the fun navigation and smooth combat. Finding secrets feels rewarding, and destroying a group of enemies is satisfying. Combining moves to do ludicrous damage and traversing chasms aboard a speedy bycicle is enjoyable.
's fun is difficult to deconstruct, but it works.
The soundtrack is both unique and progressive, and it completely fits the atmosphere that the game so perfectly creates. The often chilling (and sometimes beautifully melancholy) audio tracks are unlike anything previously created. Tracks in the soundtrack often encorporate metallic clangs, haunting chorus, and retro beeps to create funky, catchy, and unforgettable beats that will stay with you long after the credits have rolled.
If I have one complaint, it's that there are some technical limitations of the RPG maker engine. But honestly, this game pushed the engine to a place that seemed unreachable, so minor technical faults can be forgiven.
is an emotional rollercoaster that makes the player beg for more. It is a completely fresh, fun, and intelligent experience.

up right now. Set aside some time to play the game. Support the awesome developer that created this title. Do yourself a favor.

When I first bought KAG well over a year ago, when the game was still in alpha, I too thought it was an amazing game. However, anyone new to the game will quickly be greated by an utterly atrocious community and even worse developers. This has resulted in, as many of the negative reviews have already stated, two overwhelming problems: griefing and banning.
For starters, the devs have not implemeted, nor do they appear willing to implement, an in game mechanic which prevents members of one team from joining the enemy team during a game. This creates a situation in which there are no consequences for players who abuse the game by griefing the opposing team. As such, being the lazy developers they are, the devs have turned enforcement of in-game rules over to the community, who in turn "solved" this problem by simply banning any behaviour which can in any slight degree be regarded as griefing. The result is one of the worst experiences for a new player that I have ever witnessed. You see, as a noob, one is just learning the game and can sometimes make mistakes... big mistakes. This leads to noobs being misconstrued as griefers and subsequently being banned from servers thus adding to the already significant problem of griefing in general.
This has created an environment in which the community responds very negatively to new players and is often times unwilling to allow, or help, a noob to learn. I have been banned simply for saying that I was a noob and sorry for any mistake I have made. In a way, the community cannot be blammed for this as the experienced players have no way of telling who is actually being honest and who is a griefer, but the problem with the community still persists and has not gotten any better in the time I have played this game.
To be fair KAG is actually a very well made from a gameplay standpoint and I really do want to like it. Which is why I wrote the devs months ago to make my concerns known and to inform them that I will no longer play or promote their game in any fashion. I put alot of time into that letter, because I really do care, and apparently my time doesn't even merit a response from the devs which is why I assume they never did. Hell, they probably didn't even read it. Overall, if you can put up with being banned constantly and appealing those bans on the forums over and over again, then this game is for you. But for anyone who actually wants to play a game and not get caught up in the politics of community forums then I cannot in good conscience recommend that anyone spend their hard earned money on this game.
It should be noted that I have spent many hours in-game during alpha when the game wasn't available on steam and that my hours played as it is displayed on steam is in no way accurate. I have only played it on steam only to see if beta brought about any positive changes, which the devs have sadly failed to do.

An absolutely fantastic game and an amazing experience. I loved the Tolkien-esque journey Artyom must embark on to save his home station. While the game does feature mutants, communists, nazis, and a massive metro, ultimately the game is about a boy becoming a man, and the hidden morality system in the game does a great job of enforcing this motif.
The morality system in the game rewards or punishes the player depending on his or her actions, and even more brilliantly, without the player's knowledge. I would argue  that the morality system is also a wisdom system, as many points are rewarded from exploration and listening to other people. Through this system, the player either will or will not receive the opportunity to change the outcome of the game. If through your travels you have developed wisdom, awareness of your surroundings, and empathy, you are rewarded with choice and autonomy. If however you've proved to be ignorant the world, narrow minded, and ruthless, you do not get to choose. In this case, the ultimate decision of the game is made by your superior and you can only silently condone the decision or silently realize your guilt. But either way, you get no choice - you only follow orders.
In addition to being a story about adulthood, the game is also reflects upon the human condition. Ultimately, your actions decide what it is to be human. Are we a people who can realize mistakes, embrace the unknown, and conquer fear? Or are we cursed to repeat our mistakes and blindly attack those whom we consider hostile without a second thought? Will the people of the metro someday emerge from the darkness and embrace the future, or will they scurry in tunnels like rats until they finally finish each other off? You decide.

My perspective of Metro 2033
A faily engaging game that puts you in the shoes of a young Russian, living in the post apocolyptic metro system of Moscow, who is giving a big task for such a small person. Turns out that your adventure will take you all over the metro system and up to the surface in a daring attempt to save all the inhabitants of Metro.
I'll break it down:
The story - An in depth story. I'd say it was better than average when it comes to story telling. You meet different characters that have unique personalities and breath life into the world pretty effectivly. Some are good, some are bad. Some live and some die. I found myself liking each different character in the game for different reasons. You do have a sense of a living, albeit ugly, world that you are struggling to help survive. Think Fallout, but darker and more story driven then exploration driven. The overall story can be a bit unclear on the finer details but in the big picture however. I felt a bit unsatisfied with some of the unaswered questions that I had. It didn't ruin the experience but it did take away from the final gratification upon completing the game.
The graphics - The redux version, which I played, felt nicely pollished with effective lighting, textures, models and animations. I really didn't feel there was much lacking in the "look" of the game. To tie into the story aspect, I felt the graphics did a good job of making you feel like you're in a miserable, dark, and dangerous world. As far as performance, I ran the game on a mid range gaming laptop and it performed well throughout the game.
The sound - Gun noises where pretty good. Some of the weapons sounded a bit underwhelming to me, but that is an issue I find happens often even in AAA games. The atmospheric sound effects where also well executed. Possibly could have been better at sound effect variation in close quarters as opposed to outdoors, but that could be merely the limitations of the engine it was built on. All in all, sound effects of guns, environment, monsters, ect, where all at an exeptional level of quality.
Game mechanics - Overrall pretty standard game mechanics. You can cary 3 main weapons and a choice of auxiliary weapon like a knife or grenade. There were times that I wish that I could go prone but crouching was as low as you could go. There are a lot of key commands that I would forget from time to time because I didn't find myself using them that often, till I got to a point that I wanting to use the function and would get frustrated because I'd have to go look at the controls again. Not a big issue really. One thing however I felt could have been executed better. At a one point you are blocked by a bunch of spider webs and cannot continue. I don't remember anything in the game giving any sort of hint that the world had the interaction built in that if you light your lighter next to it, it'll go up in flames. It being a game, not everything you'd think should be interactive actually is. So in this situation, it might have saved me undue frustration had there been a "Hey, burn that s**t with your lighter." or anything! Before that point, I don't think I even used my lighter as your flashlight is much more effective. I think they added the lighter so that you could see your objectives note book in the dark. Cool idea, but not used very often as it wasn't very necessary. I went through more than half the game without looking at that notebook even once. This is because this game is linear. A function like the objectives marker is more effective in an open world environment. Not a linear, story driven experience. Still, these quips were minor setbacks and oversights. The game mechanics were good otherwise.
The take away - I'd say that if you like the idea of a game that functions like Call of Duty and Fallout had a baby and you want a cool, dark story to go along with it, you should consider buying this game. If this game is on sale, just buy it. It's worth the money.

God damn this game is beautiful. Breaktaking graphics that remind you Unreal Engine is capable of a LOT more outside of all those first person shooters with low resolution scaled textures, blocky maps, and generic gunplay. Both the redux and original version look gorgeous but the Redux has a touch that makes it feel more photorealistic rather than just "pretty game graphics." The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is essentially a walking simulator where the player can interact with objects and/or solve puzzles. Walking through some areas will trigger narration. The game has no instructions, only a semi linear map (I say semi because there are wide open areas with just nothing including an upwards climb into a clearing with a view of the valley but has no impact on the story whether you decide to visit it or not). Great eye candy that you can just get lost in if you don't feel like "playing" the game. Well worth the money as it comes with both the original and redux. Had to remind myself to stop taking screenshots and to immerse myself into the game LOL!
For lower end machines, you can still run original with quality settings, for hardcore gaming PCs, Redux is the way to go. I can only run Redux with 150% texture scaling (this is super scaling btw) and with the highest AA settings and it still runs pretty well (40-50 fps so long term play causes eye strain, turning texture scaling down to 100% and no AA will probably raise the FPS to a consistent 50+). Also I'd recommend turning on the camera smoothing option and raising FOV as that helps with motion sickness.

Holy crap, this game gave my mind the biggest ♥♥♥♥♥♥. I played the Redux version, and beat the whole game in one sitting, 4 and a half hours without a break. This game is that immersive. The atmosphere is so perfect and strong. Each event just makes you want to push forward more to see how the story will unfurl. The mechanics are pretty unique and interesting, sensing clues and such. Not sure if I like their creative choice on the ending, it kinda alters the feel of the rest of the game prior, I guess they were trying to go for a shocker twist, but it just kind of became "meh." Still interesting to figure out how earlier clues reference the ending. I also find it kind of cringy that they had to start the game with a screen that says "This is a narrative exploration game that does not hold your hand." So we need to be told when games don't hold our hand? I think we can see that for ourselves when we play. Although it makes it sound like this game is hard, which it is far from. Imagine popping in Ninja Gaiden and the first screen said "This game is very very difficult. There is BS enemy spawning and we're not going to let you have a moment of security. Because the game is difficult. It's hard."
I installed the non-redux version of the game to speedrun it now that I knew the story (took me just one hour), and I was surprised to find that the Redux version actually ran better on my computer, and I was playing on medium settings in that version, while the original version I had to set almost everything to low settings and I was still getting frequent framerate drops. So I would recommend sticking to the redux version, it's prettier and easier to run it seems. Also in the original version it didn't give me the Depression achievement even though I did solve Travis's murder. What's that all about?

Imagine for me this: You take the post-apocalyptic setting of Fallout but instead of guns you use fists and farts to deal damage. Then after that stir in the perversion and eccentricism of Mad Max and Escape from New York; finally bake to a tender juicy finish with the melodramatic insanity of A Boy and His Dog. That's LISA.
LISA is the type of game that doesn't come along often, especially from an indie developer. Having just scratched the surface of this game with only 8 hours of gameplay, I am confident to say that it holds its own amongst indie superstars Braid and LIMBO. The introduction alone is worth the price of admission, as it weaves a convincing story in the first five minutes of (near silent) game play than all of Twilight does throughout three films. As the player follows LISA's protagonist through a heartbreaking adventure full of perverts, drugs, and combat, he or she will find it hard to pull away from both the narrative and the gameplay.
If I had anything remiss to say about LISA it would be that sometimes the combat can seem repetitive, or the side scrolling back and forth to make sure you have explored every possible route can become tedious for the neurotic gamer, but LISA manages to mix up the perfect concoction of humor and unique combat to spin a dark and twisted post-apocalyptic tale unlike many modern games have ever done.

LISA has...changed me.
I use to be a normal teenage girl before I was sucked into the sticky black tar of Joy that is this game.
I was encased in it.
Molded by it.
Until I emerged a man...
...A very lonely and perverted man who would only wear shirts that ended above my nipples...
But a man never the less!
I don't remember much of my old life but, to some degree, I feel whole.
For those of you who don't think of that as reason enough to also get in the tar, you're the one who is really missing out.
LISA has to be one of the best RPGs on the market. Everything that was put into this works so well together to make an experience that is worth playing at least once (even if there is more than enough reason to play multiple times).
The game's art and soundtrack are amazing and go hand in hand. Both are relatively weird but so enjoyable that you want to keep going just to see what's next.
The World the devs made is awesome and filled with amazingly enjoyable characters, especially the party members. Each of them has their own distinct appeal and abilities that make them all so wonderful and distinct. Some highlights include (SPOILER)
. These characters, and more, you will meet and find the ones you appreciate the most.
