I would like to recommend this game, really, but the final act totally ruins the experience, bringing everything to a grinding halt for what is otherwise a humor and story driven game.
It's got fair-to-ok humor, lots of jokes that reminded me of the old Diskworld games, especially with the narrator interactions. However the humor is clearly targeting men, as the jokes are mostly physical humor, denigration and toilet laughs. Samuel literally pisses all over himself, and repeatedly vomits as a function of the game, which often comes across as lazy humor.
As you go through the tasks, you'll find that each act gives you the intro controls to a task before you have to perform. You'll have the chance to fail without consequence, before being put to the task. There are several mini-bosses, whom defeating is a task of memorization of attack sequences, and appropriate responses, however most bosses are only two or three stage ordeals, which the stage prepared you for by teaching the skills needed; like how to use a shield or a weapon. Generally the acts move along at a good clip, without getting bogged down in too many repetitive tasks, or punishments for awkward controls.
But then there's the final boss, where it really falls apart.
In no uncertain terms, the final boss is an absolute mess. You have to contend with a timed button pressing slider, utilized only a handful time times previously in the game, which seems to lag to respond as I could not get a reliable 'sweet spot' on the slider button press. Plus I was expecting more than 'memorize this' as the final boss fight, which was dissapointing and frustrating.
However the biggest sin of the final boss fight is how dull and boring it is. Even in the immediately previous minion fight there was quips and some attempt at humor to break up the repetition of the manual actions of combat. However the final boss fight is void of humor, narration, or anything to break up the 'try, try, try again' design of the fight.
The game is entertaining for the most part. It  does a good job of being forgiving and providing a ramped up learning curve as the game progresses. The grannies in the car stage was one of the funniest moments for me. But you will run into a wall on the final boss, and you will bang your head against that wall.
In the end the level of frustration the game presented was, for me, not equal to the level of enjoyment. This is certainly going into my 'done with' category, and I would recommend it only to those who enjoy this kind of humor, and are willing to bull through the controls on the final boss. If you don't like the humor, or controls, in the first fifteen minutes, then you will not like this game.

I'm sorry that the least good aspect about this game is the story. For me, this aspect matters the most. 80% of the events and facts are left unexplained. All you know about is that Ethan and his family are affected by an evil force. But why and how it happened? Who or what it is this evil force? The game doesn't want you to know. It wants you to stroll through beautiful scenery until you go:
"Uh, oh, a murder! I'll use my supernatural instincts to visualize what happened and ask no questions."
You walk around some more, looking at branches, rocks, dirt, and go again: "Uh, oh, another murder! How nice!".
The only and truly wonderful thing about this game is its visual graphics. It is the only reason I hit recommend. If you want a much more deeper narrative experience, I don't recommend playing it.

The game works up until a certain point and then just stops, as such. I used internal clock glitches, skipping probably well over a year of time and barely anything was changed. Yet I still persevered, but after it was clear I would earn very little extra from this, I stopped playing.
After a good amount of months I returned to find that I had a lot of offline earning (Well, as much as the 20 day cap would allow, but ok) and I restarted with the boosts that you are likely familiar with like AdCap's Angel system. When it became accessible, thank christ it was somewhat fair and playable. After the event, however, the Game of Stoned is still glitched and the main game is still only growing at a snail's pace.

This might be one of my favorite games. Ever. So I feel obligated to write a review.
The style is great. I'm huge on pixel graphics, but that aside I love the way everything looks, from the people to the backgrounds to the weird, unsettling Joy mutants. Almost every enemy you encounter has a unique sprite, keeping the combat fresh despite some trite mechanics. The soundtrack is also GREAT, I'm always getting the themes from this game stuck in my head.
Even though LISA is not huge in scope, exploration is always rewarding. There are so many weird and interesting places to find. I'm on my second playthrough right now and I'm still finding new things.
Another great thing about LISA is its humor. It comes in many shades: wacky, dark, crude, and often off-color, I guarantee there's something to split every side. However, LISA does a great job balancing humor with sobriety. Without spoiling anything, the game explores topics such as abuse and addiction with nuance. The game also does a good job creating a solid antihero. By the end, you as the player are forced to question whether the protagonist's aims are truly noble or if they're actually selfish, a question I'm still left unsure of how to answer. LISA manages to be both funny and heartbreaking, which isn't an easy feat to achieve.
The only real problem with the game is that the emphasis put on the importance of player choice in the trailers and descriptions is a little misleading. There were not as many choices as I was led to believe there would be, though I still enjoyed and was challenged by the choices I was presented with. It's delightful, in a strange way, when your choices have very concrete consequences on you, your party, and even the world, so that you're left by the end wanting more.
As I mentioned, the combat system is also nothing to write home about, with the most notable feature being unique abilities between characters and the ability to do combos, essentially extra damage. You also have withdrawal as a unique status effect. Choosing to lose your limbs permanently alters your stats, which is also pretty unique albeit frustrating at times. Occasionally the combat is difficult but after a while it mostly just becomes about oiling your enemies up and exploiting the resulting weakpoint with fire-based attacks or firebombs. It's pretty cut-and-dry, but if you're playing RPGs you're probably pretty used to combat systems being less-than-innovative at this point.
Overall I cannot recommend this game enough! You will like it if you enjoy games like Earthbound/Mother and OFF. Please check it out, totally worth it.

I used to play the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of Alien Swarm, and if you've played and liked that, get helldivers. There's your TLDR, so now lets move on to the actual review.
When you start up the game, you're met with a cinematic explaining the setting and situation. Following that, you'll go into training, where you'll learn the basics of the game; including the fact that a small mistake can mess you up BAD. Following training, you'll be sent into the field to fight the enemy on various planets. starting off, you have only one gun: the liberator, as well as a sidearm. The liberator is a very solid weapon, and there aren't really any direct upgrades to it later on. Each of the guns is unique, even if some are far better than others. There are a few kinds of planets you can fight on, each having their own specific characteristics. snow planets will slow down your walking (except for a few small areas), forest planets have puddles of water that will slow you down, desert planets have wide open spaces and narrow canyons between mountains/hills, and volcanic planets are usually black rock with geysers of lava spewing out of them; which will damage you until you get downed. There are 3 enemy factions you can face, the Cyborgs: communist robot ISIS, the Illuminates: mysterious, technologically advanced monks, and the Bugs: starship troopers: electric boogaloo. each of these factions have different kinds of scouts, that function in similar but different ways. I'd say the Illuminates probably have the most annoying scouts, because they're really hard to see until they spot you, are un-impedded by snow and water, and can move quite quickly. Each of these factions also has different units that they send after you, with different ways of deploying those units (but each of these ways are functionally the same). The Bugs will un-burrow around you, the Cyborgs will drop in from low planetary orbit, and the Illuminates will teleport onto the battlefield. The enemies that are sent at you vary in how annoying and how deadly they are, as well as what it takes to defeat them (keep in mind that hellpods can kill ANYTHING if you time and target them right). When you're dropped onto a planet, you have a list of objectives to complete, which you can see in the map at the start of the mission. You're allowed to spawn ANYWHERE on the map, even right on top of objectives. So why wouldn't you? Because enemy patrols are more frequent around objectives, you're safer the farther you are from them. On very low difficulties, you should have no problem with spawning on objectives, but on higher difficulties, you're gonna want to spawn somewhere really isolated so you have time to get all your support strategems in. After your objectives are complete, you need to head to the extraction zone, where you'll activate a beacon that will call in a dropship to pick you up. You board this dropship simply by running into the sides where the doors are. After about 15 seconds, or when everyone is in, the dropship will take off, and you'll be treated to a victory screen, where all of your experience and statistics are tallied up, so you can jerk yourself off to how accurate you were and how many kills you got. At the end of these missions, you're sent back to the bridge of your ship, where you can spend the technology points you earn by collecting scientific samples on the missions, as well as customize you outfit and read information about the aliens you just shot, stabbed, burned, and exploded. You're then able to continue your missions on the planet you were just on, or abandon that planet, lose it's planetary reward, and move to a different one. One last bit of advice, if you see a "retaliatory strike" mission, do NOT go to that planet, no matter the reward. That kind of mission is basically impossible, and you will rage hard trying to beat them.

I've enjoyed this title a lot, the variety of weapons and accessories leaves you with a lot of options in how you want to tackle the mission at hand, granted more freedom is given if you play with a group. The single player experience is very unforgiving, especially when it comes to suboptimal loadouts.
At the same time some of the most frustrating elements about the game can be the players seeing as how the screen is shared amongst the entire team all it takes sometimes is one person running off and locking everyone down. Learning to play around bad teammates was probably one of the most enjoyable parts of the game for me personally, simply another difficulty factor.
I would argue that, some of the DLC is very useful bordering on too good. Such as the terrain expert perk letting you ignore the mechanic which is meant to make snow maps difficult.
Besides that one DLC the rest is very much just more variety for your loadout and/or appearance should you desire.
Another drawback for the people starting to play the game is that the galactic campaign system doesn't do itself any favours as unlocking abilities require you to play particular planets from each enemy and in some instances those can be unaccessible for extended periods of time depending on the current War.
The game isn't without its problems but overall I think it is a very enjoyable experience.

Metro 2033 has been one of my favorite games so far that have been story driven. I rarely tend to play story driven linear games, my prefrence being towards open world games or strategy games, but this game took my intrest. I've played it through twice now (even though I said I wouldn't after finishing the library) and I have to say I love it.
The main reason for this is atmosphere, the game really puts you into the universe with ease and it makes you truly care for just about every character, and makes you feel as Artyom does throughout the game. On top of that the game makes you truly think as playing on Ranger mode is not forgiving at all for mistakes.
With this said there a few problems.
The Library mission can not be ignore as one of the most difficult, terrifying, and infuriating moments of the game. Even though this breaks immersion, I highly highly suggest you look up a walkthrough of this section, if you dont wish to, dont say I didnt warn you but I will tell you this as it isnt made obvious anywhere as far as I've been able to tell.
In the first section look at them and do not move until theyve turned to walk away, and if they dont turn to walk away walk out of their way, they shouldnt attack you although, trust me, be on your guard. In the second section (where you see the black librarian which isnt a spoiler) try to stay stealthy, there is very little room to manuver in these areas, and the librarians are significantly more hostile. I can't not explain how long this section can take if you do not do this.
The next bit is the endings. The endings themselves are fantastic, both are very intresting and make you think upon your actions, however, there are problems. The way you get the moral points (which is an amazing system and much better than the simple choose x or b for good vs bad ending) is difficult to understand and can be extremely frustrating. There have been occasions where doing everything right has given people the bad ending (although dont be mad thats the one following the canon).
Its also very aggravating that the ending isnt more clear on what to do,
The final thing is that the game is in some cases buggy. I do not know how problematic this is for other people, but near the end when you are moving through the watchmen herd in the tunnel, I have experienced a bug where it will spawn a watchman on me and that will instantly kill me, if this happens go back to the main menu and restart the mission. I havent found a fix to this.
Outside of these problems I have immensly enjoyed the game and began reading the book because of it  (which is different enough to the game to make them both extremely intresting), as well as create a similar design for kiev metro. I can not recommend this game higher, and I have even bought this game for friends for them to enjoy. All in all a totally worth while purchase.

Second playthrough:
I encounter a pirate taking advantage of some poor defenseless civilians on some world...
I decide to be the hero.
I eradicate the pirate scum, however during the battle my medbay catches on fire!
I send ensign Willow and Dolan into the fray to put out the fires.
The battle is intense, yet seems manageable at first. Then, the fire catches on in the door control room, so I send the pilot, Hector, to assist.
Both Willow and Dolan begin suffering from smoke inhalation and 3rd degree burns, so I tell them to get the hell out of there! Hector is also beginning to lost the fight with the flames, so I have him run back into the cockpit.
As I try to figure out, wtf do I do now?... the fire catches on in the sensor room. In a short time I can no longer see any room on the ship other than those occupied by the horrified crew. It seems as if the end is here, after only 2 missions, when Hector gets the bright idea "Hey, what if we turn off the oxygen systems!" (You see, the rooms were not adjacent to the airlock, and even if they were, the door control room was destroyed so there was no possibility to remotely access them anyway.)
Such a brilliant idea! It put out the fires! Then hector goes in to repair the medbay, with only 6 hp, and because, idk, maybe the fire accelerated the rate at which the oxygen was drained from that room, he suffocates and dies. But at least his dying words informed the rest of the crew that the plan indeed worked. Hector died a hero.
Knowing the risks at this point, Willow waited until the O2 systems restored life support throughout the ship before going in to repair the medbay. After Willow and Dolan rocevered from their wounds, they finished repairing the rest of the ship.
Now it is time to hold an honorable funeral for Hector.

*Before I start the review, I will note that I spent more time than what is actually displayed since most of my time was using an .exe file of the plus patch that wasn't on my steam list.*
If one was looking for a good CRPG to play, VTMB is a recommendation. I do recommend using at least the latest unofficial patch there is with just the bug fixes and not the plus content if one wants to play the least buggiest version that stays close to the original release. What makes this CRPG good is the replayability, not just in choices like sneaking through a vent or shooting down thugs in a room but also in the different abilities each vampire clan has along with what makes some of the clans unique to others such as the appearance of the Nosferatu or the insanity of the Malkavians.
The only cons to mention on the game is the fact that it has its share of bugs which most fan-patches at this point have fixed (with one said series of fan-patches having a plus option to add in some new fan-made content).

If you play RPGs not only for incredible loot and skill tree leveling, but also for the sake of role-playing a character and taking in the atmosphere, this is the game for you. While you do gain experience, and unlock new abilities, the skill tree will be unfamiliar to those not already versed in White Wolf's pen and paper games. Also, there is very little gear, whether dropped or bought and it almost feels scripted. You get to a new place, and get a new weapon or armor, at the same time on every character you make. The only other bad point i'll touch on is the combat system. While it's fun hacking away in melee, and the vampire powers you get to back your fighting skills are top-notch visually and mechanically, if you specialize in guns, expect to have a REALLY hard time until about halfway through the game, even if your ranged skill is high. On top of that, even when your wielding a trusty baseball bat knocking some punk to the floor, you literally have to wait for them to get up to strike again as the hit-boxes don't register when they are prone. But those a few minor annoyances, and really aren't the spirit of the game. You can get through many missions without physical confrontation if you are socially inclined, or can make people magically go insane. The characters you meet all have a story and each one's personality might clash with another or even yourself. It's a great opportunity to really role-play a vampire and a must have for anyone looking for more than a run-through guns blazing type of game.

After modding to be a reasonably attractive cel-shaded game, VTMB is pretty good. It is a little overhyped, but it has good story, good characters, and good music. Gameplay is kind of weak, though.
Tip: Get good weapons, you'll fight a lot.

*Many people say to get the unofficial patches.  The first playthrough I did of this game was without the patches and it was fine--still a good game--but the patches are necessary if you want a GREAT game and a more full experience, as they do restore more than a fair amount of stuff that was originally cut from the game.
This game, honestly, is one of the few I can say I've gone back and played over and over... and over and over again.  The only others I've done that with were Morrowind, Fallout: New Vegas, and this PS2 game called Romancing SaGa: Minstrel Song.  It's not a new game by any means either, which just goes to show that "new" doesn't always mean "good."
The story is enthralling, and holds up well with the lore established in the original table top games.  The Camarilla can be imposing and haughty or friendly and righteous depending on how you play, and I like that aspect of it.  You can't play as all the clans in the books, but that's not too big of a deal (though I do regret not being able to make a Tzimisce ;n; ).  The clans that are present are fairly well fleshed out, though I definitely recommend getting the unofficial patch that way you can access histories in order to add more depth to the characters from each clan that you may choose to make.
The graphics, honestly, are pretty good for a game from its time.  Not the same as today's graphics, but LaCroix looks fairly attractive (just kidding... not really.  But truly, the graphics are nice).
The music is a huge plus for me, being an avid fan of 90s/early 2000s goth music.  I highly recommend looking up the soundtrack, as I imagine the vocal tracks may not be everyone's cup of tea, but overall the instrumental tracks lend a gritty--but oddly, at the same time, soothing--feel to the atmosphere of the game (particularly the Santa Monica theme, in my opinion).
Another big plus is that you don't, by any means, need a high end computer to run it.  I have an HP15 laptop with a pentium graphics card and it runs very smoothly.  This is, of course, likely due to the age of the game, but still.
Overall, it's a great experience, with some truly horror themed quests as well as some that go more towards a drama--and sometimes even comedic--theme.  If you're interested in vampires, ghosts, demons, and any other sort of supernatural creatures in video games, then I highly recommend it.  Or if you're just looking for a fun RPG to spend some time in!

The first thing that comes to mind - the game is pretty. The outdoor environments are fantastic (indoors are much less extraordinary). I played the "Redux" version of this game. It's the same game, but re-compiled with the Unreal 4 engine. Even though Steam says I've only played this game for a few minutes, I actually have about 5 hours in.
I really enjoyed this game. The closest game that I can compare this to (that I've played) is Firewatch. Like Firewatch, it's all about the narrative. In essence, it's a walking simulation where you explore the world to solve mysteries. Where it differs from Firewatch is that it completely lacks any sort of hand-holding, in-game tutorials, or "hints" as to what you're supposed to do next. There is an extremely interesting narrative, but it only reveals itself as you piece it together. It's not a "ride" by any stretch. Where Firewatch is generally light-hearted, introspective, structured, and occasionally poignant, The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is dark, somewhat disturbing, organic, yet unquestionably beautiful.
Unlike some other walking simulator games, The Vanishing of Ethan Carter actually does require you to solve things, not just "discover" them. It rewards thorough investigation while creating enough variety so that it really doesn't get boring. I'd love to say more about the story, but I don't want to spoil anything. All I can say is that you're trying to solve the disappearance of a boy by retracing steps and events that occured in this very scenic mountain setting. The journey is intriguing, shocking, and immersive.
Things to consider: the lack of hand-holding, at times, was confusing. There would literally be 30 minute blocks of time where I was running around, not really knowing what to do or where to go next. I found myself retracing my path several times to finish pieces of the story that I hadn't finished. That's because I didn't realize their significance until later. This isn't necessarily a bad thing, but be prepared to think and explore pretty thoroughly to get through this game. There are no maps, no compasses, and no objectives. I started on mouse/keyboard, but the controller support was nice after a while. This is the type of game where you want to kick back, take your time, and take it all in. If you can, plan to play through the entire game in one or two sittings. You should be able to finish it in 3-5 hours. Beer helps too

This game is very bi-polar, it's a beautiful game, very asthetically pleasing, very immersive and historical. The gameplay captures the strategy and tactics, and the feel of World War 2. However the game mechanics involve a lot of really annoying RNG and unrealistic features, especially when it comes to the British.
Lelic has secret documents revealing that the Bofors AA gun can fire High velocity shells as an artillery suppressive barage, because logic.
Secret documents also reveal that the Germans did not execute the Mentally ill, no instead they trained them as tank crews.
Other secret documents show features that no one but Relic knows about history like...
-the Vickers, (a WW1 machine gun) was apparently the best machine gun of World War 2.
-British emplacements can "brace" making the people in them completely invincible no matter how much you set them on fire or blow them up. #realism
-The Churchill was actually just as well armored as a King Tiger, so the British can get a faster equivalent of a tiger, but it also has a flamethrower that kills all infantry in a 25 meter radius instantly, making it invulnerable.
-The AVRE has better armor than a sturm tiger, and also has the same blast radius when it fires (even tho it didn't IRL) and it can move faster, also doesn't have to stop when it reloads (but the sturm tiger does)
-The German Pak 43 emplacement can shoot through buildings and hedgerows, apparently the Germans had rail gun superlaser technology.
-The Comet Tank was barely produced in WW2, but in this game it's the backbone of the British, it's the strongest medium tank in the game, by far. There is not a single German heavy tank I would want more than the Comet Tank, it's as well armored as a panther, but can throw grenades at infantry, and do emergency wartime speed, turning it into an invincible race car.
-RNG in this game is really bad, makes for scenarios in which a T-34 will beat a Panther in a 1v1 (this actually happened to me) which shouldn't happen because panther's are twice as expensive (and the Germans literally built them to counter allied tanks like the T-34)
-RNG will also screw you over with indirect fire, especially as Germany, because of your small 4 man squads, and the fact that they really like to all clump up, RNG will often cause a mortar or rocket artillery to instantly squad wipe your men.
-Hit boxes in the environment are terrible, after a buidling gets destroyed it's hitboxes are still up, resulting in incredibly annoying incidents such as a bombing run that doesn't hit the men you targeted, instead it hits the invisible building and the bombs literally explode from impacting the air (has happened to me several times and can ruin a game.
-The Oberkommando West was actually a late-war German army but in this game they don't get the MG 42, they only get the MG 34, and all of the Allied MGs are better, even though all of the Allied MGs are from WW1 and the German ones were the best ones in actual history.
-last but not least pathfinding, it's not just the German tanks who's crews are mentally ill, every tank in this game struggles to figure out how to drive, often doing things like randomly deciding to confront an enemy tank by reversing into it and asking to get it's engine destroyed instantly. Or when you ask it to reverse out of a hot spot, it decides to do a random 360 for no reason, and then reverse, and in most cases it will be destroyed in the time it takes to turn around. The worst is when there are two tanks within the same square mile, they are bound to run into eachother and then take the next 10 minutes to figure out how to get around eachother, so most of the time they will stop and continue to turn back and forth, failing to actually go wherever you told them to, and likely dying while they sit there uselessly.
-infantry pathfinding is appalling too, first of all there are many glitches in which infantry will get stuck on a clump of trees just because the obstacle boxes on the environment are way too bug, even though visually it looks like it would be perfectly possible for the infantry to get out of there. Support teams like mortar and MG crews will often wait 5-10 seconds to pack up their weapons and retreat, which means they will often sit there under fire or literally standing in a field of lava from incendiary artillery, but won't reatreat as you told them too until after they are dead. Infantry also sometimes continue in their state of "retreat" even after they get back to your base, so you can't use them for the rest of the game and they are just sitting there hogging up population. The retreat pathing is the single most appalling thing in the game. The retreat pathing is so simple even I could have coded it, all infantry do when you tell them to retreat is take the closest path toward your base, which means in a lot of cases they will "retreat" toward the enemies that are shooting at them. I'm sure you can imagine how well that ends up going.
For a game that has so much potential to represent the feel of World War 2 combat, this game fails, there's so many gameplay nuisances that make this game geared much more toward luck than skill. Which is not the way an RTS should be. World War 2 certainly had a lot of RNG involved realistically, but not to this extreme, there were reasons besides pure luck and unrealisitc ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that the Allies won, but that's not simulated in this game.
Despite my constant bashing on how OP allied factions are , I'm not biased, I don't actually just play Germans even though that's what it looks like, I have extensive experience in my 400 hours playing with all 5 of the factions, and the U.S. is my favorite, but the game is way too unbalanced that I don't enjoy either side, I feel like a hacker playing as the invincible British, and even the Germans have really annoying things they can do like building the Pak 43 rail cannon that can phase through buildings. I'm tired of dealing with how annoying the gameplay features, bugs, and RNG is in this game, don't look at my time played, it's 400 hours too many, I'm uninstalling the game, wish I could get my money back.

I got Manual Samuel off Humble Bundle for half price.  I saw people complaining about length but they got four or five hours of it, so that can't be that bad, can it?  That's a dollar an hour.
So now that I have it an played it, how is it?
Well the video set me up for a somewhat humorous game filled with a decent number of mini games.  I kept hearing people compare this to QWOP, that old browser game and that comparison works.
This game is a bit like QWOP, a bit.  The problem is it is an easier version of QWOP, In 90 minutes I was able to beat the game, and I tried looking for "dying".  There's no "Failure" at all, given enough hours almost anyone can beat this game.  The problem there is there's no sense of accomplishment with the game, you just play through the story.
So ok, how about the story?  The trailer above is pretty funny, right?  Great idea, tons of potential.  I agree 100 percent.  And then you play the game and kind of wonder.  "Where's the stuff from the trailer."  Don't get me wrong those scenes are in the game, but in the lukewarm script they're not that funny, in fact I'd say those are some of the funniest scenes in the game.  The idea that Death wants to be a skater goes on too far, and Sam barely talks, so it's all the narrator and Death saying random things.
There's a "running joke" where instead of &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; people say "Feces".  It's clever the first time, but it gets old fast, and they keep using that joke.  The same joke is used maybe five times in a 90 minute game.  Consider that is once every 18 minutes.
The difficulty of the game DOES take a huge jump for the final boss, which is a bit of a "Yay" moment until you realize there's again no true difficulty as failing has no penalty.  I spent maybe 20 minutes on the final boss, that's close to a fourth of my play time, but the entire battle is just repetitive pattern recognition.
I wanted to like the game, it's a great interesting idea, but the problem is Manual Samuel wants to be a funny story.  It's not that funny, but it's also not a lot of story.  A shame, because the idea of the game in the pitch of the game was likely very good, but the final product?  It's just repetitive monotony for the most part, rather than a really clever game.   A shame, because a guy forced to manually control his body functions could be funny.. but that's the key.  It COULD.  Manual Samuel isn't that game.
Is it awful?  Nah, I've played worse, and there's a few fun moments in the game, but after the first real stage, the game doesn't do too much more.   Darn.  And after about 20 minutes I got most of the achievements.  I only reached 3 hours of play time waiting for the final card drop.   A game so short, I had to leave it running for a card drop... wow.

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter was a pretty big let down for me. I had heard that it was a terrific game, so I really looked forward to playing it. However, I went into it with the wrong perspective, mostly because I saw some people mention "Walking Simulator" when talking about the game. This game is not a Walking Sim. It's an open world adventure title with puzzles to find.
My first problem with this game is that the mechanics aren't effectively hinted at. I understand that the game says that it won't hold your hand, but when I hear the phrase "no handholding", I expect there to be somewhat difficult or tricky puzzles that requires some thinking to figure out. The problem with this game is that the puzzles from a logic standpoint aren't especially difficult when you actually know what you're doing; instead, the difficult part is that you have to kind of stumble into some things in order to understand the mechanics of the game. Don't get me wrong, the mechanics are fun when you understand what you're supposed to do - what is not fun is stumbling around for two hours in a really big, open world without a good way to actually know what you're supposed to be solving.
My second problem is the world. It's really, really big, and it is pretty much empty aside from the hidden sidepuzzles you, again, have to stumble into in order to find. The sidepuzzles feel like timewasters, hidden only to get you to wander around and in the end being pretty pointless for the general story (not completely, but enough for their existence to not be justifiable).
My third problem is the mine maze. Anyone who've played it probably knows why.
Basically, I spent the game being angry and feeling like the game wanted to just ♥♥♥♥ with me by design. I finished the game with a walkthrough, and I would recommend using one for the first puzzle you encounter if you can't solve it, just to get a hang of the mechanics for the rest of the game. Also recommended for the bloody mine maze.
Anyhow, you might be wondering why I recommend this game. Well, it's mainly because of the main story and its puzzles that, when you know the mechanics, are pretty enjoyable and fun to solve. The theme is pretty great, the conclusion is somewhat satisfying, and the mechanics themselves are imaginative and feel good and logical to use (again, once you figure them out). I think the story is worth the journey, it's compelling, has a creative premise and does keep you guessing until the end. With that said, not everything about it is perfect, but it's pretty damn good nonetheless. There are a lot of good things in the game; the problem is simply that they're hidden so well.
The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is hit and miss, but when it hits, it does hit pretty hard. Play it if you will; if you don't, it's not that big of a deal to miss out on it.

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a horror game for people who hate horror games. There is only one section with anything that could be remotely called a jump-scare – the game is designed to give the player a consistent sense of unease, not to startle them or produce short moments of terror.
The Vanishing of Ethan Carter concerns an introverted teenager, the titular Ethan Carter, who is constantly belittled and criticized by his family. With no one to talk to at his home in the mining town of Red Creek Valley, Carter starts a correspondence with a paranormal investigator, Paul Prospero. Prospero quickly realizes that, beneath the human evil in Red Creek Valley, is something deeper and more malevolent. Taking the role of Paul Prospero, you try to find out what happened to Ethan and his family after arriving in Red Creek Valley to find a trail of corpses.
In terms of gameplay, The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a walking simulator/puzzle game where you explore the eerily beautiful town of Red Creek Valley and investigate a series of murders which happened within. To accomplish this, you find objects involved in the murder, return them to their original positions, and order the scenes produced by using your psychic abilities on the victim’s body.
Virtually the entire five hours I spent playing this game was on the Vanishing of Ethan Carter Redux, the Unreal Engine 4 remake that comes free with every copy of the Vanishing of Ethan Carter.
Even if you don’t enjoy horror games, you might enjoy the Vanishing of Ethan Carter. The game is as much a tragedy as it is a horror game, telling the downfall of an economically-depressed family who had the misfortune to be born in a town with no future.

"This game is a narrative experience that does not hold your hand." That's the first thing that you see in this game, and frankly, it's the game's undoing. The game started out strong, and had an interesting concept. You play as a detective investigating the dissapearance of this kid named Ethan Carter after he reaches out to you for help. It started out good enough, with me solving the railroad murder fairly quickly, just giving me a glimpse of what the game had to offer. The graphics were breathtaking, and the game ran like a charm. I followed all the "hints" left by the developer in order to get to the end of the game, only for the only door in the scene to still be locked. A quick online search revealed that I had actually missed 3 of the game's "scenes", and I had to go back and solve them if I wanted to finish the game. See, if the game had let me end the game right then and there, I wouldn't have had an issue, and would have rated it 8/10 or so.
The first scene I missed takes place
where your character spawns at the beginning of the game. Really, behind! Nobody is going to spawn into this game, and think that the first place that they have to go is behind them, and not follow the railroad track so clearly marked in front of them. Thing is, this scene was meant to be the tutorial, yet the developers didn't make it optional, meaning that I had to slog all the way back to the beginning of the game in order to beat it.
The second and third scenes just emphasized how bad the game design in this game is. After solving the murder scene at the train tracks, I picked up on a hint that told be to go to location A. At location A, I picked up on a hint to go to location B, then C, and so on. Any new player who spawns into the game would think that they were going the right way, that the developers meant for them to follow this path. Yet, halfway between A and B, there would be a scene of to side,
of the walking path that you had been following. Honestly, nobody is actually going to go there, because they wouldn't expect anything to be there! It's just bad game design all around.
When a game says that they won't hold your hand, you still have to impose some restrictions. Don't let them get to the end of the game, and not be able to finish. If your game is really a good game, the players shouldn't have to look up a guide in order to finish it. The developers tried to do something new, stray away from the gaming conventions we know and love. While originality is new, there's a reason why we still have those conventions, and the devs failed to realize that.

A breathtaking 'narrative experience which does not hold your hand' as the opening title displays,
not only does what it promises but also excels at crafting a fantastic world and intriguing story for the player to discover.
On my continued journey through the 'walking simulator' genre, there was a game with raving reviews that I somehow got in a bundle and never had a chance to play. In retrospect I might regret not playing the game sooner but on the other hand, good things come to those who wait and boy this game was an absolute delight.
Visually, is without a doubt, one of the most beautiful games I've ever had the joy to play through. Majestic landscapes, brilliant light effects, captivating scenery, runs smooth as butter, the photo-realistic power of the Unreal Engine 4 really shows it's tremendous capabilities here. I could praise the graphics of the game all day long but the fact of the matter is that the pure eye candy of the game only strengthens the already majestically immersive atmosphere of the game's world.
The soundtrack and ambient music are exquisite to say the least and the change in tone and tempo is a great tool for foreshadowing the various events that will take place in the game. The music tracks are not constant, which is a great thing in my opinion, and when they're there they set a great theme for the player to enjoy.
The gameplay is fairly simple. You're Paul Prospero, a detective out in the wilderness on a mission to find little boy Ethan Carter. As you unravel the mystery, you'll be faced with several puzzles which you need to solve to progress through the plot. Mind you, some of them can be skipped but I see no reason to do so since they're fairly easy and they don't inhibit the flow and fun of the game in any way. If anything the unique nature of the gameplay, adds a very well executed otherworldly element to the story and it ties the characters and the overall narrative in a great way.
I won't spoil the story itself cause I believe in this genre it is the core of a successful game so naturally you must experience it for yourself.
The Vanishing of Ethan Carter has a perfect blend of childlike imagination, eerie and horror atmospheres, fantastic graphics and fitting soundtrack, some achievement hunting and all enclosed in a 3 hour trip which you will not regret. Fans of different types of gaming genres, like adventure/mystery/puzzle/walking simulators,
skip on this experience; a definite recommendation.

One sentence summary:  A wonderful widget game
Manual Samuel is a creative, well executed and very original 'widget' game.  Multiple solutions for various problems, a great deal of silliness, and it rewards experimentation, good play and blantant stupidity which means it's fun no matter how you play the game.  Since you can't die, you're free to abuse Samuel in a variety of ways and see how they change the outcome of the story, including at least one interseting Easter-egg-turned-brick-joke-turned-trick.
The premise is simple:  Samuel's been switched to manual mode, meaning he must manual breathe, blink, stand up, walk, drink, swallow and manipulate.
You can hurl him down stairs.
You can make him throw hot coffee in his face.
You can make him drive with his eyes closed.
Talk like an idiot.
Talk like a less idiotic idiot.
Destroy a great deal of the city, including ruining the coffee shop you helped pay for.
You can play perfectly and you can also play with calculated stupidity (neither is easy although the latter is possible to do on accident) for maximum entertainment value and the developers are prepared for many different outcomes, on purpose or otherwise.
It's not a long game, but it's a well-thought out one that's open for replay value both in Time Attack mode and for "What new stupid thing can I accomplish?".

Three disclaimers before this review:
1. I am a big RPG fan.
2. I love story-driven games.
3. If you hate to read words, then skip to the end.
I blew through the main campaign in Mafia II in just over 15 hours, and I would say that my overall rating would land very close to the Metacritic average. I'd give it a C+ or B-
Most reading this already know what kind of a game Mafia II is. For those just starting their investigation, it's a 3P action shooter/driver. There will be inevitable comparisons to the Grand Theft Auto series, but outside of the big city setting and gunplay, it really isn't. All preconceived notions there should be thrown to the wind.
What I liked about Mafia II:
1. I loved the story driven game. The writers did a good job of tying seemingly disparate scenes together later in the game. And there was enough character development to at least *begin* to become emotionally tied (or repulsed) by certain main characters. More on that later.
2. Dialogue. You're going to have quite a few cutscenes in this game. I personally thought they were well dispersed and well-done. Voice acting is *excellent* and dialogue writing is good (not great, more on that later).
3. I loved the shooting mechanics. Some will disagree strongly, but I played with an XBOX 360 controller, and I found the shooting to be fairly true to real life. You can definitely nail down plenty of head shots, but you're going to have to work to be able to do so. Pistols were actually my favorite in-game, as I could (when able) concentrate on one enemy at a time. I also loved that NPCs responded to my firing. They would behave differently when I was firing. It came in handy later in the game with larger fields of oppenents.
4. I really liked the relationship with police. They seemed to ramp up their vigilance accordingly, and occasionally, they (realistically) interrupted gunfights with other parties to try and bring order. Sometimes, this was a welcome "backup", and other times it was infuriating, but fairly realistic.
5. The length of the game. It was relatively short, but for me (parent, full-time employed) it was perfect. No grinding, very little backtracking. A clean, linear gameplay line on the main story. Note that I did very few side quests (maybe two?). This is not an open-world game (no DLC for me), for those that prefer them.
6. The settings and extras. I loved the way the seasons changed and it affected everything from driving (snow, ice) to attire and graphics. The environment really draws you into the time period you're playing in nicely. The collectable WANTED posters and Playboy magazines are a nice touch, too. Vintage specific/appropriate and a little treat. I can't imagine who is rolling through and finding all 100 mags, but that achievement is available for you perv completionists out there. ;)
What I didn't like:
1. The story. Yes, I also liked it. But there were moments where it felt forced. There were scenes in the game that I kept wondering, "What am I doing here?". But they had to be played. Those times it felt much less organic than it could've. Overall, the story was compelling, but it was close to having been truly great. The game is most certainly still worth playing, IMO, but it left me with a little twitching feeling about what could've been. While some characters were developed fully, others left me scratching my head and wondering about motives and actions.
2. The dialoge writing. There were some great dialogue moments, but there were also a few moments of gratuitous self-indulgence. I'm not a prude or a puritan, but there were a couple scenes that seemed over the top for no apparent reason. As a writer myself, I realize sometimes part of character development is showing an ugly side of someone, but in Mafia II this seemed to happen with dead ends to further development (Eddie, in particular, IMO). I just left with the feeling that someone thought this would be appealing to a certain audience. If so, that audience is younger and more crass than me (which is fine).
3. A lack of choices. This is on me, since the game isn't an RPG. *But*, due to character development (or lack thereof) in several scenes, I kept thinking, "WTF, man!? WHY am I trusting this guy? There is no sane person who would do a job for this guy after what he's done to me. This doesn't make any sense." There were also several fire fights that turned into mass murder scenes as opposed to calculated revenge kills. Those weren't realistic or fun for me, even though I *loved* the fire fight mechanics.
4. A lack of stealth abilities. This isn't the only game like this. But there were moments where it would've made sense IRL (to me, anyway) to actually be just a *bit* more subtle in entry into/exit of an enemy stronghold. It would've been considerably more rewarding and fun to at least *start* to choke people out/knock them out/muffle a shot before you got noticed. There was precious little of this available.
Overall, if you've got 15-20 hours to kill, I'd actually recommend this game highly. Especially if you've grown tired of sci-fi/fantasy settings and want to play something closer to home (Earth, 20th Century).
Mafia II has a really, really good story, some very memorable moments, some incredibly fun shootouts, and quite a few other fun missions that I've never seen in a game before. On sale, this game is well worth it, and for those that have already picked up free/cheap, I'd queue it up. I don't think many will be disappointed.

is a long-running tabletop roleplaying game made by White Wolf a little over 20 years ago and which is now in its fourth iteration (specifically, the 20th Anniversary Edition). : the game and its setting have a lot of history to draw from.  The clans, powers, politics, mythologies and permutations contained in the computer game are only a small fragment of its true form.
For this reason it's forgivable if someone completely new to the setting feels like they've been dunked in the deep end, alleviated only by scraps gleaned from the NPCs.  It's a big world with a lot of content.  I'm not going to go into detail because this review is going to be too long as is, but keep in mind that if you're new to the setting and want to take a bite of the larger picture you'll have material to be chewing for a long time.
I bought this game when it was newly released, back in 2004, and at the time it was remarkable for many reasons.  The graphics were rich.  The story and mechanics a significant improvement over its predecessor,
.  The sheer capacity to choose your clan and sex put it miles ahead.  It showcased the Disciplines (vampiric powers) in new and fascinating ways and it was just so surprisingly replayable.  Sure, there's no doubt that the stories and quests are pretty much the same, but playing as a Tremere is nothing like playing as a Brujah.
However, it was also dogged by the absolute worst loading times that were around at the time.  The transition coding, from what I gathered (I'm no coder), was outright shoddy.
Nowadays, of course, things are a bit different.
It is important, before buying this game, to understand that it's more than a decade old.  Don't expect cutting-edge graphics.  Sawing-edge, maybe, but that's about it.  This is a game that was high-class in its day but
top-class.
You may run into the same problem that I did once I bought the Steam version: it wouldn't run.  At all.  I received a rather aggravating message that I didn't have enough available memory to run the game (which, of course, was nonsense).  The reason for this is that the game was never coded to handle modern computer specs.
To solve it, find Wesp's
(whatever the latest version happens to be; you'll find it online with little trouble if you do a search for
).  Install that sucker to the Bloodlines folder.  Problem fixed.
Would it be nice if an official patch were rolled out and included with the Steam version?  Yes, yes it would.  But this game is no longer supported by
in an official capacity.  Just like the vampires it stars, the game stays alive after its death exclusively on the blood of fans.
Most cons of the game, and let me be entirely blunt, are likely to be the user's fault for expecting more from an 11-year-old game.  But of the cons that aren't the result of unrealistic expectation, let's go through a few of the more important.
This is on Steam.  If they want to supply a game then it's a reasonable user expectation that it will run.  However, I don't really know how they'd solve it - a warning note on purchase, maybe?  An agreement with all relevant copyright holders and modders to supply it with the latest Unofficial Patch pre-applied?  Not sure.  Either way, apply the Unofficial Patch to fix it.
At some point you're going to find yourself stuck between a door and a wall or locked in a staircase because an NPC inexplicably won't move.
The game autosaves now and then but not necessarily at logical moments.  Heading through a zone transition isn't necessarily going to result in a save point.  Make sure you take note of your quick-save and quick-load keys (rebind them if necessary) and use them often.
This is a mixed blessing as it allows you to go back several quick saves if you need to but if you like a nice clean save game list then you're going to need to delete a bunch of saves from time to time.
While mods can adapt the game there is no 'hot-bar'
.  It would have been nice to have the option.
Some people aren't going to be bothered by this, of course, but it's worth noting.  If you're playing a female character some NPCs
call you things like 'hot stuff.'  Some characters (including the Malkavian PC model) have jiggly parts.  One of the major female NPCs (a Toreador named Velvet Velour) wears lingerie everywhere (including official vampire meetings).  If this doesn't bother you, go for it.  If it does, proceed with caution (and perhaps mods).
On the bright side, there are plenty of pluses to the game.
This is a game about vampires written by people who were very conversant in the setting and determined to give it its due.  They've
succeeded.  The world is gritty and morally suspect.  Even acts of kindness can twist around and bite the player on the backside.  It eminently reflects your place as a fledgling in a world ruled by individuals who have been dead decades or even centuries longer than you.
There are many downright funny characters in the game, plenty of them largely unimportant as anything but vendors, but they break up the action.
People familiar with the pen-and-paper (PnP) roleplaying game will recognise the character sheet immediately.  Nonetheless, you don't need to know how to play the PnP game to play this one.  A tabletop game
translate flawlessly to a computer game but there's a balance that can be attained.
manages this quite nicely.
Your vampire elders are suitably manipulative and vary wildly in how nice they happen to be about the matter.
Many quests in the game can be approached in a variety of different ways (though, it should be noted, not a particularly wide variety) and the differences between the clans truly do keep the game's replay value up.  Often you'll find yourself wondering how
clan would have handled things.

I'm not sure if it's the Unofficial Patch or the speed of today's computers but those loading times are no longer an issue.  Bam, gone, fixed.  I suspect it's the patch (yet another reason to apply it).
Vampires don't particularly care what sex their peers were in life.  There are many female leaders and strong female characters in the game.
I seriously suggest that you
play as a Malkavian the first time through.  Leave it for later.  You'll see the game in an entirely new light.
Yes, I recommend this game, but with a caveat: if you don't want to alter it with the Unofficial Patch, steer well clear.  The developers
fix this game - ever.  The copyright holders even went so far as to crush a fan-driven project to update the game for the modern day (search
if you're curious).
Everything wonderful about this game survives because of community modders and for no other reason.

This is a pretty short game - Steam clocked about 17 hours for my first playthrough - but it is one
of a ride from start to finish. It is hilarious, sad, uncomfortable, and terrifying, but always great and rarely goes
far with its subject matter (though be warned, it still goes far). Battles are simple, but satisfying with a combo system that allows some additional flexibility with battle strategy, a varied cast of party members to play with, the occasional looming threat of instant and unavoidable permadeath for your companions (don't worry, there's not *too* much shame in save-scumming), and an absolutely killer soundtrack to accompany it. The soundtrack is stellar all around, really; if you get this game, be sure to grab the Deluxe edition if only for that.
If you're looking for a light-hearted game, you might want to skip this one; even the humor is often firmly on the dark side (though it will give you a good fart joke or two). If an R-rated, incredibly messed up Earthbound sounds like your cup of tea? You probably want this game.

If you like Earthbound, wrestling, body horror, ambiguous morals, post-apocalypic enivornments, the Power Rangers, or surreal humor then LISA is not for you because it's not for anybody.  But you'll still love it.
LISA is a
game.  You need to know that going in.  This is the kind of game that will make you slap your forehead as the game wrecks you and your player character with little warning while still giving you a fair amount of time to prepare for the hit.  It's also the kind of game where all of the characters are weird, sometimes lovable, oftentimes disgusting, and completely expendable.  Don't get too attached.
The gameplay is an interesting combination of genres.  On one hand, it is a side-scrolling adventure game with similar philosophy (but far different feel) to Flashback or Another World.  On the other hand, the game's combat system is handled as a turn-based RPG that brings to mind Earthbound.  All of which is very balanced, though a small gripe is tht screen transitions in the side-scrolling sections can occasionally cause players to blunder off cliffs resulting in damage or even instant Game Overs.
The graphics also easily bring to mind the Earthbound asthetic, especially the feel of Mother 3.  Don't be fooled though!  This game is not childish at all and will use its cartoony style to create an unsettling dissonance (which is helped greatly by the soundtrack as well) with all of the dark subject matter.
That's the final part of the game that I wish to comment on: this game covers very dark subject matter.  There is betrayal,♥♥♥♥♥♥ extreme violence, needless murder, suicide, sex-crazed wastelanders doing anything to get off, drug abuse... the list goes on and on- and it's not exclusively the villains who partake in this behavior.  It all comes together to make an excellent story with beautifully flawed characters who try to get by in this bizarre, barren, ridiculous, and harsh world.
The reason why I bring this up is that, while I love how the subject matter is handled (oftentimes like a screwed up joke that cracks up the joker but leaves the rest of the room uncomfortable), it isn't for everybody.  If you find yourself easily offended or unable to cope with uncomfortable subjects like the ones I listed in the previous paragraph then this game might make you squirm too much for you to enjoy it.  If you think you can handle it, however, this game is definitely worth your time.
One of the best and most interesting games that I've played in a while.  It continues to amaze me what creative people can manage to do with RPG Maker.

Arthur Morris (1922–2015) was an Australian cricketer who played 46 Test matches between 1946 and 1955. He is best known as a prominent member of the "Invincibles", a team that went undefeated on their tour of England in 1948. In his teens, Morris became the first player ever to score two centuries on his first-class debut. After serving in the Australian Army during the Second World War, he made his Test debut against England. He scored a century in his third match and two more hundreds in the following Test, becoming only the second Australian to score a hundred in each innings of an Ashes Test. By 1950, he was Australia's vice-captain and had amassed nine Test centuries with a batting average over 65. Thereafter his form declined, and his career ended after his first wife became terminally ill in 1955. In later life, Morris served as a trustee of the Sydney Cricket Ground for over twenty years. Selected in the Australian Cricket Board's Team of the Century in 2000 and inducted into the Australian Cricket Hall of Fame in 2001, he is widely regarded as one of Australia's most successful left-handed batsmen.

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter redux is the type of game that is best experienced by going in blind and as a result, I will attempt to discuss what I liked/disliked about it without trying to spoil it. It's highly reminiscent of how awful movie trailers are today, in attempting to describe/give a taste of what's to come, the important parts of a movie/game are spoiled. This really surprised me because even as I played through the game, certain mechanics stood out to me, but I knew that I wouldn't be able to fully discuss them because it's best experienced/learned on your own. Attempting to go in depth about the game's mechanics would spoil certain aspects of it and not doing so would result in better immersion, a big part of walking simulators like this one.
Without revealing too much, ECR is a highly atmospheric walking simulator that puts you into the shoes of a noir-type detective attempting to solve a mystery. I know that comes off as a mouthful, but that more or less covers most of what it offers without going into spoiler territory. Seeing as how it's a walking simulator, the basic mechanics are there. It consists of FPV, a few puzzles, a lot of interaction with all sorts of items, even mundane ones, reading, and cutscenes that put you in the middle of the various situations. Most people, including myself, may turn away from walking simulator games due to them mainly being seen as something other than "real" video games, but ECR offers enough that I could say it's not only a video game, it's a great one.
One of the main attractions of ECR is its graphics, this game is visually stunning. Having just recently upgraded my GPU (I went from a 480 to a 1080), I was able to fully enjoy this one aspect of the game. This is the type of game that you'll want to snap many screenshots and that's exactly what I did, it even led to what I believe to be one of the best screenshots I've taken in a video game. With the high quality graphics you will be able to enjoy the many different locations offered such as dense forests, decrepit houses/buildings, a graveyard, and large bodies of water/sunlight.
Speaking of locations, ECR's "level" design is fairly close to what I would describe as good to great and at times it vaguely reminded me of Dark Souls. When it comes to great level design, I mainly think of the first Dark Souls game, it's a massive and expansive world that when fully examined reveals intricate shortcuts/paths that showcase how well connected it all is. This is more or less what is done in ECR. On top of that, most of the locations that are visible in ECR could be visited. It's not as extensive as in Dark Souls, but it offers enough so that you will eventually begin to anticipate things to come.
For the most part, ECR's locations are what you'd expect to find in the nearby surroundings of a small town except many of the houses/buildings can be described as decrepit and then some. Everything just feels abandoned and lifeless. This is of importance because that along with low key ambient music contributes to the game's moody/atmospheric feel that can at times be described as disconcerting.
Seeing as how the game takes place in Wisconsin, most of the game takes place near/around forests. There is a specific labyrinthian location, but a great deal of time is spent in the outdoors. What's notable about this is that there's much to be discovered in these places and it could easily be missed, it requires a highly observant eye. This is of great importance because in order to progress through the game, you must find items/clues that can easily be missed.
On the subject of possibly missing out on important things, that's one of the few things that bothered me about ECR. This game was initially described as an experience that will not hold your hand and that's true. Honestly, this could be viewed as both a good and bad thing. In not having your hand held you are able to experience the game for what it is and progress feels like an actual accomplishment, it ends up being worth it. On the other hand, the game is done in such a way that missing out on important items/clues can lead to the story getting jumbled up and you ending up lost as a result of this. You are eventually able to piece things together by endlessly backtracking through the game's locations for possible hints, but it won't result in what is ultimately a specifically structured story. On top of that, it could also be a while before you realize just what it is you're really supposed to be doing in this game. The game's mechanics aren't clearly defined and it's through trial and error that things are eventually fully revealed.
Another problem that relates to being lost and locations is the lack of a map. I guess you could say that this contributes to the mysterious feeling that is generally felt throughout the game, but it could've been done in such a way that it wouldn't have prevented the story/atmosphere from being ruined or doesn't make the player suffer. Eventually you are able to orient yourself with the help of visible landmarks, but it could take a while before this is realized.
Though I previously stated that this game is visually stunning, that isn't entirely true. At this point it's probably me just nitpicking, but the textures in this game aren't as detailed as other aspects of this game. From afar, everything appears to have fluid movement and high attention to detail, but that is entirely different when up close. When viewed from that distance, things can appear to be stiff and blocky. I feel that it's important to note this because walking simulators generally consist of FPV and high attention to detail to make up for what some could view as a limiting subgenre of video games.
To conclude, I highly enjoyed ECR. Though it was a bit frustrating to be lost/confused for the first third of the game, I was eventually able to fully digest what the game offered as time went on. This is the type of game where you won't be given hints or clear objectives and it is through your own observations that you begin to learn what needs to be accomplished. I know this game probably won't be enjoyed by everyone, but I still recommend it. I will also say that even with what I viewed as its flaws, ECR is what future walking simulators should aspire to be, a narrative experience with enough to keep you occupied/entertained.

Ethan Carter is a little like that friend you had in high school who was both prom king and valedictorian. It probably could have coasted by on good looks alone, but it irritatingly insists on being well-rounded and ends up plunging you into existential angst.
Ethan gets a lot of things right. The graphics, particularly on the Unreal 4 remake, are the National Geographic kind of pornography. The developers used extensive photo scanning to create a hyper-realistic environment, and if you squint a little bit, there are times when the game approaches photorealism. Since Ethan focuses more on immersion and exploration than it does on gameplay, this level of realism elevates the game from “macabre walking simulator” to “holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ remind me not to go to rural Wisconsin anytime soon”.
The soundtrack is a fitting complement to the gorgeous terrain. Haunting but subtle, there to accentuate the experience without overly distracting from it, it adds a finishing touch of vague unease to an adventure that is otherwise largely silent.
As is true with other games in this genre, it’s difficult to go into much detail about the game mechanics and story without giving too much away, but it can safely be said that while neither approaches the stratospheric standards set by the graphics, both are original and coherent enough to support the game’s ambitions. There are a number of subtle design touches that contribute to the narrative in small but significant ways, and as a result, Ethan is a game that benefits from a second playthrough. The plot isn’t wildly original, but it does tie up neatly at the end, and the developer’s focus on weird fiction storytelling has many smaller triumphs. Ethan is less about the plot than it is about the atmosphere, and you’ll find that the synergy of the two of them is more than enough to keep you engrossed for the duration of the game.
Although the Redux version does fix a few of the game’s more critiqued flaws (the save system and the need for backtracking), there are still things to nitpick here. Aside from the main character, the voice acting is community theater quality (Ethan’s brother intermittently slips into a muted Irish accent), and the game’s dedication to creating an immersive environment sometimes sacrifices mechanical coherence on the altar of damn good looks. On balance, however, these are minor flaws, and they don’t chip away at the game’s ability to transport you to another (significantly more murderous) world.
Ethan Carter is the kind of game that you want to just linger in, and that’s a testament to the engrossing setting the Astronauts have constructed here. Red Creek Valley deserves to be savored. Turn off your lights, pour yourself a soothing glass of your alcohol of choice, and let yourself get lost in the woods for a few hours. Just remember to take screenshots.

9.5/10 GAMEPLAY
This game has taken all the wasted potential of other zombie games, and somehow managed to squeeze them all into one game. This is the definition of a pure zombie-apocalyptic game. When you start playing, things are tough, life is tough, zombies are tough. But as you progress, you can actually see how your character develops. You get better weapons, teach yourself new skills to defeat zombies, learn how-to and how not to approach a zombie, and it feels really great when you reach the point where you eventually start to ease into the life of Kyle Crane(the character you play as) in Harran(the default map), with or without any intention of doing so. And also, co-op is really fun. To be able to play a zombie game with your friends is a blessing.
9/10 STORY-RICH
Now, unlike most other zombie games which lack a storyline, and focuses on mostly just slashing-and-dashing zombies, Dying Light does a really great job at implementing a main story and many many backstories into a zombie-killing frenzied game. You get to have fun killing the infected while you watch as Kyle Crane tries to stop his life from falling apart.
9.7/10 GRAPHICS
There is no doubt when it comes to graphics, that this game is a really well done piece of art. Textures are smooth, rendering is fast, and view distance is really well done. Despite all the parkour and very quick movements of your character, Dying Light provides a smooth and beautiful game for you to look at, 24/7. Of course, I'm talking about putting your graphics settings to Max all the way. Optimization is on point. 100-150 fps constantly most of the time on my GTX1060 6GB in spite of the entire previews of many different textures you see everywhere around you. Lens flare can be a little bit crazy though.
10/10 IMMERSIVENESS
Now, there's not much to say anymore, except the fact that the developers created a masterpiece. When you play Dying Light, you're completely focused on the game. The gameplay requires you to react quickly, the graphics makes the world of Kyle Crane seem real, and the story includes almost everything that will or might be happening in an actual zombie apocalypse. There are all these conversations you can interact with, many, very different sorts of people you will meet,  even small 'easter eggs' here and there which sort of have a backstory if you actually look at stuff and think about it(or I'm just overthinking it), and most importantly, at least your character has its own voice. I'm not naming any games, but in most other games, your character does not speak at all, and that really grinds my gears, especially when communication is important in real life; therefore they lose the immersiveness of the game.
OVERALL a solid 9/11.

Three disclaimers before this review:
1. I am a big RPG fan.
2. I love story-driven games.
3. If you hate to read words, then skip to the end.
I blew through the main campaign in Mafia II in just over 15 hours, and I would say that my overall rating would land very close to the Metacritic average. I'd give it a C+ or B-
Most reading this already know what kind of a game Mafia II is. For those just starting their investigation, it's a 3P action shooter/driver. There will be inevitable comparisons to the Grand Theft Auto series, but outside of the big city setting and gunplay, it really isn't. All preconceived notions there should be thrown to the wind.
What I liked about Mafia II:
1. I loved the story driven game. The writers did a good job of tying seemingly disparate scenes together later in the game. And there was enough character development to at least *begin* to become emotionally tied (or repulsed) by certain main characters. More on that later.
2. Dialogue. You're going to have quite a few cutscenes in this game. I personally thought they were well dispersed and well-done. Voice acting is *excellent* and dialogue writing is good (not great, more on that later).
3. I loved the shooting mechanics. Some will disagree strongly, but I played with an XBOX 360 controller, and I found the shooting to be fairly true to real life. You can definitely nail down plenty of head shots, but you're going to have to work to be able to do so. Pistols were actually my favorite in-game, as I could (when able) concentrate on one enemy at a time. I also loved that NPCs responded to my firing. They would behave differently when I was firing. It came in handy later in the game with larger fields of oppenents.
4. I really liked the relationship with police. They seemed to ramp up their vigilance accordingly, and occasionally, they (realistically) interrupted gunfights with other parties to try and bring order. Sometimes, this was a welcome "backup", and other times it was infuriating, but fairly realistic.
5. The length of the game. It was relatively short, but for me (parent, full-time employed) it was perfect. No grinding, very little backtracking. A clean, linear gameplay line on the main story. Note that I did very few side quests (maybe two?). This is not an open-world game (no DLC for me), for those that prefer them.
6. The settings and extras. I loved the way the seasons changed and it affected everything from driving (snow, ice) to attire and graphics. The environment really draws you into the time period you're playing in nicely. The collectable WANTED posters and Playboy magazines are a nice touch, too. Vintage specific/appropriate and a little treat. I can't imagine who is rolling through and finding all 100 mags, but that achievement is available for you perv completionists out there. ;)
What I didn't like:
1. The story. Yes, I also liked it. But there were moments where it felt forced. There were scenes in the game that I kept wondering, "What am I doing here?". But they had to be played. Those times it felt much less organic than it could've. Overall, the story was compelling, but it was close to having been truly great. The game is most certainly still worth playing, IMO, but it left me with a little twitching feeling about what could've been. While some characters were developed fully, others left me scratching my head and wondering about motives and actions.
2. The dialoge writing. There were some great dialogue moments, but there were also a few moments of gratuitous self-indulgence. I'm not a prude or a puritan, but there were a couple scenes that seemed over the top for no apparent reason. As a writer myself, I realize sometimes part of character development is showing an ugly side of someone, but in Mafia II this seemed to happen with dead ends to further development (Eddie, in particular, IMO). I just left with the feeling that someone thought this would be appealing to a certain audience. If so, that audience is younger and more crass than me (which is fine).
3. A lack of choices. This is on me, since the game isn't an RPG. *But*, due to character development (or lack thereof) in several scenes, I kept thinking, "WTF, man!? WHY am I trusting this guy? There is no sane person who would do a job for this guy after what he's done to me. This doesn't make any sense." There were also several fire fights that turned into mass murder scenes as opposed to calculated revenge kills. Those weren't realistic or fun for me, even though I *loved* the fire fight mechanics.
4. A lack of stealth abilities. This isn't the only game like this. But there were moments where it would've made sense IRL (to me, anyway) to actually be just a *bit* more subtle in entry into/exit of an enemy stronghold. It would've been considerably more rewarding and fun to at least *start* to choke people out/knock them out/muffle a shot before you got noticed. There was precious little of this available.
Overall, if you've got 15-20 hours to kill, I'd actually recommend this game highly. Especially if you've grown tired of sci-fi/fantasy settings and want to play something closer to home (Earth, 20th Century).
Mafia II has a really, really good story, some very memorable moments, some incredibly fun shootouts, and quite a few other fun missions that I've never seen in a game before. On sale, this game is well worth it, and for those that have already picked up free/cheap, I'd queue it up. I don't think many will be disappointed.
