is a long-running tabletop roleplaying game made by White Wolf a little over 20 years ago and which is now in its fourth iteration (specifically, the 20th Anniversary Edition).  This isn't really news but it bears noting before you go anywhere near this game.  Why?  For the same reason that it's worth noting the '3' in
: the game and its setting have a lot of history to draw from.  The clans, powers, politics, mythologies and permutations contained in the computer game are only a small fragment of its true form.
For this reason it's forgivable if someone completely new to the setting feels like they've been dunked in the deep end, alleviated only by scraps gleaned from the NPCs.  It's a big world with a lot of content.  I'm not going to go into detail because this review is going to be too long as is, but keep in mind that if you're new to the setting and want to take a bite of the larger picture you'll have material to be chewing for a long time.
I bought this game when it was newly released, back in 2004, and at the time it was remarkable for many reasons.  The graphics were rich.  The story and mechanics a significant improvement over its predecessor,
.  The sheer capacity to choose your clan and sex put it miles ahead.  It showcased the Disciplines (vampiric powers) in new and fascinating ways and it was just so surprisingly replayable.  Sure, there's no doubt that the stories and quests are pretty much the same, but playing as a Tremere is nothing like playing as a Brujah.
However, it was also dogged by the absolute worst loading times that were around at the time.  The transition coding, from what I gathered (I'm no coder), was outright shoddy.
Nowadays, of course, things are a bit different.
It is important, before buying this game, to understand that it's more than a decade old.  Don't expect cutting-edge graphics.  Sawing-edge, maybe, but that's about it.  This is a game that was high-class in its day but
top-class.
You may run into the same problem that I did once I bought the Steam version: it wouldn't run.  At all.  I received a rather aggravating message that I didn't have enough available memory to run the game (which, of course, was nonsense).  The reason for this is that the game was never coded to handle modern computer specs.
To solve it, find Wesp's
(whatever the latest version happens to be; you'll find it online with little trouble if you do a search for
).  Install that sucker to the Bloodlines folder.  Problem fixed.
Would it be nice if an official patch were rolled out and included with the Steam version?  Yes, yes it would.  But this game is no longer supported by
in an official capacity.  Just like the vampires it stars, the game stays alive after its death exclusively on the blood of fans.
Most cons of the game, and let me be entirely blunt, are likely to be the user's fault for expecting more from an 11-year-old game.  But of the cons that aren't the result of unrealistic expectation, let's go through a few of the more important.
This is on Steam.  If they want to supply a game then it's a reasonable user expectation that it will run.  However, I don't really know how they'd solve it - a warning note on purchase, maybe?  An agreement with all relevant copyright holders and modders to supply it with the latest Unofficial Patch pre-applied?  Not sure.  Either way, apply the Unofficial Patch to fix it.
At some point you're going to find yourself stuck between a door and a wall or locked in a staircase because an NPC inexplicably won't move.
The game autosaves now and then but not necessarily at logical moments.  Heading through a zone transition isn't necessarily going to result in a save point.  Make sure you take note of your quick-save and quick-load keys (rebind them if necessary) and use them often.
This is a mixed blessing as it allows you to go back several quick saves if you need to but if you like a nice clean save game list then you're going to need to delete a bunch of saves from time to time.
While mods can adapt the game there is no 'hot-bar'
.  It would have been nice to have the option.
Some people aren't going to be bothered by this, of course, but it's worth noting.  If you're playing a female character some NPCs
call you things like 'hot stuff.'  Some characters (including the Malkavian PC model) have jiggly parts.  One of the major female NPCs (a Toreador named Velvet Velour) wears lingerie everywhere (including official vampire meetings).  If this doesn't bother you, go for it.  If it does, proceed with caution (and perhaps mods).
On the bright side, there are plenty of pluses to the game.
This is a game about vampires written by people who were very conversant in the setting and determined to give it its due.  They've
succeeded.  The world is gritty and morally suspect.  Even acts of kindness can twist around and bite the player on the backside.  It eminently reflects your place as a fledgling in a world ruled by individuals who have been dead decades or even centuries longer than you.
There are many downright funny characters in the game, plenty of them largely unimportant as anything but vendors, but they break up the action.
People familiar with the pen-and-paper (PnP) roleplaying game will recognise the character sheet immediately.  Nonetheless, you don't need to know how to play the PnP game to play this one.  A tabletop game
translate flawlessly to a computer game but there's a balance that can be attained.
manages this quite nicely.
Your vampire elders are suitably manipulative and vary wildly in how nice they happen to be about the matter.
Many quests in the game can be approached in a variety of different ways (though, it should be noted, not a particularly wide variety) and the differences between the clans truly do keep the game's replay value up.  Often you'll find yourself wondering how
clan would have handled things.

I'm not sure if it's the Unofficial Patch or the speed of today's computers but those loading times are no longer an issue.  Bam, gone, fixed.  I suspect it's the patch (yet another reason to apply it).
Vampires don't particularly care what sex their peers were in life.  There are many female leaders and strong female characters in the game.
I seriously suggest that you
play as a Malkavian the first time through.  Leave it for later.  You'll see the game in an entirely new light.
Yes, I recommend this game, but with a caveat: if you don't want to alter it with the Unofficial Patch, steer well clear.  The developers
fix this game - ever.  The copyright holders even went so far as to crush a fan-driven project to update the game for the modern day (search
if you're curious).
Everything wonderful about this game survives because of community modders and for no other reason.

Metro 2033 is a fun game with some minor issues. The games shooting is fun and the ranger modes are very immersive as there is no HUD. However I still think the gameplay is fun.
The way the story is told reminded me of Half Life, Artyom doesn't speak in gameplay but when loading in the next level he reads a journal entry about whats to come. The story is that Artyom needs to save his station from monsters which killl humans and have overrun other stations. Going from stop to stop through the Metro is fun and the story is well paced. I did not like the enemys though, they weren't explained in any detail and I didn't find myself invested in the end goal. The story is more about the journey than the destination.
The graphics in the game are amazing and the way Metro does lighting is very good and atmospheric. The game has ambient music which blends into the background and I honestly can't remember any of it. It does it's job and nothing else. The most obvious flaw in the game is its sounds. With the notable exception of the silenced weapons, which I think sound pretty good, the sound effects are not very good. The gun sounds feel like they have been taken from a generic movie. They just sound boring and lack punch.
The voice acting is ok though, if you want the best experience go with the Russian voice acting and subtitles. The lip syncing sucks but you won't notice; I can count on my hands how many times someone was talking with a gas mask on or during combat when I don't notice.
I think this Metro is a good game but the lack of urgency in the plot and roughness in the presentation limit it from going beyond just good. I recommend it, especially as it goes on sale for almost nothing.

Half murder mystery, half Lovecraftian eldritch horror, 'The Vanishing of Ethan Carter' is a game of many surprises.
It's boldly announced very early on that the story is 'a narrative experience that does not hold your hand', and that's certainly true - for better or worse. Loath as I am to be led by the nose through a game, there are moments in the early parts of TVoEC where I was forced to backtrack to find all the things that I had obviously missed... which, as it turned out, accounted for about 30% of the entire game. As other reviews here have noted, you may wish to consult a walkthrough for the first few minutes, just to get a sense of what it is you're supposed to be doing, and how it is you do it. Then, once you've worked it out, you can really begin to enjoy what Ethan Carter's world has to offer.
The voice acting - the scenery - the concept and conceits of the story - all come together to make a well-crafted and tightly honed gaming experience, satifyingly wrapped-up by its closing act. It's a narrative that doesn't outstay its welcome - the perfect length, though perhaps a little pricey for a game you're likely to play only once. Still, if it's on sale, I definitely recommend it.

So, I've played quite a few games in my time. Some good, some bad.
I'll be honest, I had no clue what I was expecting here. I'd picked this game up on sale and thought nothing of it at the time. Didn't really have any friends who'd played it nor had I ever heard of it before. But, eventually the time came to give it a try.
So with the night still young, a couple of beers handy, I dove right in.
What greeted me was a wall of confusion. I had no idea what I was doing or where I needed to go. Eventually I began to come across things I could interact with. Initially, neither the story nor the game made any sense to me. But as I played further, I began to discover the true nature of this game.
This is a
story driven game.There is quite a bit of narration throughout, as expected as well. If you're looking for a fast-paced, action-horror, this game does not provide that. The pacing is quite nice if you want something to relax with. Atmosphere: The game provides a very peaceful, even disturbingly so, atmosphere. A very surreal experience. You always feel tense while playing (at least I did anyway). There is a lot of anticipation. A
. It does get a bit morbid, so it's not for the faint of heart. Keep your stomach about you.
The sound is nicely done. It fits the theme quite well and also has a small tendency to really create gripping suspense. Often, the music will peak as if in horror movies. It creates tension. You await what lies ahead. Overall, it becomes an atmospheric rollercoaster.
Often, the ambient sounds are very nice. Quite peaceful and jolly sometimes, but also complemented with dark mellodies as well. The music at the end of the game is quite beautiful, I would say I really enjoyed listening to it.
I wouldn't really class this game as horror, more so a thriller. There is an element of 'jump-scare', but there is some bit of indication beforehand that it may happen.
Mechanics: There is not a lot of interaction. Your right click is all you really need for most of it. However, this game is quite a bit more immersive than a "point and click". The story is quite linear, but the map is expansive enough for its setting. Exploration is suggested, but not 100% mandatory. You don't need to search every nook and cranny. But, not everything is always as it seems.
Ultimately, do try to explore. There is some danger to missing parts of the story (this game
doesn't hold your hand or tell you what do next or even where to go, so be vigilant. Don't tirelessly run around every edge of the map either though, all you'll find is beautiful scenery for the most part. This game is in fact quite pretty. Even with my settings (see below), I could render it in a somewhat pleasant manner. If you like a pretty rural setting, this game delivers on that quite well.
Saving: This game saves very little. Only when you've done something meaningful. I reccommend sessions longer than 15-20 mins at the very least to properly digest the story and scenery. The game does inform you that it's saving, but unless you see that message, take note that progress
be lost quite easily if you decide not to finish an area after going into it. My recommendation is to stop after you see the saving notification after you complete a section if you know you won't be able to finish the next section fully.
Content/mechanical element: This game has a lot of puzzles which you need to complete to progress in the story, so if you enjoy some challenge, then this should be good news for you.
Story:
This is not a game of happiness. In fact, it's quite tragic. The setting is beautiful, but highly contrasted with the themes. You will see a very dark element of human nature, so I reccommend being emotionally prepared, if you are a sensitive person.
You will not be prepared for the ending. The more you progress through the story, the sadder it gets. All while having a very chilling, haunting presence. You will get chills running down your spine as you play. Even a scare or two. But, don't let that stop you. If your curiosity permits, push onwards. Discover the grim tale behind the Vanishing of Ethan Carter.

Parkour, free-running, call it whatever you want, this is a first-person platformer. Platformers work well in 2d, or 3rd person. Think of all the fun platformers and Prince of Persia 1 - 3, or Super Mario 64, or Assasin's Creed come to mind, but not Mirror's Edge... because 1st person platforming is a futile exercise in anger management. This is a 1st person platformer and it doesn't work. It doesn't work at all.
First of all, in 1st person mode, depth perception and judging distances are very difficult. You can't estimate distance based on only one image (that's why we have 2 eyes instead of 1, our early survival depended on judging distances). Playing the game, you have no way of confidently judging your jumping distance, or where your feet are when initiaitng a jump. Predictably, you fall and die for not pressing jump in time, or jump too soon and die just as well. The movelemt is quite fluid, but the platforming (parkouring) is a half-baked cow pat pie. If only they implemented some cues to aid in judging if you can make a jump or not, and when to jump, or switch to 3rd person view when not aimimg.
1st person platforming didn't work when Half-life tried it in 1998 and it doesn't work for Dying Light 20 years later in 2018. Bad ideas are bad no matter when they are concieved, and this game is just another very well polished turd. Its not fun. Platforming is frustrating and un-reliable in 1st person; it works in 3rd person, but not here. Additional cues are required to assist in judging distance.
Oh and the story-telling, and main plot character dialogue is absolutely♥♥♥♥♥♥ Your starting game "mission vending machine" npc produces a sound worse than nails on a chalkboard whenever attempting to deliver dialogue. His voice is profoundly infuriating. If I were to ever meet a person with a demeanour and speech manner so abbrasive and "bratty", the urge to smash his teeth in would be overwhelming. Not to mention your character, who is a neck-bearded, lumber-sexual hipster, pretending to be Solid-Snake, or Chris Redfield.
Whatever potential this had as an open world horror-survival game was sadly squandered by choosing to make "parkouring" a necessary gameplay mechanic. This could have worked so much better as a stealth/line-of sight/ambush game. Shame that the engine is so well polished and the production quality so high, for such pittiful gameplay implementation.
It's a good game.

This is a really, really good game, however there are imperfections: The AI
1. They do not take effect from having 0 gold and making a negative income per turn
Usually if your playing and your out of money and your making negative something gold then it automatically begins removing some of your troops because it cost gold per turn to manage them and if you cannot pay for them they are removed, however with AI ive seen it where they have the largest army and they are still growing and yet they are at -130 gold a turn and have 0 gold, yet for some reason they dont get their troops removed in order to decrease their debt, but if you as a player had -130 gold per turn with 0 gold they would remove your troops.
2. Happiness
Happiness is a feature to where if you have 1 or more happiness then your civilaztion produces things at a normal rate, troops do the same damage, and your cities make food at the same speed, but if you are -1 or lower then it starts to decrease, if your over around -50 then they actually begin to revolt, but for an AI they do not take effect from unhappiness, they still can do the exact same things no matter what, meaning it wont matter to them if they are at -100 happiness.
3. Get mad over nothing.
So there is another feature where you can interact with the AI diplomatically, they can get mad or have a negative opinon about you because you covet land they want, which is fine, that to me is ok because every civ has different feelings and some can get hostile and some dont at those things, however it draws the line at some places, take this scenario (Which actaually happened to me)
Two AI Civilations asked me if i wanted to join the war against another empire, i said yes, keep in mind i never went to war with that person they want me to war with, and i didnt ask them to join me in attacking them, they asked me. So we defeat them fairly easily, then my allies get mad at me for being a warmongerer what is a warmongerer? well:
war·mon·ger
ˈwôrˌməNGɡər/Submit
noun
plural noun: warmongers
a person who encourages or advocates aggression towards other countries or groups.
The AI interperets a warmongerer whenever you declared war on someone then made peace but them declared war on them multiple times, like being trigger happy, they also determine it if you are declaring war on multiple people, either at once or one at a time, However in this case my allies called me a warmongerer even though i never declared war on our enemies before, or declare war on anyone, and the thing is that they were the ones that wanted to war. So there is my lovely story with how the AI can get mad over nothing.
4. Trades
In the game your can trade with the AI, you can provide gold per turn, gold itself, luxery rescources, open borders, research agreement, resources, Even Cities, and more. The problem is when it comes to research agreements they make extremely unfair trades, now i know in some cases they may get greedy, but its EVERY SINGLE TIME.

It's fun all things considered. The visuals are nice, very reminiscent of Diablo 3. Though there is a severe lack of options. Even maxed out edges are jagged.
Sound design is solid. Guns feel punchy and have a nice audio queue when they're getting low on ammo.
There are a lot of ways to customize your loadout and approach missions.
I do however, have a few things to complain about:
The way you have to call in drops by pressing an arbitrary string of "up down left right" directional combinations on W,A,S,D while holding Ctrl, is convoluted and uncomfortable, especially on a PC with a M/KB. I suggest re-mapping this.
There's a mechanic where you awkwardly fall down when you reach half health, and in single player, this means you have only half a health bar because there's basically no recovering if a melee enemy closes the distance.
Extracting from the levels is a  little repetetive. No matter how stealthy you complete a mission, the end always amounts to a "hold out for this amount of time" (1 minute) wave survival mini-game where enemies just happen to always attack you and know where you are. Turrets counter this mechanica nicely, which means you'll likely be standing in one spot for a minute waiting for the level to end.
Everything slows and/or body-blocks you. Which means the second you have to reload you'll likely be surrounded and juggled to death.There's an unintuitive and clunky melee system in place that's good for nothing except ticking off a box that says; "yes, you can melee in this game". Perhaps this is more fluid with a controller? This makes energy based weapons far more viable, especially solo.
Enemies hover around objectives as if they know it's important. I wish this aspect was more dynamic and rewarded decision making. No matter what you do, the second you start reparing a fuel pump, or scanning for ordinance, waves of enemies start to show up.
You have to stay put while your mini-map is open. Easily the dumbest design decision this game has.
I understand why it's this way on console, but why is the PC version subject to it?
Soloing missions is possible, but you'll be stuck on very low difficulty for hours on end without some help to level up and get upgrades that allow you to solo harder missions. I can solo "helldive" difficulty missions now, but it took 20+ hours to get to that point.
Overall, it's not a bad game. Even with the issues I have with it, I can't seem to point it down.
The price point being "worth it" is subjective. If you're a fan of this genre, you're probably safe paying $20 as you'll get your money's worth. I'd however avoid the $40 version with all the DLC. It doesn't really seem worth it. I only use maybe one add-on, the snow boots.

I forgot I had this game and I am ashamed that I forgot I had it. I had a lot of fun playing this before, as I did just now, but it is late. I feel it deserves my thumbs up. I'll tell ya why.
You are a lady who finds people to join you and help out as the story progresses. The story is quite nice. The people are funny and will often make jokes and claim that they hate the hero, when really they don't.
The actual gameplay itself is typical of most tower defense. You have a grid where you place your units (the 'people' that joined you), and they fight when something is near. What I like about this game is that the different types of units work together. I won't go into any detail about this because you'll probably want to experience it yourself.
Each level is split up into four difficulties. So if you're feeling brave, you can try the hardest. Even if you fail your units will still gain experience points. If you're feeling like a wuss, try the casual setting.
The units have skill trees which you apply 1 point on each level up. I find this to be very rewarding, although sometimes when you complete a level you may have to apply a buncha points (I had to apply about 20 before after one level). C'est la vie.
It is well worth the whatever I paid for it. I don't remember buying it, but I am very glad I did. You'll not be disappointed if you're a fan of tower defense games with a hint of humour and a nice storyline.

The game bills itself as primarily a tower defense game. Tower defense games generally require you to come up with a strategy to defeat the enemies given a particular map and set of resources. Defender's Quest maps are much simpler, and to a large extent don't require much strategy. That's where the "RPG" part comes in. There's not really any role-playing going on, but your characters get stronger and you can buy better weapons and armor for them. The maps don't rely so much on strategy as on having characters that are high enough level and have good enough equipment. And that generally means grinding for XP. So when it comes to the advanced and extreme levels, it's not that the levels are possible but you have to have a better strategy. The levels are simply impossible to start with, and the only way you can beat them is by leveling up your characters.
In short, it's not a good tower defense game (because the challenges rely primarily on having high-level characters not strategy), and it's not a good RPG (because there's no real role-playing, just "numbers going up" as you and the enemy gain levels and equipment). So I think it rather fails the "tactical depth" promise.
The second promise is customization, and it does have options to rebind all the keys and change the XP scaling, character names and colors, etc., but I don't think it's a big deal. The developer also put thought into how he could accomodate people with certain disabilities (like epilepsy), which is nice.
The third is story, and I suppose that's where this game does best. The story isn't great, but it does give a reason to keep playing and it is fairly humorous in some parts.
Technically, the game is well-made, even if it appears dated. I can't recall any bugs in the game, and it has been very stable. The game runs at 800x600 resolution, which is fine for me. The sound effects and music are well-done, but lack variety, which is okay for me.
I just wish the game rewarded thinking more than it rewards grinding. It's worth a try if you can get it on sale.

Metro 2033 is a fun game with some minor issues. The games shooting is fun and the ranger modes are very immersive as there is no HUD. The gameplay is very fun and was my favourite aspect of the game. The guns handle well and you can stealth through most of the fights against humans. The fights against monsters are more frantic but feel less refined, I think running around in circles trying to use the health syringes isn't as realistic as the fights against humans. However I still think the gameplay is fun.
The way the story is told reminded me of Half Life, Artyom doesn't speak in gameplay but when loading in the next level he reads a journal entry about whats to come. The story is that Artyom needs to save his station from monsters which killl humans and have overrun other stations. Going from stop to stop through the Metro is fun and the story is well paced. I did not like the enemys though, they weren't explained in any detail and I didn't find myself invested in the end goal. The story is more about the journey than the destination.
The graphics in the game are amazing and the way Metro does lighting is very good and atmospheric. The game has ambient music which blends into the background and I honestly can't remember any of it. It does it's job and nothing else. The most obvious flaw in the game is its sounds. With the notable exception of the silenced weapons, which I think sound pretty good, the sound effects are not very good. The gun sounds feel like they have been taken from a generic movie. They just sound boring and lack punch.
The voice acting is ok though, if you want the best experience go with the Russian voice acting and subtitles. The lip syncing sucks but you won't notice; I can count on my hands how many times someone was talking with a gas mask on or during combat when I don't notice.
I think this Metro is a good game but the lack of urgency in the plot and roughness in the presentation limit it from going beyond just good. I recommend it, especially as it goes on sale for almost nothing.

A walking simulator with a creepy setting. This game is an interesting experience, with beautiful views and enjoyable puzzles. The story is presented as a mystery that unfolds as you progress throughout the game. As with other "walking simuilators", game mechanics are limited. The game consists of mainly walking, interacting, and inspecting. Overall, a worth-while experience.
Notes:
As there are no tutorials or directions, you may sometimes accidentally skip a section. However, sections may be revisited later.
There are some horror bits in the game, so keep that in mind.
Make sure resolution and graphics details are high enough, as some graphical details may not be easy to read/decipher.
Try this out if you are interested in a mystery puzzle game.

I played the Redux version first (about 3 hrs gameplay, without using a walkthrough), and then the regular version (1.8 hrs gameplay, skipping all the scenes). I would recommend the Redux version, simply for the graphics tune-up.
Figuring out the story and the puzzles on your own, all the while in a breathtaking and sometimes haunting environment, makes this one of my favorite walking simulator / mystery games. However, there is very little re-play value - once you've figured out the puzzles, it's simply an atmospheric experience. I found playing the game a second time somewhat diminished my original play-through experience.
Play Redux, play once, and play in the dark with your headphones on.

Helldivers is a Sci-Fi top-down shooter. You play as, well... a Helldiver. Your objective: Defend Democrasy! How? Shoot aliens! Yay!
You pick a team of 1-4 and you go to a planet. Complete different objectives to complete missions. You have 2-3 mission per planet. You complete the planet, you get a reward and you add influence to that sector. Get enough influence, you launch an attack on the capital of that sector, win that, move to the next sector and eventually get to the enemy homeworld where'll you'll launch a final attack.
That's the basics. Now to why I reccomend this.
I could go on and on of all the resources you have avalible. In addition to your primary and secondary weapon, you have a single perk and 4 stragegem slots. Those 4 are abilities you use to call down different things from your dropship. some things include a deployable minefeild, a heavy machine gun, an auto turret, a mech, a bomb dropped by a fighter jet, an ATV, a distractor beacon... The list goes on. Now, a lot of those need to be unlocked from completing planets, but you get a few things to start.
There's 3 races to fight and many different enemies. All races and different and are countered differently. There's a lot of diveristy in your foes. Also, planets too are diverse, from snow planets to forest and desert ones, and even urban mission in rare occasions. Lotsa different stuff.
It's 4-player, so you can bring all your friends! Also, what makes the game even more fun is that EVERYTHING can cause friendly fire. You guns do. The stragemes you drop arrive in pods at supersonic speed. If that lands on little Billy... Hell, the reinforcemnet pods and the FREAKING EXTRACTION VEHICLE all can kill you if they land on you. Fun all around!
Downsides? Weeeell, at times, the game can feel grindy. You do have to do lots of mission to get stuff. You do start with comparativly little. Once you reach the higher levels, the game I find gets bland as there's not really anything else to introduce.
All in all? Thumbs up. Go have some fun with your friends selling Liber-Tea.

Helldivers is best experienced as a multiplayer game, and joining an online session is about as quick and easy as starting a mission of your own. A couple of quick menu selections and you will, quite literally, drop in on another player's mission in progress. Local multiplayer is also an option and, in the absence of outside life, it's still enjoyable solo. Playing alone requires different strategies and offers less flexibility in strategem selection, which does make the already brutal higher difficulties seem even more insurmountable, but the satisfaction of single-handedly conquering a planet cannot be denied.
Unrelenting and brutal, Helldivers delivers fast-paced combat, epic standoffs and a comical approach to death. Its enemies are varied, powerful and a constant threat to the players. While the full impact of the larger multiplayer experience remains to be seen, it still adds a nice little scratch to the progress itch. The strategem system provides great flexibility in squad building with many ways to build out team roles to maximize defensive and offensive capabilities. With procedural map generation and just enough mission and enemy variety to prevent a sense of repetition, the twelve levels of difficulty ought to keep players challenged for a good long time.
The game is worth every penny.

I've never played Mafia even though I got it in a Steam promo.  I have played and completed Mafia II though and I enjoy the game.  You start off as Vito Scaletta during the invasion of Sicily in WWII.  Basically this is a tutorial mission and shows how Vito first gets introduced to the Mafia.  Graphics are nice and the voice acting is pretty good.  Afterwards you are sent home and manage to dodge out of going back to the war.
Early on you are taking baby steps getting used to the various game mechanics and absorbing the world.  Empire City as the name suggests is very much a stylised recreation of New York.  Everything looks right even down to the GM Loco in the credits and the look of the cars.  You can customise cars but don't expect GTA V or Saints Row level customisation, basically a couple of tuning options and some cosmetic parts like new plates and paint job.
For the majority of the game Joe will be your faithful, if bumbling companion, and he's a pretty likeable guy.  You meet others though some are forgettable others less so.
The most annoying aspect of the this game is the collectibles.  There are wanted posters, some of which are VERY hard to get, even with a walkthrough, and one in particular is an exercise in frustration.  These can be collected throughout the open world aspect of the game at any time.  The other collectibles are Playboy pin ups.  These are apparently genuine Playboy Girls and not 'made up'.  Somewhere online theres a list of their names and when they appeared.  A bit anachronistic as some appear after the game was set, and indeed Playboy wasn't even around when this game takes place, but no matter as its one of the better collectibles you can get in game.  These ones are found at particular points in particular missions.  If you miss it, tough, though you can replay a chapter.
General game mechanics are decent, the driving being okay.  I say merely okay because 40's and 50's cars don't handle like even family sedans from Saints Row or GTA, you feel more like you're driving a land barge except for some later sports cars.  One thing that sets the atmosphere is the in car radio with music and announcements appropriate to the period.  Early on you're getting schlocky music and patriotic news spots, later on you're in  the rock and roll era.
Pick this game up if you like sandbox style games, especially if you can get it cheap.

After watching Lisa speedruns and listening to the soundtrack it moved to the top of my wishlist. So I waited for a sale, and waited, and waited some more. Well last night I got impatient and said screw it, it's $10. And it's totally worth the tenner.
It's not a very nice game, bad things happen all the time! Some are even your fault! There's 30 recruit-able party members which is good because there's permadeath moves out there in the wild. There's tough life or death (or arm) decisions out there you'll have to make.
It's not all gloom and doom though, there's plenty of just whacky and weird things out there. Terry, the first recruitable character, does a sliding headbutt that does 0 damage for the first few levels. Jack the Magician has a skill that makes random things come out of his hat, one of which is a carrot that flops down at enemies feet making them wary. Foreboding music plays as one of the antagonist rides in on a cute, hoppy little deer. There's a recruitable fish lawyer. A lawyer that's a fish!
But how's it play? Lisa is a hybrid game, an rpg with a platformer overworld instead of the usual overhead or isometric view. Combat is turn based with a few twists, certain characters have a combo system using WASD which lets them do special moves during attacks, effectively giving you two turns of damage. The animations are great, getting around RPG Makers 1st person camera system by having the characters appear on screen to do their moves. It's a neat little feature that gives the game another unique property to it. There's also a lot of status effects, some not explained all that well but there's a hint sign early in the game that tells you what they do.
Almost every encounter is unique, with only a few farming spots with the standard "walk x tiles and combat happens". A lot of the fights are ambushes or ones you initiate, and some "oh the enemy hit you fight time" too.
So if you're looking for some classic RPG goodness get Lisa.

Lisa is a strange game. It’s also a satisfying, humorous, entertaining, thought-provoking, at times emotional, and more often disturbing game. It has already shoe-horned itself into my top ten list for 2014, and damn me if I’ve ever walked away from a game with such satisfaction for having seen it to the end - And end up only wanting more.
I find the term ‘Devil’s Earthbound’ when referring to Lisa is a loving and very honest way to describe this RPG, as the weight of emotions (which at times can be crushing) and bizarre nature of the encounters and world as a whole make it nigh impossible to not think of the classic SNES title. Lisa, however, bears an ‘M’ rating, and it does so with pride and effortless gusto, even telling jokes and pulling gags despite the darkness and gore of the game world. To have Brad (the player character) make a critical decision regarding his safety versus that of his allies, only to encounter a blind assassin flailing his knife at him wildly while talking mad smack should make the critical side of my brain call this out as an incredibly poor pacing of events, but the game consistently executes these wild swings on such a regular basis that you end up becoming numb to them, save for the shock or comedy of whatever the scene entails. You will encounter said shock and comedy often since the game progresses at a steady rate, even in the hub areas that make you take various paths to trigger the next set of events. Even if you choose the wrong path, you’ll end up discovering more party members to recruit, smaller plot elements to uncover, or who knows what madness that has no purpose other than putting that much more character into the game (those who had the patience for the Snake Eater climb will know exactly what I mean). With a vast majority of battles having enemies unique to one another, your journey only gets weirder, bloodier and wackier, with new things to encounter and discover, which keeps the game so fresh that I find it hard to believe that anyone can’t be excited to see what kind of psychopath is waiting around the next corner.
Lisa is an RPG, and your battles are all turn-based affairs. This is where the game unfortunately has its first major flaw after looking the past the fantastic writing and set pieces. As mentioned, battles in most cases will be unique each time in character design and flavor, but save for a few instances with bosses that circumvent this, the plan and execution for victory boils down to the same routine: Trip them, oil them up, set them on fire, rinse and repeat. The potential depth and strategy is utterly shattered once you discover party member combinations that synergize ridiculously well and end up outright disabling enemies from causing you any harm, making victories feel shallow unless they are drawn out fights. In defense of Lisa, I was building teams that maximized damage output and brought victory the swiftest way possible, and with such a wide array of party members to recruit (and possibly lose for good), perhaps your best team will greatly differ from mine. This can inspire multiple playthroughs with different teams and even challenge runs with certain conditions, though getting attached to certain party members for very long is a poor idea. The chances that all the friends you meet will make it to the end and be alive is incredibly slim; be it unfortunate kidnappings, death from a boss or even your own selfish (or arguably self-preserving) decisions. Having a reliable party member die for good is painful (although save-scumming can lessen the blow and only use up more of your time instead), and excluding scenes that are specifically for humor, it only furthers the point that your journey through Lisa will be violent and unpleasant, with the story of Brad’s potential redemption one of tragedy and pain. I haven’t felt this much pity for a doomed loser of a protagonist in ages. The relation I have to Brad would unfortunately be spoilers, but my wish to see him ascend in victory rather greatly overpowered my cynicism to see him tumble back into drug-addled addiction.
While Brad’s tale is one filled with peril, pratfalls and perverts, I do find it a shame that, excluding the villains (and near the end of the game, you can’t help but question who the good/bad guy really is) who have their intentions and motives explained to a point, the vast array of supporting characters including your own party don’t get more of their own time to shine; like Terry Hintz, the wimpy trash-talker (but somehow isn’t more of a loser than Brad) who becomes your first ally, or Buckets, the mysterious gunman who joins you after cheating death at Russian Roulette enough times to make a casino pit boss to sweat. There is plenty of closure with side-stories and a finale to be sure, but the selfish side of me just wanted to learn more about these idiots and badasses.
Lisa tore at my heart, split my face in laughter, made me shiver in fear, had my blood run hot with ire and provoked more thought out of me than anything I have consumed in the past, and all only for $11 $17 for the added digital art book and soundtrack, the latter only bringing enhancements to the atmosphere of the world and the scenes you encounter, whether good or bad things are happening. While not immediately enjoyable on its own, Widdly 2 Diddly has composed a soundtrack that only adds to the overall experience, never taking away from it. Suffice to say, I can recommend Lisa without a shadow of a doubt, with only the disturbing imagery and the shallow RPG battles as major deterrents. I love this game to the point of silliness, and I only hope that other consumers can walk away as happily as I have in the end.

This game is an absolute hidden diamond amongst the rough of generic shooters.

The amount of dedication and focus it takes for an independent developer to create such a comfortable, engaging and rewarding experience is rarely discovered nowadays, but this game unimaginably brings it to beautiful light.
As with the majority of independent games, expect no hand-holding and many hints and refrences to the world of the nerd. This isn't quite a game for the casual player; fans of 2D exploration titles such as Metroid will enjoy this, but this game has that gameplay toned down. Average play time is only a few hours, but that is entirely up to how you explore and learn.  It's not meant to be difficult or aggrivating; the controls, mechanics and features are all beautifully built with perfect pacing adventure in mind and delivered very well.
Play with a keyboard or with a controller consisting of a d-pad and one button; there's nothing complicated needed to play, so make yourself comfortable with the nostalgia, and prepare to have your platforming skills and mental map imaging handy.
If you really love platformers from long ago and want to test yourself, you will download and play this free game. Don't look up any guides or ask for help. Immerse yourself. It's very rewarding.

Ok so let me sum up this game without spoilers and things I personally liked and disliked
It's a first person - survival - parkour - hack and slash -  blow up - shoot in the head - drive over - badassery
Imagine Mirror's Edge and Dead Island having a child combined with a great storyline followed up by a DLC which, simmilar to The Witcher 3, brings in a completely new game with a ton of more content and new challenges. The ending will leave you with a bit of blue balls but other than that I have only a few things to criticise. Here comes the pro-con
Pro:
-Amazing parcour
-Think game is too easy? bump up the difficulty
-4 player coop with optional zombie invasion (a player invades your game and gets to play as a badass zombie)
-Big variety of weapons (melee weapons)
-Insane agility and mobility
-Huge open world city for you to explore (2 if you buy the DLC)
-Tons of zombies to torture, impale, shock, combust.... you get the idea
-Replayablity
Cons: (like I said, these are personal and can be different from player to player)
- Firearms have very little purpose and are heavily underpowered, they only atract viral zombies which are just pestering you
- The buggy feels a little off and the parts seem to break a bit easy. The physics on your vehicle are not very pleasant and zombies slow you down too much which in turn kills the fun of mowing down hordes of them.
________________________________________________________________
Other than that, there's a new suppressor you can put on weapons which supposedly recategorizes pistols from "dinner bell" to "pea shooter". I haven't checked it out myself but sounds fun.
The game is an overall masterpiece with gorgeous graphics, great melee combat, badass melee weapons which are upgradable might I add.
If you are a fan of the Dead Island franchies you will probably enjoy this game (they are not connected though)

This game has an interesting premise, decent visuals, and some fun mechanics.  However, there were so many negative aspects that I found myself annoyed more often than not.  This game is a platformer which requires you to be extremely accurate, but often places you in very dark places or has jumps that are frustratingly too large.  And every time you mess up in the slightest, you have to start again from the last checkpoint.  The lack of a quick reset button makes it really annoying to watch the falling animation over and over again.
Even though it promotes itself as a puzzle game, there are no puzzles.  There's simply one right way to move through each section.  At one point, you literally have to turn around and go back through what you just did, only with greater difficulty.  While the store page says "Explore the World", you don't actually get to do any exploring.  You just have to jump from platform to platform over and over again, and it gets quite repetetive.
The story was very short, almost nonexistent, and with an anticlimactic ending.  You only really meet one character.  A few others have speaking parts, but don't really contribute much to the story.  The store page says "Emphasis on Story", but the amount of time the story is actually presented is about 15 minutes.
All in all, I would say that this game is rather mediocre.  It has some interesting mechanics, but the poor story and gameplay make it fall flat on its face.  I would not recommend purchasing this at full price.  There are 15 achievements to get, but they are all so difficult, I didn't even get one during my playthrough.

I hate everything about this game.  It's set up as a puzzle game, but there's only a single linear path to follow with no allowance for experimentation. The dialogue is uninspired and the voice acting toneless, unforgivable in a story driven game.  I'm uninstalling and asking for a refund.

Manual Samuel is an awesome adventure and side scrolling game which has been developed by Perfectly Paranormal and published by Curve Digital.
Manual Samuel is an Adventure game that puts you in control of a man called Samuel. There is a slight twist to Samuel and that’s the fact that you can control Samuel with individual buttons for example, moving his left leg requires you to press one button and then the same for his right leg, not too difficult right? WRONG!!!
Samuel is known to be a bit of a♥♥♥♥♥♥ He is a selfish narcissistic rich boy who has never had to work for anything in his life and treats people as such! When he forgets his girlfriend’s birthday (for the third year in a row) Samuel ends up dead and gets taken to hell where he meets his new best friend, Death.

Death does a small deal with Samuel and gives him his life back but on one condition, Samuel must work manually, every movement, breathe and blink will take his total and entire concentration! Samuel of course agrees to this and you end up waking up on his bedroom floor!
One of the most interesting parts about this game is the narration, there is a narrator throughout the whole game who gives you a bit of a tutorial and adds a lot of humour to what is happening to Samuel especially once he becomes Manual. The voice is well spoken and British which only adds to the humour.
So Back to Samuel lying on his bedroom floor, Death begins to talk to Samuel and explaining to you what’s happening and all you can see is Samuel going blue like he can’t breathe and in actual fact he can’t! You have to manually breathe both in and out using different buttons, if you don’t breathe out you will die, if you don’t breathe in you will die, and when you have to combine this with the manual movement of using different buttons for different legs, arms and blinking, this game become a more hilarious and intricate version of QWOP, anyone remember that game!

It takes a lot of effort for Samuel to do almost anything including drinking a cup of coffee, using one hand to hold it, the same hand to drink it but you must blow on it before you do and if you miss your mouth then you get coffee in your eyes which really hurts! All the while this is happening the narrator is doing a fantastic job of narrating what is happening!
The story and the gameplay of the game is very well done, the scenes are changed up a lot and so it the gameplay itself for example, walking around as Sam can get a bit boring when you’re just walking but the game breaks it up with some driving, controlling robots and daemons and such. All the controls work sort of similar but there are twists with each one for example when Samuel is driving his car to work on the morning of his “Undeadening” (it’s a word) Death has disabled the automatic gear box because in the games language “Death is a bit of a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥”. This means that you can’t turn left or change gear without moving your hand first, then you need to think about where your feet are, whether they need to be on the clutch, accelerator or break and it can get a bit daunting especially when there are Grannies all over the road getting in the way. This gives the game a pleasant shift from just walking around, grabbing and throwing stuff.
The Control Scheme can be quite daunting at the start but once you get the hang of walking and grabbing and moving stuff around then it will only be a few stupid mistakes that cause you any issues! The game does keep witching up the scenes and levels though so it remains interesting even when you feel like you know what you’re doing!

The characters in the game aren’t entirely Deep but then again you only get 3-5 hours of gameplay from this game Max! There are a few main characters who have a basic back story and few minor characters who only show up for a few scenes of minutes but they add to the story and don’t take too much screen time away from Sam and Death. For example, Sam’s Dad adds to the story a tiny bit but you only see him 2 or 3 times.
The game has a nice soundtrack to it which you can purchase along with the game but it really helps to captivate what you are doing at the time, the music doesn’t add a lot of emotion to the game but its more there for background noise and to give you something to listen too whilst your figuring out how to make Sam not throw hot coffee in his face!
The game adds a Time Challenge mode to all of the levels once have completed them so that you can either see if you can improve upon your time or compete with others, it wasn’t really my thing because some of the levels caused me some slight frustration so I personally don’t see much replay ability in that but other people will find it very interesting.
So in conclusion Manual Samuel is an interesting game, I had a lot of fun playing it but I don’t think I will go back and play it again because the story wasn’t anything to shout about and the gameplay is one of those that once you have played it and completed it then you have had your fun. That’s just my opinion however, there may be a hidden Community that compete with each other for the fastest times but I won’t be joining them.
You can pick the game up on Steam for £7.99 and with the Soundtrack for £10.98 which I think is a little bit steep for the 3-5 hours of gameplay but it was fun none the less.

This is a really, really good game, however there are imperfections: The AI
1. They do not take effect from having 0 gold and making a negative income per turn
Usually if your playing and your out of money and your making negative something gold then it automatically begins removing some of your troops because it cost gold per turn to manage them and if you cannot pay for them they are removed, however with AI ive seen it where they have the largest army and they are still growing and yet they are at -130 gold a turn and have 0 gold, yet for some reason they dont get their troops removed in order to decrease their debt, but if you as a player had -130 gold per turn with 0 gold they would remove your troops.
2. Happiness
Happiness is a feature to where if you have 1 or more happiness then your civilaztion produces things at a normal rate, troops do the same damage, and your cities make food at the same speed, but if you are -1 or lower then it starts to decrease, if your over around -50 then they actually begin to revolt, but for an AI they do not take effect from unhappiness, they still can do the exact same things no matter what, meaning it wont matter to them if they are at -100 happiness.
3. Get mad over nothing.
So there is another feature where you can interact with the AI diplomatically, they can get mad or have a negative opinon about you because you covet land they want, which is fine, that to me is ok because every civ has different feelings and some can get hostile and some dont at those things, however it draws the line at some places, take this scenario (Which actaually happened to me)
Two AI Civilations asked me if i wanted to join the war against another empire, i said yes, keep in mind i never went to war with that person they want me to war with, and i didnt ask them to join me in attacking them, they asked me. So we defeat them fairly easily, then my allies get mad at me for being a warmongerer what is a warmongerer? well:
war·mon·ger
ˈwôrˌməNGɡər/Submit
noun
plural noun: warmongers
a person who encourages or advocates aggression towards other countries or groups.
The AI interperets a warmongerer whenever you declared war on someone then made peace but them declared war on them multiple times, like being trigger happy, they also determine it if you are declaring war on multiple people, either at once or one at a time, However in this case my allies called me a warmongerer even though i never declared war on our enemies before, or declare war on anyone, and the thing is that they were the ones that wanted to war. So there is my lovely story with how the AI can get mad over nothing.
4. Trades
In the game your can trade with the AI, you can provide gold per turn, gold itself, luxery rescources, open borders, research agreement, resources, Even Cities, and more. The problem is when it comes to research agreements they make extremely unfair trades, now i know in some cases they may get greedy, but its EVERY SINGLE TIME.

Well its because even with all of that this game is still amazing with alot of variety in what you can do, there are different ways you can win, different leaders to play, maps to play, and they are randomly generated (like where mountains are) and SOOOO much more, and also you need to think about what you do and if it will help or not, yeah the issues are annoying, but overall it is really fun!

I've never played Mafia even though I got it in a Steam promo.  I have played and completed Mafia II though and I enjoy the game.  You start off as Vito Scaletta during the invasion of Sicily in WWII.  Basically this is a tutorial mission and shows how Vito first gets introduced to the Mafia.  Graphics are nice and the voice acting is pretty good.  Afterwards you are sent home and manage to dodge out of going back to the war.
Early on you are taking baby steps getting used to the various game mechanics and absorbing the world.  Empire City as the name suggests is very much a stylised recreation of New York.  Everything looks right even down to the GM Loco in the credits and the look of the cars.  You can customise cars but don't expect GTA V or Saints Row level customisation, basically a couple of tuning options and some cosmetic parts like new plates and paint job.
For the majority of the game Joe will be your faithful, if bumbling companion, and he's a pretty likeable guy.  You meet others though some are forgettable others less so.
The most annoying aspect of the this game is the collectibles.  There are wanted posters, some of which are VERY hard to get, even with a walkthrough, and one in particular is an exercise in frustration.  These can be collected throughout the open world aspect of the game at any time.  The other collectibles are Playboy pin ups.  These are apparently genuine Playboy Girls and not 'made up'.  Somewhere online theres a list of their names and when they appeared.  A bit anachronistic as some appear after the game was set, and indeed Playboy wasn't even around when this game takes place, but no matter as its one of the better collectibles you can get in game.  These ones are found at particular points in particular missions.  If you miss it, tough, though you can replay a chapter.
General game mechanics are decent, the driving being okay.  I say merely okay because 40's and 50's cars don't handle like even family sedans from Saints Row or GTA, you feel more like you're driving a land barge except for some later sports cars.  One thing that sets the atmosphere is the in car radio with music and announcements appropriate to the period.  Early on you're getting schlocky music and patriotic news spots, later on you're in  the rock and roll era.
Pick this game up if you like sandbox style games, especially if you can get it cheap.

Helldivers is best experienced as a multiplayer game, and joining an online session is about as quick and easy as starting a mission of your own. A couple of quick menu selections and you will, quite literally, drop in on another player's mission in progress. Local multiplayer is also an option and, in the absence of outside life, it's still enjoyable solo. Playing alone requires different strategies and offers less flexibility in strategem selection, which does make the already brutal higher difficulties seem even more insurmountable, but the satisfaction of single-handedly conquering a planet cannot be denied.
Unrelenting and brutal, Helldivers delivers fast-paced combat, epic standoffs and a comical approach to death. Its enemies are varied, powerful and a constant threat to the players. While the full impact of the larger multiplayer experience remains to be seen, it still adds a nice little scratch to the progress itch. The strategem system provides great flexibility in squad building with many ways to build out team roles to maximize defensive and offensive capabilities. With procedural map generation and just enough mission and enemy variety to prevent a sense of repetition, the twelve levels of difficulty ought to keep players challenged for a good long time.
The game is worth every penny.

To start of, I myself am an avid shoot-em-up fan, and went in with a lot of anticipation seeing I could play this game in co-op with friends. Most of this hype was shattered quickly through clunky controls, repetitive missions and no long time reward thanks to DLCs. Don't get this game if you want to play a good Twin Stick Shooter! I don't understand, how so many people could give a positive review, did nobody ever play a good Shoot-em-up.
This review will mostly focus on gameplay, as that was the reason i got the game. The intro cinematic was kinda cheesy and interesting, but it lacks any kind of later story progression, which could have keept me interested.
The camera completely works against you. Enemy’s often see you before you even can see them. It takes at least a second, until the camera decides to follow you, and when it finally does it takes another 20 seconds. If you are lucky the camera actually shows what’s in front of you.
Furthermore the controls feel super clunky. The player walks slow and shooting and aiming makes him walk even slower than a snail. Dodging also isn't really an option. The classical combat roll is replaced with a move, where the player goes prone and is even more likely to get shot.
And whoever had the brilliant idea to add turn speed to a top down shooter, should get fired.
Shooting also just doesn't feel right. Weapons in your armoury are just statistics, that barley explain enough what it actually does. Then, when you go into a mission, you are limited to one gun and a mostly fixed pistol. This makes the actual gameplay monotonous, even if you have unlocked a buttload of weapons.
The idea of being able to send down further equipment and airstrikes sounds kinda cool, but its execution is mayorly flawed. You have to initiate a combination of arrow presses in form of an Quick Time Event. It greatly slows you down when use a new equipment don't know which combinations to press and when you learned and remembered them, it is just an annoyance. I thought the gaming industry realized 2010, that a large amount of QTE, are really bad.
The DLCs also killed any reward that progression would have brought. It killed any long time fun for me. If you truly want to get DLC for Helldivers, wait until you reached a higher level, before you get any DLC.
Multiplayer is also more of a hassle than help. The camera doesn't zoom out if players move into different directions making enemy’s outside your view even more of a problem. This also forces you to bunch up, but then you are more likely to cause friendly fire. You are also more likely to die to your friends than to enemies most of the time.
Oh, and the game also needs precise D-Pad input. This makes playing it with a standard Xbox 360 controller, which most people i know have, really punishing and adds unneeded difficulty.
The missions also get repetitive very quickly. After one or two hours, you've seen all variety the game has to offer. Most missions are just different kinds of walk from point A to point B, where you then have to do one of the arrow QTEs. The mission may be described differently, e.g. activating anti-air cannons, or blowing up alien nests, but completing them always needs a QTE at its core. Although there are three different enemy races, the game throws every different unit of the races at you at once, meaning after the first mission with every race, you have seen them all.
TL;DR: Don't expect a great twin stick shooter from Helldivers, maybe you can get some fun out of it in local couch co-op . And don't get DLCs after you completely sure you like the game.

Lisa is without a doubt one of my most favorite Rpg maker games ... I still am so shocked that this was created by that engine, Because its unlike any other Rpg maker game I'v ever played.
Such a brutal experience I had playing this, Its gruesome .. Sick ... Twisted ... and just Hilarious.
This game is not for kids.. thats for sure, I personally think its 18+ not 16+ but what do I know.
So now for the game itself.
The game starts with an interesting story, That slowly progresses into what your character is, Revealing bits and parts every now and then.
An interesting concept is that you can slightly control how it goes with the (Choices matter) Thing.
And the story is really dark and good.
The game-play certainly is something to notice, Because its a good platformer with many platforms to platform on ...lol
The battles are fast, They are unique and fun but being fast is an admirable feature because thats what you usually aim in an Rpg game, To not have to waste so much time watching your character do the attack animation.
The dialogues are so funny, The type of ( HAHA..ha...wait .. thats so EVIL ..HA HAHA .. I feel so wrong for laughing at this )
Everything in the game is so twisted, And the difficulty is something to count for,  Trust me DO NOT start the game with ( Pain mode ) From your first try,.
What pain mode does is , Gives an extra ending/boss/area and when you save at the savepoint it disappears so you cant save there again, So you need to go to the next one, Which is an actual pain because you'd die a lot in the game.
So its recommended to try after finishing the game once.
Characters are all over the game, There are a lot to find and get to join your party. ( And let me just say they are all pretty weird, Don't think I met any sane person )
Some wants money(magz) and others some certain stuff, But know that you'll lose a lot of them I will explain why.
Music is really good, And sound effects are good, Level designs are spectacular and characters looks great, The part I really cant deny is the animations... they're just so great.
So how the game works.
You get choices to choose from that effects how the game goes.
And one of those choices are whether to sacrifice one of your party members to keep your items, Or the opposite.
There are a lot of annoying scenarios where you'd be forced to pick between stuff like that or ( Your arm or this random party member), Later in game you'd be able to afford to lose a few party members because you'd have too much that you wont use anyway.
Resting at tents is really scary in this game, Because there are a lot of things that could happen to you after you wake up, A party member could get kidnapped, You could lose items, You'd all get poisoned or sometimes nothing happens.
I don't exactly know how deep your choices effect the game's story, But I do know you need to do your best to keep your party members alive at first because if you keep losing them, Then battles and bosses are gonna be tougher to vanquish.
Shops, Secrets, Weird events, Bikes to ride And much more content to encounter, Didn't feel bored at all.
Also a good note worthy part is the fact that this game is quite long and has some replay-value, And the achievements are really well-done.
I know you might see the disclaimer and see the review for this game being too positive you'd think I'm biased.
The only thing that could be biased is the fact that I enjoy Rpg maker games, But I dislike those that has no creativity or originality and just abuses the basic RTP library, When this one made its own design, And became a platformer unlike any other.
So the not so good parts.
- At certain parts the game felt extremely frustrating with pain mode, Making a small mistake and falling off a cliff and dying then having to restart from a long distance, So I felt like certain save points are close and others are just too far from each other.
- This is considered a con to some but it contains spoilers !!
- The platforms in the game are great, But considering this is RPG MAKER made you can feel some slight slow downs while jumping with your character, But when its on the bike its pretty smooth.
- In most parts, The game leads to you to the next area that is basically 5 different places to go to, Which you'd need to do by order to carry on with the story, I had to use a guide a couple of times because I got lost, I mean yeah there are clues on what to do most of the time, But it was designed to be hard and I got lazy after dying so much in pain mode, And used the guide which was a really informative steam guide.
- It crashed once for me, Which did not annoy me because thankfully it was a little bit after I saved, And there is this bug I encountered after saving at a tent ( Like all rpg games, Screen goes black when you sleep ) But then stayed black forever got stuck there, Had to close game and load.
So
Lisa, Is a game every big fan of RPG maker games should own.
Because it has so much originality and creativity in it that makes it standout between all those games.
WELL if you are not into platformers then this game is not for you because it focuses a lot on that, But don't forget it has a lot of rpg elements, And a really good story and the game keeps it fresh with those hilarious dialogues
Rating -> 8/10

Be warned: This game is extremely experimental (and this isn't just another way to say "it's pretentious indie crap," I swear).
The game goes out of its way to frustrate you. You are forced to make hard decisions. You will lose, again, and again, and again. There are dozens of companions in this game, and each and every single one of them can die permanently. Or they might just decide to abandon you. Your main character can lose all he has, including his limbs.
This game is absolutely nuts.
It's not quite "rocks fall, everyone dies," but at one point, it gets very, very close to that.
Absolutely loving the game just for that aspect alone already.
The story is gripping, dark, and you always know that anything can happen. I absolutely couldn't let go off this game, because I wanted to know how it was going to end.
But all in all, I've got to say the story's actually what I like the least about this game. A few times in the game, your player character will do terrible things to others. He'll just do what he wants, basically. It always takes you out of the game a little bit, but it's mostly forgivable. However, at one point in particular, towards the very end of the game, it just completely took me out of the game. I'd been there, captivated by the plot, longing to know what happens next--but then, I ceased to feel with my player character. Simple as that.
About one hour before completing the game, I was actually concerned that I wasn't going to be able to sleep easy, no matter how the game would end. But now, I just don't really care.
And when you look at it, the story is just bleak and depressing. Things don't really get resolved at all, and there's a bunch of open questions.
Apart from the last thirty minutes of the game, the story is perfect, though. Absolutely phenomenal, especially coupled with the permadeath mechanics. I can't emphasize this enough: Hard decisions have to be made in this game.
I've actually had to wrestle with myself whether to hit that thumbs up or thumbs down button at the bottom of this review. Ultimately, I went with a recommendation, because this game is just so unbelievably imaginative, daring, and provocative. Does the game go too far? Definitely. But too far is better than too little.

Many people called this a "tower defense with RPG elements" at first I didn't know what that meant but it pretty much describes the game perfectly.
Azra is the leader who can cast spells and also boost defenders - there are 6 types of defenders that have their unique abilities and advantages. While you boost the characters in battle, there also is a leveling up system in which you also add points to certain skills which actually adds a lot of depth to the game - it makes you think about what is mostly valuable of each defender and if you boost them enough for a certain skill to be used.
Some enemies go straight for Azra, some try to get Azra but attack defenders along the way, some are fast, some are slow, some have armor, some have an insane amount of hit points. The come in waves from different locations in different amounts.
It all sounds pretty basic, right?
What makes this game so special is that it introduces new variables and level designs at just the right pace; there is never too much of one thing in the game, it's never a grind, it's never repetitious. The levels were never frustrating when they were heard either; it always just made me think hard about a better defense, who should get boosted and where I need to reposition during the battle. The idea of making something challenging without making frustrating is something they absolutely nailed on this game. On the flipside, if you are convinced you have everything figured out for your defense and even need to watch - just fast foward with the 2x or 4x button (this small feature is amazing).
If you want to go back and play the battles at a high difficulty, you can do that too, which I also found the be very fun (the higher difficulty didn't just add more enemies - it also changed what types of enemies and even changes the entry points. Once again, they did a great job of preventing this game from feeling like repetitious).
The game has an accompanying story which is kind of funny sometimes. I enjoyed the animations mostly and they were well done. A minor complaint of mine would be that the humor bits would take over the unfolding of the story occasionally and got in the way. I don't feel like the story development was conitinuous enough.
The music was pretty enjoyable and fitting for the game. I will say some of the songs seemed like they were ripped from Nobuo Uematsu (Final Fantasy I - X, Chrono Trigger) but he is the GOAT.
Highly recommended.

My recommendation for this game is a lukewarm one. It's absolutely beautiful to look at, and there's a great eerieness about most of the game that had me on edge while exploring, but I also found myself getting bored and frustrated with walking around the same places over and over.
I chose to play the original version rather than Redux and therefore didn't have a reliable save function, so that's on me. In the original, not only are the autosaves somewhat spaced out, if you happen to have two puzzles going at the same time (you've inspected objects for two separate areas, for example), if you complete only one and then save, your progress on the unfinished puzzle will not be saved, and you have to redo everything. I also ran into what might have been a bug where on multiple occasions the text to interact with the environment didn't trigger properly, and I had to return to the same exact spot sometimes up to four times to get it to activate. Other minor complaints are that I wasn't that big on most of the voice acting aside from the main character, and that while I actually enjoyed most of the story (and the stories within the story), I found the ending to be on the "meh" side of things.
Overall, I don't regret spending my time on this game or money (I would recommend getting it on sale, though). Again, the graphics are gorgeous, and it's decently creepy, especially in the beginning before you've really figured out what to expect more or less. Maybe I would have enjoyed Redux more, but as for the original version, be aware of the potential mechanical annoyances. And to be entirely fair, this was my first walking simulator, and that type of game just might not be my thing; if you enjoy them and like your mysteries on the (very) mildly scary side, there's a good chance you'll enjoy this.

First off, I only recommend this game if you can get it and Last Light both for 20$ or less. The shining point of this game LL is the atmosphere. Outside of that I cannot say the AI, Technical aspect, Gunplay, Stealth elements and most importantly the story do a whole lot for the game. Especially considering a bunch of people got shafted into buying the "Ranger Mode" difficulty. The AI reminds me heavily of older 2005-2007 era games where they will do the cover shuffle, chicken dance searching, the deadly accurate blow your brains out through cover trick, and the ignore you allies to do the same trick. There's not a ton of crashes or bugs, but there is quite a few annoying quirks the game has such as bringing up the steam menu with you just pressing shift if you come back from a Alt-Tab. In ranger mode they strip the hud down to nothing except your weapons menu which lets you select nades and see how many stims you have (They remove the hud entirely in Last Light...)  The gunplay is ok but the attachment system is not noteworthy. You have to buy and unequip your attachments at stores which costs Military ammo which is costly and often forces you into a cookie cutter build, taking a page from Crysis  (Made in 2007... also has better AI) would have helped this game alot in allowing you to change attachments you already have in combat. The stealth in this game is an average light and sound based system that is quirky at best. You can dodge the ai about if you run a silencer and keep your lights off but they eventually gain the infamous Omnisiance of Oblivion guards or they act like dumbfounded chickens. The story is interesting but very thin and jumpy. I didn't honestly know what the big deal was with the dark ones until the very end and the rest of the story is forgettable. This game wasn't horrible despite my long review of negatives, but I can honestly say this game and Last Light are bargin bin material at best because if I had paid 60$ for this I would have been very mad.

While there are many, many people who say this is an utterly brilliant game, I sadly cannot verify that. Why ? Because whoever coded this made such a complete and utter hash of it, it takes hours and hours to get it to work.
There is an Unofficial Patch available, which is still being made 10 years after the original was released. This is done completely by fans of the game and is supposed to fix many many bugs. However, because of the sheer crapness of the original coding by the original developers, there are still some bugs that you have to manually fix. They include bombing out when you select New Game and crashing on game load if you have more then 4GB of RAM (these days who doesn't!). It also seems to hate Windows 8, though I've come across some people who can run it fine, and others where it just refuses to start.
Unless you have hours to kill trying to get the game to run, don't bother. For me, this will have to be a game I come back to at a time when I actually have time to to get it to run. Very disappointing.
