Well, what can you say? It’s ♥♥♥♥ing Peggle. It’s part puzzle game, part platformer, part skill, and part luck. You shoot a ball out and attempt to take out all the red pegs. Blue pegs, and many other things, give you bonus points, but that’s about it. Sure, there are powerups, different masters, all kinds of different play modes, and so on, but that’s pretty much all there is to say about Peggle.
Honestly, it’s only $15, it has a bunch of depth, it’s highly addictive, you can play with your friends, AND it’s two whole versions of Peggle. I wish there was more to say because Peggle is a damn fun game, but like many casual games (Diner Dash, Plants vs. Zombies, Bejeweled, etc.), the beauty is in its simplicity. Often you’re still playing for hours on end and you can’t quite say why, other than “just one more level.”

Once in a lifetime does a game capture the essence of fun. No other game does what Peggle does quite like it. The fun, interesting gameplay mechanic, somewhat pachinko esque, immediately captures your interest by it's quirky artwork and character selection, and leaves you hooked with it's various hilarious animations, noises and quotes from the Peggle Masters. Nothing quite beats the feeling of %100 a level and getting an Ultra Extreme Fever.
The gameplay in Peggle Nights is simple; drop a ball from the top of the screen in a 180 degree arc and hit all the orange pegs (And blue pegs for more points). You start with 10 balls and gain an extra ball every 25k points, or by landing it in the bucket at the bottom of the screen. Various Peggle "Masters" introduce new features such as the ball returning to the top of the screen after falling out the botom for a second drop, a blast that hits all pegs in a radius and so on.
The best feature of Peggle Nights is the music and background art. Each of these elements is done to insane levels, with the art painting a story in the background. The music is calm and relaxing, but changes dramatically to the Ode To Joy once you clear the last orange peg on the board.
This is the best game ever made. No other game is as good as Peggle Deluxe, or it's superior sequel Peggle Nights. Peggle 2 is decent, but nothing can compare to these two titans of games. Owning it on Steam(PC), Xbox 360 and IOS, Peggle is my favourite game of all time, and I'm sure if you gave it 5 minutes, you'd love it too.
(Pick it up in the Peggle Complete Package when it's on sale for %50 off during the Steam Sales, or if you can go back in time, pick it up in the Humble Weekly Sale for $6 along with Peggle Deluxe and Plants Vs Zombies (And Bejewled and many other Popcap Titles)).
1000000000000000000000000000000000/10

So, let's get into it: this game is fantastic. From the gameplay, to the visuals, to the community and development team, the game is worth whatever price you find it at.
The bulk of the game will have you running, jumping, scaling and free falling your♥♥♥♥♥all over the map. The parkour system is done exceptionally well and is easy to get into, while at the same time.very rewarding when you master it. Traversing the maps in this game is fun in and of itself, adding in dodging enemies and attacking from the skies just tops the whole experience off.
The combat is great fun, as well. You can purchase the Hanaan Ranger pack right off the bat, and make easy work of all the enemies, but why would you want to do that? It takes some serious work to get to a point where you can slice your way through hordes of zombies, and even then it'll still be dangerous. Weapons have a durability function, which I typically hate in games, yet in Dying Light it doesn't hold the game back from fun and engaging combat. Leveling your Power and Agility skill lines also grants access to some abilities that will spice up the combat: from drop kicks, to ground finishers.
The RPG elements are abundant and implimented well: you gain Agility xp by running around, climbing, jumping. All of it contributes. The Power line will level as you attack and take out zombies. Both take some serious time to level, short of using XP exploits. Both feel rewarding and paced very well.
The crafting system is simple enough to not require intricate items to create weapons a d equipment, and yet still complex enough that going out scavenging for the items in order to craft the next tier of weapon never gets boring. I go out for full days and nights at a time, simply to gather materials and find little nooks and crannies that I've yet to see.
The map design is impeccable and lends itself well to the parkour system. A vast majority of buildings are enterable, affording yourself a quick safe spot and a chance at some loot. It's just great fun, jumping and climbing around, to get into second and third story windows that may hold some reward.
The weapons are quite varied. There's all types of melee weapons, and the come in all kinds of quality levels. They can also be modded, adding a myriad of effects to your attacks, from electrical shocks, to searing flames. Really getting into the weapon system will reward the player with some pretty ♥♥♥♥♥in weapons capable of shredding your infected adversaries. Eventually, you'll get your hands on a gun, or many. They've been implimented extremely well in this survival game: they're quite deadly against all enemies, yet with the distinct absence of silencers*, the player must make a decision whether or not to quickly dispatch their target, and risk attracting nearby hordes. It makes for some compelling gameplay situations, in which you'll find a quick attempt to eliminate some thugs has plunged the player into a mess of swarming zombies and Volatiles.
The enemies are fantastic. Thee zombies are well done, and while not very menacing on their own, are absolutely dangerous in hordes. Sometimes the best option is simply to scale the wall next to you and flee. The game also has an upper tier of infected enemies, known as Volitiles. They come in a number of shapes and sizes, easily distinguished from the normal infected, and carrying a number of abilites unique to their type. All in all, combat rarely becomes dull or repetitive.
I have to give huge props to the development team behind this game. The Following DLC was amazing, adding some great new features to the game, along with a large new map to explore. Beyond the DLC, the team has been hard at work on a number of free releases. The game launched in January of 2015, and yet here we are in the beginning of 2018 with the team still putting out a wealth of updates, free to their playerbase. In a time of rampant monetization, sold as "necessary for cost," here is a company giving back generously to it's community, and all the while absent of microtransactions and loot boxes. The generosity and the engagement of it's community comes off as quite sincere, and you can tell theyre grateful of the community that still plays this game. Techland sets a shining example of what a truly passionate game company is capable of, and should all else aspire to be, in this day and age.
If you're a fan of action games, zombie survival games, or just want to smash some heads: I wholly recommend this game, and I give it a perfect 5 out of 7. Don't miss out on this title.

A free game that is a loving tribute to the platformers and "open world" of the ZX Spectrum/Commodore 64/NEC computer days, where the world was divided between different screens that formed the whole of a world much like VVVVVV was, rather than the scrolling with the character that came with Pitfall and Super Mario Bros. Make no mistake while this is a tribute and love letter to many a classic game in level lay out, early 80s tube computer box outline, and art style for it's game world, it is very much a game for modern design and ease of getting into.
A game where you have plenty of opportunities to learn exactly what to do due to natural and clear explanation of what to do in what is shown and required (touch an enemy and die, longer pit requires to hold the jump longer, etc), and true to it's roots it never gets too confusing in what to do or where to go unless you yourself have lost your way. It rewards mastering the jumps and wall jumps (a power up), it gives the chance for pixel perfect jumping when desired in it's normal mode, nothing is impossible to reach once you know how and can (power ups, 2 of them), and there is never a situation where one can get stuck.
As it is old school it can prove challenging to those who require a clear cut map, as none is provided and instead has one memorising the world and it's lay out until you have a good idea where to go next. As death is never a issue in it's normal mode, with Super Meat Boy like instant-respawn and an infinite number, however one is never punished for exploring and through time you learn the routes to take until they become second nature. Take as many tries as needed, never respawn too far from doing it again or leaving to try something else, it's open to you with the normal mode. As it is screen to screen, a static image as only you and enemies and some objects move in it, you learn what each one looks like with a way to remember them by a quote at the bottom to make each one stand out beyond just it's unique lay out.
Never more than a game about collecting all the money bags in the world and platforming save for one end game puzzle, which you are told how to solve by clues written on the wall, your only worry is your own skill at platforming. You jump, you wall jump eventually, you slide down, you move. The enemies are things that move from left to right or shoot small bullets in a set pattern, nothing to worry about because they never do anything different and thus you can take your time until you master them. Then, quickly speed past them and that may just be the best tactic to get through a specific screen.
As a platformer fan, as someone who loves to explore a game world, and one who enjoys creative designs with limitations on what is actually shown at any given time, I find this to just to be a spectacular and amazing game that does so many things right and is a pure example of a platformer. A game where my first play through was filled with numerous deaths, gave me the greatest sense of satisfaction in earning an achievement (Steam) when I beat the game by never dying, proving that I had mastered the game and knew exactly what to do.
Yet it doesn't even end there. For it offers a Master Quest style challenge, named Extra Spicy Mode, which completely changes up the lay out of every screen, the order in which you travel the world, the challenge offered, and you collect power ups in reverse making it that much more of a different experience. A wonderful thing to go through after I had just "mastered the game and knew exactly what to do". One section required me to do a pixel perfect landing on what normally is death for example, another learning not to jump to keep yourself alive as normal on a vertical positioned platform, and it made me work through it and improve my skill that much more without ever being unfair.
There are issues that can prevent many people from finishing it because it is challenging, those who quit games easily/rage quit may find little to love here as it's all on the player, at times easy for some to lose track of where they are or going due to no map, it won't be for all fans of platformers who want the Super Mario Bros influenced style of always moving right and holding down speed and jumping only, and there is no action/attacking some crave. Yet it is still one of the best examples of this type of platforming, a loving homage to a style very rarely seen today, and of course it's free so there is no loss in trying.

Defender's Quest is an interesting twist on the tower defense paradigm. This time, your "towers", are RPG heroes you're summoning on the battle field. This makes for a much more interesting story, with many characters voicing their opinions on what you're doing (usually to complain about it :p). The story itself isn't revolutionary, but it's servicable.
Unfortunately, by making the game an hybrid of TD and RPG, Defender's Quest brings with it the bad aspects of RPG. Mostly, the grind. There will be times where you're facing a level which you simply can't win because your characters/towers aren't levelled up enough. So you will have to grind by doing other stuff (like replaying levels on a harder difficulty) before coming back. It's even more notable and grindy when you're trying to keep your adventuring party small, like the games encourages you to do (by raising recruitement prices, but also having some achievements that only unlock if you never expand your roster).
Another problem with the small roster is that in many levels, there are some optimal positions to place your 5 or 6 people, and then you're pretty much done, you fast forward to see your team hacking and slashing away for several minutes until the level is done. There are some levels where you will more active, with your main character having to use its spells, and you having to replace some of your team in better places. But on the whole, it's a rather static tower defense, since you have limited number of people, an enticement to bunch them together (for increased efficiency) and a limited mana pool to summon.
All that bad stuff being said, Defender's Quest is still way better than most tower defense. The writing is good, the levels are interesting and you can always stop at any point. The main game is pretty easy to finish, while the main game plus will offer a bigger challenge, but also new items, additional missions and optional quests to keep it fresh, and reward you for staying with the game. So on the whole while i wouldn't classify Defender's Quest as one of my favorite games, it does get a soft recommendation from me.

King Arthur's Gold is perhaps one of the single greatest multi-player side scrolling themed games I have ever played. This game has recently been made available to purchase through Steam, but has an extensive following, manifesting itself during the Alpha and Beta stages of the games development. There is an outside Steam forum for KAG located
Where you can contact other players, and get in touch with the developers. There is also Modding tools, and instructions on hosting your own server available at the forums, which I feel is a great addition to the game, and will inherently increase the content and re playability of the King Arthur's Gold in the future.
The actual Game play is set within a Medieval Age side scrolling platform, Where Two Teams Battle it out for Dominance in Three primary Game Modes. I personally find myself going back to Capture the Flag, But Storm the Halls, and Team Death-match are also appealing. There has been a Zombie Mode introduced into the Game, however it is still in the Pre-Release stage of development. The Arcade, mode is also fun, giving a Puzzle/ Race across the Map and obstacles to the finish with different classes.
Speaking of Classes, There are Three classes released right now. The Knight is the powerhouse of your Team, armed with Sword and Shield you Glide/ Slide your way to the enemy and Charge & Slash through their noob players to Victory. The Builders role is the most Diverse, offering both offensive and defensive capabilities. They are also the resource collectors of your team, but if you find a huge pile of stone left behind from some blood crazed dead builder, carry the resources back to help your team construct your defenses. Whether you are building Shops for your Team at the Spawn, Traps and Walls in the field, or Ladders and Tunnels to Storm your enemies gates you will be the last to receive credit for victory, and the first to be blamed in defeat, primarily by the Archer class. The Archer class is unique in the they carry a type of radical grapple hook which allows you to skillfully scale almost any Wall in the game. They can also scale Trees, and have the only long range attack in the game aside from Siege Equipment.
Each Class can supplement their skills with Shops, giving your character the competitive edge and courage only a Keg of Explosives, or Explosive Fire Arrows can muster. The game at this point has some balancing issues, which is to be expected with any multi-player online game, but nothing which corrupts the overall experience and enjoyment achieved from playing the game. KAG is still popular and growing, so finding a server should not be a problem; If it is, there are ways to host your own servers so don't let that discourage you. The only thing this game is missing is more classes, character skins, Larger explosions, Steam Achievements, and a greater variety of game modes. If you end up Purchasing King Arthur's Gold you will surely not be disappointed.

To give you a hint at what I'm talking about, let me explain the beginning of the game. First, you meet Bjorn. He wants to be acknowledged as a scholar, but struggles because of his terrible name. This leads him to search in his innermost thoughts which are strangely filled with pegs, and discover that with the name Bjorn, he wonders if his parents ever loved him. Through the tragic tale, you realize that pegs are what cause all problems in life, but that without them, you would have no life to live. In a beautiful world, you may even have tears in your eyes as you journey on. Along comes Bjorn's associate, Jimmy Lightning. He loved adrenaline, but still remains fat because his addiction has become too extreme and poor Jimmy has had to resort to "chemicals." You now enter his mind, and while it is filled with chemicals, the game brings along plenty of gameplay twists to keep it interesting. As you uncover the truth, Jimmy remembers that he also had a burning passion to play the guitar, and decided to dedicate a riff to playing every time you do something really really good. Now, Jimmy also remembers that his real problem, all along, was that he was just really, really, really stupid. It's all in the experience. The issue arrives in that Jimmy is really, really, really stupid, and this prevents him from making any relavant or accurate statement. How will Jimmy reinvent himself? Lisa is a side-scrolling rpg made in rpgmaker. Mechanically speaking, it's very similar to Earthbound. Got it? Okay, now forget that. It's not important. Lisa is the most hurtful and disgusting game I've ever played. By the time I was done with it, I felt nauseous and depressed. It is also a perfect ten out of ten.
In a time where games are becoming more mainstream and developers are becoming softer, Lisa stands out as a truly satisfying game. It doesn't hold your hand other than for a brief unintrusive period, the entirety of which is witty and refreshing. You are forced to make some hefty choices throughout the game which have serious ramifications that you are forced to live with. It's never so brutal as to be game-ending, at least on the normal difficulty, but it earns its title as The Painful RPG.
The writing is hilarious and terrifying all at the same time. The beautiful sprites pop out against the bleak background, a collage of grays and browns that manage to look terrific while simultaneously poking fun at modern AAA graphics. The story is incredibly bleak, and it's told in snippets so small and unobtrusive that you could miss them entirely. If you want a bit more backstory, I would recommend playing the free downloadable game "Lisa the First" which came before Lisa the RPG (although it certainly isn't necessary).
You should be warned before you buy Lisa that it is NOT for everyone. There is strong adult theming in the game. It isn't of an overtly sexual nature but it is shocking nontheless. If you are squeamish, you should at least make sure you can handle the story before you play. That said, if you're okay with that, I couldn't recommend Lisa more. Also, if you like wrestling (poster is a lowkey wrestling fanboy), you will get so much more out of this game than the average consumer. Trust me.

With a dialogue that is unique and extremely refreshing and combine that with a story that you would never expect from the face value of this game and you have LISA. This game is a masterpiece. Not to mention the music that accompanies it is beautiful in itself. If you like side-scrolling RPG's, this one is going to be memorable for you.

I've never played the original Metro 2033, so I can't really comment on how good this remaster is compared to the original. I've heard though, that some things have been changed so that the overall game is more mechanically similar to Metro: Last Light.
Now that being said, this game is extremely atmospheric and immersive, especially if you play it in the Ranger difficulty mode, which removes HUD elements and some other things. The story is gripping enough to keep you going, and provides a vehicle to explore the cramped, lonely metro tunnels and the beautifully ruined city of Moscow in the overworld. The game is fairly linear, especially in the underground metro sections, with the sections where you roam around in the overworld being slightly less linear.
The graphics for this game are fantastic, with the remaster bringing the visual fidelity up to par with Last Light. If you are going to play this game, it's recommended that you have a system that can run this game at reasonably high settings. The high graphical quality really enhances the immersion that is one of the main selling points of this game. Be careful to make sure that SSAA is off, as that setting can cause your game to render at half the resolution, rendering the beautiful scenery and detail blurry.
Overally, a fantastic and atmospheric game with an interesting story and beautiful visuals that contribute to it being one of the most immersive games that I've ever playyed, where you can really feel the mournful mood of a world destroyed.

Man, this game. Solid shooter with a great setting, and an interesting story. I have a soft spot for post-apocalyptic settings, so this one immediately appealed to me. Same for the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. series. So, how's the game like? Well, it plays out like a run-of-the-mill FPS, with iron sights, melee and grenades, althought these are surprisingly good. Throw in a bit of stealth and a filter mechanic which forces you to keep track of the state of your gas mask lest you die to asphyxiation and you get a unique game. Oh, and don't forget the story and setting. Mostly set in the damp and dark metro, you rarely see light save for the above ground levels and even those have some indoor environments where flashlights are a necessity. Oh, and you have to recharge your flashlight too from time to time. Add in limited medkits and ammunition and you'll find yourself on your back foot most of the time...well, for the harder difficulties at least. Fits the survival and hopelessness theme really. So, it sounds good right? A perfect game? Well, it does have its quirks.
- Some of the sounds are...lacking. Sounds cheap. Like the AK family of weapons and the character's grunts.
- Stealth is...weird. You can be directly near a person and he won't even see you.
- Sometimes the game throws A LOT of enemies at you, and these ones are usually close ranged beasts. You'll really be
going through ammo for these parts.
- Voice acting, especially the children. They sound like grown men with their balls squeezed.
Most of these are minor, actually. You can have yourself an extremely immersive experience in my opinion.
So, should you get this? Well, if you're looking for a first person shooter with great shooting bits and great atmosphere, then you should totally get this. Just...a word of advice, though.
If it's hostile, you kill it.

I wrote a review for this about a year or so ago but thought I'd rewrite it as I have some different and new views on the game.
First off, this is a tower defense game that revolves around a well written story with a nicely done narrative that includes all the who/what/when/where/why questions, along with moments of subtle humor and despair. On the first play through you get all the character dialogue that propels the story but not a whole lot more. On the second play through you get the main character's (Azra unless otherwise named) thoughts after each mission is completed. These journal entries go pretty in-depth for being subtext you don't even need to go through. There are some 30 entries and I do recommend reading them.
The game starts with the Azra wondering where the hell she is and finding the first warrior, Slak, entering into a battle against the Revenant (the dead). The story progresses and you will find all the other characters (read 'towers'). There are six others you find and you can have up to six of them in that class, in total allowing you to have an army of 36 towers and Azra.
The Berserker is a hack 'n' slash guy. He wields a sword, wears no shirt, and thirsts for blood.
The Ranger is your snarky and quick witted bow expert. She often griefs Azra on menial things such as, "not being pretty enough to have her plans work out."
The Healer comes off as overprotective and cautious but holds the team together.
The Ice Mage is cold and has cynical tendencies but wields the power to stop hordes of foes.
The Knight is rightous and pledges himself to Azra. He takes down the strongest enemies by ripping them of their armor.
The Dragon is the last to join the group. She acts like a god and thinks the humans beneath her yet is impressed at how far Azra and her companions have traveled thus far. She also enjoys eating sheep.
With these characters you can create varying strategies on every battlefield in the game. Some will require a near exact positioning that you'll figure out by trial and error, while others are more liberal in placement. You can pull off a ton of combos though and it's cool to find something that synergizes well.
Now, along with all the characters, each has a skill branch (not tree since there are only two directions it goes) and with each level you get one point to put in each skill slot. Most of them are damage boosts for their attack tier (each character has a five tier attack that is upgraded through Psi that is earned by killing enemies in the level) and the rest are passive buffs. They can include skill cooldowns, range, crit/poison/bleed/blind/armor piercing chance, slow/stun/burn, group damage amplifiers and tagging enemies so they take more damage.
Azra also has six spells she can upgrade. There are three damage and three buff spells. A direct lightning attack, an area of effect crystal explosion, and a full screen flame attack. The buffs are sending your characters into a frenzy to increase attack speed, massive healing, and pushing back waves of enemies. There are also unlockable spell books that can be equipped to provide boosts.
There are three weapons in game that two classes can use. Swords for the Berserker and Knight, a bow for the Ranger, and staffs for the Healer and Ice Mage. Progressing through the story increases the price and damage of future weapons. Armor can be equipped to them as well, heavy and light variants.
The max level each member can achieve is 60 so you won't be able to max every skill on each character. The good thing about having multiple in a class means that you can have someone with a high bleed chance, and give the other person the higher armor piercing chance. At any point you can pay a small fee of scrap (currency) to respec their builds.
So that's the gist of the game. Pretty straight forward. Where things really get rolling are on the new game +. Much more challenging and rewarding. A new currency of "skulls" becomes used to upgrade the special weapons and armors you aquire through missions. It's pretty hard to get all the skulls as you'll need to grind to get your characters to a high enough level to beat the much harder than before levels. There are also a few puzzles hidden here and there that you need to keep an eye out for. I had some trouble with it and found a guide and without it there would've never been a way I'd have caught on.
All in all, more than your run of the mill tower defense game, great story, fun and unique characters, scaling rewards that only get better and better through all the challenges, and tons of replayability as there is mod support.
Oh, if you really want a challenge, there's an achievement to beat the game and new game + with only the original characters, not using any of the extra hired ones. And then getting 180 stars (awarded through level completion). That took a ton of time.

Summary - The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a story driven puzzle solving mystery game, from the role of a great detective you explore the these abandoned places in order to find what happened to the people that lived here and what happened to cause the disappearance of Ethan Carter.

Pros
- Great story, the game itself is not very story driven if I'm honest it mostly focuses on puzzles, however the overall story to the game was not predicable in any means, I had no clue the ending was going to turn out as it was
- Well layed out puzzles, the puzzles in this game are perfectly constructed, as you have to firstly fine clues to what has happened in the sence, and then you secondly get a first hand view on what went down. As if you were a detective, the way the puzzles immerse you with little things that just make so beautiful is just phenomenal
- Due to the free Redux verison, this game is unbelievably beautiful this is for sure one of the best looking games I've ever seen the attention of detail is even in the distance is just beautiful
- I experienced no glitches or bugs when playing, apart from a little texture missing in a rock, but I ain't going blame ya for that..
- Very unique, I've never played any game like this in my entire life
- Again this game is just too beautiful
Cons
- Story is short even considering the game is only 15 bucks depending in what country you're in, the game still feels short
- Although the graphics are beautiful the views are generic as it's set in the woods most of the sights are the same thing.
- Basically doesn't have any replay value
- One of the puzzles is rather hard, in my opinion
Verdict: Overall, The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, is a masterpiece one my favorite games of all time and I proudly say that with no regrets, the game is just beautiful in every aspect, views, soundtrack, story and so on. I would recommend this to every person, although note that this is a puzzle/mystery game so some people might not find this appealing to them compared to a more story driven game, the game also has no use of violence, weapons and so on are not used. However regardless of what your preference is this game is a MUST buy and I strongly recommend this masterpiece.

Faster Than Light is a 2D roguelike game set in space, the roguelike genre has been crawling its way back into the spotlight, however it's not common to be set in such environment.
You're part of the Galactic Federation that assigned you critical information that you must deliver eight sectors away, to do so you're given a spaceship that you must upgrade and fill with crew... All this, while being chased by the Rebel force, nice setup.
Faster Than Light relies heavily in random generated encounters since every time you warp to a location, you have hundreds of possible encounters with multiple outcomes, however this outcomes are sometime random as well, since the answer you gave on one playthrough might not have the same outcome on the next one. Often enough you'll feel the game cheated on you and that the result wasn't fair, however this also makes the game alive and filled with high risk high reward situations.
The combat system is pretty straight forward, when your weapons are loaded you can fire, when your enemy has their weapons loaded they can fire back, however you can assign crew members to certain stations, for example to the shield station which will make the shields recharge faster or to the engine station that will help you dodge incoming fire. Even though encounters are important you also have to make decisions inside your ship by choosing your crew members which unlock special encounters solutions but also come with their pros and cons. You'll have a whole bunch to choose from the Humans, the Engi, the Mantis, the Rockmen, the Zoltan, the Slugs, The Crystal and finally the Lanius.
The art of this game really stands out mainly the soundtrack that is masterfully done setting the perfect atmosphere for a game that leaves you on the edge of your chair, you'll know what I'm talking about once everythings starts going wrong and your entire ship is set ablaze or when you find yourself drifting  in space with no fuel, waiting for friend or foe to approach you with a helping hand or a loaded cannon.
However not everythings perfect, even though the game is filled with Quests and Encounters they somewhat lose their essence after some playthroughs when you start seeing them repeat too often with outcomes that you are now aware and can predict most of the time. Also the difficulty even on the easiest setting might be too hard for the casual gamers, which might put some people off the game after some tries.
+ Diferent Strategies and Aproaches
+ Great Variety of Items and Races
+ Amazing Soundtrack
- Encounters get repetitive after a while

I'll list the pros and cons of this briefly, from my experience.
Pros:
~ Deep and non-linear storyline.
~ At the start, you can choose your stats or 'roll' them randomly (let the game decide!), and have a choice of clans with their own personality, background, advantages and disadvantages.
~ Creative and well written dialogue, of which can change depending on chosen clan.
~ Voice acting that fits well with the characters and enriches their personalities.
~ Many hours of play filled with many missions and many choices for you to make.
~ Experience various entertaining kinds of insanity.
Cons:
~ There are bugs. The patch does help with this and is easy to find with a web search. However, it does not eliminate them completely, and this is also to be expected when playing an old game. Personally I wasn't bothered by them, as I was too busy enjoying the storyline.
~ Combat is funky. This links with the bugs, but don't get me wrong - there are tough fights.
~ Graphics can be improved with the patch I believe, but are still old. It's not disasterous or unplayable however, by any means - on the contrary, very good for an old game in my opinion.
~ For some people this will be a con. SAVE OFTEN. Your experience of the game will differ in places depending on the choices you make, and you may want to go back to have a different experience later. And then of course, there's always the possibility of getting shredded up and dying.

Just as a note. I played the redux version of this game.
First of all, this game is beautiful! Very stunning visuals, the landscapes are super beautiful both at a distance and close up. It is apparent that a lot of time has been spent creating assets for this game. I played the game with everything cranked to max and didn't notice much lag or stutter. Some areas if you pan the mouse quickly accross the horizontal axis it could stutter slightly, but nothing severe.
I had to turn of the head bobbing thing as I didn't like how that felt at all. Mouse input seems a bit laggy or smoothed, but not super important for a non-FPS game.
As for the puzzles. It took a little while for me to figure out what to do with them. Apart from the one with the portals in the house, they mostly seem very similar to each other in terms of mechanics. Basically, you have to find clues, put them back into the order they were originally. Then find the chronological order of how the crime took place. Rinse and repeat for each area. It got a bit too easy after trying it a couple of times.
Even though the puzzles might be a bit to easy, especially near the end of the game, I kept trucking through. Mainly because of the story. I really liked how you kept getting more and more details about what happened to Ethan and what kind of gruesome things occured. Also the small stories that Ethan put around the place were nice details. They felt a lot Lovecraft-esque.
I highly recommend playing this game, if you are into this genre of doing detective work, finding clues and piecing the story together. All this while walking around in a world of stunning visuals.

If you were disappointed with the EA release of battlefront and want something to prepare yoself until they release the hopefully better star wars battlefront II (EA). Look no further than the good Ol' original.
Story: Is actually interesting, it's from the perspective of a veteran clone trooper from the clone wars all the way to the rise of the empire. While the mission structure of the campaign is rather basic, if you are a star wars fan you will find it enjoyable from beginning to end. The game will run like a dream on pretty much any hardware from 2007 to the present and you will enjoy it tremendously. Overall the single player campaign is pretty awesome star wars lore and is actually a reason to buy the game.
Gameplay: If you've seen gameplay and found similarities to battlefield I guess that is omewhat accurate. Just know in terms of gunplay, vehicles and the such it will be another shooter. There are classes in the game and all have their own strengths and weaknesses as well as different weapons. There are several maps, and a decent amount of game modes. The modes are broken into three categories, Campaign, Galactic Conquest, and Instant Action. Campaign is self explanatory, but Galactic Conquest involves you conquering the galaxy while managing your resources such as the type of troops you have. Instant Action is like this, you pick a map, a game mode, an era, and play! For the game modes the most popular one is conquest which involves capturing all the points on the map or eliminating the entire enemy army to win. Another popular one I would share is assualt which is basically heroes vs. villans on a few selct maps. In addition to ground battles there are also space battles. Two teams have one capital ship, you hop in a ship, dogfight with other ships, destroy the capital ship systems from the outside, or land inside and destroy the systems from there. The best part of it all, this is all still so much fun even almost 12 years later. Not to mention the modding community is still very active and even though the official multiplayer servers went down people have found ways to play online! (I don't because I like battlefront solo) but you just might!
Bad Stuff: You might need to do some tinkering to get it to work on Windows 10
Verdict: I don't remember how much games cost back in 2005, but back then it was worth full price, the 10$ its at now is completely worth it, and the 2.49$ it costs on sale is eve better, what the heck are you waiting for?!

How would life be if you had to do everything manually? If suddenly, you had to think about breathing and blinking? "Manual Samuel" uses this premise as the game's focus point. Play Samuel, a rich kid that did not have to anything to this point, suddently having to do everything manually after a deal with Death.
Manual Samuel's focus point is that simple tasks being really difficult once you have to think about actions you unconciously do, and Manual Samuel runs with this idea. Each section is unique, bringing new tasks while advancing in this story. The humour is something, and is usually not what you often see anymore. The narrator accompanies you the whole way, providing most of the humour through their dialogue, especially when you skip cutscenes and at the end. However, it does not outshine the other characters in the game, as they each provide their own humour. The voice acting is surperb throughout, and only made the game better as you progressed.
There is no failing in Manual Samuel, only not succeeding as the game will let you try again. To compensate for this, the enemies also heal while you recover so you can go through with trial and error instead of relying on being knocked down to progress. This is important as combat becomes important towards bosses, and as you move onto completing the time trials the game unlocks.
While it is short, it is important to know that doing everything manually may become taxing on the player. The only negatives is that controls may not respond the first time (which can be annoying especially when trying to do time trials) and Sam's spine.
Manual Samual does have local co-op, so you and someone else can take control of half of Sam's functions and try to work together. It is also recommended to play with a controller than with a keyboard. Overall, Manual Samual is a fun little game with great humour and voice acting.

Without Within is a very short independent Visual Novel that was developed by InvertMouse with art by Karousel.  The story revolves around our main character, Vinty, and her struggle to make ends meet while following her dreams of being  a professional calligrapher.
From a technical standpoint Without Within does just fine.   It runs off Ren'Py so all the normal quirks associated with the engine are present.  Font is easy to read and everything functions as expected.  The music is well done, though often understated and lilting, it does fit the various scenes well.  As for art, Karousel did a fantastic job and more thought went into the design than the average reader will initially expect.  More on that latter.
The actual journey that we take with Vinty, whether she is dreaming of stardom or fending off the soul crushing nature of actual reality, is short but sweet.  Clocking at under 20 minutes to explore all of the paths (which function in a Bad End versus a continuation of the story system), Without Within can be immensely charming, funny, sweet, a bit too real at times for those of us that did a stint as a starving artist.  The story is a love letter to creative types but something everyone can relate to: It isn't easy to blaze your own trail but if it was would the journey actually be worth it?
So, is Without Within worth your time?  Absolutely!  It is a cute little tale that is short but full of character.  Is Without Within worth your money?  That is a difficult question to answer and one I leave up to the reader after they finish the story.  If you enjoyed it, as I did, I personally suggest spending the meager amount to show your support and unlock some goodies.  The Art Book in particular is very interesting as they discuss some of the design decisions for the game and you get an interesting inside look at how a small team would go about putting together a project like this.
But if you find Visual Novels even the least bit appealing, there is literally no reason to not spend a bit of time to go through this one.

At the beginning, you and your friends will flail about, and get turned into paste. In the middle, you will be fielding hard-earned new tools, and barking now-familiar terms. At the end, you will be in sync, moving as one, calmly cutting down swarms of enemies, taking objectives amidst hails of shrapnel, and fading away as reinforcements arrive to crush you.
The music, visuals and attitude are infectious in a darkly sarcastic way. This game understands Verhoeven's Starship Troopers, and adds a dash of far-out Warhammer style.
There are so many good design decisions. Many things are unlocked by filling your XP bar, but strategems, the most significant, are behind sets of missions that you must complete - you actually have to accomplish something.
The controls are unbelievably polished for a top-down shooter. The turn rate and easing, the acceleration and momentum, it all gives your character weight. It's remarkably natural to take off the laser sight, and start aiming by feel. The vehicles are fun exaggerations of this.
The gear progression is cleverly laid out like an invisible tutorial. Whether from experience or from missions, new stuff arrives in a logical order, slowly increasing the skill, risk, and reward. And for the most part, it is skill and risk that rewards you - the overall power progression is fairly flat. You do get more powerful, but only if you can use your ever-more dangerous tools competently, and in combination. Entry-level gear never gets obsolete. That makes the co-op extremely flexible between new and experienced players.
The DLC is well-crafted and fun, but very optional. I find the core content still gives the most meaningful tactical breadth. And the snow boots feel like cheating.

text:
A fun little tower defense with RPG elements. The protagonist is a librarian cast into a plague colony, and sets out on a quest to escape. She quickly discovers latent supernatural powers that allow others to defeat the zombified infected. She serves as the objective that must be defended. Besides the standard ability to summon units to defend her, she's also capable of casting spells for harming or buffing, and can equip spell books to further enhance her abilities.
Throughout the game you'll encounter characters who join with you, unlocking new classes of characters (berserker, archer, healer, etc.) that you can hire and summon to defend you. The classes come with simple skill trees that unlock new abilities or enhance them in some way, and every individual unit can be leveled differently from the other, enabling a more diverse army to choose from.
The game is made for a wide variety of skill levels. New players and seasoned veterans alike will find something to challenge them when the game gets rolling, and you can replay maps as you please for practice or for XP/money. The map's rewards are better for higher difficulty settings, and can reward unique equipment for success. The game can seem like a grindfest, but the devs wisely included the option to increase XP/money gains and to ensure all units get equal access to it, regardless of whether or not they entered battle.
The story itself is very competent. The characters are largely likeable and the writing and humor is enjoyable. The cast tend to have something of an emphasis on their quirks, but mostly avoid becoming bland one notes with varying degrees of depth.
The game is not without its flaws. Completionists can find that the New Game+ might become something of a chore, the skill trees are rather simple in their execution, and certain parts of the story or characters can become tiresome (looking at you, Slak). If you can put this aside, you still have a fun and funny game that's worth a look. Grab the demo and give it a spin. You can even transfer your save file if you choose to purchase it, and the game is set to receive an HD update (at the time of writing) and sequel.

This game is incredible, and the fact that it was made in RPG Maker really goes to show that it doesn't matter how limitting the software or engine is, there are people that are creative, bold and willing to create something unique and near flawless.

This game is good and has some awesome ideas going for it, too bad a lot of them fall flat due to balancing issues or the hit or miss community. I love the ideas of building epic structures and working together with your team to take them down with siege weaponry and cunning, unfortunately this is not usually how the matches end up. You'll go into a game hoping to create a grand structure, but you'll be one of two, or maybe the only, builder and it's just not possible to build anything large by yourself, you simply can't gather and hold enough resources to create it before the enemy shows up. And then they do... wave after wave of knights carrying keg bombs, just laying waste to your creations. Who needs a catapult when a cheap as dirt explosive does twice the damage? It's stupid, makes no sense, and ruins most matches. Then there's the lag, I'm not sure if it's happening to anyone else, but i meet the requirements to run the game and it does run very smoothly when I'm playing alone, but then i hit the servers and it all goes to hell. The match will start off fairly smooth, but then it will degrade as the match goes on. By the end I'm moving at slideshow speeds of a frame every couple seconds. MY ping is between 30-100 most days so i really don't know what's going on. I really have to wonder how people with higher pings even manage to stomach it. I tried turning on faster graphics and that literally made things worse, when it is supposed to speed them up. I find it difficult to recommend the game, but i will as if the problems i've described are fixed it will be a great title. Right now as it stands it's either fun as hell or oh-my-god-someone-give-me-a-gun-I'm-going-to-kill-that-son-of-a- kind of experience depending on your luck at the servers. So if we could just raise the cost of keg bombs, decrease their damage, get a bigger player base, and fix the framerates this game would be excellent.

But that's not the only threat the survivors in the underground stations have to face...
Your station is attacked by mysterious mutants called the Dark Ones.
Artyom is chosen to spread the word about this to a group of rangers.
But for this, he has to travel to their headquartes to talk to them...and so his dangerous journey begins...
You will sneak through enemy stations, dark tunnels and many other hostile areas....all set in a perfect atmosphere.
Actually one of the few games, that really managed to scare me in some situations.

The game looks great, especially the grand hilltop and lake views. This makes the game sometimes choppy, though I guess that depends on your settings. I suspect turning of motion blur caused it for me. There is a warning right at the start that the game does not hold your hand. And truly, while you do click on text that appears, you usually need to directly look and pinpoint some items for text to appear. In this way it really feels like an investigation where you need to FIND stuff and put it together. Trying to move from one clue to the other can be annoying sometimes as old text flashes and swirls around. But this is actually the way the game communicates with you what you should find next. The puzzles are not that hard if you play puzzle games. At first you have no idea who you are supposed to be and can only guess if this is some psychic-powered detective. Throughout all of it you put together pieces of a story. But it is not easy to get what is reality and what are just whacky stories of a little boy. The mines part was the coolest section in my opinion due to the sudden shift of tone which surprised me and was quite thrilling. It had some Cthulhu vibes which was very cool. The ending was okay, I guess, though compared to some previous scenes it felt less engaging/emotional. Worthy of note is also the Redux version which does not look better or worse but just slightly different. This version is a separate Library entry which is received upon buying the standard game. Let's do a brief summary - the game is interesting, the music great and the detective dynamics are cool. However it feels a bit short, with puzzles far from each other, as most of the game time you walk through empty places without interaction. If you like walking simulators and/or adventure detective games then this game is for you.
I also found a bug (or maybe intentional feature?) with the "Unfinished story" achievement that consists of doing 3 parts. After I did part 1 and 2 fairly early on in the game I did not find part 3. Maybe because I played the game in two sessions instead of one or maybe there is a time limit. Either way I had to backtrack all the way back and do part 1 and 2 again (they will reappear) and then to part 3 again (NOTE: see the elevator shortcut near the dam so you do not WALK all the way from where you came)

The protagonist is an aspiring, struggling calligrapher who has to make ends meet working a crappy job so she can pay for her crappy apartment so she can try to find success as a calligrapher. However, she realizes that she had been so focused on success that she lost sight of her passion for her art. Calligraphy, and the story itself, is obviously a metaphor for what this game developer has gone through, but I thought it was well written with nice artwork and an appropriate sense of self deprecation. Plus, I laughed out loud at the ending. It was truly hilarious in the context of the story.
Very well done, free to play title, and one I definitely recommend trying out. You wont regret your time spent with this game.

I'm going to attempt to give a "not recommended" rating to a game with many "recommended" reviews on here. I realize this deviates from the norm, but please read what's below before automatically downvoting this review.
Mafia II suffers from what many AAA sequels of today end up going through: attempting to build off the success of an earlier game, but ultimately it doesn't make the cut. Most if not all of the features that made the game look great, such as car customization, graphics, and little things such as getting chased by the police for speeding or hitting cars, can be seen as only halfway finished.
The graphics featured in this game are probably the only selling point, but even in that category there are faults. More than once, you'll watch your beautifully rendered character eat from plates of food that can only be described as relics from the era of PS1/N64 generation of gaming. Whether little things like this are the result of a poor console to PC port, or meeting deadlines for 2K Games, it's frustrating to watch your character swing his fork through a flat mesh of food on the highest settings possible.
Other integral parts of Mafia 2 are downright broken or poorly thought out. The game’s system of earning money swings wildly around as you play through the game, much like Saints Row or Grand Theft Auto, but unlike those games, you hardly need it for anything. Even if you are flush with money, which happens at some points in the game, it either gets taken away from you in a cutscene, or you’re required to fork it all over to someone else.
I think I need to elaborate on my earlier point about the wanted system being partially finished. Mafia 2 takes the unique step among open world videogames of making often overlooked small crimes giving you wanted levels by the police. Hit and runs and speeding, done fairly often as you blast from one end of the city to the other, will make the police come after you if you're within range of a patrol officer or vehicle. If they catch hold of your appearance or license plate, you're more likely to be chased again once you escape unless you change your clothes/car. These great features, however, can sometimes fail to trigger properly. One (albeit anecdotal) example of this in my gameplay was a time outside of missions where I walked into a gunstore and shot the owner in the face. Cops came looking for me, but I walked right out and the wanted level had already gone away for premeditated murder. No game is perfect in executing all planned features, but this one does come fairly close to perfect despite the small bugs.
Cars in general did not get enough attention, aside from graphics, the lockpicking minigame, and actually dying when you hit a tree at 100 miles an hour. Why bother tuning up a sporty car when they cost hundreds to fully repair and there’s little difference vs a car you can steal? Why bother repairing cars when you can magically fix the engine in 10 seconds every single time they break down? Why can’t I remove cars I don’t want anymore from my 10 car garage nearby my horrible apartment?
----------SPOILERS BELOW----------
The gameplay itself was hit or miss in my opinion. I played through the game on hard mode, and although most of the game was fairly simple to grasp, there were a few parts of the game where I threw my hands up in the air in disgust. In the last mission where you’re storming up the observatory killing enemies that are mostly running at you in the open, I had many unavoidable grenade deaths on the last set of stairs before the final fight inside the planetarium. Lone grenades chucked down by unseen and unshootable opponents doesn’t make it Dark Souls-esque artificial difficulty either, as this happened a few times before it mysteriously stopped at one point. Gunplay and shooting itself though, is fairly decent. It was incredibly satisfying to blow gangsters away with shotguns, and the wide array of extra weapons like the M1 Garand gave you many different potent options in battle. Fist fighting, however, is awful. Maybe it just wasn’t my thing, but there was no fun in holding down the space bar and waiting for counter punches, with the greater possibility of your counter punch missing and your foe landing an unblockable counter on you shortly after.
----------SPOILERS ABOVE----------
In terms of story, we’re given a start point and an end point with no side quests or wiggle room. The great part about the most recent installments of Grand Theft Auto and similar games are the random quests you could find, and being able to do quests at your leisure. I know I compared Mafia II to Grand Theft Auto more than once already, but it’s important to note that Mafia II is an open world action game, while the GTA series is all action-adventure games. Why make this comparison? Because without any focus on an “adventure” in an open world game, it’s very hard to consider it open world. There’s not much to do besides head to the red marker and continue the story, unless you like running over pedestrians and evading the cops a whole heck of a lot. I’m sure the DLC attempts to address this, but optional DLC addressing problems in a base game is incredibly problematic.
----------SPOILERS BELOW----------
The actual story itself is nothing to write home about. I mentioned before it’s linear, but the plot itself is poorly thought out. Your father is mentioned often early on in the game, and you find out later that you’ve been working for some of the same people that killed your father. You also come to learn, right as the game is about to end, that a loan shark you borrow money from was the one that your father borrowed from that brought your family incredible debt (that you pay back earlier in the game). They’re moments of actual character development that are abused for a slightly more emotional cover shooting event soon after. The same could be said for Marty, a forgettable companion that was heavily hinted to die at some point.
Aside from all of this, where’s all that power you’re supposed to get when you’re inducted into the family? You never have anyone working under you, you’re still getting terribly risky jobs with little backup (besides Joe yelling “C’mon chop chop! every 10 seconds), and still getting the same short end of the stick that you got when you originally started doing work for the families. Why aren’t there missions where you roll up about as with as many guys as the hostile NPCs have? Why does Vito have no clout among the families despite being brought into them very quickly?
----------SPOILERS ABOVE----------
Overall, I’d give this game a 6/10, and wouldn’t recommended it. Don’t do what I did and play through the game hoping it improves, your time is much more valuable than that.

TL;DR: Would i recommend it? If you got friends to play or just like good movement in a game, yes.
If you want to play it for the pvp? I'd rather not.
Dying light is an zombie apocalypse parkour simulator with a story and loot n shoot elements. It has relatively good story, a fair mount of janky animations and children voiced by grunchy women. The parkour element however, is relatively satisfying and fluid enough, and only has been a true problem once when i managed to stick myself into the ground through a sewerpipe while swimming. Parkour. The weaponplay was a bit hard to understand and i came to conclusion that i hate power attack and the person who designed it should get burned in a fire after being electrocuted. Gunplay, extremely satisfying and feels real enough when an enemy chunks you hard if you get shot. Coop with 2+ friends is extremely fun and shared trackingly between eachother.
And that's where the positives end. I tried the zombie mode a couple times only to find it incredibly unfair. Mainly due to the lack of balancing. There is none far as i can see, since a level 1 zombie can be tossed into a match with a 12+ player with weapons easily hitting 100 per swing. A notion when a zombie's hitpoints are at 160 by default while unpgraded.
"Oh but he gets an instant kill ability" I hear you say. UV lamps. These literally go on as soon as the player knows they've been invaded. "But it can be made immune to!" Yes, at a later level, (16 by rumours?) at which point a zombie player has probably given up, turned off the option and returned to the fun, safe environment of the dying light coop.
Now i do not know whenever they have fixed this at any point, but one can hope?
Would i recommend it? IF you got friends to play or just like good movement in a game, yes.

Before I start with my review on Vampire: The Masquerade know that it is an old game. As such the graphics are not up to par with current standards. Moreover, the base game is riddled with quirky to game breaking bugs. However, there is a dedicated patch by fans that solves all these issues and brings new (restored from the orginal concept) powers and game balances to the game. My review will be about the game with this unofficial patch for that is the way to experience this game.
VTM is a RPG about vampire in the setting of the likewise named pen & paper version. The main abilities of your vampire depend on the clan you choose. Although all of them share the greater part of skills, you have unique abilities linked to your clan that are at times shared by another but never in the same combination. Furthermore your background alters your starting proficiencies, and your sex does matter in the game at some small points.
The game seems to be made out of two parts. The beginning is a true RPG, with heavy quests and side-quests, intrigue, and the ability to stealth, talk or fight through these quests (not all of these opportunities for each quest, but most of the time at least 2). After a certain point though, the game starts more to become a Hack & Slash RPG - probably to allow you to use all those cool vampire powers you have been putting points into, but it does break the experience a bit here. Regardless of that the RPG does have some adult stuff, even if it black screens at moment supremes, it at least does not shy from it. The feel of the world is dark indeed and it feels trully unlike other RPGs.
Replaybility is supposedly low as with other story driven RPGs, but I would advice using some clans for a second or third run (I did them all) for some of them are quite the game changer - like the Nosferatu or Malkavian vs. the other clans - moreso than just another class in e.g. Baldur's Gate. Now I did all the clans for runs and you can see from my profile I do not have a huge amount of hours in game, thus it is not very long - but the price is also not high.
In my opinion this game is definately worth the pricetag for a relative short RPG in a very unique environment.

Defender's Quest is a huge little gem of a game. I believe it offers the most hours of fun per megabyte of any Steam game I've played yet. I really enjoyed playing through it twice and sweating enough to unlock all the achievements.
The game scales in difficulty exponentially. This means that the easiest battles are actually the earliest, and that the game gets harder as it progresses. This is a welcome change from most games,
it's taken to an unnecessary extreme at the end. Finishing the final 10% of a full 201 star playthrough will be where you spend the majority of your time. Thanks to the level cap - which you will get to - you'll hit a wall in your ability to improve. That makes it feel repetitive and slow, because you're just repeating the same few battles over and over again, trying to make little tweaks to survive. Most of the game isn't like that, but it's a frustrating way to finish.
The game's story and characters are quite memorable and well-written. The dialogue is funny. I wasn't expecting that at all, especially from a tower defense game. It's actually one of the main reasons I'm looking forward to the sequel: I want to know what happens in this world to these people.
The graphics are a huge let down though. With no way to scale the sprites are locked in a tiny window. I found myself squinting just to tell what was going on. And I heavily considered lowering my resolution just to make things bigger. Thankfully an HD re-release is in the works, but the level of fidelity as is leaves the game looking like a B-level mobile game.
Defender's Quest is not without flaws, but if you enjoy challenging tower defense gameplay where the story compels you to move forward then it's well worth a purchase.

At the beginning, you and your friends will flail about, and get turned into paste. In the middle, you will be fielding hard-earned new tools, and barking now-familiar terms. At the end, you will be in sync, moving as one, calmly cutting down swarms of enemies, taking objectives amidst hails of shrapnel, and fading away as reinforcements arrive to crush you.
The music, visuals and attitude are infectious in a darkly sarcastic way. This game understands Verhoeven's Starship Troopers, and adds a dash of far-out Warhammer style.
There are so many good design decisions. Many things are unlocked by filling your XP bar, but strategems, the most significant, are behind sets of missions that you must complete - you actually have to accomplish something.
The controls are unbelievably polished for a top-down shooter. The turn rate and easing, the acceleration and momentum, it all gives your character weight. It's remarkably natural to take off the laser sight, and start aiming by feel. The vehicles are fun exaggerations of this.
The gear progression is cleverly laid out like an invisible tutorial. Whether from experience or from missions, new stuff arrives in a logical order, slowly increasing the skill, risk, and reward. And for the most part, it is skill and risk that rewards you - the overall power progression is fairly flat. You do get more powerful, but only if you can use your ever-more dangerous tools competently, and in combination. Entry-level gear never gets obsolete. That makes the co-op extremely flexible between new and experienced players.
The DLC is well-crafted and fun, but very optional. I find the core content still gives the most meaningful tactical breadth. And the snow boots feel like cheating.

Only downside is that some of the DLC is a little too important for certain missions (the all-terrain boots, to be specific).
Still, the game + all of the DLC is only $40 and can probably be picked up on sale for half of that; I can't get to upset about these prices considering how much fun I've had with the game so far.

King Arthur's Gold is a fun game. I enjoy the insanity that can go on in a match. The game can turn a reasonably-pretty forest with a lake into nothing but a colossal crater.
Positives
+ The way the game is made allows for good strategic decisions, as well as teamwork.
+ There's something satisfying about running up to a well-defended enemy bunker with a lit powder keg on your back, just charging towards the bunker for a tactical suicide. I was the only one on my team that ever did that, yet most of my team members would buy powder kegs just to give to me to grab it and charge at the next wall.
+ It actually has a pretty good combat system, much to my surprise.
Negatives
- Once you've played one round you've played them all. (The main reason I stopped playing the game was because I played a round that was in a stalemate for 3 hours. It was just such a good round, that when we won, every round I played after that felt inferior and boring in comparison.)
- Playing as a Worker for more than the 60-second setup phase is stressful, and boring compared to playing as the guy that can use his shield as a makeshift glider. (There are on average less workers on a team, so one worker's working is much more influential on the team than a single warrior. I didn't want to be that guy on the team that just gets everyone else killed because he built the bridge poorly.)
All-in-all, fun and strategic game, but it doesn't have too long of a life. I played it for 11 hours, but I'm probably not going to go back to it.

Post-apocalyptic, heavy story-based shooter set in Moscow, 2033.
You play as Artyom, a citizen of Exhibition station in the underground metro system in Moscow.
Humans are forced to live beyond the surface, because a devastating nuclear war made the atmosphere inhabitable.
But that's not the only threat the survivors in the underground stations have to face...
Your station is attacked by mysterious mutants called the Dark Ones.
Artyom is chosen to spread the word about this to a group of rangers.
But for this, he has to travel to their headquartes to talk to them...and so his dangerous journey begins...
You will sneak through enemy stations, dark tunnels and many other hostile areas....all set in a perfect atmosphere.
Actually one of the few games, that really managed to scare me in some situations.
You're always in search for ammo and gas masks to be able to survive.
The atmosphere, supported by the great music and voice acting, is so dense and tight, you can almost feel Artyom suffering during his journey.
Definetly of the my favorite games.

You play as Paul Prospero, a paranormal investigator. He receives a letter from Ethan Carter saying that he’s in danger and needs his help. Upon arriving, it’s clear to Paul that something has already taken place. Now, he must put the pieces together, figure out what happened and save Ethan.
Graphically speaking, the environment of the game is amazing to look at. Whether it’s the simple detailed areas such as the trees or the abandoned homes, it’s very well presented. This is further enriched with the notion that you can explore the areas at your own pace and leisure.
While it’s pretty to look at, what about the story? Well, I suck at giving opinions about storytelling, but one area that’s an issue for me is the length. More specifically, the overall game length. The game can be completed in approximately 3 hours, and for those who go for all the achievements, same thing. For a $20 game, that’s not a good bargain.
Now something to take note on. When you buy the game on Steam, you receive the original game as well as the Redux version of the game, which utilizes the Unreal Engine 4 as opposed to the Unreal Engine 3 that’s used in the original game.
The problem here is that the original game is unstable. For example, one day, the game runs with no errors, and the next day, the game will suddenly crash. As for the Redux version, it works great with no major issues to note.
Now, I’ve noticed that an updated version of a game tends to suffer from being unstable, while the original has no issues. Usually, it’s supposed to be the other way around.
Unfortunately, as much as I liked the game, I’m going to have to say no to recommending it. This game falls into the category of “You play it once and you’re done with it.”

Note: I played the Redux version of the game, which was redone for Unreal Engine 4, and is added to your library automatically when purchasing this standard version.
Beautiful.
By FAR the most beautiful gaming experience available. Screenshots from regular gameplay look nearly photo-realistic. Even if this game didn't have any story, wandering around in the scenery enjoying the landscape would be sufficient for me to recommend this game. It's truly a marvel of graphic design for a video game.
With the simple beauty of the game out of the way, there is an actual story as well. This is a mystery themed walking-sim with a few horror-esque elements thrown in (although it's certainly not horror focused). Learning the story as you go can be a bit confusing, but when the ending cutscene played, the whole story finally came together and made sense. It was definitely well told, and a strongpoint of the game as a whole.
There are some "puzzle" elements, however these are closer to "find the thing" rather than what I would call a "puzzle" (with maybe a couple exceptions) (which isn't necessarily bad). The gameplay is not difficult, nor are the puzzles, so don't come in expecting a challenge.
This IS a walking sim, so the main point is to explore, discover, and investigate as you uncover more of the landscape and the story.
I also need to mention the soundtrack is also great, and definitely enhances the experience, although note the soundtrack is largely atmospheric, so barring a couple exceptions of a few specific songs, you probably won't be going to download and/or listen to the soundtrack as standalone music (unless you're into more atmospheric music).
Overall, in my eyes, this is the golden standard for a walking a sim. Absolutely the best graphics, and thus some of the best atmosphere compared to quite literally any other game in existence. Great story telling, no hand holding, no restriction on exploration (barring the edges of the maps), and a great pacing and overall length.
It's short enough that you could complete the game completely in one extended sitting, but it will more likely take 2 or 3 sittings to fully complete. As far as walking sims go, I would consider this a good length, although some people may call this short (I doubt anyone could get much more than maybe 8 hours, probably more realistically around 4-6 hours).
Honestly, this game is worth it just for the graphics, and to revel in its beauty and see just how far gaming has come. Just look up gameplay screenshots and you'll see what I mean.

Game mecahnics: turn-based fighting and crummy RPG Maker controls. Don't worry, the controls - tho awkward at first to someone who has never played an RPG Maker game before - are very simple and you'll adapt quickly. Just know you move with the arrows and interact with the spacebar. The game will teach you the rest.
Story, Writing, Characters: perfect. Note: this game is full of mature content - don't play if you're not prepared for that. Each character has his own personality, the dialogue is natural (for Olathe), and the story is unraveled through gameplay at the perfect pace. If you want a game that will make you care and evoke the whole spectrum of emotions - from angry to happy, laughing to depressed - this is the game you want.
Game Length: I finished the game in just under 13 hours, and I know I skipped some things, so I'd say you could power through the game in a day, or take your time, hit every nook and cranny, and stretch it out to five days or a week.  I found 13 hours to be just right. I'm not sure if my heart could have taken any more of this game by the time I got to the end, and the break of beating it is welcome. I say "break," tho, because this is a game I will be coming back to again and again (it's my new FFVI). With all the choices you make and permanent consequences to your decisions, you could play this game five times over and play it different every time.
Overall, I'd give this game a 9 / 10 (-1 for the platform choice, which is super easy to get over).
Seriously, if you've still got doubts about wether or not you want this game, check out the website at
. The gang and the music will give you a better idea for the style / feel of the game and the website should help make up your mind.
Or you could stop wasting your time and just buy the game.
TL;DR:  Don't bother waiting for a Steam sale; this game is well worth its full price.

Great game marred by terrible balance and really shameless Pay2Win hyper expensive DLC. Seriously, the commanders alone, if you bought them all, would cost you over a hundred dollars, and many of them are mandatory if you want to be competitively relevant. Even the non-gameplay stuff like skins is exorbitantly priced(Really, Relic? 25 dollary-doos for a small skin-pack for vehicles while on SALE? 35 when not? What are you smoking?). It's DLC scheme would make even EA, Activision, and Ubisoft blush. There's a 'war spoils' system where you can supposedly pick up the content for free in random drops, but the drops are few and far between, and more often than not are copies of content you already had(I have 3 copies of a USF commander I ALREADY PAID FOR. In fact I have a copy of almost every USF commander, when I've paid for every one.), with no way to trade them with other players, or means to convert your copies into something useful. Between that, and the absolutely ridiculously high pricing of commander DLC that will have you paying the pricing of an entirely new game(Heck, a bundle of two new commanders costs more than CoH2 itself does while on it's routine sale.), there's no real incentive to buy DLC.
Well, except for one: The game balance. This is some of the worst balance I've seen in an RTS. When they decided to make the move from the system of the previous game by having many, many more commanders, they forgot that they have to actually make all the commanders unique AND relevant. What you get instead is tons of reused assets, tons of gimmicky garbage that breaks the mechanics of the game, and a system of balance built entirely around seeing who can out-cheese their opponent with the latest flavor of the month unit-spam, sim-city, or exploitation of some poorly tested ability or dooms-day tank. Every other month or so, a set of new commanders is introduced with little to no testing(Or perhaps, intentionally made overpowered). These commanders are either outright broken by introducing units/mechanics that totally circimvent intended counters, or are designed in a way that an otherwise underpowered and broken faction(In the sense that they underperform/are gimped) HAS to use them in order to be relevant. And like clockwork, after Relic has collected their shillings for a month or so and DLC sales finally slow down, they nerf these commanders and prepare the next batch.
It's a crying shame, because underneath all the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, this is a game that is fun, and has a lot of potential. The cover mechanics are fun, combined arms are fun, the soft-realism makes it accessible to people that aren't the greatest at RTS games, The low learning curve makes it easy to get into, and it straddles a middle-ground where both RTS casuals and enthusiasts can have fun and feel competitive, while bridging two extremes in the genre of Starcraft and Men of War into a game where both sides can enjoy themselves.
A lot of what makes this game great is marred horribly by the poor balance, the bucking of it's own damn mechanics by devolving into unit blobbing and running across open ground, the horrible DLC implementation, And the horridly skewed level of diversity and attention to detail between the Axis faction and the Allies faction(It's no secret that Relic are tremendous Wehraboos. One look at either side reveals that Axis gets far, far more unit diversity and aesthetic, while factions like USF feel lazy, slapped together, and chock-ful of reused assets.)
I'd say, if you are really looking for an RTS with a live community that is easy to get into, pick this up on sale for no more than 12 bucks. Otherwise, don't waste your time, get Men of War instead.
