This is my first real review, and it's for a game that is free. Honestly, I don't know why it's free, because it is awesome, and the developer could easily make some good money off it. If you like platformers like Super Meat Boy or VVVVVV (which you should, because they are awesome), then you will like this game. It has cool retro graphics (like something off the Gameboy or earlier), and it's not as difficult as SMB or VVVVVV. It has a mechanic pretty similar to VVVVVV, where your screen displays one room at a time, all of which have different names (alternately cryptic, humorous, obscure, or just wierd). There are also save points in most rooms like in VVVVVV. There were just a couple times where the save points were a little too far apart, which was somewhat annoying when I got stuck at a hard part and kept having to play the same 3-4 screens over and over, but this was pretty infrequent. The music is mostly non-existent, except for some jumping sound effects and such, but that's ok. It adds to the retro asthetic.
I played through a good portion of the game with a keyboard, which is certainly doable, but eventually I got to a part where I just knew it would be easier with a controller, so I played the rest that way. The game has some cool surprises, especially at the end. Figuring out the "magic word" and the "magic number" really isn't too difficult, but it is rewarding when you get it. Also, choosing to "lose" the game is also funny, although I recommend winning first, since you lose all your powers and start at the beginning when you lose (but you keep all the stuff you've found).
Anyway, you should definitely give this game a shot. It's short and sweet, but the price is definitely right. For what it is, I give it 9/10.

Mafia 2 places you in the shoes of Vito Scaletta a boy who's parents emigrated to the USA - specifically the fictional city of Empire Bay (fashioned after NYC) - from Sicily. Think of Mafia 2 as the best of your favorite gangster movies only much longer and with you in control of the action and you'll get an idea of what the game is really like.
Gameplay is reminiscent of GTA only without the auto-targeting aspect. At its core Mafia 2 is a 3rd person over the shoulder shooter.The game takes place in 1940's - 1950's America so expect period guns (M1945, Tommy Gun's, shotguns); vehicles (not actual licensed cars but closely based on period autos); and clothing. The driving mechanics in Mafia 2 in my opinion are a vast improvement over the on-ice feel that the vehicles in GTA IV featured. Driving insane speeds is possible but expect a quick death if you crash (on hard difficulty anyway).
Unlike other open-world or sandbox games, the focus of Mafia 2 is the main story. Admittedly Mafia 2 is short on sidequests and minigames. This is generally a problem if you go in expecting a GTA clone. Mafia 2 is most definitely not that. Personally I found the focus on the story refreshing. Instead of distractions like pizza delivery missions or other time wasters, Mafia 2 is about story driven events that include everything from jewelry store heists to covert missions planting explosives to assassinate a rival family member.
While Mafia 2 doesn't feature any type of online gameplay there are plenty of collectibles in-game including Playboy centerfold magazines (complete with nudity) and wanted posters to keep you occupied. I highly recommend this title!

Ludicrous humour is unmistakably its centerpiece, complemented with perfect narration and soundtrack, inspired 70's cartoon style, measured hashtags and attitude, and a fully original premise without equal. Every character is a marvel of ingenuity, from the gangsta-wannabe Death to the overly polite Hell police.
The game has an excessively generous count of the word 'feces' but otherwise it constantly serves puns and antics worthy of the best absurd and carefree comedies.
The whole concept revolves around the one idea of using ridiculously uncomfortable controls to perform the simplest tasks. Its originality makes it an instant classic but the novelty also wears off surprisingly quickly, leaving the player with annoying limitations and a repetitiveness that would merit a negative review under any other circumstance.
Every section of the game offers something unique and most of them introduce their new ideas smoothly, perhaps with the exception of combat sequences. The final boss fight in particular is a trial and error of nonsense in a sequence that must essentially be memorized and executed perfectly.
You don't so much fail as simply not succeed, so the game lets you easily retry until you get it right, without having to reload a checkpoint. Most sections are highly enjoyable and easy enough to be completed on the first try; only a few tenuous ones can be irritating.
The game is also very short but its length is perfect for what's on offer. Manual Samuel is worth your time for its boldness and cleverness but it is as much fun as it becomes a strain to play (figuratively and literally). By the time it was over, I felt relieved, but also quite satisfied at having played and enjoyed one of the most unique games in existence.
A game controller is highly recommended along with some level of dexterity and patience. Sense of humour not optional.

However, while innovative, the controls are equally infuriating. You need to remember to breathe in, and out, and blink, and use your left and right feet systematically throughout the game. Every action performed follows this approach, and that detracts from the game's highlights.
Pair the above statement with the fact that some actions are not at all obvious, and suddenly the comic relief becomes outweighed by poor user experience planning. There will be moments amid your confusion where the game will flash 'exactly' what you need to do as a tip at the bottom of the screen. This, in my mind, is just bad UX design. I understand with a game so 'unique', it will be hard to find clever ways to express what needs to be done, but that's what game and UX design is all about.
Even still though, the game is great if your open to different ways to approach video gaming, and looking for something upbeat on a night after work. The game will last you maybe 3 hours on storyline mode.
Pros
[+] Visual Design
[+] Hilarious Voice Acting
[+] Comic Relief
[+] Unique Controls
Cons
[-] Somewhat Short (2-3 hours)
[-] Unobvious Control Schema

I've played a lot of tower defense. I used to play Warcraft III custom maps where the tower defense genre was cut from. Defender's Quest does a nice job of putting a well developed story with well developed characters into tower defense gameplay without it feeling pasted on.
It keeps it simple. There are only a few basic towers to choose from, but each tower acts like a character in your party and you can equip most of them with weapons and armor (no weapons or armor for a dragon and no armor for the barbarian/main melee guy). The maps are laid out well enough that consideration to where to place your troops does make a big difference.
There is also a nice take on the gameplay by offering 4 difficulty levels. You get rewards for completing the level, but you get bonus rewards for not taking a single point of damage. If you do that, you can get a lot of extra scrap (money) and unique items.
What I'm doing on my second playthrough is going as far as I possibly can while only buying recruits and never any items on the easiest mode. When I hit my first failure, I go back to the very start and try to complete each level on the hardest mode possible. After I fail once, I will go down to an easier mode and so on until I am right back at the easiest mode and therefore, the furthest out I've ever been.
The main game is not that long and there isn't a ton of replayability to this game once you complete it. That is why it is only worth a few bucks...but it's worth a few bucks. I hear they are making a Defender's Quest II and I hope that is at least as good. Even when it is, this is still a pretty fun tower defense and something that feels more refreshing than you might think when you come back to it after a long time.

Really fun game, especially for the first few hours. If you have a group of friends that are looking to play a game all together and want a challenge, this is a great game. Without having proper items, some missions can be a real challenge which makes it extremely fun. That being said, there are a bunch of problems.
DLCs definitely make some aspects way too easy and I think it's more fun without them. That being said, some of the DLC are almost essential in the sense that they shouldn't have made them DLC, they should just be in the standard game (All-Terain Boots especially).
The main issue is the lack of content. After a few hours you can easily unlock everything and then you're left rerunning the same missions with the same few objectives. The only variance deals with differing enemy types, but when in a war you're left with one enemy type at times and it makes it feel like even more of a grind. Who wants to fight the same enemy over and over and over again?
Stemming from the lack of content is how easy the game becomes after a certain point. If your team has all the unlocks or a bunch of DLCs, any mission becomes extremely easy. You will have more than enough ways to deal with the missions and enemies. People with only 10 hours in the game can DUO the highest level difficulty mission in the game easily if they have the right stratagems. Boss battles can take as little as one minute if you have a good team just because certain strategems are incredibly strong for certain enemy types (Explosive Mines vs Borgs).
I would recommend this game to anyone just for the first 5 hours of enjoyment you'll get out of it. The team work aspect makes the game really enjoyable and fun to play with your friends if you're all on discord.. But if you're looking for something to play for over 5 hours that isn't really over priced, keep looking.

This is an absolutely fantastic game and I highly recommend it.  I'm really not sure how to describe it without ruining any of its charm.  I'll try:
Graphics + Music = surreal, twisted world. LISA definitely has that "unique" feel the makes it a world of its own, very similar to how Earthbound felt. The more you explore, the weirder the world gets, and the more normal the characters act like it is. It's weird, but it feels right.
Game mecahnics: turn-based fighting and crummy RPG Maker controls. Don't worry, the controls - tho awkward at first to someone who has never played an RPG Maker game before - are very simple and you'll adapt quickly. Just know you move with the arrows and interact with the spacebar. The game will teach you the rest.
Story, Writing, Characters: perfect. Note: this game is full of mature content - don't play if you're not prepared for that. Each character has his own personality, the dialogue is natural (for Olathe), and the story is unraveled through gameplay at the perfect pace. If you want a game that will make you care and evoke the whole spectrum of emotions - from angry to happy, laughing to depressed - this is the game you want.
Game Length: I finished the game in just under 13 hours, and I know I skipped some things, so I'd say you could power through the game in a day, or take your time, hit every nook and cranny, and stretch it out to five days or a week.  I found 13 hours to be just right. I'm not sure if my heart could have taken any more of this game by the time I got to the end, and the break of beating it is welcome. I say "break," tho, because this is a game I will be coming back to again and again (it's my new FFVI). With all the choices you make and permanent consequences to your decisions, you could play this game five times over and play it different every time.
Overall, I'd give this game a 9 / 10 (-1 for the platform choice, which is super easy to get over).
Seriously, if you've still got doubts about wether or not you want this game, check out the website at
. The gang and the music will give you a better idea for the style / feel of the game and the website should help make up your mind.
Or you could stop wasting your time and just buy the game.
TL;DR:  Don't bother waiting for a Steam sale; this game is well worth its full price.

This is my first real review, and it's for a game that is free. Honestly, I don't know why it's free, because it is awesome, and the developer could easily make some good money off it. If you like platformers like Super Meat Boy or VVVVVV (which you should, because they are awesome), then you will like this game. It has cool retro graphics (like something off the Gameboy or earlier), and it's not as difficult as SMB or VVVVVV. It has a mechanic pretty similar to VVVVVV, where your screen displays one room at a time, all of which have different names (alternately cryptic, humorous, obscure, or just wierd). There are also save points in most rooms like in VVVVVV. There were just a couple times where the save points were a little too far apart, which was somewhat annoying when I got stuck at a hard part and kept having to play the same 3-4 screens over and over, but this was pretty infrequent. The music is mostly non-existent, except for some jumping sound effects and such, but that's ok. It adds to the retro asthetic.
I played through a good portion of the game with a keyboard, which is certainly doable, but eventually I got to a part where I just knew it would be easier with a controller, so I played the rest that way. The game has some cool surprises, especially at the end. Figuring out the "magic word" and the "magic number" really isn't too difficult, but it is rewarding when you get it. Also, choosing to "lose" the game is also funny, although I recommend winning first, since you lose all your powers and start at the beginning when you lose (but you keep all the stuff you've found).
Anyway, you should definitely give this game a shot. It's short and sweet, but the price is definitely right. For what it is, I give it 9/10.

Great game marred by terrible balance and really shameless Pay2Win hyper expensive DLC. Seriously, the commanders alone, if you bought them all, would cost you over a hundred dollars, and many of them are mandatory if you want to be competitively relevant. Even the non-gameplay stuff like skins is exorbitantly priced(Really, Relic? 25 dollary-doos for a small skin-pack for vehicles while on SALE? 35 when not? What are you smoking?). It's DLC scheme would make even EA, Activision, and Ubisoft blush. There's a 'war spoils' system where you can supposedly pick up the content for free in random drops, but the drops are few and far between, and more often than not are copies of content you already had(I have 3 copies of a USF commander I ALREADY PAID FOR. In fact I have a copy of almost every USF commander, when I've paid for every one.), with no way to trade them with other players, or means to convert your copies into something useful. Between that, and the absolutely ridiculously high pricing of commander DLC that will have you paying the pricing of an entirely new game(Heck, a bundle of two new commanders costs more than CoH2 itself does while on it's routine sale.), there's no real incentive to buy DLC.
Well, except for one: The game balance. This is some of the worst balance I've seen in an RTS. When they decided to make the move from the system of the previous game by having many, many more commanders, they forgot that they have to actually make all the commanders unique AND relevant. What you get instead is tons of reused assets, tons of gimmicky garbage that breaks the mechanics of the game, and a system of balance built entirely around seeing who can out-cheese their opponent with the latest flavor of the month unit-spam, sim-city, or exploitation of some poorly tested ability or dooms-day tank. Every other month or so, a set of new commanders is introduced with little to no testing(Or perhaps, intentionally made overpowered). These commanders are either outright broken by introducing units/mechanics that totally circimvent intended counters, or are designed in a way that an otherwise underpowered and broken faction(In the sense that they underperform/are gimped) HAS to use them in order to be relevant. And like clockwork, after Relic has collected their shillings for a month or so and DLC sales finally slow down, they nerf these commanders and prepare the next batch.
It's a crying shame, because underneath all the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, this is a game that is fun, and has a lot of potential. The cover mechanics are fun, combined arms are fun, the soft-realism makes it accessible to people that aren't the greatest at RTS games, The low learning curve makes it easy to get into, and it straddles a middle-ground where both RTS casuals and enthusiasts can have fun and feel competitive, while bridging two extremes in the genre of Starcraft and Men of War into a game where both sides can enjoy themselves.
A lot of what makes this game great is marred horribly by the poor balance, the bucking of it's own damn mechanics by devolving into unit blobbing and running across open ground, the horrible DLC implementation, And the horridly skewed level of diversity and attention to detail between the Axis faction and the Allies faction(It's no secret that Relic are tremendous Wehraboos. One look at either side reveals that Axis gets far, far more unit diversity and aesthetic, while factions like USF feel lazy, slapped together, and chock-ful of reused assets.)
I'd say, if you are really looking for an RTS with a live community that is easy to get into, pick this up on sale for no more than 12 bucks. Otherwise, don't waste your time, get Men of War instead.

This is one of my favorite games of all time.
It's an old game, so a lot of the perks that we've all become accustomed to enjoying on newer games are not possible, but there are infinite outcomes and numerous nooks and crannies in this game to be explored.  A lot of the outcomes depend on exactly how you play.
Do you choose the Camarilla or the Anarchs or niether?
Do you try to be a nice guy, or does your blood lust know no bounds?
The great thing about it is that there are no right or wrong endings.
It also uses that same old spreadsheet-style upgrade system that works by granting you points as you play the game to spend on various different aspects of your character's skill  -- this is an archaic system, but it is kind of engaging in this game.
The developers of this title also did a lot of work on the seductive and Romantic end of being a vampire.  Matter-of-fact part of your skill-set is your seduction feat.
If Activision were to ever create another game I would hope that they do something better with the character generation.  As good as the technology and the engines are now, why can't you play the game using your own visage?  And you can determine which clan embraces you by answering a few questions about your own personal skills.
The other great thing about this game is the humor.  When you enter the internet cafe in Hollywood, you'll notice all kinds of Softdrink cans lying about.  At first glance these look like Coke cans, but when you approach it, one realizes that the patrons of this Internet Cafe are drinking cans of♥♥♥♥♥♥
In your haven and in various other places throughout the game you'll have the opportunity to turn on the radio and listen to the talk show "The Deb of Night."  This is amusing in and of itself, but if you want a really good laugh, make sure to stick around for the commercials.  The satirical riddiculousness of them is absolutely delicious.
In essence, what we have here is a great story with a very rich and interactive environment that totally works for a Vampire theme.  If you like dark RPGs, I totally recommend it.

The reason my gameplay is showing so little is because I could not find the redux version on steam to review  (with my true playtime)
I do recommend this game for those that are after a story based casual relaxed pace with a dark plot.
This is a story game first formost and solely. There is no way for you to die, I played through from start to finish in approx 4-5 hours, no rushing and no using walkthrus.
It can be a little challenging here and there with a few "eureka" moments but generally anybody from teen onwards is likely to be able to complete this.
The story itself without spoiling is a somewhat cthulu-esque and will not be suitable for children under around 12 ish due to this and due to a very small amount of bad language in an endgame cutscene, it is not gratuitous and I mention only for younger gamers/parents of younger gamers.
The game is beautiful, I have played this on a not too impressive laptop on low and on my desktop on ultra settings flawlessly and is easily the best looking unreal engine game I have seen.
The music is soothing and ambient, well done and very fitting
The story is not too long as the game is not too long but I felt happy paying ten pounds i believe it was at the time of purchase, but it does involve you and I felt attachment for the central character.
It is relatively linear and the "gameworld" is not huge but larger than it really needed to be to give some feeling of exploration.
The puzzles are few due to the general length of the game and not overly challenging although I did get "stuck" a couple of times.
Lastly for me, this is a one time game, I am unlikely to replay as of course I know the story, but I still recommend the purchase just for the one time play through I had.

A Story About My Uncle has a very beautiful game world, and fairly innovative gameplay. The game looked promising at first, but started to lose its charm after the fifth or sixth time I fell (for an unnecessarily long time) to my death. Most of the platforming is easy and repetitive; the parts that weren't easy were downright frustrating. The game makes no attempt to help you when you are stuck - there are a couple of sporadic hints that may pop up (usually immediately after upgrading the suit), but for the most part, you're completely on your own. Puzzles do not get any easier or offer simpler solutions if you have failed them too many times; if you are interested in this game for the story, be ready for this. Additionally, I had problems with glitches in the menu UI elements (in particular, when I initially configured the game, the mouse sensitivity slider became "stuck" and would adjust itself according to ANY horizontal mouse movement in a menu, even while not in the controls section, and even after closing and re-opening the menu); the game also frequently fails to save your graphics settings and starts up with the defaults on next launch.
TL;DR: Visually stunning, but gameplay comes up short. Wouldn't buy unless you're getting a good sale.

VTMB is what all gothic-inspired games should strive to be. It drops you into a dark world rife with conflict and bloodshed. You start as a feldgling kindred (vampire) and slowly climb your way through the ranks of the vampiric societies, all the while fighting interesting foes, discovering entertaining characters, becoming immersed in the setting and having an all around fun time!
Whats more is that it is an open-ended RPG! Wanna use your vampiric power to rush a horde of enemies, bashing in their skulls and filling them with led? You can! Wanna slink thorugh the shadows using finesse to slowly pick off your enemies? You can! Wanna sit back and use your vampire magic to boila guys blood until he explodes? You can!
Another interesting aspect is the inherent weaknesses all vampire clans have. Sure all vamps need to drink blood and avoid sunlight, but some clans have extra special qualities to set them apart. The Tremere clan, for example, ar elike mages. They use their blood sorcery to destroy their enemies. The downisde? they cannot raise physical attributes as high as other clans.
In my opinion VTMB scores a 9/10

Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines is an open-world RPG about vampires. Go figure. In its design, it is far less similar to its party-driven "predecessor", VTM Redemption. In fact, I'd say it is more closely related to a game like Deus Ex, with its focus on stealth, player choice, and RPG mechanics. The last DE game I played was Invisible War; Apparently, VTMB seems bent on making me sit through an avalanche of loading screens as well, though these ones aren't nearly as long. Regardless, this is the least of the game's worries, and I'll get to the bigger concerns as we go along.
Trying to review this on its own is impossible; not because I am just that displeased with what it is, but because it simply does not work. A quick search on Wikipedia revealed that the game was released "in an unfinished state", but it's Wikipedia, so who knows? I had to install a mod to get it working. Then, I installed an "unofficial patch", which added a boatload of content to the game, some of which seemed a little out of place, but still enjoyable. Yet, even with these fixes, I frequently ran into a plethora of technical problems, ranging from script errors during quests to objects that appear to be floating in midair to glimpses into the textureless, surfaceless realm that I've come to know as "the void".
The options menu... exists. It won't blow your mind, but you'll find a few options to improve performance on modern toasters that have trouble rendering a game from late 2004. Other options, like autosave toggling, more specific resolutions, and FOV fixes require a trip to the console menu. On a side note, I've observed that the game has a habit of not rendering things that the player isn't looking at. I noticed it first with the buildings, which is why I changed my FOV and widescreen settings. I thought I had solved the problem, but in reality, I had just widened the borders at which this sort of thing happened. If I look quickly enough at characters who wear flowy clothing, I can see it "snap" into existence. Not really an issue, but it's fun to look at.
The game looks and sounds fine for a specimen over 10 years old. Yeah, I mentioned permanent fixtures which float and appear ridiculous when given a closer look, but it does little to negatively impact the experience. Honestly, the worst looking things are the ridiculous animations on the less relevant NPCs. Where the graphics really shine is in the main and side characters which you can interact with. Excellent facial and upper body animations during their dialogue sequences compliment their great voice acting. The music is fine too.
The quests provide the meat of the gameplay, as most exploration really takes place during said quests. However, there is often little reason to revisit a certain area after going there for the purposes of the quest. Eventually, this leads to the world feeling rather dead, and you will find yourself taking the shortest possible path through the hubs to your next objective without stopping to smell the nonexistent roses. The quests themselves often serve the player one-sided challenges under the guise of choice. When given a choice, it always seems there is one beneficial choice and one detrimental choice, with no cost-benefit analysis to be had. Depending on what mods or patches you have installed, some quests are more bound to break than others.
The classes/clans hold all of the game's replay value. Each is suited to its own specific skill set and dialogue choices that ultimately determine how you go about playing the game, like a good class system should. The player facilitates this gameplay style by distributing the experience points he or she receives at leisure into a variety of skills and disciplines. The skills are the most affected should the player choose to replay the game. Things like lockpicking and hacking can be given far less focus after the player has gone through an area once and learned where all of the keys and passwords are located.
Combat feels awkward. It's not that the enemies are too hard, because on their own, they usually aren't. It's just that the game prefers to throw them at you in excess of five at a time, and that can get a little overwhelming to the point that I've found myself playing gun peekaboo to make it through. As such, when you have the option, stealth is often the better choice, even though it often feels linear and constricted with enemy funnels, like playing a game of Operation. It does little to help prepare for boss battles. Bosses range from "Damage Sponge" to "Elusive Damage Sponge". These guys can usually be taken out pretty easily if you're satisified with spending five minutes running backwards in circles while unloading entire magazines. The only boss I had trouble with was Bach, due to the fact that he has the advantage at a distance and does a ton of damage per hit.
I think that about covers everything, or at least everything I feel like talking about. Overall, the game feels as if someone brought a Geo Metro onto "Pimp My Ride", unaware of the fact that no matter how big you make the rims, no matter how many subwoofers you staple to the inside of the trunk, at the end of the day, it's still just a Geo Metro. Would I say it succeeded at being an open-world RPG about vampires? Yeah. Would I recommend it? Sure; That is, I would, if you don't mind doing what the "pee-see masturb race" does best, which is installing a collection of mods and patches to fix something that should not have been broken to begin with. Lucky for you, the m̶o̶d̶d̶i̶n̶g̶ fixing community for this game is still nice and active.

This is a great game with amazing role playing opportunities but unless you're willing to use unofficial patches and the console to get past issues, choose a different game. On a modern system, this game won't run without an unofficial patch and even then you run into hiccups. Still interested? Well, sit down because I'm going to tell you why this game is the vampire RPG you've been looking for and more.
Ever craved more after Skyrim's tiny vampire section? Well, here it is, with fangs and bloodlust to match.
This game puts you in the middle of an urban city environment based in 2004. You've been sired by a vampire against the Masquerade and if not for Kindred (vampires) political machinations, you'd be ash alongside your sire.
Now, you are thrust into a world of politics, monsters and blood, all whilst hiding your true nature. The clan you pick has a decent factor in on this and some more than others. There are different ways to handle situations throughout most of the game and it's really just near the end where the rewarded path becomes the least successful which is quite discordant.
Each situation is very different, leaving very little of that normal copy and paste side quest/main quest situation, giving you a fulfilling storyline to warm your undead heart. Mechanics have you thinking like a vampire- a game where you are the predator and sometimes, the prey don't know how close they were to their death, spared because it was too much effort. Your judgement, skills and so on will determine how you approach things.
The penalties for violating the Masquerade by exposing vampiric activities to the Kine (humans) can be severe if you're not careful. Feed on anyone out in the open, use certain powers openly, amusement, even the wrong speech choice can get you in trouble. Five strikes and it's an automatic final death/game over. Humanity Loss, unfortunately with the XP you can spend to undo is a little less dire but be careless and not fix a severe deficit and suddenly you're looking at a frenzy where you literally lose control for a bit. Injury and thirst for blood can bring out the vampiric beast within. Mostly, a savvy player will sidestep these pitfalls but occasionally, you’ll find yourself desperate for blood and a crowd of unwitting humans after a hellish quest so stock up on those spare blood bags.
Gameplay can get frustrating and there's no difficulty bar. My best advice to new players is don't get intimidated, and you'll make it through, even if you need to add self-advantage.
I won't spoil the main game but the World of Darkness universe is an amazing playground for your vampire RPG-ing wants. You have to play it for yourself and carve out your potential eternal life, although be careful. The wrong side at the end can leave your legacy as a fate worse than death. It’s a game of consequences with logic behind decisions and outcomes based on your choices. Vampire: the Masquerade - Bloodlines is a great vampire RPG, arguably one of the only chances you'll have to play a vampire as they were made to be and it leaves you wondering why more entries couldn't have been made. It is 'the' vampire RPG everyone wishing to sink their fangs into the night must have and the price is worth the gamble to get it running on newer computers.
My final score for this game is 9.5/10 and the half point loss is for the bug that required no-clip and the fifteen reloads it took to get through to the next section for an otherwise game breaking bug. Any older game made for XP and earlier you pick up at this point will come with all kinds of issues but this game was released as an unstable beta, requiring years of caring work by Wesp5, who deserves an eternity of gratitude for getting this game to run as well as it does.

Metro 2033 is a story based FPS and should focus on scripted sections instead of these Stalker-esque sequences.

I've currently played a little over 20 hours of Helldivers and am thoroughly enjoying it. I bought the game in a steam sale for about £8.
The difficulty is really well paced, as you can choose what (hardness) level to play almost straight away.  I would strongly recommend playing the training mission, even if your an experienced gamer.
There's 3 different races to play against, the harder the level of planet you choose, the tougher the enemies are that will spawn.
The maps and missions are procedurally generated so you cant refine a route and repeat it endlessly, unless you keep failing the level.
My only major gripe is the DLC, currently £16 for all the items if purchased together or £36 if bought seperately.
In particular the "all terrain boots", make playing snow levels a completely different experience, and are only available through DLC.
The cynical part of me would think that this is a deliberate pricing plan targeted at younger players (I'm presuming it matches the console pricing).
Although i was able to finish a "Helldive" level 12 mission and a Boss battle I think I was carried by the players I was with due to them having much better gear than myself.
The game really shines in multiplayer, games can be set to public, private or freinds (so only your steam contacts can join).
Although you have health (and can equip shields) most things are insta-death,  (there is also a pick-up system ala L4D).
Lose focus for a second and you walk under some equipment that gets inserted from orbit: insta-death, shoot explosives too close to yourself: insta-death, fall off a ledge: insta-death, etc.
In single player you have a set number of respawns, increased as you complete objectives in the map.
In multiplayer your comrades can call down reinforcements (respawns), effectively unlimited as long as someone is alive to call it.
So much fun to be had I will probably overcome my skinflint gene and purchase the DLC!

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a short game - took me about 5 hours in total, and I'm someone who is very thorough with exploration - but it is beautifully atmospheric and certainly tells a story.
First off, I cannot say enough about the graphics. The environment is absolutely stunning. The characters are perhaps a bit lacking by comparison, but it isn't so drastic to be distracting. I thoroughly enjoyed unfolding the events in each "chunk" of the game, even if the mechanics are a little repetitive, and getting to watch it all play out in full. My favorite part of the investigation sequences is how much they genuinely feel like solving a "Whodunnit" case; classic formula of finding clues and figuring out the order of events, which as someone who has always loved solving mysteries, gave me a thrill. I recall the storytelling feeling dark and disturbing to a degree, which I found myself eagerly digging into to discover more, so if you're into that - you will enjoy this.
There were also some extra, we'll call them "side missions" to uncover by going out of your way while exploring and completing certain tasks. These unlock additional stories that Ethan wrote which can be fun and interesting to hear about, but ultimately serve no purpose aside from achievements. There was one side mission in particular that caused me a lot of heart-pounding anxiety, but I was determined to finish it! Overall, though, I think they were a nice and warranted touch to a game that's already lacking in length.
I will say that I was disappointed with the ending. Without giving too much away, I remember repeating at my computer screen, "That can't be it. There had better be something at the end of the credits." Sadly, no extra goodies were to be found. Regardless, this is a GORGEOUS game with an engaging method of storytelling, fun Whodunnit-like mystery solving sequences, heavy emphasis on environmental exploration, and lots of optional additional content if you're patient. Definitely recommend.

I can't say enough good things about Lisa.
The gameplay is suprisingly engaging, it takes the elements of the Mother (Earthbound) series and fixes the parts that weren't working (the repetitive, boring battles). Almost every battle in Lisa is unique and there's a massive amount of characters with entirely different abilities and play styles to test out. I'll admit I didn't even give half of them a shot, there's just too many. Some of them are mostly useless, too, which I like. We're not all heroes.
Hidden under the (wonderful) toilet humor is a surprisingly deep analyzation of the hero's journey and a deconstruction of the male as hero and female as damsel tropes. The world is interesting and enigmatic, the characters are all eccentric, the storyline is challenging and the decisions you have to make throughout will genuinely have you biting your nails trying to decide what's best. Even sleeping a night to restore your party can have unfairly dire consequences. It's a game that will subvert your expectations at every turn.
There are a ton of small details (I don't want to spoil too much) that really make the game shine, too. I lost an arm in an unfortunate situation and suddenly climbing ropes is a slightly slower action. Dingaling squeeze a lot of love into his horrible world.
The soundtrack is equally impressive. I know Virt was originally slated to write some tracks, but I'm glad in the end he wound up having too busy a schedule to get around to it. The writer/creator of the game really nailed a strange fusion of the Mother series music stylings with modern weird electronic influences and it helps immensely with the worldbuilding. Virt is one of my favorite chip composers, but I don't think he's capable of moving in this weird of a direction as effectively.
If you like challenging, unique, dark and compelling indie games, you can't pass up Lisa.

This game is good, but apart from the main storyline, it seriously lacks enjoyable side missions. It's main storyline is also devoid of any depth or character development. It's far too short in my opinion. I was playing it for 9 hours and following the storyline half-arsed because me and my friend got distracted by loot or fighting zombies. Anyways, after 9 hours had passed, I was pleased to see we had completed 9% of the game.
However, after a few hours had passed, storymode completion shot up to 53%! We didn't concentrate on the story more intensely in those hours though, so really I was expecting it to go up to 18% or something. We were just playing it as normal so it's very bizarre it did that. So, I feel like the developers deliberately did that to dupe people into thinking the storyline was going to get more immerseive when it finished a mere 2 hours later.
The last mission is really, really long, and it's really enjoyable. Lots of parkouring, zombie killing (though I just avoided them to get to the more interesting parts) and scares. But for some stupid reason, you can't co-op the last mission! What were the developers thinking?
It also seems like 50% of the game is set inside the sewers (which I just hate because there's nothing much to do in them).
While not doing the main storyline mission or the side missions you can parkour around the place (there are various challenges set up but I've played none of them so don't know what they're like).
I've been co-oping it with a friend and it's been great. But, I must say, I've been quite disappointed when there weren't sniper rifles in the game as the game seems perfect for them.
You have bows (exploding, electric, incendiary and regular arrows - although I think you can only get these if you purchase the DLC), along with one type of rifle, shotgun and pistol. For me, the assortment of guns in the game is very limiting (I wish there was a whole load more). There's loads of melee weapons (which can get boring after a while), I just wish there were more guns and even an RPG in the game (there's molotovs though).
I bought the DLC as well, so in total you have quite a large area to cover (there are 3 maps in total).
All in all, it's a really good game at a very okay-ish price (bought it for $15 through a steam sale plus the $9 for the DLC). Would I ever pay $60 for this type of game? Hell no. Would I pay less than half as much? Yeah, sure. Only buy this game if it's on sale, otherwise you might find you've been ripped off a little. Would I also ever play this in single player? Nope. I wouldn't recommend it. I would only ever do it in co-op (where you can have up to 5 players in one map).

Defender's Quest is a great tower defense game for fans of the genre. It is the only tower defense game I can think of that has a decent plot and humor. You can also adjust the game's difficulty without any penalty. (300% gold and EXP is very useful when you need to grind.) I also like how I can name and customize my units. So many tower defense games have you fill the screen with identical towers, so it's nice to create an army of unique people.
I'm not very picky when it comes to graphics, but I think the game could really use better graphics and music. It's not a deal-breaker, but it does take away from game to some extent. I know that the Deluxe HD Update has been released, but the art style still looks primitive. Also, the update did not touch the music, so get ready to hear the same 5 songs over and over again as you fight your way through this lengthy, zombie-infested pit (twice if you're up for New Game+).
Overall, Defender's Quest is a fun tower defense game that has lots of charm. If you enjoy tower defense games, I'd definitely recommend Defender's Quest for some classic tower defense gameplay.

I know that we've ALL, at least once or twice in our lives, considered how impossible life would be if we had to consciously regulate the autonomous bodily functions that we require to survive in our everyday lives. Manual Samuel takes that idea and runs with. Not just a little bit, but a lot. In fact, Manual Samuel may as well never stop running because this game is one of the most ridiculous and stupid games I have played in such a long time, and I absolutely LOVE it.
The game oozes with both cringe and charm in equal balance, and honestly leaves me in stitches, time and time again. I don't think I've had so many genuine and uncontrollable bouts of laughter from another game since perhaps my early childhood. The corny dad jokes, sarcastic British narrator, beautiful comic artstyle and Beetlejuice hell scene at the beginning of the game won me over immediately, and continues to captivate me the more I play.
The addition of coop, though I've yet to try it, is an amazingly good idea. When playing alone, you need to control Sam's arms, legs, eyelids (yes, eyelids lol), mouth, lungs, peni$ (yes, peni$), EVERYTHING. Imagine sharing those bodily functions with a partner, and having to cooperate with them in order to keep Sam functioning. Lols for days.
This game really is immensely fun and I highly recommend it to anyone that has a good sense of humour and loves a good laugh. Bloody brilliant.

Short Review:
80% story, 20% puzzles. A joy to play if you like the mystery/puzzle/story type game.  The only bad thing is that this game is way too short, which is why I recommend getting this during a sale instead of paying full price.
Longer Review:
The story is intriguing and sometimes beyond fantastical, puzzles are mostly not too complicated. The graphics are gorgeous and the music is nice. Might get a bit slow at some points, but it’s a slower type of game that relies on atmospheric story telling. A joy to play if you like the genre. And then suddenly it’s all over. Way too short of a game, this is my only gripe with it. There’s not much replay value, unless you want to re-experience the lovely views and atmosphere. This game is not on my All Time Faves list, however it is an honorable mention simply due to the feeling I experienced at the ending, something only few games have achieved. A feeling difficult to describe, the best I can say is, it touched my soul. If you like mystery/puzzle/story type games, this is a must get. However due to the extremely short length, I recommend waiting for a sale to add this to your library.

This game is not for everyone. You will most likely either absolutely hate it or think it's among the best games ever created. My opinion is the latter.
Story: 10/10- Right off the bat this game is immensely depressing; you start off as a little kid named Brad getting beat up by some of the run of the mill bullies. After they're done picking on you, Brad proceeds to head home. Upon entering your house you meet your father, Marty. He is a terrible person, instead of consoling you for getting the crap kicked out of you, he continues to insult and even abuse him. You then go to your room, cry, and then the title pops up as the intro fades. The next time you see Brad is him as an adult, he lives in a world where there are no women. The dystopia setting is somewhat similar to Fist of The North Star.  He then ends up finding a baby girl, he decides to keep her and raise her as his own. His friends think that he should give the child to Rando: More or less the villain of this game, or at least the villain from Brad's perspective. He refuses, and decides to keep the girl, who he names Buddy. To say the least, Brad is a morally gray character; he SHOULD give Rando the girl to save the planet, but he doesn't because of his ♥♥♥♥ed up childhood. This is Brad's second chance.
Gameplay: 8/10- If there was a weak side to this game, it'd be this. If I had to describe the gameplay to this game, it'd be  Earthbound with the difficulty of a traditional SMT game. It isn't overly hard, but it is still fairly challenging.  It's an RPG, but it's on a 2d plane, so exploring is MUCH easier, seriously it is SO much better than the traditional 3d plane.
Characters: 9/10- You can get around thirty party members in this game, so not every character can get lots of development, but just about every character in this game is funny or incredibly tragic. I'm going to refrain from going in depth about the main character, Brad, because if my review can convince you to play this game, then I think you should learn about Brad's character yourself.
Graphics: 8/10- It looks simple, yet charming. The graphics are VERY similar to the Mother series, which really adds to the game in my opinion. It really works well with the tone of the game. The only thing that actually bothered me is that the cloud patterns are almost always the same pattern; which is understandable, but it looks a bit lazy from time to time.
Soundtrack: 9/10- I absolutely love this soundtrack, it has a tremendous amount of variety. There are incredibly hype tracks for the boss battles, really chill tracks for strolling around, and sad orchestral songs for the depressing parts of the game.

This was my game of the year for 2014, and possibly one of my new favorite games of all time. Every single aspect of it is damn near flawless in terms of what it sets out to do- not ground breaking in terms of combat, but it's very very well made and quite enjoyable, with a ton of unique combo-based fighting systems and other fun mechanics that are quite different from any RPG I've ever played. However, where the gameplay REALLY shines is the exploration; if you enjoy games like Yume Nikki, you'll love the vast, mysterious landscapes with more content and lore than you can shake a stick at, and if you like Dark Souls, you'll love the sheer amount of tricky hidden encounters with unpredictable outcomes and rewards, often leading into unexpectedly entertaining side-quests.
But most of all, the big grade-A+ selling point of LISA is the story and atmosphere. I've never played anything like it before. Comparisons have been made to a sort of R-Rated Earthbound, but that doesn't nearly sum it up. It manages to alternate between laugh-out-loud comedy, absolutely heart-wrenching tragedy, and genuinely nightmarish psychological body horror without skipping a beat. The game's profoundly dark themes are handled tastefully, and despite being quite gruesome in many places, are never played for simple shock value. Without spoiling anything, the story deals with domestic abuse, drug addiction,♥♥♥♥♥♥ revenge, mutilation, and apocalyptic desperation in ways that surprise and disturb, but never offend. And somehow, it manages to be one of the funniest games I've played since Portal.
Absolute 10/10 for me. If you have ten bucks and you're even remotely interested in oddball RPGs, you need this game, plain and simple.

Sinlesss is not your ordinary game, so before you buy this game, you should ask yourself some questions.
1) Is a story and tight atmosphere enough?
Sinless is more of a visual novel than a game. Gameplay here is you scanning the screen for objects to interact with and frankly, this is no fun at all. Add the clunky controlls and a couple of (at least in my experience not gamebreaking) bugs to the list and it is really not a game you should consider buying for anything else
2) Do I like the atmosphere?
As stated, Sinless is a lot about its atmosphere, so you should really make sure you like what you get. Watch the trailers in full screen with sound and let them do their work. You like what you see? This is exactly what you get when "playing" Sinless. The fun I had with Sinless was about me exploring the world.
3) How much are ~2h "gameplay" and an OST worth to me?
Sinless is short. Even slower playthroughs seem to take less then 3h. If you watched the trailer and decide now that 5 bucks are okay for a short story in this setting ando/or you like to have the OST available, now it's the time to buy Sinless. Otherwise wait for a sale or move on.
With a stunning, heart-beating Cyberpunk elements and classic Point n' Click playing that Sinless was considered Adventure game benearth  neon-lighted settings, glitch music and others...

Sinless is a 2D visual novel with some point-and-click adventure elements. You explore a cyberpunk world and try to track down your missing girlfriend. Soon enough it becomes apparent that something far more sinister is afoot.
The visuals may be stylish but they are also pretty painful to look at. I wasn't a fan of the visual style at all. The low resolution font is a big issue too and makes all the text a massive pain to read.
The game does not support 16:10 resolutions.
The sound effects are pretty basic but get the job done. I wasn't a fan of the sound track and found it rather annoying and repetitive.
The gameplay is very basic. This is certainly more of an interactive experience than a proper game. You simply explore the locations, talk to characters and pick up an item or two. There are no real puzzles to speak of.
The game is extremely linear too and to make any progress you need the complete the required actions in specific order. This can feel extremely artificial at times.
Overall finding the interactable hotspots is reasonably easy, but many of the area transition hotspots are somewhat hidden. The travel system in general is quite annoying and the game has a lot of backtracking. This gets extremely tedious since every single area transition comes with a lengthy loading time.
Sinless is a very easy game. Most of the time your next course of action should be obvious and there are no real puzzles to speak of.
The controls are rather basic but for the most part functional enough. There are some incredibly badly designed UI elements, however, and the dialogue window in particular is just a massive mess.
The writing is pretty terrible. There are quite a few typos and way too many cheesy pop-culture references. The story itself is rather derivative and not particularly interesting.
The game isn't very polished and there are a number of issues with the scripting. You also can't alt-tab out of the game at all.
I found Sinless to be a pretty terrible experience. Between weak gameplay, poor writing and a terrible art style there's little here to like. Best avoided.

Is this game good? Yes... at 50 cents. I bugged my friend to get me tthis game when it was on sale for 50 cents as I couldn't sell anything yet.
You can easily beat this game on a casual playthrough in less than 2 hours, heck, I beat it in 2 hours and I got stuck on some parts of the game. Anyway, this story IS good for the latter half of the game, I'd say it's similar to Fahrenheit 451 in a way, but without the books.
One of my biggest complaints about this game is the lack of dialogue progression. For an example, in the beginning of the game, there's a shop you have to shop at to buy a bus pass. The dialogue comes and goes, but later in the game, if you go back and talk to them again, the same series of dialogue shows up, and you pay for it again and again, but it doesn't spend you money. I think it's lazy on their part.
Another minor complaint I have is the travel system. In the beginning of the game, you're in your bedroom and have to go into the living room. You have to select the lower left corner, even though there's absolutely no indication that a door to the living room was there.
Now let's go to the good parts.
The story, is, like I said, pretty good but it could be better. There's a lot of holes in there, but its probably explained in the other minorly different endings, but I don't feel like replaying the game.
The visuals on this are actually very unique in my opinion. In most parts, it looks very beautiful. At other parts it looks too bright, too many glares and such.
The main catch of this game is the OST. The OST is great, and was one of the main reasons why I bought this game too. The OST is a hidden gem, so it's hard to find on youtube or various other sites. It's not my type of music persey, but if I liked it, I'd be jamming to it every day.

This game. This is most likely the biggest surprise in my entire library.
I originally bought this game about two years ago. The Steam Trading Card system  had just launched into beta (remember when everyone thought it was going to be huge and a card could be worth $5?) and I had gotten in. Curious to test the system out, I found I at the time did not own any games on the short list of applicable games. I immediately did two things. First, I purchased Half-Life 2 since I had played that game on another account and knew it was good. Second was I started scanning the list for cheap games. This was on a daily deal sale the following day.
I checked it out and saw that is seemed like a pretty generic, if solid, tower defense game. Felt like one of those particularly good flash games on something like Kongregate or Armor Games. Still, for 5 bucks, I figured it was worth a shot.
And I wasn't entirely wrong in my expectations. This does very much feel like a buffed up flash game in a lot of ways. And then I asked myself if that was a bad thing. The gameplay is simple and understandable yet plenty difficult. Creativity is encouraged and different strategies will be required. The graphics weren't amazing, certainly not HD (though a HD update is on its' way at time of writing) but I feel like the art has character to it. This of course is helped by the fact that there actuually is a solid storyline in the game, more than many games I've played. The characters don't have a lot of screentime for development, yet I still feel like they are real.
All in all, this game I found to be a very good surprise. Don't expect a AAA level game, but do expect a game whose simple charm and solid gameplay will leave you satisfied. This game doesn't amaze, but it does the one thing that all games have to do. It's simply entertaining. The devs (who btw are super communicative and dedicated to their games) really did a great job with this one, and I look forward to their future work.

Not a good game.
It was as if the devs made sure it had all the elements to sell, but none to make it fun.
Not an enjoyable 17 hours.  I wasn't smart enough to stop.
(1)  The tower defense gameplay was poor.  The appeal of tower defense games is usually to try and optimize your defense to be efficient and effective as possible against the oncoming force.   In Defender's Quest there are very few places where your characters can be placed rationally.  In other words, there was only one strategy to place your characters when you setup.  Since there were no other real elements to the game, this made it very boring.  When you lost a mission, you couldn't try and refine your process as there was nothing to refine.  You just needed to level up to get stronger.
(2)  The character leveling up process was poor.  I decided to buy the game because the game boasted an RPG leveling-up process.  Although this is technically true, you DO HAVE TO CLICK A BUTTON in order for them to get more powerful, it could have been done automatically as your choices were thin, uncreative, and obvious.  Again, there was no game element in it.  You put the point where it was supposed to go and done.
(3)  The storyline was not worth it.  I don't remember the storyline other than it seemed shallow.  The characters were the best part of the game.  Each character seemed unique and full of personality, but the storyline needed more to take away from the poor gameplay.  Because I liked the characters and I thought they were unique, it was a big letdown to find out later that you get more characters just like them gameplay wise.  Here you thought you had a unique crazy berserker guy or a badass ice mage, but no, they are just one of many.
(4)  The enemies were uncreative.  The enemies were similar across the board.  At no point do you need to change your strategy based on the different types of enemies coming our way.    Some tower defense games have VERY uncreative enemies, but they don't need varied enemies as the game element is in the placing of the towers/characters, abilities, and tower synergy.  Defender's Quest did not have that.

I am not a fan of "twitch" games, especially as I get older and my reflexes get even poorer.   Nevertheless, I found Defender's Quest to be, although rather small in scope, to be engaging and enjoyable.    Lots of interesting planning at each new level, some role-playing aspects, and graphics that are good enough for the purpose intended.   This is not the game of the decade or anything like it, but it will deliver some real fun, and was a nice change of pace for me.

Mafia II is a great game, let me just start with that. The guys at Illusion Softworks have done it again. The game engine is fantastic, and makes everything feel realistic. The driving (in simulation mode), the combat, the cover system,the guns, the AI, the lighting, the textures, cutscenes, animations and of course, PhysX  are all brilliant. I'd go as far as saying that this game's visuals and physics programming are superior to that of GTA IV. On top of that, the game is of good length and has decent characters and a nice story. BUT MAKE NO MISTAKE  this is not even in the same league compared to the original. The first game really had it cracked  the pacing, the level design, the variety, the characters, the story, the soundtrack, the realism etc. Mafia II is still a Mafia game  it's not a generic third-person shooter and is character driven, so don't expect much free-roam. I'm glad that this isn't a GTA clone, but in some aspects it has tried to be to appeal to a wider crowd. I felt like this game was heavily influenced by Grand Theft Auto IV. The story and missions aren't anywhere near as special as The City of Lost Heaven, and the characters are more shallow. Joe is almost a clone of Roman from GTA IV. There's also no Free Ride mode as in the first game either. However, what this game manages to do is make you feel like you've actually lived a day in the life of the main character, because each chapter Is packed with content and is of perfect length. Overall the game is a bit more predictable and more generic, and does nothing new. It's pretty much a combination of Mafia and GTA IV, which isn't a bad thing but the story isn't as good as in Mafia 1 and there's no extra content such as multiplayer or free-roam and side missions. It's worth playing if you liked GTA IV but if you're expecting it to even come close to touching the first game on any department, you're gonna be disappointed.

As the store page for the vanilla game is still available (i.e. the Redux edition does not make the original disappear) I am only going to concentrate on the new aspects of the game. Should you be interested in what Metro 2033 about feels free to read my review on the vanilla game's store page.
Initially, I thought this Redux edition was only a graphical enhancement to the game released back in 2010. Make no mistake: the creators have done a superb job! Redux sports better lighting effects, more detailed textures and, to be honest, we have so many bits and pieces here that it is simply better to use YouTube and look for some comparison videos.
But is this good for us? Well, yes! Remember when Last Light came out? It offered better graphics so much so that we can say it was as Metro 2033 was originally intended to be. So, the developers picked this upgraded, more refined engine and remade all the levels of Metro 2033. We have the ultimate Metro 2033 experience now!
And the upgrades do not stop there: some new elements introduced in Last Light were also borrowed. For instance, melee was not possible but finally, taking out enemies silently is possible not just from the distance. Also, diary pages are now hidden throughout this game. Since you explored everything for the extra ammo now you can find these and read more about Artyom's thoughts and emotions.
Some sections were expanded upon and there are new sections such as the hall in Polis where you can stop by and marvel at the establishment along with the bartender who you can drink with. Besides the diary pages, there are many safes hidden, as well. Keys to them appear on dead bodies or simply on shelves and while they glow in red due to the cobwebs sometimes it is difficult to spot them. Oh, cobwebs! We now have these and setting them on fire with the lighter is as fun as it was in Last Light!
Redux is the definitive version of Metro 2033. A version that expresses that this is how it should have been all along back in 2010. You can dismiss the idea if you want due to the fact that money is - once again - asked for it. However, if you are a true fan of Metro and you liked its sequel I'm sure it will be an immediate purchase for you. :)

I finished this game yesterday and I am still thinking through the storyline and the characters.  Much like a really good book, I couldn't put it down for long.  I just had to know how it all played out.  I will say that those expecting the protagonist to be packing a BFG and taking out evil, then this is not that type of experience.
First off, the game itself is gorgeous and just drips with melancholy emptiness.  There is a an evil just beyond the veil of beauty and the story brings that out.  Fans of
and
would likely feel right at home.  Don't ever trust that picture-perfect small town.
Puzzle elements are very light and forgiving.  The worst that may happen is you reset and start again.  I did not experience a single glitch in my playthrough.  There were a couple of jump scares, and yes - I did jump . . . slightly (don't judge).
I did find myself wishing there was a run setting or warp function.  You move through the game at a purposeful trot at best (aka walking simulator).  But aside from going back for a couple of bonus items, the game was linear, moving from one scene to the next as the story unfolded.  And that is the focus here - the story.  "Gameplay" takes a back seat.
And then it was all over, the story was told.  No strategy, score, or massive shoulder pads.  Just the story and its lingering lessons.  And I will likely experience Red Creek Valley again at some point.  My thanks to The Astronauts for creating this title.

This is a beautiful game. Beautiful in terms of its music, its ambience, and most definitely its graphics. And in terms of its appeal, it is definitely one of those "Walking Simulators" you've heard about.
There's certainly actual concrete "gameplay" here, but it is light and never really what keeps you playing. You also don't really have to worry about death or failure in any way, at worst puzzles simply reset your position.
Beyond simply exploring, the other main draw is the series of unique and interesting vignettes that offer a small self-contained 'experience' when you encounter them. These, in addition to investigating the scenes of the murders in the own, offer the concrete gameplay of Ethan Carter.
The game has you playing paranormal detective Paul Prospero as he searches for a lost boy in a small town that reeks of death and the occult... and that's about as deep as I'll go before I'd inadvertantly start dropping plot spoilers. If the player character and plot premise sounds somewhat flimsy and weak, setting you up as a cornier pacifist version of Harry Dresden... you wouldn't be wrong. Infact that's definitely the major flaw of the plot for me, the premise was so paper thin at points that later plot twists didn't end up being twists for me. The plot had made itself transparent in very major ways so that the ending simply ended up as "Oh, that seems about right. Yes." rather than anything mindblowing.
Graphically this game is stunning. It uses phototelemetry to build up 3D versions of actual objects using a multitude of photographs and the result is actually pretty mindblowing. Though sadly it means the parts of the graphics that have to use conventional methods, folliage and characters... well they can't measure up at all.
The game is so scenic that simply exploring the town and the surrounding woods becomes a mesmerising experience, helped along by some really beautiful atmospheric music.
The actual puzzles in the game arn't really that great, generally revolving around you solving murders by finding relevant objects (which can turn into a bit of a blind hunt at times) and ordering the sequence of events by way of psychic memories left in the enviroment. This ends up being a combination of trial and error and obviousness. There's at least one of them so easy to solve that you're simply ordering them 1 to 10 in a straight line.
In terms of content this game has horror underpinning with strong references to the Cthulhu Mythos. There is a fair amount of gore present in the murders, but generally no other life so it never really graduates from 'creepy' to 'scary' with the possible of one segment of the game.
This game is relatively short, clocking in at around 3-4 hours of playtime (which may make the non-sale price steep for many), but offers something unique and memorable. The main draw for me was a combination of exploration and the unique vignettes, so I'd class The Vanishing of Ethan Carter as more of a short experience than a 'game'. Sadly the story fell just short of engaging me due to it playing its hand earlier than it intended to, but I'd still recommend this game any time it is on sale.

I played the Paranormal Investigative game all in one sitting. The game Last seven hours, taking into account some time used actually trying to figure out the clues or where to go next. I'll address this later.
-Firstly the story:
If you like the paranormal, Noir detectives and murder mysteries. This is your game, and I would recommend you get it ASAP. The narrative of the game is explained to you through flashback sequence; which occur when the player completes all the "clues" for a scene in the game. Even then it's not overbearing. A simple line from the protagonist and player, Paul Prospero details everything you need to know without taking you out of the immersion of the game. Another thing this games does very well.
-The games world:
The map of the game, although small, is detailed meticulously. This fact and the use of the engine mean you can immerse yourself in the world incredibly easily, with the help of the subtle narrative. I cannot imagine what this would be like in VR. The game play is not completely linear, but there are aspects; and rightly so, that are. Such as areas being blocked or just hidden until an event is triggered in the story. Otherwise you can visit anywhere in the map without restriction. One downfall to this is it can lead to a lot of back-tracking, which does cause annoyance at times. When you really just want to progress the story to find out what is happening.
-Game Mechanics
As mentioned earlier the game tells it's story through a sequence of flashbacks, that the player instigates from restoring items to their original places at a crime scene. Adding, partially, the element of paranormal. Otherwise the game plays like a first person point and click adventure really. Personally I think that's what makes it good. It's not over complicated; and doesn't bar people from entry into the game. Also, more importantly, it doesn't take away from the detective work.
One thing that I both praise and criticize the game in, is the lack of hints or hand-holding. On one hand this means how well you progress through the game is entirely up to your skill. However in certain cases this can lead to frustration when, to progress onto the next area you have to do something that isn't obvious at all.
To conclude I definitely recommend this game. It's a fun paranormal investigative game, which had me on the edge of my seat throughout and left me wanting more when I had finished. While I haven't played this in VR I think it would add to the immersion of the whole game, while there probably wouldn't be a high chance of motion sickness due to the walking nature of this game. However if this is the case then there's an option to add a sight in the middle of the screen that could help.

Before anything, know that you will need an unofficial patch to run this game. I cannot tell you how much of a headache it was not knowing this. After you get past that issue, this game is a must-have.
It is a gem of an RPG with tons of replay-ability because almost everything has multiple options you can take in different playthroughs.
Most quests have this open ended sort of nature. There is no super protective hand holding here. You are given a goal and that is pretty much it. You can solve every problem in whatever way that you fit. Every type of person is welcome, from the sneaky sneaks to the testosterone fueled run & gunner. Sometimes quests may come with some parameters the quest giver wants. These are mostly optional but you will be penalized (EX: being told to go sneaky but going guns blazing = a scolding)
The gameplay is also solid and gives you options as well. Are you a fan of 3rd person melee combat? We got you covered! You a fan of FPS shooting mechanics? We also got you covered too.
One of the oddest things that I really enjoyed and respect the most from this game is in character creation. When you start, you get to pick a vampire clan to belong to. Certain clans have certain quirks to being them. For most, it is just minor changes in dialog where people would reference it. The 2 clans that are exceptions to this are the Malkavians and the Nosferatus. Malkavians are usually pretty insightful but it is lodged in crazy while the Nosferatus are so deformed that they should never be seen by humans. So what did the devs do? Malkavian players hear whispers in their ear and are given really insane dialog options for everything that can range from gibberish to cryptic hints for both. 80% - Mafia II: The Real Mafia Experience
This game opens up as an interesting story that keeps going until ends up on an even more interesting story, going from a thief wanna-be that joins the US Army Light infantry Airborne unit to ends up as one of the biggest Mob leaders of New yor...... Empire city.
The first mafia has been just a rip off from The Godfather (IMHO, best PS2 game ever). But this game REALLY does a good justice to the genre of mobsters sandbox. Of course, there are flaws, but nothing too big. The weapons are somewhat lacking, and the ammo is not universal between some of them like how it should be (the .45 ammo used in both M1911, and both Thompsons) and the Crosshairs are not really useful either at all... but this is not the first time we have seen this, so its not really game-breaking.
The graphics DOES looks dated somewhat, then again, we are talking about an 2010 game here, but trust me, it won't look like that in a lot of times, the biggest complaint would be also that the Cutscenes are not rendered with the same quality than the in-game engine, but that they are inferior too (something odd and EXTREMLY rare in games). But the shadow quality is at least, good, and i cant say much bad about the textures either.
The game tries too hard to be interactive, maybe a little bit too hard. Some parts of it itself are glitching because the interaction is up to where your character is looking, not where you are pointing at, and being a Third Person Shoter, that's not a good idea. Not that its a big problem, after all, almost nothing that you can do inside your house is really useful... you will be only using the fridge, the guardrobe, maybe the radio, and the phone for certain missions.
Talking about the radio, a big complain would be the lack of radio stations, in the first part of the game that takes in the 1945 has just 3 radio stations (too little) but at least the song in them its not bad, its pretty good. Then, after the second half wich takes you into the US of 1951, the radio stations are there, with the music of the time, not even their names changed.
Now that i mentioned the second half, i have to say, its REALLY well done as an enviroment, some places changed, the cars changed, and you can see everything by yourself how the whole US changes in the time of the war and after the war.
The main difference of the 2 parts would be the weather, wich in the first part is snowing (vehicle handling is affected) and the second part is Autumn/Summer.
About vehicle handling: Its no TDU or car simulator, but its doing a pretty damn good job at it. I haven't touched the arcade setting, but the realistic vehicle handling its just fantastic.
The AI its just the good old classic Sandbox AI, TERRIBLE. And the cops may look like if they took car driving lessons from the ones in GTA. But at last, the Cops AI its not so bad, it does behaves somewhat in a realistic manner, the only exception would be that going over a red light its not considered law infringement, or at least i haven't been chased by passing over a red light.
This game is FORCING YOU to stay in cover, wether this is good or bad, its up to you. Also, i should be explaining that the AI only reacts to you, yes, granted, this is better than COD, friendly AI actually does something, but the game really put the spotlight on you.
The system to buy things is bad. You cant buy cars, the tunning its not good until you have unlocked everything in the last section of the game, and the cloth stores do not tell you wich item you have already bought before, or wich one you haven't. This is turning the game into a more GTA IV style approach, as you cant even buy houses (not that it really matters, as there are just 4 houses for you, starting one, first half, mid half, and a bad last half one).
The dialog is greatly written, and there is nothing else to say that i just love it.
You WILL have to remember that this game doesn't give a thing about your money, as in 2 parts of the game they force you to leave everything behind.
There is a lotpicking minigame to steal cars, but dont get too excited, it may be silent, but its still attracting cops, its not really realistic at all (how hard would it be to make it realistic? really!), but its a nice add to the general game.

At first this game looks very promising. It's a pity the only included single player campaign is designed only around the Knight.
Multiplayer will actually play out much like modern FPS games. Yes, there are rocket jumping knights in this game. Here are the unique abilities of each class:
Archer: Grappling Hook, Charge Attack (fires 3 arrows if you keep clicking), Fire 4 arrow types (normal, water, fire, bomb).
Builder: Mine, Build, Deconstruct. Builders make all things including workshops to manufacture items for the other classes.
Knight: Block, Charge Attack (breaks through block, and a quick 2nd swing usually kills the knight),
Use Bombs (water and explosive), use heavy demolition, fly with shield (further with chicken), bomb jump, weaker deconstruct (knights can chop through wood and dirt, but must bomb through stone). They can also surf over rough terrain using their shield.
As you can imagine most multiplayer sessions devolve into rushing for bombs and demolitions and then most players switch to knights because they are so overpowered. The game could be much better than what it is with a few simple changes to the knight (remove charge attack, have shield only block arrows and melee, make stone blocks tougher, remove supply drops). But as it stands the combat oriented players will win every time over builders and their traps.
It would also be nice if you could make a custom castle or fortress and then use that at the beginning of every game rather than having to rebuild it at the start of each new game. Sadly I cannot recommend the game in its current state, which feels very pre-alpha to me.
