Many people say that this is a glorified walking simulator and while there is a lot of walking in The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, there is also a lot of puzzle solving. It's interesting, weird and “hard to understand without a guide” puzzle solving, but it's much more than walking.
Please keep in mind that this playthrough was for the "redux" version. That version apparently doesn't have reviews applied to it on Steam.
I got the chance to play The Vanishing of Ethan Carter during a day when I was at home sick. That meant I had a good uninterrupted play-through of the game, which I fully recommend if you're going to play it. From what I gather from the story (more on that in a second), you're a detective who has come to a small abandoned town to solve the mystery of a boy named Ethan Carter who has gone missing. I’m not sure who called you or why you’re there in the first place, however, it's immediately apparent that there is MUCH more to this town than just a missing boy.
There are many things to like about Ethan Carter. One is the fact that it is a gorgeous game. The landscapes and environments are top notch and for a game where 70% of your job is walking around this small town, that's important. I found myself taking pictures at many times where there was no story being told, just because it looked so beautiful!
Also, the atmosphere and overall feeling of the game is just something that doesn't seem to exist in other games. This town you're investigating truly feels abandoned and creepy and you're never sure what you're going to stumble upon next!
However, there are some issues with the game as well. As a game where a lot of walking takes place, the movement can feel super slow at times. There is a run button, but it doesn't make your character move all that much faster. As small as the town is, I think the game could've done well with some sort of fast travel system. Especially when you find out you have to back track a bit when you haven't solved certain scenes. Finding out you have to return to where you started from the last crime scene in the game is kind of a let down.
For some, the story might be an issue, as the game doesn't divulge the last 75% of the story until the very end. If you're ok with going through a mysterious, abandoned town and not fully know why things are happening until the end, then you should be fine. However, even the ending, while it gives you an idea of what happened in this town, it doesn't completely fill you in.
The positive part about the story it is that all of the good and creepy stuff feels like it's right out of a Stephen King novel or a Twin Peaks episode. I found reading through Ethan's short stories to be some of the best stuff in the game, next to the visuals.
The pace of the walking and the story would be forgivable if it weren't for this next thing that got on my nerves. It's obvious that the team behind this wanted to create a murder mystery that felt like Myst or another similar walking while puzzle solving game. The issue is that Myst was created back in the early nineties. 20 years later, we should've learned from such a game that explaining a few things about how your game works isn't bad!
The game starts by telling you that they will not be holding your hand in this adventure. Fine, I get it, you want us to figure out the mysteries ourselves. However, what this actually means is that the game has no tutorial whatsoever, and you're left to your own devices to sort of figure everything out.
In this game, you will be trying to solve and put together how a crime scene happened. I managed to get to about the mid-point of the game when I realized how it’s actually supposed to work. The issue is that there are several crime scene investigation parts and then there are other random puzzles. Sometimes it can be hard to figure out which is which when you stumble upon them.
On top of that, the game doesn't give you a lick of information on how to start looking into these crimes. I had fun with the game, but after the first 2 hours and then not progressing for a bit, it's hard to know where to go, what to inspect, what to do and all the while you're slowly wondering around this town looking for clues. You could be hot, you could be cold, but you won't know until you stumble upon a clue.
Perhaps this is what they were going for? They wanted it to feel like you were really solving the case and you had to solve the cases with nothing but your wits...and paranormal powers. However, I think putting a quick few notes within the first crime scene, or even a small help guide in the options would’ve been just fine to help the player out a bit. If you don’t want to help with the optional puzzles, I get it. But it would’ve been nice to not have to look at a quick spoiler free guide on Steam to help (though I will say that I am very glad it exists, because it helped!).
This is a tough one for me to decide on recommending or not. I enjoyed it and didn't mind a little help from a spoiler free guide, but not having the basics explained to you during the game is a real killer. I'm going with recommending it, with the caveat that you should really read about what you're getting into here before taking the plunge. Getting it cheap doesn’t hurt either, if you just want to see the beautiful visuals.

The graphics are good( just know it's from mid 2000's) and everything looks like it's riped right from star wars, even things made just for the game. The stages are nice and have some easter eggs as well. Over all this totally nailed the look of star wars. This all goes for the sound as well. Laser sounds are iconic as are the lightsaber sounds. And the sound track is nostalgic gold. The controls are a little clunky but nothing game breaking. But be aware you will be dealling with around three control styles. Land,vehicle, and space flight(and a few others less common) and all are pretty diffrent from each other. And it can be difficult to be precise sometimes, but it never hurt the battle too much unless I needed to hurry somewhere.
There is quite a bit of content as well. Campaign, galatic conquest,instant action, and of course online play. You also have four default classes that are good at certain things(vanguard is effective vs. vehicles, sniper attacks long range,ect.). And two uniqe classes for each faction, of which you need to earn points in battle to use them in combat (since they are better than the default in most cases). You can also use heros when you fulfill certain conditions. Which are all from the movie like luke skywalker and darth vader. I didn't like the campaign very much. It was more of a tutorial for multiplayer and less a satisfying experince. And the story feels tacked on. It deals with the clones perspective of the rise of the empire. It could have been interesting and humanized the clones a bit, but it never really did much more than a cutscene saying "yup, we were there at this point". It all seems like a missed opportunity. The galactic conquest is much better. You get credits for how many planets you own which you can use for different advantages like extra troops  or more fire power. And you must attack other planets  and take them from opponets. The only nitpick is that you can play the same planets and space battles a lot, particularly when you are on the last few planets since the opponet is limited in movement.
Instant action is what it sounds like. You choose the rules and era, and then you battle. There are also some rules not in the other single player modes like XL( large scale battles) and hunt(kill certain species). And there are plenty of stages and their size is not too big (draging out fights) or too small(making them clutered). They are just about right. My biggest issue with the game is the A.I. It's pretty bad, as i've seen some just stand there and do nothing or not defend posts like they should. I should say "sometimes" as they never got me killed too often, but be aware you are pulling your team 100%.
It's strongest point is the multiplayer no doubt. And it still seems to be very alive. But there is still a lot of fun to be had in single player. Overall, yes I recommend this game. Any flaws in the game are countered by the fact it's still a lot of fun to play.

Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines sounds like a sequel and there was a game before it, but it starts fresh and doesn't seem to carry any baggage from the previous game. You play with roleplaying-style skill points which increase as you buy into the higher levels. Your skills range from melee, to stealth, to guns, to computer hacking, and everything in between!
When creating your character you choose between male and female, and then one of many different families. These families give you your vampire powers, like terrifying presence, or moving in super speed.
Your job as a newly converted vampire is to do the will of your Prince and leader. During your missions you'll meet so many creative and unique characters. The world you're put into is just so unique and enjoyable from everything else out there right now, it's really hard to describe how this game's story was.
Bottom Line: Get this game. If you like great stories and/or role-playing games, then this is a gem I had missed for years and I wouldn't want any of you to miss it any longer.

How this game starts gives me a strong sense it was influenced, at least partly, by the concept of 'The Matrix' reality system. The game upholds a typical cyberpunk scene where you play as a good citizen of a seemingly flawless system who starts to discover there is a darker twist to his reality. A short game with only one chapter complete (I shall re-evaluate my review once this game is updated), so the game as it stands is incomplete and ends on a cliffhanger, leaving the player anticipating for more. The game could use a touch up on the text dialogue with interactable characters, but to be fair I found a number I did interact with rather either amusing or fitting. The background music fit perfectly with the theme, which although hard to follow at first, made sense the more you play through. I enjoyed the artstyle in this game but it could be an acquired taste for some.
I'd like to see this game developed further so the story is finished, as I anticipate to see where this journey will lead me.

[Setting]
The unique artstyle combined with the little details give the impression of being in a living and breathing cyberpunk world.
[Story]
Right now there is only one episode (looking forward to the next ones) which would be a good intro into the game itself.
It sets up the plot and ends in a cliffhanger.
But that's what it is, an intro: The path is as linear as can be (and I think I did everything possible in the game) meaning that there are no consequences whatsoever. It doesn't matter what options you pick in a dialogue because you can repeat most dialogues until you get the desired result.
[Negative stuff]
You can't manually save in this game.(You can if you follow my guide in the discussions)
To get the achievement of reading all the news, you have to read the news in each act in one playthrough. You can't load a savegame of act 1, read the news, load a save from act 2, read the news, load a save from act 3 and read the news.
[Overall]
The story and atmosphere are unique and very good but the game itself needs more fleshing out. If this episode is being kept as an intro and if the next episodes are more fleshed out, then this will be a great game. Sadly I haven't seen any information about the next episodes and there is no sticky thread in the discussions to communicate with the developers. I hope that they are still working on it and have not abandoned us.(I don't mind a long wait for a good game but it would be nice to get some updates)

Verdict: A wonderful take on the often stale Tower Defence genre, with light RPG elements, solid gameplay, excellent art and soundtrack and a simple but endearing story. 8/10
Story: The story is simple and humour-orientated, but endearing and, at times, surprisingly engaging given that is delivered through static art cut-scenes and text speech bubbles. The characters are distinctive, fun and memorable. 7/10
Gameplay:  The gameplay is solid Tower Defence with light RPG elements. You equip and level up your heroes, which you place as towers to fight off the waves of encroaching enemies. Placement is key, such as placing your ice mages a good distance from your fire-breathing dragons as their abilities will counteract one another, or ensuring your knights will be able to shatter the enemy armour before your archers rain down their arrows for maximum impact. 9/10
Graphics: Simple, pixelated graphics are stylistic and get the job done but have been done better elsewhere. Sprites look good, environments are dull and a bit repetitive. The cut-scene art is fantastic. 6/10
Sound/Music: The sound effects are basic and appropriate to the pixelated presentation. The soundtrack, on the other hand, is superb. 8/10

A great zombie/survival sandbox that executes on its systems better than pretty much any other game in this genre. It is somewhat held back by its throwaway story.
The gameplay design is where this game shines. The melee combat is some of the best I've ever seen in a first person game.  You could almost buy this game for that system alone. The skill tree is one of the better ones I've seen in a game like this, and gives you very useful upgrades that almost completely change the way you play the game. The new skills are insanely fun to use and harmonize really well with the core mechanics. You end up with this really fun mix of "fight moves" to use in between slashing/shooting zombies. Some mechanics like the "stomp" are a little bit overpowered, but they are incredibly fun and fluid. The experience of simply living in this world and trying to survive is when I felt most engaged, and that experience gave me a stronger narrative than the written narrative.
The biggest criticism I have is the quest/narrative design. It's easily the worst part of the game. Thankfully all or most cutscenes are skippable. You'll find yourself being sent to mainly run boring errands. These boring quests are mostly saved by the polish of the core gameplay systems - but there's no reason why these quests couldn't be more interesting.

I played through the story on medium.
The story was pretty good but nothing stellar. If you've watched a lot of mob movies (Godfather, Goodfellows, etc.) then you'll get a good idea of what will happen. The end bits feel a bit rushed and they do jump around a bit but it's above average, even if it doesn't cover new ground.
The open world that's in the game is beautifully done. Everything from the shops to the kitchens are filled with details. The problem is that there isn't much to do in the world. You can steal cars and rob shops to gain money but there isn't much to do with it that many times it's not even worth it. The main reasons you need moeny are story based and the story will provide and take away from you as it sees fit. There were a few times where I loaded up with guns before a mission only for that mission to have me stripped of them. A few story events have you gaining and losing large sums of money so your previous work doesn't really matter.
The gun play is ok but nothing special. The driving is good but driving laws are enforced and the police will chase you for speeding, meaning you won't have the oppurtunity to really test them out. You have to pay for the repairs so you can't go too out of control with cars from your garage. A lot of the missions involve you driving people around and doing it safely. Pressing "L" makes it so your car doesn't go over the speed limit so that helps a bit but it does get kinda boring driving everywhere.
The game had a few graphical glitches for me and sometimes characters would get stuck, forcing me to restart missions. A few cutscenes lacked characters and had a voice coming out of nowhere. Most of these were solved via restarting the game or mission. It was frustrating but I've had worse.
Overall the game is pretty good but probably not worth full price to you. If you can get it cheap and like mob movies, go for it. Otherwise you aren't missing much.

I can safely say that Lisa is personally the best game from 2014, and now one of my most favorite games of all time! Thank you so much Austin for such a fantasic experience!
From what I understand, besides the music, this game was made by one man; not a big deal to many people these days. "Sure many indie games are made by just a couple of people, big whoop", you may say. Of course the man himself who made this game, Austin Jorgensen, didn't just make a game; he made a truly emotional story, one which I feel surpasses the average indie game, let along RPG Maker game!
For a basic rundown of the plot, you are Brad Armstrong, a former Martial Artist Instructor who lives in a post-apocalyptic world where all the woman of the Earth had mysteriously vanished... Except for one; your daughter Buddy, whom you found one day and raised as your own. I don't want to spoil anymore for anyone who hasn't played it yet but the story after this point divulges in an incredible way that can only truly be appreciated first-hand. This game will give you a laugh from its quirky/dark-humor, references and cameos then beat you down for every choice you make, then leave you in tears at its dramatic and sad plotline.
The game's combat system and art is very reminiscent to Earthbound, to which the Developer admited was indeed a source of inspiration for some of the game's aspects, which means if you liked the style of Earthbound you'll definately find this a choice game to play. The 2D Platform style seems very unique compared to Earthbound and other RPG Maker Games, but that's just my personal opinion.
There are over 30 party members to choose from in this fantasic game, each of whom with there own special skill sets and stats. There are many points in the game in which you have to make very difficult choices or gambles that can involve these characters and permantly affect the environment and yourself, but leaving no truly "good" choice.
The music of LISA is very nostalgic, again reminiscent of Earthbound, but completely original and fantasic to listen to. I have never gotten tired of hearing the amazing soundtrack, and even bought the DLC Soundtrack and Art Collection (Which you should totally get if you enjoyed it as much as I did)!
I only encountered a few glitches in LISA, but nothing game-ruining or even worth mentioning (especially since they occured in spoiler territory). I feel it is a very well polished game and very enjoyable throughout though I only have two issues. First off is that it could have included more random encounters or events after returning to an older area since they were usually a bit more monotonous, but it didn't take away from any gameplay. Secondly is that I was a little disapointed to not be able to play buddy as the strech goal for the original Kickstarter Program had suggested, but I feel that there are multiple reasons as to why it didn't come to pass and agian it did not take away from any gameplay at all.
All in all this is definitely an amzing game full of tounge-in-cheek humor and very strong emotional moments and I would suggest it for anyone who has ten dollars and an eagerness to feel the best kind of painful experience! 10/10, will play again and again and again!

The gameplay is good, and you can easily tell the difference between a good commander and a bad commander.
The balance is fine, and each army provides clear strengths and weaknesses, some moreso than others. The decisiveness of weapons in the game feels impactful, and I take my hat off to the brains behind the creation of Ardennes Assault.
If on multiplayer you are looking for each army's strategy
-Russia:These guys are literally the essence of Starcraft 2's zerg. Overwhelm with massive numbers, hit them with cheap units and keep sending more than your opponent keep up with. No one out-produces the bear that is Russia.
-Wermacht: Similar to the russian playstyle, but has more quality units, and is pretty good with dig-in tactics. A jack of all trades.
-Oberkommando West: My personal favorite military. Your base is mobile, your troops are all quality, but costly to produce. They even have higher veterancy, so the longer an OKW player survives with squads, the harder they become to kill.
-U.S. Forces: Hit 'em hard and Hit 'em fast. Their infantry is the best, barring the OKW infantry, they adapt and try to use their versatility to take over the early game and counter their opponent's movements.
-Brits: Honestly, I havent had too much experience with the brits overall, but they dig in like ticks, and can't be moved, good for establishing a line and slowly pushing forward.
The gameplay is good. The game company is♥♥♥♥♥♥ Bugs in Ardennes Assault were recently fixed, so my thumbs up was finally earned.
If you were expecting something completely different from CoH 1, I don't really know what to say. A lot of the barebones ideas were still intact, and its still got that same feel to it. Is that a bad thing?

Story
Paul Prospero, a calculating detective attuned to his senses and surroundings, arrives in Red Creek Valley after receiving news of a missing boy named Ethan. With a supernatural ability capable of digging up events from the past, you must shed light on dark happenings and piece together a chain of murders in your quest for answers, but most importantly, Ethan Carter.
Gameplay
Vanishing plays like a minimalistic walking simulator, no HUD, no inventory management, no menu for reading past discovered letters or journal entries. Environment interaction is limited solely to what is relevant to the case (with the exception of a few puzzle solving instances) your building and learning about the troubling past of the Carter family.
During your search for Ethan you will come upon gruesome murder scenes, which you can dive into after you’ve discovered all the evidence in it’s surrounding area. Then, using Prospero’s supernatural abilities, murder scenes come to life with holographic like figures frozen in time, it’s up to you to number them in chronological order based on your findings and instinct. If successful, they come to life and play like an eerie reenactment before your eyes, if out of order, you’re reverted back into Paul’s shoes to correct your mistake. These scenes are clever and enjoyable to uncover, keeping you in your seat for longer, however the empty gaps in-between playing lost hiker and supernatural detective leave more to be desired.
The puzzles along the way are difficult enough to keep you from rolling your eyes at their simplicity but not too challenging where they’d induce frustration. Vanishing is prefaced with the notion that the game does not hold your hand, which is both a valid statement and an arguable idea. Yes, you have a great deal of freedom as you roam Red Creek Valley for clues. Red Creek teases the idea of open world, boasting it’s vast size, however a great deal is filler with little to no reason. And arguable in the sense that, while hidden, every relevant object bears a large word or instruction overhead once in their proximity. All in all, the game takes a hands off approach that allows for player freedom, but it’s suggestions are not entirely absent.
Sound
Soft and magical music composed by Mikolai Stroinski sets a beautiful tone while you wander Red Creek Valley. Filled with wonder and mystery, it alone boosts the quality of this already enjoyable experience. Prospero’s narration provides insight to his problem-solving process, his feelings, and his genuine thoughts on the events that he’s uncovering. While scarce in dialogue, it only makes each word that much more important. Superb voice acting from all involved. Sound effects only build on the experience, from the wisps of wind flowing through the branches of pine trees, to the dense wall of wind that rushes over the dam. The crackling of a slow burning fire or a slow humming tune of a train car’s engine, everything whispers it’s own identity with fantastic sound.
Graphics
Unbelievable. Not many games can make a forest or house feel like a living breathing thing but Vanishing does just that, masterfully. The kind of graphics you wish every game you play had. The detail put into each surface is astounding, blades of grass hide most of the textured ground floor, pebbles and stone walkways follow no blocky pattern, each rocky surface appears unique, weathered wooden boards layer the houses, and the list goes on. The Vanishing of Ethan Carter flaunts it’s beauty in every direction you look, and every object you examine. Runs smooth throughout the entire experience even with added visual effects. Hands down one of the most beautiful games I’ve played.
Replay Value
Like many mystery narratives, the story builds and builds, relying almost entirely on it’s ending to gauge the overall quality of the complete story. Vanishing is one of those narratives and after your journey through Red Creek Valley is over, there’s really no reason to return.
Wrapping Up
The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a very impressive work of art, both visually and aurally. Offering an interesting story, solid ending, and an extremely fine-tuned gameplay experience that is both satisfying and challenging. I personally found the pacing between walking and detective work rather slow, and it’s concept of “does not hold your hand” odd, however they’re not strong enough to blemish this incredibly polished game.

Sinless is a short point & click adventure game. I finished the game in less than three hours. That includes playing the two minigames for a while in an attempt to get the Steam achievements for them. So I guess the main game takes only about two hours.
In the end, Sinless felt more like an interactive short story than a game, mostly because it was pretty easy to solve and because it felt very linear, even for an adventure game. The story's setting and characters are all weird but in an interesting way. A commendable effort was made to create a unique futuristic world with its own social structure and lore.
The story has an ending of sorts but it leaves more questions than it provided answers. Some people like open endings, others don't, but let's say in this case it's very, very much open-ended. According to a lot of reviews and discussions, a sequel was always supposed to be made to continue the story, which would make sense.
Technically, I had a perfect experience with Sinless (no bugs, no crashes), but one thing I do have to mention: you see a 'loading...' screen for a few seconds every time you go to another screen, which is very often. Sometimes, when you know you need to go to a place that's 5 screens away, you'll be looking at more 'loading...' screens than actual game screens for half a minute. And when you know where you need to go but you don't remember how to get there exactly, you'll feel the urge to grab a guide, just to avoid as much of those pesky 'loading...' screens as possible.
A word about the typical Steam features. Sinless has six trading cards. You'll get three from running the game. The achievements are mostly easily obtained, but:
I hope this helps you decide whether to buy Sinless or not. As for the question '
' that Steam needs answered, I think I have to put it this way: it very much depends on the price. I bought this game for 49 cents (-90%). In that case: yes, I certainly recommend Sinless if you're at all interested in point & click adventure games and/or (weird, dystopian) futuristic fantasy worlds and stories. But at its full price of a fiver? No, I wouldn't recommend it. It's too short and too open-ended to stand out among the dozens of stories/experiences to be found on Steam these days.

Hello to all and the dev! (I know you'll read this eventually since you seem to be following fan feedback very closely from what I've seen :D)
So I saw this game on the Steam front page and I figured "Well hey! It's a free game and judging from the reviews it doesn't take that long to complete!" So I installed and played it.
Is it absolutely amazing? Eh I wouldn't say so. Did I feel that it was worth my time? 100% so and maybe even more than that!
When I walked away from Without Within I felt not the amount of immense triumph and satisfaction that I get from the best games ever made but instead a small warm feeling at the pit of my heart.
I am currently a Master's student in Taiwan (So yes I speak Chinese :D) who is pursuing a degree in digital software, and gaming in general so I have felt more or less the experiences a creative person goes through. It is not uncommon to lose sight that you do what you do simply because you love it. It's unfortunate but it happens.
After playing Without Within though I experienced a nice slice of a relatable experience through Vinty's short little journey. Despite the fact that being supported is every artist's dream one should not forget the reason that you started off: Because you love it. Vinty lost her way for a moment and I'm happy to see that she found it back.
When you love what you do it will show in your work and that will be what gives it its soul.
If I want to be a bit critical I would say that the biggest current problem may be in the pacing of the story. The story tends to jump around an awful lot and scenes don't seem to pan out properly before they go on into the next one. Also many of the endings seem to cause the game to end very abruptly which just leaves me sitting there baffled at what had just transpired. It's seemingly a small problem but one that bogs down the experience from being a much better one. It can be easy to lose sight of pacing as an author of a work so lots and lots of beta testing will definitely help one stamp out errors such as these in the final release!
Even with that being said though I liked the 10 minutes that I spent with this game. So...thank you InvertMouse. Thank you for this short and relatable experience. I wish you the very best of luck in your future endeavors! :D
I will be sure to tell my friends about this game and tell them to go check it out for a nice little 10 minutes!
And for all my fellow gamers who happen to be reading this....the game is free! Go play it and have a nice little 10 minutes :D

Machanically, Mafia II is cover-based shooting at its dullest, framed by a stupidly predictable storyline. Worse still, probably half of the game is entirely redundant: theoretically, you can drive around town like it's a sandbox game, but there is no reason whatsoever to do so. Game developers need to understand that not every game that takes place in a big city needs to be a sandbox. More to the point, pretty much every mission forces you to drive from home to whoever you happen to be working for at the time, then drive them to where a given task takes place, drive to a safehouse to drop off your mate, then drive home through the lifeless town. They are nothing but unnecessarily interactive cutscenes.
Mafia II is not a bad game, strictly speaking. It's just not good either.

Ok, so I will begin by commenting on the story, it is great. If it was a movie, it would have probably fared well, you know with all those gun fights and Mafia meetings and going to prison and such. It is not so much a sandbox game, it is more of a shooter game, I know because when I played, all of the difficulty of the game rests on the gunfights and covering system, and even some stealth. The "sandbox" aspect of the game is where you have to drive to every objective, they are long drives, and sometimes when you miss an exit, you have to circle all the way back again and drive for another 2-3minutes, you can buy clothes and guns, and that's about it, oh and take care not to speed or else the cops will be at your tail fast. Also there are plenty of fist fights, where you push the right buttons and you win. The graphics though are really novel and crisp. Even at low res, this game looks amazing and sharp and performs extremely well. This is in fact your standard third person shooter, and if your good at shooters, than this game is for you. As far as "freedom" and "sandbox" go, there is not very much to it, I might compare it to Prototype without all the optional side missions. Anyway story is good, gun and fist fights are good, just needed a little bit more development in the "sandbox" aspect of it.

Most people love the first game. It was original, brutally mature, and insanely addictive.
In this game, you start as a soldier in WW2 where you see some intense "Brothers in Arms" action.
Next, the game brings you back to the States in February, 1945 - and I won't spoil the storyline any further.
The game doesn't throw you into driving right away. you actually get to enjoy the view of the city.
The cut scenes are interesting to watch to say the least. I like GTA games, but I don't remember being able to sit through a single cut scene, it just never stuck with me. However, in Mafia 2 as well as Red Dead Redemption, you DO want to watch the cut scenes. Read Dead for instance, was filled with some good, albeit heavy well-thought out secular life philosophy. That isn't exactly the case in this game, this IS a gangster game after all. However, it IS impressive how they managed to keep the story strong without resorting to the well-known cliches that are associated with Italian gangsters, plus there is some good vulgarity, nudity, adult magazines and great original one-liners.
The attention to detail is simply outstanding. I wouldn't be surprised if the developers hadn't taken their time to create every shelf, every book and every street corner for that matter, with the utmost care to detail. The NPC models are numerous and if you dont scrutinize the NPCs too much, you just wont often find same NPCs, just let the game flow over you. The interior designs are amazing too look at and the icy roads are a b1tch to drive on.
Having played the demo, and getting my first glimpse at the map, I was disappointed. It is small in comparison to Just Cause 2 and Red Dead, which is still a bit of a turn off for me. HOWEVER, the major point is how they managed to utilize the city to its fullest potential. Meaning, the miscellaneous stores and buildings often have an interior with and without people that you can see, which only adds to the sheer depth of the city. You actually get a feel that you are standing next to an apartment building filled with people. In GTA series, buildings were but lifeless texture blocks. Also, there are plenty of missions that take place inside buildings. One of them, involving a safe, will put a long smile on your face as you listen to the conversation between the two security guards. The shootouts are okay, the usual shoot -take cover type of action. The funny thing is that whilst completing the shooting missions, I found myself wasting time by observing the details of furniture and other objects which are greatly polished.
Its also fun to see the well-familiar WW2 American propaganda posters. Remember, the walls have ears... There are plenty of artifacts in the game indicating your 1940's era. Babe Ruth's posters, movie posters and what not.
Some random conversations in the game are outright genius. "Extra! extra! I am freezing my ball$ out here..." or "Spending nights with Rosy Palm and her five sisters" are just a few of them.
The radio broadcast gives an incredible insight into how people talked and thought. The then-live broadcast of WW2 events and battles is interesting enough for you to stand and listen, getting more and more immersed in the game.
I also wouldn't mean hearing some original Italian Language with English subtitles. That is how I played Assassin's Creed II actually.
The lock pick system is reminiscent of the Watchmen game, but it is MUCH easier to handle
Another cool thing is that you can pimp your ride, AND you can customize your plates. Go vulgarity!
Also, for those of you still yearning for the good old days of the first game, tune in Empire Radio whilst driving and feel yourself get a decade younger for a moment.
The Brooklyn Bridge replica is impeccable. I ride the Brooklyn Bridge on my bike quite a few times every summer, and let me tell you, the game nailed it the bridge where GTA 4 failed. Enough said. Also, there is a nice replica of the Brooklyn-Bridge Expressway as you take the right exit off of the Brooklyn Bridge - on the Brooklyn Side.
The docs are also in the right place.
The fist fighting is reminiscent of the Bourne Supremacy game, plus there are some cool easy-to-pull of combo moves
The cut scenes actually retain the car damage that you may have sustained completing a mission
The BAD:
The lip sync is not exactly top notch, in fact its bad.
You can tell they just had the characters flapping their pie holes whilst adding the relative dialogue. I guess only Bioware can pull a well-made lip sync, among other companies.
I also think that the main character could use a bit more charisma and inner thoughts just like Tommy in the first game.
Another thing is that after a couple of hours of playing, you find that there isn't really much to do in the city besides enjoying the scenery, driving and going to bars. But, I guess that's why the developers tried to push the game into linear play in an open-world map.
But it's all good. The city itself is a part of the story and while you don't get to visit every corner in the city during the story line it is sitll nice to know that you can explore this very polished world.  It is sad that the game's engine hasn't been used since in many other game, it really has a lot of potential.

Mafia II does a few things right, but it's more of a driving simlator than a game, and is ultimately boring as hell. Here's a quick breakdown of what you'll be doing: cutscene, drive, cutscene, drive, shootout, cutscene, drive, drive, cutscene, drive. It seems all you do in this game is drive from cutscene to cutscene, which wouldn't be bad if the story was compelling in the least, but it wasn't. I didn't give two ♥♥♥♥♥ about Vito or any part of his life, which is a shame, because the voice work, atmosphere, and look of the game are incredible. They did do a couple neat things, though, and as you'd guess, they all revolving around driving. You can run out of gas, get pulled over for speeding, take health damage (and possibly die) if you get in a bad enough accident.. all things that make sense and bring another level of realism to virtual driving. However, this is all squandered once you realize the police in this game are absolutely useless. Got caught speeding or running over a civi? Stop your car, wait for the police to get out of theirs, then take off. That's all it takes to ditch the cops. And there goes all the tension of running out of gas during a high speed chase. Or worrying about trying to drive under the speed limit. Because it doesn't matter. The cops may as well not even be there.
ALSO. If you're an achievement ♥♥♥♥♥, beware. There are three separate collectible achieves in this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. THREE. Collect all 50 Playboys, drive 30 of 36 cars, and find 150 wanted posters. That's nearly 250 different things to find. Whack. Totally and utterly whack. And this whackness doesn't even factor in the DLC achieve which involves driving 1k miles- an estimated 10 hours of time.
Boring game, punctuated by horrible achieves. Save your money. Buy something else.

Dying Light is a game about avoidance, or at least that's how it's presented. There are zombies, but they can't climb very well. To avoid them, you're going to learn to be an expert at parkour, but don't expect Titanfall / Mirror's Edge wallrunning here. Climbing, jumping, and running are your entire arsenal.
In the resource-starved city of Harran, guns are hard to come by, and ammo is scarce. If you want something reliable for dealing with the zombies, you need to find a melee weapon. Luckily, debris is plentiful, and improvised weapons, like pieces of pipe or lumber, can be found without much trouble. You'll also get help finding gear from the allies you make in town. Most importantly, you can drop kick the zombies. Yes, you can drop kick them into all sorts of hazards, whether it's off the side of a building, into spikes, or into whatever deadly debris is lying nearby. The drop kick is your most potent ally for keeping zombies at arm's length, and you'll use it a ton.
Unfortunately, any weapon you find will start to break down as soon as you begin using it. This is one of the more frustrating parts of the game, as that metal pipe you just grabbed disintegrates after two hits, leaving you with nothing in hand to deal with the now-agitated enemy. You can improve durability as you progress through the game, but the unpredictability of it is definitely a turn-off. Even worse is the stamina meter. Especially early in the game, you get only a few swings with your weapon before you're too winded to fight. It makes little to no sense when your "special-ops guy who just parachuted alone into a zombie-infested city" character is too winded to fight back against the undead monster in your face, and it definitely breaks down the character and the narrative when it happens.

If parcour and zombie slashing seem like great hobbies, look no further. Dying Light is the kind of game that combines a well-detailed and thought-out zombie apocalypse with parcour, giving the ability to climb out of reach from some zombies, but you become a great target for others. I'd say this makes Dying Light one of the most dynamic sandbox-with-story games out there.
The magic of the game is that once you played the opening missions you get the freedom to do whatever. You can dive into the main story and into the zombie gore, or you can build some skills and get decent weapons by doing side-missions first. Most situations can be handled at your own discretion. You can either remove all undead obstacles from your path, or run past them of you feel like it. The first option is generally more fun, but the second can be a necessary option if there is more zombie than weapon in your direct area. You can parcour over the rooftops to avoid the horde, or you can smash your way through. Several skill-trees can grant you skills which can really help achieve your playing style.
The story of the main game is not that original, but it is very well executed and I would still recommend it for the story. In the DLC 'The Following' the story is something else which at times was really nice, but at times would seem slow. The boss fight on the other hand is, depending on your choices, amazing. The continuation of some of the sub-plots of minor characters was really nice. It is very much recommended to play the main game before you start the DLC, both in terms of story and experience.
There are also many side-missions ranging from fetching some items to destroying enemy bases. Because of the way the game plays it's never boring. At the worst it's just killing zombies with some extra steps, and at the best they give you proper challenges and nice side-stories.
All the missions, challenges, skill-trees and other activities give a lot of things to do. I'm 59 hours in according to Steam, and only just finished the main and side quests and most of the basic skill trees. Turns out, (minor spoiler on game mechanic) there are even more skills to unlock and improve on, and many more objects and challenges to complete.
I'm definitely going to need another 50 hours at least to get most things done. In terms of value per hour played this game is a bargain. And I haven't even touched the multiplayer yet.

This is a tower defense/RPG hybrid where your towers and home base are all characters that level up between battles, giving you points to spend on stats and extra abilities. No tower mazing is involved, and there are enemies that can attack your towers, necessitating armor, dodge, and healing abilities in addition to strong damage output, slowing attacks, buffs, debuffs, and knockback. Defender's Quest succeeds in blending tower defense and RPG gameplay thanks to strong design on many levels.
pros:
+ core gameplay is fun -- character and enemy design are good and placing/upgrading your characters always feels strategic
+ excellent balance and tuning with multiple difficulty settings
+ the interface is intuitive and well-designed

Thank you, Dingaling/Jason, for this piece of soul-crushing art. It deserves lots of attention.

Pop culture has an obsession with being “edgy,” whether it be through grittiness, hyperviolence, or manipulative melodrama. “Edgy,” as a term for describing somehow-exciting and somehow-different new art, has seemingly been drained of any positive connotations. It has become a word that’s to be used exclusively with a sarcastic tone, mocking the tryhards that would use it unironically to describe their supposedly daring and incisive new thing.
So what is
? A game with the unofficial subtitle of “The Painful RPG,” that touts a post-apocalyptic setting defined by amorality and violence, that features amputation and drug addiction as game mechanics—it’s edgy, certainly. But
is an effective reminder that “edgy” doesn’t always have to be said with an eyeroll and a scoff. Developer Dingaling has put in the effort to present a game that varies wildly in tone and charms, that does all it can to dodge the fatal one-note nature of so many other games that have tried and failed to claim edginess.
is a Venn diagram of “disturbing” and “silly” with a surprising amount of overlap, making its tangents purely into either side all the more effective.

If on multiplayer you are looking for each army's strategy
-Russia:These guys are literally the essence of Starcraft 2's zerg. Overwhelm with massive numbers, hit them with cheap units and keep sending more than your opponent keep up with. No one out-produces the bear that is Russia.
-Wermacht: Similar to the russian playstyle, but has more quality units, and is pretty good with dig-in tactics. A jack of all trades.
-Oberkommando West: My personal favorite military. Your base is mobile, your troops are all quality, but costly to produce. They even have higher veterancy, so the longer an OKW player survives with squads, the harder they become to kill.
-U.S. Forces: Hit 'em hard and Hit 'em fast. Their infantry is the best, barring the OKW infantry, they adapt and try to use their versatility to take over the early game and counter their opponent's movements.
-Brits: Honestly, I havent had too much experience with the brits overall, but they dig in like ticks, and can't be moved, good for establishing a line and slowly pushing forward.

I think it's a bit unfair to call this, as others have, a walking simulator given how that term connotes an experience where there is just a lot of walking and very little game to enjoy. Ethan Carter has plenty of walking for sure, but there are some substantial game elements here as well, which means exploring the open world feels purposeful and worthwhile.
Design-wise, it's intelligently thought through: you are given clue scraps that are vague enough to sustain mystery, but directive enough to help push you through the relatively small, but beautiful open world without meandering aimlessly for long. The gameplay element consists mainly of "mini-games" whose end goal is to make sense of the various goings-on.
Ethan Carter impressed me in terms of its polish, graphics and considered approach to story-telling. Visuals are superb: the landscapes are like paintings and the level of detail on everyday objects found throughout the game is very impressive.The only let down are the character models: they are excellent, but being "cartoony", they don't seem to fit well with the photo-like world they inhabit. Music and sound are evocative and create a suitably creepy atmosphere, working well with the visual style.
The story itself is dark and enjoyable; however, I found the script and voice-acting a little weak which detracted from the potential impact the game could have made emotionally. Although I sympathesized with Ethan, I was never too invested in him or his plight.
The thing I most dislike is scouring the landscape for small objects scattered randomly about. It's just a tedious process. Given this is a major part of the game this is a big reason why I like rather than love this game.
Overall, The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is excellent. I'm a fan of developers who try to do something a bit creative with their game design, and this indie game is polished to AAA standards.

My review so far on the game Dying Light.
Bought the game on the 24th, 32 hours played already.
+ Combat
It's pretty cool dude. You can spin around with axes and hammers, slice and dice some zombies with your machete, blow some head with your guns, bows and crossbows.
+ Movement
You can climb pretty much anything. Be it cars, towers and buildings. And im not talking about some random ladder you find, no, window bars, ledges, lightpoles, ziplines, you can even go mario mode and jump from a zombies head.
+ Enviroment
At day, you are the hunter, you smash through undead with breeze, be as loud as you want because some weak runners will only be your ''danger''. And then nighttime arrives.♥♥♥♥♥♥fool i kid you not, you better be in a safe house or your cherry butt will get a new tint. You're blind without a flashlight, volatiles all around you, and you cant be as loud as you want. Unless you are stacked with gear because then nighttime is daytime with a new color.
+/- COOP
It's okay, didnt really use this feature but when i did, i got some polish kid with static mic or a nice guy with the quietest microphone since 1978.
+/- Crafting System
You can craft some cool stuff, be it to electrify your meele weapons, silence your pistols or craft some firecrackers. Nothing special.
+/- Story
The story wasn't bad, it wasn't the greatest either. But it was okay, quite cliche at some points, but otherwise an enjoyable progression.
- Bugs
There aren't many, but once you find one, you will notice it. I used the grappling hook to climb a building, and once i reached the ledge, i fell down  and died from fall damage. Happened about 1 in every 30 grappling hook scenarios. So it wont really ruin your experience unless you were on some tight schedule.
Overall, buy this game, the Enhanced edition is 19.99 euro at the moment because of the christmas sales. It will be worth your time, and you will have a really good time.

Most people love the first game. It was original, brutally mature, and insanely addictive.
In this game, you start as a soldier in WW2 where you see some intense "Brothers in Arms" action.
Next, the game brings you back to the States in February, 1945 - and I won't spoil the storyline any further.
The game doesn't throw you into driving right away. you actually get to enjoy the view of the city.
The cut scenes are interesting to watch to say the least. I like GTA games, but I don't remember being able to sit through a single cut scene, it just never stuck with me. However, in Mafia 2 as well as Red Dead Redemption, you DO want to watch the cut scenes. Read Dead for instance, was filled with some good, albeit heavy well-thought out secular life philosophy. That isn't exactly the case in this game, this IS a gangster game after all. However, it IS impressive how they managed to keep the story strong without resorting to the well-known cliches that are associated with Italian gangsters, plus there is some good vulgarity, nudity, adult magazines and great original one-liners.
The attention to detail is simply outstanding. I wouldn't be surprised if the developers hadn't taken their time to create every shelf, every book and every street corner for that matter, with the utmost care to detail. The NPC models are numerous and if you dont scrutinize the NPCs too much, you just wont often find same NPCs, just let the game flow over you. The interior designs are amazing too look at and the icy roads are a b1tch to drive on.
Having played the demo, and getting my first glimpse at the map, I was disappointed. It is small in comparison to Just Cause 2 and Red Dead, which is still a bit of a turn off for me. HOWEVER, the major point is how they managed to utilize the city to its fullest potential. Meaning, the miscellaneous stores and buildings often have an interior with and without people that you can see, which only adds to the sheer depth of the city. You actually get a feel that you are standing next to an apartment building filled with people. In GTA series, buildings were but lifeless texture blocks. Also, there are plenty of missions that take place inside buildings. One of them, involving a safe, will put a long smile on your face as you listen to the conversation between the two security guards. The shootouts are okay, the usual shoot -take cover type of action. The funny thing is that whilst completing the shooting missions, I found myself wasting time by observing the details of furniture and other objects which are greatly polished.
Its also fun to see the well-familiar WW2 American propaganda posters. Remember, the walls have ears... There are plenty of artifacts in the game indicating your 1940's era. Babe Ruth's posters, movie posters and what not.
Some random conversations in the game are outright genius. "Extra! extra! I am freezing my ball$ out here..." or "Spending nights with Rosy Palm and her five sisters" are just a few of them.
The radio broadcast gives an incredible insight into how people talked and thought. The then-live broadcast of WW2 events and battles is interesting enough for you to stand and listen, getting more and more immersed in the game.
I also wouldn't mean hearing some original Italian Language with English subtitles. That is how I played Assassin's Creed II actually.
The lock pick system is reminiscent of the Watchmen game, but it is MUCH easier to handle
Another cool thing is that you can pimp your ride, AND you can customize your plates. Go vulgarity!
Also, for those of you still yearning for the good old days of the first game, tune in Empire Radio whilst driving and feel yourself get a decade younger for a moment.
The Brooklyn Bridge replica is impeccable. I ride the Brooklyn Bridge on my bike quite a few times every summer, and let me tell you, the game nailed it the bridge where GTA 4 failed. Enough said. Also, there is a nice replica of the Brooklyn-Bridge Expressway as you take the right exit off of the Brooklyn Bridge - on the Brooklyn Side.
The docs are also in the right place.
The fist fighting is reminiscent of the Bourne Supremacy game, plus there are some cool easy-to-pull of combo moves
The cut scenes actually retain the car damage that you may have sustained completing a mission
The BAD:
The lip sync is not exactly top notch, in fact its bad.
You can tell they just had the characters flapping their pie holes whilst adding the relative dialogue. I guess only Bioware can pull a well-made lip sync, among other companies.
I also think that the main character could use a bit more charisma and inner thoughts just like Tommy in the first game.
Another thing is that after a couple of hours of playing, you find that there isn't really much to do in the city besides enjoying the scenery, driving and going to bars. But, I guess that's why the developers tried to push the game into linear play in an open-world map.
But it's all good. The city itself is a part of the story and while you don't get to visit every corner in the city during the story line it is sitll nice to know that you can explore this very polished world.  It is sad that the game's engine hasn't been used since in many other game, it really has a lot of potential.

Mafia II does a few things right, but it's more of a driving simlator than a game, and is ultimately boring as hell. Here's a quick breakdown of what you'll be doing: cutscene, drive, cutscene, drive, shootout, cutscene, drive, drive, cutscene, drive. It seems all you do in this game is drive from cutscene to cutscene, which wouldn't be bad if the story was compelling in the least, but it wasn't. I didn't give two ♥♥♥♥♥ about Vito or any part of his life, which is a shame, because the voice work, atmosphere, and look of the game are incredible. They did do a couple neat things, though, and as you'd guess, they all revolving around driving. You can run out of gas, get pulled over for speeding, take health damage (and possibly die) if you get in a bad enough accident.. all things that make sense and bring another level of realism to virtual driving. However, this is all squandered once you realize the police in this game are absolutely useless. Got caught speeding or running over a civi? Stop your car, wait for the police to get out of theirs, then take off. That's all it takes to ditch the cops. And there goes all the tension of running out of gas during a high speed chase. Or worrying about trying to drive under the speed limit. Because it doesn't matter. The cops may as well not even be there.
ALSO. If you're an achievement ♥♥♥♥♥, beware. There are three separate collectible achieves in this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. THREE. Collect all 50 Playboys, drive 30 of 36 cars, and find 150 wanted posters. That's nearly 250 different things to find. Whack. Totally and utterly whack. And this whackness doesn't even factor in the DLC achieve which involves driving 1k miles- an estimated 10 hours of time.
Boring game, punctuated by horrible achieves. Save your money. Buy something else.

Don't let the trailer's lack of action decieve you. This game is full of adventure and extremely challenging parkour. If you haven't realized it already, your main gameplay consists of grappling from one object to another to make it to an objective. You'll have to fly through beautiful fantasy lands and breathtaking visuals and swing your way into finding your uncle, who's been missing for almost half a year, trapped in this strange world. But the catch is that your grappling hook only has up to 3 uses while you're airborne, making every tether, swing, and inertia count. You'll also be able to super-jump, either if there's a high object or if there's an platform a ways away from you. As well, you'll eventually aquire rocket boots, which only gives more of a challenge to a puzzle. There are 5 collectables per level that are hidden in really hard to reach places, and some that are merely blind to the focused eye required for the game's parkour, which becomes extremely difficult as you progress. However the difficulty doesn't swing from peaceful to intense like some other games, so you'll be wearly of what may lie ahead of a challenge. Some parts of the game had me boiled from rage, and some parts were easy to accomplish as it focused more on the jaw-dropping scenery.
However there is only one factor that I feel to seem that lots of players will dislike about this game. As you probably already saw, my time for playing this game is only 4.3 hours. Minus .3 hours for control setup, and you've got yourself a 4 hour game. This game is very short, and seems like the developers rushed the ending, and I was surprised that the ending of the game was just where I thought its falling-action would seem to start to kick in. Immediately after an agonizingly difficult parkour session, you're thrown into the game's ending and credits roll. That's the only concern you should have before purchasing this game, and it is a big one for most consumers.
All in all, I feel like most players will see that this game isn't worth its price for its very small amount of gameplay, but I believe that the game's visuals, scenery and landscape, parkour, challenge, and small story will all make up for the player's demand for more. But if you don't mind short stories and gameplay, then this game is definitely for you.

is a visually stunning first person, swing-type platformer where you as the protagonist must journey through an unknown world to find your uncle. This strange world is inhabited by these equally as strange anthopromorphic frog people, but only like four of them talk and only one is actually important.
Now before you read the rest of the review, keep in mind that I really liked this game, it's just much easier for me to critisize than praise. Also ****Warning: There's going to be SPOILERS, especially near the end of the review.****
So first things first, this game is absolutely beautiful. The bright starry skies and glowing crystals and floating islands in general make this game very appealing to look at as you travel from place to place. The atmosphere that each location portays is pretty spot on, with the warm, bright yellows in the village and the dark, cold blues in the caves. I never got used to the scenery, every place I went I was astounded by the colors and expansiveness of the world, even in the ice caves where all the walls and platforms mixed in blues and blacks, the glowing crystals just made everything so alive.
Second, the frog people. They're not inceredibly appealing to look at, but it's to be expected, since, you know, they're frogs. I wish there could have been a lot more interaction with them, because it would have be really cool to hear their accounts of their lives in the caves or maybe how they came to know your uncle, to give him a little more characterization, but I suppose they weren't really the main point of the story. The first person you meet in a young frog girl named Madeline, though people always call her "Mad Maddie" (I actually have no idea why that is, even after finishing the game), who seems to be very close to your uncle, saying she's "known him all her life" even though he's only been gone for a couple of months. She's your generic 'I don't wanna stay in my hometown cause it's boring but no one will let me explore cause it's dangerous' character. I hated her, mostly cause she was annoying to me and follows you around for the half the game, but she's not actually that bad. Just a little underdeveloped, like a lot of other things.
Now, ASAMU is supposed to be praised for it's story, but I honestly see it more for the puzzles and visuals.; the story is actually pretty lackluster. And the ending, wow, I did not like the ending. So you fly and fall your way all the way through the crazy, difficult-to-navigate, challenging world, dying about 300 times, just for your uncle to tell you he's staying there and he's going to send you home. Honestly, it's so plain and badly planned, I would compare it to the ending of Firewatch. But, unlike Firewatch, this ending more or less to be expected, since nothing was ever built up throughout the game. You just travelled from place to place to find out that your uncle had gone somewhere else.
There's a lot of mysteries and questions that go unanswered in this game. Like, what's the point of the weird symbol language? And what was with that weird fish monster thing? And why was there a dead whale on the floor of the ice caves?!? Based on the pen and paper role playing game of the same title name, Bloodlines tells the tale of various breeds of vampire living in the world of humans, trying to uphold the Masquerade that they're just normal everyday humans... Which means fit in, or they're going to be sending the disciplinary squad after you!
The game opens up as pretty much a turf war, and later descends into an end of the world prophecy story. Your progression from lowest rung on the ladder to working for the big cheese/being responsible for the fate of the world is jarringly fast...
I did have to use a patch to get the game to work on Windows 7, even through Steam (which seems crazy that the game "as it comes" doesn't boot), so its hard to say how much was the original game and how much had been modified...
But in the form I played it the game still looks pretty damn good aesthetically and the voice acting holds up, adding a lot to the memorable cast of friends and foes.
The early game missions are easily the best bits the game has to offer, the later ones feeling like an unnecessary dragging out of the game, especially with the number of "dungeons" that are incredibly dull to walk around. They're also where most the roleplaying goes out the window and it's just straight up combat.
This was the most disappointing part for me, I chose the "cop" backstory, and felt I was going to try and stick to that, putting my "level up" tokens into boosting my deductive or intimidation skills, putting very little into fighting... This left me at quite the disadvantage in the late game, leading to a lot of dying, reloading, and subsequently, frustration. The worst part is that the game colour codes dialogue options to let you know "you have this options because of your observation skill" for example... But there aren't many situations where these come up and when they do, they only have minor changes to the outcome, sometimes none.
In addition to this, I found the powers you unlock as a vampire ultimately kinda sucked, though they may be different for each faction (I only played as Gangrel). I could summon birds to fly around and distract a character, but in combat, the moment I got close the spell would cease and they'd return to slapping me around. There are stealth sections, but only if you choose to treat them as such (there's no real penalty for just slaughtering everyone except some angry dialogue from the boss), and really they're not difficult to get through without utilising powers. Ultimately the heal spell was the only boon I seemed to get from being a vampire.
Fortunately despite this, there's a whole load of vampire related side content that really helps flesh out the world in ways the main plot fails to deliver on. In mean this in the sense that outside the main players, the other kindred are just generic cannon fodder in the same way they are in any game, other than being more grotesque character models, and perhaps some pouncing attacks, the fact they're vampires themselves is kind of forgettable. Other than it taking place in a kind of seedy, shadowy underside to the city, the kinds of tasks you end up doing feel incredibly generic and fail to take advantage of the fantastical setting. The side quests however are generally more personal tales of the vampires dealing with their day to day business that humans don't have to deal with, or at least if they do, this is a more messed up take on those activities.
Though it has to be said, despite my personal disappointment with the aspects the later game decides to focus on, there is some gold in the main story, including dealing with vampire hunters, a really messed up torture sequence, snuff films, a haunted house... When the game dabbles in the more mystical side, it's absolutely fantastic to play through.
This is an incredibly story focused game. If you're not interested in that and seeking out side quests, really you're not going to get anything from this game, the combat is weak and the dungeons being not all that interesting to fight through compounds that problem. But if you're willing to forgo the annoyance of some substandard fighting mechanics, you'll find some incredibly well done story beats, some of which are pretty unique to this game.

Marrying two uniquely intricate genres of games, RPG and Tower Defense, Defender's Quest: Valley of the Forgotten displays a very well-balanced gameplay and an incredibly enticing combat system. Essentially placing stationary combatants that may be bestowed special abilities (your Towers) by investing numerical value of "Psi" into them, on a grid-like environment overlay, coming in a variety of different classes, unlocking new classes as you progress the main storyline. Each class a page out of a classic RPG history book, they each carry their own bevy of abilities based on the type (Berzerker, Archer, etc.) that will bolster your defenses either for the better or worse depending on placement and Psi investment. Characters may earn EXP by being used in battle, growing levels as the criteria becomes met and allowing the player to invest skill points into a basic (yet vital) skill tree.
The overall feel of this game is very old-school, but executes sleekly by today's standards. The World Map (level select screen) features a beautiful score, quite reminiscent of early RPG soundtracks. Interestingly enough, the site for Defender's Quest 2 claims to have musical talent brought forth from none other than Nobuo Uematsu himself. One of the millions (billions?) of Final Fantasy players and avid enjoyers of their dynamic, emotionally-captivating soundtracks, this notion that an industry veteran so well known is working with an indie developer brings me hope for the future generations of gaming. Imagine the experience this renowned professional can impart upon this team, and how this team may in turn inspire Nobou Uematsu, thusly conceiving the music that highlights some of gaming's most touching and well-loved moments. Relationships like these in the game industry are vital for its continuation as the younger generations may offer fresh ideas while in turn being nurtured by the experience and wisdom of seasoned developers having been in the industry since its near-conception (decades, folks!). I sincerely hope that veteran talent continues to  reach out to budding indie developers like Level Up Labs who clearly have a passion for delivering a lasting entertainment experience that is indeed inspiring to all.

I tried to play this game years ago and abandoned it after a short time due to the amount of bugs rendering it unplayable. After rediscovering the game a far corner of my steam library, I decided to give it another go.
Io and behold! By now, a very active community of enthusiasts has fixed 99% of these problems with their unofficial patches. And the game is an absolute gem. Brilliant writing, memorable characters, dialogues and settings. I Recommend it wholeheartedly. Where else can you play a batshit crazy vampire who ventures to have a conversation with a stop sign?
While the story is quite linear, it provides reason to replay it because the different clans of vampires provide very unique game experiences: Some, like Toreador and Ventrue, will be able to talk themselves out of most situations. The Nosferatu look like the monsters they are and will cause a panic the moment a mortal sees them, which leads to a focus on sneaking and exploring the sewers of the city. The Brujah are combat experts, inviting a hack'n'slash melee-fest. Others, like the Tremere, focus on magic.
And then there's the Malkavians, a strand of vampires who's very blood causes insanity, leading to some of the craziest dialogues in video game history. They can (temporarily?) cause insanity in others - who wouldn't want to make their annoying ex think you're their long lost pet turtle? It also allows them a near prophetic insight into their conversation partners' thoughts and motives - That is, if you listen to the right voices n your head and ignore the others...

It's a free game, so I shouldn't be expecting too much, but I would have appreciated a bit more effort being put into this game.
My main problem with this game is that it seems to be trying to mimic older games.  Maybe.  Unfortunately, YHTWTG manages to fail at trying to provide a *good* retro experience.  The game can be frustrating, borderline cheap at times, and while I have no problem with difficult games, I like games to be fair as well.  There's also virtually no soundtrack, which just makes the game boring to go through.  Coupled with the game's frustrating difficulty spikes, this severly hampered my enjoyment with YHTWTG.  There's also the lack of a map, or really, just any direction.
We're not in the 80s anymore; people shouldn't be making games like this.
This game is obviously very "inspired" by VVVVVV, with all the spikes, the high difficulty/low playtime, and every room being named.  VVVVVV did things right; it had hard, but fair gameplay, it wasn't confusing, and it actually had a soundtrack (and a damn good one at that).  So, in summary, YHTWTG tries to be VVVVVV, but ends up being the opposite, much to my dismay.
It wasn't a totally negative experience, but I wouldn't recommend the game, even though it's free.
Edit: Oh, and how could I forget?  Another thing about the soundtrack is that the trailer for the game on Steam has music playing, but like I've said, there's barely any music in the game.  I find that to be somewhat misleading, honestly, and it's a shame that there's little music, as the tune for the trailer is actually not half bad.

Sinless is a flawed but enjoyable game. If anyone remembers the old Cryo Interactive adventure Dune, this game has a very similar feel to it. You move from static screen to static screen, engage in dialog and occasionally look at objects or scenery. Much like Dune, both the graphics and music are absolutely terrific. The art direction really lifts this game up; the stylized cyberpunk vibe is fabulously well-realized. On the down side: i don't mind the familiar plot, but the dialog is a big problem - the characters lack depth and personality, and do too much exposition. And, well, the pixel hunting is painful. There aren't many puzzles in the game, but you will spend a lot of time mousing over everything just trying to find out where the exits are. If it wasn't so beautiful, i would probably give it a thumbs down, but the aesthetic is right on the money, so if you're a fan of cyberpunk i'd definitely recommend giving this a look.

This is my third edit of a Review of this game .. and while I can't fault the gameplay nor the content ..  both are good .. there is one fatal flaw this game exists with .. and that is the Save Game feature.
Like many games this one Auto-Saves and does not allow the player to manually save.
The glaring problem with this is .. you cannot go back to an earlier desired point to recover from a mistake, such as selling a much wanted piece of equipment.
I did this, sold a gun I really liked, went back to the ingame vendor and clicked 'Buy Back' .. and there was nothing to buy back even though I'd only sold the gun a few minutes previously.
The 'Buy Back' feature only exists for the particular session you are interacting with the Vendor.
Once you exit out of that session, the Buy Back feature no longer exists.
Some sort of 'Lock' feature for equipped items would have got round this problem easily.
Even though I have put 'Not Recommended' for this game generally speaking it is a good game .. but, it has some deep flaws which will ensure I do not return to this game after I have completed my first run through.
I know this game is old now and the developers don't give a flying f*ck about it as they've already made their money and moved on.
But, for anyone coming to this game as a new player .. consider .. you may not have much control over the zombie hoards that want to eat your brains .. you have equally as little control over your personal progress if you make a choice and move on from it .. and I'm talking only a few minutes after moving on .. there's no going back.
A single Save File that is constantly over-written as the game Auto-Saves is such a sh*t idea I'd personally like to slap the idiot who thought of it.
___________________________
A new edit ..
If you like games where you have no control over when and how you save .. and if you die you are  respawned without your ammo and wear on your melee weapons being replenished .. but, you have to fight the same creatures OVER and OVER again from that spawn point .. then this is the game for you.

The original Mafia game still rates highly as one of the best games ever. Even six years gone, it still looks beautiful and has a deep, rich setting. Its main weakness was in its gameplay, with some unforgiving missions and little to do with the expansive game-world outside of the intense storyline. In almost every way, Mafia II looks to continue the tradition of its predecessor.
Mafia II is gorgeous. I know graphics are supposed to run second to gameplay but its hard not to get swept up by this game's good looks (especially the nighttime winter levels at the start). The fictional city of Empire Bay is exceptionally well detailed and the cars are unbelievable; Mafia II could almost stand alone just on its driving mechanics, especially if you play in "simulation driving" mode. That there's a strong story mode is just icing on the cake; the missions are well designed and always entertaining, albeit sometimes a bit stingy with the savepoints.
It's true that outside of the main story there isn't too much to do and, unfortunately, the latter will take you 10-15 hours to complete. Compared to the Grand Theft Auto series, there is much less actual game (even more unfortunate, the disc comes with "free-roam" modes installed but disabled unless you purchase some downloadable content; 2K games is nickle-and-diming its fanbase). But what the developers do provide is so rich and exciting that it is hard to fault them for not giving us more, especially when I enjoyed the experience much, much more over that of numerous shorter games. I definitely got my money's worth.

This game is a rouge strategy game, where you are in command of a space ship. Your goal is to flee from the rebels and at the end to destroy the enemy flagship. You are not direct control of steering your ship; rather you jump from planet to planet using "light speed". On each planet, you encounter different aliens and scenarios via text based information, you fight aliens and if you win, you salvage scrap, fuel and drones. You use the scrap for buying new upgrades or weapons for your ship. You are in strategical command of your ship via a control panel and your crew via a grid like overview of your spaceship.
The game is very challenging and unforgiving even in "normal" mode. That is mainly because of the randomness. Although the game gets progressively harder as you come closer to your goal, you may get unlucky because of the randomness. For example, in a scenario you have the choice to help someone on a space station with "giant alien spiders" or do nothing. Here you may make you lose one of your crew or get an additional crewmember if you choose to take the risk. Another example is that you may run out of fuel if you do not find a shop in time.
Secondly, you cannot save. You need a good strategy to survive; if you make a wrong choice early on, it may have detrimental effects for you later. You face different enemies and challenges that have their weaknesses and strengths. It is hard to stay alive and (at least for me) 90 % of the times you will not make it.
