King Arthur's Gold is a wonderfully frantic, visceral little hack&slash.
If you have any experience with games like soldat, or any recent 2d creative games you'll feel right at home here. Controls feel exactly as you would expect them to; responsive and precise, and combined with the ability to wallrun/jump, hookshot, glide/surf on your shield, or just build yourself a ladder you couldn't ask for more mobility.
Combat is simple, yet still has some depth. You have a main attack, a secondary (shield, grappling hook), and an item (bombs). You can attack with quick weak bursts, or charge up for a power attack. Charge slightly longer and your weapon will shimmer, allowing for multiple power attacks in a quick row, beyond that and your attack will fail. It's just enough to add some thought and variety to combat, while still keeping things simple.
The building aspect really enhances the game. Stone deposits can be found throughout the ground by digging, and trees will grow on the surface providing wood. You can build walls, towers, pitfalls, tunnels, spikes, traps, doors, etc anywhere on the map. You can even build siege weapons like catapults.
Each game typically starts with a build phase, where each side of the map is blocked off, providing you time to construct some basic defenses. After that, all bets are off. Items like doorways and spikes react to the proper team, meaning that careful building can really change the flow and control of the map. When those fortifications eventually fall, they do so with full physics, crumbling down and crushing anyone in their way.
It's already worth every penny, and it can only get better.

Magicka is a tough act to follow and while Magicka had those unforgettable multiplayer shenanigans where you accidentally cross beams and kill your entire team, I believe that HELLDIVERS offers the superior multiplayer experience.
Now before I start, let me address the fact that this game HAS to be played multiplayer since that's the only way for you to truly experience the craziness and create memorable moments that you'll be sharing with friends (both old and new) for weeks to come.
GAMEPLAY: The gameplay itself is nothing special, a classic twin-stick shooter which although it was one of those classic arcade genres has been flooded recently with indie games lacking polish and originality (Zombie-themed high score crunching mindless wave-shooter). It is however, still very fun and tries to incorporate unique elements such as the magicka-style quicktime event "special items" known as Stratagems which are very powerful and quite often, deadly to both friend and foe alike. This creates some very dramatic moments where your friend is surrounded by enemies with no hope and all you can do is toss a grenade or fire a rocket launcher, sacrificing your friend in the process so you can hopefully revive them at a later time where they will often have to do the same as soon as they spawn in.
In fact, these dramatic moments ARE the gameplay... Those tense moments where you are a mere 100 kills away from clearing an elimination style mission before realizing your party is out of weapons, out of Stratagems and 3 out of 4 of your revives are still on a 1 minute cooldown. The shuttle arrives just in time and you manage to scurry your way to the safe confines of the ship, your friends however... Not so lucky, you tossed out a revive just before boarding in hopes that they can somehow fight their way through the hordes but to no avail, the ship leaves as you can do nothing but watch helplessly as their corpses are devoured by the bugs below as you scream out to them in chat, tears streaming down your face from a strange mix of laughter and genuine sadness.
COMMUNITY: The community in this game is fantastic as most of the players I have encountered have embraced the ability to troll other players without abusing this power. HELLDIVERS also does a fantastic job of connecting players with an absolutely genius in-game multiplayer UI allowing you to connect to other players without having to open Steam, navigate server lists, port forward etc. It also has an option to send out an SOS signal in the middle of a map allowing people to spawn in and lend a helping hand if a mission is too difficult (again creating dramatic moments where you get wiped out but a player or two spawn in to save the mission).
BALANCE: There are some insanely powerful Stratagems which can seem a bit overpowered at times but with great power, comes great responsibility. You can spawn in a tank which your party of four can commandeer around the map offering a great deal of firepower however there is a massive amount of risk associated with this, namely the fact that if your tank explodes with everyone on board... Well, you know how that goes. There's also airstrikes which can wipe out entire hoardes but often kills your own teammates as collateral. Most Stratagems also have cooldowns which emphasizes tactical usage and have to be picked up to be used which is always complicated since fighting your way through the hordes to get access to your upgrade can be difficult.
The guns all have their place and are standard shooter fare, shotguns, pistols, assault rifles, SMGs and sniper rifles. Each has their own little upgrade tree which offers very minor customizations such as a bayonet for more melee damage/range or armor penetrating rounds for those pesky armored enemies. But I always feel like there aren't many options for my weapons and I feel like weaponry could have been a really exciting area to create interesting combinations tuned to your playstyle.
The enemies each have their own strengths and weaknesses and are brutally difficult but you rarely feel as though they are unfair, there have been a few times where enemies spawn around me in a circle, effectively creating a wall around me as they swiftly strike me down but that's a fairly rare occurence. The difficulty system is also fantastic with missions that will challenge even max-leveled players so it should never feel as though you "faceroll" the content.
GRAPHICS & SOUND: The graphics are top-notch for a twin-stick shooter style game with flawless animations, vivid environments and a nice color palette as opposed to most twin-stick shooters which always seem to be quite boring with their color choices, often sticking to dark tones resulting in a "muddy" look. The character designs are very aesthetically pleasing, in fact a few look very inspired by Star Wars armor designs while the enemy designs are all very distinctive from each other and the enemy designs are all very distinctive which helps with determining enemy weaknesses quickly amidst the chaos.
CONCLUSION: HELLDIVERS is a fantastic game and i'm so thankful that it was part of the Humble Bundle as it alone is worth the $10. The incredible moments from the online multiplayer make the HELLDIVERS experience a memorable one that i won't soon forget.

I've become quite fond of Arrowhead as a development team, they don't have a lot under their belt as of yet but all the games they've released so far have been great fun. I was really taken with the pick up and play co-op nature of their brilliant adaptation of the arcade classic Gauntlet, but they've taken this about twenty steps further with Helldiver's. To sum it up Helldiver's is an online co-op twin stick shooter with a living campaign, what that means is that as you play online you're taking part in a game of intergalactic conquest, each mission you complete contributes to the war effort which will in time determine whether or not the titular Helldiver's manage to conquer the galaxy so that their home planet Super-Earth will prosper, or whether their enemies will overcome their efforts and leave Super-Earth in ruins. Once a campaign is complete it resets and a whole new campaign begins, it's a neat idea and it gives you a reason to log in every couple of days to contribute to the battle.
Gameplay is fairly straightforward but with a few neat twists. You and three other Helldiver's embark on a series of three missions to conquer a planet, each mission is made up of mini sub goals, such as defending a tactical point, retrieval and delivery of sensitive information, taking down anti aircraft systems so your allies can call in an airstrike and so on, all while enemy scouts patrol the area attempting to discover your presence, which if they're successful causes them to call in reinforcements, resulting in you and your allies fighting off waves of enemies. Once all your objectives are completed you're to locate an escape point whereby you call in an evacuation ship to pick you up, it's very fast paced and arcadey and yet due to it's objective based nature manages to portray quite a bit of depth, which is backed up by the levelling system allowing you to grind missions for experience and rewards with which to upgrade your Helldiver. Any experience accumulated in missions is converted into points which you can use to purchase new gear for your Helldivers ranging from different weapons and upgrades to strategems, which is where the game boasts it's tactical depth. Stratagems are specific abilities you can call in mid mission, you do this by holding down your map button and inputting a sequence of button combinations, not all too disimilar to entering cheat codes, these relate to the strategems you chose to bring with you on the mission of which you can carry up to four. Strategems come in three flavours, offensive, defensive and utility. Offensive stratagems are generally attack based such as calling in an air strike, napalm and orbital lasers. Defensive strategems take the form of AI controlled gun turrets, mine fields, defensive walls and other such tactics. Utility strategems are the most varied, these can be weapons, vehicles, mechs, ammo drops, or even extra equipment such as an energy shield, a jet pack or a utility drone. The drivbe to unlock all of these really gives you an incentive to keep playing.
As for the Helldivers themselves you unlock aesthetic gear as you level allowing you to change their appearance slightly by picking from a range of helmets, armor and cloaks that don't stray too far from the stormtrooper motif that the Helldivers represent. To best describe them they're like a mix of the Imperial Guard from Warhammer 40k, the Stormtroopers from Star Wars and the titual army of the movie/novel Starship Troopers. They're basically an army of elite soldiers fighting for the totalitarian regime of Super-Earth that seeks to "liberate" the galaxy, see Helldiver's has a very tongue in cheek style in the way it parodies imperial governments and the propaganda they utilise to push their agenda. You'll often hear your characters yelling about freedom and liberty as they blast the hell out of the three enemy races and it's played for laughs as you're very clearly playing as the bad guys masquerading under a facade of political benevolence. They may say they want to liberate the cyborgs, wipe out the threat of the bugs and establish diplomatic relations with the illuminates but what they really want to do is quell the cyborg rebellion, breed and slaughter the bugs for fuel and steal the illuminate's tech and they don'tr really go to great lengths to hide it, this is all told to you through news bulletins as the campaign progresses that really give the game a snarky charm that wants you to be in on the joke.
All in all I can't recommend this game enough, I've sunk a lot of time into it playing with friends and randoms online and I've enjoyed every minute of it. I really hope Arrowhead puts together a sequel in the future as the creativity displayed here would yield much potential in a future installment. Definitely be sure to pick this game up, you won't be disappointed.

Sinless is a point & click adventure game made to resemble golden adventure classics from 90s and yet introducing some novel improvements to the genre.
The game play itself reminds me the polished version of the classic adventure from my childhood days "Rise of the Dragon". It has the same cyberpunk feel to it without going overboard with it.

The game has some really fantastic audio-visual presentation. If I had to compare it to some animated movie, it would be famous "Ergo Proxy" anime, which has similar distinctive theme.
The game starts a little slow, but after a while you just can't get away from it.

Suddenly coming to his senses at the top of a set of escalators whilst the night's heavy rain thrashes against the all-glass exterior, the first words your player character utters are "What
the! Where the hell am I?". Those questions will circle around in your own mind as you descend, only to re-emerge at the top until eventually, a mysterious creature offers you a strange blue substance for tasting. As you oblige, reality warps around you and your adventure begins ...
Sinless is set in a utopian World which wants to distance itself completely from the now-bygone, "primitive" AD era. Due to catastrophic flooding, civilzation was forced to build it's habitation upwards, simultaneously diving the population geographically and caste-wise into lower, middle and upper classes. All citizens interface with scheduled programs through ports on their augmented bodies. These "progs" dictate what activites are acceptable on any given day. Anything else is considered a deviation from the "prog" and results in immediate punishment.
The omnipresent 'OmniCare' is the megacorporation pulling the strings, insisting it's all for the public good; a mandatory ruleset that eliminates anti-social behaviour, resulting in a healthy, happy populace. A world without sin ...
Sinless has a strong sense of it's own aesthetic style and it's a pretty unique one: predominantly dark backdrops are flooded with neon-like bloom/lens flare lighting effects from the red/pink area of the color spectrum, corners and objects are semi-obscured with blurring or pixelization and characters are animated in a very minimalist, odd, entrancing way. It's a style that always leaves something to the imagination which really helps to immerse the player in the cyberpunk world that MGP studios have created.
Gameplay is essentially a visual novel with point 'n' click elements. Making the wrong decision or provoking the warth of the law can result in a 'Game Over' screen, but it's fun to discover the many ways you can end your character's existence. Interactivy is relatively limited: your standard "examine/look" and "use" actions are the staple here once again and there is no great deal of exploration or sidequests to be had. 2 mini-games and 2 instances of a puzzle are decent little bonuses.
Second to the unique presentation, sound and music is where Sinless really shines. The game comes with the OST included, which for many would probably be worth the price alone. Headphones are definitely recommended here (as advised by the developers) to experience the heavy electronic score. Most impressively, the intensity of the tracks increases as cetain revelations and milestones occur on-screen. It's a perfect compliment to the visuals and the combination of the two enhances the immersive experience.
The story is not particularly deep and influences from popular science fiction are evident. Little or no connection is made between any of the characters and most of what they have to say is strictly related to your progression through the story. There are however some interesting observations and theories relayed by a few of the seeminly inconsequential characters. At the same time, a strong argument could be made to explain this pervading, distant behaviour as a plot device. I suspect a clearer picutre will be painted in part 2, which I'm very much looking forward to.

Sinless is a cyberpunk point and click adventure game, and manages to be dizzyingly beautiful and an aural treat, dragged down by everything else. This is part one of a three part trilogy, and unfortunetly there is no satisfying conclusion yet. The story isn't terribly interesting and unfortunetly filled full of contemporary video game references. It feels cheap and I can't say I really care for the developer's taste in games. The characters are pretty much stock standard and the dialogue is just ok. It really just doesn't bring any interesting ideas to the table, it's mostly full of tropes. I could excuse this if there was a philosophical theme, but this doesn't really happen, the game takes a more action approach and prefers to dazzle with it's atmosphere.
Where the game truly shines is it's ability to create an immersive environment. This is a game you want to wear headphones with, the music and sound effects really bring you into the world. The visual design is quite unique and uses massive amounts of lens flair and bloom on the lighting, as well as blurring and pixilating everything. And it works well. If you take a close look, it looks like quite a lot of the assets are actually photographs put through a filter. I'd consider this a cheap way for the developers to create assets, but it works fine for most of the part. The asthetic is something resembling Deus Ex: Human Revolution if it were set in Japan. It's not 80's cyberpunk, but it still has a lot of the Asian influence. The game also delivers on the classic bleak rain, neon lights, dark alleys, illict augs and a lot of drugs. It's used somewhat sparingly and works well in the games context.
However, I had quite a lot of difficulty navigating through the city. Unfortunetly, the visual design doesn't lend itself to guiding the player well. Unless you take note of everything on the screen, you may find yourself not knowing how to continue.  I'm fine with a bit of exploration, but it's never clear exactly where you can go. I also found it easy to miss dialogue options, as the section requires you to click and drag to scroll and will often add new options without marking or otherwise bringing them to your attention. Like most players, I go from top to bottom in the dialogue list, but I've seen cases where the options are added above your last clicked dialogue option, making it a little confusing.
As of the first release, there are a number of issues with graphics failing to load, leaving you with a black screen or only part of the scene. At this point, the only thing to do is to reset. Luckily, the game will always bring you back to where you are, so it's not a big deal, but still an annoyance. I expect this will be patched fairly quickly.
Although Sinless fails on many fronts, I feel it's definetely worth the small amount of money, just to experience the atomosphere.  I got around 2 hours of playtime out of it, and I'm quite happy with the game and am anticipating the second part.

Some notes on my review, I payed $20 for the title and have all DLC. I played exclusively on hard mode, never touched anything else. I played 17 hours solo at time of review. I only used guides to find police vanes on the map and when trying to figure out how to cross the bridge otherwise played blinded.
First of all let talk about something that impressed me about this game and that is how well it handled alt-tabbing. As a user that frequently tabs out to change music, turn on netflix, answer emails and of course bring up guides I was very happy to find that the game doesn't suffer any issue while doing so. The game alt-tabs out quickly and returns just as fast without hitching or stuttering. I also noticed no problems alt-tabbing while in loading screens, which cause alot of games problems. Alt-Tabbing ability is a 10/10.
Fast load times for an open world game, I am using a Samsung 850 Evo so your milage might vary, I am usually in the first load screen for about 5-10 seconds. All subsequent load screens are near instant. Also loading after death is instant allowing you to get back into the game right after consumption by zombie. 10/10
Lets talk about game flow. This game flows a standard open world zombie formula. There are lots of zombies, you gather supplies, you can craft items (primarily weapons and medkits), fallout 3 style lock picking, first person parkour system, trap activation, safe house clearing, quarantine zones that act as pseudo-arena and range/melee combat. Dying Light features no thirsty/hungry meters and only has health, stamina and weapon durablity as perameters to manage. Weapons can be repair but only limited number of times. Stamina is regain by waiting. Health is regen small amount naturally with large chunk being recovered over time by using medkits.
Zombies, Zombies, Zombies. During the course of the game the primary enemies you will face are zombies. They come in several types, most common as the slow walking(occasionally, jogging forward) zombies. The fast moving 28 Day later zombies with the ability to climb structures. This zombies are normally handled by simple using the parkour system and traps to escape the horde. You rarely feel threatened by them and the normal infected as essiently unable to the kill the player who is being vaguely cautious. Most death to these zombies come from trying to press your luck or ingaming in trap baiting or combat for fun. Otherwise they are mostly teethless.
Outside of that we have the standard Left 4 Dead special infected. A few large high health tanks, spitters and boomers(minus the attracting goo). The special zombies only occasionally require a change in tactics. With running away being a fairly safe tactic in most cases. With the exception of the Volatiles, which are basically hyper fast hunter zombies. They move faster than you and deal extreme damage. While the tactic of running and avoidance still occurs when encounting Volatiles the franctic and immediate pressure of escape make these encounter the most enjoyable. As the player try desperately to jump building to building, change direction constantly to break line of sight, and avoid certain death.
Crafting in this game is simple and to the point. Supplies were plentiful in hard mode and I never had trouble crafting what I needed in the moment. The game allowes the creation of new melee weapons and melee weapon mods. Because of the limited number of uses melee weapons have and the number of hits it take to kill zombies, even with mods, made the crafting system unrewarding to invest in, I never felt attached to my weapons or creations. I usually end up using basic weapons as electrifying weapons or adding poision damage didn't make a noticely difference to the combat for me. As of 20 hours in I haven't found very main weapon blueprints and of the ones I do have none of them add much to gameplay for me.
The craftable throwables suffer from the similar problem as the melee weapons, simply being too weak taking nearlly 20 throwing stars to kill some enemies because of this I mostly stick to the tactic that works the best, firecracker(noise maker) and molotovs to kill most hordes of zombies. This leads to a rather boring but effective strat of throw firecrackers then molotovs till the horde is cleared but then that begs the question why bother? when running and avoidance is more effective then fight.
Finally we have firearms. There extreme rarity in the early game makes them increabiliy important in early encounters. I remember finding my first hand gun with 10 bullets. I know exactly where I put those 10 bullets. 5 went into bandits to clear an early mission and the other 5 went into a tank like zombie who was guarding a supply crate. When faced with tough enemy I had to make a conscious decison to use my bullets here or not. The uncertainity of how long it would take to find more ammo and the pressure to make each shot count add tension to the game and made firearms feel right.
However this tension is thrown out during a story mission 1/3 the way through where I left the mission with 8 rifles in my backpack and maxed out ammo for pistols and rifles. After that ammo wasn't an issue to gather for me. I still mostly use the ammo on human enemies and super zombies making ecounter that are clearly designed to be difficult a 5 minute walk in the park.
Next I need to address the parkour system which is focused on 1 button, space bar, much like Assassin's Creed. Like all games that feature a single button doing too many tasks you will run into an occasional problem but over all the system works well when you are free running in the over world. The system involves either hitting space bar to jump or holding space bar and looking at a ledge to grab. Often the character grab ledges outside of what is preceived to be possible to grab(i.e. grabbing a ledge a clear foot highier then his make jump). This leyway with ledge grabbing allows the games parkour to be forgiving however sometimes the character will fail to grab some ledges, air conditions, while grabbing unintend ledges like, window seels, this creates an occasional inconsistent feel when trying to be precious with your free running. I have discovered in my time playing it is often best to just follow developer intended path through areas (stair step roofs or duke of hazard style ramps) to traverse the over world.
I wanna take a brief second to discuss the lockpicking. Lock picks are plentiful and you will never run out. It does a fallout 3 style lockpick system but it is real time, no pausing. If you loath this style of lockpicking prepare to cry as it is used in several story missions, usually done will surrounded by zombies, and is used to acquire guns, ammo and supplies from various caches. I would call the lockpicking a major game feature since it appears so often. I would have liked to see more innovating ideas or features attached to lockpicking. Maybe skills or a different style as the Fallout 3 style is nearly a decade old and the game uses a carbon copy of it.
Finally lets talk story. Its a standard video game story mode featuring simple motivations, cardboard cutout quest givers and black/white morality. Stuble isn't a language present in Techlands story department with the evil guy being a standard issue sadist and the good guys being underdogs who just wanna help. You got hotheaded younger brothers, sister who are forced to become parental figures, double crossing seen from a mile away, and you, player characters the hero(aka errand boy) of the whole country. Luckily all of this can be skipped by hitting your trust space bar.
Despite flaws and critisms I can't deny the game is fun and enjoyable. What other meteric do you need to rate a game on so thumbs up.

But beware: that video shows the solution for a whole part of the game so I don't recommend watching it but I recommend reading the completely spoiler-free version below instead.

I had this game on my wishlist for some time. I wasn't really sure if it'd be my kind of game, or that it was worth it's $20 price tag, so I waited. And I waited until it was on sale, I can't remember the exact price I paid, but let me tell you, it is worth the money.
This game, is just utterly astounding. I didn't know what direction it was going in, but the ending just blew me away. It has such amaizng story telling, along with an absolutely gorgeous environment.
I will admit originally I wasn't sure what was going on, or how some of the mechanics worked. I DID have to look it up eventually. And I did miss some key parts in the game. BUT, you are given the opportunity to go back if you missed something. I am not sure if not knowing was on my behalf, or the game not explaining what to do well enough.
But honestly, even with that, and having to backtrack because I missed a few things, I STILL will say this has to be one of my favorite games. I haven't played a great game with an amazing story like this in a long time, probably since I played Life Is Strange.
This game just really hooks you, drags you in, and takes you for a ride. Immensely wonderful story, with some breath taking visuals to it's aide. Give it a go, take your time, and EXPLORE. This game is filled with more than just beauty, but it is most definitely covered in it.

Overall, I'd give this game a 7.5/10. Note: I played the redux, so don't mind my hours.
Pros
- Stunning visuals
- Interesting plotline
- Great voice acting
- Fun and unique puzzles
- Atmospheric horror (rather than a bunch of cheesy jumpscares)
- Great plot twist and ending
Cons
- Plotline can get slow at times
- Occasional glitch (i.e. can't pick up an object that I need to continue)
- Shorter than expected
- "Detective-view", or whatever it's called [right click] can be frustrating to work with
In summary, if you like walking simulators with mystery and can handle a little horror this game is a great buy. But I wouldn't recommend it until it goes under $10. If you're on the fence, wait until it's $5 or under. It's a solid 3.5+ hours of gameplay.

(cue power surge just after I cloaked to avoid a barrage)
In case you couldn't tell, no. I didn't finish the fight. And legend has it, the salt remains in the heart of this review's writer to this very day. Or not. I'm writing this at 1 AM just a few minutes after it happened. It sure feels like it'll stick with me for a long time though. Maybe I'll upload this review, if not just to relive the bad memory the next time I wonder
"Wait, I 've reviewed games on Steam?"
That reminds me. This is supposed to be a review, not a blog to vent about my shortcomings in video games. FTL fun if you delude yourself into thinking that luck isn't the main deciding factor in runs. You always know deep down that it's something of an elaborate gamble. Sooner or later you'll remember, and it'll lose some of its appeal in gameplay. You'll see all of the beaconevents before too long, and every conceivable dramatic, emergent comeback or situation will occur to some degree if you play a bit longer. Once those lose their charm, it becomes harder and harder to come back to. At least it has for me.
I suppose a ten dollar indie game doens't advertise infinite replayability, so you know what, I'm going to begrudgingly reccomend it despite coming in here to fervently denounce the game with the hopes that maybe my spite would be resolved if I was lucky enough to see the positive review percentage drop by a digit following my submission. I've had a lot of frustration with this game, but I think overall, if I look way back to 2012 (when good indie games were released on Steam on a regular basis, if anyone can imagine that.) Good sequel to Coh: New Steam Edition (old servers gone, now on Steam). With a new Russian faction, and substantial re-working of familiar ones, this is definately a sequel worth a discount price. Why discount? Because some of the strategies you live by in Coh won't work here. For example, don't expect to rush a bofors position when fighting the brits; those things are now lethal to infantry/vehicles/light tanks AND aircraft. Also, not all of the commanders are worthwile, and you won't get them all in a few hours of gameplay: still haven't got the great ones at this time (300+ hrs in).  Least you get the choice of 3 throughout the battle, similar to choosing a doctrine in Coh.
Don't expect all the bells and whistles in customization either. From custom unit decals (vehicles only), custom killstrikes (attack an HQ upon victory with 200 medic airdrops...or whatever), custom color patterns, and variable faceplates (surrounding box outline to customizable area), you will typically get an 'X player has a mod that others haven't installed' error.
You'll have to troubleshoot in-lobby; just stick with default stuff (usually with a rarity indicator, like common/rare/whatever as oppossed to 'custom'). This defeats the entire purpose of allowing this level of customization in the first place, and that's not touching the custom maps/mods you may encounter. FYI: YOU DON'T DOWNLOAD THE SAME MOD VERSION AS IN-GAME IF YOU ALREADY HAVE A DIFFERENT VERSION. Maps are fine, but that could be that no one's really making new maps.
Overall, not bad. However, after you beat the Campaign/Theatre of War, you will likely see the most variety of multiplayer action over the first 30 hours or so. After that, it's back to Coh usuall: compstomps aplenty (though new maps help) and player matches not even remotely close (especially if one side has several "paid for" commanders than the other). Get this game when discounted.

This game is entirely free and that's a wonderful thing, because it's definitely worth a few bucks. And besides, who doesn't love something for nothing? I know that I do! I mean, free stuff is awesome. But I digress...the first thing you may or may not notice about this fantastic little platformer, depending on the year you were born, is the fact that it looks and feels exactly like an old-school classic NES title from that colorful decade: the 80's. The 1980's, not the 1880's, of course. That may be the first strike against this game to some of you, but for me this game feels just as reminiscent as those classics I sunk so many hours of my young life into way back when my mother was still picking out my clothing for the day.
This game is also surprisingly challenging despite the fact that it looks rather easy. There's also no music, extremely limited sound effects, and the only action your character has is to jump. But despite all of this the game still works extremely well as a whole. And for these reasons and these reasons alone, I feel compelled to yell at you to get out there and try this game. You don't even have to wait until the next big sale because did I mention earlier that it's entirely free?

A very authentic throwback to the pre-NES PC days. As someone who actually knows what a 5.25" floppy drive is, I really appreciated this. The use of the 4-color CGA palette, sprite and tile design, physics, and PC speaker beeps, and especially the level design philosophy are all spot-on. The CRT screen emulation is also genius. I've played every Civilization (a.k.a Civ) game up to this version. Every game added more content, better graphics and GUI, and consolidated features for smoother gameplay. The one feature that does not get enough attention has always been the AI or computer players. In Civ V, the AI doesn't do well by the end-game because as the focus becomes less about settling/expansion and more about economics, culture and diplomacy they have a hard time adapting which leads most AI to just declare war regardless of their capabilities. I enjoyed the combat in Civ V vs. Civ IV because it is less about RNG and more about how good you are at strategizing. However, if you are one of those conquering types, the warmonger penalty is annoying because you cannot get rid of it and diplomacy with AI becomes a no go. The religions are more customized based on player choice. Espionage is less annoying in regards to AI constantly stealing your techs, which it still can do, but a lot slower and you can build up protection against it. The best feature of all about CIv 5 and some previous versions is the hotseat multiplayer whereby I can put the game on my big screen TV and play with my friends as if a digital board game.

Metro 2033 redux is improved version of Metro 2033,FPS set in  Post-Apocalyptic Moscow about 20 years after Nuclear Dewastation of..everything.This review will be short and i won't say anything about fighting or soundtrack because nothing changed from normal version!(I haven't reviewed first game because i played on xbox)!
Changes in this version are:
-MUCH better graphics.I played on highest settings and game looks beautiful.In metro maybe you don't see that much of change but on surface it looks amazing!
-They removed some of loading/end of the level screen.I will explain.Dead City in Metro Redux is one long level from metro entrance to vent.In Metro 2033 there was a Dead City 1 which started from metro entrance to a Stalker hideout near staircase after meeting a eating body demon.Then there was Dead City 2 from staircase to vent.This is very good change because you don't lose as much of that feeling on loading screens as in first game,and of course less loading screens=better.
-Levels are little changed.If you played normal Metro at least twice you will be good. Some bigger changes are:
a) when on level "Trolley Combat" there is no tank fight,you just simply ride across bridge
b)In Market you can try your shooting skills to get bullets! (10 to enter you can get 40 if i remember)
c)Added shooting ranges near SOME trading shops,not every shop have that.
d)On level "Armory" you CAN'T  buy any suits so you don't have any stealth or armor bonus.Be careful.
e)On "Dry Station" it's harder to play without killing because game gave a lot of obstacles and changed a station with added walls.
f)On level "Cursed" there is no MG :(
-Gameplay changes...well they added stuff from Metro Last Light such as cleaning your mask and a melee fight (stunning or killing).You still can beat most levels with humans without killing anyone(thanks to stunning) or if you really need to fight...just fight.Grenades still suck tho.
-Of course Remaster could not be a Remaster without "ALL DLC'S!!!!" so we get Ranger Pack because it was the only dlc for Metro 2033.In this dlc we get new difficulty called "Ranger Mode" and 2 guns.Heavy Shotgun and Miller's Electric Gun.Same thing as in Metro 2033.One change is that on level "Armory" you won't get them.You can only buy them or wait for church level after the Library where you can have all guns for free
So game which was good now is even better and if you haven't played 1st Metro you need to buy that! Great atmosphere,gameplay and graphics are making this game very good! 9/10. You need to play!

I really wish I could love this game, but there's too much in the way for that to happen...
On the one hand it's got a great atmosphere and immersion. The environments and the level design is on point and the enemies look scary. It really makes you feel like you're there among them. The stations have a cool vibe and they managed to keep the UI to a minimum.
But then there are things like the gas masks that can run out - on paper this sounded like a cool and logic addition, but now that I played it a while, they really limit the time you have for exploration and force you to rush through some sections of the game - even playing the ranger mode (or whatever it was call - the one with a lot of loot lying around) I once ran out of masks and then you're more or less forced to restart the whole chapter...
Also the levels are extremly linear. Even more so than most shooters I played so far. This quickly becomes frustrating during stealth sections where you pretty much have to pull out the compass every few seconds to find where you're supposed to go. The stealth is also extremly unforgiving on even the easiest of difficulties - one tiny moment in the wrong spot and you are almost immediatly dead and have to restart the save-point... this requires serious patiences.
The scaling of difficulties also was way off. I played the easiest available and the enemies were bullet sponges. Some took half a mag to kill - and the game sometimes throws 10 to 20 at you and you're out of bullets immediatally! The lack off hints and tutorials etc. doesn't help either.
Also, the controls felt a bit weird. I tried to rebind some keys but I couldn't get it to a point where it all felt comfortable.
In conclusion:
If you like difficult games that require a lot of patiences and are willing to redo some check-points over and over again than this might be perfect for you.
If you like exploring and taking your time and prefer a more casual experience then this is most likely not your kind of game.

Very rarely do I write reviews.  When I do, they are for the most deserving of games.  This is just such a game.
If you're looking for visual fidelity, exemplary immersion, an impressive plot twist, or even novel control schemes, The Vanishing of Ethan Carter delivers.  There's little else I can offer in the way of explanation or backstory without giving away key details that might spoil the surprises for you, sadly, but I can at least attest that the experiences that await you here are equal parts suspenseful and cerebral.
I only have one area which detracts from the game's value, and that is how short it is.  Most can easily beat it in a single night with a little concerted effort, and you'll be left wishing the experience had lasted longer.  In terms of getting your money's worth, it still easily trumps the average passive movie watching window (and allows you to live through it in first person instead of watching a movie as a casual observer), but there's no explaining away the desire for more of a good thing.

I usually prefer to wait until I finish a game before I review it (barring episodic games but even then I finish the episodes that are available THEN review) but I enjoyed this game so much I figured I'd might as well review even before I finished it -- especially since it seems like there's so much to do!
First of all, I'm not normally a tower defense fan; I actually picked up Defender's Quest as part of a Humble Bundle female protagonists deal. I don't even remember why I decided to try the game on a whim but I'm SO glad I did. The story is interesting and, even better, funny. There's tons of really good characters and the devs have done a good job of creating a story that walks the line between silly and serious pretty well.
In terms of the gameplay, like I said -- I don't particularly enjoy tower defense, mostly because the ones I've played previous to this have all seemed far too complicated to be worth the time and effort. Prior to Defender's Quest, the game that I've enjoyed the most in the genre was Plants vs. Zombies. Defender's Quest is a step above that, really, because DQ actually attempts to have a story and character development, though the basic goals of the two games are the same. I'd say DQ is a little bit tougher than PvZ, if only because there's a lot more variability in the maps, whereas PvQ was a fairly straight-forward flat plain. DQ offers maps with multiple enemy spawn points (three is the most I've seen so far), different terrain (e.g., water vs. land), and various restrictions in routes for enemies (and placement for allies). I especially enjoyed the way you can change battle speed to slow down -- or pause -- the enemies spawning to catch up or speed up (4X is amazing) if you're sure your allies can handle the enemies without much management. It's a nice mix that I liked, because I prefer to micro-manage at the start, rather than during the battle. Even better is the different battle difficulty settings, so you can go back and replay battles on a harder setting (same map, different enemies) PLUS bonus challenges and (so the achievements would suggest) a new game plus mode -- means there's tons of stuff to do. Playing DQ actually makes me want to go out and find similar tower  defense games to play because I enjoyed this one so much -- which is probably the best compliment I can give a game!

Can be a fun game until you get to the end. The final boss is basically a checklist to make sure you're incredibly overpowered or have a some kind of way prepared to cheese it. Really, have so much as one weakness, and the Flagship will use it to tear down your hull to nothing. I had a fully decked out arsenal, pre-igniters, maxed cloaking. My one weakness might've been my modest crew size of 5. Then, my gunner is mind controlled. Make that 4 crew. 2 Humans board. Well, it's hard to get away without piloting the ship in the final fight. 3v2? Seems it'll have to do. Just gotta keep trying my best plugging away at the Zoltan shield. It's a bit tougher when I have to keep my weapons from taking damage when an enemy combatant I both don't want to kill yet need to constantly fight is in the same room as them. Ouch. A wayward rocket in the medbay while cycling injured fighters in. Goodbye crew member. Oh boy. 2 more humans boarding. No use in trying to man the blast doors, they're right on top of me. Just gotta vent them out into space. Now let's fix up my weapons.  Here I am with 2 crew with a silver of health left each. Could I possibly finish the fight? (cue power surge just after I cloaked to avoid a barrage)
In case you couldn't tell, no. I didn't finish the fight. And legend has it, the salt remains in the heart of this review's writer to this very day. Or not. I'm writing this at 1 AM just a few minutes after it happened. It sure feels like it'll stick with me for a long time though. Maybe I'll upload this review, if not just to relive the bad memory the next time I wonder
"Wait, I 've reviewed games on Steam?"
That reminds me. This is supposed to be a review, not a blog to vent about my shortcomings in video games. FTL fun if you delude yourself into thinking that luck isn't the main deciding factor in runs. You always know deep down that it's something of an elaborate gamble. Sooner or later you'll remember, and it'll lose some of its appeal in gameplay. You'll see all of the beaconevents before too long, and every conceivable dramatic, emergent comeback or situation will occur to some degree if you play a bit longer. Once those lose their charm, it becomes harder and harder to come back to. At least it has for me.
I suppose a ten dollar indie game doens't advertise infinite replayability, so you know what, I'm going to begrudgingly reccomend it despite coming in here to fervently denounce the game with the hopes that maybe my spite would be resolved if I was lucky enough to see the positive review percentage drop by a digit following my submission. I've had a lot of frustration with this game, but I think overall, if I look way back to 2012 (when good indie games were released on Steam on a regular basis, if anyone can imagine that.) I've gotten more out of it in fun than what it has taken from me in the form of torn out hair and swear jar change.

I have played several RPG; on consoles, on the PC, and even tabletops. This one, with one, big, major flaw (which is fixable with a little bit of work!) is the _best_ videogame RPG I have ever played! I tested several characters, different builds, different approaches. I was never disappointed. The world is detailled, there are funny moments, there are intrigues, dead ends, confusing things, dark myths you try to solve - all placed in the "World of Darkness", a well known setting in the tabletop community. The story is awesome and one might be thrilled to look it up, but this would ruin your experience, so I will say just the basics:
You are choosing a vampire clan and the gender of your character when starting a new game. In the story, you are "embraced" (turned into a vampire) without wanting or knowing that. So, basically, the character doesn't really know what is happening and so are you, if you don't know the WoD-setting already. You are thrown into dirty politics, shady business and immor(t)al situations.
Your choices and behaviour actually change the game experience: While playing one character, I was surprised by a situation: I wanted to talk to a robber so he leaves me alone; it has worked with another character I played before. But my character had a very low humanity, so he decided to just drink him dry, leaving me in lack of control. This is only one example of the possibilities which are waiting for you. While revealing the secrets of the mainplot, you can side with different parties, thus changing the end of the game.
There are seven playable clans, and two of them are offering a very different experience: The ugly-as-hell Nosferatu which are forced to be unseen (if you don't want to get into trouble) and the incurable insane Malkavians, which are seeing the world totally different. So, you can play the story at least three times without being bored. For noobies, I suggest to start with one of the other clans, for WoD veterans: Have fun, you know the deal.
Graphics may be outdated, but I don't care. Gameplay was always more important for me than uber-gRapH1x, and this game got an immersive atmosphere with unique characters, cool details (you can listen to radioshows and watch the news on TV; there are references to the story in both of these!) and a nice soundtrack. Plus: The voice acting is awesome.
I have to be fair, though: The game was rushed and did not get the blessing of fine tuning, thus, it is, when played in the downloaded steam-version, very buggy and unstable.
BUT there is an unofficial fanpatch which fixes 99,9% of the bugs and even adds bonus stuff if you enable it! The patch is still (!!!) being worked  on (but it is in a very, very good state, it's just finetuning) and there are even some cool mods which are altering the game in a nice way.
So, to all those who are lamenting like "I BOUGHT GAME I WANT IT TO WORK WITHOUT EXTERNAL PATCH!!!111":
I understand you. Yeah, this is not what one might call "customer friendly". But the developers are gone, there is noone official who could fix that. But, think about it: It has become quite a norm that unfinished, crappy early access games are popping up like mushrooms in the forest on steam. Some of them are boring, some totally bugged, a lot of them not even in a state of what one might call "pre-alpha".
This brilliant jewel of RPG here can be fixed with a third party patch which is easily accessible in the internet (just look for the "unofficial patch"), so do give it a try if you are looking for a good vampire game. If you are a fan of the WoD, you may already played the game. If not: Do it. The disciplines have been changed a little bit, but this game is awesome; even with the little mistakes in the lore/setting. Don't expect a perfect tabletop->PC port, but it is damn good anyway. You will even meet some known characters from the books.

If you take every horror movie stereotype and Frankenstein it together, would the creation somehow mould its way into the hallowed halls of the A-movie? Probably not. But what a kick♥♥♥♥♥game it would make! This is that game. An RPG first-person shooter hybrid, where the strengths of these horror cliches are celebrated, and the atmosphere it creates is eerie, even startling. But it's not a scary game. It shouldn't be. After all, in this game, you are the nightmare. You are the vampire!
This game derives so much of its atmosphere from its music. It's fitting then that the first thing to introduce you to this bloodfeast of unholy gore is a score that perfectly sets the tone of the game; dark, but with a simple yet energetic beat. The heartbeat of the game. The visuals do a great job of creating an atmospheric world, but that atmosphere flourishes in the presence of such a masterful score. The darkness is all the more tangible.
The visuals, though a bit dated, are still nothing short of impressive, presenting a world that is dark, cold, harsh and inhospitable. Nothing of this world is beautiful, except how beautifully unpleasant a world it is. It's the detail in the decay; the rust in the infrastructure, the trash littering the streets, even the people are decayed by disease (of one form or another). That which looks beautiful only succeeds in looking artificial. The exception being anything of nature, what little of nature there is. And even then, nature, more often than not, has fangs. Truly a masterfully designed world, both from a graphic and architectural perspective.
Lets delve into some of the juicier aspects of the game. Starting with the creation of a character. There are several (literally) vampire clans to choose from, each with their own advantages and disadvantages. But all of them do serious justice to the name Vampire. That being said, some clans are easier to play than others. For instance, the Nosferatu clan is so hideous that they cannot be seen by humans, lest they violate the masquerade, a crime punishable by final death in the world of darkness. This requires them to stick to the sewers or sneak from place to place. Then, of course, there's the Malkavians, who are insane. With dialogue options so confusing that anyone playing as one might go insane! Every clan has various abilities. The Tremere has Blood Magic to literally suck the life from their opponents. The Malkavians have Dementation. Go on. Spread the insanity.
The RPG element is clever. Instead of earning experience by grinding enemies, you instead earn experience through completing quests. Some quests have alternate solutions, which sometimes net extra experience points. These can then be used to upgrade whichever stats suit your personal play style. And lets be honest. There are a huge variety of options! You like swords? This game has em. Guns? Try the convenience store. You like kicking♥♥♥♥♥using every violent means imaginable? Is using Vampire magic to literally boil an enemies blood until they explode gruesome enough? (Sorry, no ripping out hearts... that I'm aware of).
Guns did not suit my play style. But from the few times I used them, I found their accuracy and damage to be heavily influenced by skill, timing, and stat based luck. This is true for any weapon, but I found it easier to use melee weapons. Unlike guns, melee fights take place in third person mode (all the better to see thine♥♥♥♥♥kicking action). And once you get close enough to an opponent, dishing out a combo of damage is almost certainly assured. Regardless of weapon of choice, strategy is required if you want to survive.
The story is a fascinating exploration of darkness in all its forms. The vehicle for this exploration is the society that the monsters have evolved, and the multiple factions all struggling for what they desire. At the heart of this struggle lies the Ankaran Sarcophagus. And the secret sealed within. The first of these factions is the Camerilla, a near worldwide group that is grounded in structure and order, laws and politics. They want to establish a social hierarchy in Los Angeles, shielded by the masquerade of maintaining order. This is greatly in opposition to the Anarchs, who desire freedom over rigidity, though not to the point of stupidity. Revealing themselves to humans would call forth the hunters, those who would destroy any monsters in the name of god. And then there is the Sabbat, a group who relish their inhuman power, willing to lord it over both humans and any monster weaker than they are. They embrace their inner beast, regardless of danger. These are just some of the many factions dancing as puppets in the hands of the chess masters.
As the newly born pawn on the block, you are persuaded (forced) to do the bidding of one Prince Sebastian LaCroix, leader of the LA Camarilla. It quickly becomes apparent that not only are you LaCroix's pawn, you're everyone's pawn! But that has its advantages. You learn about the world and everyone in it by proxy and necessity. LaCroix's ambitions drive the main plot, but the rest is decided by you.
It's worth mentioning that while the voice acting is not of movie quality, you can tell that everyone put serious effort into their roles, even the minor characters! Extra points on that alone.
I'll admit that the ending was interesting, not as epic as I would have liked, but somehow far more satisfying than I imagined. A game every RPG fan should play.
It takes place in LA, putting you in the shoes – or heels – of a freshly made vampire. They have a secret society and live among us with a certain set of rules to maintain order and ensure that their existence won't become widespread knowledge. This is the Masquerade. You become the new pawn for the local leader in his political wars. Not all is well in vampire community, and some factions are eager to change things.
It's a comfortable entry – just as you're in the dark, so is your character, letting the two of you learn together who's who and what's what in vampire life. It's a pretty crazy one, too. Violence and sex are plentiful and the game doesn't shy from either. You'll find it hard, and not too rewarding, to play your regular Good Hero sort. It's also a very humorous game with plenty of moments that made me chuckle. The voice acting is terrific and there are many great characters. I found myself often just standing still and listening to the in-game news report on the TV, or the late-night radio show for the laughs.
The story develops in unexpected ways and the ending managed to surprise me. Maybe I haven't found them out yet, but I didn't feel as if my choices bore significant consequences. It didn't really bother me, though, because the ride was a good one. The game is divided into city hubs that open one at a time after plot checkpoints, and you can jump from one to the other freely once they're available. You won't find the trademark "collect 10 donkey tails" side-quests that pollute fantasy RPGs, but instead many fun investigative missions outside the main plot. Backtracking can be annoying, though.
While the story isn't too divergent, the gameplay is. It shares similarities with Deus Ex – many missions (though not all) don't offer just one way to the solution. Usually you can take a stealthy approach as well as the loud and bloody one. If your hacking skill is low, often your lockpicking will let you do the job instead – or vice versa. And while, like many other RPGs, it has its skills which aren't as useful as the others, I was happy to find out that many non-combat ones are still well utilized in the game. I won't write down a guide to power-building, though. One, because you can easily google it. Two, because it's hard to suck at the game.
You can focus either on guns or melee. I did one playthrough of each, and while I felt that later on my gun-focused character was stronger, the melee was more satisfying, despite how simple it was. I really liked playing an immortal psychopath who charges into a room while people shoot at her and she just jumps around slashing everything. However, just like the graphics, keep in mind the year of the game and don't expect anything advanced in terms of combat mechanics.
The game also has serious replay value. I'm already during my 3rd playthrough, and I'm not crossing out the possibility of a 4th sometime in the future. It's not due to different choices, because – as I said – they're not too significant here. It's partly due to reviewing the story with the insight of the twist at the end and partly due to different approach in mechanics – like many RPGs. You don't choose a specific class, but instead a clan. They're set apart by their own few unique abilities (some even have different dialogue options, which is pretty amazing if you ask me), while the bulk of the simple ones are shared between them all.
Before you start, two things. First, the game is buggy as hell and you shouldn't play it without the unofficial patch. Google it, it'll come up. Second, don't play the Malkavian clan in your first run – they're lunatics who hear voices, and their dialogue is completely overhauled and special, partly due to their weird insights into matters. So without understanding the plot after a complete playthrough, and knowing what happens in each interaction, playing a Malkavian can be really confusing. But after your first playthrough? Highly recommended. They're very entertaining.

Good:
- The story is amazing. It's entertaining, dark, and is completely engrossing. Seriously, it's one of the better video-game storylines out there and holds up well even today.
- The voice acting is spot on. All the actors/actresses hit the notes perfectly and every character sounds like a real person.
- The atmosphere is very good and really sells the idea of a dark, gothic LA underworld
- Oh my god the soundtrack
Bad:
- You will have to do some SERIOUS patching to get this game to work. It's all readily available online but you will have to put in the effort before the game even starts running.
- Combat is clunky and can be really frustrating at times - especially the melee combat
- Animation is dated - the character models are fantastic... when they're holding still. Once they start to move, they really show their age.
Neutral
Customisation is a mixed bag. On the one hand, you are given a choice of "race" at the beginning which influences playstyle, dialogue options, and avaliable powers. This is actually an amazingly deep system and playing as two different races feels like playing two completely different games. On the other hand, there are only two preset character models per race (one for each gender).
All in all, Bloodlines is one of those flawed gems. If you can put up with the fiddely mechanics, the sort-of-dated visuals, and the massive amount of patching needed, you will find it has a lot to offer in terms of character-driven narrative.

Before I begin, I'd like to say that though I have given this game a positive review, my personal rating for this game would be about a 6.5/10. I will go through the pros and cons as to why I feel that way about this game below:
Pros
- Games are pretty quick as planets take around 5-10 minutes to clear (more if soloing harder planets but still pretty quick as they clock around 15-30 minutes)
- Plenty challenging even as a team because of the co-op mechanics and accidental deaths, with ramping difficulty so even new players can enjoy the game
- Wide range of things to unlock and a plethora of upgrades
- Ability to play solo or co-op with up to 4 people
- Randomly generated planets ensures no planet mission is ever the same
- Magicka-like keyboard pattern generated skills (called strategems in Helldivers)
- Drop-in drop-out lets you join other players mid mission to help out and you can also leave anytime if you have to go
Cons
- A lot of the good weapons/strategems are only obtainable by buying the DLCs, and they make a decent amount of the missions types much much more easier to complete
- Upgrading stuff requires "research points", which you only get one of each time you level up or after you collect 10 "samples" from planets -- these samples are COMPLETELY easier to obtain when you have a certain DLC to detect them on planets
- No campaign and is purely mission based
- Mission objectives are recycled and after playing for a while they become stale, as they're just always the same missions repeated
- No customization of your character and the cosmetic items are mostly unnoticeable
- Enemies are divided into 3 regions, and once a region is complete you cannot fight those kind of enemies again till the other regions are complete and the whole community warfront is reset
- Even if you play offline, if the region is locked, you cannot play on that region unless you go online when the warfront resets
In summary, Helldivers is definitely more fun when you play with at least one other friend, as the game promotes co-op play and the harder planets (which give better rewards) almost always requires co-op. Yes, you can play solo, but the game requires you to put a massive amount of work into it before being able to solo. This is made easier if you have the DLCs, as a few of them provide perks that make soloing much easier. That is not to say that the DLCs are required, as you can still have fun and play without them. But even for the co-op experience, having some of the DLC loot helps a lot for many situations. With that said, because the game is so bare in terms of map environments and mission types, I'd be hard-pressed to say I recommend this game to everyone. If you're looking for a co-op top down shooter and don't mind grinding repeated missions and etc. then pick up this game. If not then I'd avoid it because the amount of money you pay (in my opinion) doesn't warrant the amount of game content. If you're on the fence like I was, just wait till it goes on sale and then pick it up and try it. If you don't like it, you can always refund it.

I really wish I could love this game, but there's too much in the way for that to happen...
On the one hand it's got a great atmosphere and immersion. The environments and the level design is on point and the enemies look scary. It really makes you feel like you're there among them. The stations have a cool vibe and they managed to keep the UI to a minimum.
But then there are things like the gas masks that can run out - on paper this sounded like a cool and logic addition, but now that I played it a while, they really limit the time you have for exploration and force you to rush through some sections of the game - even playing the ranger mode (or whatever it was call - the one with a lot of loot lying around) I once ran out of masks and then you're more or less forced to restart the whole chapter...
Also the levels are extremly linear. Even more so than most shooters I played so far. This quickly becomes frustrating during stealth sections where you pretty much have to pull out the compass every few seconds to find where you're supposed to go. The stealth is also extremly unforgiving on even the easiest of difficulties - one tiny moment in the wrong spot and you are almost immediatly dead and have to restart the save-point... this requires serious patiences.
The scaling of difficulties also was way off. I played the easiest available and the enemies were bullet sponges. Some took half a mag to kill - and the game sometimes throws 10 to 20 at you and you're out of bullets immediatally! The lack off hints and tutorials etc. doesn't help either.
Also, the controls felt a bit weird. I tried to rebind some keys but I couldn't get it to a point where it all felt comfortable.
In conclusion:
If you like difficult games that require a lot of patiences and are willing to redo some check-points over and over again than this might be perfect for you.
If you like exploring and taking your time and prefer a more casual experience then this is most likely not your kind of game.

Bitesize Review - Gunman Clive
The Good:
- Artstyle is nice
- Music is simple and fits the game's style
- Low price matches quantity/quality of content here
The Bad:
- Can't aim your gun like enemies do
- Some levels can be really frustrating
- No real story here or characters
- Very short game, I beat it in an hour
- No real reason to play again
The Verdict:
Gunman Clive is a cute sidescrolling shooter that takes place in the Wild West. The story is essentially your girl is taken and you need to go save her by running to the right through 20 stages. It's got a good style, and has decent music. The problem with the game is that it really is a bare bones side scroller. There is no story, no real characters, there are a few really frustrating levels and the game can be completed within an hour. After you complete it you can play through the game again as a passive duck (I am not kidding haha) but other than achievements there is really no reason to replay this.
HOWEVER all that being said, the developer's are obviously smart enough to know that their game is tiny and lacking on content. Since they have priced the game accordingly.
The game only costs $2 ... a toonie as we say where I am from. So I can't really knock the game due to that. If it was $5 or more I would be tearing this game apart here, but it's not. It's a little cute game that has a little price tag. For what it is, I do recommend it.

From indie developer Level Up Labs, Defenders Quest is a Tower Defence game set in the fantasy world of the Ash Kingdom. Hailing to the final fantasy tactics series with its strategic character placement and pixel art sprites. The unique blend of tactical RPG and Tower defence mechanics offers something familiar but fresh. With a fully customisable cast of characters and intricate levelling system, Defenders Quest is a western effort to try reinvent a diluted genre.
You play as the heroine Azra, the former royal librarian of the Ash Kingdom who is exiled to the ruinous outskirts of the city when found dying from the plague. On the brink of death, Azra awakens in a purgatory state to be attacked by a swarm of zombie like creatures or 'Revenant', and by using newly acquired magic and the assistance of a fellow surviving berserk mercenary – you journey through the Pit to uncover the secrets of these creatures and the valley. As you progress you accumulate a small army of companions of different class from swordsman, archers and dragons to face off against a number of tyrants to free the land from the plague.
The game primarily revolves around a linear story driven campaign that places you in the overworld of the pit. From here you enter battles that charge waves of enemies at you from designated points, trying to reach and attack Azra. To defeat each wave you tactically place your available units across the map using your Psi resource to do so. Each unit has unique abilities and resistances to overcome each wave. You can also recall and reposition each unit, but this consumes further Psi. Azra also has a host of abilities that can boost her own units and fend off the waves of enemies. Each battle has 3 levels of difficulty and as you progress on normal you can revisit a previous battle to gain further XP and stars.
The Overworld also acts as a hub for towns and lairs. Before battles you can visit these locations to recruit units or purchase more effective weapons and armour.
You can also complete bonus levels that offer intense challenges for greater reward after gaining enough stars.
Defenders Quest is highly accessible but introduces a depth to tower defence that elevates it requiring the player to strategize and carefully consider how each unit is levelled and their positioning in battle. The character development is clearly influenced by role playing games, whilst removing the repetition and time associated with grinding. This effectively ensures your steady progression through the story whilst each battle holds new challenges.
The narrative is also highly original and maintains intrigue and invention that is expected of a good RPG. Azra is the sympathetic protagonist facing off against an unknown villainy.
The ability to pause a battle at any time emphasises the necessity to properly prepare your units placing them in the most effective positions and levelling them appropriate to the incoming enemies.
The game aesthetic is very nostalgic, calling back to the pixel art of classic JRPGs such as Final Fantasy and Chrono Trigger. Each recruit can also have a custom name and colours, allowing you to personalise your army.
The main campaign is appropriately paced across seven acts, but encourages you to revisit past levels for bonus equipment and increased challenge. You can complete your army with any class of your choice as their unlocked, further increasing the range of tactics when battling and tailoring your strategies the units you've selected.
The breadth and uniqueness of the story is commendable and gives engrossing context to the battles. However the static cut-scenes through which its told at times become unnecessarily prolonged and tedious, after the initial character introductions we generally skipped through them to get to the battles.
Furthermore there is a distinct characterised design to the figures in these scenes which drastically differs to the more befitting pixel models. This lack of consistency is also noticeable against the painterly backdrops.
Defenders Quest is strongly reminiscent of its influences, but also tries to introduce a more detailed textured interpretation of its characters, that unfortunately leaves to big a void in the games overall presentation.
What starts out as a charming and casual game soon evolves into a challenge.
Unlike most tower defence games there is no such thing as the ultimate deployment to beat every level. Each battle requires a unique strategy, that sometimes requires you to fine tune each unit.
Whilst tower defence remains primarily a casual genre, Level up Labs have crafted a game with a refined battle system and immersive world that requires a fair investment of the players time. Through adapting existing RPG conventions and introducing a few new parameters, Defenders Quest's perilous journey is worthy of the most battle-hardened players.

At first glance, Defender's Quest appears to be a silly little indie game with big dreams. The characters are bright and cartoony, and their dialogue is marked with sass. Their battle sprites display whimsical touches, like the ranger who spins her bow before firing. One of the promotional spellbooks Azra can equip, the Book of Face, introduces the Internet's beloved Trollface to the otherwise sword-and-sorcery setting. Focusing on the one-liners would be simple, as they are good. However, the core plot has heft: it would make a good Dungeons and Dragons campaign or fantasy adventure novel. Royal librarian Azra must survive in a quarantine pit the size of a small nation, while she's pursued by mysterious figures. It features conspiracy, betrayal, and explosions. Careful gamers shouldn't be surprised a USDA-certified English major wrote the script. The wacky comedy and childish in-fighting among Azra's companions allows the team to quickly bond. These light-hearted intra-party friendships and feuds add personal stakes to the more pervasive dangers of the pit. The story is delivered in slideshow style before every town and battle, tying the narrative neatly to combat.
Combat is handled like a tower defense game. Enemies travel in waves from spawn points. As they walk into the attack range of stationary heroes, they suffer the effects of the heroes' attacks. The heroes are unable to move from where they're summoned, as they're doing combat on a spiritual plane where bodies just get in the way. The cornerstone of battle strategy comes from placing the six types of heroes in the appropriate location. After recruiting story characters (such as Slak, the madcap, murderous berserker), faceless extras of the same type become hirable. If that's all there was to combat, it would be a delightful diversion. However, each character gains experience points, which can be spent to learn new combat skills or boost existing ones. Once learned, most of these skills can't be used immediately. Characters must be boosted in battle, which draws from the same Psi pool Astra uses to summon allies and cast spells of her own. It can be a challenging balancing act to position the proper allies, keep them boosted, reposition troops to respond to new threats, and maintain wide scale battlefield control with Azra's spells. Thankfully, slowing the game's speed (and pausing it altogether) are simple options. The keyboard commands are simple to learn and encourage faster play, but nothing's wrong with the mouse either.
With all the moving parts that go into battle, the multiple levels of accessibility are a nice touch. Each character has nine different attack modes including "attack the strongest enemy" and "attack the enemy with least immunity to status effects." Understanding the interplay between these attack modes isn't necessary for most of the core game, but integral to completing the optional levels. Furthermore, failure isn't necessarily punished. The default settings infer experience and money penalties for losing battles, but these can be changed based on individual preference. Redistributing skill points to explore different character builds costs money, but not a fortune. The steepest cost is the time it takes to click through all the advancements. The largest concession to the casual-vs.-hardcore debate is the option to increase experience points. Players who care more for the story and the thrill of rapid advancement can run with it. Players who want their hardcore bragging rights can lift their noses at the low-hanging fruit. True challenge-jockeys can set their sights on the more exclusive achievements, many of which are challenging even with gushing wells of experience points.
Defender's Quest is a short game, but provides plenty of options to extend the experience. Completing every level at the highest difficulty takes about twenty hours; increasing the experience and money levels in the options decreases the playtime. However, the New Game+ mode, which becomes available after completing the base game, adds considerable challenge. The core story stays the same, but combat's modified with new enemy powers, new maps, and new bonus stages. The New Game+ also provides a delicious means of upgrading the magic items earned in the core game, unlocking unique modifiers for each relic. As enjoyable as these new features are, Azra's journal is the best addition to the New Game+. After every major battle, Azra updates her journal with commentary on the story. In the process, she details her internal struggles and fleshes out the world. The extra character moments in Azra's journal are enjoyable enough that their inclusion as bonus material seems strange. They'd serve the story better as part of its body rather than as bonus material.
In spite of all this praise, Defender's Quest isn't perfect. Despite the snap and crackle of the script, it features several glaring spelling and punctuation errors--especially in Azra's journal. Purchasing equipment isn't as interesting as other elements of character customization, but the numerical benefits encourage frequently clicking through upgrades. The music is initially encouraging, but loops quickly. Thankfully, it can be toggled independently of the sound effects, which provide texture and valuable combat cues. The final battle song is a notable exception. That beast should be blasted loud and proud.
Between its addictive gameplay and sliding difficulty scale, Defender's Quest offers gamers a great deal for such a small investment of time. It probably won't make a true believer out of anyone whose parents were killed by tower defense games, but it's good at what it does: drawing people in and refusing to let them go until they've finished "just one more level."

I'm super impressed with this game! After getting it on sale for 50 cents, even more so it almost seems like a crime to buy this for less then 5 dollars! Anyways here's some pros and cons:
Pros:
-Relaxing soundtrack, very well composed!

Overall this is a fantastic game especially considering the price tag! Please consider giving this game a shot, you won't regret it!
