TL;DR--Procedurally generated levels can make progression impossible. It happened to me on the first boss door of my first play-through and, unwilling to deal with BS like that, I'm refunding.
Approaching 100 total games on my account, this is the first game I'll be (hopepfully) refunding.
I more-or-less knew what to expect from this game, and I got it on sale for $0.50, so I didn't need much to be satisfied. I've played and enjoyed a game very similar to this (not on Steam) and, by comparison, that game had better controls, graphics, and smoother gameplay--but none of that was a deal-breaker with regard to DungeonUp. For the price, those aspects are serviceable.
The issue is that I needed a red key to open the door to the first boss. The sole red key available was trapped behind a wall (not a wall with doors, but a solid wall), and the game provided me with no possible means of acquiring it. I knew, from reading reviews. that things like this were possible, but I expected them to be infrequent. Fortunately, this game-breaking experience occurred so quickly that it's within the refund period, but I've no doubt it could happen later in a play-through, meaning you'd have wasted all the time you invested (assuming you actually care to complete the game).
Inexpensive though it is, I can't recommend a game with such a glaring flaw. I like the potential which procedural generation has in a game like this, but it needs better implementation to avoid screwing the player through no fault of their own.
Edit for devs: The game I mentioned before had a 'cheat room' at the start of the dungeon which would allow you to get infinite keys and money, while requiring you to forfeit your score to use it. Though it served a slighly different purpose in that game, this game could benefit greatly from something like that, given the potential for unfair 'checkmates'.

There are also mini-games to unlock, one of which, the Diamond Mine thing, is a fairly addictive little puzzle game in its own right--but, from what I've seen so far, if you're not into mini-games (and usually I am not,) you can also pretty much ignore them.
Visually, the game looks good. It's colorful, the graphics are sharp, movements are smooth, sound effects are nice and relaxing--which is a good thing when you run into a difficult level and are close to running out of time. I haven't run into any problems or bugs. All in all, this is a great match 3 game, and one that any fan of the genre should enjoy. It's not going to haunt your dreams or call to you when you're busy doing other things, but it is an enjoyable diversion.

A lightening pearl in a World of Darkness, which I had forgotten eventually for ten long years. In December 2004, I installed this game for the first time, but at that early point in time, this game was released unfinished. At the same day, i happily uninstalled it to never play it again because of the heavy load of bugs and crashes.
10 Years and a lot of unofficial patches later, in December 2014, I bought this game on Steam for 5€, installed the 9.2 patch and completed it with much joy in 43 hours, with no frustrations at all and even without having to use a single cheat. Even installed on a Windows 8.1 x64, the game did only crash twice, both times in the very beginning while configuring my character.
I enjoyed every minute of it, and I will certainly play it again in the future. Who could have ever imagined this game would become such a Cult Classic? A must-have for fans of RPG, vampires or just all good PC games.

This game actually made me like vampires, something that I'd never thought would happen. The world and lore are really interesting, and you find yourself reading the loading screen splashes and milking every dialogue tree for all their worth. Sadly, it seems unlikely we'll ever see a similar game in this universe, which is a shame after seeing, reading of hearing about the various supernatural beings inhabiting it. I would've wanted to learn more about the werewolves, the Giovanni, the Society of Leopold any many other things, damnit!
It is also a fairly complex RPG, and both creating your character and levelling up will probably require some contemplative chin-stroking and sipping a beverage of your choice. I especially loved the game's multiple social skills, which put Bioware's simplified NICE GUY/BAD GUY systems to shame.
Unfortunately, both stealth and combat kind of suck, but they aren't bad enough to be a real annoyance until the game's later quests, when the amount of fighting goes up as the plot intrigue and character interaction goes down.
Yes, unfortunately the quality does suffer a bit towards the end, but the journey there will still be memorable enough to heartily recommend this game.
NOTE: I played the game with Unofficial Patch v9.2, which fixes bugs and restores cut content

I just finished Austin Jorgenson's LISA and can say that, without a doubt, it is among the strongest indie RPGs I have ever played. I was hooked on the world of LISA with the slight taste given by the prequel, LISA: The First, which had me eagerly awaiting this title. The developer cites Mother as a key influence and that shows, but even more than the abstract game OFF, LISA has taken the wacky humor and surreal style of Mother into a dark and very adult place. Dingaling is able to take simple, old school pixels and work them into truly disturbing imagery. Lately, we have been inundated with post-apocalyptic settings that are xeroxed and re-sampled at will: zombies, plague, fallout and bad weather. All of those settings, done to death, are fairly grim, but none of them can even touch the misery suggested by LISA. Here we have a world where women are extinct and the surviving men, seeing no future for humanity, have transformed the society into a sort of prison yard where hopelessness is drowned in drugs and alcohol, and memories seem uniformly sad. The main protagonist, Brad, is driven by a past filled with abuse and grief, and literally sets himself against the will of the entire world. The player will be forced to make tough decisions in this game and to eventually think about and judge the outcome. Even as we laugh at sight gags and endless pro wrestling references, one cannot ignore the uneasy slithering quality of LISA. My greatest hope is that the game does well and Dingaling games develops more titles where the heart of the game is a great story, not the ability to snipe someone in multiplayer. Bravo!

I enjoyed the combat in Civ V vs. Civ IV because it is less about RNG and more about how good you are at strategizing. However, if you are one of those conquering types, the warmonger penalty is annoying because you cannot get rid of it and diplomacy with AI becomes a no go. The religions are more customized based on player choice. Espionage is less annoying in regards to AI constantly stealing your techs, which it still can do, but a lot slower and you can build up protection against it. The best feature of all about CIv 5 and some previous versions is the hotseat multiplayer whereby I can put the game on my big screen TV and play with my friends as if a digital board game.

Defender's quest is a mix of a tower defense + rpg elements and the result is a very addictive game.
You're Azra royal librarian casted into the pit because you got the plague, but for some reason you get a strange vision about a golden man and discover new powers capable of destroying revenants for good, now gathering new allies you on a search trying to get out of the pit for your freedom, but also learning why you're special.
During the game you will unlock a total of 6 classes of heroes each with different pros and cons, archers low dmg but great range, knight high dmg but slow attack speed, berserker high attack speed medium dmg, ice priest area attacks with crow control skills, priest healer and buffer and dragons overally awesome.
There's a total of 30 levels each can be replayed on higher difficulties for more rewards (xp or unique gear for your defenders) but doing higher difficulties requires higher leveled defenders so they can unlock/upgrade skills and passives, unlike other TD games you upgrade the hero to give him a bonus in all stats and unlock his following active skill, which requires previously to level them up outside, kind of confusing but easy to understand as soon as you can see it.
There's a set of really hard achievements such as get 180 gold stars without buying generic heroes, reaching wave 100 on endless challenge, and killing a extremely overpowered sheep.
Once you beat the game newgame+ gets unlocked, tougher waves, newer gear, 7 side quests which some of them add a lot to the plot, journal logs after every level for more detailed lore about Azra's thoughs about everything than been happening, and items to upgrade the unique gear obtained from doing 3 star levels in normal play, can switch back and forth between both styles at will.
Highly recommended even at full price, good TD system and interesting storyline with some (a lot) of funny scenes, i even played 4 hours on a row without even realizing.

DungeonUp makes me realize the importance in all those small details and mechanics I take for granted from great roguelites and dungeon crawlers. There's no real sense of progression or discovery here. The levels are randomly generated but every run consists of "use as few yellow keys as possible, collect yellow keys, find the red key, find the boss floor, kill the boss. Get a soulstone which you could use to buy new items (pretty much necessary to progress) or to respawn (only worth it if you have a winning run where you die). This creates this loop that is essentially - grind as many soulstone until you get a really great run and can do it all in one go. Games like Rogue Legacy do this well imo, with a huge progression system to keep you scaling. Binding of Isaac doesn't have your run carry over, but you still constantly unlock new items and floors, plus the room layouts and item variation is huge.
I know not all dungeon crawlers can have the depth and scope of BoI but this does not even come close. A game with this little variety in items and enemies shouldn't be so much of a grind. To me it feels like DungeonUp is unsure of what it wants to be. It wants to be endlessly replayable but doesn't have any of that staying power you come to expect from games like this, so it instead wants you to beat the same boss over and over until you have enough soulstone to get good items and scale with the floors until you have one really strong run and win the game. In a way similar to Rogue Legacy but with not even 1% of the scope/depth or progression.
If you want a rogue-lite with emphasis on the lite, feel free to give it a chance but my personal opinion is that there's better games for your time and money.

I just finished Austin Jorgenson's LISA and can say that, without a doubt, it is among the strongest indie RPGs I have ever played. I was hooked on the world of LISA with the slight taste given by the prequel, LISA: The First, which had me eagerly awaiting this title. The developer cites Mother as a key influence and that shows, but even more than the abstract game OFF, LISA has taken the wacky humor and surreal style of Mother into a dark and very adult place. Dingaling is able to take simple, old school pixels and work them into truly disturbing imagery. Lately, we have been inundated with post-apocalyptic settings that are xeroxed and re-sampled at will: zombies, plague, fallout and bad weather. All of those settings, done to death, are fairly grim, but none of them can even touch the misery suggested by LISA. Here we have a world where women are extinct and the surviving men, seeing no future for humanity, have transformed the society into a sort of prison yard where hopelessness is drowned in drugs and alcohol, and memories seem uniformly sad. The main protagonist, Brad, is driven by a past filled with abuse and grief, and literally sets himself against the will of the entire world. The player will be forced to make tough decisions in this game and to eventually think about and judge the outcome. Even as we laugh at sight gags and endless pro wrestling references, one cannot ignore the uneasy slithering quality of LISA. My greatest hope is that the game does well and Dingaling games develops more titles where the heart of the game is a great story, not the ability to snipe someone in multiplayer. Bravo!

Dear lord, where do I begin??
Aesthetics-wise LISA (all caps because this game is ART) is pretty much a sidescrolling, edgier, blander, less-interesting Mother 3. Environments range from a brown mountainous area with ropes and doors everywhere to a yellow desert area with ropes and doors everywhere. There are even caves! Enemy variety is appallingly low; nearly every enemy you fight is a human with a knife and boss encounters range from "two tall guys" to "several yakuza members". Even the hidden superboss that you can only fight on secret hardcore difficulty is
. The mutant enemies that you encounter (of which there are around 5 total whoopie) honestly could have been interesting but they have no real bearing on the plot and nobody ingame seems to acknowledge their existence (just another facet of LISA's deep story...).
Atmosphere deserves a special mention because there is none. The Mother 3-styled graphics and samey sprites completely detract from any sort of emotions I am supposed to feel when I play this game. Really, that's all it felt like: a video game. I am playing a video game, I am going from point A to point B, I am fighting the boss, I have defeated the boss. The final boss of LISA is
. I said a similar thing with Shovel Knight: it really seems like the dev wanted to make a game like Mother 3 but completely failed on the execution.
When it comes to gameplay battles are standard RPGMaker fare, but this time with a premium price tag. In terms of party members the dev opted for quantity over quality; you will find many party members, all of whom possess little to no backstory. LISA features such endearing characters as "fly man who lives in garbage town", "man who talks a lot", "guy who loves chickens", "man with tiger head", and "fish lawyer". Outside of the 1-2 minute sequence where you recruit a character, you will hear nothing out of them. With this in mind, we come to the gameplay element that makes LISA a mature video game for adult gamers: THE CHOICES!!! In LISA, just like in real life, YOUR CHOICES MATTER! At various points throughout the game you are forced to make a decision, often involving the life of a party member. Of course, since a normal person has zero attachment to any of these characters the choice just comes down to whether the party member in question is useful or not. One of the goofiest moments of the game has you forced to choose between
. In every single one of these SuPeR dEeP mOrAl DiLeMmAs it's basically a choice between an option that would make the game more difficult, and one that I guess is supposed to guilt you but ultimately has no effect on the outcome of the game. Oh no, my character
but he's pretty much the same as he was when he still had both of them! I honestly don't even remember what the other option was there; it was probably killing off one of your dudes. The Russian Roulette segment is pretty goofy too; you can either just expend the party members you aren't using or savescum your way out of it. Really the whole permanent death thing is pretty poorly-implemented; the mutant enemies have an attack they like to use that permanently decommissions a member of your party which basically just means it's time to reset and hope he doesn't use it next time. An excellent mechanic! However, this isn't to say that the game is difficult; as I mentioned earlier the enemies are all pretty much identical, not just in appearance but also in battle tactics! I legitimately had trouble figuring out when I was fighting a boss because every enemy just seemed the same to me. It doesn't help that everything is weak to status effects, meaning that Fly Guy can puke on an enemy and stop them from doing anything until they die.
Bland graphics, poor gameplay, choices that don't matter... a game can have all of these and if its plot is decent I can just pretend I'm reading a book and be happy. Unfortunately the story is pretty much just "Bald man addicted to not-meth has to go find his adopted daughter; hijinks ensue!" which would honestly be okay if the characterization was good... or the environments were interesting... or if the writing was half-decent... or if the game was fun to play... Oh no the daughter is rebellious!! Oh no Bradley
! There are attempts to flesh out a backstory for our main character and his dark past as a karate instructor for first graders but in the end I could not find myself caring for him at all, or for any of the one-dimensional characters in this game. This game tries to be quirky, it tries to be deep, it tries to be emotionally stimulating, and in all of these regards it fails. Even at this point I would forgive the dev with a pat on the shoulder and a "better luck next time" but there are actually GOOD games made with RPGMaker out there that don't cost money to play.  Maybe "good" is an overstatement, but similar games such as Space Funeral and Off! (meme game that it is) actually manage to do one or two things right. So just play those instead.

It should be noted straight away that this game cannot be run on modern operating systems without unofficial patches. For those who don't want to take the time to figure out how to do this, you'll probably want to avoid purchasing this game.
That said, if you're comfortable with spending a few minutes finding and installing the unofficial patches, you might find this game interesting. You should probably wait for a deep-cut sale though; $20 for a 10 year old game that barely made it out of production is a little silly.
The good:
- Excellent writing (easily the best aspect of the game)
- Compelling storyline
- Interesting lore and characters
- Voice acting is very well done
- Play as one of seven vampire clans with differing abilities
- Allows for several different play styles
- Explore side quests in a non-linear fashion
- Multiple endings
The bad:
- Combat feels very clumsy. The defensive stance in melee combat is essentially worthless. It is difficult to maneuver and avoid being hit by enemy attacks.
- The game favors melee combat until much later in the game where guns are very powerful. However, since this is an RPG, the player must level up their skills one way or the other. Certain boss encounters are very difficult for players who choose a melee play style.
- There are stats that are basically worthless to invest in, such as haggling. Lockpicking and hacking can be useful for those in a hurry, but are in most cases not needed since keys and password notes can be found nearby. Other stats such as those used to influence others in dialogue are useful early on in the game, but aren't used at all later on.
- It is not possible to remain in first-person view at all times. The game forces you into the third-person view when engaging in melee combat. Ranged combat functions like a first person shooter.
- The player can make many different choices, but there are no diverging story paths. All choices the player makes eventually lead to the same outcome.
- The graphics aren't terrible, but look quite dated.
- At times there are graphical glitches or weird physics.
Those Earthbound vibes though <3

A wise man once told me: "Don't let nostalgia fool ya. You'll only end up disappointed." Damn, was I foolish to not listen to him. Some things just belong to Memory Lane and ought to never be touched again.
Back in the day - 2010 - I had only recently finished reading the book this game is based on. I was 13 years old. It wasn't that much of a problem to download well- functioning torrents on reliable pages. When I found out that Metro 2033 had been made into a game, I didn't hesitate. After tedious hours of downloading that meant that neither the internet nor the phone could be used properly for a fairly long amount of time, I launched it. It was cool, it worked as it should. It was atmospheric. It was scary. I enjoyed it a lot. But then, maybe in the middle of the story, the game kept crashing. Well, damn, it was an illegal copy, so I had to stop at that point. Period.
Around 2014, I began collecting games for my steam library. Old Games I saw as 'must-haves', AAA-games, new Indie games. A friend of mine had shared his library and in there were a few games I had already played a few years back. All of which I wanted to have as well, of course. Instead of just using the share, foolish me. One of those was Metro 2033. The thought of playing it again, to see what would be after the crash of my illegal copy, it kept popping into my mind. But I didn't let it stay. Until last year.
In a sale, I decided to buy the Redux package containing Metro 2033 and Metro Last Light. I was simply curious. But then again, I played loads of other games instead. Time passed. Last week I finished reading Metro 2035, I saw the announcement of Metro Exodus and I finally told myself: If you don't play it now, when will you?

After 7 hours of playthrough, I didn't manage to see what I had liked so much about this game. 7 years have passed since it has originally came out. And in my opinion it hasn't aged well, to say the least. I don't know what changes the Redux version has brought to the original game. At least what good changes. The only thing that popped into my eye as new were the virtual copies of Metro 2033 and Metro 2034 that lay around various places. As if the creators decided it was a good idea to keep reminding you: "Hey dumbass, this game is based on a book. You should read it! It's good! And do not try to immerse yourself into this game!! The book is much better!!!" Sadly, I'd have to say the same: read the book, it's better.
But enough ranting, let's talk about the game.
20 years ago, the world has bombed itself to smithereens during WWIII. The story takes place in Moscow, 2033, where numerous people have managed to survive the bombs by hiding in the Metro. They have grown accustomed to life in the tunnels. The stations of the Metro have organised themselves under various ideologies. There's the Hansa -mainly merchants-, there's the Reich -idiots that have adopted Hitler's ideas to their own patriotic russian standards-, and there's the Reds -well, also idiots, but communist idiots-. These are some of the many factions in the Metro that are in conflict with each other. You play as Artyom, a 20-something-year-old from an independent station right at the end of the Metro. There have been numerous attacks of the so-called Dark Ones, highly intelligent mutants that use their psychic powers to pit humans against each other. At the beginning, your step-father is visited by an old friend who brings him the message how much of a threat the dark-ones are. So you have to set out to the centre of the Metro and deliver this message to the 'authorities' at Polis.
The story is as close to the novel as it possibly could. However this doesn't mean that it's good. Characters are hollow and don't develop at all. Artyom is just a hull for the player seemingly without motivations of his own. The Dark Ones almost don't play any role- although they should be the major threat, they show up only once or twice (I'm not counting the 'dreams' that Artyom has about them). The people of the Metro and the other, more 'unthreatening' mutants and anomalies are the real danger instead. Huh. I thought the motivation of all characters that help Artyom along the way and die in order to protect him was to annihilate the Dark Ones? Meh, whatever. And the aforementioned virtual copies of the Metro books are immersion-breaking.
Thankfully, the atmosphere is much better. Whether you're fighting against waves and waves of mutants whilst your comrades are trying to comedically deal with the sight of death; or you're walking through a deserted station, cautiosly looking around every corner; it never fails to drag you in. Albeit you should definitely play with headphones - or else you most probably won't feel a thing besides frustration for dying so often.
My PC set-up isn't exactly the best. But even in middle settings, Metro looks good. There are actual effects for almost everything: fog, radiation, electricity. All of which make the levels seem more dense. The voice actors however don't. So, take a breath for a moment. Breath out and try to imagine what they sound like. Remember, it's a game that takes place in Moscow. Right! They all sound like they're trying too hard to sound like Russians. But then again why are they speaking English? It's just awful. And also, in comparison to the book, some of the names have been 'westernized'. For example, there's Miller whose name in the book is Melnik.
There are also many immersion-breaking moments. Damn, I can't stop talking about these stupid virtual copies of the Metro books. But also, there are moments where the writers decided to put references to works which have inspired Metro 2033. For example Roadside Picnic by the Strugatzky brothers. Again, something that feels like they're wanting to tell you: "Hey you dumbass. Look how smart we are. No one needs these references but we're going to put them in the game nonetheless." Also there are the voice-overs of Artyom at the start of almost every level. Retrospective ones, an older Artyom telling his story.
But you haven't finished Artyom's journey yet. You still have to fight against Nazis, Communists and mutants. Gunplay is standard, but it seems that all of the many guns do the exact same damage. So, what's the point in using different guns instead of just bying three AK: on the first you put a silencer, on the second you put a bigger ammo clip, on the third you put a scope. That's possible by the way. The only differences in enemies is how much bullets they can digest and how many there are in different areas. All of them just charge when they see you. So just lean back, hide behind a pillar or something and shoot them one after another (at least in normal difficulty that is). The only time that you-yourself- have to charge are a couple Railgun-sections (standard thing in the FPS-genre) and various sections where the game forces you to sneak by some goons with heavy armor and guns.
The only interesting part of the gameplay starts whenever you leave the tunnels of the Metro and get to the surface of Moscow. There, you have to keep different things in mind: ammo is more scarce; your gas mask needs new filters every few minutes (which are also rather scarce if you don't get on with things fast); your mask gets dirty and you have to clean it so you can see what you shoot at; also you try to outrun various types of mutants that can one-shot you. So, while combat inside the Metro is rather tame, combat outside the Metro is way more interesting and gets very hectic at times.
Metro 2033 Redux is like Call of Duty basically. But with mutants and more atmosphere.

At a glance, this may seem like some kind of rip-off of Terraria, but after playing it for a few minutes, you will realise it is very different. 3 multiplayer game modes including:
Challenges- Complete simple objectives in the shortest time possible. This isn't the best part of the game, but it has some great variety.
Capture the flag- You get a set up time to create defenses for your flag including reinforced walls, archer towers, catapults, and explosives and different types of arrows. You can also prepare for the offense by building a few different kinds of boats to gain the advantage on your enemy. Use ladders, trampolines, and even catapults to make your enemy's walls pointless.
Capture the Halls- This has all of the fun stuff from capture the flag, but you must research some of this (which is done automatically, the things researched are voted on by the team). Use your setup time to create a fortress to defend your halls, and to equip yourself to destroy your foes
There is also a single player tutorial, save the princess (a great way to practice), sandbox, and challenge mode.
Also, Shark and Buffalo riding.

Gunman Clive is a charming Mega Man-style action game with a zany, unexpected sense of humor.  For $2, you can't go wrong.
One of the things I love about Gunman Clive is how it taps into an often-overlooked value of retro games: replayability.  Mega Man was a great way to kill an hour or two.  You could beat the game and feel satisfied.  Games have gotten longer over the years and, likewise, platformers have too.  And while I'd never begrudge something like Shovel Knight for its length, it does lack that pick-up-and-play appeal after finishing it.  It feels like a commitment - to unlock the stages, to buy the items and upgrades, to fight the various minibosses, and so on.
Gunman Clive cuts right to the chase and I admire it for that reason.  It's just the right length, has a surprising number of gameplay variations to keep you hooked, and multiple reasons to replay it.  There's no "fluff."  You came here for some fun platforming challenges and things to shoot and Gunman Clive delivers exactly that.
Across 16 levels set to wistful and catchy Western-themed music, Clive can run, jump and fire his six-shooter to the left or right.  As in Mega Man, you can only have 3 bullets on screen at once, but this changes based on your power-ups.  Enemies often drop these, including a spread shot, a single powerful bullet, homing shots and more.  You keep these power-ups until you get hit.  On Normal difficulty, Clive can take 4 hits.  Cake, randomly dropped by enemies, restores health.  If you perish, you restart at the beginning of the level, but lives are infinite.  While a couple levels can get irritating because of restarts, none are so long that it gets frustrating.  The difficulty curve is balanced and gentle.
Clive's goal is to rescue Miss Johnson, the Mayor's daughter.  In a fun twist, you have the option of playing as Miss Johnson and rescuing Clive.  Johnson has more air time, but cannot shoot while moving.  There's a third character you unlock at the end, who carries no weapon, and serves as yet another challenge to play again.
Did I mention it's $2?  Go buy it, now!

This may be an unpopular opinion, and it pains me to say this because I wanted so badly to like this game, but I cannot recommend The Vanishing of Ethan Carter.  I'll go into detail below, but simply put: the game's disconnected narrative, requisite backtracking, convoluted progression and lack of any redemptive feeling upon completion outweighs any positives that could be mustered from the experience.
The game is visually appealing, and anyone with a halfway decent graphics card will be blown away by this game's immersive environment.  The creators really focused on the environment as a focal point, and it shows.  It is by far the strongest part of this game.
The puzzles are challenging and force the player to think outside the box, for better or for worse.  I truly enjoyed some of the game's puzzles, however others required so many tedious attempts that it's almost not even possible to progress through unless you look up the solution.
The story is intriguing from the outset, however the method of storytelling employed leaves the player confused, and by the end of the game it's very difficult to piece together how the events took place.  Despite things coming together fairly well during the ending sequence, I was still left puzzled about a large portion of the game's events with little closure on aspects that made the game intriguing at first.
You definitely should not play this game if you aren't prepared to play a walking simulator type of game with lots of cerebral elements.  The game tells you that it does not hold your hand from the beginning, and boy, is that the biggest understatement ever!  I don't personally mind a challenge, but having to walk across the entire map just to find out I didn't even complete a portion of the game correctly and have to go back and do it again is not exactly my idea of an enjoyable challenge.
Even if you are prepared for the aforementioned cerebral, frustrating walking simulator experience, I'm still not convinced that the game is worth your time.  I left the game feeling pretty empty and did not come away with much emotionally or mentally.  The story had me thinking at first, but by the end very little is explained and I did not feel attached to any of the characters or experiences.

[Redux Review]
+One of the best walking sims in existence, because it's one of the few which has both gameplay and narrative, not one or the other.
+Better graphics than most AAA studios.
-Could use some more interaction, but fits in with the story.

I saw one of my best friends, Zoerith, purchase this game... And that got me to check it out, saw that it was on a pretty wicked sale, and decided to pick it up, as she has a really good taste on platforming games. And you know what? I don't regret it. Now as usual, I will start my review on the negative parts of the game. Granted, I didn't find many stuff to talk about...
...But the biggest downside to the game is how short it is. I barely reached two hours on it. (EDIT: 2,7 hours to be precise) Sure, I will come back and probably try to get all the achievements and hidden stuff on it, but it's sad that a game with such potential decides to just last two hours. Infact, when I reached the ending and saw the credits roll in I was shocked and dissapointed, as I expected it to keep going. It's a 13€ game without sales. I do NOT think a game that lasts 2 hours is worth that. At all.
The other complains I have about it are rather minor stuff:
-When doing a Sprint-jump, you can't steer yourself in the air. You can steer in ALL other jumps except that one, and it feels more like they forgot about it.
-There are plenty of areas where you can sort of cheat through a section. If you manage to land somewhere, your hooks and rockets recharge, but I found plenty of areas where I was NOT supposed to land, keeping me away from falling to my death and cheating the area entirely. You can also clip through some rocks and walls in weird ways, for similar effects.
-The voice-acting and music is good... But the main character and narrator of the story sounds bored. I don't know, it's almost like he doesn't care at all at times. There are moments when he says stuff like "This is awesome" while sounding extremely bored and that's just anti-climatic.
-The hookshot range seems to be a bit random at times.
*EDIT*-The animations on other characters are really weird at times. Maybe those needed some extra polish, as they usually feel unfinished.
That being said, is the game good? Yeah, I do.
The story is good enough, and it gets the job done. It would do better if it was longer, but you know...
The sound design is really good, and if the main character didn't sound so bored, it would be even more amazing. The soundtrack is also really great, fits perfectly with the relaxed gameplay.
Where this game trully shines however, has to be n the levels. It's rare to see games push the engines on making levels this big and with so much detail. And it also doesn't run badly at all, it's really well optimized. The loading times are also nearly non-existent, which is great.
Gameplay, as I said, is really relaxing and simple. You can jump, you can use your suit to jump really far, you can use a weird laser-hookshot and later on even get something extra. There were a few areas where the gameplay conflicts with those weird bugs I mentioned above, but it was fresh throughout the entire game.
There are also unlockables and collectables. I didn't really mind them much, but found most of them on my first run. I will say that it's cool to change the color of the laser... But why the hell did the game need a Goat Simulator reference on them, I have no idea. The achievements are also REAL achievements and not like most other games, being harder to unlock. I only got two out of 15 or so on my first playthrough, and that gives me prupose to get back to it at some point.
So, in the end... Is it good? Yeah. However, I do NOT recommend it at the current price. I got it for like, 2€ or so. That's a really great deal, but I'd say more than 5€ could be too much. Bellow that, it's a garanteed must buy.

Quick summary: if you play casually in the easiest mode and do not care for achievement hunting, this is a FUN little game. Otherwise, be prepared to spend an awful LOT of time redoing some of those long levels!
These days I've been playing a lot of little match-3 games because they're quick to play and this prevents me from having to choose what 'big' game I'll be playing next, ah ah. I spent 200+ hours on Witcher 3 on GOG, so I come to Steam for shorter game sessions, out of habit. I'm giving this one a negative recommendation but a positive review, because if you're like me you tend to read negative reviews mostly and prefer to see well weighed opinions that will focus on the negative issues but still encourage you to try out the game if they don't bother you.
Out of everything I've played these last few weeks (Heroes of Hellen, Bejeweled, Montezuma, Luxor and a couple others), this is on par with Hellen in terms of complexity (although not as interesting), and much worse when it comes to readability. I think this is very important in a game, and if I fail some boards because some of the rules weren't properly explained, or because the rich graphics hurt your eyes (for instance, good luck trying to determine if that special tile needs brown, red or orange matches!), I tend to be unhappy and give up. The problem is that it gets excruciatingly long to finish a single board after the first few tutorialesque wonders. Indeed, after a while your levels will consist of 5 things you'll have to do and be careful about (1) destroy all tiles behind the gems by having them in a match, (2) destroy metal tiles twice, (3) collect up to 5 different resources from special gems (which will take the most effort to do, and don't even try to forget a single one if you don't want to waste more time!), (4) be careful with the board layout, as it often gets convoluted and forces you to use destructive powers in a few places, and (4) do a specific color match on two specific tiles (later in the game, the 'singled out' power-up will help you with those, but by the time you get it, you probably won't need it anymore.) And finally, (5), after you clear a board's tiles, a special gem drops that you must guide to the bottom of the board to finish it. At that point it's time to make sure you gathered all resources, and then use the Column power-up that will save you a lot of time.
I've just finished the main game after about 10 hours, and I'd estimate the latter half of the game has levels that would take more than 10 minutes to finish without power-ups, and you never have that time if you're playing in normal mode, so you'll have to use power-ups on a regular basis (thankfully, some of them like the slime monster recharge very quickly). I made a break of a few weeks between my first and second session, and totally forgot the game had power-ups, so... just don't, really, or your self-esteem will suffer. Early levels can be completed without them, but the latter half will systematically give you a shorter time than needed, and you'll have to rely on some of them regularly.
I need to mention achievements. Many Steam users enjoy trying to perfect their game, and this one isn't going to be easy. You can easily get two thirds of the achievements by the time you finish the game casually, but some of them are a bit unfair. For instance, there's an achievement you can only get when you finish it in normal mode *and* do not fail a single board. If you do fail one (and it will happen if you don't use power-ups regularly and watch their recharge status), you need to restart the current wonder from the start to ensure you get the achievement. Given that there are a minimum of 7 boards to complete before you can finish building a wonder, it means failing a board might actually force you to spend the next hour or two redoing what you previously completed successfully. This is a game that is best played in Zen mode, I imagine, and let's consider 'Normal' mode to be targeted to hardcore casuals; yes that category exists, that is, regular gamers who haven't come out of the casual closet yet. Ask your aunt what she does at night on the computer, she can give you advice.
There are also a few mini-games, some of which are fun (I like the lab one and the map parts one), but they're tied to achievements that require you to finish them all. Completing levels in 'Diamond Domino Mine' is very luck-based (you depend on a draw of items, and you have a limited number of redraws), and if you make a wrong move, there's no 'undo' button, you have to restart the level from scratch. Since that game itself isn't particularly exciting, after a while you just give up on it and the idea of perfecting your game achievements.
Other aspects of the game are pleasing, but I think the other reviews mention it enough. I would like to mention the spelling, though. I'm not an English native so I'd be the last person to be a grammar Nazi, and yes I'm aware that this was developed in Russia, and yes story is just a pretext, but there are typos here and there, and if they didn't caught by the US producers, then what can I say... Shows some lack of quality control.

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a beautifully rendered map with a tacked-on walking sim on top, an unfortunate union that failed to meet each and every one of my expectations. What a beautiful disaster.
I'm not new to walking sims. Ever since I started with Dear Esther years ago and kept going with the likes of Gone Home, I've thoroughly enjoyed this narrative genre and what it can offer in terms of ambience, feelings and story. I've had this one in the oven for the longest time, hearing all the praise it got. I saved it for a rainy day, one where I really craved a good story and a satisfying time.
Ethan Carter, to date, ranks as the worst walking sim out of the mainstream/famous ones.
In this game you're Paul Prospero, a paranormal investigator called to Red Creek Valley by a boy (the titular Ethan Carter) who is in dire need of your help. Arriving at the location through the woods, you'll start making your way toward the inhabited areas with long walks peppered with sparse first person narration.
The roads and rivers and hills are all beautifully rendered, really immersive and a joy to look at. The Redux version kicks everything up a notch and makes the lighting even more beautiful than it was before. It's a really well constructed map, with a great sense of scale and reasonable topography. The dam is really massive and imposing.
As you traverse these beautiful and eerily abandoned locations, you'll stumble upon murdered individuals; this is where the supposed "meat" of the game is. You need to recreate the scene of the murder by placing each item into its original position so you can use your paranormal sensitivity; by doing this, the spirit of the deceased will present you with a few character models scattered in the vicinity, representing the few minutes that precede their death. You'll then have to put these in order to see the relative cutscenes in motion and hear them talk, finding out bits of the mystery surrounding the valley.
This, sadly, is nothing but a gimmick that happens a very few times throughout the game. You have no real edge on this task, no skill or intuition will help you make it more satisfying: you simply walk until you find all the objects, place them in the only interactive slots that pop up, then order the trivial scenes that lead up to the murder. Don't worry, you can try again if you make mistakes.
Other interactions with the game are a handful of sidequest which feel entirely unrelated to the reasons that led you to the valley and absolute curve balls on top of that. These interactions vary from always walking forward, walking to follow an NPC, finding and clicking all the items, walking a maze and clicking on all the items. There's only a very interesting one, involving doors and impossible spaces, a minigame that I hoped was an integral part of the gameplay at the point in my playthrough. It wasn't.
The musical score is pretty good and really helps getting in the mood, be it relaxed or anxious. I have some issue with the sound design, as loud constant noises (i.e. a waterfall, the engine you're sitting on) go crazy when they're directly behind you, but other than that it's quite alright.
So that was the pretty and the neutral. Here's the bad.
The walks between each instance of interaction/narration are so long that this game ends up feeling more empty than regular, "pure" walking sims that have no interaction at all. While walking around with just the sound of the birds and the wind, I ended up asking myself "nice, but are we there yet?" at least 3 times throughout this 2h long game. This doesn't take in account the shorter walks where you can see your goal (so you know you're not there yet) but that still feel excessively long.
The characters are one-dimensional madmen, and the story is so dull that only a masterful narration and direction could've possibly saved it. As you can already imagine, none of that is present here. The re-enacting that lead up to the deaths are devoid of any drive and pathos, and failed to make me love or hate any of them. I was wholly indifferent toward them. The story, as cheap ones tend to, pulls a couple of twists toward the end that may catch you off guard but still not save the situation.
So that was the bad. Ready for the worst?
Imagine having gone through most of the above, and you're now at the ending. You've found all the characters, solved the mysteries and find yourself at the centerpiece of the narration. There! You've finished the game. Wait... no, the game stops you. Unfinished business? What? Well, you have to go back and clear all the sidequests you missed or skipped earlier in the game in order to see the ending. Not the extra ending. Not a secret ending. THE ending. The game even gives you a convenient map with the location of said sidequests so you can find them and trudge through them, then get back and see the ending.
I could've glossed over the neutral and the bad, remembering just the pretty, but the worst really did it for me. This game opens with a smug "this is an open narration, there's no holding hands here" and puts me down a very long (albeit deceptively large) corridor, only to tell me at the end that I have to go back and check all the (few) boring or hidden rooms the game itself led me to think I was allowed to skip.
That was the last straw. I quit the game and checked the ending on Youtube.
What started as a promising experience and slowly turned into an unimpressive sequence of tasks, ultimately ended as an infuriating husk of a game and an offence to my intelligence, my money and my time.
Please consider carefully before purchasing this game. It's not bad per se, but it's a poor walking simulator, unredeemed by its bland and gimmicky interactions, and an even worse experience overall if you've played more than a handful of games in your life.

After reading all the good reviews and getting a "its alright" from a friend I finally bought this game.
But why does my opinion differ so strongly?
First of all the positive: It looks really nice, nothing mindblowing, but nice sceneries. Sound design is good too.
But then the game just fails in all other aspects unfortunately. I am not sure how people can find the story anything above average. The characters never get any color or depth, no mystery that gets "unmystified" or something and no real writing you can dig into either. You can sum up the story in about half a page wihtout missing any details at all and it would blandy reveal how simple it is without the graphics.
I'm not the biggest walking simulator fan there is, but I had much fun with them in the past. I would like to especially compare it to Gone Home, which was more interesting, with a much more satisfying ending and it had even less gameplay than Ethan Carter.
Lets get to the worst part IMHO, the "game" or the "naration method" if you like. It consists of a few "puzzles" while only 2 of them are even close to being puzzles at all. Which was very disappointing because there was one door puzzle which was really neat, but nothing good came after it. The other main part of the story mechanic is just a useless run around and inspect stuff mechanics, which then tells you about a interaction between people that happened there, only that the stuff that happened is completely uninteresting and does not really contribute to make the overall plot more interesting.
Last but not least the gameplay/narration concept is just a big hypocrite. At the start the game tells you something along the lines of "this is a narrative game that doesn't hold your hand". Sounds good right? Sounds good until it shoots itself in the foot. One step before the ending you get told you have to solve all puzzles to progress further which completely torpedoed the promise at the start. What use does a "free narative game that doesnt hold my hand" have when in the end it slaps me in the face and sends me back to the start in the worst case. Unbelievable.
To end on a positive note, it was nice to figure out the mechanics and especially the good puzzle completely by myself, instead of getting tutorialed at the start. But that does not save the game unfortunately.
Do not buy unless you love walking around in a neat environment for some hours + sale.

I bought this game on sale for around $3, but still can't help but feel dissatisfied.
Pros:
As mentioned in other reviews, the game is visually stunning. It simply looks great. If you're after a piece of eye candy to view on your high end PC, this game is for you. Furthermore, the soundtrack was on point for most of the game, and fitted the game's atmosphere.
Cons:
I had some crashes, freezes, and bugs, that forced me to restart the game multiple times throughout my playthrough. This caused me to annoyingly spend time backtracking and redoing tasks already completed which weren't saved by the game's autosave feature. I hear that the Redux edition mostly fixes these problems, but I've yet to play it myself. Regardless, the problems I have with this game are one's that can't be solved with tweaks and updates, and instead come from the core elements of the game itself.
The biggest problem with The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is its bad plot and weak story telling elements. The story is interesting in the beginning, but your interest steadily deteriorates as the game progresses and the game's lackluster plot   begins to emerge. What is toted as an engaging mystery, ends up becoming a monotonous one packed with mediocre puzzles and player interaction.
The story is presented through a traditional mystery game format, the clues given via multiple fragments and in a non-linear fashion. However, as the clues conjoin and the pieces of the story are put together, you're left with an impression of complete indifference. What could be an intriguing mystery ends up becoming a washed up version of a horror-adventure game. The character development is non existant, and what characters are developed are boring and dull. These characters are tailor-made cliches stamped with bland characterization, and you find it difficult to remember their names and their personalities. In addition, the voice acting is sub-par, and the dialogue is not convincing or at all interesting to read and listen to.
There are some areas where the story peaks your interest, particularily in the examination of the game's written clues. However, these brief moments of intrigue soon lead to continued boredom and disappointment. Whatever story you've managed to collect and understand is made completely redundant by the terrible ending of the game, which is presented to you in a "twist ending". You hoped as you played the game, that maybe a great conclusion would tie together the loose ends of the story and leave you with a satisftying smile on your face. This does not happen. Perhaps, with better writing and plot progression the "twist ending" would still be satisfying, but this is not the case. You hoped through your playthrough that it would all come together in the end. It didn't.
A good analogy for buying this game would be this: You're hungry for sweets and so you go out shopping. You look around, not sure what to buy. Then, you come across a beautifully decorated cake. The icing covering it looks incredible, and the patissier crafted it delightfuly. You buy it and take it home, for a fair price too. You open the box of cake and cut your first slice. It looks great! But as you lift the slice and place it onto your plate, you realize that the inside is rather dark. You prod the piece with your fork, and it feels hard. You scrape some icing off the top and you discover that it's burned. Uh oh. Well, you got it on sale, what can you expect? Plus, you're hungry, so you decide to eat some cake. Your fork manages to cut a piece from your slice of cake and you put it into your mouth. You first taste the sweet icing and you momentarily convince yourself that the cake is good, that your purchase was well justified. But as you continue savouring the flavour, you realize that the icing on top cannot cover the burned texture of the cake itself. It slowly begins to taste worse as you continue eating it, but you do so because you're hungry. However, the icing's sweetness begins to loose its effect as you continue eating and the dull, burned, flavour begins to overpower you. You're completely disappointed, but you tough it out. It's not bad enough to make you spit it out, but it isn't good either. Finally, you finish the cake, and look at the now nearly empty box the cake once lay upon. You see a single cherry in the box! It must have fallen off the cake! You reach for the sweet looking cherry that will surely clear the bland taste of the cake from your palate and throw it into your mouth. It's extremely sour! What a twist! But, wait. It doesn't fit with the cake at all, and it doesn't taste very good. What a disappointment.

LISA is probably one of the few games that are really able to make someone heart strong for a good thing and let it shatter into a thousand pieces that can not be glued together.
________________________________________________________________________________
***Story***
The story is set in a postapocalyptic world where all women are gone. There are only men left, with their brutalilty, ignorance, but vulnerability and wretchedness as well. Not every men is a warrior or born to be wild. Some of them are simple losers or complete dip♥♥♥♥♥ who want to have a part of the big price: The only girl that can save humanity, and I do not need to explain how. Your mission is to walk after her, make friends who help you and save her from them all. Besides that, the game does not tell you everything you see or hear. That gives you enough space to start thinking and to create lore for the game.
***Grafics***
The grafics are drawn with love. It is not just some pixel♥♥♥♥♥♥like games you are used to play nowadays that are oh-so-retro. From kind of sexy (I loved those posters of women in the Tower of Power) to absolutely disturbing and mind ♥♥♥♥ing.
***Music***
The sound design and the music are amazing. Darkly mixed psycho-hiphop reminds of the good old days where you fought Giygas in Earthbound. HIGHLY RECOMMENDED. BUY THE SOUNDTRACK.
***Gameplay***
Typical RPG fighting style, SP replace Mana while TP (Technique Points, there are only 2 characters that I saw who use them) have to be build up every time a fight starts. The system is round based, so you have enough time to think about what to do next. LISA is most definitely my GOTY 2014. And I've played a lot of games this past year. Everything about it is amazing to experience, from the music to the gameplay, to the characters, to the story.
When you first start, the introductory story segment draws you in to the point where, when the gameplay was being introduced, I worried it'd suck, since the story was so good. It didn't. The gameplay's fun as ♥♥♥♥. The battles are challenging, especially so on Pain mode (the hardest difficulty), and the events of the game that can seperate you from your most valued party members are brutal. By the way, those events aren't scripted. Olen can get his head bitten off, or Nern can be kidnapped. Or vice versa. Really, no one is safe. Be ready to lose those you value most.
The battles run a little like the Mother/Earthbound games. The characters in your party lack the typical class of Fighter/Mage/Rogue, and instead have abilities based off their actual character. For instance, Nern, a really chatty fellow, has abilities that involve around talking. Telling Ghost Stories to spook your enemies into not acting-- insulting them to make them go berserk. Discussing health with an ally to recover HP.
These quirks help flesh out these characters, and you'll quickly find yourself favoriting some over others, based off their skillset/character setup.
As for the diversity of these characters-- there are around 35, if I remember correctly, each with skills unique to themselves. There can be some similarities between them, but nothing that makes you think they're a copy of another character. Roles can overlap, though this isn't a problem due to how sparesly that occurs, and how many options you have for your party.
Recruiting these characters can be as simple as buying them a drink, to holding their lover hostage so they join you.
The story. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥the story. Depending on the choices you make, you'll either feel awful about yourself, or you'll feel oppressed by everything around you. I won't say how (it'll be obvious when you encounter it), but it's possible to complete the game with no arms-- just kicking, biting, headbutting, and tackling everything in your way. The story is one of the best in any game I've ever played. I'll just leave it at that. The atmosphere while playing reminds me of the tense darkness, and the maddening overlay that Hotline Miami has. That depressed, insane, vibe. The music also is reminiscent of Hotline Miami, and fits the game's style great.
I've already bought this game for two people, and I'll probably buy more copies for others. It's a shame this game isn't more well known, it's amazing. For 10$, it's a steal. I completed the game in 13 hours on the painful mode, and I still didn't do everything I could've. About to start my second run after I finish this review.

DungeonUp is an interesting little puzzle game with slight RPG elements, with procedurally generated levels. Sounds like a good game with lots of replayablity right? Well, yes and no.
Let me first explain something. This is NOT a Rouge-like! A normal Rouge-like game loves to provide little to no info on ANYTHING, and the only way to figure out what things are, like an item, you have to use it and suffer the effects if it's good or bad. Rouge-likes focus more on trial and error, and whether you feel lucky or not. This game does not do that. This game tells you EVERYTHING you need to know! It tells you exactly what each item does (before you even pick it up,) the stats of each monster, and whether you will survive the fight or not. This is a pet peeve of mine when people miss-use the term Rouge-Like and even Rouge-Lite. This is 100% a puzzle game with slight RPG elements, and heavily relying on RNG. *mini rant over.
The main objective to DungeonUp is to level up your character's stats, so you can fight and kill the harder monsters without dying, then fighting the boss at the end to move onto the next zone. You repeat this until you finish the game. However! This is not a straight forward run and kill everything. This game requires a little bit of strategy, as most monsters are way more powerful than you at the start. You will be avoiding most monsters at first, finding small upgrades and big upgrades to increase your damage and defense. Only then are you able to start attacking monsters and having them deal less damage to you or no damage at all.
How the procedurally generated levels work, is there is certain floors that will always be the same, such as the starting room, altar rooms, boss rooms, and certain special rooms. Otherwise everything is randomly generated, and you are at the mercy of RNG. This does provide lots of possibilities, but also limits the game as well. You will end up seeing tons of useless rooms, doors, monsters just being put into areas that you really don't want to waste keys just to go kill that one monster for 2 gold coins.
You don't gain any XP in this game, instead you earn gold coins from defeating monsters. Your main currency is Gold Coins, and you use it to purchase an item(s) from randomly placed Merchants through out the game, or save them for purchasing upgrades from altars. The upgrades you can purchase from the altars is either small health boost, more attack, or more defense. Each time you purchase 1 upgrade, the price goes up. Now it's in your best interest to NOT buy any upgrades right away, but to actually wait till you get farther to the later alters, as the upgrades are might higher. When you reach the first altar in the first zone, each upgrade only gives you +2. Now if you waited till the third zone, the upgrades will be +8 Attack/+16 Defense, for the same price! Meaning if you didn't purchase any upgrades, your first upgrade would only be worth 20 coins! You can really up your stats that way and make the game that much easier.
You also have a second currency, Soul Stones. These are only be acquired from defeating bosses. You can use Soul Stones to purchase rare artifacts in the altar rooms, use them to give you 1 yellow key, or even use them to revive yourself if you die (which reverts you to the start, or last boss you defeated.) Even if you die and choose to retry and it keeps your Soul Stones, making the game slightly easier so you can purchase the expensive rare items.
Now this is considered a puzzle game, as you only have a limited amount of keys to open doors. There is 3 different keys, Yellow being the common key, Blue keys, and red keys being the boss/final locked door. You will find these scattered around the levels, mostly guarded by monsters. You can sometimes be lucky and find a hidden passage that can let you bypass a door all together and help you save your keys. There is points in the game where you do need a blue key to progress, and a red key to open the boss battle. You have to plan out your actions, cause if you open too many wrong doors, you can screw yourself over and not be able to progress.
Now this is where I have a complaint. As all the maps are procedurally generated, you are at the pity of RNG. For most of my games, I've been f*cked over by RNG MANY times! One example is having the game spawn the same rare item 3 times! Causing the other items you need to beat the game to not spawn. My case was having the "Wand of Flight" spawn 3 times, so I could never get the "Holy Cross" and the "Ring of Anti-magic" thus not being able to beat the game. Another case was having all the Blue keys being blocked by enemies that were impossible to kill at my current stage, and could not progress because I needed to pass a blue door. So I could not beat the game.
So all the boss fights have a "strategy" that will help you either make the boss a little easier to fight, or it's the only way to beat the boss. You are given hints about this from NPCs you find along your path. Some are not as obvious though, and can make certain boss impossible to beat. So you need a guide to be able to beat the bosses. Combine that with the RNG and possibly not spawning the correct item(s) you need to beat said bosses, can make the game seem unfair.
There is another gamemode called "Maze Mode" where you have limited resources and limited information. Maze Mode is played on a HUGE randomly generated map, where you will end up just going in circles being lost and trying to finish the one map. Having played a few maps, I was not able to complete a single map. I strongly do not recommend playing this mode, as it's not very fun.
DungeonUp also includes a map editor that can upload to the Steam Workshop. This sounds like a great idea to allow people to make some well planned out and great maps. But there isn't any, and there really isn't anyone making maps for it. Part of the reason why is the map editor is TERRIBLE! There is no tool tips, and hovering over an item does not tell you anything on what it is, so you have to be very trial and error and see if things work.
PROS:
- Great sounds and Soundtrack. (Can get repetitive, but can be disabled.)
- Graphics are nice.
- Good selection of special items.
- Procedurally generated maps.
- Takes some strategy and thinking.
- Achievements.
- Steam Trading Cards.
CONS:
- Very repetitive.
- Monsters can seem too powerful.
- Procedurally generated maps. (RNG can make sh*ty floors.)
- RNG can not work and screw you over easily.
- Bosses require guide to beat.
- Maze mode is horrible.
- Map Maker has small issues make it a struggle to use.
By no means is this game horrible to play, it just has minor issues that prevent it from being super good. For $5 it's not that bad of a deal, but when in doubt, get it while on sale.

Take note, though, that this game is pointedly not an open world game. It is procedurally generated and has branching paths, but there is no turning back, and you can only play out one scenario- a quest to defeat the rebel flagship. It's challenging enough that you'll probably go through a number of playthroughs before you even see the flagship for the first time, much less defeat it. But once you've done it a few times, you might find yourself wanting for something new, even if you haven't technically finished the game.

Welcome to the HELLDIVERS elite infantry unit, recruit. We are the personification of humanities greatest accomplishements. Listen closely and maybe you will survive your very first mission!
-We are the good guys! - A wonderful sense of humor in the fashion of Paul Verhoeven (Starship Troopers).
-Grow and learn! - A progression system that gives you new character skins, weapons, perks, stratagems (airstrikes, heavy weapons, vehicles, tools like attack- and repairdrones etc..) and upgrade points to enhance your favorite play toys.
-Adapt! - No classes, just pick your loadout before every mission. Look at your comrades equipment and take the stuff your team lacks. Or just play your favorite and most effective build which suits your personal playstyle most.
-Be proud! - Individualize your HELLDIVERS elite soldier with tons of helmets, armor and capes.
-Know your enemy! - Fight 3 different factions: Cyborgs, Bugs and Illuminates. Each with their very own units, different strategies, advantages and such.
-Be percise! - The game controls just awesome no matter if you use M+K or a controller (The game detects every controller just fine and lets you rebind keys).

-Watch your step, watch your aim! - Friendly fire is always on - Everything is able to kill you. Everything!
-You are the veterans of tomorrow! - 12 different difficulties for a challange. The higher the difficulties, the more teamplay you need to be succsessful. The game is pretty well balanced. Almost every mechanic is a risk/reward one of some sorts.

-Do your duty, soldier! - Take part in an actual war. Every single player has the responsibility to change the tides. Take back the galaxy bit by bit as a whole community.

Gunman Clive is a very unique, super polished, platformer.  Taking place in the old west, you embark on a rescue mission.  There isn't much of a story but that doesn't matter.  This highly-stylized adventure is not only beautiful but a blast to play.  It may take a lot of inspiration from classic platformers but the game is a whole new twist on the genre that is definitely worth checking out.
At its core, the gameplay is quite simple.  Dodge enemy bullets, return fire, and navigate the various obstacles in your way.  Your reflexes will be tested as the action is fast.  This helps simulate the feeling of being stuck in the middle of the shoot-outs you see in a classic western.  When you're not exchanging fire there a plenty of platforming segments as you jump around various moving objects.  The tight controls leave no need for guess work.  You'll feel great with the mobility of your character feeling very fluid and natural.
You can choose to play as Clive or Ms.Johnson, the other of which will be kidnapped.  There isn't too much of a difference between the two, Clive can move a little faster and Ms.Johnson can float for a bit.  After beating the game a third character is unlocked that plays dramatically different.  As you proceed on this rescue mission you pass through several different environments.  These include the desert, the woods, a cave, and beyond.  Each area provides new, varied, obstacles and enemies that will try to slow you down.
One of the neatest parts of this experience is the artwork.  The backgrounds and characters look like they popped right out of a stretch book.  As the lines shift and dance on screen it really feels like a drawing has come to life.  The arrangement of the soundtrack is also superb.  Clearly who ever composed the music for this game knew exactly how to set up a wonderful atmosphere.  As you play through the levels, even if you die, the music keeps playing.  This really helps keep you in the game and ready to face the challenges set before you.
I absolutely adore this game.  From the beautiful artwork, to the smooth platforming, everything about this game fits perfectly.  If you're a fan of old-school platformers you need to play Gunman Clive.  Even those who don't play this genre as much can enjoy this game for its atmosphere.  I'm still having fun in my second play-through and I'm really looking forward to playing the sequel.  So put on your cowboy hat and charge in guns blazing.

When it comes to me and my relationship with video games, Point & Click genre games are my main one. They speak to me the most, fit my personality the most, are the ones I have the best mind for, and a pretty good one at that, at least I believe. It was while I was seeing if it was plausible to get a twitch streamer I use to watch to play a fav of mine, that one or two other watchers said in the chat that this game was the new hot point & click game to play.
I prefer my point & click games to be ones where you socialize. Ones where you talk to people and are immediately told where you are and what the deal is. So I was off put at first that this game doesn't do either of those things. You're completely lost, isolated, and don't know where you are, and no one is around. It's a game where you're supposed to feel lonely. Since I suffer from chronic depression IRL, partly caused by loneliness, I really disliked at first this aspect. After the second attempt to play this is when I got successfully hooked.
I hate the gamer mentality of "I dub this game really good at being pretty, beautiful, and atmospheric, RIGHT NOW AS SOON I'M STARTING IT!" It's pretentious, and puts pressure on people thinking of playing the game to display as much "good behavior" pretension. I say no, it's better to be an "a**hole", and appreciate the beauty and atmosphere, IDK, when your on your flippin' death bed, as long as it's after playing the game for a nice long time/well after you've finished it. I don't give an f when I first start it, no one deserves to get that much sucking up. It's better to never say the game is beautiful than to say it is at record speed.
The memory I have of the feeling I got from the game after getting into it AFTER A GOOD WHILE OF PLAYING IT,  I liked quite a lot. That's what is suppose to happen. The key to games like this is suppose to be time, and a lot of it. I REMEMBER it being beautiful and atmospheric in a pretty solidly good way. It's mechanics and challenges took some getting use to, but they where pretty good too.
My biggest complaint is the story. It's a good story up until the end. To keep this spoiler free, I'll keep it to just saying this: 60's and 70's folk music artists like Simon & Garfunkel, who sang regularly about how much it sucks to live in the big city and how they'd rather feel the earth beneath their feet, apparently where completely wrong according to whoever wrote this game. According to him, if you move out to the wilderness with your family, the adults you live with will apparently NOT WANT YOU to enjoy the earth beneath your feet. They rather you burn to death than experience the outside. So stop complaining and just shut up Simon & Garfunkel, the city is just fine to be trapped in. THAT DOESN'T MAKE ANY SENSE!!!!
I recommend this game, just ignore to asinine writing toward the end.

LISA is most definitely my GOTY 2014. And I've played a lot of games this past year. Everything about it is amazing to experience, from the music to the gameplay, to the characters, to the story.
When you first start, the introductory story segment draws you in to the point where, when the gameplay was being introduced, I worried it'd suck, since the story was so good. It didn't. The gameplay's fun as ♥♥♥♥. The battles are challenging, especially so on Pain mode (the hardest difficulty), and the events of the game that can seperate you from your most valued party members are brutal. By the way, those events aren't scripted. Olen can get his head bitten off, or Nern can be kidnapped. Or vice versa. Really, no one is safe. Be ready to lose those you value most.
The battles run a little like the Mother/Earthbound games. The characters in your party lack the typical class of Fighter/Mage/Rogue, and instead have abilities based off their actual character. For instance, Nern, a really chatty fellow, has abilities that involve around talking. Telling Ghost Stories to spook your enemies into not acting-- insulting them to make them go berserk. Discussing health with an ally to recover HP.
These quirks help flesh out these characters, and you'll quickly find yourself favoriting some over others, based off their skillset/character setup.
As for the diversity of these characters-- there are around 35, if I remember correctly, each with skills unique to themselves. There can be some similarities between them, but nothing that makes you think they're a copy of another character. Roles can overlap, though this isn't a problem due to how sparesly that occurs, and how many options you have for your party.
Recruiting these characters can be as simple as buying them a drink, to holding their lover hostage so they join you.
The story. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥the story. Depending on the choices you make, you'll either feel awful about yourself, or you'll feel oppressed by everything around you. I won't say how (it'll be obvious when you encounter it), but it's possible to complete the game with no arms-- just kicking, biting, headbutting, and tackling everything in your way. The story is one of the best in any game I've ever played. I'll just leave it at that. The atmosphere while playing reminds me of the tense darkness, and the maddening overlay that Hotline Miami has. That depressed, insane, vibe. The music also is reminiscent of Hotline Miami, and fits the game's style great.
I've already bought this game for two people, and I'll probably buy more copies for others. It's a shame this game isn't more well known, it's amazing. For 10$, it's a steal. I completed the game in 13 hours on the painful mode, and I still didn't do everything I could've. About to start my second run after I finish this review.
Buy it.

The Artstyle is
for this game. It's inspired by the cult classic
, but still maintains its own sense of style and personality, setting it apart from other games entirely. I instantly fell in love seeing it for the first time. The world itself isn't the only thing that's beautifully crafted, the battle system is still quite charming. When you preform moves and combos, your characters will actually do animated attacks, instead of just effects. Enemies do not, but that's a minor issue, it feels natural. The only issue I had was that the background of the battles feel a little uninspired and not very colorful, just sort of bland.
The music is perfectly crafted to fit to the theme of this game. Often I would find myself leaving the game open just to listen to the slick tunes. The sounds tie together the feeling of this game, neither being boring or intrusive.
This game is both visually and soundly a treat to anyone who enjoys retro rpgs and sidescrollers.
Much like
, this game doesn't let you spam attack and win. Every character is unique though, some of them preform moves based off a combo system, some characters work off a resource called "Technique Points" which build up by preforming standard attacks and taking damage, while other characters keep the standard "Special Points" casting like Magic Points. It keeps fights from feeling mundane and keeps you on your toes. This game isn't a pushover, either. It's initially a bit scary, as the world doesn't entirely restrict you from running into dangerous areas. Over time you will develop strategies that can break the game, but this is part of the fun of it. The status effects are entirely original, ranging from ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to 'weird' to 'drunk', in addition to your standard 'poison'. The enemies isn't the only thing out to get you though, as you will run into thugs and thieves looking to take your buddies, mags, and even your arms! Choices have permanent effects that you must live with. This game also allows you to set up your own party", picking from 30 total characters to roll with on your journey, allowing you to play exactly how you want.
If the game is too easy for you, you can also play the much harder "Pain" difficulty, only letting you save once per savepoint, adding more difficult bosses, and even bonuses.
My personal gripe is that a lot of the moves feel very "samey" and fail to explain very much.
This game has a perfect mixture of lighthearted humor and dark mature themes. It's not afraid to jump from one to the other in a moment. This is definitely the strongest point in the game and will keep you wanting to go on. This is difficult to talk about without spoiling anything, because this is an experience that has to be felt first hand. The choices feel real and the danger feels real too, the entire game will leave you asking yourself "
".
If this game was released on the NES or SNES, it would be a legend. It stands out from other indie games by both being quality but also well written. There are a few bugs and hitches from the RPGmaker engine, but anyone could overlook them and forget about it because of how well put together this game is. I recommend it with all of my fury, it's the best RPG I've played in a long time. The devs are also very helpful and active, please give this game a chance so they can make more wonderful content in the future!
