Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

A short (1-2 hours long) retro-styled platformer with a focus on non-linear exploration.  It does a good job of making simple power-ups feel rewarding and the map connects in interesting ways that makes backtracking not feel too tedious, which is important since you'll spend a decent bit of the game retreading old ground looking for areas that are now reachable due to your newly found power-ups.  It really captured the feeling of "oh cool, that's how I get over there."
There are some annoyingly hard rooms, but checkpoints are frequent and you respawn immediately.  If the CRT and visuals aren't to your liking, you can modify them in the options to be more colorful and drop the monitor within a monitor effect.
There's also very little hand-holding involved.  You basically start up the game and explore with no intrusion.  A fun little game which has more depth than you'd expect for a free, retro-themed platformer.

Oh boy, where to begin?
Vampires : The Masquarade : Bloodlines is one of those games that become classics the moment you turn them on. The closest thing I could relate it to, both in terms of gameplay and overall feeling is the first Deus Ex, as in both games you are some kind of superhuman who gets to master disciplines and powers in an RPG fashion in a game that gives you complete freedom in how to tackle the problems it throws at you (The third Deus Ex could qualify as well, but it tends to make the various intended paths obvious to you right off the bat, rather than letting you think of creative approaches yourself), and each clan (read : Character class) helps complement those playstyles.
I'm not really going to say much more, because at this point, you should know whether the game interests you or not, but know this :
- Steam only provides the retail version of the game, which is notoriously buggy (not just minor stuff, I'm talking about the game being outright unbeatable or just crashing all the time) because Activision insisted that the game be released the same day as Half Life 2. This version only includes the most critical fixes, like getting the game to start on computers with more than 1GB of video RAM. You definitely should download the unofficial patch (which actually includes "official" fixes) at this adress :
- As enjoyable as I found the experience, the game really begins to lose itself in the last few missions, where levels become longer, much more linear, and where non-combat builds start becoming a lot less viable. The last bosses (which one you get depends on your choices) are especially bad about this, as you probably won't leave a scratch on them unless your combat skills are at least level 8 or 9, but they go down in seconds once they are. Just keep that in mind if you're planning to go down a more non-combat route.
- If you go for stealth, prepare for some set pieces to look weird., like enemies busting in through a window or blowing up a wall and then stand there doing nothing.
This said, if you're a fan of RPGs, and especially if you liked the first Deus Ex, you owe yourself to play that game.

TL;DR:  As a “classic” game in the modern era, Star Wars: Battlefront 2 holds up quite well to modern standards and is very much playable even if for just nostalgia’s sake.  Despite older graphics, minor AI issues, and the need to now use third-party software for multiplayer, the game proves itself worthy to stand as an example of what the Battlefront series should represent – chaotic combat, open-world maps, and team-based gameplay.
With the advent of EA’s Battlefront, who are now releasing their Battlefront 2, I figured it was high time to write a review of the original Battlefront 2 game.  Having not played EA’s Battlefront, I cannot say I like or dislike it, but I can say that I believe I would put many hours into it if I could.  But that is even more reason why I think this Battlefront 2 should get more recognition as “the original”.  This game did a lot considering when it was made and should be looked at as how a Battlefront game should be made in my opinion.
Star Wars: Battlefront 2 is a third-person/first-person shooter that allows the player to experience some of the largest, most well-known battles in the Star Wars universe as well as some of the lesser known battles.  This is done through both ground and space battles and with a wide variety of both character and vehicle classes.
There are three primary modes of gameplay:  campaign, galactic conquest, and instant action.  The campaign tells the story of the 501st legion, Vader’s Fist, from their trial by fire on Geonosis to their final raid on Hoth.  The story isn’t exactly compelling, but it provides an interesting view from a different side of the Star Wars story.  Galactic conquest allows the player to pick a side, either Droids, Clones, Empire, or Rebels, and gives the goal of conquering the galaxy.  The player is provided credits for holding and capturing planets and can used those credits to increase the ranks of their army, buy a fleet, or buy bonuses.  Instant action allows the player to create a playlist of different maps and game modes and jump right into the action with or against friends.
Gameplay is simple:  You choose a class, such as sniper or anti-tank, and spawn at a friendly base.  Your goal, generally, is to capture enemy bases, but that can vary in modes such as capture the flag or the interesting Hunt mode.  Vehicles will spawn at bases for the players to use, ranging from light attack vehicles to transports like AT-ATs…and that is basically it.  The real fun comes when combat starts and you have infantry and tanks mixed together fighting for a base.  The ensuing chaos is, honestly, one of the best things about the game.  While you can use the character and vehicle classes to your advantage (and you should), it is just as fun to be a regular clone or rebel and hop into the fight.  Losing doesn’t feel like losing because it happens so spectacularly, something that especially holds true on maps like Tantive IV and Polis Massa.  Space combat is no different, and dogfighting can be equally as fun as boarding the enemy ship.
For a game that is over 10 years old, this game did a lot:  upwards of 20 maps, a full campaign, an updated galactic conquest mode, 32 player battles (64 on PC).  It isn’t without issues.  The AI can be…weird, getting stuck on walls and committing suicide and the like, and as fun as the map is, Tantive IV is still a bit buggy.  Some may find the graphics unappealing, but there are plenty of mods for the game that deal with that and much, much more.  Sadly, multiplayer servers have been shut down, but there are ways to play with friends through services like GameRanger.  Overall, it is a fantastic game worthy of a spot in your library and a great game to play with friends.
Whether due to nostalgia or curiosity, you should buy this game.  You won’t regret it.  May the Force be with you, watch those wrist rockets, GG and Good Hunting.

Years later, an unknown cataclysm has rendered the earth near uninhabitable, with all women gone and the world's remaining men dying off

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a visually stunning game that is set in an open world environment in which the player can roam and explore whilst trying to find out what happened to Ethan Carter. As you first start the game, the visuals and atmosphere instantly hit you. You will find yourself constantly panning the camera throughout the game just to take in the scenery. It really is breathtaking.
As you progress through the game, you will have to use your paranormal abilities in order to solves crimes, such as sensing where important objects are located, or puzzles, such as reassembling the timeline of events tied to a certain deaths.
The majority of puzzles are moderately easy to solve through logic and common sense. There are one or two that might prove tricky to you, but not enough to ruin your experience and the flow of the game where you will be constantly pausing to look at walkthroughs. Each time you complete a puzzle or you correctly assembled a death sequence in the right order, more of the story and more answers as to what is happening will open up to you, such as completing a death sequence will show you who killed who and what their motive was.
The story is full of mystery, intrigue and on the dark side. Overall the pacing of the story is great and the telling of the story is well balanced. The game gives you enough bread crumbs so answers to questions will appear, but not enough to the point where the plot is ruined and you know how the story will end. There will be times where you have no idea what is happening and why. Some things might seem out of place to you, but as you progress through the game, the story starts to wrap up very nicely with some twists along the way.
Overall, The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a fantastic game. The only downside is that the game is rather short and the achievements are easy to obtain but if you're looking to play a game with a fantastic story in an atmospheric world then this is a game I would recommend.
Overall score 9/10.

First off, just a friendly note~ If you're easily frustrated, don't like losing, are ill tempered or impatient, don't get this game.
FTL is a rogue-like game where you take the role of the captain of a Federation ship on a mission to deliver a message to the Federation fleet and fight the Rebel's flagship. This is no easy task.... At all... In fact, it takes people hundreds of tries to finally defeat the flagship. It's a task even to get there, BUT! That's part of the fun! The difficulty makes for an exciting story and with the free "Advanced Edition", adds even more complexity to an already astounding game.
The game relies heavily on stats, RNG and getting everything just right. Someruns will be perfect, others, you'll have your rear end handed to you on a silver platter. It's exciting to see your ship and your crew make it through not repairing for 8 sectors, the thrill of getting a brand new weapon of mass destruction, and the tension of first fighting the flagship.
But it doesn't stop with the Kestrel! You can complete tasks and quests and in some cases, very very difficult, convoluted and secret missions to obtain new ships and ship layouts. It's all very very satusfiying once you do, and some of them make the game easier whereas some other up the difficulty. Each ship has its own play-style as well. I, alas, only have experience with the basic layouts of the first two: The Kestrel and the Engi ship who's name escapes me. The Kestrel is an allaround workhorse ship. It'll do nearly anything you need it to. The Engi is a fragile ship but comes standard with and ion weapon to disable an enemy's shields and a drone bay to launch an attack drone.
The game is extreamly rewarding if you have the gall to face it.
I hope this was helpful and happy hunting, commanders!!

I'd always heard the name FTL being mentioned as an amazing game. Unfortunately I was never smart enough to look up more than a screen shot or two. I got it on a whim during a sale...oh my.
FTL has very little to no story but still manages to build a world inside your head. Where it shines is in it's mechanics. It should be said from the get go that this is a "roguelike" and a difficult one at that. Death can happen at almost any point, sometimes due to bad play or just hard luck. Many people will see some of these deaths as plain unfair, and that's fair enough. As for myself, i loved that aspect. No matter how much i grew to understand the fundementals, how stong my ship was or how trained my crew were, there was always a chance of flying into a sector (could be classed as rooms?) and being overwhelmed by evnviromental hazards, a pirate ship, or ,erchants who may or may not be who they claim to be.
You play as one of many Federation ships carrying vital information that you must travel across the galaxy to deliver whilst a Rebel fleet are constantly in your tail. You must travel from beacon to beacon across 8 or so sectors (floors?) to fight the Rebel Flagship and destroy it to emerge victorious and win the game. You will have to manage crew members, along with your ships weapons and systems. Crew members can man systems such as the Cockpit, Engines, Weapons etc... and get better get better at manning each individual system. Struggling to dodge those pesky lasers or missiles? Maybe Bugsy Face slasher or whatever ridiculous name you decide to give that crew member who's been hanging around the ship being useless, could jump in the engines room and after he spends some time will grant you some extra dodge chance. Or you could just invest some of that scrap (currency of the game) that you stole from those pirates into upgrading the shield systems. I'd recommend you do both, but hey, you're the captain!
Battles occur in real time but you can pause at anytime Pausing is crucial to your survival and tactical planning. For example, an enemy ship will fire a laser at you, which will begin recharging as soon as it fires, however they also have missles. While you may have good enough engines and piloting to maybe dodge the missile, maybe it's better to let the laser fire, and pause on and off to see if the missile will fire before the laser makes contact with shield or hits a vital system in your ship before you activate your Stealth systems, allowing you to dodge both projectiles.
Members of your crew can die and will die in a variety of ways. Your Oxygen system can be completely shot down, meaning you'll have to scramble amongst crew members who haven't already taken damage to rush and fix the systems, rapidly losing air and their health in the process. Some Races are better than this than others. The Engi, for example are not good fighters but their repair skills are unmatched. Mantis crew are great at hand-to-hand combat, making them excellent boarders using Teleporters or defence against enemy boarders.
Teleporters are one of many Systems you can install on your ship, allowing a certain number of crew to jump onto the enemy ship for some close quarters battle. There are Cloning Bays that will replace Medbays, allowing your crew to come back from the dead, as long as you can keep it powered. Stealth systems to cloak your entire ship giving you a much better dodge chance. Drone systems which will allow you to buy and equid a variety of offensive or defensive drones. These systems along with the rest of the game will take some time to wrap your head around but once you do, you will be comfortable enouh to decide which ones to use and which to avoid for better or for worse as your ship only has so many slots for these systems.
Every jump to a new beacon, you will be met with one of many situations, be it a crew of passive locals who needs some spare fuel or equipment, a hostile ship armed to the teeth, honest travelers, conniving captains, or just the lonely occupancy of empty space. You will find shops, allowing you to spend scrap on getting that sexy new gun, a well needed drone or just repairing your ships hull (HP).
This can become overwhelming very fast in FTL. A crew of dangerous Mantis can board onto your ship. Fires will spread damaging important systems. Shields system can be severly damaged and your enemy has lasers firing everywhere and drones tearing your hull to shreds, you can only hope you can get crew to fix it back up before your mulch. Your Weapons systems could take a missile hit  just as you found a vital opening In the enemy's shielding forcing your weapon charge to deplete until the system is repaired. Many situations like this will happen and they will challenge your multitasking abilities, all the while planning every move you have yet to make. Do you have enough fuel to get to the store and repair? Do I save my scrap to buy that well needed weapon or will I need a shield upgrade before then?
It sounds intimidating and it can be, but once you learn the ropes I've yet to find a greater sense of accomplishment and joy. I've been blown to smithereens repeatedly whilst learning the core basics of the game but once I did I spent many, many late nights with headphones on, losing myself in this little game that was made by 2 people. Yes, the graphics may not be to everyone's taste for those who are only into top quality AAA visuals but for us indie lovers, the graphics and music (my god, that music!!!) will immerse you and draw you in, time and time again.
Not for the faint of heart, but then again, you can't be a captain without diving headfirst into certain doom!
If you love rougelikes/roguelites and sci-fi you will simply adore FTL. I've logged in quite a few hours so far and honestly I just wanna log in some more.

Let me preface this review by saying first that I like Helldivers. At its core, I think Helldivers is a great game with solid mechanics and execution. I enjoy playing it most chances I get. If I could've, I would've made this a neutral review, as this is the first game I like that I've given a negative review. Unfortunately, Helldivers doesn't want to play with me.
Helldivers is one of the few games I have ever seen that is actively trying to sabotage itself. A major component of its multiplayer is the galactic campaign system; the community, as a whole, is responsible for pushing enemies back to their homeworlds and wiping them out while simultaneously defending conquered territories from enemy advances.
On paper, this sounds like a great idea. It offers a long-term incentive to continue playing the game and a goal to strive for. In the game itself, it's one of Helldivers' weakest elements, randomly locking out factions and terrain types as a result of the community - not you, the player - playing the game too much.
Content disappears as a result of the unseen actions of a faceless mass as a "reward" for dedication. More problematic, new players are confronted with a sense of total helplessness and given little ability to improve their equipment; on many occasions, the game locks itself to a stalemate at enemy homeworlds. Only on non-homeworld planets are players able to unlock new stratagems - vital equipment ranging from secondary weapons to airstrikes - and, for some, only against specific factions.
Smaller failings contribute to the sense that Helldivers is a game that wants to be left alone. A confined, team-locked camera that restricts player mobility has been a contentious point since the game was released. Poorly-planned enemy balance and a wealth of equipment balance inconsistencies keep gameplay just below perfection. An almost entirely meaningless slog of a grind from level 25 to 50 offers little incentive to continue playing for progression.
Without any kind of consistent story mode, no means to select missions in already-conquered territory, and a campaign that seems to breeze by without any player action, Helldivers is a game that is almost totally apathetic about you playing it. It doesn't care if you want to fight cyborgs or bugs, if you want to play on a volcanic or ice planet, or if you have no anti-tank weapons and
to unlock one. Starting up the game is complete potluck as to what you'll get in the worst way possible.
With all that said and my most serious grievances aired, it is no mistake that I have, at the time of writing this, nearly 260 hours invested into Helldivers. I've gotten ahold of most of its content packs and use most of their items regularly. The statement I opened this review with is one I wholeheartedly believe; Helldivers, at its core, is a phenomenal shooter from a developer I've always wanted to see more of.
Helldivers follows a few simple rules - armor penetration, center-of-mass-based damage - that blend together with its fast-paced combat and incredible variety of weapons and enemies into an immensely fun shooter. Always-on friendly fire encourages tight teamwork and accurate, split-second decisions, lending tactical elements to its gameplay that would otherwise scream "murder everything in sight".
The spontaneity and unpredictability of the game go beyond its difficulties with the galactic campaign and into the far more applaudable territory of randomly-generated maps and objectives. Few maps are ever the same and every map has a different set of objectives in a unique set of locations. While this detracts from some of the game's personality, it offers an incredible depth of potential replayability.
Variety contributes heavily to Helldivers' replayability, as well. Even in the core game alone, there is a weapon for every task and nearly every niche. There is no shortage of stratagems, from anti-tank railcannon strikes to airdropped combat walkers, and no painful gaps in the player's arsenal. Dropping into a mission is solely at the player's discretion; you can start wherever you choose on the map, even if it's right on top of an objective.
Enemy variety is yet another selling point and one of the biggest reasons why I hold so much ill will against the galactic campaign system. There are three factions with a unit type for every level of difficulty and every role they could need filled. Each faction comes with its own distinct playstyle and its own strengths and weaknesses that interact in countless different ways with player loadouts and planet types.
Good music, sound design, and visual flair make for an inviting game that runs well and maintains its tone throughout every situation. Unfortunately, Helldivers' story - as brief and predictable as it is - gets lost in a hurry in favor of a far stronger focus on the gameplay and style rather than any kind of plot. The endless campaign that never seems to fail only drives home how meaningless even a Magicka-styled series of jokes would become.
In the end, I'll say it again; I like Helldivers. I
Helldivers. I want to keep playing it and play more of it. The problem is that Helldivers doesn't seem to want to play with me and didn't seem to care when I first started playing. As development has been considered complete and updates have ground to a halt, it's unlikely that will change.
As a result, I have to give it a negative review. I might not be able to take the hint, but I certainly understand the message - and I certainly don't ever want to see another game make Helldivers' mistakes.

This is going to be a long passionate review, so if you're not in the mood for that then just take my word that the game is incredible and you should buy it.
A long time ago... in a room not far away from me... I was just a child, with my lovely PS2, who loved Star Wars to death. This day I remember perfectly, it was a cloudy day, me and my dad went to the store to get my long awaited Battlefront 2 game for the PS2. I was so excited for it, and when I got that game box on my hands, the smile from my face never went away as I couldnt stop looking at the cover of the box with the Clone trooper in beetwen Obi Wan and Darth Vader. And to this day, I still have that box saved in my shelf with my other PS2 games. When I got home, I quickly put the disc in my PS2 and the game started running, I heard the wonderful OST of Star Wars in the main menu and I just got so many goosebumps inside of me...but there was only 1 problem... since I got the game from a German shop, the game was in the German language, which I didnt speak much of it, so I didnt really understand much of the dialogue and the main menu options, but I didnt complain, I was grateful and happy for what I had, the language of the game didn't stop me for playing that game day and night, day and night, constantly, even to this day I look back at my younger self and I ask myself, how didnt this game get boring for me? I constantly played the same maps 10 times in a row and then did it with the other maps. The game never stopped being amazing. Eventually though, I got a PC, and I slowly stopped playing on my PS2 and began with PC gaming, but to this day I still remember all the wonderfull times I had with my PS2 and with Star Wars Battlefront 2.
Now almost a decade later, I bought this game for the PC version. And the nostalgia hit me hard, its still such an incredible game to this day and in my opinion, I find this game more enjoyable than EA's new Battlefront games. Now the best part about the PC version of this game, is the ULTIMATE PACK! The Ultimate Pack is a collection of mostly all Star Wars Battlefront 2 mods which bring many new eras, many new units and game modes and much more! And it all works with a simple game launcher which allows you to choose with which mods you'll play it, and there's also this submod you can download which allows you to play multiplayer, its very simple! (You can download the Ultimate Pack on its official website
). The Community of this game really surprised me, I also never knew the community itself made a ''1.3 patch'' which adds new features to the base game and even a free camera mode during battles which lets you take incredible screenshots which I absolutely love.
Star Wars Battlefront 2 is still and in my opinion always will be an incredible game no matter what, and with the Ultimate Pack, it brings endless fun and enjoyment!

Bought this on a whim, wasn't expecting much, to be honest. But I do love tower defense, and it runs on linux, so I went ahead with the purchase. Very impressed, this game is actually very excellent and has an old-school SNES feel with modern tower defense. I've been playing it over more publicly accredited games (it actually has pulled me away from DOTA 2), so decided that a positive review would help out a bit because I feel very strongly about how this hidden gem wasted an entire Sunday for me, and I'm still not done beating it 100%. I rarely care about beating games 100%, I think the last time I did it was for a little-known title called Goldeneye in the 90's.
Excellent concept: merges RPG with tower defense. That's all there is to say, really. Units seem to be all useful, but as with ANY old-school RPG combat it can get super easy or impossible depending on whether or not you grind. Regardless on that, there are technically four difficulties (if you count casual) that change each battle's difficulty hugely. Story is alright -- the humor isn't my cup of tea, but then again, I have a picture of the dude from The Human Centipede 2 as my steam picture, so I just gotta say it's a me thing.
Looks like they're making a sequel. Good, I'll be sure to buy it.
If you're on linux and can't figure out why the game doesn't start without an error message, you need Adobe AIR. Their website is quite good on showing you how to get it running. A minor setback, I'm sure with licensing reasons Steam can't install it as a dependency. However, it almost made me assume the game was poorly ported and bugged (like Dead Island which doesn't boot on linux for some and nobody knows why, LOL).
The devs obviously cared a lot about this game: it's not junk meant to be sold to chumps where they buy it on sale, play for 15 minutes, then never open it up again. The writing is good -- not perfect, but meant to be (ugh) all ages. It's not a super deep story, though I feel with more practice they could pull it off if they feel it wouldn't detract from the gameplay in the sequel.
I would advise the devs to look at their website and tone down on the humor -- had my bored, cynical♥♥♥♥♥seen it without playing the game I would've assumed this game would be♥♥♥♥♥♥
The art isn't AAA title, but as an indie game, what the ♥♥♥♥ do you expect? The battles are mid 90's SNES quality (though better than Breath of Fire II, worse than FF6) and the cutscenes are adobe flash-esque and very similar to the indie game Sequence (minus the voice acting, plus more character gestures).
If the game was a teensy little longer and made for the SNES, with a little more "professionalism" mixed in, it would've been a classic everyone would've known about.

After playing this game for a decent deal of time, I feel that I've played enough of it that I can give an honest review of the game. Unfortunately, unlike a typical review this isn't just going to be about the sheer mechanics and style of the game but also of the implementation of the game's most notable "feature".
For starters the game itself is genuinely quirky and entertaining, it is a simple enough earthbound-esque jrpg with a few interesting button combo attacks for the main character and a few of the myriad followers. The followers themselves each have their own personality. Unfortunately, except of a few of them, you will only witness a few lines outside of post-battle text. That being said, each character is entertaining enough that before the repeats begin to wear on you, you will likely enjoy their little quips and phrases. This all comes together with the games comical and dark atmosphere to make the game itself a quite entertaining if not slowly paced adventure(even after finding the bike).
Then comes the games affectation, the spice thrown in with the assumed hope of making the game become a tad darker, a bit more uncomfortable, a little more harsh and a smidge less "stern bald man's feel good psychadelic ponchoventure".
I'm speaking of course of the ambush choices. Various times in the game, you will be ambushed. And upon being ambushed you will be given a choice, the choice is always something along the lines of, your friend dies, a town dies etc.. With the alternate choice being something like, we take all your things, we take all your money, we remove one of your arms.
These could happen for a number of reasons, you could be caught off guard, knocked out, wake up to them, walk through a door, proceed forward into a new area, beat a boss, or really just anything. Although there are a few ambushes that are random chance, the vast majority of these are literaly unavoidable. They are not consequences, you do nothing to assume them upon yourself, they are roadblocks and you must go forward through them in order to proceed in the game.
As you may have gathered by now, I am not a huge fan of this idea, but the presence of it is not the issue I have, its the implementation.
First off, although some of the choices at least affect gameplay, such as the arms and the towns, none of these crucial choices affect the ending or story, which is entirely left up to whether or not the player chooses to alleviate the ailment of his drug withdrawl random stat drains by taking "joy" pills. So their addition becomes wholly auxillary, a sort of negative power up that you are forced to swallow every 20 minutes of gameplay.
Secondly, the choices don't have any rationale into why they can't be avoided or stopped. As a silly joke, one of the  times you are asked, you are also given the choice to fight your assailant, you then are sent into a fight with a singular man who uses one attack that does 15 times everyones max health to every member of your team killing them in one blow. He then tells you shouldn't have tried that and removes the option and asks again, because apparently forcing the choice upon you is precious beyond killing you within the context of the game.
A rare few characters have longstanding beef with the main character, and so them wanting to torture you at least makes sense. But a good portion of the time, the assailents will have no apparent reason for these proposals, and you will be forced into these "choices" by whoever the ♥♥♥♥ and his gang of the same amount of people you♥♥♥♥♥whooped ten seconds ago, and the option to fight them will never even be offered.
Moreover, even if you do find a working strategy to beat one of the intentionally overpowered bosses, apparently the game will call you a cheater and start screen you afterwards. Protecting the choice sequence at all costs.
This all leads to my final point about these sequences, which is that they feel shoe-horned into the game. The choices spit in the face of, if not wholly ignore the game at large, nearly only serve to cripple you, and seem to be only for the purpose of establishing atmosphere and not actually furthering the game itself.
Instead of working with and inside of the game, they work outside and against it, and as a result make the game substantially less entertaining. They don't seem to add anything the game already didn't have. They don't add to the atmosphere, as it is already plenty depressing, even with the comical bits. They don't add to the gameplay, as only a select few characters have genuinely efficacious techniques that you would have to work around losing. They don't add to the difficulty, as any money and items can be farmed (slowly) from a few areas with respawning enemies. And there are more than enough characters that your ambushers could slaughter them like flies and you'd have a fresh supply up again. The only "interesting" and fleshed out effect is the heavily advertised arm removal, but this singular dramatic game altering choice seems to be the only attempt at legitimacy these choices were given. But choosing it either time instead of anything else would be profoundly foolish given the circumstances.
All in all these surprise choices could have still actually served the game well if they at least made sense, but seeing as how they are both unavoidable and utterly unaffected by anything you do, while at the same time bestowing mainly the chore of regrinding upon you, they only serve to cripple the game as a whole.
The developer said that the game's biggest risk and goal was that these choices would upset people, and he was right, they should. But not because they are sad, or hard, or difficult to make, but because they have been sternly forced into what would have been an entertaining game.
TLDR: The game is fun, but the choice system is the dev's baby, and the baby's needs came before the game's.
*Edit: Apparently about 4-6 hours in (the time of the above review) is when you are hit the hardest by ambushes, with there being around five in an hour and a half period, in addition, you are able to control, or at least influence, who is selected to be killed by swapping your party in advance(in my case Terry who I saved earlier). Also the aforementioned ambush by the pathetic gang of six guys CAN actually be fought off as easily as assumed, and the option that they give that you would presume surrenders a town, actually starts a fight with them. This, combined with what I've encountered since continuing the game, means what I've said above, much to my chagrin, is largely incorrect. In addition, the charm and humor of this game far outweigh any and all shortcomings I have found.
In closing, this is a fantastic game, and there is no reason any sane man shouldn't buy it. I'd be incredibly surprised if this game doesn't go down as one of the best this year.
PS: The moment I was finally won over was when I entered the pretty boys camp.

LISA is a fantastic visual and emotional experience that will have you questioning your morals throughout the entire game.

Are you willing to make personal sacrifices to save those who you've become attached to? Are you willing to do questionable things in the pursuit of personal gain? You will find yourself answering both of these questions over and over again, leaving you in a position to question yourself if you've done the right thing...or if there really was a "right" all along.
I personally recommend this to anyone who is a fan of dark humor, heartwrenching tragedies, classic RPG battles that manage to break away from cliches, and a unique, yet punishing, storyline.

I don't know if it is the dark humor, the well placed moments of tension and emotional story-telling, or maybe the fact that it is a side scrolling RPG. Then again maybe it is all of those things wrapped in a nice little package that fits neatly into one game - either way I consider LISA to be one of my new favorite games of all time.
The game may not be for everyone, but it definitely is something I enjoy.
I can suggest this game to anyone that has a morbid sense of humor with a sprinkling of weird. If an individual gets offended easily by certain themes or subjects, then it is probably best they scoot along and find another game to play.

Gunman Clive is a beautifully simplistic platformer with a futuristic wild west setting featuring charming sketch like visuals and an absolute superb soundtrack. Tight controls that feel precise matched with fair platforming creates an enjoyable experience. New elements are introduced every level, however some are gimmicks only appearing in their respective levels, due to this it should also be noted whilst playing the duck some of these gimmicks feel like a hindrance to endure. It is very reminiscent of Megaman and Donkey Kong Country as many levels feel similar to those I have played in the aforementioned games. However whilst the game is great, there are some issues; Difficulty only changes how many health/hits you can take whereas I feel the game would benefit more if it were to modify the levels and enemies in a way to increase the challenge.
Indeed the game is short, say 2 hours for your first run of each character combined, I wouldn't necessarily say it gets repetitive, each character handled slightly differently, where Clive was the standard all-round character, Ms. Johnston played a lot like Peach in the sense her floaty jump has an extended reach. The duck was by far the most enjoyable to play for me, it was more challenging due to the fact you had to avoid enemies rather than confront them. I definitely recommend this to everyone from casual players to platformer fanatics.

First off, just a friendly note~ If you're easily frustrated, don't like losing, are ill tempered or impatient, don't get this game.
FTL is a rogue-like game where you take the role of the captain of a Federation ship on a mission to deliver a message to the Federation fleet and fight the Rebel's flagship. This is no easy task.... At all... In fact, it takes people hundreds of tries to finally defeat the flagship. It's a task even to get there, BUT! That's part of the fun! The difficulty makes for an exciting story and with the free "Advanced Edition", adds even more complexity to an already astounding game.
The game relies heavily on stats, RNG and getting everything just right. Someruns will be perfect, others, you'll have your rear end handed to you on a silver platter. It's exciting to see your ship and your crew make it through not repairing for 8 sectors, the thrill of getting a brand new weapon of mass destruction, and the tension of first fighting the flagship.
But it doesn't stop with the Kestrel! You can complete tasks and quests and in some cases, very very difficult, convoluted and secret missions to obtain new ships and ship layouts. It's all very very satusfiying once you do, and some of them make the game easier whereas some other up the difficulty. Each ship has its own play-style as well. I, alas, only have experience with the basic layouts of the first two: The Kestrel and the Engi ship who's name escapes me. The Kestrel is an allaround workhorse ship. It'll do nearly anything you need it to. The Engi is a fragile ship but comes standard with and ion weapon to disable an enemy's shields and a drone bay to launch an attack drone.
The game is extreamly rewarding if you have the gall to face it.
I hope this was helpful and happy hunting, commanders!!

I'd always heard the name FTL being mentioned as an amazing game. Unfortunately I was never smart enough to look up more than a screen shot or two. I got it on a whim during a sale...oh my.
FTL has very little to no story but still manages to build a world inside your head. Where it shines is in it's mechanics. It should be said from the get go that this is a "roguelike" and a difficult one at that. Death can happen at almost any point, sometimes due to bad play or just hard luck. Many people will see some of these deaths as plain unfair, and that's fair enough. As for myself, i loved that aspect. No matter how much i grew to understand the fundementals, how stong my ship was or how trained my crew were, there was always a chance of flying into a sector (could be classed as rooms?) and being overwhelmed by evnviromental hazards, a pirate ship, or ,erchants who may or may not be who they claim to be.
You play as one of many Federation ships carrying vital information that you must travel across the galaxy to deliver whilst a Rebel fleet are constantly in your tail. You must travel from beacon to beacon across 8 or so sectors (floors?) to fight the Rebel Flagship and destroy it to emerge victorious and win the game. You will have to manage crew members, along with your ships weapons and systems. Crew members can man systems such as the Cockpit, Engines, Weapons etc... and get better get better at manning each individual system. Struggling to dodge those pesky lasers or missiles? Maybe Bugsy Face slasher or whatever ridiculous name you decide to give that crew member who's been hanging around the ship being useless, could jump in the engines room and after he spends some time will grant you some extra dodge chance. Or you could just invest some of that scrap (currency of the game) that you stole from those pirates into upgrading the shield systems. I'd recommend you do both, but hey, you're the captain!
Battles occur in real time but you can pause at anytime Pausing is crucial to your survival and tactical planning. For example, an enemy ship will fire a laser at you, which will begin recharging as soon as it fires, however they also have missles. While you may have good enough engines and piloting to maybe dodge the missile, maybe it's better to let the laser fire, and pause on and off to see if the missile will fire before the laser makes contact with shield or hits a vital system in your ship before you activate your Stealth systems, allowing you to dodge both projectiles.
Members of your crew can die and will die in a variety of ways. Your Oxygen system can be completely shot down, meaning you'll have to scramble amongst crew members who haven't already taken damage to rush and fix the systems, rapidly losing air and their health in the process. Some Races are better than this than others. The Engi, for example are not good fighters but their repair skills are unmatched. Mantis crew are great at hand-to-hand combat, making them excellent boarders using Teleporters or defence against enemy boarders.
Teleporters are one of many Systems you can install on your ship, allowing a certain number of crew to jump onto the enemy ship for some close quarters battle. There are Cloning Bays that will replace Medbays, allowing your crew to come back from the dead, as long as you can keep it powered. Stealth systems to cloak your entire ship giving you a much better dodge chance. Drone systems which will allow you to buy and equid a variety of offensive or defensive drones. These systems along with the rest of the game will take some time to wrap your head around but once you do, you will be comfortable enouh to decide which ones to use and which to avoid for better or for worse as your ship only has so many slots for these systems.
Every jump to a new beacon, you will be met with one of many situations, be it a crew of passive locals who needs some spare fuel or equipment, a hostile ship armed to the teeth, honest travelers, conniving captains, or just the lonely occupancy of empty space. You will find shops, allowing you to spend scrap on getting that sexy new gun, a well needed drone or just repairing your ships hull (HP).
This can become overwhelming very fast in FTL. A crew of dangerous Mantis can board onto your ship. Fires will spread damaging important systems. Shields system can be severly damaged and your enemy has lasers firing everywhere and drones tearing your hull to shreds, you can only hope you can get crew to fix it back up before your mulch. Your Weapons systems could take a missile hit  just as you found a vital opening In the enemy's shielding forcing your weapon charge to deplete until the system is repaired. Many situations like this will happen and they will challenge your multitasking abilities, all the while planning every move you have yet to make. Do you have enough fuel to get to the store and repair? Do I save my scrap to buy that well needed weapon or will I need a shield upgrade before then?
It sounds intimidating and it can be, but once you learn the ropes I've yet to find a greater sense of accomplishment and joy. I've been blown to smithereens repeatedly whilst learning the core basics of the game but once I did I spent many, many late nights with headphones on, losing myself in this little game that was made by 2 people. Yes, the graphics may not be to everyone's taste for those who are only into top quality AAA visuals but for us indie lovers, the graphics and music (my god, that music!!!) will immerse you and draw you in, time and time again.
Not for the faint of heart, but then again, you can't be a captain without diving headfirst into certain doom!
If you love rougelikes/roguelites and sci-fi you will simply adore FTL. I've logged in quite a few hours so far and honestly I just wanna log in some more.

My first play session lasted 5 minutes before I stopped and uninstalled
A while later I thought let me give it another try - and I haven't stopped since. KAG is a 2D medieval fast paced teamwork PvP based game with vibrant colours and a fun art style.
The game is extremely simple on the surface, build stuff, shoot stuff or slash stuff. As you play around you start seeing the depth of each class. As a builder you build defences for your base, and with time you invent creative ways to assist your team, or hamper the enemy's movement. You can be the reason why your team wins or loses. As an archer you rain death from afar, and with your trusty grappling hook there are very few places you can't reach. Don't forget to grab a few fire arrows and watch entire wooden structures burn to the ground. Knights are running tanks who love to grab a chicken and glide with their shield over enemy fortifications. Practise your bomb jumping or shield skiing for maximum fun.
Game rounds can last anywhere from 2 minutes when sneaky archer ninjas steal the flag to several (2-4 hours) of tug of war, multiple failed stalemate votes and thousands of hilarious deaths.
The only complaint is the griefing in the game. There are normally mods available to hand out bans, and players can start a grief kick vote to rid themselves of team griefers, albeit normally after your last line of defence was collapsed as the enemy approached.
All in all this game comes highly recommended by me. Buy it, equip a crazy hat and start fighting those pesky enemies! Take a break, read some wiki's and go at it again.

LISA is an impressive balancing act, teetering on a razor sharp line between comedy and horror, and yet it works. It never feels like it's trying to make light of the world; that's just how things are. And the way things are is, well, crushing. No matter how light-hearted the game may get, there's always this opressive fog looming over everything; with every element contributing to this depressive atmosphere. From the brutal gameplay and how quickly you can (permanently) lose party members to the many songs and their themes.
It's a good deal more disturbing than a good many of horror games I've played, and I don't think that I'll forget it any time soon.

Taking inspiration from Earthbound, LISA is every bit as "painful" as the game's creator, Dingaling, marketed it.
But the implication therein assumes such a word to be bad, in this case "painful" is actually good; it's the best way to accurately describe the roller coaster of emotions I experienced from this sidescrolling RPG. Filled with equal parts chuckling at a denizen of the post-apocalyptic world just trying to get through his day, and regret and remorse at the lengths the protagonist, Brad Armstrong, will go to to get back his daughter, Buddy, LISA is very much a game about "pain" and the emotional response the player has to various trials and tribulations and overall wackiness that will occur.
"Stylized" is another word I'd use to describe LISA. One glance at the game and the visual look of the characters portrays a slightly off-beat, darkly humorous nature about the people that inhabit the landscape. The music is equally brilliant, as ecclectic and diverse as the people you'll get to know and possibly recruit into your ragtag party. I've found myself many times listening to the game's soundtrack, and as of right now am listening to "Live in Joy" as I type this review out. Tracks range from pulsing electronic beats to catchy hip hop montages, to some pretty sinister and darkly pieces that pepper the game's world. Perhaps the master piece of music is "Summer Love" that seems to play in different measures and times throughout the game's many villages, that signifies just another day in post-apocalyptia.
As mentioned, the game draws heavily from Earthbound's well and that's no different when it comes to combat. Even though damage isn't represented by rolling numbers, it does feature a similar artistic aesthetic in both background design and the interface. More than once I've found LISA to resemble games such as Paper Mario or the more recent South Park: Stick of Truth from the unorthodox ways to inflict status effects on an opposing enemy.
LISA is very much a game about pain. It really is a painful experience, but there's a lot of laughter and a lot of charm as well. You'll probably end up hating one or two characters, but you may just find yourself attached to one or two characters as well. And you may regret becoming close with any of them at all. In short, "don't ever tell anybody anything. If you do, you start missing everybody."

The game should have some sort of hint feature, for if you get stuck and don't know what to do.  There are lots of questions at the end of this game, such as the purpose of the grenade and sniper rifle.  Were the murders real, or just part of Ethan's crazy imagination?
Overall, I recommend giving this game a playthrough.  The visuals alone should satisfy any gamer's basic needs, but the story is very hard to naturally complete without external support.

To start: I used to add a header to these reviews, but since it once too often made the reviews too long to submit, I've decided to leave it on my Backloggery page. Not that this review should push the length limit, but I'd like to stay consistent.
Gameplay: It's hard not to look at this game and think, "Oh hey, a Megaman-esque game." You really wouldn't be wrong thinking that, either. It's also got a little bit of Contra/Probotector in it, with weapons that you can pick up throughout the levels and lose once you get hit. As far as the levels go, they've got a pretty Megaman-ish feel to them, although the game sometimes hops onto the Donkey Kong Country train. When it does, it's not exactly subtle about it, either. There's a minecart stage and there's the ladder-enemy-avoidance-thing from Vulture Culture. It's not bad, but it does feel pretty uninspired whenever these sections roll up.
In fact, the most original feeling levels are the ones at the very beginning. Now, even some of the less inspired levels do make good use of the design mechanics... sometimes. For example, there's a really neat jump you've gotta do in the Gravity Man stage that makes clever use of momentum. Even though they may not always be the most inspired, the levels are still pretty fun to play. As for the enemies and bosses, there's a pretty good variety of enemies, if once again some of them are blatant ripoffs of Megaman enemies (the five-way turrets, for example). The bosses - of which there are four - are all pretty fun to fight.
You can play as three different characters: Clive, the man protagonist; Ms. Johnson, the not-man protagonist, and a duck, the not-hu-man protagonist. Clive and Ms. Johnson play pretty similarly, with Clive being the hardier of the two while Ms. Johnson has a better jump as well as having a hover. The duck, oddly enough, was the most fun to play as. Since you are a duck, you can't fire a gun. As such, the game becomes about avoiding enemies. This does force you to look at the stages in a different manner, allowing for some pretty neat twists on level design. Of course, since you are a duck and cannot fight things, bosses have been removed.
Overall, I had a pretty good time with this game. My current playtime of 1.8 hours reflects my playthrough of the game as the three individual characters. I normally consider a $1/Hour of Gameplay to be an ideal value for a game, and this game certainly delivered that. It may not always have the most original level design, but it's still pretty fun nonetheless. 7/10.
Story: Sometimes you are a man rescuing a lady. Sometimes you are a lady rescuing a man. Sometimes you are a duck rescuing... I dunno. Anyways, the story ain't the focus of the game, or even a major element, so I'm leaving it out of the scoring.
Graphics: The main draw of this game, almost certainly. I'm sure I don't really need to tell you that this game looks utterly fantastic, so I won't even bother. You've got eyes. The game does have a bit of an issue with alt-tabbing when in fullscreen (throwing an error along the lines of "A Shader has failed to compile"). The one time I alt-tabbed out of fullscreen I didn't bother to check whether the game still worked or not. Anyways, this isn't too big of a detriment. You can choose your resolution, and the game otherwise worked perfectly fine for me. 5/5.
Sound: The music sure is good in this game. You can get the OST by doing a little directory digging in the files of the game (/SteamApps/common/GunmanClive/data/sound, and the music will be the .oggs). As far as the sound design, I found it a bit lacking. Hitting enemies just doesn't have the punchiness I would've liked. It just makes things feel a little flat. Apart from that, there really isn't much else to talk about. The music is great, but the sound direction could've had a little bit more. 4/5.
Overall scores are: 7/0/5/4; cumulative score of 8.0/10. I'd say it's worth the $2, definitely. If it's ever on sale for any reason, it's definitely a steal.

Defender's Quest (DQ) is a tower defense meets RPG hybrid. You go around with your ragtag bunch of misfit heroes, trying to save your skin and possibly the world. As you make your way, battle after battle, through hordes of zombies... I mean, Revenants, everyone's skills improve, making them harder, better, faster, stronger at slicing-and-dicing more undead meat.
Is that all? No. DQ has a delicious old-school feel, partly thanks to the pixellated sprites, partly because of the great soundtrack which will make you think of the glorious days of SNES JRPGs. It also has some notably well-written dialogue, snappy and fun (though let's face it, the art in those scenes leaves something to be desired...). DQ also has lots of challenges for you. Playing levels at regular difficulty is getting too easy? No problem, you can replay them at Advanced or Extreme to get bonuses and goodies. Finished the game? No problem, there's a New Game+ with more difficulties awaiting for you. The learning curve is extremely well-balanced and I especially enjoyed being able to complete the main story without ever getting really stuck but with a very real sense of increased hardship towards the end (the last two-three battles, especially, I barely managed to power through).
It's definitely a very good game, especially if you like tower defense. Get it.
EDIT: the developers released a "DX" patch for this game adding new content, remaking the engine with HaxeFlixel and redrawing the art to be better - thus the only complaint I could ever muster about this game has now gone. This is nothing short of a masterpiece, and quite possibly the best tower defense game you'll find on Steam. Search no more.

TL;DR:  As a “classic” game in the modern era, Star Wars: Battlefront 2 holds up quite well to modern standards and is very much playable even if for just nostalgia’s sake.  Despite older graphics, minor AI issues, and the need to now use third-party software for multiplayer, the game proves itself worthy to stand as an example of what the Battlefront series should represent – chaotic combat, open-world maps, and team-based gameplay.
With the advent of EA’s Battlefront, who are now releasing their Battlefront 2, I figured it was high time to write a review of the original Battlefront 2 game.  Having not played EA’s Battlefront, I cannot say I like or dislike it, but I can say that I believe I would put many hours into it if I could.  But that is even more reason why I think this Battlefront 2 should get more recognition as “the original”.  This game did a lot considering when it was made and should be looked at as how a Battlefront game should be made in my opinion.
Star Wars: Battlefront 2 is a third-person/first-person shooter that allows the player to experience some of the largest, most well-known battles in the Star Wars universe as well as some of the lesser known battles.  This is done through both ground and space battles and with a wide variety of both character and vehicle classes.
There are three primary modes of gameplay:  campaign, galactic conquest, and instant action.  The campaign tells the story of the 501st legion, Vader’s Fist, from their trial by fire on Geonosis to their final raid on Hoth.  The story isn’t exactly compelling, but it provides an interesting view from a different side of the Star Wars story.  Galactic conquest allows the player to pick a side, either Droids, Clones, Empire, or Rebels, and gives the goal of conquering the galaxy.  The player is provided credits for holding and capturing planets and can used those credits to increase the ranks of their army, buy a fleet, or buy bonuses.  Instant action allows the player to create a playlist of different maps and game modes and jump right into the action with or against friends.
Gameplay is simple:  You choose a class, such as sniper or anti-tank, and spawn at a friendly base.  Your goal, generally, is to capture enemy bases, but that can vary in modes such as capture the flag or the interesting Hunt mode.  Vehicles will spawn at bases for the players to use, ranging from light attack vehicles to transports like AT-ATs…and that is basically it.  The real fun comes when combat starts and you have infantry and tanks mixed together fighting for a base.  The ensuing chaos is, honestly, one of the best things about the game.  While you can use the character and vehicle classes to your advantage (and you should), it is just as fun to be a regular clone or rebel and hop into the fight.  Losing doesn’t feel like losing because it happens so spectacularly, something that especially holds true on maps like Tantive IV and Polis Massa.  Space combat is no different, and dogfighting can be equally as fun as boarding the enemy ship.
For a game that is over 10 years old, this game did a lot:  upwards of 20 maps, a full campaign, an updated galactic conquest mode, 32 player battles (64 on PC).  It isn’t without issues.  The AI can be…weird, getting stuck on walls and committing suicide and the like, and as fun as the map is, Tantive IV is still a bit buggy.  Some may find the graphics unappealing, but there are plenty of mods for the game that deal with that and much, much more.  Sadly, multiplayer servers have been shut down, but there are ways to play with friends through services like GameRanger.  Overall, it is a fantastic game worthy of a spot in your library and a great game to play with friends.
Whether due to nostalgia or curiosity, you should buy this game.  You won’t regret it.  May the Force be with you, watch those wrist rockets, GG and Good Hunting.

LISA is an RPG about regret, shame, and suffering. It combines tight writing to push painful moments and excellent comic timing to relieve that tension to produce a compelling narrative about failure, trauma, desperation, etc. But all that aside, it's also a very satisfying traditional RPG - the diversity of characters provides enormous flexibility in playstyle, the mechanics are complex enough to reward mastery while simple enough to be mastered. There's also plenty of side-quests, which add depth but aren't necessary to complete the game.
The setting is compelling enough that it'll itch at your mind for a while after you finish the game. I'm very much looking forward to the next game in the series.
Beating LISA took me about 13 hours of play-time, accounting for save-scumming. In terms of entertainment value per dollar, it's not unbeatable, but it's pretty good!

A solid RPG videogame, LISA is packed with 10-20+ hours of good humour, discomfort and uncomfortable humour.
The game plays like EarthBound (albeit with a 2d side scrolling view) and the battle system also resembles it too. But be prepared for a lot of customisation as unlike the Mother series, you get to change party members from a large selection that's essentially the size of a miniture Suikoden cast.
There's 3 major HUB areas in LISA that lead to other areas filled with content. Your decisions and outcomes matter in this videogame so expect some things you wouldn't find in a conventional videogame. For example; at one point you're forced to survive 3 full games of Russian roulette to progress the plot. It can be a very unforgiving experience, but even when it screams "screw you" it finds a way to make it hilarious.
The theme and story of LISA is as unsettling as it is funny, it's set on a world where everything went to crap akin to the Australia portrayed in the original Mad Max trilogy except without women. The dumb, crazed and depraved acts of men trying to entertain themselves in a dead world can sometimes turn from funny to depressing when you're reminded of their bleak future or the happier pasts they might have had. There's a lot of scenarios in the game and I heavily enjoyed the fun or depressing character arcs that the game puts you through. I struggle to explain any direct example from the setting, plot or themes as I don't want to spoil the smallest things but I can gurantee LISA is compelling from the very start.
Most of the time the music is intentionally weird but there's a few genuinely great tracks that are very easy listening or funky. The bathhouse's theme may be my favourite out of the lot.
It's one of the better videogames I've played in recent years and I'd like you to consider purchasing it. LISA is likely going to appeal to you if you're a fan of Mother series, Yume Nikki or Mortis Ghost's OFF as it presses all the weird buttons fans of those games have. Game creator Austin Jorgensen should be proud of this title and I hope he finds time to make another videogame (similar to LISA or not) if he can make a viable career out of this.

It would be impossible for me to not write a review about this game.
The game immediately harkens to the 'Mother' series with it's visual/art style, it's gameplay mechanics, unique cast of characters, humor, profound story and tweaking of the jRPG genre. With 'Mother 3' inparticular coming to mind in reguards to all of that. But it also has a air of a Alejandro Jodorowsky movie; with it's surrealistic/psychadelic nightmare worlds, blisteringly dark humor and it's depths of probing the human soul (the pancho doesn't hurt either).
I am impressed and staggered by this game; it forces you to evaluate the difficult decisions your characters are often forced to make, making me more than once pause to consider all the ramifications. It's a hard game, with a sharp learning curve that changes on a dime, and while that can be frustrating, it makes sense in reguard to the story.
There is so much I want to say about this game; it was a strange personal journey I took with these characters that I can't really explain in a short review. But it was depressing, funny, mind boggling, crippling, it was so much to me and I think a lot of other people got their own experiences from it. There are tons of strange characters to choose from, and it's often hard to decide on what team you want, but for me, when I made that decisions I stuck with them for pretty much the whole game. I can't reccomend this game enough. But, I don't think it will be for everyone and that's a good thing.

It's not often I write Steam reviews (this is my first), but this game really struck a chord with me.
Story: It's hard to get too detailed without spoiling, but the basic premise is that the characters are in a post-apocalyptic setting in which only men are left alive (it's unknown what happened to the females, at least far as the player sees), yet the main character, Brad, came across a young baby who just so happens to be female, so he takes her in to raise her and protect her from the outside world. As you may expect, a human is a difficult secret to hide; she eventually gets kidnapped, so Brad goes in search for her and the story starts.
The main, overarching story is told a bit slower, really coming more to the forefront at the end of each hub area, but it's very interesting when it does. There exploration in between the story segments is still extremely interesting though, since it's filled with plenty of events and things to see, many are very quirky and humorous (and the humor is excellent, very reminiscent of Earthbound), though some things can be pretty unsettling (the game constantly walks a fine line between these two distinct types of emotion, and pulls it off surprisingly well). There's also the backstory of the game world and main character, which are also hinted at in various ways as you explore many of the areas, so even between the bigger story sections, there's still a lot to hold your attention and get you continually more interested and invested in the game world and characters.
True to the game's tagline of "The Painful RPG", things can get downright dark and painful at times, especially with some of the choices the game forces you to make. I'm not going to spoil those, but you're not going to come out of this game feeling like a saint. It's an interesting contrast to the choices of many other RPGs, where there's often an obvious "good" and "bad" choice. While LISA's choices tend to affect the gameplay (for which the consequences can be pretty big) more significantly than the overall narrative, there is a degree of story impact from some of these choices.
Gameplay: I enjoyed Lisa's battle system quite a lot. It's fast paced and frantic, and as soon as you're done issuing commands, moves execute quickly, rapidly, and with a lot of nice but quick animations for each move. Some characters, like the main character, Brad, also have a combo system of sorts, where you input commands with the WSAD keys to pull off a combo, which I found pretty fun (you can also automatically use these combos through the skill list, but they'll do less damage that way). Unlike many RPGs, status ailments are also extremely useful, even in boss encounters. This is partly balanced by bosses often being durable and hitting hard, and status ailments not being completely reliable, since they may fail to activate, and can sometimes wear off quickly (especially the more crippling ones).
There also aren't many spots to grind. It's possible, but very ineffective until one point very late in the game. I see this as a good thing though, since the game is well balanced around this aspect, and as long as you explore the different areas, your team will quickly grow powerful enough to tackle the ensuing obstacles.
The game also has a very survivalist feel: Consumable items are often harder to come by (some are available to buy, but it's a very limited selection for the majority of the game), and money can be pretty scarce, so you need to use your resources wisely. Exploring can help a lot in accumulating items and gear, speaking of which, the exploration in this game is pretty fun, since there are a lot of secrets to find, and you'll constantly be running into little events and interesting characters along the way.
This game also has some things that can cause you to permanently lose an ally, like permadeath moves (these are rare, and mainly used by certain bosses), and the chance for a party member to walk out or get kidnapped while you rest at certain camps (there are a couple safe resting spots that cost money, too). While perfectionists can potentially avoid these through caution and savescumming, the game also has a total of 30 allies to recruit, so as long as you aren't overly careless, you should be fine with a couple casualties here or there. It still hurts to lose a favorite member of course, so that danger can really keep you on your toes, and motivates you to be careful. The large amount of allies can also make replays more fun, since it gives you a lot of different party setups to try out.
Soundtrack: Absolutely wonderful. Lots of tracks that range from loud and bombastic to more subtle and mellow, so there's a lot of variety, and they're all utilized very well throughout, totally nailing the atmosphere of the different scenes and locations. It's also impressive just how little repeat there are of the tracks; I honestly lost count of how many battle themes there were (and all were awesome), and most areas have their own BGM (with the exception of smaller connecting areas, like caves). There's also a very definite Earthbound influence throughout, so fans of that game's soundtrack will likely feel right at home here.
Graphics: The graphics are very nicely done, often quirky, nicely stylized, and vibrant, yet fairly gristly and and gory with the darker parts of the game (the cartoonish style somewhat balances this out, but it can definitely be unsettling, especially to someone unaccustomed to horror). The art is also very consistently polished; this isn't like some RPG Maker games with an awkward mix of default resources and custom assets; everything here is original, and you can tell the creator was both very talented and knew exactly what he was going for.
All in all, LISA is a very well made game that I deeply enjoyed from start to finish. It may not be for everyone (especially with how dark and disturbing it can get at points), but it's very polished and packed with content for a game that costs only $10, and I've honestly gotten more enjoyment out of it than many games that cost much more than that.

Helldivers is a very challenging and addictive Co-Op Shooter.
In Helldivers you play as an elite unit working together to protect the planet Super Earth from invading aliens and enemy races along with liberating their own planets.
The game focuses on completing missions on different planets while fulfilling a set of different random objectives, these objectives range from killing a set number of enemies, to destroying and protecting equipment and even rescuing survivors.
You can play solo or up to 4 players Co-operatively, obviously the more people you have and the more well rounded the team is, the easier the game will be on higher difficulties.
After each successful mission you earn xp which will level your character up so you can unlock more weapons and abilites called Stratagems. Stratagems range from Turrets and Player controlled Mechs, to ammo drops and airstrikes. These Stratagems are integral in completing the harder missions so you need to think about which ones to take with you on each mission and the best times to use them.
The Presentation is well-rounded with both crisp, clean graphics and satisfying weapon sounds and decent voice acting, the music is also catchy.
There are a few issues with the game, for one a lot of lines your fellow helldivers say can get very repetitive, the game also often goes into a event where you can't complete certain missions or boss battles until it's completed.
Overall though Helldivers is a very satisfying top down co-op shooter that requires a lot of teamwork but rewards you with plenty of replay value.

This game is probably one of the best roguelikes I've ever played. The base scenario is compelling - you are running a ship across the galaxy, picking up upgrades and crew where you can to confront a final enemy.
From that simple scenario sprang a multitude of deep and satisfyingly fulfilling strategies that you can use. The ways you can defeat your enemies (or be defeated) are countless, from mass teleporting combat crew in to take over the ship, to setting multiple rooms on fire, to disabling shields and letting asteroids do the rest, never get old. The random procedurally generated world really challenges the player to find ways around obstacles, make real choices and take real risks. Every new ship and layout also plays like a completely different game as they present you with different challenges.
I also don't say this often but the game is pretty much perfectly balanced. There's no one overwhelmingly dominant strategy that you use over and over. Every strat has a weakness and failings depending on the random encounters you receive as well as the weapons and augments you find. The various difficulties are perfectly balanced just by the simple adjustment of rewards. The game is statically difficult but the rewards make the entire difference between snowballing into an unstoppable killing machine and being ground down into defeat. The simple brilliance of balancing makes this game playable by anyone.
If there's only one roguelike you need to play, it's FTL. All the others have some flaw or failing that makes second rate compared to this. Do yourself a favor and pick it up if you haven't already.

A short, Western-themed 2D platformer in the Mega Man vein.   A solid little game which can beaten in around an hour.  Levels are short but have no checkpoints so dying restarts the level.  Not too much of a problem except for a couple of levels that accounted for over half of my deaths.  Some of the level design is of the "you need to die once to know what to avoid next time" variety.  There's also the feeling that the devs went down a platformer checklist when creating level features but some of the stuff they did is pretty cool.
Bosses are pretty standard, not great, not bad.  Enemies drop gun power-ups and they're mostly in the Contra style.  There's no up/down/diagonally shooting, though you can shot while crouched and jumping and this stops feeling restrictive with a couple of minutes of playing. Your health bar doesn't do a particularly good job of conveying how many hits you have until death, as you'll get killed at times with what looks like to be a decent chunk left.  Game would've been better off just having some type of numeric representation of health, those this isn't too big of a deal.  There are no game overs, you have infinite attempts at levels.
There are three playable characters, Clive, Ms. Johnson, and the duck.  Ms. Johnson is clearly inspired by Peach from Mario 2 in how she controls, with the big difference between her and Clive is that she can float for a bit on her jumps.  The duck cannot hurt enemies but can jump/fly and is more of a challenge run character.
All said, a decent little game with some replayability, though a bit on the boring/bland side at times but hey, it's 2 buck at full price.  Worth picking up if you're looking for a Mega Man-esque platformer.

I quite enjoyed this title. Haven't read the book nor played the original. Sure the scale isn't grandiose as the heavy weight titles such as COD or Battlefield but Metro has a distinct style, engaging story line and overall enjoyable gameplay.

What can I say about Metro... Well, for starters, it is a unique survival horror title with an amazing story, great gameplay mechanics and a great sequel to boot. What makes Metro so good is, for one thing, it's combat mechanics.
There are two types of bullets: Regular and Military Grade bullets. Regular are pretty simple; you shoot and they kill, where as Military Grade does more dammage, and they work for almost every gun. Something to know is that Military Grade bullets are also the main currency in this game, and if you are low and need money, you can exchange regular ammo into currency, however you don't get much for these trades. For example, you trade in 10 shotgun shells for around 2 Military Grade rounds. Now bullets aren't too common, and on hard they're scarce, so there is a lot of mannaging what you spend and what you keep.
You also have the choice of being loud or stealthy. Being loud, of course, means you kill everything in sight, but doing will obviously blow through ammo quick. Stealth allows you to preserve ammo, but it takes WAY more time, and often a lot of trial and error. Use the dark, and turn off/avoid lights, as this does keep you hidden, but most of all:
You will need to be precise and make sure when you shoot, the body isn't too close for other enemies to see. (My reccomendation for a good stealthy weapon is upgrading your first gun to have a good stock, sight and surpresser.)
That's just a few aspects of Metro I can give out of many. Over all, I highly recommend Metro 2033 as well as Last Light.
Oh, and be certain of your actions and choices throughout parts of the game(s).

In this day and age vampires are often a mockery in pop culture, thanks in large part to sensations like Twilight. But let me tell you, this game has no glittering pretty boys. It's a true painting of what the modern vampire should be- they walk among us in society because they look like us, often using their intelligence and sex appeal to feed and maintain their powers. The game largely focuses on the politics within vampire society known as The Masquerade- it's this web of politics that sends you off on several quests where, depending on how you've chosen to level your character and converse in dialogue with NPCs can play out very differently.
The side quests are also very compelling. And I'm usually incredibly disinterested in these- the lore and the characters are all just so well written it made me want to explore the game more.
If you're looking for an obscure gem, excellent writing, unique atmosphere, or just tired of seeing Vampires suck♥♥♥♥♥like they have been in recent years this game is up your alley.
