You Have To Win The Game is a short retro platformer game designed to look as though it is being played on an old CRT monitor. The game is deliberately evocative of ages past, and contains various standard platforming puzzles.
Story
The game has no story.
Gameplay
At the start of the game, the character can do two things – move, and jump. Over the course of the game, the character also unlocks the ability to double jump and to wall jump, as well as activating red and blue walkway bricks; all four of these things open up new places for the player to go. The platforming starts out pretty easy, but gets progressively more difficult throughout the game. There are no bottomless pits in the game, but as per usual, there is lava and spikes.
Enemies in the game exist, but there are only a very small variety of them; however, this isn’t really a problem as the game is so short and the gameplay so basic. Touching any enemy is instant death, and there are fundamentally two kinds of “normal” enemies, creatures which crawl on the ground (snakes and crabs) and creatures which fly through the air (bats). In addition, there are a small number of unique monsters which spit out patterns of projectiles that the player must navigate through to win.
Most of the gameplay consists of exploring the environment, collecting all 64 money bags (though 5 of them are actually hearts instead, they serve the same purpose), unlocking all of the abilities, and navigating through to the end of the game, where there is a little mini-puzzle which allows you to “win” if you solve it. Winning or losing brings up a short message on screen, then sends you back to the beginning of the game without any upgrades, but all of the other collectibles remain collected.
The platforming is very basic, and overall the gameplay is very evocative of older platformer games, with very simple gameplay that isn’t anything special, but does what it needs to do. Unlike older platformers, are bells scattered throughout the game which serve as checkpoints, and their extremely high frequency means that the player is never sent back too far if they die; in this sense, the game is rather evocative of VVVVVV, in that the platforming deaths have little consequence because you can immediately try again, which is a good thing as it reduces frustration. The game gets to be fairly difficult by the end of it, but even still, the game is quite short; 100%ing the game took me under two hours, and to do that, you must beat it twice.
Graphics
The game is meant to look like it is being played on a computer out of the 1980s, and the game does a great job of achieving exactly that. This means, however, it isn't really very pretty to look at, though it is mostly reasonably clear what is going on; a few of the money bags are deliberately hidden by maching the surrounding colors closely, which is a somewhat questionable decision from the point of view of collectability, as all the others are simply hard to get to, whereas those two are easy to simply never see in the first place.
Final Summary
You Have To Win The Game is exactly what it promises to be – a retro platformer out of the 1980s. It isn’t the best platformer ever, but it is competent enough. However, there’s really nothing to recommend it either – if you miss out on this game, you aren’t missing anything from your life. If you get a free copy and are bored, you might get some enjoyment out of it, but there’s a reason games have moved on from such basic mechanics – they’re too limited to really grab you and leave you feeling as if you’ve done something new.
VVVVVV meets Super Meat Boy.

Although a short game, it's a very good game. There is not much story to speak of, but it isn't necessarily the most important part of this kind of game - the title describes the objective, and a counter in the bottom right hand corner describes the win condition.
It's easy to see where the developer has gotten his inspiration from (among others VVVVVV and Super Meat Boy (and, while I'm not quite sure as it might have gotten inspiration from the same sources, I might want to add I Wanna Be The Guy to the list, too).
The game is hard for pretty much the same reasons VVVVVV is hard - it's difficult to remember how to get where, and it's easy to get lost in the numerous level screens. Some parts of the game requires some "grinding" (if that's an appropriate term to use for trying again and again in a platformer), and some levels are pretty boring to do after a while. But the save-points are plentiful, and collection of money/artifacts/things are saved upon collection.
All in all, a really good game. It took me 1 hour and 50 minutes to get to the end without losing, and completing the game 100% took me 2 hours and 10 minutes (that means 20 minutes extra from my first, any%, win to my second, 100%, win. After this, I have three achievements left, which I'm going to go finish pretty soon. Other than getting 100% of the achievements, it doesn't look like there is a lot of replayability, as much of what makes the game great is the exploration.  However, it could be a fun game to run through once in a while, just to see if you remember every level and how to do them.
If you like this game, I'd recommend also checking out VVVVVV, Eversion, and I Wanna Be The Guy. This game reminded me a lot of those three, and I have enjoyed all three of them a lot, just like I did with this one.

It's rare that I find myself writing Steam reviews, but in this case I find that I really should.
Having finished the game, and only done maybe about 3/4ths of the content that the entire game has to offer, I can easily recommend this to anyone as my Game of the Year for 2014. There is a unique world presented in LISA that's both heartwarming, terrifying, and altogether tragic.
For every single moment of laughter, there's a moment that comes where a decision you make permanently affects the denizens of the world. Whether it's your own character, a character you've come to enjoy, a character you despise, or an entire town of strangers you'll more often find yourself resting your chin in your palm and scratching it until the moment passes and you've made your final decision. Even once I did, I still found myself asking if what I had done was right.
That said, the gameplay will not be for everybody. It's incredibly difficult to get started and quite often you'll reach decisions that seem deliberately designed to royally mess you up, and even then it's possible to keep pressing on. There's also a deliberate pace and VERY unsettling subject matter and atmospheres, however the game never feels like it's forcing you into bad situations for the sake of it, despite a handful of cheap shots that get pulled you quickly learn this world cares nothing for you right until the very end.
If you enjoy Shin Megami Tensei's punishing difficulty, Earthbound's quirky and often heartwarming but sometimes dark humor, and a decent turn-based experience loaded with interesting moves and decent status effects. LISA is just the game for you. However, if the thought of losing characters, making heavily burdened decisions, or extremely mature and unsettling subject matter leaves you shaken, this may not be the title for you.
Overall, I can't recommend this game enough, it truly stands as a paramount to what people can achieve when giving it their all with RPGMaker. Not all games need a happy story, but it doesn't take a happy story to provide an unforgettable experience, and I feel that's something worth exploring in the realm of gaming. LISA can proudly stand next to titles like Mother 3 and NieR for boldly exploring darker themes and handling it all in a mature manner.

This game is probably one of the best roguelikes I've ever played. The base scenario is compelling - you are running a ship across the galaxy, picking up upgrades and crew where you can to confront a final enemy.
From that simple scenario sprang a multitude of deep and satisfyingly fulfilling strategies that you can use. The ways you can defeat your enemies (or be defeated) are countless, from mass teleporting combat crew in to take over the ship, to setting multiple rooms on fire, to disabling shields and letting asteroids do the rest, never get old. The random procedurally generated world really challenges the player to find ways around obstacles, make real choices and take real risks. Every new ship and layout also plays like a completely different game as they present you with different challenges.
I also don't say this often but the game is pretty much perfectly balanced. There's no one overwhelmingly dominant strategy that you use over and over. Every strat has a weakness and failings depending on the random encounters you receive as well as the weapons and augments you find. The various difficulties are perfectly balanced just by the simple adjustment of rewards. The game is statically difficult but the rewards make the entire difference between snowballing into an unstoppable killing machine and being ground down into defeat. The simple brilliance of balancing makes this game playable by anyone.
If there's only one roguelike you need to play, it's FTL. All the others have some flaw or failing that makes second rate compared to this. Do yourself a favor and pick it up if you haven't already.

Dying Light's premise is a good one. You're in a Zombie Apocalypse and have to survive with parkour skills, wit and blunt force if you can't avoid a fighting situation. It has excellent crafting/upgrade/skill mechanics, and both looting and skills very much matters in the game. Still, I can't recommend it, except *maybe* on sale.
The reason I can't recommend it is due to a lot of bad game design factors. Some are annoying, while others are keyboard-crushing, soul sucking kind of decisions.
Parkour climbing/grabbing of edges is done automatically, but what you can grab is inconsistent and not always obvious. Grabbing some ledges (even in the tutorial!) requires perfection and anything less than that, and you fall to your death. This game doesn't let you manually save either, so expect trying parkour missions over and over again, from the point where the game decided to save for you. Also when you respawn you don't get back any of the equipment you used.
Some keymappings are dual-purpose and the game designers picked some of the worst combinations they could come up with. For example, the crouch button is shared with "slide". What happened to me was that I wanted to crouch after a jump to avoid being spotted.. but instead I slided outside a balcony, to my death.
For the first 6 hours of the game (at least) you only have melee weapons, and they break easily. Weapon/equipment wear is nothing new and can great, for example in System Shock 2. But in this game it's damn annoying. Most weapons unless they are of very high grade breaks after a few swings. We're talking *minutes* of usage. After you have repaired them so many times, they get broken and unusable permanently. This gets worse combined with a tiny inventory, and you can have maybe 3 or 4 weapons on you at any time. And again, they will mostly be melee weapons until you're lucky and get your hands on both a rifle/pistol *and* ammunition. Which is rare.
But the worst offender is the fighting mechanics. It is stamina based. Without any skill upgrades, the player character has minimum fighting stamina, and you have to run away to recharge after 3 or 4 swings with your weapon. It's a major chore and not fun at all. Now combine waiting for a stamina recharge while you're low on health and your weapon is "broken" all happening at the same time.
I lasted single-player for about 12 hours. hoping I would eventually 'get' the point of all these awful game mechanics. I did not complete the game before writing this review, nor have I tested coop or multiplayer.

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a haunting, story-driven exploration game. It isn't a horror game, at least not in a conventional sense, but more like Dear Esther and Gone Home with its spooky, lonely atmosphere.
The crux of the game is figuring out why Ethan Carter has gone missing and why everyone in the sleepy little mining town of Red Creek Valley is dead. Red Creek Valley is entirely abandoned. Traces of what happened to Ethan Carter's family can be found throughout, cleverly placed in an order that funnels the player in the right direction without railroading them--you can stumble on encounters in different orders, though the intended order is very clear.
Each area in Red Creek Valley has its own story to tell. Solving the mystery behind each of Ethan Carter's family members involves identifying all the key evidence and reconstructing the scene of their death. Once this is done, our protagonist, the (deliberately) clichéd hardboiled detective Paul Prospero, can use a sort-of psychic power to access a flashback of a sequence of events leading up to the person's death, which you must then order chronologically based on context clues.
The detached second-hand experience of these ghostly premonitions enhances the lonely and eerie atmosphere of the game and the subject matter at hand, working in its favour rather than against it. The basic detective puzzle minigame itself is perhaps a little contrived and contextless, but it serves a purpose both in the game and in the narrative.
Red Creek Valley is stunningly pretty, thanks to deft use of photogrammetry and baked lighting techniques. I've only played the Redux version, but it is a highly optimized, fully realized, seamless mini-open world with just one loading screen at the very beginning of the game. I love seeing asynchronous asset loading used to create non-traditional open world games like Ethan Carter, Dragon's Dogma and Dark Souls, and I want to see more games outside of the Ubisoft sandbox formula use it.
Gone Home's environmental storytelling is more densely packed into a smaller space, though Ethan Carter's is a better narrative that meshes well with its gameplay. With that said, I think Ethan Carter is the better example of what a quiet, story-driven walking game can be.

Enjoyable at first, in the end, only tedious. No real challenge... or even tower defense.
Where most tower defense makes you think about how best to place towers and what to upgrade when, this game is completely stripped of thought. You learn the optimal locations for each "tower" type early on, and, as evidenced by "hero mode", the levels are almost all designed with a choke or two that takes full advantage of a single group's optimal patterns, so most levels play like this:
1. Plug one, rarely two, "tower" groups into obvious optimal
locations
OPTIONAL: Spam archers
2. Upgrade (Mostly whenever, you'll have plenty of 'power'.)
3. WIN
The "RPG" side certainly gives math nerds something to obsess over, but it's similarly simplistic:
1. Level up!
2. Damage +1
OPTIONAL: Reset points at any time, because you somehow screwed that up
That's it. You want your healers to heal, of course, (skip Holy Light completely) and to take advantage of each "tower's" secondary effects, (armor break, chill, bleed, range, light/blind, devour) but for the most part, you'll just have to decide which usually low-end skill or two to neglect. Usually the lowest. You can safely ignore most defensive skills. (The actual numbers are utterly pointless because adequate info to calculate DPS and some secondary interactions aren't provided, and you learn how effective everything is by "feel"/sight same as any TD game anyways... but don't tell the math nerds!)
And that's the game for you. The art is bland, the story is absurd, but occaisionally amusing. Nothing to see here. While not a "worst game ever", if you're out for an actually good tower defense/game, look elsewhere. You might enjoy this if you're a math nerd, part of the Number Enlargement crowd, or just want something easy and amusing to click on and only plan to throw a few hours away with it anyways. Don't expect the game to get better as it goes on, it just doesn't. It never could, because it's fundamentally flawed.
Unfortunately, I have to add:
The game runs in Flash/AIR and suffers from the usual "looks like an old DOS machine could run it/practically requires a super-computer" issues. On a less powerful CPU, it may take twice as long to get the same amount done, and you will lose input control if you button-mash the one spell you'll want to button mash. But don't worry, you'll only notice it at critical moments, and only cause you to lose your "perfect" completion on a couple 45 minute boss battles... before you learn. Or your RSI flares up.

This is a must-play for any fan of retro platformers.  If you've played and liked VVVVVV, you will like this.  You might even think Terry Cavanagh designed this game.  He didn't.
The good:
- Great retro visual aesthetic
- The game's simulated projection from an old CRT monitor is clever and effective.
- There's a overarching puzzle element to the game that isn't intrusive and encourages exploration.
- It's free, apparently, which is awesome.
- The jump mechanics are tight, and well-programmed.
- You get power ups that allow you to access previously inaccessible parts of the map which you probably overlooked before, which gives you nice warm feelings of exploration and freedom.
- It has achievements and collectibles. I like OCD.
- It has 3 game modes. One has save points, the others do not.
- Despite the (intentionally) crude graphics, as the game progresses, a menacing atmosphere develops. It's effective.
The bad:
- No music.
- It's kinda short. But it was free.
- There's a couple cats in it, and I don't like cats. Woof.
Other comments:
- It's not terribly difficult.  Even the hardest platforming portions took me a couple minutes maximum to get past.  It's nowhere near as challenging as VVVVVV.
- It's a rather short game. I beat it in about 1.5 hours.
- There's no plot as far as I could tell.  Just win the game.  Some people might be bothered by that.  I wasn't.  Better for there to be no plot than some languishing backstory that's fed down your throat.
So yeah I'd recommend playing this. I enjoyed it.

Vampire; the Masquerade - Bloodlines
Before purchasing please note you will need to download an Unofficial Patch to fully get the game to work.
Storyline, lore and depth is heavy in this game. When you first lay eyes on it, it might be an eye sore, but trust me. Start to sink your fangs into the first few victims and get lost into the twisted personal horror game that lets you cling to your humanity while witnessing unGodly, unspeakable things... or let loose and become the monster you always wanted to be all the while walking the thin red line of not breaking too many Kindred laws.
The RPG element comes from the table top version of the game, point in intel, point in strength, point in charisma or melee, the concept is easy to use for beginners and easy to follow if you hover your mouse over any stat. It will tell you exactly what other stats benifit from your choices. Lacking in Hacking? Lacking in lock picking? (Dues Ex - like skills) Just add points to whatever helps you make you better at what you like doing.
Game play: When you start you pick a clan, each clan has their own strengths, their own weaknesses. Adding to the replay value of the game. Brawl your way, punk your enemies into submission, lie or whisper sweet nothings into the humans' ears to manipulate them into giving you what you want. Stealth your way through the city via sewers and back alleys, stick to the shadows - or walk among the humans and other vampires as their superior. It's all up to you.
Lots of side quests and though the world is not too vast (hence the game was made in 2004) you will have plenty to do with the portions of the city you have access to. Some you will need to gain specific skills, others you will get to as the game progresses.
The music is awesome. 90's and early 2000's gothic/rock, dark metal music. Will be looking for the OST of this game.
Voice acting, Jeanette! And many others. Even a popular actor from the TV show Futurama voice acted in this. Jeanette's voice actress did a role for Harley Quinn as well. Love her work! One of the strongest parts of this game is conversing with the NPCs. Some are funny, others will make you annoyeed, but none will be boring. Certain powers and certain social skills will effect how NPCs interact and react to you. Some you will need to threaten, if your threat is high enough, some you will have to persuade, others you have to flirt with, and some (if you pick clan Malkavian) you can just talk crazy talk with them. All adding to the depth of each NPC and some making you wish you could talk with them all night long.
The game is a Horror game, and some jump scares, but the feeling I get from playing the game... CREEP FEST. The atmosphere of the game when you get into a haunted house, or exploring a mad house, or going into a den of those trying to hurry the end of the world... and the sewers! It will make you think twice about opening a manhole, in real life and in game.
Over all this game is a CULT CLASSIC. If anything, get it and play it so when you nerd it out with your friends online or in person, you can give them lots of bloody tales of your own experiances in Vampire - Bloodlines.
9.5 / 10 Play it! Worth every penny at full price and at 75% off. No reason not to on a big sale!

I played the redux version of The Vanishing of Ethan Carter before doing a speedrun of this version, which is why my time in the game is relatively low. It took just over 5 hours for me to reach 100% completion in my first playthrough, and just over 2 hours to speedrun the original game to 100% completion.
The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a blend of the walking simulator, point-and-click adventure, and puzzle game genres. The game begins with a disclaimer that it will not hold your hand, and this is certainly true. There is no inventory, or notes, or objectives, or any explanation of what to do whatsoever. You are dropped into a (relatively speaking) large open world, and left to explore it as you see fit.
The problem with the open world format is that small objects are hidden within it, sometimes in places you have no reason to look, which are required to complete the puzzles in the game. In addition to this, large areas of the world serve no purpose whatsoever, but you will not know which sections those are, or if there is anything to be found, until you have expended a fair bit of time exploring the world.
The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is more obtuse than it is difficult. Most puzzles in the game can be completed within a matter of minutes, once you understand what you need to do. The final couple of puzzles are significantly easier than the rest of the game, to the point that I wondered if they were necessary at all.
While both versions of the game are visually and aesthetically beautiful to behold, the redux version in particular is one of the nicest looking games I have ever played. If your computer can handle it, I strongly recommend playing the redux over the original. Interestingly, both versions of the game come with trading cards and achievements, so there is some argument to be made for playing them both. One minor criticism is that the faces on characters seem... off, somehow. Perhaps it's the uncanny valley, but they don't seem quite natural.
I found the music of The Vanishing of Ethan Carter to be haunting and beautiful. It helps build on the already exceptional atmosphere the game presents. The voice acting and sound effects are competently handled.
Gameplay is a bit hit or miss. Overall the puzzles are clever and well crafted, but there are situations where the solution is counterintuitive or unclear. Combined with the necessity of exploring everything on your first playthrough, this does sometimes make the game feel like it is dragging its heels.
The story is interesting enough while you are playing, but for me at least ended on a somewhat unsatisfactory note.
Overall I would give The Vanishing of Ethan Carter a tentative recommendation if you are a fan of puzzle and point-and-click adventure games, and don't mind a game which does not hold your hand.

This is a recommend with a lot of caveats.
The core gameplay is exceptional. Rhythm and RPG are a surprisingly effective combination, with the game rewarding good spell and tactical choices as much as mastery of the rhythm mechanics.
HOWEVER
The story is, at best, cringe-worthy and cliche, written by someone who clearly thinks they are incredibly clever. There's a few good moments, but nothing that's worth it. So, if you play it, after the tutorial, skip every single cutscene and rush through every single bit of dialogue.
And expect a lot of grinding for random drops. You need drops to craft items, and you need XP to craft them. But you don't just spend XP, you choose how much XP you spend to improve your CHANCE of crafting that item. So even once you have all the materials, a couple of unlucky breaks and you're back to grinding again. The worst thing about it is that there is actually a much better mechanic for it ALREADY IN THE GAME. When you learn a spell, you pay a certain amount of XP to take a short trial, and if you succeed, you get the spell. Why couldn't this have been done with items? To pad for time! Of course.
In summation: Before the Echo is a fantastic core game with an awful story and a lot of grinding. Once upon a time, when this was $30? I'd never recommend it to anyone. Right now, at $5? Probably worth it if only so you can see what it could have been.

I played this game once, on normal and stopped at level 6 (out of 7) ...
I played this game a second time and stopped at level 6.
And yet I'm going to give this a thumbs up.  Before the Echo is what happens if you take DDR and make the player use the controller (So Stepmania), approach it from a multi lane system (like frequency or amplitude) and then add in RPG elements (puzzle quest).
And the end result is... well pretty impressive.  The game is played like an RPG, with the main character exploring floors.  Well "Exploring" in reality he chooses one of three monsters on each floor to fight, and is sent to a combat screen.
The combat in this game will be recognizable to anyone who has played a rhythm game before.   You press buttons to trigger different directions on three grids, each doing a different task.  If you are on the defense grid, you're blocking attacks, if you're on the mana grid you're gaining mana, and if you're on the spell grid you're casting your magic.  And you'll be switching between the three grids as you play the game.
There is also a similar mini game to learn spells.  The entire time there's quality music being played, a selection created specifically for this game, and while I won't be humming these songs later, the music is enjoyable.
There's also a rather solid story to this game, the player is locked in a tower with 7 floors and must reach the top level to ... well honestly I don't know because I never reached there, however the first 6 floors had a relatively engaging story, even a few twists that worked well.
However the first problems with the game is around the 5th level the game gets annoyingly tedious.  Enemies get too much life, and there's a time limit to every battle (the length of the song) but they also start throwing VERY powerful attacks that the player.  Wait long enough for a really good spell? Well you might have to choose between taking massive damage (20 points where you might have less than 150 total points) or skipping that spell that's lost forever and needs to be recharged
On top of this, the enemies start having 3 digits of life, usually more than the player, and they will be punishing.
There's even four difficulties of the game which is a good start, it does add notes and movements to songs, and that's a cool feature, but even on easy, the sixth level is tedious.  In fact it's always tedious. It's not impossible, but... well then there's the other part of the game, crafting.
At first the crafting system is cool and new.  You kill monster get items (up to three different items per enemy, though on item per type)  and then can make stuff out of it.  On Level 1 there's only 4 or 5 craftable items.  Each level adds 1 more recipe, so level 6 has around 10 recipes, by that point you either have played entirely too much of the previous levels, or you got sick of them and have a ton of unmade recipes in your inventory.
But the problem is every drop only comes from one monster.  If you don't like fighting the insect on level 6 (A decently fast and hard fight)  too bad, you have to.  And the other side of that is you don't fight him once, you will have to fight him two or three times just to progress because the key to the next level is craftable to, and even more if you want to make everything.
So even if you somehow beat him you'll have to go and grind him again and again which is where the real tedium comes in, and that's assuming you don't get unlucky and miss a potential drop (as each drop has a percentage chance to appear).   It artificially lengths the game in the worst way.
The other side of this system is that while the player gets more powerful as he plays, he doesn't feel more powerful because the enemies on each floor are significantly more powerful too.  When I went back and fought someone from level 1 I realized how much of a god I had become, but you only get that feeling if you return to very early floors, on level 6 you feel like you're the same weakling you always were.
However with that being said, I LIKE the core gameplay of this game.  I like the concept, I even like the story, I really like everything in it, that it hurts me that I just didn't want to finish it.  It is a really terrible feeling to say "I wanted to see it, but I can't stand the monotony. " Yet that's where I ended up.
So I recommend it, because I did put in some good hours into it, and it is a really fun game and concept.  Just realize if you aim to beat the game, you WILL be grinding, and not in a mindless way due to the combat structure.

This game was absolutely awesome! As a very experienced and advanced Dance Dance Revolution, Osu, and Stepmania player, I tend to fly through many rhythm games, especially those involving arrows. However, I was on the medium setting, and the game was challenging for me. The challenge is in the arrows, of course, but it is more so in the strategy of the game, such as navigating between the arrow screens, casting spells at the right time, making sure you have enough mana, trying to defeat the enemy before time ran out, not getting hit, and balancing experience points, as the experience points are also currency for synthesizing and crafting items.
I loved that mechanic of the game because it was not a set value to craft an item, but instead you can decide how many experience points to use. The higher you want your probability of success to be, the more exp you sacrifice. The probability also caps at 95%, so there are no free rides. It's a good way to keep people battling and playing and makes one think carefully before deciding what to create. Quite a few times, I had to go down a level to create something I needed. I also liked how in this game, you have to accept that you will lose hp in battle in order to defeat the enemies. This is not a huge deal because all your stats reset after every battle.
The story itself was also very original, although it didn't get very deep until the end. When it did get deep, though, it went far. There are a lot of twists that are less predictable than I had anticipated, and the plot gets into the nitty-gritty of what's going on while still keeping secrets.
Playing for acheivements does actually expand gameplay, and there are quite a few little secrets in the game that lead to one large secret.
The voice acting and audio are beautiful. The voice actors were pretty talented, and the audio was high-quality. The music during the rhythm battles was a bit underwhelming to me as a ddr player and sounded more like background music, but it was very well produced and some songs were cool. It made sense in the context of the game. The art was beautiful, too. I think the aesthetic fit the game very well, and the main characters and enemies are well-done and very pleasing.
I highly recommend this game to people who like rhythm games like DDR, Stepmania, and Osu, as well as people who just like RPG-style battles or intense games. This is a different kind of game that is very well developed and that I'd like to see more of.

This game is an amazing Visual Novel, one of the best I've seen since I first started playing dating sims on Deviant Art. Gorgeous art work, beautiful music, and amazing voice actors. I'll admit though, some parts of the story line are a bit... lacking in depth but that's why I feel those parts are fleshed out more in the sequel, Demon War. But this isn't about the sequel, this is about Seduce Me the Otome by Michaela Laws.
Whenever I play a VIsual Novel that entertains the idea of sex (even if it's of the implied kind), I get turned off by it, but somehow the idea of Incubi(?) and Succubi(?) giving the player's character (or just the main character) a chance to turn down the offer of sex is a great and there are very few VIsual Novels (from what I've played) that actually toy with this kind of idea. But there's more to Seduce Me than a girl meeting five hot incubi guys that can seduce her with their powers.
It's about a girl named Micah (though you can change her name to whatever you want), who, after her grandfather dies, inherits her grandfather's estate (and all his other assets it seems) and she meets six incubi brothers, James, Matthew, Sam, Erik, and Damian. The six brothers escaped from the demon world and are being hunted by a devil named Malix. So in return for her letting them stay at her grandfather's house, the brothers decide to help Micah with her own problems (that's all I'm going to say to help avoid spoiling more than I already may have).
Each path in this game is generally about two, maybe three hours long, at least depending on the guy you're going for and the choices you've made. There are even four "secret" characters you can unlock and woo if the six brothers aren't your thing. Three of those choices are ladies if any girl playing this game wants to have the yuri side of things. But that's about all I can say about this game.
It was fun getting all of the achievements and even more, I'm glad I discovered this free otome because now I can move onto Demon War and finish the story there.
All in all, I give this game a 9/10. I took one point off because the second half of the story somehow seems to slow down a bit and turn into a more of a drama fest (which is still fun but I kinda wanted to see more about the Devils that were after the boys) but thankfully, the sequel has more about the Demons and the boys' backgrounds and home in the sequel. So get this game, play it and be seduced by the lovely voices of the guys and their story.

It's difficult to fully do the game justice without writing a novel, so I'll try to sum it up in as few words as possible.
The sheer scope and breadth of the game is incredible. Randomised galaxies for each play, a huge variety of ships which can be unlocked via different methods and a fairly impressive and unique set of alien races for your crew. Power distribution and the layout of your ship are both intuitive *and* important to your strategy. My favourite part, though, is the immersion - the game's plot is a simple one, but the way in which the game draws you into it is truly wonderful. You will be on the edge of your seat, you will agonise over which decision to make, you will become heavily invested in your ship and your crew - and you WILL wile away hours and hours of your time without realising it, because you will find yourself starting a new game if you fail, or if you win. It matters not, because the game supports so many playstyles, you will always find another way to play. If you fail, you will vow vengeance on the Rebels and start again - and if you succeed, you will decide to punish them again anyway, with your new ship and crew.
This game is an absolute steal for its asking price. If you have a spare few quid sitting around, use them to buy this game - you won't regret it.

A straight and forward tower defense game. If you like the genre, I very very highly recommend this game. If you don't like the genre, I doubt any game would be able to change your mind, and suggest that you carry on.
Defender's Quest managed to impress me by literally exceeding the average in every way I can think of.
+ Not a rehash of another tower defense game - it didn't really do anything extraordinary within the genre, yet I can't think of a single game I'd call it similar to.
+ Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ the story is actually good, the characters fun, and the funny parts actually funny.
+ There is no ultimate strategy that works for the game (build/upgrade order, etc). Each map forces a new strategy based on the availability of locations to place your characters, and enemy monster types.
+ There are dozens of maps, with 4 different difficulty settings, all of which have a New Game+ version which play differently. This game will take many dozens of hours to complete.
+ The music is good. Nothing spectacular, but for the genre and the pricetag, exceeds standards.
+ Lots of things to play with in the options menu.
+ Family friendly - I would see absolutely no problem in an 8 year old playing this game.

to hit that sweet spot between the two, while offering a much different sci-fi experience.
has a VERY strong Starship Trooper vibe, but it is used to good effect; while clearly taking its own unique creative queues. As a Helldiver, you are out to protect humanity from all manner of hideous alien species, in all the hostile planets around the galaxy. Each mission is randomly generated, offering different goals and layouts each playthrough. Along with this, there is also a number of different specific scenarios including some challenging boss fights in the late game plus a whopping 12 difficulty levels to choose from!
In conjunction with the design choices & combination of mechanics used,
offers up some intense coop gameplay, that actually encourages team work. Design dictating behaviour; It is nice to see a commendation/reporting option built in to encourage the community to govern itself against troublesome players. The coop/team work/community focus is strong throughout.
Levels being objective based, have tasks like bomb disposal, arming a missile silo, blowing up an alien hive or recover an important item. Each almost always requires team work to complete the task &/or to provide defensive cover. You also need to share ammo and supplies to best survive harder incursions.
Many of the objectives also require you to input a series of directional presses in sequence and without mistakes to progress. These start off easy but get quite long in harder levels, increasing the pressure & punishing mistakes harshly. This combo mechanic is also used when calling down your personal

. It is fundamental to the gameplay experience, and used in perfect balance with the shooter/action aspects of the game.
One of the other key mechanics vital to the experience is friendly fire. Normally, unless playing with friends this can lead to frustration in online gameplay, actually turned out to be an absolute BLAST
, offering up some of the most hilarious, calamitous failures & occasional epic recoveries I've seen. Lot of laugh-out-loud moments, such as the inevitable time when your team mate drops a reinforcement
to revive your dead Helldiver, only to have the capsule kill them on your decent!
Surviving your team mates can sometimes be harder than the aliens :)
Controls via controller are responsive, precise & there are some challenging achievements to acquire on the side.
Another impressive element of
is the great customisation over your loadouts, each offering something different, but well balanced in a way not to have a go-to loadout. This encourages experimentation, keeps things fresh & used as a reward/unlock mechanic as you level up. The DLCs offer a much wider range of weapons & outfits to choose from, not required by any means, or offering any distinct advantage, but would recommend picking up the
with the 'Snow Shoes' as that is necessary in the Arctic scenarios. Working with your team mates' loadouts can greatly enhance your survivability & becomes crucial on harder difficulties.
The Mechs you can pilot are fantastic carnage inducing fun too!
Aside from the high quality, detailed animations & environments, there are three alien species change up your strategies, all performing very differently from each other. My favourites are the Bugs, perhaps it’s the throwback to Starship Troopers, but I do find them the most fun to play against. Cyborgs get on my nerves with some of the blocking mechanics used & swarms of Illuminate can be hard.
These alien species are tied into a rather unique community feature where there is a War fought by all players in the Helldiver Community. Each mission success accumulatively counts points towards victories against the three different alien species, ultimately leading to a campaign to conquer their homeworlds. If players do not work together & push the aliens back, then they can overtake our homeworld. I really like the way this works, offering something to keep you loading the game back up on a regular basis, but it does unfortunately have one limitation in that it can prevent you from being able to play against some of the alien species at some points in the war.
You may log in and find you can only fight Cyborgs for example, which can continue for many days!
With all the variety in the levels, objectives, weapons & aliens coupled with the solid team oriented mechanics there is a lot of replayability to be had for the money, but ultimately as you progress to the top levels, seen a few wars & have everything unlocked the experience can become repetitive. Levels generally play out with similar tactics outside of the core scenario changes.
With such solid foundation & super fun gameplay overall, I would love to see content expanded for veteran & new players alike. More map variety
, more level modes/sizes
, more aliens or some sort of a game-plus mode or campaigns. Perhaps in a Helldivers 2: Search for More Democracy?
Although at time of writing this the online community
is still active, I have also unfortunately experienced many an issue connecting to games over my time playing. Does work 90% of the time, but some will simply not connect & dump you back at your ship. When it does connect, the game performs well.
Best played with friends,
is well worth a look for any fan of coop games or twin stick shooters.

I've played the best part of an hour and thought I would leave my initial impressions.
Great music. I love it. It's a bit of a mix of the old school chiptune vibe with a twist of the contemporary.
It doesn't have the option to rebind keys but the default is a fairly common WASD setup. The native xbox controller support works like a charm and it makes use of the analogue sticks with progressive flight controls(push it a little to fly slowly, push it a lot to fly fast) so I would say a controller is the way forward.
If you've played a roguelike before you'll be familiar with the ?? pick ups. Instead of potions and scrolls you get alien artifacts and alien technology. They come in usual buff and debuff flavours but are all themed to fit into the world. Blindness/confusion potion becomes a Sensor Disrupting artifact etc. After you've use a ?? mystery pick up once, it's identified and the next time you get it, you'll know when to use it or if you just want to jettison it right away.
There's no XP system but there is equipment to loot, which is all procedurally generated a la Borderlands, which is great. I found a couple of different shields, one had a higher total capacity but slower regeneration, a low capacity shield with very fast regen and I found a few ship accessories. One boosted fire rate at the cost of shield regen and the other allowed me to regenerate armour.
The other way your ship progresses is through upgrade parts. They are like skill points you can find and then you can choose to add another weapon slot, the only gun I found on my run boosted my front fire rate a fair bit but also had a rear fire which was great or  you can increase your hull/cargo capacity and thrusters.
The "overworld" isn't too dissimilar to the FTL star chart. You move from left to right and you can branch off now and then taking a longer route to the goal to go hunting for loot and upgrades. While you are in the overworld aka space you can identify your mystery parts and potions.. I mean artifacts and you use your upgrade parts. The UI is simple but effective and very easy to work with.
When you are done messing around in space you pick the planet on the star map and get down to business. I think I seen 4 different kinds of planet. Desolate, Ice, Forest and Water. There are some cool environmental effects like a Sandstorm type deal that blows in from the left or right and slows or speeds you up depending on which direction you are going. On the Ice planet I noticed a nice little fogging/frosting effect at the edges of the screen, while on the jungle planet I think I was attacked by some sort of space locusts.
It's really not as punishing as most games with roguelike elements. I was reduced to zero Hull(that's after 0 shield and 0 armour) a few times and was allowed to carry on but my equipment degraded. Shields regenerated at half speed, my gun lost x amount of power. So while you pay a bit of a price, there is enough loot that at least a placeholder item wont be far away. You can save and quit anytime, too. That's always good.
Anyway, this is just supposed to be a bit of a rambling first impression seeing as there were no reviews at all when I got it. So far I really like it. I should add that the little writing I got to experience was well done.

King Arthur's Gold (in the following text written "KAG", to keep it short) is developed by transhuman and takes place in a medieval world, which is ruled by battles from two teams. That describes it roughly. Very roughly. KAG isn't a game that cares about story, it delivers it's awesomeness through the multiplayer. In the coop, you mostly build your own castle with materials that you farmed before from the destroyable world. While you are busy building a nice home, your comrades are trying to stop the other team attacking your castle. You see, there's a lot to do and it feels like that to. You can really feel the tension on the battlefield. The keeps this feeling up. It's pretty fast because of some movement-features, that help you climp walls or jump on to the right spot. For example: You are lost on the map, running away from your enemys. You could jump from a platform to a safer place, but it's hard to land there. When you're playing as knight you can use your shield to floate in the air and land softly on the saving platform. That's another thing, the classes. There are 3 to choose from: The knight, the magician and the one with the bow. So pretty classic, but they are designed very well. Each one plays in another style and has other advantages. Also nice: Avery single movement has an own animation. That sounds dumb when is say it, i know. but come to think about it. Not every game, especially indies, does this. And in this manner, you're leading your pixeld hero through a battlefield with up tp 32 players. That's a huge number for an indie game of this size and style. The only complain I have, is the not completely functional crafting system. It works for the most part, but sometimes there are some graphic-bugs or it doesn't place items right. The last great thing i want to mention is the Challenge-mode. When you play it you get a specific time to do something like "kill all enemys" or "get to the other side of the map". It really shows the oppurtunities for this game in the speed-running branche.
KAG is this kind of game that shows the advantages of the internet. Because of steam everyone can have it and play with other people, which is a thing many will do because it's hillariously fun to play. On the other hand it's great for hardcore-gamers to compete or build tournaments for. So many great things in one small game. one of the best multiplayer-games on steam so far. 8/10

Good game!  Definitely worth your time if the preview videos look like your kind of thing.  It's short - think hard before you pay full price (I got it for $3 on Humble Bundle) - but those 3-4 hours are quality time.
In case you didn't read the sales blurb on the store page,
is a story about a psychic detective investigating the circumstances surrounding the disappearance of a young boy, which takes place in the "town" of Red Creek Valley - a few scattered buildings way out in some remote woods.
The game prides itself on not holding your hand, which is great, but I could have used SOME handholding on the controls.  Turns out that when flying words tell you you have to find a clue, that does not mean to leave and go look for that clue.  I spent two hours angrily scouring every inch of the woods trying to find a hand crank before I read a review that told me that the flying words themselves are the starting point.  Of course, I then watched a friend play it and she "got it" immediately; maybe I'm just stupid.
Anyway - other than that, I found everything very intuitive, the few puzzles were enjoyable, and the story was suitably creepy.  Some players were disappointed by the final reveal, and I think that's a valid view, but personally I thought it was fine.  The story's strength is in the telling, not the justification.
Graphics, music, and performance are top notch.  No bugs encountered.  You might want to turn the music volume down as it competes a little too much with the environment and dialogue.
Overall, a good mystery/horror story that lends itself well to this type of game (as opposed to a book or movie).  Slow paced and pretty straightforward.  Avoid if you demand twitch action or painful difficulty.  Buy if you enjoy slow burning horror or detective adventures.

)
Note: This review is for the Redux version, which for some reason I cannot give a review for.
You are Paul Prospero, noir detective extraordinaire, with a special ability to see into the past when you touch stuff. Thank goodness you can, because you will need it to help solve some murders. Nobody else is going to help you: Red Creek Valley is literally a ghost town. When I mean literally, I mean literally
. The clues you are going to get are mainly the visions of ghosts of the deceased and their final movements. Otherwise, there is nobody.
Hang on, why do you have to solve murders when we have this Ethan Carter boy to find? He is the only person mentioned in the title, and he is kind of important, right? Yes, he is. Indeed he is so important to the story that every single murder you have to solve is about his disapperance. And you might want to solve the mystery quickly, because he is only a young boy, and children don't tend to live for very long in horrific situations.
Did I mention there is nobody to help you? This extends to the gameplay: complete open world with no hints whatsoever on what to do. No tutorial, only the occasional instruction to click on something. Yes, the whole game is one big puzzle. You have your main plot, of course, but you also have your sidequests. All of them are a lot of fun and mildly challenging. The puzzles are intuitive and based on the real world. You are encouraged to explore, to go into the grass and push buttons. Indeed, you might start doing that not because you want to find clues, but because the whole place is so
. For a supposed horror game, the scenery is gorgeous. The game is also devoid of any cheap horror tricks, such as jump scares (on the most part) and scary monsters, which was nice. And the music. The music fit the game so well.
However, the gorgeous scenery is a double-edged sword. It is so photorealistic I got severe motion sickness if I play for too long. There are tips and tricks for reducing that and you can find them in the discussions. But please keep this in mind if you suffer from the same affliction as me.
Overall I think this is a gorgeous puzzler. Please do not rush this: not only will you miss clues, you will also miss out on a beautiful experience. It is a game to be savoured.

Partly due to its troubled history however the game has its problems. The bugs were well wiped out thanks to community effort but still has minor annoyances. Nothing game breaking but like e. g. when You face a boss, there is some talking and after that You have to reselect Your weapon. Things like that, nothing major.
Steam has the latest official version, some of the major bugs were addressed in that but You would probably do Yourself a favor installing one of the community patches:
True Patch Gold aims to totally conserve the original gameplay while addressing the bugs.
Unofficial Patch has two flavors, the basic patch more or less does the same, though some minor changes were made to the original to make some things more logical. In the expanded 'plus' version (it is one download You decide which to use while installing) however the creators tried to restore and even recreate much content cut from the final game, including places, weapons, abilities, weapons, dialogues, quests etc.
If You are a purist and want to experience the original game, True Patch Gold is for You.
If You do not mind a few changes but want the original experience, UP basic might be the way to go.
If You want to see the game as what it could have become if not for its troubled history, choose UP plus.
And please, please do not ask in forums which to choose, the above should be enough information. There is a years long flame war involving the patches, their creators and their supporters. Don't spill oil onto the flame. It is a shame, both are great, took up a lot of time and work, both deserve respect.
As a closing, a few notes, hints, advices:
- save often. Really. There is a quicksave function, You can have a few, it is nat too hard to press F5 (or whatever).
- spend some time studying the character sheet and understand how feats work, what adds to them etc. Don't throw around Your points, there won't be that many.
- understand how skill books work so You can get the most of them.
- specialize. It might be hard, You'll need some unarmed to feed, also there is a quest which is very hard without celerity discipline or ranged - on the other hand the game seems to push You toward melée.
- have spare XP points unspent as many as You can. The amount in later game may go up to 50-60. You never know when You'll need to spend a lot to buy in to a skill that You need to complete a quest to Your satisfaction. You WILL need for example high computers and lockpickig, if You spend all Your hard earned XP on fighting/social skill You will be in trouble with side quests, maybe even main ones. Btw, You might think that the game will throw a lot of XP at You later in the game, it won't. Conserve.
- if You are completionist, and Your ego can stand it use a walkthrough, otherwise there will be a lot of saving/loading and running around. You don't know beforehand which solution to a quest will yield the best reward. Dialogues are also unfriendly: if You choose the wrong line You might never get to the option that gives the best option. Also NPCs are rarely very clear concerning their wishes. If they hint that it would be appreciated if You did X quest without bloodshed that means that You SHOULD do it that way for the best reward. They are often not even this clear.
- if You want to have all endings as an option in the endgame You have to forget about roleplaying and go for shameless bootlicking and say to all major players what they want to hear, all the time.
This is it. Well, not much of a review, but at least it is long 8).

A third-person action/RPG that is true to the old whitewolf roleplay system.
Pros:
- The game is true to the old pen and paper whitewolf system, you'll feel like you're really playing Vampire: The Masquerade
- Fun character generation with all the classic vampire clans complete with most of the old powers
- Immersive environments that make you feel like you're really in a vampire run city
- Intrigue and political tactics true to the setting complete with clan biases and alliances
- Interesting items and weapons that seem appropriate for the setting
- Different playstyles depending heavily on clan and powers
- Interesting quests that add a lot of color to the world
- A real feeling of power at higher level, but also danger as the game never becomes easy
Cons:
- Buggy, lots of crashes and locks can make things annoying at times
- Lots of prep work needed to get the game running, you usually have to use one of the fan-created patches to get this to work on steam
- Some knowledge needed, building a character poorly can make the game very hard to progress in
Overall:  This game is a great experience, even with the work needed to get it running (which is usually an instant fail for me), I have to recommend this game.  It's worth the investment to be able to immerse yourself in a game and a world that pays so much respect to the original Whitewolf source material.  And even if you've never played Vampire before, you can enjoy it for the interesting story and unique world.

I quite enjoyed this title. Haven't read the book nor played the original. Sure the scale isn't grandiose as the heavy weight titles such as COD or Battlefield but Metro has a distinct style, engaging story line and overall enjoyable gameplay.

What can I say about Metro... Well, for starters, it is a unique survival horror title with an amazing story, great gameplay mechanics and a great sequel to boot. What makes Metro so good is, for one thing, it's combat mechanics.
There are two types of bullets: Regular and Military Grade bullets. Regular are pretty simple; you shoot and they kill, where as Military Grade does more dammage, and they work for almost every gun. Something to know is that Military Grade bullets are also the main currency in this game, and if you are low and need money, you can exchange regular ammo into currency, however you don't get much for these trades. For example, you trade in 10 shotgun shells for around 2 Military Grade rounds. Now bullets aren't too common, and on hard they're scarce, so there is a lot of mannaging what you spend and what you keep.
You also have the choice of being loud or stealthy. Being loud, of course, means you kill everything in sight, but doing will obviously blow through ammo quick. Stealth allows you to preserve ammo, but it takes WAY more time, and often a lot of trial and error. Use the dark, and turn off/avoid lights, as this does keep you hidden, but most of all:
You will need to be precise and make sure when you shoot, the body isn't too close for other enemies to see. (My reccomendation for a good stealthy weapon is upgrading your first gun to have a good stock, sight and surpresser.)
That's just a few aspects of Metro I can give out of many. Over all, I highly recommend Metro 2033 as well as Last Light.
Oh, and be certain of your actions and choices throughout parts of the game(s).

It's hard for me to explain but I like this mix of RPG elements with Surival, Parkour and Zombies it just works so well and is really enjoyable.
There's a few major points though.
First being the exploration of Harran and Old Town the two areas of the vanilla game now while Harran itself isn't exactly anything special it's what you can find while you run around what gets my interest. it's not just finding weapons, it's the people as well sometimes you'll find a survivor who needs help and will hand over a new weapon at the end or a survior who doubles as a handy merchant. You can also find neat places to explore like train tunnels which feature all sorts of rare items and weapons.
Second is the crafting system which returns from Techland's previous title Dead Island. Both games feature a plethora of weapon blueprints which grant you access to all sorts of weapons a sword that sets zombies on fire, a Khopesh that freezes the enemy, a hammer that sets a zombie on fire and blows their head off in one swing.
Third is the variety of the zombies. Like any decent zombie game Dying Light features more than your average flesh biters they also have the quick paced Virals which are drawn to explosions and gunshots they can also climb up objects and in some cases buildings, Toads which shoot poision at long range but are utterly worthless up close, Volatiles which are big angry zombies that make Lickers from Resident Evil look like angry dogs the Volatiles are a tenacious and incredibly durable type of zombie which can not only run but they can jump as well, they can easily scale buildings and attack in groups of up to 4 to make matters worse Volatiles have a variant known as Spider Volatiles which have increased health.
The game also features Brutes which are bigger, stronger and weilding rebar versions of standard zombies they're a challenge to start with but become rather simple to deal with. The Demolisher on the other hand is one zombie that pretty much stays the same at every point in the game it's a zombie with high attack, high defense, high speed and high health. They hit like a truck and look like one too, the best way to deal with them is easier attack their back or run.
Lastly is the Expansion DLC for Dying Light the Following which features an incredibly interesting story line with a new assortment of weapons, zombies and missions. It is by far the most satisfying DLC granting you access to an entirely new area about as big as Harran if not bigger and adding in the buggy which is the most fun I've had driving in an apocalypse.

Helldivers does a lot of things right and a few things very annoyingly wrong. It's a fun, chaotic top-down RT shooter with gobs of different equipment that allows for different playstyles. It has three types of enemies that feel nicely distinct from each other, rewarding different tactics and loadouts. The player shouts are great and very in-line with the atmosphere of the game, which ventures heavily into Starship Troopers type territory. The weapons are also very different from one another with good feedback and sounds.
The game can be played with up to 4 people, and loudouts are designed to make that possible. The team can take an APC and roll across the map with all 4 protected to get to the objective or can instead bring lighter weapons and try to use stealth by taking out sentries early. There's an interesting campaign structure that takes into account everyone playing the game and can be 'won' or 'lost' regardless of individual contributions.
There are some problems, however. First, there is no real option to disconnect from the 'global' campaign either to play solo or with friends. That means if the campaign has progressed to a point where there is only one enemy left out of the three, you have no choice or variety anymore. You're stuck killing bugs or cyborgs or (shudder) illuminati until things change- and you can do very little to effect the broad campaign. The game will work 'offline' but you will be stuck with things as they were when you last went online.
'Retaliation' missions are also stupidly difficult in solo (and for that matter are pretty ♥♥♥♥ing stupid in general). In solo play pause should also be available- no reason not to have it. There is no need to spend time programming bots for solo play but some more thought could have been given to single-player, especially in the campaign mechanics. It's idiotic that cyoborg tanks can spawn basically right on top of you in single player and renders any tactics up to that point basically useless.
To add insult to injury, if you die and respawn in single player you start right where you died- IE where there are a dozen heavy enemies ready to kill you and you probably don't have all your weapons. Weapon selection is terribly awkward and slow- VERY bad on this point and it feels so cheap when you get killed because your stupid marine doesn't switch weapons. I'm also not entirely convinced the campaign mode won't get screwed up when the player base shrinks enough.
Additionally, there is the 'screen' issue. When playing multiplayer, everyone has to stay on the same screen. If people don't move together, no one can move- and no one can see past their nose. This forces teamwork but doesn't work well in a game where you have scouts you have to take out from a long distance. You'll find that a lot of fans of the game freak the hell out whenever anyone mentions this but it's an ugly mechanic, and it just sucks. Imagine the strategies and choices that could be implemented without it- and if that isn't desired, the screen should have at least some elasticity; maybe just half the screen-width. As it is, the devs have said they want it this way so they're not changing it. That doesn't negate criticism.
This isn't a huge negative but a lot of the strategems feel redundant and make for a huge money sink in terms of research. The grind in the game- for research points and unlocks in general- is also a bit much.
I like Helldivers and am going to continue to play it and I recommend it to people who want a good co-op game and especially like the style. I'd suggest watching a let's play or something to get an idea of how it goes. Don't buy it for solo play, it's a waste of time.
Note: Played the game with friends for the most part (no randoms) with some solo play as well and all the DLC available at the time of review.

Between its addictive gameplay and sliding difficulty scale, Defender’s Quest offers gamers a great deal for such a small investment of time.

Defender's Quest is a case study in covering your weaknesses and emphasizing your strengths. Shoddy writing? A beautiful "skip" button in every cutscene and dialogue can be turned off. Difficulty? If you hit a brick wall in story mode you can go back and do slightly harder versions of prior maps to level up. Tower diversity? Unique equipment means your second Berserker probably won't be as good as your first, so it's harder to spam one tower. The slog of New Game+ not going fast enough? Triple experience is an option in the menus. All this lets you focus on the core tower defense game, which is best played at 4X speed.
Plenty of weaknesses can't be worked around, though. Workshop mods are few in number, and the first one I tried locked up the game in the first level. Character level is too huge a factor in whether you pass a level or not, meaning few maps feel appropriately scaled to your level at any given time. The game has a fixed resolution, even in fullscreen, and in fullscreen Steam notifications will leave artifacts on the screen. It's a little too easy to fall into a "two of each" mentality, setting up two identical sets of towers on the two major paths of most maps, with the only major variance between maps being what towers you level up first. The tower "skill trees" don't contribute much especially for those towers that only have variants of "melee attack" or "shoot arrows".
For all the weaknesses I've pointed out, there are few high points in the game. The boss fights are excellent, requiring you to balance "kill the boss faster" against "kill the creeps faster". Otherwise it's the usual tower-defense game of setting up your towers and watching them slaughter thousands of zombies. The game demands enough of your attention in boosting your towers etcetera that it's not a good "put something on in the background while you play" game, but isn't demanding enough to be a thoughtful or engaging experience.
All in all, it's hard to recommend Defender's Quest unless you're just dying for a tower defense game where you make a bunch of bars go up a la Progress Quest.

I like this game a lot! The story is entertaining and the characters all have very distinct personalities. Your character is a high school girl who inheirits her grandfather's house after he mysteriously dies. Your father pushes you to move into the mansion your grandfather left behind (your father is a very pushy person). When you move in, you find demon five brothers hiding there from the devils they were fighting. Demons are neutral (some good, some evil- depending on how you play the game) and devils are evil- this distinction will be announced later when you encounter the devils. The brothers stay with you to help you prepare for a party that your father wants you to throw for the people at your family's company to prove you have what it takes to be CEO (this is one of the achievements if you answer the questions correctly). The game really picks up with the fantasy plot after the party. BUT whoever you pick to help at the party set-up is who you can choose to date (it's only the brother you chose for the rest of the game), unless you go out with your friends instead which allows you to pick between them.
Five Demon Brothers:
James- Responsible firstborn son, very polite and gentlemanly
Erik- Comes off a bit like a lady's man and very flirty but he's not what he appears
Sam- A bit hard-headed and aggressive, the toughest fighter, but also extremely protective
Matthew- Childish and Sweet but a bit of a cry-baby
Damien- Quiet and pensive, he has the ability to read minds, he also seems a bit shy
The five demon brothers all have varied personalities and powers. And if you're not interested in dating them you have the option to date your friends:
Naomi- a girl who is very girly, always follows the rules and likes hanging out in cafes
Suzu-a tough talking tomboy who chills at the arcade
or Diana (a powerful succubus who is very sassy) , too I think, somehow (though I haven't figured out how yet).
I like that there are options to date either guys or girls since a lot of dating games are usually only straight. It's just refreshing to see a dating game where the main character could canonlly be bisexual. I greatly appriciated that!
There are other events in the game that potentially have nothing to do with romance (like a third of the endings any way). So if you don't want to date any of the characters, you can still play for the story. There's enough of a plot and a world to get into with this game that it's an option as well. This is a believable fantasy world with its own full cast of characters, supernatural races, magic, and lore. If you like fantasy and otome (anime-styled dating games), then you will probably enjoy this game like I do! :)

To start: I used to add a longer header to these reviews which explained my reviewing ethos, but since it often made the review too long to submit, I've opted to leave it on my Backloggery.
Gameplay: This game has been described quite a lot by now as a darker Earthbound, and that's not the worst comparison. I'd call it a sort of hybrid of the classic Shin Megami Tensei style of team setup where there are many people throughout the world which you can recruit into your team (unlike Shin Megami Tensei however, you can't recruit enemies) and the combat formula of Earthbound without some minor things like gradually decreasing health bars. There's over thirty members which you can recruit over the course of the game, and as the description of this game says, there is indeed perma-death, albeit not in as harsh of a manner as you may think.
Running out of health in this game results in you getting KO'd, not dying. Characters can die either through scripted story events or random enemy attacks; the latter of which I don't find particularly good. While it did force me to use other characters than my powerhouse team, it did feel frustrating getting punished just because of RNG. Unless I've completely missed something, there is no way to counter or predict killing moves; a design decision I feel would benefit the game. While it is funny that characters can just get their heads bitten off, it can be rather frustrating when that character is your powerhouse. Since it is RNG-based you can save-scum the game (in fact, you can scum the scripted sequences as well, but I'll let you figure out how to do that). However, if you choose not to scum up everything, you'll find yourself actually facing some pretty challenging decisions. Talk about these decisions, however, will come in the story portion of the game.
The comparison to Shin Megami Tensei earlier wasn't just one made to compare party systems; this game is pretty hard as well. Combat isn't as in-depth or tactical as something like Nocturne or Digital Devil Saga, but as far as the challenge goes, it is on the level of Digital Devil Saga's normal mode, with the aforementioned unavoidable lethal attacks included in that comparison. If you're looking for a relaxing RPG, this game ain't the one for you. It's not gonna blow your face off or anything, but it definitely has some expectations from you as a player.
Overall, I had a pretty good time with Lisa. It's about eight hours long (for me; I also know I missed a fair bit of stuff), so the $10 price fits the bill IMO. It's also the kind of game I could see myself playing sometime down the road, mainly for using different characters and seeing the other endings. This probably won't be for a while, but hey; at least it does have me interested in replaying at all. That's a lot better than other games have done for me. 8/10.
Story: From the trailer, I was expecting this to be a schadenfreude-laden adventure in which we enjoy partaking in the misery of this man named Bradley Armstrong. What I didn't expect was for the game to actually get kinda dark and heavy on me. This game walks a damn fine rope between dark comedy and just plain dark, frequently tilting to one side but never falling off. If you're looking for a happy game, go away. Now. If you're looking for a game in which teenagers go out to save the world from [Evil Entity X], you're in the wrong part of town.  If you're looking for a story that wraps itself up conclusively, well... sorry to disappoint you, but there's a lot of interpretation that you can have for this game. The funny bits in this game are great, the dark bits can be downright upsetting at times, and the ending could get a little too real for some. If you're interested in a dark and macabre tale about a man potentially ruining the future of humanity and in the process stepping on about forty rakes in a row for a cheap knockoff karate scroll, this game is for you. 10/10.
Graphics: Well, it's not gonna tax your system; that's for sure. If you can run Steam, you can run this game. As for the art style, I could see it being a love it or hate it kind of affair. Some of the enemy designs can get downright grisly at times. Other times, you're kicking the crap out of/headbutting an adorable deer. The art does a pretty good job of conveying the mood for the area. There's a lot of silly stuff and a lot of gory stuff. The stage design does leave a bit to be desired IMO. Often, it just comes down to a reskin of a generic mountain, and it all would look exactly the same if it weren't for variants in the palette. I don't know if this game engine has the capability for slopes, but it would help the game world look a lot better. Plus, there are a few unfortunate areas in which vital things like doorways are obscured by foreground elements (namely in the motorcycle race toward the end of the game, ramps and the doorway to exit are hidden by grass). Despite some disappointments which may just be incumbent on the engine, the game does look pretty darn alright. 4/5.
Sound: Man, this game has a trippy soundtrack. If you liked the weirdness of Earthbound's OST, you'll be right at home with  this one. In fact, it almost feels like you could switch the battle themes around and they'd work just as fine on each other's games. It's definitely one of those games where I'd suggest getting the OST if you're into it; you should play the game first just to see if you like it or not, of course. The sound design is pretty good as well; hits feel punchy, meaty stuff sounds juicy, and it's just all-around a good job on that front. Of course, there's no voice acting, so there's no point in going over that. Overall, a once again very good effort. 4/5.
Overall scores are: 8/10/4/4; cumulative score of 8.7/10. It's darker than what you'd expect from the trailer and lighter than what you'd expect from the intro. Definitely worth the purchase if you can stomach a sometimes very brutal game.

Sleeper hit of the year. With RPGs like Dragon Age:I, Banner Saga, and Wasteland 2, it's good to go back to a much simpler time to have a few laughs and even shed a tear or two. Taking a large amount of inspiration from the Earthbound/Mother series, LISA is a much more surreal and darker take on the genre.
Set in the post apocalypse with a men only world driven by unwholesome amounts of sex drive, you play as Brad; a broken man on the hunt for his adoptive daughter who is the only known female since the apocalypse. Your journey leads you into generally unwelcome terriorty filled with quirky characters chocked full of bizarre humor at every turn. With combat working like a traditional RPG style with an added combo system which can be controlled through the players input to preform special attacks.
The game is a roller coaster ride of emotion, morals, and choices, both which have a dark side to them. So much that you'll choke up on the many curve balls the game throws your way. These curveballs include sacraficing party members for your own skin or even the other way around;  where you yourself are offering an arm or an eye to save them at the cost of losing your combat prowess.
Overall it's a great game with a lot to offer and plenty of content. If you're a fan of the Earthbound/Mother series, you won't be disapointed! Buy this game!
