I played the "redux" version but it wouldn't let me write a review there.
Anyway, the best parts of this game are the story, the atmosphere, and the graphics.
It's hard to say much about the story without giving anything away, but I found it interesting and compelling and wanted to complete it.
The graphics are extraordinary (again, I played the Redux version, so I don't know what they were like beforehand). I've played games with much worse graphics ran much worse. I'm not sure how they did it, but the environments, in many cases, felt almost real. Photorealistic might be an overstatement, but not much of one. The lighting and sweeping vistas and beautiful forests and landscapes... all amazing.
The atmosphere is great. Spooky, creepy, lonely, but with a feeling that this was once a living place with a real history. Even though not all of that history is written out and explored, you FEEL like it's there.
There is no way to view a map or your inventory. While the inventory would have been silly (most items are used within eyesight of where you found them), I wanted a map several times, or some way to quick-travel to locations. I know, I know, that would have ruined the atmosphere I just praised. But when I realized I had missed 2 puzzles early on, and had no choice but to wander slowly back to them from the very end of the game, it was frustrating.
Sadly the puzzles were one of the weakest parts of the game. Solving the murders was interesting, but frequently turned into a first-person version of pixel-hunting. Yes I know I need a doodad to insert into the thingamagig. That's the puzzle. But HUNTING FOR the doodad isn't fun or compelling. They're never in a logical place -- they're just somewhere random nearby. There were whole sections of the game that I missed because I didn't find the exact right place to see a thing I needed to click on.
If there's something I can't stand about puzzle games, it's when I, the PLAYER, have solved the puzzle, but I can't figure out exactly what I need to click on so my CHARACTER can solve it in the game.
There were also puzzles where it wasn't clear what I was trying to do. I didn't know I needed to open a particular pathway, for instance, so there was no reason for me to be clicking on things trying to figure out how to do it. If I found the thing to click on, there's no reason for me to think it opened up a pathway elsewhere. The things weren't part of a logical chain I could follow. It was just "until you click on this thing, you can't go that way" even though I didn't know the thing was clickable or that "that way" was a way I could go.
Many times I resorted to looking for online hints to tell me how to progress. There are two ways that can go:
1) I feel like an idiot because I should have been able to figure that out.
2) I feel vindicated because there was no logical way for me to figure something out, or it required "pixel hunting" to solve.
I am recommending this game with reservations. I found it fun to explore and solve things up to a point. But scouring the game environment to find a doodad that isn't in a logical place just isn't fun for me. If you're like me, you might as well just play with a walkthrough open so you can experience the story without the frustration.
Here are some examples of where I got frustrated, in spoiler text.
So like I said, as a puzzle game I found it frustrating (not in the good way) and somewhat lacking. As an interactive story, I think it was great.

Pros: Diverse gameplay drawn from a solid, simple foundation - you can quickly grasp what each thing does, but the way that individual mechanics and ship quirks work in concert allows you to have moments where you feel really damn smart figuring the best ways to utilise them. High replayability if you enjoy the "roguelite" genre of procedural maps and randomised spawns, a wide variety of starting "character" setups, and character advancement during an individual session.
Cons: The AI you face in every combat is acting randomly - there is no tactical play from the enemy, so you're sometimes up against foes which could cripple you in a single barrage, but fail to do so. If you want an evenly-matched tactical fight, rather than combat where you use tactics against RNG, look elsewhere. If Roguelites are not your thing, this will not be your game.

Alright ladies and gents, here I go again. I'm making this reccomendation after putting five hours into this little gem.
I've gotten a good feel for the gunplay, the mission structure, the story, and just the general aesthetic and based off of that I can safely suggest you buy this, now!
First, you might notice the lukewarm reviews from some big name game critics. The problem is they went into this game expecting a GTA style experience. This is an open world game in the sense that you can drive wherever the hell you'd like. However there are no side missions spread out for you to complete at your leisure nor are there any activities. This is a purely story driven adventure, and it's a damn good one.
You essentially start as a war hero, broke, trying to help his family. You find work with the local italian mob and work your way up, from shaking down dock workers to pulling big time heists and hits that almost always lead to excellently choreographed shootouts. The environments come apart, the bodies rag doll, and the weapons feel damn good with each shot you fire into your advesary.
The setting is incredibly well done, with authentic music from the era blasting over the speakers with the 1940's New York skyline working as the back drop. The cars handle as you'dexpect, these are 1940's vehicles folks, not race cars, please keep that in mind before you ♥♥♥♥♥ about handling. Also, I love that cops will pull you over for speeding and running lights and arrest you for hit and runs, it adds to the feel of it all. You're also welcome to fuel up your chosen ride when the gauge is running low. Mafia 2 has an extremely involving setting and it's truly the little details that make it work.
So, if you love a great story mixed with a healthy dose of mobster fueled action that never feels stale then pick this up, the critics got this one wrong, it's not a GTA clone and its not trying to be, it's a top notch title that carves its own path.

Defender's Quest is an extremely fun and addicting tower defense/RPG hybrid.  There are so many viable strategies for you to experiment with.  The way you can get your different characters to work with each other is very deep with different talent trees to choose from, weopons and armor to collect and level up, spells for your main character to choose from, and placement of your troops.   I found it very enjoyable and satisfying to beat both the normal game and the new game plus (hard mode) first in "hero" mode where you only use the characters introduced in the main story line and then go back to recruit extra troops to tackle some of the more advanced extreme difficulties.  There is an interesting storyline to follow.  The dialog between the characters has a sometimes wacky sense of humor that I really enjoyed, while the overall storyline was still serious.  I thought they struck a nice balance.  While the game may look simplistic in graphic design, the experience is anything but and I got my money's worth many times over.  Just a very fun game and well worth your time if you have even a passing interest in either RPG's or good tower defense games.  Greatly looking forward to the sequel that is in development!

I am enthusiastically recommending this game, but I feel I need to write 2 separate review to fully cover the experience.
Review 1: Level 1-20ish
This game is a blast, From the hilarious but still effective tutorial the game had me hooked.  The planet/mission select screen plays out like Christmas morning as you select missions based on what reward you want. Mechs, guns, utility gear, justice from heaven, all can be earned for your part in spreading managed democracy. The sweetest gear is often found on the more challenging planets, but a quick drop of an SOS beacon will usually get you teamed up with a group of Helldivers who are just as enthusiastic about earning that laser canon or APC as you are. Early on, I found the community to be very civil and helpful. A point I was skeptical of considering my previous forays into 'online co-op' had been in MOBAs, and I don't need to detail how that went.
Overall, the game is great fun. There are DLC packs which expand your arsenal, but I wouldn't go so far to say you HAVE to buy them ( the exception being maybe the Terrain Specialist Pack to get the All Terrain Boots perk, more on that later). Buy this game now!!!
Review 2: Level 20 – 50
Once you've unlocked most everything and find yourself only really challenged by the difficulty level 9 and up planets, the game changes quite a bit. Level ups become far less frequent and you find yourself playing with the more grizzled veteran players. Again, the community is still far better that any other co-op game I've played, but you start to run in the the “optimal” crowd. I first ran into one of these players on a snow planet. It was a mid level mission, so I was a little surprised to see a level 40+ drop into the fray. Snow planets slow down your movements speed. The only way around this is to equip the aforementioned All Terrain Boots. It is an unspoken rule that you MUST wear boots on the snow planets. 'Why do you say unspoken, Mittens?' Because every time I got slowed down by the snow, the veteran player would march back to me and literally rifle butt me in the face. It's true that the game has built in voice chat functionality, but it's extremely rare to run into anyone using it. This leads to communication being achieved by cape spins and spamming of the built in “no” command. Kind of a minor issue really, but it was a noticeable change from the more casual early game. This has not been enough to get me to stop playing, and even if it did, I got more than my money's worth. You can always jump into a lower level mission or, better yet, make friends with fellow Helldivers that share your playstyle.
Just as before, I recommend the game. Just realize that it gets very grindy in the endgame.
Thanks for reading, and have yourself a cup of Liber-Tea!!!

In LISA: The Painful, you are the father of the last and only woman alive in the lands of Olathe. In a world populated entirely by men it's survival of the fittest, with everything and everyone out to get you.
LISA is an RPG with alot of unique twists to combat and exploration. For starters the world is 2D with three main hub worlds. Certain areas can only be accessed once completing certain requirements and after completing some parts others change in various ways.
Combat is typical of most RPGs but the changes made strongly stand out with aspects like the Combo Dial, a feature utilized by some character that allow you to input five attacks by pressing the WASD keys, with different characters having combos that can be performed with said inputs. The 30 recruitable party members are all unique in their own ways, take my personal favorite: A drunk by the name of Birdy. Birdy has no standard attack, instead he takes a swig-increasing his ATK power and raising his special bar (labelled as TP). The only way for him to attack is to use one of his specials, but his value comes in the form of support. Not only is he able to heal his team mates but he can also spit oil at his opponent, making fire based attacks deal rediculous amounts of damage.
One of LISA's greatest feats is the choices you are forced to make. Choices in LISA don't affect the story, but rather gameplay. Do you sacrifice a party member to keep items or do you make yourself weaker losing your combo potential? That's up to you. Do you take the drug known as Joy which causes all of your attacks to become critical hits and recover all of your HP at the cost of more periods of suffering withdrawl where you deal practically no damage? Again it's up to you.
Enemies and Characters are also unique in the fact that aside from wildlife and a couple reused enemy sprites for Rando's Army, every Human character you meet/fight is one of a kind. No reusing the same generic soldier character over and over, everyone is different.
Game takes roughly 10 hours if you know what your doing, and then you've got Pain Mode to tackle where enemies are significantly stronger and each savepoint can only be used once. All in all this is an RPG that carries the spirit of Earthbound that I highly recommend.

Clearly I could be talking of no other game than Gunman Clive, a western side-scrolling shooter with a stylish look and a budget price tag, originally released on the 3DS and now making its way to PC.  It’s a simplistic game that could have easily felt at home on the NES, featuring many of the basic design philosophies common in that generation. You have a very limited range of moves, capable of jumping and shooting and little else, and are sent through short platforming levels with only spouts of variation therein, ending with a climactic boss fight that seems designed more to test who has the fastest trigger finger than anything else.
There are a few ways to look at a game of this nature. On one side, side-scrolling shooters have seen a great deal of innovation in recent years taking advantage of modern technologies to create games the likes of which could never have existed on the limited tech that started the genre, and making something like this seem a tad outdated in comparison.
On the other there’s absolutely nothing wrong with a simple, dare I say retro, simplicity which Gunman Clive so fully embraces. In some ways I enjoyed having such an uncluttered and uncomplicated direction that doesn’t require a great deal of thought to play, and is almost refreshing compared to more advanced titles of recent memory. All that said, what developer Bertil Horberg never managed or even attempted, was to outdo my expectations.
Every set piece, enemy encounter, and platform design felt like something I’d seen and played a hundred times over already, and eventually began to grate on me as scenes unfolded with so little originality. I can forgive a game to paying homage to others, but there’s something so...generic, about the way Gunman Clive plays, that I found it hard to be impressed after the initial awe of the fantastic visual style. The cheap deaths and lack of any checkpoints within levels also proved frustrating, for however short they may be.
Were it to cost anymore I might have a hard time recommending Gunman Clive in any great respect, but for $2 it’s a perfectly solid (if often unremarkable) experience, that most should have no trouble finding an hour or two of enjoyment in. I would have liked for the developer to have spent more time designing and fine tuning the levels and controls, as most of the budget and focus seems to have been spent on the visuals (which while great, can’t make up for average to mediocre gameplay), but all the same there are far worse things to spend $2 and an hour of your time, provided you know what you're getting.

This game plays a lot like Mega Man, albeit at a slower pace. Still, the game is well-designed in most respects, and the boss battles are both well-executed and impressive to behold. Gunman Clive is a pretty short game, but it's still worth checking out, especially when you consider its low price.

The game also rewards players for not receiving any damage, or making a speed run, which should appeal to the real hardcore crowd.  This game is definitely for the fans of the old school and new gamers alike.

It's almost like they ran out of time, money, or just gave up at the end. The last "mysteries" can be solved easily because they're so painfully obviously in order. Maybe it's for the best since the earlier ones were more trial and error than actual detective work.
If you're still interested, I can't see spending more than $5 on this. Yes, the art direction is fantastic, and the score is beautiful, but that really doesn't matter. They should have designed an engaging game, and they didn't. It's simply not worth your time.

Not that there is much to be attacked in the game but the only thing you DO in the game is interact with your environment. Two power-ups unlock blocks a-la color switches in Super Mario World, and the other two are a double jump and a Mega Max X-esque Wall Jump ability.

Dying Light was released on January 27, 2015. Dying Light: The Following, released on January 9, 2016. To this day, December 21, 2017, Techland is still releasing new content and patches issues for the game. THAT is how a game is supposed to be supported. Dying Light was developed by Techland (Dead Island 2011 and Dead Island: Riptide 2013). If you enjoyed the Dead Island games, I HIGHLY recommend this game. Be sure to purchase Dying Light: The Following - Enhanced Edition. This includes the following: Dying Light, Dying Light: The Following, Dying Light Season Pass, and Dying Light - Crash Test Skin Pack. $60.00 value. Totally worth the money, even with the season pass today. You get a lot of content. Be sure to check out the DLC individually and check to make sure you do not purchase content twice. If you purchase the Enhanced Edition and you would like to purchase the DLC as well, be sure to exclude Dying Light: The Following, Season Pass, and Crash Test Skin Pack so that you do not re-purchase them.
Dying Light: The Following is the continuation of Kyle Crane's journey to help the city of Harran. The voice actors did a great job. The game mechanics are amazing, with a glitch here and there just like any game, there are not bugs like Dead Island has that were never fixed. Techland has been doing an outstanding job at taking care of their game. Dying Light is THE ZOMBIE GAME we have all been waiting for. The game allows you free roam, to focus on missions and side missions, Parkour missions, crafting of weapons, blunt, bladed, and firearms. You will learn many skills on how to defeat and or avoid the undead. There is day and night time change, weather change, and best of all, at night....you will be hunted. You can play the game singleplayer but I recommend cooperative at least with one other friend. Cooperative allows up to 4 players. You will hunt and loot for supplies and food. There are a plethora of collectibles to find. Also, the game replay value is endless.
Dying Light: The Following introduces the Buggy! You get to upgrade the vehicle with better engine parts, refill it with fuel you find, and add weapons to it! You can carry a buddy in the back seat and you can switch off and let them drive yours, or they can drive their own! Mowing down the undead with the Buggy is very satisfying to say the least. There are more missions and more collectibles to hunt for, so you will definitely be busy!
Let's not forget the amazing soundtrack to go with this kickass game. The game music was composed by Paweł Błaszczak, who also composed Dying Light: The Following, as well as other titles like Dead Island and Dead Island: Riptide. The music adds so much life to the game and has an old horror movie sound to it that Paweł was striving for when he wrote it. The music has that old George A. Romero Dawn of the Dead or Day of the Dead sound and feel to it with electronic and synthesizer sounds. Dying Light and Dying Light: The Following soundtracks can be found and purchased online. The Dying Light soundtrack was released on February 4, 2015, and the Dying Light: The Following soundtrack was released on February 23, 2016.
Once again, I highly recommend this game. Buy the Enhanced Edition. Thank me later.

I have played and beat the pre-release of LISA two times and now again for the third time on steam.
I will try to collect my thoughts, that gathered up during that time with the game, into this review. I will try to avoid spoilers.
LISA without a doubt is a
. It is one man's passion project. (scroll to the end for TL:DR version)
Special games such as this are rarely made to completion, and when they are, their nature is such that it demands concessions.
This is a technically weak game for what people might expect from a commercial title, options are scarce, controller setup highly counter intuitive, resolution non-adjustable, and full-screen mode hard set. It has all the issues you might expect from a game made on a RPG-maker platform, such as an antiquated battle system and very rigid platforming.
If technical shortcomings of a game turn you off, I would like to suggest that they shouldn't, as a game is not a car or a tool judged upon its specs primarily, however if you are not willing to make some concessions to a game over its technical aspect LISA is not for you.
-Thomas Hobbes
Such is the view of life we find in LISA, it is cheap, plentiful, yet brief and ends ignobly in violence. The game mechanics work in concert with the narrative splendidly here, by offering plenty of wonderfully varied and interesting companions to recruit, all with a distinct look and behavior, you could even swear each has a deep and sorrow filled backstory even when they don't, it is all to easy to get attached to these men before they die permanently.
People almost act like a secondary currency, you soon find out that your allies are just another resource that you expend to get where you need to go, but thankfully they never feel like that, making each death at least somewhat painful.
While gameplay and narrative work together great, LISA's
hands down. What at first seems like a regular "save the damsel" story, is actually so much more. Some minor spoilers coming:
The only girl character- "Buddy" is a messiah character, she is the only known female, and is seen as someone who can "save" the world. However, you (as Brad) want to save HER from the world she is meant to save.
The game asks, what is the dignity of a child? Should a world that can produce nothing but misery be allowed to perpetuate at the price of yet another innocence? The answers that emerge through gameplay are often truly shocking and makes decision making very hard.
These themes of tragedy are suggested to be rooted at the core of all characters you meet,  through encounters like with Horace and understanding the backstory of Rando. The villains and allies you have are often more like you than is often comfortable and everyone partakes in a brotherhood of misery.
As you play you may choose to go with this world's depravity or constantly struggle against it, with more or less success, while becoming more enmeshed into this world as it builds on you, thematically and narratively, with its punishing gameplay. It culminates in one of those rare satisfying endings, which was the only video game ending to truly make me cry.
I can not commend and recommend this game enough. Also the game has a gorgeous soundtrack, and tons of secrets, even whole large areas/towns that you wouldn't otherwise find casually playing the game.
: The fact of this games existence is worth celebrating and forgiving the inevitable vices it had to possess to ever be made. This game is excellent not for polish, but for its grand, bleak vision and meaningful story, that together make for a truly painful game. [Pain/10]
Advice: I suggest not abusing the "reload feature" if someone dies, or you make a choice live with it, what is the point otherwise?

Before the Echo is a perfect mash-up of the rhythm and RPG genres. You use DDR style mechanics to cast powerful spells, restore your mana, and block incoming attacks as you make your way through the increasingly dangerous dungeons. The characters are really likeable, and I found myself enjoying the story way more than I expected. The villains in particular are quite entertaining, and while I won't spoil them here, you're likely to remember them long after you stop playing this game. The mechanics here are rock solid, and the difficulty curves quite nicely at each level. I mostly played on normal, since I sadly don't have the time to practice enough to master the hardest difficulties, but there's definitely enough value for both hardcore rhythm gamers and players new to the genre who want to see what it's all about. If you are new to rhythm games, be aware that grind is an essential part of the experience. You're going to be fighting the same monsters time and time again on each level to unlock the items you need, and the drop rates ensure that there's a random element that can halt your progression and add some frustration. In another game, this would be a huge negative, but rhythm games are based on the idea that you're going to play the same levels over and over again to master them. I never found the grind to be an issue, but I also beat Knights of Cydonia on Expert in GH3. My tolerance is pretty high for this kind of thing.
If you love rhythm games already, buy this game. If you're not sure whether you like rhythm games but really like character focused RPGs, buy this game. If you hate rhythm games, I don't know how you got this far into my review, but this isn't going to be the game that changes your mind. I loved this game, and if you found this page in the first place, I'm willing to bet you will too.

For a game made back in 2004 this game has aged supprisingly well. It's certianly earned the reputation it has as one of the best RPGs ever made. Even if vampires aren't your thing you should still give this game a look, it's that well put together.
The complaint I have is that for most systems you will have to download an unofficial patch in order to make the game playable. Step by step instructions on where to get the patch and how to apply it are stickied on Steam's forum for this game, so it isn't much work; all said it's a pretty painless process.

The stronger points of the game are that it has a fantastically dark atmosphere, believable and often intense characters (something which alot of games lack), and a solid storyline that does the game justice. Also, you choose at the beginning which bloodline (faction) you are part of, which will directly affect your relationships with the characters in-game, offering variation and replayablility, if you don't mind already knowing the storyline the second time through. Finally, the level design is very well done, giving varied and interesting locations that will keep your interest, no rampant cookie-cutter design here.
On the down side, it is a dated game, having been released in 2004, so you will probably only get the most out of it if you don't mind the avatars looking a bit blocky compared to what you might be used to. I'm sure it was 'fairly' close to cutting edge graphics in 2004, but if you can look past it, the game will suck you in and you won't notice.
It was mentioned that the game doesn't feel finished by one reviewer, and while I disagree, I can see why that might come up. The game is completely set at night, so far as I can remember, so you won't get the bustling city feel that daytime would bring, and also it doesn't have a huge amount of side quests that seem to pack into games these days (to cover up lack of original content), but there is plenty to keep you occupied.. you won't get bored.
Also, apparently the game was quite buggy at release. I'd used the official patch when I played it, and didn't come across any problems. I certainly didn't come close to checking on forums, as one or two others had, but everyone plays a game differently, and it's becoming standard practice to check forums rather than think a problem through, or work around it. Regardless, apparently the unofficial patch made by fans is the best, from what I gather.
Overall I greatly enjoyed the game and thought it to be underrated, definately a pleasant surprise. At no point did I get bored, even though there are many areas, nor did I question whether I'd see it through to the end, unlike quite a few games which get churned out. The storyline was interesting, and I found myself carefully watching the behaviour of all the characters, not quite sure who to trust, as it should be in a vampire underworld. The hotel level was especially spooky, I might add ;) good job on that. I only wish that there was a sequel.

This is a nice, completely free-to-play 2D retro style single player platformer along the lines of VVVVVV with a lot of exploration and traversal. One might call it MetroidVania style since its a big open world that has you moving from screen to screen. Each 'room' is only a screen like the original Zelda. Since you are exploring, there is no map. The controls are simple, left and right to move and a jump button. On certain platforms you can hit down on them to fall through the platform like many old school 2D platformers.
Where's the challenge? When you get hit by an enemy or spike you die instantly. Luckily there are checkpoint bells everywhere on almost every screen. When you die, you instantly respawn with no load times. It really keeps you in the action. It is very similar to VVVVVV but much easier and relaxing. If you get frustrated easily, this might not be the game for you, but since you respawn, there's no real punishment for failing.
The game takes an hour or so to complete. For the most part the game is easy fun. It starts out calming and relaxing as you explore, but eventually has tricky platforming areas and intense bullet dodging boss battles. Along the way you'll find loot bags. What do they do? Nothing but an achievement at the end if you collect 100% of them.
Progressing through the game, you will enable different things such as solid blue blocks, solid purple blocks, double jump and so on. To enable each thing, you must get past the boss. I say get past, because you are just a boy in this game with no combat. You will dodge enemies and in the case of a boss, dodge dozens of bullets on screen at once. The bosses fire in patterns, so you will get the hang of it. There is not that much enemy variety, bats, snakes and crabs move left and right, spiders move up and down. The game's main enemy is spikes.
Since this is a retro style game, by default the game has a 1980s monitor feel. Thankfully you can turn off the 1980s monitor and see everything full screen with no added glare. For anyone that finds the game too easy, there is a remixed level design which is much more difficult yet still forgiving with checkpoints everywhere. If you are brave enough there is cat mode that features 9 lives and YOLO that has one life and then its game over.
This is an easy recommendation, but if it was $1 or more challenging I'd be hesitant to recommend, but this feels like a good game for the developer to make a better game with. Solid controls, the understanding of an easy beginning headed toward difficult end.

The plot, the voice acting, and the character personalities are the good qualities of this dating sim. The storyline flows in an easy to understand, linear fashion, and seems as though a lot of thought was put into it; the political systems of the fantasy realms alluded to are all explained well, the foreshadowing isn't overbearing, and the character arcs are well-executed. The voice lines are read with the perfect amount of emotion, and are present throughout the entire game. Since this is a reverse harem situation, the characters do have personalities limited to specific archetypes. Fortunately, their quirks set them apart from characters of other otome, and their backstories are enough to gain the affections of the player.
While these are all great characteristics of the game, their are a few weak points to address: repetitiveness, grammar, and art quality. Playing this game as I did, trying to unlock every end, was incredibly tedious. as the storyline is ultimately the same for each character, and there are only slight differences that occur simply due to the personality of the character. After my first playthrough, I was pressing the skip button for almost the entirety of the game. The composition of the narration and dialogue was also something I couldn't quite get used to. To be blunt, proofreading and editing would've done the game wonders. Finally, the art wasn't very appealing at all. The character portraits are tolerable, but any art used for a specific scene looked awkwardly drawn, and reminded me of wikihow illustrations.

Mafia 2 is one of those games you pick up, and wonder how on Earth you could have overlooked it for all those years.
Starting out in the 1940’s and going into the 50’s, you play as Vito Scaletta, a young criminal “entrepreneur” looking to make his bones in organized crime. You start off small, taking on bigger and bigger scores, until you’re finally in way over your head.
That’s perhaps the one flaw with the otherwise engaging story. It’s thoroughly enjoyable until roughly two thirds into the game. After that, everything starts going south, as somewhat of a cringeworthy moral reminder that in the end, crime doesn’t pay.
It’s not so much the turn of events itself that leaves a bit of a sour taste in my mouth as it is the painfully obvious way it’s being handled. You just know♥♥♥♥♥♥is going to hit the fan as soon as certain events are set into motion - and how - yet there’s nothing at all you can do about it.
Vito was never the sharpest tool in the shed at any point in the story, yet he's portrayed relatively consistently until the turning point. After that, it's almost as if Vito has conveniently taken leave of his senses so as to allow events to unfold the way they do. Willing suspension of disbelief is stretched a  bit thin as crucial information being plainly spelled out to him is being blatantly ignored multiple times, and for no good reason.
In all, the story isn’t bad, though; it’s actually reasonably good (apart from the somewhat cringeworthy turn of events). Furthermore, the atmosphere as portrayed in this game is just incredible. Personally, however, I can’t help but feel that the story of Mafia: Lost Heaven (the predecessor to this game) was better still.
Gameplay in Mafia 2 is rather reminiscent of the Driver series of yore and resembles the GTA series quite well. Needless to say, you’ll be driving around a lot. With Empire Bay, the developers have crafted a beautiful, teeming city, but unfortunately not very much is done with it. It mainly functions as the backdrop for the story you’re going through and the missions you’re completing.
During and in between these, you can free-roam in your car and rob a limited number of stores – gun stores, restaurants and pubs, clothes stores, gas stations etc. – and sell stolen cars to one or two people. This quickly becomes a bit old, though, once you realize there’s not much else to be done around these parts.
It would have been really nice if they’d delved deeper into the vast potential this game has to offer, such as extorting money, loan-sharking, investing in businesses, setting up “shop” of your own, etc. There’s so much potential here that’s tapped into only superficially.
There’s a couple of bugs here and there, most of which seem to be related to the graphics card and/or graphic settings. One particularly annoying bug involves the Steam overlay – if you shift+tab and open up the Steam browser during gameplay and shift+tab again, the vertical synchronization setting might randomly freak out.
The DLC offers a change of pace from the main story. Here, you’ll find little in the way of an actual story (with cutscenes), instead you’ll be completing a series of (usually timed) objectives in the city. While fun in and of themselves, they’re unfortunately somewhat less compelling than the main story.
To conclude, this game offers an engaging story with an incredible atmosphere. The favourable impression is somewhat lessened by the shortcomings – a few bugs here and there, a somewhat less than compelling plot turn and the "story" DLC itself falling a bit short of the mark set by the main story – but all in all this game is still a thoroughly recommendable experience.
Be sure to pick this one up if you have a more than fleeting interest in the fascinating (virtual) world of organized crime.

DDR-like rhythm game with a repetitive and grindy RPG bottom line.
----
The gameplay of Before the Echo involves swapping between three different screens of falling arrows to hit in the right rhythm. Each screen has a different effect - one is for generating mana with which to cast spells, one is for casting spells to damage your opponent or for a variety of other effects and the last one is to defend yourself from enemy attacks which deplete your hp.
The gameplay itself is quite good. The falling arrows are tracked well with the music on all the difficulties and swapping between screens adds an interesting multi-tasking and decision making aspect.
Where the game falls down is the RPG elements. You're given a bunch of recipes to craft which require materials dropped from battles. This involves repeating the same battles with the same music over and over again to get the required materials and then actually crafting the recipe has an experience point cost. In my two hours of playing I leveled from 1 to 4 and then back down to 1 again after having crafted all the items for the first floor and eventually finished on level 3 again at the start of the second floor. You can see why this is a problem.
By the time I arrived on the second floor I was looking forward to a new set of songs at least and was unpleasantly surprised to find that the three battles for that floor were all tracks I'd heard before. Two out of three tracks were songs I'd just spent an hour on for the previous floor. Exactly the same. The prospect of grinding more battles on songs I've already heard for item upgrades and character level downgrades made me uninstall right then and there.

As someone from the DDR generation, it takes a lot for a rhythm game to receive a good review from me. Keep that in mind when reading this review.
Before the Echo is a very interesting approach to the genre. It combines RPGs and rhythm. During the game you equip your character with various equipment and spells and fight monsters.
Fighting monsters is accomplished by toggling between a magic, defense and mana field and trying to hit the arrows at the proper point. You will frequently find yourself choosing between recharging your mana, defending against enemy attacks, and using magic against the enemy.
This combat approach is very well implemented when using a controller. They obviously put a lot of thought into it, and it makes sense.
The music is fine. It didn’t stand out as anything special to me. I didn’t really “feel” it though, so it was more a matter of watching the arrows than listening to the beat. This can probably be improved by ensuring your audio settings are correct.
I have mixed feelings about the tutorial and plot. The tutorial accomplishes its purpose well, after playing through it, you know how to play the game. The plot consists of waking up in a tower, having a snarky/sarcastic woman tell you what is going on, and then fighting monsters to get a key to move to the next floor. I don’t know more than that, as the game quickly lost my interest.
I was very glad we have the ability to skip the plot scenes. I found the character’s interactions very annoying.
Despite being well designed, the game didn’t grab my interest. It felt like it was missing something. It is inexpensive enough that fans of the genre might as well give it a try, but casual players should look elsewhere.

The mashup of RPG/rhythm is very cool, and switching between the different aspects of the battle is a great idea.  That's where my praise of this game ends.
In one of the worst openings to any game I've ever played, we are immediately subjected to terrible dialogue with worse voice acting.  Every line is delivered awkwardly and with a shoehorned-in joke.  The writer goes out of their way to try to poke fun at RPG/gaming stereotypes, and not a single joke lands.
If that wasn't bad enough, we're subjected to approximately 20 minutes of tutorials before we can even play the game.  A character even calls the game out on having too many tutorials, which begs the question why this was not fixed prior to release.
When we finally get to play the game, we find that we're in for a repetitive, non-stop grind.  Let's go through the steps it takes to learn a new spell:  1) grind multiple battles against one or more enemies. 2) craft the spell, which may fail, requiring repeat of step 1. 3) learn the spell, requiring you to play a mini-game, which is a more boring version of a regular battle, oh and by the way the song is the same song you heard 6-7 times during step 1.  What should be an exciting aspect of an RPG (learning a new spell, oh boy!) is instead reduced to a slog.  And that, in a nutshell, is Before the Echo.
Stay away from this one.

Jump #8 - Ambushed by cloaked Rebel Interceptor waiting at the jump beacon. Life support took heavy damage. Charrl got sucked into space trying to repair a hull breach. Life expectancy on this mission kinda blows.
Jump # 9 - Ran across critically damaged civilian ship being pursued by bounty hunters. Bounty Hunters didn't offer a very good bribe so we killed them. Sadly the civvies all suffocated because their life support failed while we were busy fighting.
Jump #10 - Crew morale was low and our hull was in serious need of repair. Arrived at federation-friendly station. No life-signs aboard. Crew wiped out, Rebel AI running the systems. This galaxy sucks.
Jump #27 - Navigating a nebula when our Rockman weapons officer was mind-controlled and allows himself to be teleported off-ship by Slug kidnappers. They held him for ransom, which we couldn't pay. They blew his brains out right there on the viewscreen. Mantis crewman was quite excited to use the weapons console, we killed them quickly as vengeance.
Jump #42 - Mantis crewman revealed she had an illicit liason during a stay aboard a space station in the last sector, and became pregnant. Being in deep space and not really knowing how else to deal with a hormonal alien killing machine, I congratulated her. At that point she revealed her offspring had already hatched and was pretty much fully-grown. In honour of the alliance between our two people she named her child 'Daughter'. Truly, a strange people.
Jump #64 - Holy frak, that Flagship is HU-

Gunman Clive is a western platformer, in the simplest sense. Its price of $2 is well-justified as it's short, sweet, and gives enough good times to outweigh the bad.
On the whole though, I was kind of bored with the whole game. Even with a length of approximately 30-45 minutes, this game that was originally on the 3DS and phone devices also isn't one I would normally even glance at. However, I enjoy platformers and thought the art style looked nice in videos so I decided to check it out. You play as Clive, or a female character who is the daughter of the mayor of some town (and whose name I forget). There's also a third playable character but I'll get to that in a bit. Clive controls similar to how MegaMan does in that series of games, minus the special moves, and the female lady (from now on I'm just going to call her "Umbrella) walks slowly but can float after jumping. For some reason I decided to play as Umbrella and she gave me some added challenge which was nice. I imagine playing as Clive would not be as fulfilling as her clunky slow speed made the game quite a bit more challenging.
In fact, I'm happy to note that this game does provide a decent challenge, even for experienced gamers. Enemies, which consists of bandits, wolves, and ducks oddly enough, move fairly fast and can appear at any time so you have to be on your toes. There are about 20 levels in the game, each of which are fast (about 60-90 seconds long each) and good for quick play sessions or a full playthrough in one run. In each level, your goal is merely to get to the end usually, unless it's a boss.
Now, I'm really not a fan of the bosses in this game. They all feel the same because they mostly kind of are. Usually they just blast bullets at you and move around a bunch. They're bland a little boring sadly, but I guess for the price you can't expect much variety in the bosses. Maybe it was just a personal gripe but on these levels I usually blazed past them and didn't care for their designs or making a strategy at all. Blasting bullets right back at them usually worked every time for me.
The length may be an issue for some. Really that's what this game being a good buy or a bad buy for anyone comes down to. Now, I've heard some say this game can be beat in an hour, but I beat it in about 35 minutes without rushing at all so that seems a bit off to me. Considering this game is less than an hour long, I wouldn't say it's worth the $2 if you just run through it once. I like to play games for at least as long as I payed for, and if I payed $2 for it I'd like to get at least a 2-hour game back.
Now, I'm not actually discrediting the game by saying I don't like its price as I do in this case. When you beat the game you unlock a third character, a duck. Yes, you get to play through the whole game again (minus the bosses) as a duck that can fly for brief periods of time and can't attack. It's pretty funny seeing a duck waddle past the enemies you had just beaten and it also provides a great extra layer of challenge that more games should try to do, even if it's as a joke. The duck mode is actually pretty tough and took me 30 minutes to get through about 1/4 of the game. There's also achievements for beating each mode with a gold star (for speed), not dying, and not getting damaged (which is crazy!). These can be pretty fun and hard to try and attempt, so in terms of replayability this game isn't too bad luckily. I've seen some people on the forums who have 5-10 hours and have all the achievements, so you can definitely get your money's worth if you don't mind trying some tough challenges.
The graphics are point that many love to mention when talking about this game. They're definitely very cool and "artsy" I suppose. It feels like you're playing something an artist doodled on a notebook, but brought to life. The dusty colors are nice to look at too. Overall, this game looks pretty good for what the developer had to work with, and it's probably one of the shining points of this game. The sound is sadly not quite as good, with basic sound effects and just "okay" music. Nothing was really memorable, but I enjoyed the main menu theme and a few songs slightly.
If you're looking for a multi-hour long game, this isn't it. In fact, it isn't even an hour long unless you're very slow and die quite a bit. However, the potential replayability with the fun (and hard!) duck mode and the pleasant art style may suck you in. It's worth a shot, if you pardon the pun. ;)

Simple, inexpensive indie TD with a nice twist. Each "tower" is a character and levels, equips and spends skill points independently. The campaign has a nice length to it. I'm not finished, but I'm over 20 battles. Each battle also has multiple difficulties that give greater rewards, including unlocking bonus missions.
The native resolution is tiny, probably 800x600 if not 640x480 and there is no way to increase it in windowed mode that I can see. Also the generic characters you make have the potential to be clones of your main heroes, each class' talent tree provides customization but (at least at low levels) leaves little advantage to stray. It would be nice if each character could learn different active skills from their brethren that share a class.
There is a sequel in the works and I look forward to it. It would appear they are addressing my main issues and thensome.
Bottom line, I'm enjoying this title and while I'm a sale hound, if I had paid full-price I wouldn't have been disappointed. If you are not a huge TD fan, this may leave little to desire.

So I really enjoyed this game but some of the mechanics and choices of the game design completely kill this game for me. First, progressing through the levels requires you to farm monster drops from the various enemies. Normally, this wouldn't be too bad but getting screwed by RNG never feels good in any game. After you finally get all of your materials to craft a key to progress, you spend experience to increase the chances that your crafting succeeds. The decision to implement F2P game design into this game is mind boggling.
So after you spend all of your experience to craft your key, you end up losing levels and stats which makes you much less likely to be able to beat the boss. In a normal game you could just trust your skills to get you through the level. However, if you don't do enough damage to an enemy before the song ends then you end up losing the battle. I really wanted to enjoy this game. I really did. But the implementation of the rpg system and the horrible crafting system really made me hate it.
With the bad being said, I would still have to recommend this game. Even wth all of the systems that I really dislike, the game still has me enjoying the musical gameplay while frantically switching between the different styles.
TLDR
Pros:
unique gameplay
good soundtrack
Cons:
hate the story and characters (subjective)
annoying rpg/crafting system
can't turn up/down in game sound
RNG sucks
Grindy
Woud still recommend even with the cons

I was a fan of the pen and paper game and bought this when it was released.  It was really buggy and initially impossible to finish.  If it stayed that way I'd be writing a pretty scathing review and am still disappointed in Activision because of this.  Thankfully the game attracted some talented fans who've fixed it up and made it a really enjoyable game for the rest of us.  There are still modders working with this game a decade after its release which means it'll work with newer versions of windows.  The fact that it's held the attention of a cult fanbase for so long is a testament to how great the game is.  I saw it on the Halloween sale and just had to buy it because I felt myself longing to play it again (lost the disc version a while back, no disc drive on this PC anyway).
The storytelling and most of the voice acting are pretty top notch.  The game is customizable and has multiple paths and options depending on the skillset you decide to develop.  This means replayability is very high.  Especially when you consider the uniqueness of the Malkavian and Nosferatu playthroughs.  It also covers many different types of vampires as well from the seductive humanlike bloodsuckers in clan Toreador, beastial brutes in clan Gangrel to the truly hideous monsters in clan Nosferatu.  You be the vampire you want to be.  Axe wielding melee master or gun-toting vamp.  I feel like this game was way ahead of its time and if it hadn't been so mishandled it could've been a booming success launching expansions and sequels.
My recommendation isto buy it on sale.  Not because it's not worth full price but because the people who profit from its sale don't really deserve full price due to their lack of support and release of an unfinished product.  Too bad the fan modders who made it playable don't get a cut.  They certainly deserve it for rescuing this gem of an RPG.

This costs less than buying a
in TF2 and will (probably) provide you a lot more satisfaction. It costs less than a delicious, but ephemeral, giant chewy candy bar.  It costs less *guilt-inducing frown* than a cup of coffee.
The distinct visual style is charming. It looks gimmicky in screenshots, but when you get the game loaded and see the fluid, scratchy style you'll immediately appreciate it more. It works, the art is tightly-controlled, and you immerse in the game rather than being distracted by the stylistic effect.
It's definitely short and sweet, but this is a simple, simple game that doesn't try to do anything except provide you the ability to: Run to the right, jump, climb ladders, ride mysteriously-levitating platforms, and shoot cowboys, ducks, jackrabbits, pelicans, wolves, and more cowboys.
I don't agree it's quite like classic Mega Man. You have special jumps (the girl can fluff her skirt to fall slower, for example), you can duck, and you don't collect new abilities from enemies — gun powerups just drop randomly that change how your bullets fire (heatseeking, shotgun spread, etc). You can only have one special shot at a time (new ones replace it).
It is like Mega Man in other ways: you can't aim (you just fire whichever way you're pointing), and the enemies have simple patterns you quickly learn.
For $2 this is a few solid hours of amusement, and then a pleasant diversion you can pick up again and again for 10 minutes any time you feel like having some very simple run, jump, shoot side-scrolling.

Basically, Gunman Clive is what happens when an author decides he's going to make a solid, oldschool platformer (just like, say, Mega Man 5) and yet somewhere along the way gets confused, forgets what he's doing, and just actually makes Mega Man 5.
This is both the highest praise and harshest criticism anyone can really bring against this title- it's 99% derivative, and 1% sepia-toned cowboys. Despite its looks, every gameplay element present is lifted directly from oldschool platformers, and anyone who's ever held a game controller ought to know exactly where those disappearing blocks, one-hit-kill spikes, and inexplicably missing sections of mine cart track came from. Among them all, Mega Man 5 seems to have been borrowed from most liberally, with shoutouts to Charge Man, Star Man, and Gravity Man's famous levels, nevermind the fact that Clive himself handles exactly like the original Blue Bomber himself (with his pre-90's control scheme, specifically).
Like similar indie title Bleed, Gunman Clive is a love letter to these games of yore, and to its credit, it executes the mechanics pretty perfectly, remixing incredibly familiar elements in comparatively new and challenging arrangements. Furthermore, the skin stretched over these old cogs is a surprisingly pleasant one. While embracing minimalism is hardly a new trend for these retro-style indie games, Gunman Clive actually does it gracefully, foregoing rehashed 8-bit-style graphics for something more contemporary- specifically, a combination of 3D models and artful shading for a simplistic, sepia-toned storybook visuals. The similarly minimalist story of silent-protagonist-saves-the-girl is at best unintrustive, yet still manages to be charming, if only for the sheer ridiculousness it quickly devolves into. Adding further charm is the story's feminist-friendly inversion, where Clive himself plays the hapless damsel while the armed and ever-capable Ms. Johnson takes it to the bad guys with her own victorian style.
Disappointingly, despite drawing most of its appeal from his ability to emulate classic platforming adventures, Gunman Clive doesn't necessarily attempt to surpass them. While the Mega Man series famously featured selectable levels and a generous handful of bosses, Gunman Clive is content to remain linear and dishes out only a precious few boss encounters, not a one of whom will be bestowing their signature weapon upon defeat. There's a justification for this lack of ambition, however, and the proof is in the price tag. The asking price for Gunman Clive is two dollars, which might be less than you've ever paid for a video game that wasn't 90% in a Steam Sale.
For its asking price, you'd be doing yourself a favor to give Clive a fair shot, especially if you've got any love for oldschool video games. It's all too short, but every bit as sweet.

When I saw this game got a steam release I just had to have it. This was a real standout game on the nintendo store and it still holds up on the PC. First of all I'm very surprised by how good this game looks on a monitor with the art style looking just as good as ever. It looks as though it has been sketched out with constant movement even in motionless objects somewhat similar to the A-ha Take On Me video. What you really want to know however is if this game is any good or not.
It plays almost identically to early Megaman games. You jump, sometimes you shoot, pretty self explanatory but the main thing jump and shoot games need to have is very tight controls and this delivers. You never really feel like a death is cheap as damage is always avoidable with quick reactions. The game itself can be quite challenging at times but this is a good thing. After a death you get straight back into the action starting at the beginning of the level almost immediately making you want to keep going to complete that final level.
So for the game length my first play through on the 3DS took me just under 2hours or so but I can see this being much shorter if you're not terrible like me. So for the replayability there are 2 additional characters along with Clive himself. Ms. Johnson has a slightly different mechanic in that she can float in her jumps allowing you to do some little extra tricks but mostly the same kind of gameplay. However the third character is the Duck which is hilarious to play as and surprisingly saftisfying as you have no attack and must avoid all enemy contact (which means a few of the levels are skipped as they would be impossible to do). Along with the additional characters there are also awards for taking no damage in a level and also for speedrunning it which are for nothing more than bragging rights and steam achievements but give you something else to aim for.
All in all the amount of content in this game and how good it feels is more than enough to warrant the small price tag. I'm just glad I got to support this developer twice with my purchase as there is so much potential. So if you're a fan of the Megaman series (specifically 2) or you just want a classic feeling jump and shoot game I cannot recommend this to you enough. There is so much character to this game you'd be doing yourself a disservice by not playing it!

Gunman Clive is one of those games that many might think is just another derp smartphone sidescroller (this was an Android/iOS game first), but once you get into it you see a higher level of quality. With each successive platform release of this title (Desura first, then Mobile, then 3DS, then Steam) it has improved on each port, and the Steam version is certainly the cream of the crop, despite how good the stereoscopy looks on the 3DS. The artistic effects are tuned to perfection on this release, looking completely awesome in HD, yet still maintaining the sketchbook cartoon look. The Desura release had responsiveness issues which have been cleaned up in this version, and just like in the 3DS version, there's three playable characters for you to use, adding replay value.
That isn't to say this game isn't worth playing over and over again with just Clive. The levels are fun and challenging, and while they start off like an old west shooter, they quickly evolve into a crazy, off-the-wall platforming adventure. Runaway minecarts evoke Donkey Kong Country. Floating platforms recall Super Mario Everything. Boss designs recall familiar characters and franchises, but are clever and charming in their own right.  At one point aliens invade and steal your damsel in distress. In the second level there's a Portal-esque sign with a silhouette figure and an arrow pointing toward the end of the level. The simple jump-and-shoot formula works a treat, although there are times I would have preferred to have the ability to shoot upwards. The boss fights themselves are fast-paced and tricky, but just like older games, a simple attack pattern and basic AI is all you need to worry about.
The game is short, which is a bit of a disappointment, but it is fun enough to keep playing off and on for a while. Plus, at two bucks regardless of platform, you really don't have much to lose purchasing Gunman Clive.

Summary: Pleasantly surprised with the game since it is free to play, but lacks uniqueness in routes.
Speaking as someone who has finished 3 routes (Damien, Sam, Matthew), plus multiple endings
Pros
- Character sprites (especially for the boys) are very nice
- Voice acting is really good
- Each boy falls into his own personality type so there are various options if you have a specific type you like (Tough guy, Intellectual guy, etc...)
- Ability to quickly skip through routes to get to specific point
- Free to play
- Heroine feels relatively fleshed out
- Several characters are fleshed out well; you may begin disliking one and end up really liking them by the end
Cons
- Art direction looks like it was done by different people. Sprite art is great, CG art feels out of place (honestly looks like pictures taken out of a WikiHow article)
- All routes feel very similar; a lot of recycled content. Seems like there's only one route of all the boys who has more content than others
- Following this, routes are so cookie cutter you could change the boy you pick halfway through and it wouldn't affect the story
- Game lacks a lot of background music. There are a lot of scenes that are completely devoid of sound
- UI is sometimes hard to see for timed choices- I didn't realize some choices were timed because the timer is near invisible
- Key story elements not explained in every route (This is a con if you don't plan to play every route)
If you're not playing for completion, I recommend playing Damien's route the most, as that seems to be the most unique of all the routes. All in all, a fun experience, and I will be playing the sequel when I finish all the routes.

This is actually a pretty hard game to review properly, as it has many faults and is in many aspects hard to recommend, but also feels like something that a lot of passion and genuine effort went into. I will go with recommendation mostly because it's free and it doesn’t take that much time to explore the most interesting story routes, so you don't risk much trying it. I also have to stress that I was interested primarily in the yuri routes, so my review mostly reflects that part of the game.
I will start with the most obvious thing - the art in this game is not good, as times being acceptable and sometimes being atrocious, especially when it comes to female characters. Guys seems to look ok and some drawings where actually nice to look at, but a few sprites of Diana or Naomi seriously made me cringe. Voice acting is a mixed bag at best, with main characters being mostly ok and supporting ones mostly poor. The whole project has this strong amateurish feel to it, but it’s somewhat expected with a free game. The end effect is not bad enough to scare you off, but it doesn’t help the storytelling, to the point that one could wonder if it the whole thing wouldn’t be better as a text adventure rather than following the VN format.
Production values aside, the story content is also a bit questionable. Above all, for the most part it lacks any deeper intrigue or unpredictability that would make it interesting in anything apart from the romance. The romantic arcs themselves are also so short that it’s hard to take most of them seriously, slight exceptions being the ones with protagonist’s high school friends – those at least have a lot of history between the characters and are developed from the first moments of the story – and especially Diana storyline, which just felt written and acted better than all the other ones. Most of the time tought the whole thing felt like a simplistic dating sim rather than a proper VN, the large amount of routes available meaning none of them had appropriate depth and impact. On the other hand, the game actually offers quite a lot of choices and multiple endings, pretty distinct from each other. It also doesn’t force you into uncomfortable territories, giving you full control on what romantic interests you do or do not pursue (if any at all).
With all that said, I can’t say I had a bad time with this game. It has some amusing writing and interesting moments, athough it simply falls flat as a romantic VN that should produce some deeper emotion (apart maybe from the Diana route, but only to some extent). It was amusing enough for me to not regret a few hours of messing around with it and I actually think it’s worth your time if you have a sleepy afternoon to fill. Just don’t expect anything beyond mild amusement.

The story keeps its ground in the idea that humanity has almost brought itself to extinction and continues to survive in the underground Metro system, while also adding in fantastical/mystical elements that bring the story to a whole new level. While the game can be relentlessly difficult should you choose to play on Ranger mode (where you have no HUD, little to no hints, and you and the enemies do way more damage) and some level design can be very annoying, this was an amazing experience in both the FPS/horror-ish genre. A must buy if you're looking for a nice short-ish length single player survival game.

This game is free, what else do you want?
OK, I get it, this sentence has some negative aspects these days, but I can assure you that this is really a complete free-to-play single player game. Not surprisingly though, since it's quite short.
Story
Well, there is actually no story to tell here and it doesn't really matter. Just jump through the game and imagine your own story.
Gameplay
This game is really your most basic Platformer Game. You can jump and walk and if you touch an enemy you'll die. The world is divivded in seperate screens, which even have their own unique names. Something that helps if you talk to someone about the fastest possible route. YhtwtG has a Metroidvania styled gameplay, so you need to collect different upgrades and go back to previous regions to use your new upgrades. There are four upgrades you can find. a red and a blue power up to activate colored blocks (it's up to you which one you want to find first), the classic double jump and at last a pair of Spider gloves (used for Wall Jumps). It's not too difficult to learn how the game works and if you're good you can finish it in even under 10 minutes.
Graphics
Fitting for a 80s retro game YhtwtG uses an EGA graphics mode. The entirety of four colors at your personal disposal. Believe it or not, there are actually games out there which only have four colors. But don't worry, there is an option to change it to an eight color mode if you want. There is even a nice little option to set up a VGA monitor bondary with a twisted screen on the edges. The only way to reach more nostalgy in this game is to deliver it on a floppy disk.
Conclusion
If you have a sudden wish for nostalgy or if you just want to see how games looked in the stone age of the computer technology, You have to win the Game is cleary something you need to try out. And that all just for the price of a little space on your hard drive.

Steam now has thousands of thousands of games, but there are a few which will stand the test of time and FTL is one of those games. You can look up screen shots and game play vids in youtube (or just the teaser vids if you are lazy) to see what it is about, basically it is a top down spaceship management game where you simulate being the captain of a space ship ala Star Trek and you go around with your crew customizing your ship, blowing enemy ships and engaging in "Choose your own adventure" style events while listening to some of the best music ever put in a video game. If that even remotely sounds like something that is appealing to you then by all means buy this game, it is one of the highest rated games in Steam and has given players thousands of hours of value comparative to its low, low price, esp. if you can get in on a discount it's like cheaper than a cup of coffee in starbucks.
While the base game (and FREE EXPANSION) are already amazing in its own right, what actually makes it one of the best  indie games out there is the mod support, unfortunately steam workshops isn't enabled but if you go to the game website you will see an entire forum dedicated to the extensive mods done, esp. the captain's mod which adds like 10x more content to the game. This game basically started the roguelike/roguelite  craze which is why you see tons of games out there in the roguelike/lite genre.
All in all definitely a great buy esp. if you are a gamer on a budget and/or have low pc specs.
Other games you might consider (low price+great mods which add value): space pirates and zombies, mount and blade:warband, torchlight 2, Fallout: New Vegas, Civilization 4/5 and Xcom: Enemy Unknown.

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is decent if rather short indie first person adventure/mystery game. I played through the Redux version, so I have minimal playtime listed for the base game. The redux version is simply a remake of the original game in Unreal Engine 4 with improved graphics and few minor gameplay tweaks.
The graphics are definitely the highlight here. The Vanishing of Ethan Carter has some of the most impressive nature scenes ever seen in a game. It's also a very atmospheric and immersive experience with pretty minimal handholding.
Unfortunately the gameplay is somewhat disappointing. While the core mechanic of reconstructing murders by finding and ordering the clues is interesting enough, the game could have taken this much further. As it is, almost all the puzzles are on the simple side and way too much of your playtime is spent hunting for the puzzles themselves and any clues you may have missed.
Overall, the Vanishing of Ethan Carter felt more like an impressive tech demo than a full game. I'd still recommend it, but only during a sale.
The good:
- Extremely beautiful natural environments
- Atmospheric and immersive
- Reconstructing the murders is an interesting mechanic, even if the game should have done much more with this
The bad:
- Quite short
- Most puzzles are pretty simple
- Too much aimless wandering looking for both clues and the puzzles themselves
- The story is not that good

--  The first person swinging physics stuff - basically the "grapple hook" thing the whole game is centered around - is a very cool concept, and I'd like to see more of this kind of thing.  And throughout the entire game one thing at least remains constant: the beautiful environments.  If the game had more open world maps it would be fun just swinging around all over the place, exploring and taking in the sights.  Sadly, the game is pretty linear for the most part, but at least it looks great along the way!
The voice acting is pretty good, but not fantastic.  The way it's implemented is crucial to the telling of the story, and the game wouldn't be the same with out it. However, I found some of the speech disconnected and awkward at times.  Still, I'd say it was done quite well overall and more of a pro than a con.
Also, I noticed other reviewers consistently put the game's short length in the cons category, but I'm the opposite.  I think this is a wonderful thing!  I barely got through the handful of hours as it was.  If it took twice as long to finish I'm not sure I would have been able to tolerate it enough to finish.
-- Considering this is called "A Story About My Uncle", the story side of the game is pretty awful.  The grown up version of the main character is telling a bedtime story (iirc) to his daughter, and rightly so, because it would make just about anyone fall asleep.  The story is as simplistic as it gets and extremely anticlimactic.  I was completely dumbfounded at the end, like, "I went through all that, and that's all there is?"  Very disappointed about this.
So what did I go through exactly to get to that lame ending?  Lots and lots of falling/dying and just as much frustration, that's what.  The whole goal throughout the game is to grapple and jump from place to place, often with a bottomless cavern or some such below.  A single mistake and you plummet to your death before being taken back to the previous checkpoint, which can be pretty far in some places.  This creates a lot of repetition that gets old fast and generates a lot of frustration indeed, maybe even rage depending on your level of patience lol.
What makes that even worse is the inconsistency of the grapple.  In one area you'll be able to grapple super far, and then five minutes later you're somehow not in range of a giant rock at half that distance.  Also, the surfaces that the grapple will work on is inconsistent as well.  You can grapple on to every surface in sight one minute, but then when you're trying to grapple that big floating rock just a few feet away, hovering above a cavernous pit, suddenly your grapple only works on a few square centimeters of the entire thing and if you don't hit that exact spot you fail.  Honestly, it feels like the devs deliberately tweaked the range and grapple-able surface area in certain spots simply to increase the difficulty.  But it does't make the game harder, just incredibly annoying and sometimes infuriating.
Finally, because a lot of people are OCD about getting achievements, I'll add something here.  You'll probably find it extremely difficult to get more than a few achievements in this game since they are mostly challenges that require minimal uses of the grapple or not falling.  As for myself, I'm not sure I want to put myself through the misery of trying, but we shall see.

wanted to enjoy this game... but I didn't.
has so much potential in so many ways, but it fails due to it's own clunkiness and inconsistency, not to mention a lame story when that should probably be its best feature given its title.  There's no way I can recommend this game in good conscience, but should you feel the need to try it for yourself (based on all the positive reviews or whatever), I do recommend that you at least do yourself the favor of catching it on sale.

From Michaela Laws comes Seduce Me: The Otome, an anime visual novel about a girl called Mika, who ends up in a love triangle with a bunch of incubi.
You play as Mika Anderson, a girl with two friends, and the daughter of the CEO of a toy company. One day, you get taken to live at your grandfather’s estate after he passes away. Everything seems fine, until you get there, and there are five injured men lying on the lobby floor. After a little while you find out they are incubi, male demons that feed off the sexual energy of humans to survive, but will you kick them out? Will you want them to leave?
I downloaded this purely because it was a free otome novel with some Steam achievements that I could play in my spare time. Upon playing the game the first time around, I was utterly shocked to find how quickly I fell in love with it.
Of course, it’s not that great; it’s the exact same route most of the time in just different locations, but for once, I didn’t really care about it. Each romantic interest was a well developed character that was fun to get to know, and it almost felt like they were real. Along with three female romantic interests as well, there were quite a few routes to take, and you’re able to switch it up without too much fuss, and without as much repetition. The character designs themselves, again, are pretty simple, and it’s the very generic demon design – although it was fun to see how each design changed with each demon. The soundtrack was also quite generic and didn’t have much to it, but I found the story line itself the most important and interesting thing of the game.
The story line really took us around things, and everything was explained pretty well. It was well rounded, and each story line finished off beautifully. A couple of the story lines had me in tears.
I would really recommend this to otome lovers, and I cannot wait to buy and play Seduce Me 2: The Demon War. This does a really, really good job of making players want to move onto the second game in the series, and it does its job. I would definitely recommend it.

Everytime you mention Bloodlines, someone installs it, or so it's said.
Anyway, onto the review!
Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines has a ridiculous title but that's alright. It's based off a tabletop RPG called Vampire: The Masquerade by White Wolf Publishing.
It's set in Los Angeles by night where the player controls their own vampire. There are seven clans to choose from and each has their own "thing". There's a clan which focuses on art, one that speaks in riddles, one that lurks in the shadows etc (Also adds replayability!). The PC is sadly not customisable, but it's possible to play as female or male. Gender doesn't have a very big impact on the game, but it affects NPC interaction a couple of times.
There's also some crazy♥♥♥♥♥♥going down in game. I won't be going into too much details but it can be kinda scary sometimes. Also there will be gore, sex and even a snuff movie. And maybe about two jump scares.
BUT WAIT. Luckily there's a console in case you really don't want to/can't do something. Hooray!
There's no such game as levels in the game. Like a real RPG, there's a character sheet and you can upgrade your abilities by spending experience, which you get from completing quests.
Questing is fairly fun in this game. There's no such thing as mindless farming! The first challenge is getting the quest, through picking the right dialogue. In some cases, if you pick the wrong dialogue you're missing out on quests and thus, experience.
Quests can be completed in different manners. You can either kill everything, stealth and in some cases just with dialogue, which is nice for the lazy people among us. Sometimes it affects the experience gain though. (For example, getting 3 XP instead of 2 if you aren't seen).
Combat is decent-ish, but at least you can switch between first- and third-person perspective.
The game isn't sandbox, but there are a few hubs you can go to as you progress through the game. You can travel as much as you want, as you have your personal vampire cabdriver! Awesome!
NPCs are all voiced and depending on the clan, even the whispers in your PCs head too! Isn't that fun, you'll never be lonely again! Anyway, it kinda adds to the already dark atmosphere of the game.
And unlike a lot of games, choices DO matter, throughout the whole game. If you aren't nice to someone, you might miss out on a quest/experience/ending.
The downside is that combat becomes more important as you get closer to the ending. This is probably because the developers were in a rush to finish the game. The vanilla game has some game-breaking bugs even, but if you use a patch by Wesp the game is definitely play-able.
There are also a lot of loading screens. Fortunately, loading times aren't long.
True, it's not a game for everyone. But what game is? BUT. IN THIS GAME...
You'll meet fellow vampires, werewolves, ghosts, zombies and humans!
You can be nice, sarcastic, or really mean!
Your vampire can dance just as good as you can!
Also you can make people explode so their blood is everywhere. Did I mention that? 'Cause that's cool you know.
For a rushed game from 2004, it has a lot of mods and some even revamp whole game mechanics. So I guess it's kinda hard to get bored of it.

C:\Users\YOURUSERNAME \AppData\Local\4A Games\Metro 2033\1100001183987d6

For keyboard mouse acceleration: mouse_curve_coef 0, mouse_curve_num 0, sens_border 2
FOV: r_base_fov 55 [This is 100 degrees horizontal FOV at 21:9]

Joe's Adventures is absolutely disappointing. I thought that I'd get more of what I really liked in the main story, but this is nothing like it. Two words: Fetch quests. And missions with time limit!
