The Vanishing of Ehtan Carter is a game that knows exactly what it is, and revels in it.
The core of The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is the telling of its story - and I won't spoil any of the story here - and the world that the story exists in. A lot of effort has been spent creating and rendering a consistent and believable world from start to finish. Unlike most games, The Vanishing of Ethan Carter isn't about understanding, learning and exploiting game systems or rules, but it's about exploring a compelling environment that is largely system-less.
The gameplay relolves around walking around a large rural environment and solving the puzzles that you come across. Those puzzles vary slightly and are, with one exception, quite easy. There are times when the "puzzles" are so straightforward that it is no exageration to say that you can complete them without trying. That doesn't tend to matter, though, because the experience of the game itself is so compelling. The game strives to create a coherent world, and injecting complicated or contrived puzzles into that world would feel out of place. The few times when more traditional puzzles do appear coincide with jarring narrative beats that match the unexpected change in gameplay.
Ultimately The Vanishing of Ethan Carter feels crafted. Its pieces all fit together and work to compliment the whole, leaving the player satisfied with the experience.
Visually, the game's environments are stunning. The character models and animation, unfortunately, don't match the quality of the environments. Similarly, the ambiant audio and sound effects are perfect, but the voice work is merely good.
I had no problems with performance running on a GTX 1070, but I did run across one bug that would have been game-breaking. If you are using a Steam Controller with the intention of mixing mouse and direct input controls then the game will stutter tremendously whenever the input switches from mouse to direct input. The solution is to set the right thumbpad to be input as a mouse-like thumbstick instead of a mouse.
Overall, I would highly recommend The Vanishing of Ethan Carter to gamers who enjoy slower-paced, narrative games.

Date: 2/26/16
Review Number: 28
Game: FTL: Faster Than Light
From (Creator Publisher): Subset Games
Played On: Laptop
Steam Price as of Review: $9.99
Total Time played: 45 Minutes
Review:
Next game on the randomizer was one on the significantly shorter list of my personal collection of games that I didn't purchase while on deep sale or as part of a bundle.  I don't recall now exactly how I had heard of the game in the first place, however I do distinctly recall knowing that this was a game I could totally end up playing long term.  And lo and behold that has generally been the case.
Now the premise of Subset Games FTL: Faster Than Light is more or less a typical space opera sort of thing, you are a lone ship, fleeing a great and terrible army in your spaceship towards some sort of base at the end of the map, at which time you give the secret to a military hub only to have them tell you that they don't want it and that it's your job to destroy the enemy’s secret weapon anyway.  One would wonder why they didn't just tell you that at the beginning of the map, but regardless you can still take all that time traveling inexorably rightwards to build up your ship with numerous types of weapons and sundry to make the job slightly less impossible when it happens.  The game is largely text based, with most of the game's story communicated via dialog boxes, and combat more of a point and click adventure game than a space battle, but the fighting still manages to keep you entertained, not dragging on too long to be annoying, but not so short as to seem to be tacked on at the end.  The game is very roguelike, with each star system having the possibility of throwing you a bone with some nice loot, or a pitched battle with a pirate battlecruiser.  You definitely can feel the hand of the random number gods all over this game, and in many circumstances you will most certainly find yourself backed into a corner regardless of having done everything right.  But the game does take great pains to not make the game seem completely unfair, and even the longest streak of bad luck really just seems more like you didn't do enough to make it work than any sort of random chance.
In the end, as far as roguelike games go, I can safely say this is probably my second favorite, blending strategy and gameplay in a simple game that you can jump right into, get blown apart a few times, then feel like you've learned something, only to get blown apart a few times anyway.  Buy.
Game’s Fate: Kept.  This game works brilliantly as a quick and easy time waster and a long and drawn out roguelike.
Buy/No Buy: This game will not appeal so some people, for many different reasons.  All those people are horrible.  Buy.

Another flaw is combat. It can be a bit boring and way to difficult, especially melee because it is clunky and awkward. There is supposed to be a system of pushing directional keys to vary your swings, but it doesn't work well. I high recommend playing a gun-wielding character.
However, in the long run, combat is mostly avoidable (more on that later), so it doesn't matter too much.
Other than that, this game is perfect. You get to play as a vampire for one thing, which is awsome. I know of no RPG like this except Oblivion, but those aren't real vampires in that game. The world's lore about secret vampire societies and laws is really well thought out and interesting. The sheer amount of it shows you how much work the developers put into the game.
Another great feature is the story. I just felt that it was really cool and interesting. It's very subtle and mature without being too long-winded. The dialouge is really awesome as well. In fact, both the voice acting AND the writting of the characters made me feel like I was watching a movie or reading a novel.
The gameplay and rules system is also extremely well done. You're assigned experience for completeing goals. Thats it. No XP from killing things. A lot of RPG's award too much XP for killing, and as a result you're actually punished for finding alternate soloutions because you'll be under leveled. In VTMB, there are always multiple ways to finish a quest. You could be a cowboy and fight your way through it, or you could look around for a way to sneak in. Or maybe you can hack a computer? Don't forget charming, persuading, or intimidating people to get your way. You're allowed to play any way you want and have tons of freedom. More RPG's need to be this way.
All things considered, VTMB is an awesome game that compensates for it's flaws with a legendary story and backdrop. It's a must have for RPG fans who like vampires.

contemplated a bit whether I should buy it or not.
so without further ado here's my review on whether you should buy it or not:
Gameplay:
The game is a hardcore top-down twin stick shooter if you're the same as me the "hardcore" part probably turned on that lightbulb above your head. so I'm going to summarise the gameplay in a way that'll let me vent my anger and frustrations, my tears of sorrow and happiness.
"YOU WILL DIE" so many times that you'll grow tired of it but keep coming back because your a masochist and you know you love it but on a serious note the game is straight up true to their word when they say hardcore.
You'll die when your friend accidentally shoots you with his shotgun close range. you'll die when your friend and you argues about whether or not to get that nearby research point. you WILL die when your friend or that random stranger just threw a Nuke near you didn't notice. the game makes teamwork near essential with the end game missions.
Next is the aiming system. you may find it hard  at first to target anything especially your friends when first playing the game. the game was specifically designed for a console so you may have to adjust to that a bit but in all honesty the port is done right, with a few performance issues here and there.
TL;DR "YOU WILL DIE A LOT!"
Story:
The story? there's none well at least none that your hoping for if your looking for a story.
Graphics:
It's not rocket science but it's good it's the type you'll expect from a console game not too bad not too realistic it's just right.
Should you buy it?
> depends, do you plan to play this with friends?  if yes then buy it.
> if not don't the community died at of this moment public matchmaking is near null. so good luck looking for people to play with in the "helldive" difficulty missions.
> Are you a masochist who likes to prove to the world that I can play this "hardcore" game solo? by all means buy it.
Overall I'd recommend this game for people who likes a mix of RPG, and Diablo-esque style games with that tinge of Dark Souls feeling of achievement.

Mafia 2 is a fantastic game, in the same vein as GTA.  It has a heavy focus on storytelling which it does quite well, but less of a focus on the open world aspect.  Many locations are only avaialble during certain missions, though there are three different time periods you visit during the course of the game.  The weather, people, cars, radio stations all change throughout the game giving it more of a living feeling than a lot of games manage.
The cars generally don't drive very well (as expected, it is around the time of World War 2.)  The physics can be a bit too realistic though, which makes it very difficult to drive with a keyboard.  The AI drivers seem to respond a bit more intelligently than most games in this genre, though occasionally they'll get stuck and even make you fail missions because the person you're supposed to follow decided to stop.  One quite interesting thing though: this is the only game I've played where the cops will actually come after you for speeding.
The graphics are decent, not great, and the game runs well even on old hardware.  The PhysX code seems very poorly written though and causes the game to run very slowly, even when there's no special physics effects being used.  On a better note, the voice acting is very good, though the game really could use Rockstar-quality facial motion capture (maybe for Mafia 3?)
The real disappointment of this game is the DLC.  Both packs are just loosely collected missions with very little story, where the point is to rack up points during these missions.  You gain points by doing things like shooting bad guys and destroying cars, which of course causes every policeman within 10 miles to want to kill you.  It's the same kind of annoying gameplay that Red Faction Guerilla is full of and it just plain sucks.  Don't get the DLC unless you're a hardcore completionist and don't mind driving in circles for 40 hours to get one of the achievements.  No, I'm not exaggerating.
I've heard people say this game is really disappointing after Mafia 1.  Mafia 1 must be an absolute masterpiece if that is the case.  All I know is, this is a great game and I highly recommend it.

At first, I was a bit worried by the somewhat cheesy lines delivered in the opening sequence by our intrepid detective 'Paul Prospero', but it didn't take long for these concerns to diminish and to become engrossed by the amazing visuals, music and story in this game.  The game crafts a rich atmosphere that feels very considered.  As it turned out there's a reason for the detective's manner of speaking that is part of the story but that is in spoiler territory as to why.  The rest of the writing and voice acting is superb (especially Ethan's).
I like to call the game a supernatural, first-person, narrative-driven, detective adventure game.  The environments are like nothing you've seen in a game before.  Despite how well they're crafted they took extra care to make it 'feel' real with wind through the grass and trees and leaves blowing in the breeze.  At the same time, the environment is completely devoid of people and animals (except for the puzzles) which makes it feel lonely and a little creepy and sinister.  I would've liked to see a few animals like birds to add to the realism but not too many to detract from the general vibe.  I highly recommend playing this game at night with either good speakers or headphones to experience the atmosphere to its fullest.
The puzzles mostly revolve around establishing the sequence of events of various murders you find around the game.  On one occasion I had to consult a guide to understand why I couldn't solve it (the hidden room puzzle) but once I figured out that there were options I wasn't seeing it was easy enough.  If I had any criticism here I'd say the game can feel a bit 'walking simulator' at times, but with visuals this good I didn't mind that much.  On a technical level I noticed the standard version of the game was fairly jerky on my laptop but the remastered version played smoothly, so best to stick with the update.
I'd say it’s a 4 to 5-hour game at normal pace, more for intrepid explorers, wanderers or the snap-happy and less for the 'efficient' or impatient.  Sure you could watch a play through on YouTube but you'd be denying yourself the full experience of one of the truly great indie games in recent years.  The ending was truly cinematic and a beautiful conclusion to this amazing gem.  It left me feeling like I'd experienced something genuinely hand-crafted, original and filled with love and care, just the way a fine film does.
I feel with this game they bit off just as much as they could chew, preferring a polished quality experience than to drag on or deliver more of a game that is incomplete or rough around the edges and I always prefer it this way.  This game is indie gold and I can't wait to see what's next for the cool guys at The Astronauts.

A mix of a Walking Simulator and a 3D Hidden object.
I find both genres utterly boring in general.
Puzzles were mentioned, but finding hidden objects is no puzzle solving. Resolving sequences of seemingly unrelated events, neither (although it can get pretty intriguing).
A few items were collected, but no inventory. Not that it that it would be of much use.
No map either. That would be of much use. Or, at least, a compass. After all, the forests have a reputation of disorienting the non-elven races. A minimal story was there. Not a bad one, to be sincere, but too short nonetheless. Hadn't I wasted so much time in random forest walks (evening tea not included), it would have taken about an hour to finish.
Yet I somehow liked this game.
Somehow, while aimlessly wandering with the petty excuse of searching for clues (actually admiring great landscapes in an almost totally inanimate world) the game managed to create an atmoshpere that thrilled me. Sometimes even scared me, for no apparent reason.
Well, I managed to die once. (which must be some kind of a negative record).
Once is perfect. Not too many to become frustrating, but enough to keep you thrilled.
Perhaps the previous, enthusiastic critics clouded my judgement. Or, meyhaps, I've grown too old, and too cheap, and got carried away by the amazing artistic work, both in music and visuals (in expense of an actual gameplay). Or it was beacause of the smaller things, as the relaxing experience of using a joypad and moving at my own pace.
Sometimes I imagine the game makers, having created a great 3d-modelled enviroment, coupled by an excellent soundrack, and then struggling to give the gamer a purpose to wander in it. From this point of view they did a great work. Definitely not overdoing it.
In conclusion, yes I'd recommend it. Not a 20$ recommend, but on a discount it is a very good offer. After all, and despite having to install both game versions just for reviewing it, the fact that they provide fresher graphics for free (in the era of payable useless DLCs) is something I really appreciate.

Don't be fooled by the modest visuals - this is a fantastic game. As an RPG Tower Defense hybrid, it's a blast. Solid mechanics that allow you to micro-manage as much (or as little) as you like, while offering simple tweaks to XP accumulation, allow for a high degree of accessibility. On top of that, the story is great. It does its own thing without relying too heavily on established fantasy tropes, and also mixes in some really successful humor - it actually reminds me a bit of Avatar: The Last Airbender.
If you're going to pick the game up, I'd highly recommend heading to the game's site. There's a sequel in development, which will have a score by no other than Nobuo Uematsu, and pre-ordering it there will net you a free copy of this game as well.
Bonus Note: For a more classic RPG experience, don't pick up any additional recruits in the towns you visit along the way. Instead, use only the characters you get directly through the story, and bump up experience gains to 300% - this will lend itself to a few special achievements, minimize micro-management headaches, and generally let you bask in the glory of your awesome, uber-powered characters.
Bonus Note+: The New Game+ is incredible, and so worth playing. It adds side quests, and a journal (which is actually really well written), giving loads of meat to the story and characters that was only hinted at on the first playthrough. Stick around for it - it'll be worth your time.

An interesting blend of RPG and rhythm game that works incredibly well.
Before the Echo is a game that combines the usual mechanics from rhythm games, where you have to press keys/buttons with the precise timing according to the music played, with elements from RPG games - leveling up, acquiring new gear, crafting, etc. And it does so very well. Basically, you have 3 screens - Attack, Defense and Mana. You use the Mana screen to recover Mana spent, the Attack screen to cast spells and the Defense screen to block incoming enemy attacks. To advance through the game, the player needs to know how to administer all three screens, changing between them whenever needed and using the proper timing to cast spells so that they're not cast at the same time an enemy attack is coming. The player can then learn new spells with varied effects like damage, damage over time, healing, creating a protective barrier, etc. The stronger the spell, the harder it is to cast it. Items improve the character's stats, making the character cause more damage, take less damage, recover more Mana, etc. Bosses have special abilities of their own that makes the battle harder.
At first, the story seems to be overly simplistic, but as the game develops and the story unfolds, it's revealed that there's a lot more to it. Characters are interesting and there is character development throughout the story and the voice acting is very well done.
For those who like a challenge, the game has four difficulty levels, with the hardest difficulty being for those lovers of rhythm games. The easiest difficulty still presents some challenge at later levels. (I actually had to reduce the difficulty to Easy for the last boss)
And, of course, the soundtrack - truly amazing. I would have expected a good soundtrack for a game that is heavily based on music, but even then, it surpassed my expectations.
Highly recommended.

Grappley's Review:
A beautifully challenging game! From the moment you shoot your first bandit untilt he challenging boss battles and attacks from bunnies! This game will amuse you and challenge you all together. The graphics of this game are fantastic, detailing a 3D yet 2D style along with a truly western soundrack that really puts you in the moment. I love the moments where I can cruis into the view and take out 4 bandits without being injured, Yee-haw! There's just too much to this game that makes it wonderful!
The Negatives
~~~~~~~~~~~
Well sadly this game had a few problems, but that's to be expected for Indie, right? Of course. So here's my list of cons and how they could be improved:
- A Tutorial; for many new players to this game, it's techniques can be confusing and I found many of times that I would experiment and end up dying. It's a great game and easy to pick up but it needs some information for new players.
- Restarting...It's A Little Disheartening; I understand that this game trys to challenge you, but really, I'm so proud of myself when I conquer a difficult part of a stage...but then I die on the next part and have to start the whole level again, A little annoying.
- Control Mechanics; I've learnt to enjoy the basic Up+Down+Left+Right controls for the character but it would be helpful if the game would add Mouse Clicks for shooting/jumping, it would generally make it easier and more helpful, Along with this I also found that jumping could be a tad hard, when I found that whilst running, I could only jump twice in a row before I had to stop running and try jumping, sadly I found this out the hard way...while jumping at a spiky hole :P
Apart from these, this game is a fantastic platformer and for only $2, you certainly get 5x the amount of fun and skill then you should. I recommend this game to anyone who is new to Steam and wants to add a game to their list. But of course even the most hardcore gamer will love this game for a break from Battlefield or Assassin's Creed.

Overall, I liked Before the Echo. I'm quite fond of rythm games in general (hard player on Guitar Hero, but not expert) and I liked the mix of rythm and RPG elements here.
At first I wasn't much into the artstyle but I got used to it and kinda like it now. Same went for the dialogues which are a bit cheesy, especially in the beginning but then you get into the story and it's all ok. I found the story interesting and mostly went to the end of the game for that. Oh and the voiced credits is a nice little bonus ^^.
As for the game mechanics, they mostly work well. You got stats to increase with stuff and level up, and spells to unlock and select for your build. The "line" selection during combats gives you control on how to spend your time and keystrokes.
Though, the main negative point I have with this game lie in the game design. I started the game in Hard mode because I'm used to rythm games, it gives a little challenge and at first it was all ok. But, as after floor 3 you can't change difficulty, I regretted that choice much later when I needed to unlock more spells and couldn't because it was too hard for me (struggling with keys and controller, more used to frets). So I finished the game with only 7 of the 20+ (?) spells unlocked. And I unlocked 2 of them out of necessity for the floor 7 boss and final boss.
The second complain I could make about the design of the game is about the final boss. On floor 7, once beat the boss of the level, you immediatly encounter the final boss and start the battle. There is a noticeable difficulty increase from the floor 7 boss. Therefore if you barely beat the previous boss, you can't beat the final boss and you have to go back and farm to level up and increase your stats. Also, because the damages notes are random, and in the battle the rythm of the song varies a lot, you end up in a total random fight when casting your spells and it ends up being infuriating. I lost my temper there with 20-30+ tries. I guess it's mostly because I didn't have the right spells unlocked but I was also struggling to unlock them.
So, could be a bit better on some points, but overall a good and enjoyable game with a nice story to it. Liking rythm games is recommended to play this one ;)

TL:DR
Pros:
Fun for a few hours.
Cons:
Progression slows to a crawl after a short time.
Too few milestones to aim for.
Bad mobile port.
Developed bugs and now fails to load.
Has a hidden "Facebook Ad Tracking" checkbox.
Full Review
_____________________________
I was prepared to recommend this game after about 7 hours of playing, as it initially starts out mildly fun for a "clicker-style" game.  However, I decided to mess with my system clock to see just how long it takes to progress later.  Doing so drastically changed my view.
The game starts out fun enough.  The first half hour or so you progress at a decent rate, upgrading your crops and buying trimmers and upgrades.  Then you plateau.  Not a problem though, just close the game and play/do something else for a while.  When you come back you'll have earned enough money to purchase a few more things.  Rinse and repeat.
Once you're not earning enough money to buy many upgrades or more plants after a few hours away, you reset and gain some Puff-Puffs, which increase your money gain slightly.  Then you do repeat the same process.
Eventually, the amount of money required for upgrades increases so much resetting barely feels like it helps you progress.  I suspect this is when the devs hope players will spend money to buy gems to buy manure which dramatically increases profits from one crop.  This is where I decided to fiddle my clock.
Up to this point, I had almost no problems with stability or bugs.  Sure, the port from mobile was poor, so the menus feel like they were meant to be portrait and scrolling with the mouse wheel is painfully slow (you can scroll faster by left clicking and dragging), but I did not experience the crashes and bugs preventing upgrading as others have mentioned (outside of the "Trimmers" upgrade "glow" preventing being able to click on the majority of "Upgrades" and "Up In Smoke").
Once I diddled my ticker, I started to experience these bugs.  Upgrading a crop would cause a "Cash explosion" animation to freeze and block out most of the upgrade buttons for other crops.  Going "Up In Smoke" would freeze a smoke animation in the middle of the screen which seemed to lock out everything.  Resetting the game fixed the issues.  Finally, for some reason, the game now refuses to load.
In all, I reset my grow around a dozen or so times, by moving my clock ahead a few years in total.  If I were to continue until I could "complete" the game by unlocking all the achievements, it would have probably taken a few decades.
Now, I don't have a problem with "clicker-style" games having long term achievements, I've put 7,000 hours into Time Clickers in order to 100% it.  However, this game has very little progression after the first few hours and too few milestones to aim for.
The final nail in the coffin was discovering a hidden "Facebook Ad Tracking" check box in the menu.  Click the stoner picture, far right option (question mark I believe), scroll to the bottom, then click as far to the bottom as you can and drag the mouse up.  It's impossible to uncheck because of what you need to do to reach it.  I'm fairly certain it's a hold over from the mobile version, but the slight possibility that the game is potentially having hidden Facebook metrics is a big turn off.

Haunting best describes this atmospheric mystery. The music, sounds, and visuals all work together to make the world of Ethan Carter feel very big and very lonely. The story is intriguing and poignant.
PROS: The way the plot is revealed is very well done, through reconstructing crime scenes and reliving short stories written by Ethan. There are many surprises, and the parallels between Ethan's stories, the events involving the adults in his life, and the revelation at the end are all intertwined extremely well. There's a lot more going on in this game than meets the eye.
The music shivers and surges at just the right times and was never intrusive.
The visuals, even on mid-low on my system, are stunning.
CONS: A down side to this is what the game warns about at the very start: it does not "hold your hand." While it's nice not to be force-fed tutorials, it's too easy to miss vital story components simply because you don't know they're there.
Case in point, I nearly reached the end of the game before quickly checking online for things I had overlooked. I found I'd managed to skip almost HALF of the story. What I wrote off as a "weird house I'll understand later" I was supposed to actually patiently pick apart right then and there. Some clues are even spaced so far apart they don't seem important or related. Compounding this problem, the game makes no indication when you've moved on too soon.
To avoid this problem, I recommend finding a list of game areas but NOT using an actual walkthrough. Merely knowing you're supposed to do something of importance in an area will solve the problem of the game's absence of player guidance. This information is actually given to you near the end of the game in the form of a map, but save yourself the backtracking. A simple cue like "I'm not finished here yet" or "I should take a look around" might have helped.
Despite that small issue, this was a very worthwhile experience. There are plenty of surprises and just a heavy aura of mystery that kept me playing. The game is short, taking me about 4 1/2 hours, but I finished feeling like I'd just read a good book.

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a cyclical adventure game in the first person perspective featuring you, a detective tasked with unraveling the mystery behind the disappearance of a young boy who has witnessed bizarre and paranormal happenings in a small isolated town.
The visuals are pretty and the ambient sounds, music, and narrator’s voice are quite cozy and form a nice kind of aesthetic to drive the player forward from area to area. As I mentioned earlier, the game is cyclical, however this is in an almost purgatorial sense in that you will be doomed to walk one gigantic circle until you solve every single puzzle in the game.
How are the puzzles solved, you ask? Normally, when you come across a puzzle, you will be able to hold left mouse to reveal a shimmering and incomplete dreamlike overlay. By finding the right items and pairing them with their respective alcoves you can trigger specific events to expand that overlay until it covers your entire screen, completing the puzzle and unlocking the second phase of that particular puzzle. In the second phase, you simply need to discover and order a paranormal re-enactment of the events that came to pass (the game will allow you to proceed once you get it right).
I’m going to be blunt here, this is basically a walking simulator tied to a very simplistic adventure game. Depending on how you enjoy this kind of thing you will either find it really relaxing or incredibly boring. The game has one section (underground mines) where the devs thought it would be fitting to shoehorn in some awkward and easily avoidable jump-scare mechanic which was kind of lame.
Given the general lack of playtime I can hardly recommend this game at the prices it’s often seen at; considering I finished the whole thing half-drunk in about six hours total. Best to wait until it’s near-free and maybe with a VR headset to squeeze the water out of this stone.

I'm quite skeptical when it comes to indie games, because the lower budget often means worse graphics. Nevertheless, The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is definitely one of the best-looking games I've ever played, and in that it's quite ahead of AAA titles like Far Cry 3. What you get is what you'd only expect from a short demo for benchmarking, to see what kind of effects your graphics card can handle. With Ethan Carter, it lasts 4 hours and you're in full control.
As for the story, there's a mystery at its core and a twist, as in a detective novel. I did not like it much, but it was not boring. I also didn't like the game's attempt to mimic Amnesia at one point. It should have stuck with being an amazing walking simulator to solve clues, with decent voice-acting and beautiful background music. It's definitely not a horror game.
Get the game if you like adventures and crime solving, or if you're captivated by astonishing visuals and sounds. Keep in mind that it's quite linear and short though, which can still be a good thing if you need a break from those 30 hours long open world games.

FTL is amazingly enjoyable, and even more frustrating.  The entirety of the game is a battle between risk management and a bipolar RNG.  Easy and normal modes are a painfully fun grind of learning all the ins and outs to unlock ships, achievements, and victories, but hard mode becomes a masochistic trudge toward arbitrary accomplishments.  The creators of the game even admit that hard mode is intended to be won 1 out of 10 tries.  If you ask me, this is a real killer.  I don't want to put in an hour of really good gameplay to have RNG put me in a literally unwinnable situation.  All that said, FTL is a hell of a fun game.  Even in easy/normal modes at first it can be punishingly difficult, but not without a lesson learned from each failure.  The most fun part of the game is unlocking all of the ships, and trying to defeat the Rebels with as many as possible.  Once you really have everything unlocked, it can get boring and frustrating, but that really does take a while.  For the price of this game, I don't think you can beat it.  Just be ready to angry cry a lot.  And swear more.

A Story About My Uncle (AKA: ASAMU) is a narrative platforming adventure starting the main character retelling his tales as a young boy looking for his Uncle Fred, a bright minded inventor who spends most of his time spanning the globe and tinkering with experiments. But one day, Fred vanishes again and doesn't call back. No post cards, no nothing! So after suiting up and preparing himself, his son delves into the underground world and the mysteries that lie within.
ASAMU is a Fantasy adventure platformer. Spanning across lovely environments from underground villages to sky-bound cities almost like Bioshock infinite. The player gets around with a grappling hook, allowing high-flying Parkour that can be fun, with more additional features unlocked in later chapters. However, it isn't without its problems as you'll soon find yourself missing easy landings because the collision box is slanted the wrong way.
The Parkour lets you the freedom of taking your own path, allowing some rather amazing bounds and turns. However as a result the game has no clear marker of where to go most of the time. More so, you can easily get lost or end up going in circles most of the time like I have several times. And when you hit
you might as well be playing super meat boy. I'm pretty sure I broke my mouse a bit because I smashed it in rage over slip-sliding over an unfortunately slanted Collision box and falling off, going back quite a ways.
Which brings me to my next issue:
There are far too few for how difficult the game can be at times. By the time you're in the third-fourth chapter you will struggle a lot to get anywhere. Spending up to an hour on a 'simple' bit simply because you hit your head. For a game with basis around momentum, it sure seems to struggle with the concept!
Anyway, Verdict.
: In my opinion? Not for the $13 it was asking. Maybe $10, probably $5, definitely at its current (At time of writing) price of $1.24

You will often hear that this game is the child of Dead Island and Mirror's Edge, taking place in COD-favela-like setting, and that is pretty accurate description. It's also a quite well done and fun mix.
I didn't really like Dead Island, so I approached this title with a healthy dose of skepticism. And I was pleasantly surprised. Turns out that the idea of parkour during zombie apocalypse works pretty well. There is an enjoyable freedom of movement, good level of character immersion via body awareness and combat is somewhat refined compared to DI - bashing zombie heads and cutting off limbs feels pretty satisfactory. The novelty will eventually tire itself out and the game will become repetitive - but you can actually squeeze a pretty decent playtime out of this purchase. There are quite a lot of things to do and many creative ways to kill zombies to discover.
Now some criticism: I didn't really like the whole idea of 'elemental' weapons upgrades - things like electrified gas pipes and blow torches taped to swords are ridiculous in my opinion. However, using them is optional, so I just played without crafting such oddities. The story has holes here and there and the main comic book villain is totally silly, but it bears little effect on the overall game, it's not like anyone will actually play this type of game for the nuanced narrative.
Overall, a really solid title - one you can enjoy with friends or just play at your own pace alone.

It was a similar thing with cash as well, I failed a few times by buying too much ammo for my ranged weapons and not enough blood to heal myself with.
Having to take that time to think made the game a lot of fun to me, it's not as fun when there's no challenge in it.
The graphics might not be anything to write home about, but it's an old game, that's something you should expect. They're still pretty decent in all honesty, and the actual design of the characters is lovely and one of the things that endeared me to this game.
I loved the music in the game, especially the music in the club areas and how it differed depending on where you went and I will admit I was happy when I heard a few songs I recognised.
For me I think the biggest plus of this game was the characters, all of them were amazingly voiced and had fantastic depth to them which can sometimes be lacking in games. I quickly found myself loving some characters and vampire clans, while others that I thought I would like at the start found themselves in my bad books because of how they acted and helped the game develop.
I have been pestering a lot of my friends to get this game since I started playing it, and I would gladly suggest it to many more.

The game is genuinely good and fun to play, but it is an open world game.  As such, repetitive gameplay is a staple of the game that must be acknowledged.
If you're completely new to Saint's Row, then imagine GTA with a slapstick sense of humor rather than a dark one.  If you've played 3, then this is going to feel like nothing has changed.  Specifically, the world is reskinned and the super powers from the DLC are the only "new" mechanic that differentiates this entry.
If your experience with Saint's Row is either the origingal or 2, then be prepared for a very huge tonal shift.  Whereas the original entries are GTA knock-offs, this it more like a clone decided to steal a gallon of nitrous oxide and fall into a vat of chemicals.  The resultant monster is funny at times, depressing at others, yet thoroughly worth your time.
As far as DLC goes....maybe wait for the complete pack to go on sale.  Most of the DLC is just character clothing, with the occasional item thrown in.  My experience is that Gat out of Hell is the only really great content worth seeking out on its own, but given what happened with 3 you won't have to wait too long before everything will be put out in one discounted pack.

Summary:
[+] This game is a wonderful one. It's fun, has a lot of small things to take into account and a great variation depending on which team you play. The small things matter which is always lovely in a strategy based game. Many maps and a hell of a war-feeling to it.
[-] However, the current state of the Matchmaking system, is seriously broken and will put you up against people with 10-20 times the in-game hours you've got.
Verdict: Don't buy this game unless you're prepared to spend numerous (hundreds) hours playing against bots. Because the MM will show you just how bad you are at the game and you won't get a chance to turn the games around or understand what you did wrong, because the good players are so beyond your level of play that you'll be a bleeding kitten swimming in a pool of hungry piranhas.
------------------------------------------------------------------
At the moment I've invested 31 hours into this game. I played CoH back in the day and had a lot of hours and know the game mechanics fairly well. When me and a friend (40 hours played) search for matches, we get matched with people who've prestiged one, two and sometimes even three times.
How can they claim the MM-system is a working one?
I have yet to have a game with people at the same skill level as me. At the same time they claim that the MM-system actually is fair and should match you against players at the same level as yourself.
How come it doesn't then?
I see a lot of posts on the internet regarding this, some people (good at the game, many hours) defend this, because if they get matched with a good player(s) they will have a chance because of their skill level. Many people (mostly not so good, few hours) are complaining they simply can't use MM at all because of the uneven matchmaking that currently rules the games.
I will lose interest in this game way before I reach that level. It's simply to challenging and not fun to be matched up against players with 700+ hours. At the same time it's not realistic that a game forces you to play 200 hours against bots before you can even try to make a difference in 2v2, 3v3, 4v4.
The 1v1 is pretty much 50/50. Sometimes you get a player closer to your skill level, sometimes you get one with a hell of a lot more time invested than yourself.
I'm sick of this and I have yet to find a post from developers that take this criticism seriously, no matter how constructive it might be.
I'm sad to give this a bad review as I love the game, the feel and everything around it. The MM-system is what's broken and has to be fixed. I rather stay in a queue for 25-30 minutes than get matched after 5-10 against opponents who will stomp with ease.

While both rhythm games and RPGs are not unknown land to me, a game that combines both of them in an almost seamless way made for a very unique experience.
The overall visual design is good, especially in terms of colour and consistency, and the voice acting just adds another layer of quality. The story itself puts a bit of a twist on the caught-in-a-video-game trope and is well-worth the play, and the characters are quirky and unique enough to be interesting. What stood out in terms of writing though was the humour which was present throughout the whole of the game on many different levels, such as dialogue but also e.g. weapon descriptions. It knows its audience well.
Of course, as a combination of two genres, the game, while scratching the surface of many gameplay features (e.g. crafting, character equipment choice), cannot reach the depth of e.g. an RPG in terms of gameplay, and, unsurprisingly, every rhythm game could do with even more songs. Still,
is a lowly priced and highly recommended hidden gem.

Mafia II, in short, is a pseudo open world third person shooter set in the 40's and 50's. Sounds pretty cool, and personally I thought it was alright. The combat is solid, the graphics are pretty, and there are immedietly noticable technical issues. There are a few key things though that hurt the game. As I mentioned earlier, it's a pseudo open world game. True, there is a large city that you can drive around, but it all honestly feels like an oversized hub area. Just a place to transit between mission sections. There was nothing to explore (unless you count the randomly placed vintage Playboy magazines, which may or may not be where you find them depending on what chapter of the game you're on), no side missions to do, and the city just felt empty, despite its best attempts to feel lively. This definitely hurt it the most, not to mention a total lack of ability to free roam after you've finished the game. If you're looking for a 40's-50's GTA or Saints Row, you won't find it here, at least not in the way you were hoping for. However, the story makes up for it. Memorable characters, great voice acting and dialogue, and decent writing keeps it interesting. Be warned however: The ending is horrendous. I enjoyed it, but unfortunately was nothing more than average. Very fun, but very average.

Full review:
Gunman Clive, what an excellent game. The game follows Clive and his journey to rescue Mayor Johnson’s daughter, who was kidnapped by a group of bandits. Although that may be extremely generic, this game was built for its gameplay, not its story.
The game packs sixteen levels and a few boss fights as well. Each level takes about one minute of your time, although this is not including the various times that Clive dies, of which, there will be several occasions. A few of the levels took me a very long time to complete, mostly due to a few challenging mechanics that were only present in said levels (rolling rocks and mushroom jump-pads). There was a level that featured mushrooms as “jump-pads” which I had a difficult time with, as in, it took me quite some time to master how to actually use the mushrooms to boost myself up to where I needed to be.
The graphics are definitely one of the game’s strong points. The game features a unique, minimal artstyle. It looked like everything was done with crayons or colored pencils of mostly yellow/brown shades. It fit the game well, surprisingly, and I really enjoyed this style. The music was not too spectacular, but wasn't that bad.
Gunman Clive is an excellent platformer-shooter overall. Like I said, it’s essentially MegaMan, but western, which is an excellent combo. And with a $2 price tag (on Steam), it’s a steal.

The controls are easy to adapt to from the classic WSAD format. Along with the controls, there are many button combos that can perform dash moves, devestating attacks, and quick escapes. The classes are a main feature in this game. There's the knight, the archer, and the builder. The builder is essentially the heart of the team. This class can build war machines, defenses, castles, spawn stations, and tunnels through the desrtuctible enviroment of the map. The knight is the one that charges in hacking and slashing. They have the ability to use bombs and several sword attacks. And don't forget the shield, an important factor in combat. The archer is the ranged attacker. With light armor and a deadly bow and arrow, the archer is quick and deadly. This class has the classic bow and arrow, but also a grappling hook, for daring advances and quick escapes. Another great future is the destructible enviroment. The bombs launched by kinghts will leave holes below your feet along with blood and dismembered limbs. Arrows will stick to everything, including human flesh. The gamemodes are fun and creative like the Create-Your-Own Castle and defend it (Take the Halls), Team Deathmatch, CTF, Zombie Fortress, and Challenges (minigames). Overall, its a really fun and  unique take on the claasic side scrolling genre that I believe everyone will enjoy.     8/10

On balance, yes, I recommend this game.
On its own, Saints Row IV is a fun, funny, highly customizable persistent world action game that is well worth a look.
Compared to Saints Row The Third, however, and the picture is a bit more mixed. On the one hand, the brand of humour is more refined and less cringe-worthy, with more heart and less slapstick. Superpowers feels like a piece of the puzzle the last game was missing, and opens up whole new possibilities for action and mayhem. Activities are more refined and enjoyable. Despite the over-the-top sci-fi turn, the story feels more coherent and more focused, and the finale is more satisfying.
On the other hand, there seems to be less actual missions; most of the so-called "side missions" are just pre-set Activities chains, which diminishes the sense of freedom. While Volition did a decent job mixing things up, a return to Steelport, of sorts, still gives off a strong sense of deja vu, and much of the content and gameplay systems are recycled from the last game. Unlike the optional collectables of the last game, this game's collectables are relatively more important, and collecting them can be a monotonous chore. Aside from the optional Challenges, there is a feeling of even less things to do, especially after completing the game.
Still, overall, Saints Row IV is a fun game, and highly recommended.

I finished this game in four hours.  This is a difficult game to review because I absolutely don't want to spoil it for anyone.  Avoid spoilers at all costs.  The game is worth it.
TVoEC is a beautiful game.  It is visually stunning, has great sound effects, and an amazing score that never gets in the way.
The voice actors were outstanding.
This is a game with mystery, exploration, and discovery.  It tells a story, and sets up characters, in a very unconventional way.
It was a very emotionally moving experience to play.
I found only three cons, and they're 100% opinion, and based only on my own preferences.
1.  Although the game largely gave the illusion of freedom of movement, and largely avoided the feeling of herding me down a corridor, there were some immersion-breaking moments where I found myself somewhat boxed in by rocks, trees and drops, and felt the protection of invisible walls.  Not a huge deal, but I would have preferred just a tiny bit more openness, with a little tiny bit more to fill some of the open spaces.  But this is a very small gripe.
2.  The game warns us from the very beginning that it will not be holding our hands, and respect that, but there were times when I wanted them to hold my hand just a tiny bit, so that I had more of an idea of where to go or what to do.
3.  There was one tense, scary point in the story where I looked on the internet to avoid the situation.  In an otherwise casual and laid-back experience, that scary place in the game kinda jumped out and grabbed me suddenly.  Not actually a jump scare, just a moment of tension.  I like horror games, but that one was too much.  Good job, devs!
Overall though, this was a very satisfying experience and I highly recommend it.

I enjoyed this game very much. The quality is amazing for a free to play game, and there are no added in-game purchases - it is an honest-to-god FREE game. That being said it wasn't what I'd call a perfect visual novel, but there rarely are any.
The CG are a huge part for me in otome and visual novel games. The CG in this one sometimes looked strange and disproportionate, but for the most part they were well drawn. I was a little disappointed at how lazy the demon forms looked, but I love how each one was individualized to the characters personalities.
The story as a whole was good, but again some parts felt lazy. Certain scenes between the protagonist and the brothers were almost carbon copies of each other. I was especially disappointed that the love scenes were like this. It didn't feel worth reading through everything again. Each route was so similar that I ended up just skipping through most of the text after I completed the second route. The one thing I liked about the love scenes is that you could actually skip them and still end up with the character, which is perfect for those who might feel like things were moving too fast in the game.
I absolutely love that you are able to romance your two best friends, an heir to his father's company, and one of the enemies. This makes it worth while to go through every route possible. Some people only play just for the initial romance routes since the "normal" endings aren't usually good. I won't spoil it but towards the end of the game you'll be presented with three options, one that leads to a surprising result. I was shocked this ending was even placed in the game but was totally pleased by it.
The brother's each have thier own back story for thier mothers (they are all half-brothers) so each flashback and item is unique to the specific route you're on. Damien has a somewhat extended ending from the other brothers - they all have the same scenes with different locations, but Damien has an extra one.
I was also happy that there was a sort of secret ending to the game. Once you've completed a route you recieve a letter (as in a character fromt he alphabet). Once you have completed all the routes, you unscramble the letters and type the result into the password section to get a sort of teaser.
As I said, the game isn't perfect, but Seduce Me has been and is still on my top ten otome and visual novel games. The fact that this one is free and has no extra purchases makes it that much more worth playing it.

OUTSTANDING game.
First of all, I adore indie games. I love the creativity and teamwork that comes with creating indie games, and they are my favorite genre to play and watch. I picked up this game on my queue during the Steam summer sale, but let me tell you, it's at least worth the five dollars standard price.
As an avid lover of rhythm games, I was pleasantly surprised at the complexity of each level. The difficulty increased without overwhelming the player, and the spells come in a great variety that essentially allow the player to beat the game in their own style. The art style is consistent, entirely due to the fact that every visual was created by the same artist! And it's so very sweet on the eyes.
Moving on to the characters, I have to say that while it is a rather short game (I finished all achievements in around 2-3 hours, after resetting my glitched game, a result of an error on my part) and thus we don't get to see much in terms of character depth or development, the characters' presence was enough to add quality and personality to the game without taking away the mystery and shock of the plot (I loved each of the Guardians and applaud the voice actors, as well as the artist, for providing such animated spirit). The ending leaves several questions unanswered, and if you're ambitious enough to get the hidden ending, you get a taste of even more secrets yet to be revealed.
I couldn't put this game down. It was funny, intriguing, and the artwork and music are STELLAR!
Now, to be fair, the game did have some drawbacks. I feel like the characters were a bit flat, but, if you play the game, you'll figure out why they seem to be so...scripted. It is a short game (hence the low price), but the crew that worked on it was so small! Aside from the voice actors, very few people put together a game that I will proudly call one of my all-time favorites. Iridium Studios, thank you for this masterpiece; I will cherish it for years to come.

When I was a kid, I really liked DDR.  I bought this game because I thought it would be like DDR.  I am disappointed that this game is not a whole lot like DDR.
I'm having trouble separating my disappointment of this game as a scratch to my DDR itch and how I feel about the game as its own thing.
So first I have to say, if you want to buy this game because you're like me and want to scratch that itch, give it a pass.  The objective of this game is to miss a bunch of notes on purpose, which drives me absolutely insane.  Just watching arrows pass by without being pressed.
By itself?  I dunno, it's got a lot of cringey humor and some mediocre voice acting.  The RPG elements seem kind of compelling?  But also really confusing?  It just feels really unpolished, I had a lot of trouble grasping how well I was doing because the visual feedback is less than great.  I think, mechanically, this kind of step rythm game just wasn't meant to be mixed with an RPG.

Definitely an awesome game for anyone that enjoys step mania, DDR, and possibly even rhythm and music games in general.  However, if you find Step Mania or DDR challenging or frustrating, this game is likely going to be too hard for you.  It forces you to not only hit arrow keys in time with the music in the same fashion, but adds even more layers of difficulty.  There are no color codes on the arrows themselves to tell you what beat the note is on.  So you have to go purely on listening to the music, and sometimes the arrows are just on really awkward notes or tones of the song, like a series of 16th notes where only a few of them have arrows on them.  Tack on that you are watching three sets of arrows at once instead of only 1, having to swap fields of arrows to be hitting, and apply strategic thinking to when to cast spells and what to cast SIMULTANEOUSLY and you need to be so good at something like Stepmania that you don't even have to think about the arrows.  You have to be able to do them almost completely subconsciously to keep up with this game (At least at the Hard difficulty level)  If you're that good, this game will knock your socks off.  It's incredibly fun.
The only real downsides to it come from sheer lack of variety.  The game has RPG mechanics for sure, and that includes trying to collect items with a % drop rate.  Meaning if you get unlucky (And you WILL get unlucky) you may be grinding the same exact monster for half an hour.  Which means the same damn song for half an hour straight.  What is worse, each monster does not have it's own song.  Some repeat.  This can get seriously old.
For 5$, this game is awesome.  Something I've never seen before and very well put together.  And at that price, the lack of variety is understandable.  Personally, I'd love to see a sequel, and would be happy to pay four times as much if they just make sure to really crank up the variety so the game isn't such an awful feeling grind at times.  The foundations of this game are rock solid.  It just needs a few more coats of paint.

Mafia II, in short, is a pseudo open world third person shooter set in the 40's and 50's. Sounds pretty cool, and personally I thought it was alright. The combat is solid, the graphics are pretty, and there are immedietly noticable technical issues. There are a few key things though that hurt the game. As I mentioned earlier, it's a pseudo open world game. True, there is a large city that you can drive around, but it all honestly feels like an oversized hub area. Just a place to transit between mission sections. There was nothing to explore (unless you count the randomly placed vintage Playboy magazines, which may or may not be where you find them depending on what chapter of the game you're on), no side missions to do, and the city just felt empty, despite its best attempts to feel lively. This definitely hurt it the most, not to mention a total lack of ability to free roam after you've finished the game. If you're looking for a 40's-50's GTA or Saints Row, you won't find it here, at least not in the way you were hoping for. However, the story makes up for it. Memorable characters, great voice acting and dialogue, and decent writing keeps it interesting. Be warned however: The ending is horrendous. I enjoyed it, but unfortunately was nothing more than average. Very fun, but very average.

This was a rather great game you can view this as you want but here's my view on it: The game lacks any sort of direction as to where you need to go (no way points) which to me is preferable because it forces you to think and explore. The whole "limited resources" adds another challenge to the game to make every shot count, use your gas mask filters wisely, search every nook and cranny if possible to find spare filters/masks and ammo. The weapons in the game are very customisable so you can play how you want (CoD style spray bullets everywhere, or fun and stealthy/careful), there's also a difficulty/style that makes it a bit more "run and gun" that provides more resources if that's your style.
One thing I did hate about the game was the level "Trolley Combat," it puts you in the gunner seat of a trolley/car thing that has rather wonky controls (makes you aim up and down with your mouse (or Right stick with up-down movement only if you use a controller) and rotates the turret left and right with 'A' and 'D' keys (left stick with left-right movement only if you use a controller); in this part of the level you cannot heal yourself with your med kit, so if you've taken an excessive amount of damage and hit a checkpoint right before the enemies arrive you're kind of screwed, at this point your only option is to restart the level and try to take less damage and be more accurate with your shots. I was finally able to pass it by putting the difficulty to the lowest setting (which you can nicely do at any point in the game) and set it back after.
But not to end this review on a bad note, the game was phenomenal with interesting characters, many different enemies: Nazis, Communists, and various mutants which can resemble a sort of animal (or human) that it mutated from. It has very interesting lore and just might make be buy the book series it's based on. The soundtrack is also a masterpiece that adds a good feel for the atmosphere, especially the ambient guitar being played by a refugee in the metro.
On to the next game, and excited for the new one coming out, it's definitely a great series.

I became deeply invested in it, and only took breaks when I couldn't figure out a stealth section or where to go.
Pros:
Environment: Creepy, desolated, and crude are all terms that could apply to the envirnment. You don't get the massively detailed vistas atop high mountain tops of other games, but you do get the gritty feel that you are exploring the underground of the apocalypse.
Characters: Oh boy you go through these a lot. You'll often receive travelling budies or escorts, but don't expect them to hold your hand the entire game. A large portion will be spent alone, daring the underground with nothing but your map, flashlight, gas mask, and your arsenal of crudely-made high-powered weapons.
Story: Really good story, with felshed-out characters and backstories.
Unorthodix solutions: You will get to navigate a library where you have to stare down giant ape-like monsters that will murder you if you turn your back to them. You will be in a vision where you basically have to platform run your way from floating rock path to floating rock path. It certainly keeps the combat from getting stale.
Cons:
Combat: Meh. Takes an unordianry amount of bullets to kill humans and the monsters can be much harder. Standard shooter mechanics. A few secondary throwables I never used.
Stealth: The stealth is okay, but ends up being either "You must quickly silent-kill or knock out enemies when their buddies turn their backs and then take them out and follow the semi-obvious path" or "Whoops they saw me enter GUNS BLAZING MODE!"

I adored Dying Light for the most part. I loved the way it presented itself as a first person open world rpg zombie game. I personally play a lot of zombie games. Dying Light as a whole thrived on its open world concept and having the player choose what to do next for the most part. I loved scavenging the city of Harran for weapons and supplies to craft with. Those mechanics in my eyes would have made a FANTASTIC open world multiplayer survival game without quests. I remember spending hours on end just beating zombies to a pulp and I never lost the smile on my face.
However Dying Light disappointed me and many others towards the end of the main story. At a certain point in the game, The design felt rushed. All of a sudden the open world aspect was taken away completely. Not only that but the end game forced players almost entirely to use guns where its main focus in every other aspect was melee weapons that didnt make noise. Also the most disappointing part was the final boss fight, which can't even be considered a boss fight as it was the only quick time event in the game. That part left me extremely disappointed. I enjoyed the conclusion of the story. I wish that a little more effort was put into the end game though to go out with a spectacular finale to an otherwise extremely fun game that left me with many fond memories.
I give dying light a 7/10 for its great concept but its rushed ending

Probably for me one of the best RPGs there has been - although it should be noted this is a story based RPG where the focus is interacting with the NPCs and working out what is going on and finding a way to survive all the machinations and chaos going on around you. It isn't a loot/xp grind type RPG, so if that is your cup of tea, look elsewhere.
The story is pretty well done, with a series of very different chapters as you move through the different regions of the city and encounter different types of threats. There are numerous memorable characters you interact with along the way, particularly Jeanette and Therese, Nines, Sebastian, Smiling Jack, VV, etc. Even the minor characters are generally done well enough to help flesh out and pull you into the world more convincingly (see especially Romero, or the surfers at the beach), which is essential to this sort of game. As others mention in their reviews the voice acting is a particular strength here.  While some of the characters/situations are a bit (or a lot) cliche, for me they are done well enough for that not to hurt things.
There are also a couple of particularly good set piece events in the game which really raise the bar - the key one being the mission to the Hotel towards the end of the first chapter, and the second being towards the middle of the game when you go up to the observatory. The mission for Romero in the graveyard is pretty amusing as well.
In terms of gameplay it is all fairly solid - combat is generally somewhat challenging -  not so hard that you die all the time and lose immersion, but not so easy it just feels like filler in between story advancement. Items and skills gained from levelling are powerful and can make certain situations (combat and not) a lot easier, but there are no required skills - there is always an alternative path or three to progress. This is particularly shown if you play through again as a Nosferatu which have to travel through the sewers for most of the story to avoid being seen by any humans, but also in the dialogue expanding skills to persuade or intimidate (or try) different reactions and courses of events.

On balance, yes, I recommend this game.
On its own, Saints Row IV is a fun, funny, highly customizable persistent world action game that is well worth a look.
Compared to Saints Row The Third, however, and the picture is a bit more mixed. On the one hand, the brand of humour is more refined and less cringe-worthy, with more heart and less slapstick. Superpowers feels like a piece of the puzzle the last game was missing, and opens up whole new possibilities for action and mayhem. Activities are more refined and enjoyable. Despite the over-the-top sci-fi turn, the story feels more coherent and more focused, and the finale is more satisfying.
On the other hand, there seems to be less actual missions; most of the so-called "side missions" are just pre-set Activities chains, which diminishes the sense of freedom. While Volition did a decent job mixing things up, a return to Steelport, of sorts, still gives off a strong sense of deja vu, and much of the content and gameplay systems are recycled from the last game. Unlike the optional collectables of the last game, this game's collectables are relatively more important, and collecting them can be a monotonous chore. Aside from the optional Challenges, there is a feeling of even less things to do, especially after completing the game.
Still, overall, Saints Row IV is a fun game, and highly recommended.

Being a bit spread thin from the holiday season and entertaining my nephews over the last week, I decided to try out a cheaper game this week. Gunman Clive’s regular price of $1.99 is pretty easy on my wallet and the art style looked decent enough to give it a try.
Don’t expect a deep story or anything for your $2 but you do get a fairly clean, straight forward, old-fashioned style action platformer set in the old west. You play as Gunman Clive and save the damsel in distress as you go shooting your way through some old west themed areas. If you’re feeling the damsel in distress scenario is a bit sexist, you can reverse the rolls and play as Ms. Johnson while she saves Clive instead. The game is a fairly even mix of tricky timing platform puzzles and action combat. Controls are fairly smooth, action is good, and the game doesn’t last long enough to get too repetitive.
I see many parallels to Contra as a side scrolling style shooter even including the ever effective spread gun as one of the upgrades you can find. Although the wild west model only shoots three bullets instead of five. When not slaughtering cowboys, wildlife, and aliens there are a few jumping puzzles that really offer the most challenge from the game. The hardest of these, I found, are the dang Spring Shrooms. I had a really hard timing when I’m supposed to hit the jump button after I hit them to maximize my spring, and ended up having to take a break due to raw frustration.
The game does do a good job of mixing things up and adding more complexity as you go along. Jumping over bottomless pits turns into jumping over spikes with moving platforms, which turns into spinning platforms while dodging spinning blades, which turns into crazy disorientating gravity switching. All quickly escalating fast enough to keep you from getting bored. I really have only two major complaints of the game. First I hate that taking damage sends you on an uncontrolled backwards jump. It leads to several ‘OH C’MON!’ moments when you complete a tricky set of jumps only to have your character get pushed off of a ledge to their doom when they get hit by a duck. Secondly the game is short, really short. I suppose you shouldn’t expect an epic game for two bucks but you can easily beat this game in less than an hour on your first play through.
To add a little bit of re-playability, you can try beating the game with each of the two starting characters, Clive and Ms Johnson. Ms Johnson, kinda like Peach from Mario Bros 2, can slow fall a bit. And after you’ve beaten the game once you unlock… duck mode. Which lets you play as a duck. Despite your ability of some flight the game is a heck of a lot harder without the ability to fight back. Duck mode also skips boss fights, so there’s that. If you really want to squeeze all your money’s worth out of the $2 it might be worth it but I started getting bored by then.
Still for two bucks you can do a lot worse. It’s a cheap and fun way to kill an hour or two. The art style is pretty easy on the eyes, the music ain’t too bad, and it is fun. I would have liked to see a few more levels that had all the different elements in it as I felt the gravity changing areas were under utilized. All in all, if you want a simple western game that reminds you of some old classics, give it a try.
Final Score:
Graphics: 7/10
Game Play: 8/10
Music / Ambiance: 8/10
Story: 5/10
Value: 10/10
Overall: 7.6/10

Haven't finished yet, but I truly love the style, gameplay, concept, and mechanics of the game!
Imagine an RPG style "guitar hero like" rhythm game. Got you hooked yet?
Simply put, the player switches between 3 "fields" or screens (Defence, Spell, and Mana) while in game as arrows move down in each field.
There's a great deal of multitasking involved because of casting spells, defending yourself, and gaining mana.
You win by draining the opponent's HP to 0 by casting damaging spells, but you can lose by losing all of your health or by not winning by the end of the song. It's a great game that keeps you on your toes and equipping the right spells.
That being said, don't feel as though there are "wrong" or "right" spells to use. Some are better for certain levels or battles, but I've been able to use the spells that fit my playstyle.

Company of  heroes is probably one of the best WW2 RTS games out there on the market. Personally, I love strategy games, planning a way to defeat your apponent with the rescources you have, to the hard AI that tests your abilities. From playing the past Company of heroes games, this one is amazing. The graphics are beautiful if you have a good computer, and feels like your their in the battle. I can tell they made the AI smarter than the past Company of heroes, so you wont get away with a win that easily. The physics and realism is excelent, and the maps are colourful. I highly recommend purchasing the masters collection before getting the main game. If you want to play all the factions, and make the war more intereting, buy the DLCS. Buy it, and go into a time portal to the great wars of our past.

Company of Heroes 2 gives an experience that few other games give. Where Men of War gives you a more technical picture of the Second World War Company of Heroes gives a cinematic experience that I have seen in few places. The sound of the engines grinding across the terrain, the dirt being kicked up by the treads and the haze generated by artillery bombardments really helps to immerse the player in the world of the Eastern Front. From a mechanical standpoint this game differs little from its predecessor and remains a solid Relic title. I have little time logged into multiplayer but from what I understand the community is a healthy one. If you want an a WWII title that is pleasing to the eye and can give you a truly immersive experience as far as sound design, set pieces to battle over as either the Wehrmacht or the Red Army (There are other factions available if you feel so inclined to purchase the DLC) this game really is a great place to start before you venture further into the WWII RTS genre.

This is one of the best RPGs ever made. Period. The atmosphere is amazing, it feels like a horror game set in a human world, meaning you get genuine horror moments fighing vampires and other monsters, but then you have times you're chatting to humans and having some interesting and some funny conversations. The writing is amazing and the story is gripping, with some amazing characters with grade A voice acting. The side quests are interesting as well, adding hours to your game time. I love the early 2000s Nu metal, industrial metal/goth atmosphere this games gives while also supplying Californian surfer and overall a realistic view on the humans living in LA. It's dark, and the way horror and real life contrasts is amazing. It really reminds me of Blade and An American Werewolf in Paris because of the Gothic church nightclubs playing metal in the background.
As for gameplay, it's very fun. You have hubs that are these urban areas with loads of buildings you can enter to get quests or just expore and meet characters. The combat is the only thing I have an issue with, it's fine but somethimes it's feel so cheap. For example, after a few hits your character has to wait to attack, letting the enemy hit you and when you're attacking the mouse often goes into awkward positions.
The diffuculty is fair, but sometimes when you're doing a quest, it feels as if they were designed for specific vampire species. Like in one mission you need to be stealthy but you haven't got an invisibilty power or when you're fighting the bosses, which are very challenging, you can die a lot which can be frustrating. Also, when you die, it takes you ro the main menu which is boring and annoying to see over and over again.
Overall, it's amazing. It's dark, has amazing atmosphere, diverse locations, genuinely interesting characters, top notch voice acting, a wide range of quests and weapons and will scare you in some missions, I dare not spoil the Ocean house hotel mission, but believe me when I say...oh, god. Anyway, I don't think there is any better game to play at halloween or in general, pick it up. It's worth the generous £14.99 it costs.

Star Wars: Battlefront II is the epitome of great games. From Galactic Conquest to Multiplayer, this Star Wars game hits every segment well. The Campaign has a selection of great maps from the Clone Wars Era and the Galactic Civil War Era, with two difficulties to select from. AI can be set according to difficulties set by: A. Campaign Settings, Instant Action Settings, Galactic Conquest, and Multiplayer. Classes for each faction are set in a balanced and competitive way, with each of the four different factions having two unique classes for each faction. Each map allows for unique faction heros to be played by the character, depending on the current game session's settings. Vehicles are a great asset to the game and provide another unique perspective into the universe of Star Wars gaming. From AT-AT's to speeder bikes, the game offers plenty of rides for the player. Space Battles are another masterful piece of the game. The space battles are arranged in different formats for each of the Eras represented in the game. Capital ships act as the home base of the factions, while frigates support the faction's starfighters with anti-air cannons. Objective points are secured by taking down critical parts of the Captial ship's systems from the outside or from within, as the player determines the course of action for victory. Frigates can also be completely eliminated to secure more points for the player's faction.
I would recommend this game at a solid 10/10. Great gameplay experience!

I saw this game popup on Steam and it caught my eye. I watched the video, which seems to be purposely a bit campy, and it sold me. King Arther's Gold is one of the few games on Steam I paid full price for and I was not disappointed. This game has some history and has seen several revisions before it hit Steam. There already seems to be a fairly established online community of gamers so finding a populated server hasn't been an issue for me.
King Arthur's Gold is a 2d online pvp game where two teams build up their base and attempt to destroy the opponent's. The game features four game modes: capture the flag, team deathmatch, take the halls, and challenges. There is also a single player gamemode called "Save the Princess" which I have not played as I assumed this game is multiplayer in it's focus. Capture the Flag and Team Deathmatch are fairly common in pvp games so I won't explain them. Take the Halls is essentially point control. Challenges vary map to map but this mode digresses from the other three as Challenge maps often pit players against NPC oppoonents.
Capture the Flag matches tend to last around 30-40 minutes. Take the Hall matches tend to take a lot longer (upwards of 2 hours). I have noticed this game can get a bit unstable after a few hours of gametime and/or with matches with lots of people.
The mayhem advertised in the video is absolutely accurate and I highly recommend playing this game.
Score: 9/10

Metro je skvělá jak hra tak kniha. Pokud máte ve hrách rádi skvělou atmosféru tak je Metro 2033 přesně pro vás. Popravdě koho by do hry nevtáhla post-apokalyptická Moskva. Hra by se nechala rozdělit na dvě části. První se odehrává v moskevském metru, které je naprosto dokonalé. Druhá část se odehrává v  rozpadlích ulicích Moskvy kde musíte být rychlejší, protože na povrchu potřebujete plynovou masku a do ní musíte sbírat filtry jinak se udusíte, no a těch filtrů není moc. Nepřátelé: Jelikož je Metro trochu survival hra tak musíte hodně prohledávat každou místnost, každou škvíru ve které by se mohla schovávat munice, když dělat nebudete dojde vám munice a roztrhají vás příšery na které budete narážet skoro všude. Typů příšer je opravdu hodně některé zalézají do škvír okolo vás, některé budou lítat a obtěžovat vás ze shora nebo jsou tu knihovníci (ty se nachazejí jen v jedné kapitole, která se odehrává ve Velké knihovně) a ty se pokoušejte obejít potichu, nebo do nich samozřejmě můžete plýtvat munici ve velkém.
Já Metro rozhodně doporučuji je to opravdu zajímkavá hra.
