What's this? An artsy game that's actually... good? Nah nah nah nah that's not possible... No developer could possibly make an artsy game without the pretentiousness that comes with it...
Except for this one.
This "game" (rather, interactive narrative), sets the bar for every indie developer out there looking to make the next "Her Story" or "Gone Home" or any other pretentious "game" out there.
The visuals are stunning; Unreal Engine 4 makes the game look absolutely gorgeous. The plot remains interesting throughout the entirety of the game, and I was never drawn out from the experience. The music is beautifully written, and the dynamic of it is superb (dynamic meaning it changes seamlessly depending on whatever you're looking at).
I also love the stylization of the text whenever you inspect clues; it adds to the immersiveness of playing as a detective.
My only complaint is that it's not worth $20. Pick it up whenever it's 75% off though, and you'll definitely be intrigued finding Ethan Carter.

Having no prior knowledge of this game, I found it quite intriging. The story was well crafted and kept me hooked throughout the entirety of it.  One of my favorite features is that it doesn't hold your hand. You are encouraged to explore from the get go.  This can lead to some frustration when you have to loop back to areas again to find clues that you may have missed.  The game, albeit fun and engaging, is a little short.  I took a leisurely stroll through it and completed it in 5 hours.  The only element that felt out of place was the jump scare.  I felt it wasn't needed and could have been left out.  Overall, I feel that if you get this on sale it is a fantastic game for the value.

When I realized of the great revelation in the ending chapter of "The Vanishing of Ethan Carter", I almost burst to tears, not only for the deep amount of sadness and melancholy of knowing the unexpected truth, but also of how beautifuly this story had been told, the acts and misteries along the tracking of the missing boy. Of how the story unfolds itself through the eyes of the detective Paul Prospero, as he tries to find 12-years-old Ethan Carter by following the clues written on the letter by the kid. Is he still alive?
This was, no fear to admite it, one of the most shocking, powerful and memorable experiences ever achieved in a videogame. More than a game, this was... a emotional healing scar,

Before going further, keep in mind that it took 12 hours to complete the game on maximum difficulty, so It's not exactly the most challenging game. It's more intended to be a fun co-op game with friends, If you intend to complete it alone for the story this might not be the game for you.
Dying light is fun, but it does a lot of things wrong.
First, the difficulty curve is really weird, for the first half of the game, you can kill about two enemies before having to repair your weapon. Making most missions extremely difficult unless you exploit broken mechanics. And as soon as you get your hands on a gun, the game becomes a cakewalk. In the main story, ammunition is pretty common to find after a certain point, and most enemies die from one or two shots to the head, making melee weapons almost useless. To balance that, you get stripped of all your weapons before the two boss encounters in the game. Instead giving you really weak weapons to beat them, If balance was done correctly this wouldn't need to be the case.
Once again, the whole weapon crafting and upgrading system is fun on paper. But what's the point if all of the good gear you can find or craft is useless compared to firearms which you can't craft? For the last half of the game I only ended up using melee weapons against the weakest of enemies in order to conserve ammo, which ended up being useless because you're stripped of your gear before bosses.
And also, I don't see the point of a skill points system if there's no classes. Unlike Dead Island where you have to pick a class and specialise, In Dying Light you have 4 distinct skill trees, and the points you gain are linked to said trees. When you fight, you gain fight experience, when you parkour, you gain agility experience, etc. All skills in the trees being locked by level, everyone has to play by almost exactly the same build, so I really don't see the point. Sure, you have a choice to make, but most of the time it's a no brainer, like who wants a slight stat increase over a drop kick? And in the end you're gonna end up picking both, because the tree doesn't let you pick what you want.
Last thing I found really weird was the story. Yes, this has the plot of a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ action movie, but a well done story even if pretty dumb, can give personality and set a good mood for a game. Just look at the last DOOM, you can't make more simple of a story, but it just works perfectly for the given game. But in dying light, damn was I disappointed. The main character is this generic action game blank slate guy, but annoying as hell. He fits the cliché of the American guy who doesn't shut up, saying """badass""" stuff when confronted with adversity, like "SON OF A ♥♥♥♥♥", or "WILL YOU SHUT UP". The minority of characters that are likeable are either unimportant to the story, or are killed off for no reason. Don't get me wrong, some drama is good. But this feels forced and redundant really. I get it, it's the apocalypse, and the Die Hard villain has a thick foreing accent and tattoos so you know people are going to get killed. But a tragic death should be at least a bit of a surprise you know, or come after a minimum of character development. And I say all that as an action movie fan, seriously, Rambo 2 characters were better than this, this was a really dumb story with even dumber dialogues.
If you like games like dead Island, you're definitely going to like that. Besides the class system that makes more sense in DI, everything is done way better in this game in my opinion.
So yeah, if you want to play a game with a compelling story, deep lore and challenging gameplay, stay away from this.
If you want to drop kick people off building and break their legs with rebar, this is the game for you.

Pros:

An open world, good graphics, zombie smashing and an interesting leveling system drove me to this game, but unfortunately the cons started to hollow out the gaming experience after a while.
The open world of Dying Light is more like a gamey sandbox than a well designed immersive game world. I got frequently lost in the tower headquarters at first, with all its blocked stairs and elevators. Maneuvering the tower is initially more dependant on writings on the wall than easily understandable visual design.
The city itself looks and feels a bit samey, with the same buildings, shops, encounters, loot and enemies. You'll meet random people that are just waiting around to tell you their whole melodramatic life story, all while the zombies close in on you both. Time and again you'll stumble upon the same shopkeepers that mysteriously end up in trouble, over and over again.
Enemies and loot are everywhere, but the way lockpicking and looting is implemented, slow and clumsy, it feels like more like a chore than a positive experience.
Still the worst thing to me was when those virals started to spawn all too often, after a few hours of game time. I tried to keep going, but every time I was in the zone and had some fun, mizing traps and weapons the best I could, I always ended up on a roof with a handful of virals on their way up. After repeating that 10 times for a 5 minute game session, and naively repeating that over a few days, I just started to feel pretty much done with the game.
So, here you have a zombie killing game with loads of weapons, traps and weapon upgrades which all is fun in itself to explore, but then the game punishes you for using them, with an annoying enemy that takes the fun out of the gaming experience. I can understand that they wanted a game mechanic like that, but  the way it was implemented just made my brain implode...somewhat of a waste for a zombie game, perhaps.
Overall Dying Light is a hollow yet entertaining zombie-killing sandbox that will leave you a little dissatisfied if you crave a more substantial experience. After a while you might feel like you've had cake for dinner a whole week; it starts out pretty fun, but in not too long you just feel fatigued. There's plenty of in itself entertaining things to do in this game, and I think it's a bit overly crude to go either thumbs up or down, but because of the virals...computer says no.

This game's Very Positive rating at the time of this review really boggles my mind. It's not that the game is bad, rather that its an idea who's implementation seems inherently flawed.
The base mechanic of the game is the traditional "press one or more of the 4 directions on the beat as instructed". However, the twist is that you have three panels of arrows to rotate between and timing your presses correctly on them has different effects. There's your mana regen panel where each correct press earns you a little mana to cast spells. There's another that represents spellcasting where successfully landing a series of presses will cast a spell (more on this later). The last one represents defense where a sequence of arrows represents the enemy's attack; if you miss any here you take damage.
The problem is that the defense panel's arrows (i.e. the enemy's attacks) occur at random, but you have to manually trigger your spellcast sequences. You may already see the issue here: you build mana, cast an attack spell, and arrows start to fall in the spell cast panel and defense panel simultaneously. The game's prescribed cure for this is to constantly keep up a "barrier" spell which effectively mutes the enemy. So the game requires you to continually recast this barrier spell so that you can actually cast the spells you want in between each barrier cast. In my opinion this is a kludge of a game mechanic. You get involved with a whole lot of busy work just to occasionally do something meaningful. Perhaps it all gets a bit smoother with some practice, but whats to engage you enough to want to get that good?
I found a majority of the music to be ignorable at best. I've enjoyed some of Ronald Jenkees' music, but what's offered here I'd be reluctant to classify as even B-side music. The dialog is atrocious, the story is insignificant, and the graphics are the kind of crappy animatics that have now become standard fair in a sea of indie game dev mediocrity. The game would be perfectly suited for two hands on the keyboard, but I was forced into using a controller. (Oh I hope this wasn't just because I had a controller plugged into my PC; I'm not going back!)
Perhaps worst yet is that the game devolves into a grind as each enemy you face has the chance to drop (at most?) one of three items of increasingly rarer chances to drop. You can face an enemy multiple times (enjoying the same music each time!) to get all items from an enemy. Why? Did the game need a time sink like this? Again, its more poor game design that not only contributes nothing fun, but actually contributes frustration.
I really wanted to like this game. I had it on my wishlist as soon as it was released and bought it while it was still named Sequence. Despite the game's somewhat novel concept, it seems like the developer tried to throw a hodge-podge of ideas and twists at the rhythm genre, but just ended up with an overly-complicated and unfun mess.
Unless you're some kind of rhythm game fanatic, skip this one. 6/10

Company of  heroes is probably one of the best WW2 RTS games out there on the market. Buy it, and go into a time portal to the great wars of our past.

Company of Heroes 2 gives an experience that few other games give. Where Men of War gives you a more technical picture of the Second World War Company of Heroes gives a cinematic experience that I have seen in few places. The sound of the engines grinding across the terrain, the dirt being kicked up by the treads and the haze generated by artillery bombardments really helps to immerse the player in the world of the Eastern Front. From a mechanical standpoint this game differs little from its predecessor and remains a solid Relic title. I have little time logged into multiplayer but from what I understand the community is a healthy one. If you want an a WWII title that is pleasing to the eye and can give you a truly immersive experience as far as sound design, set pieces to battle over as either the Wehrmacht or the Red Army (There are other factions available if you feel so inclined to purchase the DLC) this game really is a great place to start before you venture further into the WWII RTS genre.

RTS is probably my weakest genre, so with that in mind, I will mostly just say that I enjoy the game for its detailed and convincing special effects and sound design. It has lots of dramatic gut-wrenching explosions, and there is much fun to be had laying waste to the environment and your opponents alike with heavy mortars and satchel charges. One compelling knock against the game, which I have heard, is the flattening and simplification of the progression system, compared to its predecessor. That is disappointing, because to me, good RTS design is all about that progression, and the complex and interesting ways in which it can lead to a dramatic and often catastrophic crescendo at the end. I think few games do that as well as the classic C&C: Generals.

I have been waiting to play this game for quite some time to fill the void left by Alien Swarm and finally picked it up when it was on sale for $15.99.  For the first few levels this game is fun.  Until you realize the 3 MAJOR design flaws that you will be fighting with every single time you play.  Bear in mind that I am playing with a mouse and keyboard.
1)  You are tethered to your allies and CANNOT ZOOM OUT.  Many of your weapons can fire off screen... there is NO WAY to spot off screen and if you look at your map when there are enemies around 50% chance you will be dead soon.  I understand that this is done to "increase teamwork"  or "strategic gameplay" but it is a terrible handicap that you will be forced to die for over and over and over and over.  THERE IS AN INVISIBLE BARRIER THAT YOU CANNOT MOVE PAST.  This is what is really happening, you are being forced to stop by an arbitrary obstacle that is completely made up.  This is WORSE than Alien Swarm the game from 2010.
2)  Your aiming mechanics (with mouse and keyboard) are sluggish and poorly designed.  If I am on foot I can move the mouse around but until I aim, I will not look in the direction I was mousing over.  However, when I am in a mech the aiming is linked to my mouse cursor location.  This is totally inconsistent and stupid.  It obviously should always follow my mouse cursor like in the mech.  Why this was overlooked is idiotic.  This is WORSE than Alien Swarm the game from 2010.
3)  Your cursor is barely visible until you aim (with mouse and keyboard).  Yet, when you aim you slow down.  This makes something as simple as running from a group of enemies and turning around to shoot them sometimes too clumsy to pull off... as you will still be aiming in the direction that you were running when you try and turn around to fire.  This can sometimes take 1 to 2 seconds which will kill you if you are running from cyborg dogs for example.  Because your cursor is barely visible until you aim, you will lose sight of it on a regular basis.  The option that states cursor is always on does NOT make your crosshair on all the time and therefore the option is completely useless.  There is no option to change the color of the crosshair or make it so that it actually IS always on, or even change your crosshair type.  This is WORSE than Alien Swarm the game from 2010.
I do still recommend this game as it is a lot of fun and the multiplayer is great.  Unfortunately, this game could easily have been the greatest of its' genre, but it is reduced to merely above average due to EXTREME flaws (or incredibly poor game design whichever you believe).  For some reason Helldivers insists on making walking around and shooting♥♥♥♥♥♥unneccessarily comlicated and somehow manages to be worse at it than Alien Swarm despite knowing EXACTLY what made that game so awesome.  This game does offer more replayability and options, however in the game mechanics department this game is not as good as the 6-7 year old Alien Swarm in the game and that is both sad and pathetic.

It is very very fun and highly recommend it for people that play with smaller groups. Game is not bad solo, but I would point towards playing in a group. The match making system works decently well and if you find a bad group just leave and hop into the next group.

Use the unofficial patch or this game will be too broken to even touch.
Now:
Probably the best overall writing ever seen in a video game. Deus Ex, Thief, Morrowind, System Shock and Pathologic were all excellent in their own respects --- but this game beats them all in terms of consistency and believability. Characters actually have personality, conversations actually flow, and every single NPC that can be interacted with has a ton of depth and maybe even a few ulterior motives. This game is easily tied with Deus Ex as the closest we've ever gotten to Warren Spector's "one city block" vision. It simply has to be experienced to be believed.
Unfortunately, the game is even more broken than Deus Ex. While Deus Ex was marred by half-baked and unsatisfying systems that would make for a terrible games on their own, this game is marred by a ton of systems that are either there for no reason whatsoever or just outright don't work. The Seduction skill makes Deus Ex's Swimming look useful, and there is absolutely no reason to use firearms at any point in the game. Not even the tutorial for firearms requires that you use them --- they are that useless. For the first two areas, the game is a brilliant collage of choices and possibilities, surpassing even, yes, Deus Ex, but that vision becomes more and more distant as the game goes on, to the point where the latter half of the game is a concoction of horribly rushed and bland dungeon crawls and some of the worst boss fights even seen in games and the final area is almost entirely devoid of any complex architecture, sidequests or secrets. The story comes to a similarly rushed, mean-spirited and silly conclusion. If there was ever a game that deserved this kind of fate, this one wasn't it.
Overall, this game is Deus Ex taken to the extreme in every aspect --- while the world of Deus Ex occasionally felt real and personal, Bloodlines' world bursts at the seems with life, and for a precious moment, one could be forgiven for seeing the World of Darkness as truly alive and endless. While Deus Ex was somewhat weak in its mechanics and failed to retain its momentum into the latter stages of the game, Bloodlines barely functions at all beyond its first few stages and completely falls apart in the latter half. This game is utterly brilliant for its first half, but the second half will make any player mourn for what it could have been. Considering the fact that Troika closed its doors after Bloodlines' release and nobody has so much as attempted something approaching the first half of the game ever since, it's unlikely that we'll see a happy ending for this kind of game, so we have no choice but to enjoy this precious specimen.

This game is a cult classic.
You should be warned that this game is broken and will not function on most modern machines.  There is an Unofficial Patch made by Wesp5 that fixes nearly all issues with the game and also adds new content.
Based on the board game, and sequel to Redemption, you play as a fledgling Vampire in California.  The story starts as you create your character.  Here you choose your background, bloodline, and gender.  Backgrounds change your stats slightly and your powers as a vampire will differ depending on your bloodline.  Some bloodlines have some side effects, however.
The best examples are Malkavians and Nosferatu.  Malkavians are insane and schizophrenic.  You'll talk like a crazy person, hear voices in your head and see things other people don't see.  Nosferatu are cursed in a different way as they can't be seen by humans without violating the masquerade.  This does not make it impossible to beat the game as a Nosferatu, because the main quest NPC's will still be approachable.
The masquerade is a system in the game where if you get 5 bad marks it's game over and you'll be executed by your peers.  You earn bad marks by displaying certain powers in public or are seen feeding.  You can redeem yourself if you have bad marks by protecting the masquerade.  This usually involves killing someone who is speaking  too much or who isn't playing it safe like all other good little vampires should.
Graphics are decent and passable.  The game is an older game, so don't expect mind blowing visuals.  City hubs are fairly small but there's a lot to find if you set your mind to it.  There are some nice facial animations that you won't even see in games nowadays which adds to the immersion.  There's also several mods for the game to add atmosphere and even more depth to the classes.
Gameplay is basic.  You shoot things, you smash things.  You talk to people, you kill people.  There are extra dialog options if you level your seduction, intimidation, or persuassion skills.  These skills can be vital to completing some quests perfectly.  You can also recieve bonuses from certain NPC's for having them at the required level at certain points in conversation.
You gain experience from doing quests and you level up to gain strength, wisdom, guile, skill, and become more attractive.  If you're sexy enough you get free hookers! Just like IRL! =P
The beginning of the game will mostly be fetch quests, with a few baddies to either slaughter or let live.  It's a game where you can put the fate of nearly everyone around you in your hands.  Being good is rewarded with extra perks like your very own slave ghoul girl, or an extra item/money/experience.  There's also a decent but easy stealth system that's based on how many points you have in stealth.  If you max out stealth, are in the shadows and crouch you're pretty much invisible.  There are also assassinations you can do with each weapon while stealthed and behind your victim.  My favorite is the baseball bat.  :)
Audio is very good as well.  Just make sure you turn Environmental Effects off or there will be a constant echo.  Voice actors are all top notch and AAA grade ones that you'll know if you've heard them before.
There are some very good mods for this game available as well.  My favorite being the original Unofficial Patch Plus, but there are other that increase the difficulty of the game and add new quests and bloodlines to choose from.  When installing these big mods you need to remember that they aren't compatible with eachother.  E.G. Final Nights mod will not work with Camarilla Edition nor with either work with the Unofficial Patch.  Both mods have an Older version of the Unofficial patch that come with it, which still fixes a lot of bugs.  There's also several mods  that are still being produced constantly by fans.  Every now and then you should check up and see what new mods are out to keep you coming back for more.
All in all, if you are in need of a good RPG that's open world with a lot of freedom and are tired of Fallout 3/NV, Skyrim, etc.  Then you should definately check this game out.  Especially if it's on sale.  Well worth every penny spent.

Please don't mind the time I played this. I played it offline and Steam doesn't seem to count that. I am at about five hours total.
I can recommend this game. When I finished it, I had goosebumps for quite some time and I kept on listening to the soundtrack afterwards. I played and finished the game in one session, therefore I was deeply connected to the story and the character(s). The story itself is interesting, although with a somewhat disappointing conclusion. An unusual part of this game is that you can technically ignore almost the whole number of sidequests. The world is almost completely accessable from the beginning. But I don't want to tell too much about the content.
The graphics are stunning. Unfortunately, my computer was barely fast enough to play this on low settings, but even then it was pretty. Watching the game online on maximum graphics makes my heart ache. It's just beautiful.
The story itself really captured me right from the beginning. At first I was like "who is that? what the hell are they doing to each other?" but over the course of the game I managed to recognize every character and kept track of everybody, where and when they appeared and so on. Since the game has barely any barriers, you could see parts of the story whenever you wanted, leading to situations where you suddenly understood that that particular part of the story was earlier in reality etc. Personally, I enjoyed setting up the whole storyline in my head.
I only see two real drawbacks: First, the time. As I said, it took me 4-5 hours to finish the game. But on the other hand, I luckily managed to do everything in the right order without "skipping" anything and having to backtrack too much.
Second, the glitches. Especially one of the achievements had me running back and forth, not understanding what I was doing wrong. A short online check told me to restart the game and then focus on it, and it worked. It was nonetheless rage-inducing. I heard that these glitches among many others were fixed in the Redux version that comes with the original for free. I can neither agree nor deny it since the Redux is definitely too demanding for my comfy old computer.
All in all, I strongly recommend this game to people who can enjoy atmospheric and rather slow games. As for me, it gained a "special place" in my Steam library. I must admit that I am listening to the soundtrack over and over again even now. The thing that hurts me the most is probably that I can't erase the memory and re-play it. The journey of Ethan Carter was sad and beautiful.
Oh, except that miner puzzle down below. Screw that. I almost died of a sudden scare.
Just kidding, still love the game.

The vanishing of Ethan Carter is a strange game. Obviously, it's beautiful and looks great, but is there more? A classic soundtrack is triggered whenever necessary to support the strong, mystical and somewhat threatening mood. The game consists of ten different puzzles. Put together they tell a story. Personally, I did not like the story. Until the decryption of the last riddle there are quite a number of aspects in the story that make no sense.
Some years ago I read a book that in the end turned out to be a dream, making the whole story meaningless. In a similar fashion this applies to 'The vanishing if Ethan Carter'. I don't think it is possible to find a clear verdict if this game deserves a recommendation or not. It's simply a matter of taste. And while I do understand the many positive reviews for this game, I can not join the group of proponents. You have to find out for yourself if you like this game or not.
Pros:
- beautiful graphics
- strong atmosphere
- good music
- easy achievements
- a piece of art
Cons:
- somewhat a walking simulator
- very brutal
- dark, strange, bizarre story
- short (10 puzzles)
- linear
- few moments of surprising joy
- only things to do: read notes, find half a dozen items, arrange story events in the correct sequence
- no side quests
- you can't make any decisions
- didn't touch me emotionally
- no direct dialogues with NPCs, you can only listen
- not challenging

Before the Echo (or Sequence as it was formally called) is essentially a dance dance revolution/stepmania RPG.
Mechanics:
- In battle, you can switch between three "dance" screens (where you match the sequences given like in DDR). Each screen is useful for one of three things: Mana, Attack, or Defense. So in order to prevent damage to you, you match the sequence on the defense screen.  You also collect items and abilities that you can use during battle.
Another interestign mechanic is the game provides you "recipies" on each floor. In order to get the items needed to make something, you have to defeat an enemy. Then, to actually craft it, you get a 50% chance of success. To make it greater, you can sacrific XP 9and potentially level).
Pros:
- Mechanics are fun
- Music is catchy (although can get redundant)
- Cool crafting system (although not terribly deep)
- You can level up above the necessary requirments if you feel like it to make it easier.
Cons
- Can get grindy

It has a set of amazing soundtracks,  great gameplay, very interesting characters and a clever story premise. If I have any complaint, it'd probably be the grinding you have to do to craft the recipe items, but even so it wasn't that bad and hey, what's an RPG without a little a grinding am I right? I'm definitely recommending this amazing game, 9/10

I have been waiting to play this game for quite some time to fill the void left by Alien Swarm and finally picked it up when it was on sale for $15.99.  For the first few levels this game is fun.  Until you realize the 3 MAJOR design flaws that you will be fighting with every single time you play.  Bear in mind that I am playing with a mouse and keyboard.
1)  You are tethered to your allies and CANNOT ZOOM OUT.  Many of your weapons can fire off screen... there is NO WAY to spot off screen and if you look at your map when there are enemies around 50% chance you will be dead soon.  I understand that this is done to "increase teamwork"  or "strategic gameplay" but it is a terrible handicap that you will be forced to die for over and over and over and over.  THERE IS AN INVISIBLE BARRIER THAT YOU CANNOT MOVE PAST.  This is what is really happening, you are being forced to stop by an arbitrary obstacle that is completely made up.  This is WORSE than Alien Swarm the game from 2010.
2)  Your aiming mechanics (with mouse and keyboard) are sluggish and poorly designed.  If I am on foot I can move the mouse around but until I aim, I will not look in the direction I was mousing over.  However, when I am in a mech the aiming is linked to my mouse cursor location.  This is totally inconsistent and stupid.  It obviously should always follow my mouse cursor like in the mech.  Why this was overlooked is idiotic.  This is WORSE than Alien Swarm the game from 2010.
3)  Your cursor is barely visible until you aim (with mouse and keyboard).  Yet, when you aim you slow down.  This makes something as simple as running from a group of enemies and turning around to shoot them sometimes too clumsy to pull off... as you will still be aiming in the direction that you were running when you try and turn around to fire.  This can sometimes take 1 to 2 seconds which will kill you if you are running from cyborg dogs for example.  Because your cursor is barely visible until you aim, you will lose sight of it on a regular basis.  The option that states cursor is always on does NOT make your crosshair on all the time and therefore the option is completely useless.  There is no option to change the color of the crosshair or make it so that it actually IS always on, or even change your crosshair type.  This is WORSE than Alien Swarm the game from 2010.
I do still recommend this game as it is a lot of fun and the multiplayer is great.  Unfortunately, this game could easily have been the greatest of its' genre, but it is reduced to merely above average due to EXTREME flaws (or incredibly poor game design whichever you believe).  For some reason Helldivers insists on making walking around and shooting♥♥♥♥♥♥unneccessarily comlicated and somehow manages to be worse at it than Alien Swarm despite knowing EXACTLY what made that game so awesome.  This game does offer more replayability and options, however in the game mechanics department this game is not as good as the 6-7 year old Alien Swarm in the game and that is both sad and pathetic.

Gonna write a more recent review real quick now that this game's on sale for a little longer.
The game's great. If you liked games like Magicka, then you may like this one even better. Or at least I do. Perfect little twin stick shooter with an infinite amount of gameplay that mixes intensity, action, and satisfying shooting, with goofy little "accidents," like teammates killing each other or accidently dropping strategems on each other.
The entire game is just a bunch of randomly generated missions, all of which contribute to topping the scoreboards, getting new gear, and conquering the galaxy in the name of Super Earth. (Seriously, once everyone takes over enough regions of the galaxy, you get a final cutscene, the credits roll, then things just reset so you can keep playing. Have yet to see too much repetition either.)
The gameplay itself works really well, both in singleplayer and multiplayer. The game by itself is amazing on it's own but if you can get a few friends or people you know into the game with you it'll just get even better. And the amount of stressful situations it puts you in, like surrounding you with waves of enemies as you and your teammates are very low on ammo, giving you close to no time to request an ammo drop gives the game so much intensity. And rushing to the extraction point getting chased by an army of aliens as the most cinematic soundtrack you've ever heard plays is an amazing feeling. If you're alone, you'll be able to revive yourself and have a certain amount of respawns. If you're with friends, you can revive them if they get downed. But if they die, you can call in a reinforcement drop, and they'll come out in a little drop pod with a new set of guns and ammo. (Don't stand under the drop zone though)
Wanted to make this quick, the sale's about to end soon. But to my friends, and anyone else reading this, get this game ASAP. The more people helping take over the galaxy the better. 9/10

Here's a review after finishing the game with both the main characters and trying the third, hidden one.
TL:DR? Challenging 20 levels of platforming with wild west style. Like Megaman, if you're familiar with those.
Gunman Clive is a short but challenging platformer of minimalistic but nevertheless adequate graphics. There are three playable characters, one of which you have to unlock, each with their special skills. There are about 20 levels, every 5th of which is a boss battle. They take you through the wild west and the story hilariously hyperboles towards the end.
Levels are sidescrolling action that last only a minute or so per stage. However, they're also quite challenging, requiring multiple tries to get through. Bosses have anywhere from 2 to 4 different attack types. Challenge rises from the low health of the player who can take only two hits before dying (on Hard difficulty) and also from death falls and insta-kill spikes of certain levels. Obviously, once you get familiar with the game it becomes a lot easier to avoid enemies and go through the previously difficult spots. Warning though if you're easily irritated, you might get momentarily frustrated with some spots.
After a while the game begins to resemble very much the Megaman games of NES. While you have infinite ammo, your rate of fire is limited by your weapon. Many features of the levels from enemies to obstacles also resemble Megaman, from moving platforms to appearing and disappearing blocks to alternating gravity and wind machines. Admittedly, these features are part of virtually any decent platformer, which this one certainly is. There are also a couple of special levels with slightly different moving capabilities akin to Gradius (continuosly moving, sidescrolling shooter) and just about any sidescroller with rideable minecarts.

SPOILER FREE REVIEW: To say I am smitten with this game is a bit of an understatement. I went into it with an open mind but fairly low expectations, and for the first few minutes I was pretty meh about it. Then things like her ringtone, I really enjoyed. I started to notice how good the sound track is, and the environment design, and the writing of the dialogue. That kept me playing a while longer. Then BAM! SO MUCH PLOT. SO MUCH STORY. SO MANY ENDINGS, CHOICES, OPTIONS. The characters, every single one, are all excellent, well thought out and perfectly voice-acted for the most part. I am hooked AF with this interactive visual novel. Looking at this from an artistic perspective, they are a few minor inconsistancies in the art work at times but I will happily overlook that completely for the depth and complexity of the plot, the universe and all the characters. I have played this game for 5.6 hours so far, and I still have four of the main boys paths left to follow, as well as many other endings as it would appear that there are a LOT of different endings. I found myself genuinely caring about these characters, on all sides of the story over and over.
I keep saving in new slots at crucial points in the hopes I don't miss anything but I suspect I have. If you are going to play this game once with one main character for one ending I assure you you are missing out on a LOT. I am so glad there is a second game coming out this month, I am only sad that it was announced as the final installment! In all seriousness with every ending I find I struggle to stop playing! The plot even has my partner reading and listening to dialogue over my shoulder out of interest!
Would recommend this to pretty much anyone. Great game! I will be watching the creators closely for more great content for sure!
BTW - Listen to the bloopers if you unlock them. Hilarious!

And without spoiling too much, I would like to have a quick word with those of you who claim that the ending makes "any analysis of lines of dialogue, narrative, and story telling null and void": You obviously don't understand much about human psychology. Everything you experienced in the course of the story
matter. It is a display of human relationships and emotions, of pain and abuse, of how a child feels under certain circumstances within the boundaries of their family and expresses their feelings and finds a way to vent in order to escape said pain. Ultimately, the tragedy unfolding before your eyes explains
you saw, heard and felt prior during the course of the story. The mystery part is just a nice bonus to it all. If you aren't capable of understanding nor feeling that, then you must be quite an unempathic human being and this game is not meant for you.

I am not the only person that hates this level and fears to play it either. Just check out reviews and the forums for the game on Steam!

Had this game recommended to me as a good music game hybrid, and was pleasantly surprised.  I'm not usually an RPG fan, but this game is enjoyable so far and there's no question that I'll see it through to the end.
As a long-time DDR/stepmania player, I stepped quite easily into hard mode.  The charts themselves are still pretty easy for me, and I can easily get 100% while unlocking spells.  However, during regular gameplay, coordinating switching between panes with hitting notes is a new and interesting challenge.
The biggest downside so far is the lack of content.  The soundtrack, while well-made, is extremely limited, and you'll end up hearing the same handful of songs over and over (so far maybe a half dozen songs in the first 4/7 floors of the tower, compared to dozens/hundreds in your average true rhythm game).  That coupled with the fact that I'm better than halfway through the game in under 4 hours suggests that this game won't have replay value.
Other thoughts:
- The art is somewhat low-res (720p?) and you can't change resolutions.  You can choose full screen or windowed though.  Not something I notice during gameplay, but nowadays I'd expect full HD (or preferably vector) art.
- So far I've only gotten one defensive spell and it's not that powerful.  There's a huge emphasis on attack-heavily-and-occasionally-heal with not much in the way of actually defending.  Some battles you can coast through without using the defense pane much at all, so it's not equally balanced throughout.
- A lot of the items/spells seem ignorable in general, unless you're a compulsive completionist like I am.
- Each floor of the tower has 3 different enemy battles (each with 3 different item drops), plus a boss battle.
- It's interesting that the item drop probabilities are shown, that way you can quantify how bad your luck is when grinding.  Sure, I got the 35% item in 3 of my last 4 battles, but I only got one of the 85% item that I need three of.  Haha.
- The boss battles don't seem to be replayable, but they do unlock new songs when you complete them that will be used in the higher levels of battle.
- Most people complaining about the name change (from "Sequence") have no idea how trademark law works, or why companies are obligated to protect their trademarks.
Overall, this game is well worth that 99c sale price, but it seems like something I'll play through once and then forget about.  I absolutely love the concept, but it needs more content for sure.

Helldivers is a twinstick PvE shooter, which crosses the 'starship trooper' feeling of Alien Swarm with Magickas friendly fire happiness. You can play solo (avoids camera issues) or have fun with friends - or public randoms. The matchmaking (aka: p2p hosting with a 'server' list) works pretty well and fast - just choose a running mission and drop in. Or drop a SOS beacon to increase your spot in the server list, so people find you easier (and join to support your strife for liber-tea!).
The game is cross platform (PS 4) and has a decently big player base (december 2016). You can play it well with both keyboard/mouse (my personal choice as a pc gamer) or with a controller. Here is my thoughts after 18 hours of gameplay (lvl 18, did all three homeworld solo-helldives, didn't have the pleasure to fight the three unique bosses yet though):
Gameplay-wise, you run from objective to objective, while carefully gunning down patrols to avoid alarming bigger mobs. The objectives come in different flavors: "Keep this area secure for x seconds", "Destroy these buildings", "Escort this thing/these guys", etc .. or things like "gun down 300 aliens in this claustrophobic arena".
Things should get easier the more players you get? Eeeh.. not always. When doing a solo run, you can pretty easily do missions (except of the arena type) on the highest difficulty (12, hell dive). Why? Because as a solo player, you can properly spot and shoot patrols, before things go horribly wrong.
The camera is always pointed at the middle of the (living) squad and the line of sight of enemies is comparable to yours - so the more players there are, the harder it gets to avoid alarms. More alarms mean more enemies means more mayhem. That's not necessarily bad: I think the coop mayhem is just more fun than solo runs. On a solo run, the chance of random accidents happening is just low - and you barely want to get into real gunfights.
Do you _have_ to play coop to progess? No. Like I said, you can solo hell dive for lots of research points (= upgrades things) and exp (= rank, unlocks stuff) without much issue, if you know what you're doing. I would actually say that soloing is the optimal way to progress quickly.
BUT: It's not the fun way. You'll never feel like you drive your APC through a warzone, being surrounded by enemies, while the action soundtrack plays. And you will never accidentally crush your allies while respawning, because they didn't pay attention :D
That's why I personally can live with the 'camera issue'. While it makes things harder (very hard to shoot the patrols before they sound alarm), it makes things more fun too. Calling down supplies and reinforcement beacons in the heat of battle is just more fun than a well controlled stealth mission. Why? Because you better make sure you enter the correct code (wasd combination) for the beacons quickly, before you get eaten alive.
One feature that may be a little annoying can be how the meta-campaign works: Once the players together pushed the fronts to the homeplanets of the races, you can no longer unlock new equipment by finishing planets (aka: 2-3 missions in a row). Simply because there is only one planet there.. instead you get twice the experience, which is nice.. but if you really want that one toy, you have to wait for a) the community going to sleep (and hope the AI pushes the fronts back, so normal regions/planets become available again) or b) 'democratize' their worlds with your fellow helldivers within the next 48h event... which takes a lot of effort and missions by everyone (= 'influence' point treshhold based on how long the community needed last time).
The DLC itself contains some very useful items/unlocks - and for 12 eurs (instead of 8 eurs without them; both -60% sale price), and they're definitely worth it.
Overall I think Helldivers does a pretty good job at what it wants to do. 18 hours of fun for 12 euros, with the possibility to have more fun? Fine with me! So spread 'democracy' and 'freedom' one bullet at a time. Because those aliens just don't want to listen (except to the occasional 'truth transmitters').
PS: In case you didn't notice: Yeah, lore wise, the game is cheesecake :D

This game is a cult classic.
You should be warned that this game is broken and will not function on most modern machines.  There is an Unofficial Patch made by Wesp5 that fixes nearly all issues with the game and also adds new content.
Based on the board game, and sequel to Redemption, you play as a fledgling Vampire in California.  The story starts as you create your character.  Here you choose your background, bloodline, and gender.  Backgrounds change your stats slightly and your powers as a vampire will differ depending on your bloodline.  Some bloodlines have some side effects, however.
The best examples are Malkavians and Nosferatu.  Malkavians are insane and schizophrenic.  You'll talk like a crazy person, hear voices in your head and see things other people don't see.  Nosferatu are cursed in a different way as they can't be seen by humans without violating the masquerade.  This does not make it impossible to beat the game as a Nosferatu, because the main quest NPC's will still be approachable.
The masquerade is a system in the game where if you get 5 bad marks it's game over and you'll be executed by your peers.  You earn bad marks by displaying certain powers in public or are seen feeding.  You can redeem yourself if you have bad marks by protecting the masquerade.  This usually involves killing someone who is speaking  too much or who isn't playing it safe like all other good little vampires should.
Graphics are decent and passable.  The game is an older game, so don't expect mind blowing visuals.  City hubs are fairly small but there's a lot to find if you set your mind to it.  There are some nice facial animations that you won't even see in games nowadays which adds to the immersion.  There's also several mods for the game to add atmosphere and even more depth to the classes.
Gameplay is basic.  You shoot things, you smash things.  You talk to people, you kill people.  There are extra dialog options if you level your seduction, intimidation, or persuassion skills.  These skills can be vital to completing some quests perfectly.  You can also recieve bonuses from certain NPC's for having them at the required level at certain points in conversation.
You gain experience from doing quests and you level up to gain strength, wisdom, guile, skill, and become more attractive.  If you're sexy enough you get free hookers! Just like IRL! =P
The beginning of the game will mostly be fetch quests, with a few baddies to either slaughter or let live.  It's a game where you can put the fate of nearly everyone around you in your hands.  Being good is rewarded with extra perks like your very own slave ghoul girl, or an extra item/money/experience.  There's also a decent but easy stealth system that's based on how many points you have in stealth.  If you max out stealth, are in the shadows and crouch you're pretty much invisible.  There are also assassinations you can do with each weapon while stealthed and behind your victim.  My favorite is the baseball bat.  :)
Audio is very good as well.  Just make sure you turn Environmental Effects off or there will be a constant echo.  Voice actors are all top notch and AAA grade ones that you'll know if you've heard them before.
There are some very good mods for this game available as well.  My favorite being the original Unofficial Patch Plus, but there are other that increase the difficulty of the game and add new quests and bloodlines to choose from.  When installing these big mods you need to remember that they aren't compatible with eachother.  E.G. Final Nights mod will not work with Camarilla Edition nor with either work with the Unofficial Patch.  Both mods have an Older version of the Unofficial patch that come with it, which still fixes a lot of bugs.  There's also several mods  that are still being produced constantly by fans.  Every now and then you should check up and see what new mods are out to keep you coming back for more.
All in all, if you are in need of a good RPG that's open world with a lot of freedom and are tired of Fallout 3/NV, Skyrim, etc.  Then you should definately check this game out.  Especially if it's on sale.  Well worth every penny spent.

This is by far one of my favorite games. I seriously play it at least once every year or so. VTMB is not your basic Vampire RPG. The game allows you to switch between first and third person, features both melee and ranged combat, and allows you mutliple paths to any of your goals. This is set in White Wolf's World of Darkness universe. If you are familiar with table-top RPGs and the World of Darkness, good, if not that is okay (I was not).
The World of Darkness is your basic modern urban fantasy universe. You the player take the part of a newly created vampire thrust into a world of intrigue and darkness where ancient vampires pull the strings of humanity and each other in ever-shifting alliances and plans. The game allows you a high degree of customization, when creating your character you can choose from one of 6 clans, which feature different superpowers that your character can build as you level. There are no classes, you build your stats how you want them. Your quests almost all feature multiple paths to completion. Need to kill a vampire hunter? Well you can talk your way into her place of work (if you got the speech skills), sneak around the pack and pick some locked doors (if you have the stealth and lockpicking skills), maybe hack some computers to put the place into lockdown and get civilians to leave the area (if you have the hacking skills), or maybe you just want to kick in the front door and go to work with your katana/shotgun/teeth&claws. In this game there are mutilple paths to your goal. A few different endings (choose one of the factions or yourself), and enless playthrough ability. Visit the community forums for this game and download the fanmade patches, they will give you extra quests, clans and plug some bugs.
Seriously. I can't reccomend this game highly enough.
lots of places where the game feels fairly uninspired and repetitive (mostly the "action" oriented areas), but overall it is remarkably immersive and memorable, despite its age.

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is a game that's been out for a while now, so I won't waste your time with in-depth analysis of the story or gameplay; many others before me have already covered that ground. I'll instead tell you why I believe it's a game that is worthy of your time and money.
Very few games display the caliber of writing and storytelling that TVoEC delivers. It's a story that will stick with you after you've finished the game. I was immediately drawn into Red Creek Valley, and the mysteries and secrets of Ethan's story are as dark and tragic as the scenery is serene and gorgeous.
On the subject of graphics, TVoEC is simply put one of the most visually stunning games I've ever played. The amount of loving attention paid to every little detail is impressive to say the least. During my first playthrough I found myself often just wandering around drinking in the landscape, mesmerized by its sheer beauty. Most impressive to me was the game's ability to create a steadfast sense of underlying unease in such a breathtaking environment.
Lastly, I'll say this:
I initially played through the Redux version, but you can only write a review for the original game (the Redux version doesn't have its own storepage). Also turns out that you have to run a game for x amount of minutes in order to write a review. So I installed the original version with the intention of only running it long enough to be able to write a review. Guess what? I ended up playing all the way through it (and unlocking all achievements) again. It's that good.
Call it an exploration adventure or a walking simulator, I call it a one of a kind experience.
I loved The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, and I totally recommend it without hesitation.

It's even more amazing if you have a 3440 x 1440 monitor.  It's too bad I don't have VR because this is the type of game that I think would get great use out of it.  The game itself is essentially a walking simulator like Dear Esther with the exception that there are some pretty intricate puzzles scattered across the map that help tell the story.  Some of which are pretty well hidden if you don't take the time to explore.  The game itself is pretty short and depending on your pace you could end up beating it in a single sitting.  I was able to unlock all the Steam achievements (although I did use a guide for the grenade/sniper rifle puzzle) in just under 4 hours, and I did a fair share of exploring.  Overall, I would give the game an 8.5/10.

Software Inc. is already a thorough simulation of what it's like to develop software both at the scale of two kids developing indie games in their garage and the scale of hundreds of employees in a multi-floor office tower. The process of developing an individual software package is detailed, the process of developing multiple software packages that are inter-dependend is intense. You can build a game using existing 2d, 3d editing software and an existing engine, or you can develop your own engine and your own editing software in house. You can even release your own OS and then build a whole suite of software around it like an office suite (From a simple wordprocessor to a whole package of office software with spreadsheets, presentation software, clipart, etc.) and anti-virus software. You can even just play datacenter/host for the online storage needs of other companies.
There's a lot to do, and that's not evening mentioning the possibility of trading stocks, IP buying/trading and other parts of the economic simulation.
There's just as much detail to building your own office, which allows more freedom to build walls and place objects than the Sims by allowing you to resize the grid, rotate the grid and re-colour every single object.
But it's not entirely finished. The interface is not ideal, the tutorials are unhelpful and there's not yet enough options to customize software and differentiate yourself from your competition. However, I wholeheartedly recommend Software Inc. to any fan of simulation games, from the old Theme Hospital and RCT, to Dwarf Fortress and Prison Architect.

Star Wars: Battlefront II is the epitome of great games. From Galactic Conquest to Multiplayer, this Star Wars game hits every segment well. The Campaign has a selection of great maps from the Clone Wars Era and the Galactic Civil War Era, with two difficulties to select from. AI can be set according to difficulties set by: A. Campaign Settings, Instant Action Settings, Galactic Conquest, and Multiplayer. Classes for each faction are set in a balanced and competitive way, with each of the four different factions having two unique classes for each faction. Each map allows for unique faction heros to be played by the character, depending on the current game session's settings. Vehicles are a great asset to the game and provide another unique perspective into the universe of Star Wars gaming. From AT-AT's to speeder bikes, the game offers plenty of rides for the player. Space Battles are another masterful piece of the game. The space battles are arranged in different formats for each of the Eras represented in the game. Capital ships act as the home base of the factions, while frigates support the faction's starfighters with anti-air cannons. Objective points are secured by taking down critical parts of the Captial ship's systems from the outside or from within, as the player determines the course of action for victory. Frigates can also be completely eliminated to secure more points for the player's faction.
I would recommend this game at a solid 10/10. Great gameplay experience!

Once you've played one or two tower defenses, you've played them all, right? YES. Well, almost completely yes.
I hate this genre with a passion. I enjoyed those first one or two tower defenses I've played, and I'm consistently disappointed with every successive iteration that there is basically no variation whatsoever, especially given how crowded the genre has been. I think it's to do with tower defenses being easy to make, in terms of design, programming, and graphics, so that a lamentably successful game can be made on a dime.
However, I do have to give this one game a recommendation. As much as I dislike the genre, this one definitely feels fresher. It blends significant RPG elements into the usual formula. Firstly, it has an engaging story, with plenty of humour and quirky characters. The levels support the story, including the occasional boss fight. Your "towers" are in fact your party members, belonging to six classes, who gain experience from encounters and level up to gain additional skills, or hone their own skills further. This allows for plenty of variation amongst your party, although I found myself sticking to a single formula for each of my types.
The gameplay itself is not typical of tower defense. There's no placing your people so that they block enemies; they must be placed on the sidelines of a preset path. Also, there isn't an emphasis on placing more and more towers to increase the length of the gauntlet. Although you can place all 36 members of your party in a level, doing so is generally not recommended, because it is far more efficient to simply upgrade the party members you have. The end result is a far more sparse tower defense game, one that greatly favours tactical placement, and consequently, can be fun for the most jaded tower defense anti-fan.
I also appreciated the difficulty system, whereby you can choose from three difficulty settings when playing each level (and a fourth that doesn't exactly count, for casual gamers). You can also come back and play the level on a higher difficulty setting, with different enemy types and levels, to get greater rewards (like unique items). It really added to the longevity of the game. Add in some challenges to complete, and you well and truly get your $15 worth.
So, for the first time, I have played a tower defense that has left me wanting more! I'm keeping an eye out on Defender's Quest 2, which is currently in development. If you too are as jaded as I am, don't instantly discount this one. Give the demo a try.

As a puzzle game, I think its better than the likes of Puzzle Quest, because you're essentially managing a party of heroes, and placing them in dungeon sets and hoping that your customisations and placements pay off. It doesn't hinge on playing a very abstract match 3 game. Its a hybrid of an adventuring party management game, and a battle based puzzler.
The fact that it sort of follows Tower Defense rules, in that you have waves of enemies, and they follow known paths, is all by the by. Goblin hordes usually follow dungeon tunnels anyway as they charge the brave adventurers!  I've played my fair share of Tower Defense games and hundreds of them bore me to tears, but this one seems to get the balance between RPG party management and planning, and the try it and then refine it mechanic. It's not overly complex, each class (and there are about six in total, I think) have skill trees that are only two branches. You need to earn money (loot and scrap) to purchase more adventurers to sign up. Then you have to train them up from level 1, and customise their skillsets to complement the team you already have.
There are beserkers who lend the chopping/slashing muscle - for corner killzones - and your archers can thin out the horde on the way, as well as try and catch the speedy monsters early. You also have (so far) Ice mages, for slowing effects and mages for healing or area of effect spells. You can specialise zerkers as damage soakers or fast dps dealers. You can specialise archers as heavy critical hitter, or speedy bleeders. Plus you've got the inventory to manage with different armours and weapons etc.
Some of the harder levels later on in the story, require a little bit of farming to get enough money and people to do them. It just hit a sweet spot for me, in terms of low maintenance RPG adventuring, with just enough tweaking, twiddling and puzzling to keep me going back to it over and over again. Repeating the same levels with harder foes doesn't seem to get old, you have to adjust your tactics for a longer harder game. All the while you're crafting up a team whose skills work intimately with each other, making the sum of the parts greater than the individual.

Originally titled
,
is the first game released by the indie devs Iridium Studios. It was later followed by
, a real time tactics voice controlled game released on Steam in early 2015. According to Before the Echo’s Steam Forums, they had a copyright claim thrown against them by another developer over their name. So, Iridium Studios had to rename Sequence to something else in order to avoid legal trouble. A rather unfortunate turn of events. However, I will say that Before the Echo might have been a better choice anyway, as Sequence isn’t particularly memorable for a name. I myself only discovered Before the Echo when There Came An Echo was released and got a lot of press attention for its unique voice control mechanics. BtE has some interesting ideas of its own though and I don’t think it should be ignored.
A rhythm-based-combat RPG with a story driven narrative has a decent amount of content, especially if you decide to go for as many recipes as possible. The rhythm mechanics are a refreshing change of pace from the normal choose-spells, counter as best you can and win over and over again. It forces you to pay attention to what you’re doing and continually improve as the game goes along. This is even after my initial skepticism that this game had few legs to stand on. After all, we’ve had plenty of rhythm games before. What could possibly make BtE stand out? Well, a good story with an amusing banter between the two protagonists and a decently diverse set of characters to fight out against with their own particular personality doesn’t hurt. Neither does a refined rhythm system that requires you to pay attention and react quickly to three different fields of falling arrows.
The player is following the story of Ky, a hacker who finds himself waking up in a mysterious tower called, well, the Tower. This seven leveled tower isn’t something to scoff as he’ll soon learn that he can die in this tower. Upon awaking and talking to himself about what’s going on, he’s greeted by Naia, a “shepherd” that has few answers for Kai but seems to be on his side or at the very least trapped by her own circumstances. She’ll help him out by guiding him through the tutorial and each level. Ky must do this, defeating monsters to grow in strength to eventually defeat the seven guardians that stop forward progress. The plot has lies and half truths a plenty. Not everyone is telling the truth and there’s something sinister going on in the background. It seems to be set in the modern era though no country or actual year is dropped. The characters do seem to imply this is all happening in the 2010s.
In Before the Echo’s battles, you defeat monsters and bosses by following the beat of the music and destroying the enemy’s health before they do yours in. This is accomplished in a dance-dance-revolution type battle where you’re trying to cast spells, block their attacks and regenerate your mana when possible. To do this, you’ll need to press the right direction on the d-pad and letter keys of your controller when arrows are at the right time. You’ll often need to use both set of controls in order to handle all the arrows falling. Keyboard and mouse can also be used but I find the controller to be a little bit more enjoyable and easier to use for this game. To further complicate things, you’ll need to select and cast spells using the controller’s joystick while keeping an eye on arrows. This can be a little tricky to figure out at first but I eventually got used to it.
Settings are a little bizarre here. Fullscreen on/off is the only traditional video setting to be found. Particle effects can be turned off, there’s a lag calibration for your controller, gem and text speed can be changed and a lot of other different functions important to the rhythm mechanics. Resolution options, AA, V-sync and other settings are missing as well. The one game I actually desire individual sound volume options doesn’t have them at all. I found the SFX was just a bit too loud over the music and people speaking but not unbearably high. For such an audio-intensive game, being able to adjust the different volumes seems like an obvious thing to include in your game. Voice acting can be turned off but I don’t know why you’d want to do that. It’s pretty good voice acting. I was surprised to hear the voice actor for Dust from Dust: An Elysian Tail in this title too. He plays one of the guardians.
Before the Echo is a good and different experience that’s both decently approachable but difficult to master. The combination of RPG and Rhythm mechanics just works here, the mechanics blending well together and never allowing things to get dull for long. Though there are fights that can be overly frustrating. It’s also not too hard to lose concentration and find yourself in an unwinnable situation. So, you’ll need to stay on your toes or take a break if it’s happening too often. The story itself is pretty good, I found myself chuckling at the banter between the two protagonists from time to time. It does lean a bit too much on tropes but I think it does them well enough that I’m not bothered by it. It’s a good time “dancing” to the beats while playing a more traditional RPG game. I definitely liked this mix of genres and I recommend checking out when you have the chance.

I enjoyed this game.
I know there are those who decry these "walking simulators", aka exploration Adventure games, but I am not one of them. I can enjoy a game that when done right allows a person to explore a world and soak in the atmosphere while trying to figure out what the world is about and what mysteries it holds. I appreciate a game with visually pleasing artwork for me to walk through and take in, especially with some lovely vistas and other sights .Most importantly, I don't mind hunting down for clues and putting things in their places or reading/listening to be told what has occurred.
So for me, The Vanishing of Ethan Carter was a good game. A tale of mystery and death, strange happenings, and a certain somberness all in the setting of a child like view of small wooded town of the past.
It is by no means a great game for me on the mystery front, where I rarely had trouble figuring out how the murders happened or how to solve a puzzle beyond the rare prompt not showing up the first time through, but for a once-through I enjoy the story as it went through much in the same way I would an old Amazing Fantasy, Outer Limits, or Twilight Zone, Ultra Q, and their kin because I was interested in what would happen next. Though I will say one thing took me by surprise that I had passed off previously when seeing the clues as an oh so standard static game image
It's story was well done and that's always the main crux of an Adventure game of this ilk, and though I expected the ending, it held it's charm and let me walk away happy with my experience. Even the final achievement ties in well to the final bit, though it left me wanting more...
Now perhaps because I was playing the original version, rather than redux but I did have some problems with the audio. I can pass off some complaints with it's "out there" or "things are just not quite right" atmosphere it's going for, but I did not care for sound just dropping out as though I entered a tunnel just by walking into a building nor the same sound for a trap ready to be sprung occurring in areas where no traps were present, and thus confusing me. Minor issues all together, but I thought it was worth mentioning as otherwise it's quite nice with headphones on.
I'd recommend it to others who like exploration Adventure games, as long as you don't expect it to be a great mystery game or demand much in the way of puzzle solving with some potential "where do I go now?" if you miss a clue. Just play Redux.

Alright! I've been playing non-stop for the past week and I think I've done everything there is to do and more. Overall, great game! It adds a ton to the genre while maintaining the usual core features. Here are some but not all of my thoughts... I might add to this post later.
----What I LIKED the most...----
--Building offices. This was extremely fun... Getting the rooms right and positioning everything to minimize worker downtime while maintaining aesthetics was an amazing experience. Most of the productivity is lost through workers having to walk across a carpark or to go to a meeting room or get food. I think I came up with something quite scalable and optimal. I think logistics is a massive selling point of the game and building on this would be a great decision.
--The market and company system. This was so much better than what's in Game Dev Tycoon. Managing competition and watching the market is really fun and engaging. My strategy is always rush to dominate one or two markets and shut down competitors, just like in real life I guess. Perhaps a little more depth though. I think the stock system has huge potential but is very lacking atm.
--The early to mid game. By far the most fun part of the game is building up the company from nothing and trying to keep it afloat while the company rocks on the edge of chaos. There's an easy strategy where you have your founder develop an OS over 3 years and it will bring in 4+ million per month but even then the mid-game is still quite challenging. The late game needs to be overhauled.
----What can be SIGNIFICANTLY improved----
--Managing teams and employees. It is VERY clunky and sometimes even bugs out.
There should be a way to set HR management and time schedules on multiple teams at the same time. You need 3 of each team to cover three 8-hour shifts to maximise productivity. Multiply that with several teams and adding additional teams and it gets really tedious.
I don't know what's up with HR education but it's either EXTREMELY slow or it just doesn't work. I just had a game where three identical teams with the same setting except for arrival/departure time. Two teams were sent to class and one team never gets sent. And it appears they always were sent on 1-month courses. It's better to just manually mass train employees on 3-month courses (Good thing that you can send multiple at the same time).
It should be allowed to reserve or prioritize parking spaces for specific teams or employees and staff. Currently, it seems to just flood the carpark from right to left, which is highly inefficient.
Also the functionality to set multiple roles on employees (Yes I heard it's coming in A10... Just wanted to mention it here).
--Products and technologies. Right now all the different products are basically the same in terms of gameplay. X amount of code. Y amount of art. And a combination of required specializations. Similar for tech and research. Each just adds a little more to a specific product but nothing really unique. Art/code/design are also very similar. Same workspaces (Yes, I know about the add-ons you can place next to computers), and extremely similar development mechanics. The overall effect is extremely repetitive, grindy, and bland gameplay.
This can be spiced up in many ways. Different types of workstations and environments for different specializations and sub-specialisations. Office furnishings that boost specific jobs but are detrimental to others. Technologies that add unique requirements and pros/cons to a product. Some of the technology combos don't make sense. A MMO game with local multiplayer? A touch OS with no GUI? These should all have a huge negative impact on sales but right now it seems like you just want to research everything tick all the boxes.
--The interface. It does very little to lessen the apparent complexity of the game. Every window is information overload. I'm 100% used to it now though and see the value of all the information but when I first started out it was VERY dizzying. Many windows can be simplified in ways such as grouping columns that are highly related together and apart from others, being able to collapse columns and sub-windows and setting some less-important information panels/columns to be collapsed on default to lessen the initial impact. There also no icons that allow for quick recognition anywhere apart from the buttons in the main UI. Everything is labeled with text including action buttons. Pop-up tooltips at the cursor when first opening a window would also be really good.
The WORST thing is the list of current tasks at the right. At first, it's great but as my company grew to a very large size it was quite hellish to manage that list. Even just reversing the order and putting new items at the top of the list would help massively.
--Building rooms and mass placing objects is very clunky. A MASSIVE improvement here would be the ability to place snap and guidelines on the grid.
A marquee tool to select objects would also be extremely helpful and time-saving. A lot of the time I want to select some of objects X, Y, and Z in a room but not all of them. Like just the printers or workstations in the corner or whatever. I have to individually select what I want at that point.
----What I absolutely HATED and I think should be just scrapped----
--Project Management. Either I'm not using it right or this absolutely SUCKS. It takes years to finish a project and the end completed product sucks. Not to mention that it starts marketing way too early.
BUT EVEN if project management was as good as manually managing projects I wouldn't like this feature. This feature aims to completely trivialize a huge portion of the game. Managing projects is quite an engaging part of the game. Sometimes I need to take an art team off a project to prevent it from going overboard. Sometimes I need to re-prioritize teams to prevent a disaster with support. Managing multiple projects at the same time and getting it all on schedule feels amazing but that might just be me.
--Contract Work. Also might just be me but this is probably my most hated part of in this game genre. It feels like a chore to do at the start of the game. It's not engaging or in-depth or challenging in any way. No thought and minimal strategy involved. It's a bore. Completely revamp contracts so they 1. scale into the late game and 2. are fun and in-depth. This is an area where the genre needs big innovation.
----Other Suggestions----
--Modding. It seems right now mods are limited to just adding predefined product and tech archetypes. I'd really like a much more extensive mod system, if that's possible. I wanted to create a mod that adds and improves to HR management but it didn't seem like that was possible.
--Reviewer employees. How about permanent employees that constantly review the development of games? An estimated score will be shown at the development panel of the right and constantly updated as the reviewers work. Highly skilled reviewers know how to be unbiased.
--Resource import system. Products with extensive features need additional resources to develop like arts and craft supplies. I think this would work really well with the hardware mods. Those mods right now don't really make sense with all hardware being developed on a computer and then printed or even digitally distributed.
Overall
Gameplay: 8.5/10. Good stuff! Quite innovative, much more-so than the other games of the genre! Needs a lot of polish but the core game loop feels amazing.
Graphics: 8/10. I suspect the dev went with a typical looking low-poly unity style because it's a one-man team. Though for one person it's impressive. Though granted, I'm already lagging when 300+ employees change shifts.
Sound: 9.5/10. The music and effects are on-point! I like how when I zoom in on workers I can hear their chatter.

This is one of those odd games that is both loved by gamers yet, somehow, seems to slip under the radar in a lot of discussions by the gaming press. Perhaps that's due to this developer's early games having some significant technical issues or maybe because the game is a few years old at this point. Either way, one of my favorite games of all time. I've played the crap out of it in singleplayer on both ps4 and pc(you can double the hours played stat) and have also had tons of fun in co-op on ps4 as well. It shines in both. Main complaint is dealing with human enemies; they're dumb as rocks and can be total damage sponges...in some cases more than the zombies. If you could take the human AI/damage model of a game like Far Cry and paste it in, the game combat would be damn near perfect. As it is, human enemies are sloppy-yet-still-fun irritants but definitely play second fiddle to the zombies, which is fine, considering the focus of the game.
The parkour elements are exceedingly well done and even the ability upgrades like the grappling hook and dune buggy, which would seem to be a recipe for disaster(by upsetting play balance), are really well implemented. Special credit as well for the lovely, detailed game world. Sure there's a trade off in terms of lack of physics for game objects, but the art direction in this game is consistently fantastic. Definitely a game to own on the PC for the framerate alone but PS4 still holds up. On the PC side, I absolutely recommend the minimal HUD mod to clear the UI cruft so you can further enjoy this fantastically realized world. Enjoy!
