this is probably one of the most underrated games of the past decade. even though (at the time of writing this review) it has overwhelmingly positive reviews and critics seemed to rate it well on release back in 2015, i still don't see that much talk about it and didn't when it came out.
the best way to describe this game, as other people have described it, is it's essentially dead island with mirrors edge style movement. you can see immediately that this is made by people who designed dead island, it even runs on the same game engine, and yet it is superior to that game in every concievable way.
This is the game every zombie lover needs to own. You're flung into this world which you can almost immediately explore and can go about the game however you like. Exploration is great, looting is deep (you can enter most buildings and loot cupboards, bins, etc .. even loot vehicles for gas, engine parts and stuff in their trunks!), there's a 3-tier levelling system that expands to 4 with The Following, where you'l learn a variety of new moves such as drop-kicks, slides, tackles etc. There's weapon crafting with hundreds of different possible combinations of bats, swords, knives, axes, hammers. There's pistols, shotguns, rifles and a sweet crossbow with The Following content so you can feel like Daryll from the Walking Dead. Headshot a zombie and recover your bolt. Badass.
The game is best played with a friend in coop mode but i finished most of it solo and enjoyed every moment. Once you get to The Following content you eventually gain access to a buggy which you can also upgrade provided you have the materials found in the world such as screws and metal components (which you can loot from the abundence of broken down vehicles in the world).
Aside from the occasional glitch where you might not grab onto that ledge you were aiming for and you fall to your death the game is basically flawless. The story is solid but not groundbreaking, the graphics are still top notch even in 2017 provided you have a decent system, and you could easily sink 50+ hours into this before you complete it once over if you have The Following add-on as well. Buy it, bring a friend, and enjoy hours and hours of post-apocalyptic exploring and zombie slaying.

Dying light is the game Techland wanted to make after splitting off from Dead Island. But is it worth the price?
TL;DR -

Dying Light has aged well. Like most wine. For such a rough start, the game runs well on most DESKTOP computers, looks beautiful, and contains a fair amount of content for the price of a new game.
The base game’s story is mediocre at best. The characters are dull and insanely idiotic. Most of them end up dead. The boss battle is drawn out so much, to end up with QUICK-TIME events. It’s so painful when you die, and the game punishes you for it way too much. There’s no quick travel, so you have to walk everywhere, which seems really fun at first, but transversing the whole map gets really dull really fast.
But for everything that is bad in the game, there’s something to redeem it. There’s a grappling hook late game which helps insanely with moving across the map. This makes moving a bit less tedious. Crane’s comments to everything makes the player seem like you’re not insane for thinking that everything going on is insane.
Honestly, I found more humor in the main story by just laughing at how dull the story was. The side quests made the game a lot better, and thank god for objective markers.
The gameplay is the best part of this game. The amount of fun you can have and the stupid animations for some of the attacks are the best. But you need a friend to make the game this enjoyable.
With a friend, you can have someone revive you when you’re down, you can watch the best animations, and the banter you can have as you’re smashing zombie’s faces in is amusing. Especially looking at some of the outfits you can wear in the game. You can also get experience for helping your friend up, which makes the game slightly more easier, beside the fact that there’s two of you to deal damage.
But everything comes to a close, and you and your partners have to do the ending by yourselves. Which, isn’t that bad, but would’ve been more fun to run and scream with your friends.
While there’s a lot of cosmetic DLC, the following is a complete expansion to the base game. You can use your original character for it, and this is an upgrade to the base game in many ways.
Instead of that cliche bs the game gave you in Dying Light, The Following’s story is genuinely interesting in my opinion. If you want spoilers, you can search it up. But it’s such a step up from the base game, that I find it best to experience it for yourself.
But wait… there’s more! Instead of just grappling hooks, you get a jeep. It certainly makes movement faster, and almost every area on the map can be reached with it. While it favors road (even though it looks like something you’d see only on offroading), the jeep certainly is a godsend. It mows through zombies like nothing, and it’s SO enjoyable to hit things with. Maybe not the easiest to drive.
Best thing to come to co-op. I recommend delivering letters in the side quest. That’s a good quest. Also, two people can ride in the same jeep, and you can shoot from inside of it if you’re in the passenger seat. It’s scary at night, and well… You’ll find out.
The car has got a lot of customization, and it’s got it’s own skill tree to give you really cool additions to your car, like a ramming bar and shock cage.
But wait. If you have your friend just drive you around everywhere, you won’t level up. Which means if you’re alone, your car will be♥♥♥♥♥♥
Does that sound familiar? Oh yeah. That was a flaw from the base game. With all the improvements, you would’ve thought that they would’ve thought this one out. So since I had my friend drive me around everywhere, the end is nearly impossible to do without any upgrades. You just can’t move fast enough.
And that’s it. For now.
There’s still content drops, and the new expansion, but I wish to see another big expansion sometime. I’m not sure how it would fit, but I want to see what new they can bring to the game.
Final Score: 85/100 - Okay, but you need DLC, friends, and not a laptop.

This is a pretty decent Otome game for being free. I picked this up because I was bored, and haven't really regreted it. Definitely worth your time if you're in the mood for some hot otome romance.
It's pretty unquie in how many different romance paths it offers you, including serveal none romantic endings and lesbian ones. I also find it interesting how endings that aren't either the "Super bad endings" or the "True endings" are simi pushed to the side like they don't really matter while other otome games I've seen usually have each and every ending as part of their achievements. In a way, I really like this, because at the end of the day the only endings worth getting are the true endings. I rarely achievement hunt, but I found myself doing it anyway. The voice acting is also very good. The voices fit the characters well and capture the moments. The art is also pretty nice, even if it's not my favorite style.
That being said, this game is not without flaws. It's pretty blantely obvious what the right and wrong answers are once you get into a romantic route. In fact, the only real one that's potentially difficult to decide who it goes to is the dinner scene on the first night. All of the other answers are obvious. However, that's not really an issue for me.
My REAL issue is that the five the main guys' romance routes are pretty much exactly the same aside from minor story details. The only one that gets any form of unique route out of the five of them is Damien (he's a wonderful character though). Aside from that, basically each option is copy pasted the same. Kiss them there, keep going, set her straight. What makes matters worst is that not only is this the situation but a lot of the scenes are the exact same text with just changed names. Which, to be honest was rather boring to read when trying to find the other endings. Granted, there are plenty of other endings in the game with other characters that are unique and techincally each ending is simi-different, but it was still annoying to have the same make out scene with all five guys.  As a writer, I understand this would have been extra work and everything, but still, it ruins replay vaule and breaks the uniqueness of each of the guy characters. I would have understood rehashing maybe "Wrong choice" lines but all of the other lines are REALLY important!
So yeah, this game is worth the first playthrough with the main guys, and then I'd also say it's worth going after Andrew, Diana, and one of the girls. (the chaos ending was also really entertaining), but past that it's kind of just same thing. That being said, I'm kind of into this whole world and will probably buy the sequel. I hope that they don't do this in the paid version...

Over the last five years indie games have gained a steady and impressive following among both PC and console gamers, giving rise to a rebirth of many classic game types and the birth of many creative new game styles as well. One of the game types that has benefitted the most from the rise the indie market is the Tower Defense genre, and there are few games that exemplify the quality an indie title can reach like Defender's Quest: Valley of the Forgotten.
At first glance Defender's Quest does little to inspire confidence in the overall product. With a rudimentary title screen and an almost complete lack of graphics options the game will seem lean on content to start with. Even the cinematics in the game are somewhat jarring and a let down, consisting of still images that, in all honesty, would feel more at home in a flash game than a title developed for sale.
Delving deeper into the game, however, will quickly show you the quality that lies beneath this initially lackluster veneer. The in-game graphics are a wonderful modern take on the 16-bit era, colorful and with enough animation to keep battles fairly lively and interesting. While the graphics options are sparse at best, the game wows with how much customization it allows in its gameplay experience, allowing players the option to tune experience gains, character downtime penalties, and even monetary gains to suit most players from the most hard-core strategy gamers to those who are looking for a more relaxed experience. Despite the less than stellar presentation for cutscenes the characters themselves are all colorful and fun, and the art design itself only fails due to a lack of consistency between cinematics and gameplay. Characters offer a rudimentary RPG-style skill and level up tree, and combining that with the ability to level up characters mid-level to gain access to more advanced combat techniques gives the entire game a great deal of depth. The equipment system is underwhelming, with new swords and armor offering nothing in terms of rewards beyond an incremental stat boost, but the entire design shows a great deal of promise, if not polish.
Gameplay is often quick, but can be paused to allow the player time to consider strategy as often as one needs to. Overall the difficulty curve on the game is well managed: with rewards turned up the game is a relaxing affair that still manages to hold your attention, while turning them down increases the difficulty and need for strategy without ever becoming unfair. Controls with either the keyboard or mouse are generally responsive and convenient, and there is next to nothing in the experience that will frustrate most players unduly. Level design is well handled as well, with the levels scaling nicely to present new placement and enemy challenges as the player progresses through the game.
With an intriguing storyline, good characters, and incredibly scalable gameplay that allows it to appeal to audiences of varied skill or dedication, Defender's Quest succeeds in presenting its players with a high-quality product worth investing your time in. While visual presentation suffers due to a mish-mash of different styles, it is only a minor flaw in the face of an otherwise well-made and solid game.
Final Rating: 8 out of 10.
Despite its visual shortcomings many game designers could learn a thing or two from Level Up Labs about accessible gameplay. By appealing to users seeking a hardcore strategy experience as well as those looking for a more casual game the creators have come up with a stand-out strategy title for both markets.

You might be forgiven for overlooking Defender's Quest. Exceedingly generic title attached to yet another tower defense game... of course, you'd be missing out on a whole lot if you let that get in the way of you playing this game.
Let me get this out of the way first: I don't like tower defense games. They usually bore me or frustrate me, and in worst case scenarios they do both at the same time. Defender's Quest deftly combines core tower defense play with RPG elements, a story that'll actually hold your attention, and beautiful artwork in and out of combat.
Say what you will about simple spritework: it looks fantastic here. Units are distinctive, animate well. I absolutely love the artwork out of combat, and the writing is fun as hell. I came to really love the cast, and was sad when it was all over- well, not for long. Game features a New Game+ option that not only ups the difficulty a ton, it gives you access to plenty of sidequests and some very powerful items if you play your cards right.
I've seen some complaints about this game lacking in depth of strategy- I don't find this to be the case, especially in maximum difficulty New Game+ battles. But one of the many wonderful things about this game is that its accessibility options allow you to tune the difficulty to your liking. Are you terrible at tower defense but want to see the storyline play out? They got you covered. Still having trouble? You can grind experience on earlier missions, too. Do you want this game to give you a merciless red♥♥♥♥♥beatdown and make you hate your life? Also an option! A+ to the devs for making sure the widest audience possible could enjoy their story until the very end.
Defender's Quest: Valley of the Forgotten is a wonderful little gem of a game that should not be ignored. Highly recommend you give it a shot- I have a pretty good feeling that almost everyone is going to find something to like here.

Oddly one of my favorite games that I continue to go back to.  There is no mindblowing gameplay or jawdropping graphics.  What it does it does small scale, but it delights in in each area.
Story:  A very solemn themed game about war, sacrifices, dark gods, etc.  Fortunately the main cast have great (sometimes insane)  personalities and have wonderful, surprising, and often hysterical interactions.  This is where the writing really shines and is honestly probably the strongest part of the game.
Gameplay:  It's pretty standard tower defense.  Each class has skills, attack range, hit points, etc.  Set them up in likely positions and away you go.  Fail?  Try a different set up.  Characters also level up with experience for new skills, high attack, so forth.  Getting too easy? There's a Newgame+ with harder enemies and achievements that will test you.
Graphics:  During gameplay it is high quality pixel art style, detailed and well done.  Cut scenes before and after battles are...I'm not sure what to call it.  Cell shaded stop motion?  It's nice and it does the trick without being flashy.
Like I said, I just keep coming back for more, figured I might as well review it.  If you like tower defense games with interesting stories and well written characters, get this.

There are two big complaints I have for the title though. The biggest is that you have to run it at a fixed resolution in windowed mode. The window is so small it could very well fit on an 8" tablet. This means playing for an extended period will likely hurt your eyes. I really wish I could make the game bigger without having to use fullscreen. The second complaint is the sound. It gets very bad when you have a healer and ice hero on the field. Especially a 4x speed. I would recommend turning the sound off and either listening to the in game music or playing your own. There is not voice acting so you wont be missing anything.

I was really excited to play this game, investigating a paranormal mystery in a beautiful environment, it sounded so promising.
My initial reaction was, “wow this looks great.” That was until I started moving then my reaction changed to, “oh god what is wrong with my eyes?” The motion blur on this game is horrific, it quite accurately recreates the way you eyes feel when you are so tired that you can no longer focus properly. This quite quickly gave me a headache but fortunately you can turn off motion blur and then you can actually enjoy the gorgeous scenery.
Now getting to the actual game, it is like someone played Dear Ester and thought we should make a game like that but add some more user interaction like some puzzles or something. This in itself is an excellent idea and could have resulted in a great game but this is not it. Where Dear Ester subtly guides you along a fairly linear path and advances the story, this game just give you an expansive environment and makes you go and find tiny objects hidden about the place. You spend ages scouring the forest getting more frustrated, that is if you don't miss the puzzle entirely. This scenario needs a team of scene of crime officers to systematically search the area not a nut job paranormal investigator erratically running about the forest tampering with crime scenes. As you do manage to complete the puzzles it progresses the uninspiring story. Then just when I lost all interest in the story it surprisingly managed to culminate with a nice conclusion.
So yes this is beautiful and the ending is quite good but in my opinion rest of the game make it not worth bothering with.

This game is incredibly story-rich, the developers put alot of time into really working up something amazing.
As usual, i don't want to spoil things so i will just say that the story is complex, is twisted, and makes you ask yourself dozens of questions.
I will start by pointing out few small things, first, don't get me wrong, but i felt the game was slightly boring. I loved the atmosphere, i loved the story, i loved the looks, i loved everything, but i felt like something was missing.
I wasn't also pleased about the fact that you don't have a journal of activities you've did, or anything to point out certain things you need to do, you just walk, and search for clues for various cases.
But, please, don't get this the wrong way. Some things cannot please everybody on every 'plane', and despite the fact that i got slightly slightly bored, i loved the game, and i do really recommend it to you.
I only played the Redux version that uses Unreal Engine 4, and what can i say... Graphics were astonishing, and the game/engine were also optimized quite decently.
You have to find cases, and then find clues for them, you investigate murders, but you have to find them first, you might love this, or may not. I personally would've preferred to have something to keep track of events and such.
The thing that i loved most about the gameplay is that you basically can solve the cases in absolutely any order you want, you are not limited in any way.
Searching for clues something can be a bit annoying because you have to 'expand' your search area, without you even knowing, but... that's puzzle for you!
As someone who isn't a fan of puzzle games, i am not ashamed to admit i used walkthrough guides on numerous occasions, this is what i actually wanted this game to be for me, more of a walking simulator, but the puzzles, many of them i still tried to solve myself without looking at the actual content of the guide. I mostly just wanted to know the locations of 'action'.
If you want a challenge, you can do it without the guide, as i said, this game doesn't prevent you from solving cases in any order you might like.
If you just want a walking simulator, to become just an explorer in an amazingly beautiful place, you can look inside a guide, no reason to feel bad about it.
The atmosphere, a
, is as beautiful just as it is scary.
It felt amazing, that whole place felt very real to me, and i wished so much that i could somehow be there, instead of being behind a monitor, moving with few washed-off keys instead of my legs.
The simple music fits the game perfectly, it's relaxing, it's soft as it should be, i loved it, not much i can say about it.
Atmosphere overall is beautiful. Extremely Beautiful.
I feel i need to say this out loud, so here it goes.
These are the devs people should support in my opinion, they created this beautiful piece of art that will be forever remembered by putting their hearts into the game.
Every aspect of it, you just feel that passion they had, you can feel their struggle and teamwork at every grain of sand you step on, and at every leaf that falls.
A very talented team, that i sincerely hope will get as far as possible into the gaming world.

100/100 - Story (Unique, that touches people in so many different ways, and it's also very complex)

I'm conflcted in reviewing this game, because I both enjoy it and resent some of its features.
First, the good points:
+ Nice music
+ Fun gameplay, has a nice flow to it
+ Love the variety of spells and possibilities for spell combos
+ The narrative is neat and has entertaining humor and characters
+ Pretty artwork, and solid-looking characters
Now the not-so-good:
- Not much song variety. New levels and challenges for unlocking spells tend to recycle songs from previous levels.
- Item crafting is done by sacrificing some exp. This in itself isnt horrible, but when paired with the tiny song selection, repeating the same fights over and over again to craft your armor and weapons and keys to unlock the next level all while trying to maintain a level that allows you to continue playing comfortably becomes tedious.
- In short, grinding becomes pretty much mandatory.
- Not much selection in craftable weapons and armor. Each level supplies you with crafting recipes for one armor and weapon item at its beginning. Additional items can sometimes be dropped by enemies, but I have rarely found these helpful. When I saw the crafting screens in the trailer, I was hoping there would be more variety in items for the player; a build with a ton of attack and no defense, or a ton of mana but not much health would be interesting challenges to make repeating songs less tedious.
Additionally, controllers are supported by the game, but only 360 controllers as of right now. I used the program ds4windows to make my ps4 controller compatible with it (running on Win8.1), and I have seen others find supporting programs for different controllers. Using a controller makes for comfortable gameplay.
Overall, I'm not sure I whether I would recommend this game. The core concept is interesting and the spells are fun. Playing the faster-paced songs is a blast. the first thing I want to say is that this game is not perfect, the review scores and constant praise as being 'the best zombie game ever' may make lead you to believe this but this game is HIGHLY floored.

the story is standard, and the writing is utter, utter drek, like, really, really bad. Every character is poorly introduced, and the game expects you to care for them far too quickly and
. Every cutscene feels like a burden but they are all skippable and in the end, it commits one of the greatest gaming scenes (very minor spoiler)
the game is not free from mechanical sins either, plenty of bashing 'f' to open doors and that kind of thing. Occasionally they work in the game's favour, leaving you wondering if you have enough time before something comes from behind and gets you but most of the time it really doesn't, the game also has better examples of this when picking fiddley locks on trucks on open, infested roads.
the combat, overall, is visceral, satisfying and fun. cutting zombies in half and drop-kicking bandits off of rooves will NEVER get old. The combat in the begging is a slog though, I don't think that's a bad thing, it makes sense with character development and it encourages you to learn how to use parkour to avoid a lot of earlier fights. That being said the combat can feel unfair and I dare say I wasn't the only one who suffered a few ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t deaths from smacking a boomer without looking. The common infected feel a bit.. 'sticky'? running past them they'll often get a swipe in and they are SUPER grabby. You will be grabbed, a lot and sometimes it will fell like there was nothing you could have done to prevent it, it can be very frustrating
the parkour is overall very solid and stringing together parkour moves and gliding around the city is satisfying. Generally, the game is good at making what is and is not grabbable/climbable fairly clear but not perfect. I found that the fall damage felt to high, your character can't take a fall much further than a couple meters without cracking a rib apparently. One final note on parkour, the wall jump ability is not worth the pain of accidently jumping to your death from a sky scraper.
overall the game is fun, lacks a bit of polish, makes a few very weird decisions and has a story worth ignoring but the core mechanics make it worth your time and money (the amount of content you're getting for your money is fairly excellent)

I decided to try this game, both because it seems to be one of the more revered of the otome genre, and the fact that it was free. I mean, if you are going to try some new type of game/story, and you find one free, why not? Thing is, this particular one is better than some games I've played that cost $30! First, being able to name your protagonist is a fun option (though as such, it appears none of the voice parts say more than "her" or "Miss Anderson").
Now, the story is broken into two parts. First, there's the inheriting a mansion from your grandfather, founder of a famous toy company (and who left a few secrets). One secret he left behind was letting five incubi stay at the mansion to recupperate. He wasn't expecting the protagonist's father to want her to move in so quickly. This leads to a few awkward situations, and later to the beginning of a relationship. Thing is, the incubi are recovering from a run in with some diabolic punks, and they are still looking to finish the job on the demons.
Once that is taken care of, you get a choice of letting the brothers stay or letting them go (they leave automatically if you didn't begin a relationship with one). At this point, a succubus with a... rather strong need to get those brothers back shows up. (She happens to be voiced by one of the creators; possibly the main author.) Now, if the boys stayed, you can continue your relationship, really annoying the succubus off, and eventually after driving her off (well, except for the illegitimate brother's route), you can consummate the relationship. Yes, you actually get a choice whether you are ready to give yourself to your paramour.
If they have left... well, things can get interesting. Depending on what you did during the first half of the game, there are three other options. Two are your school friends, both girls. The third is the son of your father's hated rival. Considering that boy is also in the running for becoming CEO of the company... well, there's a reason the heroine makes mention of Romeo and Juliet a time or two in that path. Now, the succubus shows up and offers... well, demands... that you forget all about the demons and magic... Apparently, there are Rules in place, and without the brothers around you... can't stay the way you are. In order to pursue one of the three above, you have to let those memories go.
There are a couple more options (that don't end with your becoming kibble). One of them is to pursue the succubus. And if you do that right... you'll change her point of view...
There is apparently a sequel, though I'm not sure what paths it follows (I do hope that there is some sort of questionaire so you can continue with the chosen incubi [or succubus], and perhaps also a question of whether you gave yourself to the incubus in question [because that seems like a rather important point since it appears you get dragged to the demonic planes by minions of their father; demons might like the idea of defiling her] [you are "innocent" in the biblical sense at the start of this game].)
I would definitely recommend this game.

All in all, I think the game is quite enjoyable- a fun, easygoing introduction to the genre.

This is quite a fun action game with emphasis on action and fun. You are a Helldiver, an elite strike team member, trained to launch from an orbiting battleship in a Hellpod and to rain death on the alien enemy scum.
Your strike team will consist from 1-4 helldivers, depending on how many players join the game, and the action takes place in one single screen that scrolls with the squads as you complete objectives in missions.
You will be facing a cadre of faitly typical enemies. Bugs that are of the typical aliens/starship troopers variety and remind of Zerg, Cyborgs hellbent on "improving" themselves trough modifying themselves and Illuminate, an advanced alien race using shield and stealth tech and energy weapons. These all have their individual weaknesses and strengths which adds some tactical element to the game in form of loadout selections.
Speaking of loadouts, you are not left wanting in variety.
Assault Rifles, Anti-Tank Rifles, Battle Rifles, Grenade Launchers, Laser Rifles, Machine Guns, Plasma Cannons, Railguns, Rocket Launchers, Shotguns, Sniper rifles, Tanks, Mechs, Drones, Automated Turrets, Decoys, Supply Drops, Air Strikes, Orbital Bombardments, Tactical Nukes, Jetpacks, Personal Shields, Mine Fields, Strafing Runs and all sorts of goodies. Some of these come in form of stratagems or calldowns in other words. You hold down a key and perform a key sequence to dial the item, drop your beacon and wait for a few seconds.
Which brings me to the interesting part. You perform battlefield actions such as interacting with objectives and using calldowns by using keyboard combinations such as up-up-down-down-left-right-left-right, which completes a sequence and does what you request. This is sometimes nerve-wracking as you try to call down the extraction pod and enemies are getting closer to you, which adds quite a lot to the excitement.
Death can come in many forms on the battlefield. A bug chewing your face off, A cyborg burning you to a crisp. Or the most likely cause of death: A careless teammate mowing you down from behind with their machine gun by accident.
Death in this game is not permanent, and you can always be called back into the game with a reinforcement calldown, and the action can continue. It is not worth getting upset about. Dying in this game is very easy. Ger overrun by a tank, wander under the landing zone of a shuttle/supply pod, falling into lava and so on.
The game has community-based star campaign progress which resets and begins anew when a "war" ends (20-30 days). During these campaigns you unlock and upgrade better arsenal such as better tanks, better mechs, bigger guns and tactical nuclear strikes to lay waste to alien scum.
The community for this game has been quite nice so far what I have seen.
There is also a commend/report system will ensure that griefers and rude players who get a bad standing will only get to play with other bad players, and well behaved and nice players who get commended by their comrades get to play with other nice players which is a nice touch. The bad reputation is not permanent so if you end up with a bad standing you can eventually get back to the good side if you change your ways and don't get more reports for a while.
Would I recommend this title? Yes, I would. Definitely worth grabbing on a sale.

I bought the game while it was on sale for 85 percent off, and having finally beaten the game, I can safely say that while this is a good game, its not worth 13 dollars. It's a puzzle platformer with a charming, simple story leading your character along: your uncle Fred has gone missing during one of his adventures, and you want to know what happened to him.
I will praise the game for its environments. I enjoyed entering a new area and getting to look around at everything. The only downside to this is if you have♥♥♥♥♥♥reflexes or suck at puzzles (as I do), then looking at these pretty areas can get a bit tedious after twenty deaths, and you'll long to either go forward or back just to get a change of scenery.
The story is, as I said, simple and charming. You meet a couple of characters, but I was disappointed to see a lack of world building. You enter a new area, but no details are given about it. In one area early on, you're given the impression that everyone fears a place called the Chasms, and yet none of the locals sit down and explain why. You couldn't go up to random NPCs and talk about what was going on. You couldn't trigger conversations with Maggie once she was on your back. For me, I love a good story that has a bit of that in it. The lack doesn't make the story bad, its just a personal preference of mine.
I will say that the ending, for all its build up, seems rather abrupt. After chasing Fred all around these fantastical places, and wondering what would lead him so deep into this realm, the answer you get is... lackluster. It makes sense, logically, and it ties the story off, but if you were craving some kind of big dramatic ending to go with the story like I was, it won't give you that.
All in all, I give the game an 8/10. It's got heart, its got charm, its beautiful and it doesn't stick around longer than need be. If you're here for a simple story, no great big strings attached, then that's what you'll get. Enjoy it for what it is, but don't expect much more than that.

A unique "walking simulator" that can be easily put on the top 3 adventure games. It successfully manages to create a truly astonishing world which you can explore and get immersed in, by using a special graphical technique called "photogrammetry". By doing so, it eliminates the "tiling effect" which can sometimes be very easily observed and can break the effect of immersion - basically, this means that almost every texture in the world created by the developers is unique: it simply looks gorgeous! And all of this is accompanied by the fact that the developers put the same amount of effort into the game's sound design, voice acting and story, all being excellent.
In conclusion, even though it is a little bit short (it took me just 4 hours to complete it - I know it says that I've only played for 1.5 hours; It is not true because I've played the Redux version, which is separated from the base game), I definitely recommend this game when it's on a sale - basically it is a steal! A must-play for every adventure enthusiast our there!
Also, be sure to play the Redux version that comes for free when you buy the game, if your computer can handle it! Not only that it comes with improved graphics and features which can be important to some, but it also fixes some gameplay aspects that some complained about.

More than 20 years ago, when i first played
i remember thinking, well, this game seems cool and all, specially the graphics, the story is very vague...and i don't really see too many things to do...i hope i soon have some things to do.. because if i don't i'm not so sure this is gonna work out....aand, of course, turns out, in myst, i did have some/several things to do, but in an original and unexpected way and there was a story, although not like you were expecting it to be, and it became one of the most known adventure games of the 90s (even though, it wasn't considered an adventure by many...). And that's fine, because the game was anything but a normal adventure, it was something else. You could like it, or hate it, but it was difficult to remain indifferent (once you played it).
Playing The Vanishing of Ethan Carter was the first time since playing Myst...that i had a similar experience... a sort of experience that not even the following game Riven could replicate, or the other games that followed in the series. Riven was a great game, even better than Myst, but it didn't replicate this feeling, of being in a real place. That's one of the things that's amazing from The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, it's been a long time since i felt this way about a virtual designed place.... this place....this creek valley....it could exist, it could actually exist (i believed it could). And i know is not real, CGI place of sorts, and the graphics were great of course, very good, but not the greatest, and still.... and that's what surprised me, there was something else happening, i don't know, maybe because of the photographic textures, maybe just by a design choice of space, or maybe the way each stage was presented , that something in my mind, told me, this could be real.
This proves to me, basically, that no matter how good the graphics are, there's something more needed for a place to be "believable" Something that has to be well though out and put into place. Something does have to work in a practical way.
One thing that this game dares to do, is design a place and then put all the different interactions in a organic way. Meaning, if you are in the woods, and there's something to do there, and then there's a bridge in the background and there's something more to do over the bridge, you are not just gonna jump from one place to the other....you are gonna have to walk all the woods and arrive to the bridge, and then if you wanna go to the house over the hill, you are gonna have to cross the whole bridge, and climb the hill. There's just no shortcuts in graphics and places, it's all there, you believe it could be some real place. Maybe that's the part that could come across as "walking simulator" because you do have to walk "a lot" but you also do have quite a few things to do, and an investigation to complete (also you can sprint fast). You are a detective of sorts, and you have to learn what happened to Ethan and his family. And whats this weird energy around  the valley where the games takes place.
I was surprised by this, because, yes, the game is in part a walking simulator (you do walk a lot) and the game itself is not overly long. But , in this case and for this game, thats perfect! for once , it made sense to me to have a game where you do walk a lot while doing some interaction with things (it's part of the experience, to discover each corner of this place, and investigate) and it's fine for this game to not be really long, because the story doesn't need it. But it doesn't feel cheap, and it doesn't feel short. A movie takes about 2 hours, and we don't think it's short or cheap. This game takes something between 6 to 8 hours, and it doesn't feel short  at all.
Also, while doing the investigation you will come around certain objects, that you will look closely, sometimes even pick them up to use them someplace else. And in certain scenes you' re gonna have to reconstruct a chronology of events. Telling more would be spoiling it...because, the same as myst, this game tries to be something else...it has to be discovered... and it does succeed in making you believe it is real.
The story is good, very interesting, it's presented in a very good pace almost all along and the tension remains almost all the way. I would say that during the last scenes it was a little let down, not because of the ending, but to the contrary, because before the ending you would want to know more about the characters and their story, and how it happened all that came to be, before the ending. That's in fact a testament to how good the game was at times, although not perfect.
I would say the story is good enough, but no great, and what truly is great here is the experience of discovering and learning about the game world.
Playing this game makes me realize how gaming has come along these last 20 years that we are now seeing new genres (or variations of existing genres) and in this parcticular case, that not all games have to be a 60+ hs experience to be valuable (especially if its not justified) Sometimes, less and minimalistic, is just as good.
I was just ready to quit for good these so called "Walking simulators" because i'm bored to death of them, i hate just walking around, if it is for the story i play it, then i just prefer to watch a movie, really.
But, The Vanishing of Ethan Carter showed me that, if there's a good reason to make a "walking simulator" (with a good amount of interactions, albeit minimal) and it is justified,it can be a great gaming experience, different than a movie. A gaming experience, that if done right, could be the first of a new genre, like
did 20 years ago.

Techland is a 'medioce at best' gaming producing studio (My opinion). This game proves that point. I'd go into more detail into why, but I'd find myself bored explaining why. Pros and cons below.
Pros:
- Fun to play with friends. (The only real pro of this game so far)
- A dollar an hour game. (Worth the money if you buy it on sale, when it's $15-$20, anything more is asking a bit much)
- Fun on normal difficulties. (Look up the rewards you get for doing hardest difficulty and ask yourself if it's worth it)
- Decent parkour. (A tad wonky, but it has its charms)
- Funny easter eggs.
- Incredibly funny when they hold some events (ei. Kicking a zombie from one side of the map to the other side).
Cons:
- Disengaging story (Obvious, unexciting, uninventive, useless. Must of been written by a small group of 20yr olds).
- Awful voice acting (Accents aren't the worst of it).
- Mediocre graphics (Graphics take away from the atmosphere that the game tries so hard to have).
- Terrible map size (For a parkour game, the map gets stale quickly).
- Unrewarding gameplay (Game makes you feel like you're doing tasks for someone else's benefit, not having fun).
- Stale gamplay (I found myself wishing this game was better than it was, instead of actually enjoying it).
- Vaas ripoff (Game tries WAY TO HARD to recreate Vaas from the Farcry series, it takes away from the game).
In conclusion, I found it far easier to speak about the negatives of this game than the positives of it. This might be because my own experiences, I don't know. It's not a bad game, but that doesn't excuse Techland for their dull, and boring games. Undead Labs are a smaller studio and they were able to create a better game than this (State Of Decay). I recommend this game because I don't think people should avoid playing it. It's a real hit or miss. I personally found myself wanting to go back to Left 4 Dead 2 because it was just better in terms of enjoyment, but I know people will disagree.

Clever is the word for this game.  The gameplay is tight, well-balanced, and clever.  Tower defense games are rarely this clever and the RPG system rewards good play.  The downfall of virtually all RPG systems is a sense of grind - you want the best stuff, you're going to have to perform repetitive tasks until you've got the prerequisite numbers.  Grinding reminds me of a job.  Defender's Quest lets you bypass that - anything you'd have to grind for is optional, and if you want the optional content, then you can toggle the exp and gold gain.  This also lets you set the difficulty to as difficult or as easy as you want.
The amazing thing is that the gameplay is so good, and the rest of the game is also so good.  The graphics aren't the modern blockbusters, but the character art is charming and clever, and the dialog is well-written and allows you to connect to the characters.  Fun gameplay, thoughtful gameplay, good art, good dialog, fun plot.  The game can even be replayed, and the new game+ has additional insight into the world if you're that hooked.  It also ramps up the difficulty if you like a challenge.  To top it off, the game is inexpensive.  Why have you not already bought it?
Hilarious and well balanced.  Excellent game and you should buy it.

The main storyline in Seduce Me is, at its core, pure fanservice. You are a high school senior living in a mansion inherited from your late grandfather, who turns out to be the sugar daddy of 5 incubi brothers. Despite being sex demons, they are all very nice and selfless and talented (how are they so good at chores, when they were all demon princes who have been living in the human world for a few months at most? we just don't know) and willing to serve you and fall in love with you for no other reason besides you giving them a place to sleep, one or two makeout sessions, and being overall stupid (and the worst part is that the MC is
stupid with other characters, just with these). Also, MC got cool demon powers just by reading some of her grandpa's magic journals once. And she can bang your incubus of choice in the end. So, a game that tackles all female fantasies of love, wealth, sex and overall being a special snowflake.
BUT, if you're not interested in that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, that's where the game's pros come into play: you don't need to pick any of the demon brothers! You can keep them at a distance from the start and send them away as soon as Antagonist #1's♥♥♥♥♥is kicked. Then, you can move on to any of the actual good routes in the game: Antagonist #2 (who also turns out to be the best character of all), Cute Human Boy, 2 female childhood friends, or you can just be free and not date anyone.
Now, the reason why I say these routes are the decent ones (despite me liking
of the demon brothers) is due to the lack of repetition between them (most situations between each incubus route are recycled, which feels off since they have very different personalities) and because these characters have actual reasons to fall for the MC. Their relationship is either based on realistic interaction and traits in common (Andrew) or slowly built over time (the 3 female routes). Plus, none of these are as heavily based on tropes as the incubi (the girl friends kinda are, but they still have more depth than the incubi). It just looks like MUCH more effort went into these routes than the demons'.
These side routes, along with the voice acting (yep, this is a fully voiced
VN!) and the variety of endings, are the reasons I recommend this game. You may feel disappointed at the incubi since they are the main pursuable characters, but the others are worth it. Other downsides include the art, which is overall inconsistent, with subpar sprites and some CGs that are quite odd while others are pretty nice; and some writing issues, such as a few contradictions. On the bright technical side, there is a variety of choices, over 10 endings, and extra content including bloopers. The incubi routes can be boring, but they're barely half of the whole game. So rather than "recommending", this is more of a "play it, but be warned" review. I mean, it's free and not the worst VN ever, so why not?

I was not sure what to expect when first loading up HELLDIVERS for the first time. I checked out the store page and watched some YouTube videos of the game but I honestly was not sold on the game until I played it.
In HD there is a constant war going on between humanity and the rest of the galaxy. You’ll find yourself up against the Cyborgs, Bugs and Illuminate, fighting to spread democracy wherever you go.
Each faction has its own portion of the galaxy and is trying to eliminate humanity. You’ll be tasked with deploying behind enemy lines to complete objectives and secure the future of Super Earth. Each mission will comprise of 1-4 players deploying to an enemy planet and occasionally one of our own worlds to beat back the enemy.
During your time in HD you will unlock many stratagems which are supplies and tools to aid you on missions. You’ll unlock these by completing world missions and leveling up. There are 4 types of stratagems to use, Supply, Defensive, Offensive and Special. Special stratagems are mission specific and you won’t need to pick these. They’re given to you automatically.
The screen is locked to you and all other players in the mission, meaning that you can’t split up and do your own thing. This is a game about teamwork and completing objectives, it’s not a mindless shooter. Teamwork is very important to being successful in HELLDIVERS.
Overall I absolutely love HELLDIVERS and I highly recommend it to anyone that likes actual team based play. You can’t go wrong with this one, it’s honestly a wonderful game and I really hope we’ll eventually see a HELLDIVERS 2 in the future.

Pros:

-interesting twist on the vampires - 7 playable clans, each with their own strengths and weaknesses
-nonlinear gameplay - sneak around without being seen or slaughter everyone with a gun
-diverse 'disciplines' (basically supernatural powers) - invisibility, charm, induce insanity and more
-decent dialogue system
-good plot with ingenious quests
-strong cast of characters
-can be witty at times, playing with stereotypes and such
-length - it probably took me around 30+ hours to finish, including most of the subquests (don't mind the hours on record, I often play in offline mode)
Cons:
-the graphics (that is to be expected from a game released in 2004) - clipping issues are unfortunately quite common
-difficulty spikes - very easy at first, can be frustrating at the end depending on what weapons you're using
-lackluster and unbalanced combat system - upgrading your melee comabt skills will only increase the damage you deal, the movesets and attack speed remain the same (or improve just slightly); there is also no good reason to choose unarmed combat over melee weapons
-hubs offer relatively little to do once the sidequests are finished (justified in that you only ever walk the streets at night)
-buggy (be sure to install unoffical patches)
-the inventory can be messy
-price - about 20 bucks for a ten-year-old game that isn't even a cult classic (albeit, for what it is - a very decent RPG, perhaps it should be)
My rating: 7.5/10

This is an overall great game. There are a few flaws, but we'll get to them.
The visuals are out of this world. Seriously, it's been a while since I've seen something so beautiful and pleasant to the eyes in a game. The soundtrack is also amazing, so aesthetically, this game is a really good experience.
It is a bit short (and expensive, so I'd suggest you to get it on sale like I did), though, and the story (especially the ending) might be kind of frustrating or unsatisfying for some. Personally, I really liked it, and the final twist, while it's something I don't often appreciate in the stories I follow, made sense to me. The gameplay is simple and interesting. But I think it's fair to warn that in a specific point of the game there are jumpscares, and to me this is one of the flaws: not only they didn't add anything relevant to the story, but they also killed the immersion and the eerie, tense atmosphere from the earlier scenes. It also has zero replay value, sadly.
I played the Redux version, so it did demand a lot from my computer. I could run the game nicely, but loading it took some time, and the camera didn't respond as well as I wanted it to. I can't say about the original version, though.
TL;DR: really good game, really beautiful, but overpriced and with a few flaws and points that not everybody will like. Get in on sale and you won't regret it.

Graphically astonishing and atmospherically imposing, The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is one of the best walking simulators I have played. The writing, chock-full of noir platitudes and smug nods to pulp/weird fiction, is neatly justified with a clever twist in the ending. The puzzles are not implausible; the flavour text offers an engaging breadcrumb trail to the observant player. It doesn't hold the player's hand, as they deign to warn us in the opening, but it does hold our attention.
The redux version is definitely more impressive and has a more stable framerate, but the original version leaves nothing to be desired. My first playthrough was on the original; the second on the redux right after. And I enjoyed both.
Brief and to the point, an interactive nonlinear narrative with no tricks up its sleeve. A story is told and told well. It lacks something in replay value, but you could probably go back to it at some point to walk through the woods and listen to the soothing soundtrack.

In my view, this is the best zombie game on the planet.  Unlike many of the other survival games the action is superb.  The enemy AI makes sense and gets better as you go.  The environment is so realistic, the sound so immersive, the situation and the enemies so believable, that you'll find yourself feeling like you are actually part of a zombie apocalypse.  You'll shout at the enemies, goading them out loud in your room so you can whack on them, starting to believe that you can actually do this (admittedly exaggerated) parkour, and just having a whale of a time.
If you liked any of the Dead Island series, if you are looking for a System Shock 2, Deus Ex series, Bioshock series like game set in a zombie environment where the ACTION is a whole lot more INTENSE, this is the game.
Scavenging is well done.   You can look for loot in car trunks, trash cans, inside houses -- in cupboards, closets, fridges, cabinets, satchels, and the like.   You'll find shops to raid, some seeming to be garages, pawn shops, restaurants, pharmacies, and so on.  You'll also find scattered around special larger chests in varying colors, many are locked with varying levels of difficulty to lockpick.  These chests, and the police cars and police vans, often yield some of the best loot.  In this game, the best and most reliable weapons are melee weapons -- if you know Dead Island you'll get the idea although it is much expanded here.   Firearms, bows, explosives, and many craftable blueprints, as well as upgrades to weapons can be found.  These all come in various varieties and many in different tiers of capability.
It's as if an action game of the quality of the Far Cry Series had decided to tell the in-your-face story of surviving in a totally quarantined city in the middle of a zombie epidemic and your the stunt man in the action movie.   You have a good range of zombies to take on, as many as in any other game.  They work together and remind one of The Walking Dead TV series.   There are the normal biters, acid spitting toads, adrenalin fueled Virals who can dodge and run, Nightwalkers who are even worse and tougher, Goons who can take a beating and dish out huge damage but are slower.  There are Demolishers who can throw boulders and pieces of concrete pavement, Volatiles which spit and run and do parkour as well as you but are much tougher than a human who come out only at night or in the always dark areas.
In addition, there are bandits and Rais' men -- who try to control the access to the limited drug suppressant to the infection -- the sole way to keep alive if you are infected.  These arrive in air drops, which are important to get to quickly and acquire, as Rais' men intend to gather and hoard it for huge profit for themselves.
Quests abound.  Tons of side quests, GTA like Parkour challenges, killing spree challenges, and the like.  Main story quests  also abound.  While you explore and move about the map, well I should say several huge maps, you may run into random encounters.  Here you can interact with fellow survivors, assisting them, protecting them, meeting random vendors who may have some of the best loot, and meeting special zombies.
The Story is more than good enough the characters are believable, english voicing good.
The environment looks like survivors have been fighting hard to survive, even preparing traps and other contraptions all over the city maps.   You can knock a zombie into a bunch of spikes set up against a wall and kill it that way.   You can use car traps, electric fence traps set on the ground to electrocute them, UV light traps at night to discourage the Night Variants from coming near you, and so on.
The combat is incredible with tons of moves you can make even unarmed.  Ever want to dropkick a zombie, it's a skill.  Want to jump with a weapon from a building and crush a zombie's skull as you land with a weapon thru its brain, you can do that.   If you sprint and want to knock the legs out from a zombie you can do a slide, later it is upgraded to a leg-breaker, making the zombie unable to use that leg.  Combat animations are superb.
Firecrackers not only attract zombies they can light up oil slicks in the environment and if there is a fuel barrel nearby, kaboom.   Some zombies have Hazmat suits with a gas tank on the back, if you hit the tank with a weapon, it begins to hiss as it leaks, and soon that ignites with resounding fury -- so don't be close.   The game has so many things in it that are interrelated that work as you might imagine -- you can't help but be immersed in the environment.
There are multiple difficulty levels.  Normal, Hard Mode, and Nightmare Mode.  Plus a New Game Plus allows you to slightly increase the difficulty even more, but lets you keep all your skills you acquired, plus any loot you have already in your basically infinite stash. But don't worry, you'll be using up all these weapons, explosives, firearms, in that stash as well.  Stashes are located in Safe Zones, which you have to find, clear out, and make safe.  Hard Mode omits the usual pausing with the inventory open, it doesn't produce as many purple and orange high tier weapons, and zombies are tougher and do more damage.  Your flashlight now also dims out as it is used compared to normal. In Normal you can pause the game even when in the environment but in Hard kiss that goodbye.   Hard Mode gives more experience, but you lose more upon death.  Nightmare takes it even to a higher level of difficulty, but the flashlight does not dim, etc.  Gold Tier Weapons begin dropping in H and N.
Experience is gained by doing many things.   There are Survivor Skills which level up also the loot and difficulty it seems in the game.   Agility Skills which you get by using cool parkour moves.   Power Skills which are gained by doing cool combat moves.  There are 73 skills in all, but only about half are actually new skills, I'd call them moves or abilities that you can do.  The rest are mostly upgrades to a higher level for those skills.  You can even camouflage yourself like a human hunter does in the wild, by using zombie corpses to camouflage your scent, giving you some periods of relative peace but at the cost of some visibility (tinted view and some blood splotches if put on too much).
It is an extremely well balanced game.  Plenty of options for your computer and for your gameplay as well as for difficulty.
I could go on, but what is the point.   It's really a great game.  Get the Enhanced Edition, it will include the Following all all the DLC except unneede special stuff in Harran Ranger, Gun Psycho, and Volatile Hunter bundles, all of which are not key to the game.
I've played this game for over 180 hours and I'm still not done the first map on Normal.   You can control the pacing and the risk by doing things your way.  Scavenge more and conserve the good stuff, or take on the world full blast with your best stuff, it is up to you.
It's a forgiving game in that you never just die.  You just lose experience. Saves system seems very solid.  Plus there are other modes in Co-Op and also a Be The Zombie mode, where you can either play the top echelon Night Hunter Zombie, or be one of the 4 humans trying to survive its Hunt and achieve your mission.
Lots of game and some more smaller content drop downloads supposed to come this year, mostly weapons and small new challenges.
NOTE: If you have an INTEL HD GPU, I cannot recommend you play this game with it.  You can expect 11fps or less in any resolution, even if you try 800x600.  It is possible that AMD/RADEON integrated GPUs may often be similarly out of luck.  But any decent gaming Video Card, I use an Nvidia Geforce GTX 750 Ti with 2 GB of VRAM, will easily play this game well.  Just make sure you have something that can game, doesn't have to be the best, the card I use or something in that ballpark will serve you well at very low cost.
Here's to your enjoying this game as much as I do.

It's been five years and 6 complete sectors now, surely we must be close to our goal. The Federation outpost's signal's weak on my radar screen, it must still be pretty far out man (note to self: get crew to boost the HMS Starman's nipple antennae).

Defender's Quest is a Tower-Defense/RPG Hybrid (Think Final Fantasy Tactics meets Tower Defense).
Defender's Quest tightly focuses on three things: tactical depth, customization, and story. That means no random encounters, no spikey-haired emo kids, no forced time sinks, and no tedious, repetitive battles.
The battle system builds off of tower defense, with individual characters taking the place of towers. Each character levels-up, learns skills, and equips gear individually, allowing the player to customize their battle experience and strategy. The overall game structure is similar to "tactical" RPG's, but with a real-time battle system. Game speed is adjustable, and commands can even be issued while the game is paused.
It also features an engaging, character-driven story written by an actual English major! The story strives to be fast-paced, snappy, and always relevant to gameplay. Events and dialogue explain things as they become relevant to the player, minimizing exposition.
Finally, it's got options and accessibility settings out the wazoo, so that you can have the best possible experience!
It has no frills what so ever. but it's a fun and enjoyable time waster.

This is a bit of a mixed review. The battle system is pretty interesting with the switching between screens and thinking up the best strategies to beat the enemies. I also have fun with the crafting system (but it does make the game grind-y; I find grinding rewarding so I enjoy it, but if you have little patience for that sort of thing, trying to gather all the materials and experience points to craft stuff might get on your nerves). Overall I've spent a lot of hours entertained by the game and am invested enough to want to get all achievements, craft all items, etc. So for the price I think the experience is really worth it (and I even got it on sale).
That said - I expected an RPG with a rhythm game gimmick, and got a rhythm game with an RPG gimmick instead... the rhythm game battling is like 90% of the game. But it's not quite strong on its own to be what I'd call an "amazing" rhythm game... the music is a bit bland and sounds more like a nice BGM than something to actively enjoy. I also appreciate sleek visuals/designs in rhythm/music games but the battle screen looks pretty basic. This would've all been 100% fine if there was just more besides the battles to the game... like if you could actually move through a map and  meet the monsters in random encounters or something, in a more RPG-y way. Or if the story and characters were more unique and there were more and better written narration and dialogue, in a visual novel-y way. The characters are pretty basic and the dialogue is cringey at times (trying a bit too hard to be witty/funny to be taken seriously, kinda generic, uncomfortable moments like one point where the r-slur is used). Basically I feel like the game is fun but falls short of being Great. Better visuals/music, more varied gameplay, better story/writing - if it had any one of those 3 things, I think it might've been enough. I wouldn't even demand to have all three at once. But as it is, it feels like it falls short of its potential. I think the core idea of integrating rhythm games with RPG in a battle system is really great and that the game could've been better.
But like I said, since it's cheap, I do think it's worth its price. So if you enjoy rhythm games you might as well get it because it'll probably provide quite a few hours of fun. If you don't like rhythm games, I'd just say you won't be missing out on much if you pass.

A Story About my Uncle is a lovely little game that will occupy your afternoon.
The game is basically narrated by a father telling his daughter a bedtime story about the fathers Uncle, Fred. The story is narrated as you play through it. You start off in Fred’s house, you make your way upstairs and there’s a funny looking suit made to fit you. You put it on only to find a ‘waste disposal’ platform. After activating it, you are transported to a distant land of frog people and floating islands.
The gameplay is very enjoyable (what little there is of it unfortunately). You use your grapple and jump abilities to move from island to island, upgrading your grapple and eventually even getting a pair of rocket boots you can use to fly with. You then move on to increasingly difficult levels to find your Uncle as you tell your daughter the story. The narration and story are a sort of background so that the player doesn’t feel like they’re on an LSD trip, flying through floating islands. It does add to the game, but not significantly enough for you to really care. It’s a nice addition, but mainly there so it’s not a silent jumping game with another mute protagonist.
Overall the game was very enjoyable. The playstyle is something that is relatively new to me and very arcade-esk. There are also little collectables that unlock certain modes (such as goat mode, but I’ll let you find out what that is) and time trials. I feel though, that this game could’ve benefited from a workshop feature so that people could create their own levels and share them with the community. This would’ve changed it from a 3-4 hour game, to a 15-20 hour game if you enjoyed it. But unfortunately this was not to be.

Graphically astonishing and atmospherically imposing, The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is one of the best walking simulators I have played. The writing, chock-full of noir platitudes and smug nods to pulp/weird fiction, is neatly justified with a clever twist in the ending. The puzzles are not implausible; the flavour text offers an engaging breadcrumb trail to the observant player. It doesn't hold the player's hand, as they deign to warn us in the opening, but it does hold our attention.
The redux version is definitely more impressive and has a more stable framerate, but the original version leaves nothing to be desired. My first playthrough was on the original; the second on the redux right after. And I enjoyed both.
Brief and to the point, an interactive nonlinear narrative with no tricks up its sleeve. A story is told and told well. It lacks something in replay value, but you could probably go back to it at some point to walk through the woods and listen to the soothing soundtrack.

It took me a leisurely 5 hours to complete the game; it is relatively short and the plot is fairly straight-forward (although it might not always seem so).  The game draws some limited inspiration from Lovecraft, but not too much.  Both the game's tone and visuals remind me of Dear Esther, but with a real plot and puzzles.
Unfortunately the game does rely on an abudance of exploration to find all the clues--which wouldn't necessarily be a bad thing if the map wasn't as large and linear (taking a LONG time to walk to the other side of the map).  Some plot elements are placed well off the main pathways and can require a keen eye (and luck) to discern.
On a scale from 1 to 10, I'd give this game around a 7.  Visually, it is stunning.  The story unfolds in a compelling manner and MOST of the puzzles are fair and help push the narrative.  Unfortunately some puzzles are too simple, while one in particular can be extremely difficult and is not coherently presented within the narrative.  It is a short game, but well worth picking up.  If you have a GPU capable of running the Redux version, don't even bother with the "original" game.
FWIW, I found the game's conclusion to be satisfying--YMMV.
Pros:
Beautiful graphics (Redux version)
Interesting plot
Nice soundtrack
Cons:
Some critical data is located far off the obvious pathways.
At least one "puzzle" (house portals) is not presented logically within the plot and can be dificult to discern what is required.
The map is fairly huge and can require time consuming trips from one end to the other if you missed something (which is likely).

One of my favourite RPG game of all time. Fans of Fallout and the Elder Scrolls will love this game.
Straight off the bat you are giving choices on how you wish to play the game. You first get to choose which vampire clan you wish to be and this choice impacts the game. Certain clans get secret missions, some are shunned by the other clans, some will only feed off rich and pure blood, some can shapshift, some are monsterous which forces you into using the sewer system least your ugly mug violates the masquerade on the streets above, and some are batshit insane. Each clan gives you an entirely different experience and different abilities.
The game has something for everyone. Love first person shooters? Go in guns blazing. Prefer third person melee? Well go grab a sword and start swinging. Stealth? Be prepared to sneak around, hack computers, pick locks. Magic? Theres a lot! Explode some homeless guys face, have them eaten by swarms of beatles, summon spirit wolves, and control minds!
The quests in the game can be complelted in a variety of different ways including the main story. Do you kill the human who has discovered that the things that go bump in the night exist, or do you convince them to keep his mouth shut? Or tell him the whole thing was a great big joke and all his friends have just pulled a fast one on him. What ever you choose you will be rewarded in different ways.
The game is somewhat linear however. Sure there is free roam but each area feels quite small once you get used to the layout of the neighbourhood.
So do you like guns, magic, swords, side quests, multiple endings? Do you like seducing women in clubs and draining them of their bodily fluids? Or would you rather suck off some homless dude in a back alley and have a rat for lunch?
If the answer is yes to any of these buy this game.

TL;DR: Buy it! Most fun I've had in a long time, great for playing with friends and a great price point.
Haven't played too much of this gem yet, but I have to say that the antics that can result from this game are staggeringly awesome. I haven't cackled with glee this much and this often in a game for a pretty long time. And if you add in friends, it becomes that much more amazing.
I think there's a few kinks that can be worked out, and some additional steam functionality (like being able to join your friends from the drop down menu would be awesome) would be nice. But despite this being released on steam, it's basically a beta. And that's not a bad thing. Actually I'd say that's one of its strongest selling points, that the dev team is constantly working on things, tossing out updates at a decent pace it seems, and it's already this addictive and fun.
To people wondering what this game is about: Looking at it from an outside perspective, it seems a lot like Terraria at first glance. But it's really only a superficial similarity. The aesthetics aren't really the same, the mechanics are much different, and the whole point of the game is worlds apart from Terraria. If Terraria is the rpg dungeoncrawler with building elements, King Arthur's Gold (or KAG from here on out) is two teams of kids waging imaginary medieval warfare on an epic scale against each other. If you've ever done things like that as a kid, or can picture it, you can see why this concept is pretty damn appealing. Everything about the game from the ground up is designed to aid and facilitate your war. Just to give you an idea of the things that are possible, here's just a few things I've seen happen or done myself in my short time of playing: Won a game by literally loading knights into catapaults to shoot them over the other team's walls. Won a game by sneakily tunneling under a team's base, setting up a tunnel there (for people familiar with Starcraft, think nydus canals) and flooding their base from below with an angry legion of molemen (actually knights), tunneling into their flag room, and stealing their flag, bypassing almost all their fortifications, I was giggling the entire way back while I was also desperately dodging arrows with no defenses of my own being a builder. I've also been a knight and relay raced a powder keg to collapse someone's tower as their panicked archers kept trying to kill us and prevent us from getting that keg to their tower.
The community has its share of problematic people I think, but in general people are quick to jump on griefers and get them out of the server, and for the most part I find them to be a pretty cool group of people. They're pretty tight knit, having been around since the game's inception almost 3 years ago, but in general they've also been pretty welcoming to fresh blood. For icing on top of the cake, the devs seem to play their own game and make regular appearances on servers, and there's a team of mods that are dedicated to going around the servers to weed out griefers as well.
There's honestly too much for me to say about the game, but even with minor kinks in the game it's one of the best purchases I've made in a long time. There are so many good memories and fun stories to be told in this game, especially when you have a group of friends on skype all yelling at each other as we try to work together (or work against each other) to win. One of my greatest laughs so far was when I was fighting another friend and managed to knock her into the waiting mouth of a shark. Instant chowtime, outraged cries and hilarity ensued.
I can't praise this game enough, for ten dollars it's worth it. And at the time of writing at 25% off during the Autumn sale, for single and 4 pack, I don't think there's any real reason not to get this! This is my favourite game in years.
It's a tower defense game where each of what would normally be a tower is actually a character that levels up, like in an RPG, complete with a customizable skill tree, equipment, etc. These levels are earned from level to level, so you're constantly improving your party.
This superficially simple gameplay concept is backed up on all sides by a great story, deep strategy elements and amazing replayability.
Azra (or the name you choose) is the royal librarian that ends up in The Pit, a wretched place full of zombie-like creatures called Revenant. Using mysterious special powers (that excellently explain the tower defense gameplay) and the help of a band of ragtag adventures you'll pick up it is your job to guide her out of the pit. There is more at stake, and the plot has plenty of developments to keep you interested, but what surprised me the most were the story's pacing and its humour.
No story segment lasts more than a minute or two, excluding the ending but not the opening, yet it tells a cohesive and engaging story. You'll never feel like the levels are just there to pad out the story or vice versa.
Within levels you get to place your defenders along the paths your enemies will take to reach Azra. Doing so spends mana, so unless Azra has a lot of Mana (maximum mana increases by increasing her level) you'll need to consider which allies to summon. You can 'boost' these allies to unlock more attacks and increase their core stats, up to 5 times, this is equivalent to the traditional tower defense game's tower upgrade. Combine that with being able to place allies whenever you want, advanced targetting settings and certain allies working very well together while others negate some aspects of other powers (frozen vs. burning) and you have a deeply rewarding tactical system.
Is this required to enjoy or finish the game? No.
The ability to play and replay any level you've cleared at any of 4 difficulties means that you set your own pace and your own challenge. On the lowest difficulty you can basically breeze through the game and just enjoy the story, never having to put a lot of thought into tactics or grinding, and the hardest difficulty will have you either rethinking your tactics or grinding a few more levels.
Clearing the game once, with any of its 5 endings (only 2 distinct ones really, one just has 4 different versions) will unlock new game+ mode parallel to the regular game mode. This features new powers for all enemies, several sidequests telling the story of one of the characters relevant to the plot, the ability to understand the 'ancient language' spoken in some of the dialogue and a 'journal' that offers lovely (and often hilarious) glances into the protagonist's mind as her journey progresses.
It will challenge you and reward you, and this is completely free extra content that was released months after the game was originally launched that is automatically included. I've put dozens of hours into this game and still revisit it regularly to see if I can't beat a few of the levels I still have problems with on a higher difficulty or to work on my Hero Mode run.

DO YOU LIKE TYCOON/BUSINESS MANAGEMENT GAMES?!
Well despite being anti-capitalist, I really do. Don't ask me why, I honestly couldn't tell you. Maybe I just really like micromanagement.
If you, like me, enjoy games like this for some inexplicable reason, you should pick up Software Inc. The premise is simple, starting in the 1970s and with one person, you build a software company from the ground up, complete with design teams, programmers, artists, a marketing department, server farms, and an office building that you design yourself.
Think Game Dev Tycoon meets The Sims.
You can create a small company that solely makes RTS games, or you can create a megacorporation that designs operating systems and buys out smaller subsidiary companies. It's up to you, the player.
The thing that sets this game apart from others like it, is how complex it's game systems actually are, while remaining simple to understand and "game-like". Most other games that set out to achieve what this game does, are either overly complex, or too dumbed down. This game maintains a perfect balance between complexity and simplicity.
The one negative thing I can say about it is that once you figure out what works to make a profitable company, it becomes way too easy. However, this isn't where the meat of the game's fun lies. It lies within the satisfaction of being creative within the game's systems. Building a cool office building, designating tasks for your individual teams, finally making making a piece of software that sells millions of copies. Stuff like that.
In conclusion, if you like tycoon and business simulation games, Software Inc is a must have.
