This would be the first game I'd recommend if you hated Dear Esther. It's hard not to compare the two, but The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is more of a game whereas Dear Esther was an experience or experiment in storytelling. To me it was an unforgettable experience, rarely a game has crawled under my skin like Dear Esther, but truth be told, I've only finished it once. That doesn't take away the goosebumps and the emotions I went through, but replayability is an important thing to any gamer. I can't help but sneer at the term walking simulator though, cos it sort of closes the door on any experiment or game not conforming to the norm. While gameplay is king, I'd rather have access to new ideas than play the 400th Mario game, because the platforming is so timeless. Restricting player movement in a game goes against every instinct in your body, cos games are supposed to be liberating experiences, but on the other hand you have highly scripted games that are rewarded with your hard-earned €60 for doing the exact same thing.
Our notions of pricing is another thing that's put to the test when playing these sort of games, which is understandable, but Ethan Carter steps comfortably out of the danger zone of being completed in 2 hours on your first playthrough. It lets you experience its story by having you solve multiple murders and puzzles, but mainly murders as you walk or run through the absolutely stunning Red Creek Valley. Considering how believable the location is and my cursed compulsion to seek out every corner, I would've hated this game with a passion if I hadn't had the option to sprint and I mean properly sprint not just walk faster, which some games seem to mix up. Sprinting would've destroyed Dear Esther, but here it's unavoidable, especially with the risk of backtracking.
The Vanishing of Ethan Carter looks so good you wish you had the PC to be able to max it out, at least in my case, cos with the use of photogrammetry it literally looks picture perfect. You would gladly walk, admire your surroundings and forget the gameplay, but there is no need to go exploring every nook and cranny. There are only a couple of items off the beaten path; this is no game of collectibles. The words Inspect and Read hover over every item worth looking at. To avoid backtracking though you need to pay attention, cos every puzzle needs to be solved in order to finish the game.
I can't say what the story is about without spoiling it, but you'll notice right away that this isn't a detective story rooted in reality. It's a nice mix between Dear Esther and Alan Wake. Often times I was enjoying the sights and the simple gameplay of putting murder scenes together that I didn't bother putting the actual story together, cos you're so used to a paranormal angle that it's become normal, which is why I was caught off guard by the games ending. Having only played the Redux version, which has a better save system though higher system requirements and the risks of backtracking aside, the gorgeous game world, its Lovecraftian tone and a good story make it a worthy experience.
EDIT:
A tip from grandsong: If you're not interested in walking, in keybindings change Run to W, so you can rest that pinky finger of yours.

A Story About my Uncle is a lovely little game that will occupy your afternoon.
The game is basically narrated by a father telling his daughter a bedtime story about the fathers Uncle, Fred. The story is narrated as you play through it. You start off in Fred’s house, you make your way upstairs and there’s a funny looking suit made to fit you. You put it on only to find a ‘waste disposal’ platform. After activating it, you are transported to a distant land of frog people and floating islands.
The gameplay is very enjoyable (what little there is of it unfortunately). You use your grapple and jump abilities to move from island to island, upgrading your grapple and eventually even getting a pair of rocket boots you can use to fly with. You then move on to increasingly difficult levels to find your Uncle as you tell your daughter the story. The narration and story are a sort of background so that the player doesn’t feel like they’re on an LSD trip, flying through floating islands. It does add to the game, but not significantly enough for you to really care. It’s a nice addition, but mainly there so it’s not a silent jumping game with another mute protagonist.
Overall the game was very enjoyable. The playstyle is something that is relatively new to me and very arcade-esk. There are also little collectables that unlock certain modes (such as goat mode, but I’ll let you find out what that is) and time trials. I feel though, that this game could’ve benefited from a workshop feature so that people could create their own levels and share them with the community. This would’ve changed it from a 3-4 hour game, to a 15-20 hour game if you enjoyed it. But unfortunately this was not to be.
Yes you heard correct, the game is only around 3 hours long. However, if you are a completionist, you may be looking at a bit more as the achievements are extremely difficult to earn. Would I say this game is worth it? Yes, but not for £10. I purchased this from EBay for 99p, and for that it is a fantastic game.
In short, really enjoyable, too short, could’ve benefitted from a Steam workshop to add to the games length and diversity.

The Metro franchise holds a special place in my heart. I owned both 2033 and Last Light on the Xbox 360 upon each of their releases, and played them endlessly. Replayed both Redux versions on pc, and in light of the recent wonderful announcement of Exodus, the spark has once again been ignited.
For those of you that are interested by the look of this game and don't know too much about it, Metro 2033 is a harrowing tale of the apocalypse, set in the heart of Russia. In 2013, we saw WW3, and when the bombs inevitably fell the denizens of Moscow fled to the Metro system to seek shelter. Fast forward 20 years, and here we are. The surface is a frozen nuclear graveyard of the world before, home to horrifically irradiated creatures. The Metro, is filled with arguably worse, us.
If you're gonna pick up these games, then Redux is your only worthy option since it looks downright gorgeous and it improves on a lot of the original's gameplay features.
Both games feature solid, satisfying gunplay, an incredibly bleak and compelling storyline complete with morality choices and optional story arcs, and an terrifyingly depressing atmosphere that never lets up.
Though a linear FPS, each chapter has a plethora of areas to explore, bringing supernatural terrors and contextual tales of Russian lives gone awry.
I'll try to keep this relatively short, but this game is nothing short of a masterpiece. Don't wanna ruin the surprises for you guys, but if you're a fan of the end of the world, then please, buy this game.

This is a surprisingly good little tower defense game with RPG mechanics. As a commander, you can recruit troops, equip them with weapons and armor and control their few skills when leveling up. It is pretty basic, yet very deep. The levels are single screen and grid based. You place your characters down and they automatically attack as enemies approach them. There are 6 classes, a basic melee, long range, healer, ice mage, slow defensive breaker and all powerful dragon with short and long range attacks. It costs PSI to place your characters, and more PSI to retract them (to move them).
How do you get PSI? Well you start with it, but then as you kill enemies, you gain more PSI and you have a maximum of course. You are defending a summoner against the waves of enemies and the summoner (your player character) can take a beating and has plenty of HP, so the game is forgiving, but rewarding if you make it through the level without being damaged.
You can 'boost' your characters at the cost of PSI. There are many levels of boos that enable skills that you've unlocked through leveling up your characters. When you level up your characters, you select their perk. Which has a simple perk tree of skills and passive abilities. It is a nice little system, but I find myself making the same perk choices instead of diversifying.
Oh and death is not perminant for your characters. If someone dies, just use PSI to bring them back. If your player character dies, you lose the level and need to restart. These levels are quick, especially at 4x speed, so nothing is really lost.
While the game boasts a rich story.... I found myself hitting the skip button. I just don't play games for the story. You read the story as you unlock new levels and progress through a Mario World style map with all of the levels plotted as map points.
The game is very easy to pick up and play, but not just that, it encourages replaying the levels with 3 different difficulties (and a 'casual' difficulty as a 4th). If there's an insurmountable level.... replay old levels *cough* grind. But replaying old levels never seems like a chore, its more of a joy. Even if you keep replaying the same level on the same difficulty, every playthrough is different, since your characters level up and you can change your tactics.
The game is a lot of fun, and while its deep, its never overwhelmingly deep. There's not an overwhelming micro management either, even if you can micro manage everything.
I highly recommend it. Its a fun little game, relaxing and never gets all that intense. I found myself playing it on 4x speed and that seems like it should be the average speed. Is it worth the $15? Its a game you can sink hours and hours into, so you'll get a lot of relaxing playtime for your dollar.

This is a bit of a mixed review. The battle system is pretty interesting with the switching between screens and thinking up the best strategies to beat the enemies. I also have fun with the crafting system (but it does make the game grind-y; I find grinding rewarding so I enjoy it, but if you have little patience for that sort of thing, trying to gather all the materials and experience points to craft stuff might get on your nerves). Overall I've spent a lot of hours entertained by the game and am invested enough to want to get all achievements, craft all items, etc. So for the price I think the experience is really worth it (and I even got it on sale).
That said - I expected an RPG with a rhythm game gimmick, and got a rhythm game with an RPG gimmick instead... the rhythm game battling is like 90% of the game. But it's not quite strong on its own to be what I'd call an "amazing" rhythm game... the music is a bit bland and sounds more like a nice BGM than something to actively enjoy. I also appreciate sleek visuals/designs in rhythm/music games but the battle screen looks pretty basic. This would've all been 100% fine if there was just more besides the battles to the game... like if you could actually move through a map and  meet the monsters in random encounters or something, in a more RPG-y way. Or if the story and characters were more unique and there were more and better written narration and dialogue, in a visual novel-y way. The characters are pretty basic and the dialogue is cringey at times (trying a bit too hard to be witty/funny to be taken seriously, kinda generic, uncomfortable moments like one point where the r-slur is used). Basically I feel like the game is fun but falls short of being Great. Better visuals/music, more varied gameplay, better story/writing - if it had any one of those 3 things, I think it might've been enough. I wouldn't even demand to have all three at once. But as it is, it feels like it falls short of its potential. I think the core idea of integrating rhythm games with RPG in a battle system is really great and that the game could've been better.
But like I said, since it's cheap, I do think it's worth its price. So if you enjoy rhythm games you might as well get it because it'll probably provide quite a few hours of fun. If you don't like rhythm games, I'd just say you won't be missing out on much if you pass.

Dating sim games tend to bore and annoy me.  I love the idea of them but generally I'm not a fan.  That being said, I LOVE this game.  It has a few flaws that are par for the genre, but what sets it apart from other games of this variety is its understanding of its audience.  This game acknowledges that women are type oriented.  Your potential love interests display a range of personalities, so whatever you're into is more likely to be represented here than in the typical dating sim where all of the characters are exactly the same: tough and mean or stoic and surly.  There's a smart responsible guy, a jerk guy, a bishie♥♥♥♥♥♥guy, quiet shy guy, a cute sweet guy, and a couple of hidden female options, if you happen to swing that way.  Personally, I'm a sucker for sweet goofy guys, so Matthew is my hubby when I play this game.  His voice actor really puts it over the top for me and I am so super stoked that this game acknowledges variety in human females by including him as an option.  So, yea, this game hits all of my buttons in a way that most dating sim games ultimately fail.  Highly recommended.

It's like Twilight for boys -- a totally non-special guy randomly ends up in a magical world where a woman with a sexy voice flirts with him. I'm looking for something a little more interesting than sarcasm. I don't need an elitist lesson in how everyone but the dev pronounces "mana" wrong -- I'm sure there's an audience that resonates with, but it isn't me.
The actual gameplay is not terrible, and involves rotating through 3 DDR-style tracks -- one to defend, one to regenerate mana, and one to cast spells. Again, it's academically interesting, but gameplay-wise, it's just kind of infuriating to constantly be shown the opportunity cost of the choosing the track you're currently on.
So maybe that's my gripe -- the game always made me feel like I wasn't doing what I should be doing. The game wants me to take risks with my EXP wagering and to not care about the other tracks during gameplay, but my personality doesn't let me switch into that mode. My personality isn't changing, the game isn't changing, and we're just not a match. If you're not like me, this might be the game for you!

This game, visually, looks pretty good, and not just in terms of fidelity. It has a discernible style that separates it from an Unreal Engine tech demo. The premise is that the player is a detective searching for a boy who wrote him a letter (with a twist that I won't spoil). The detective's investigation leads him to an abandoned mining village in American backcountry, populated by dilapidated quasi-Victorian buildings cutting into the dense surrounding forest.
Most of the story is provided by flashbacks that are activated through environmental cues. The rest is supplemented by minor diversions concerning its paranormal elements. Strictly speaking, there are no characters to interact with directly--only to view from a spectral distance.
The exposition accounts for an interesting tonal difference in the presence of architectural decay. Exploring ruins lacks the familiar feeling of melancholy due to the continuous distraction of exposition, and to the story clarifying much of the surrounding mystery of the world. Taken with the vibrant foliage and sunny glow, the visual atmosphere is almost hospitable enough to contradict its darker narrative.
Unfortunately, the story is sometimes tonally inconsistent. The aforementioned paranormal elements and the cliched twist make it feel a bit silly, but these inconsistencies are also sometimes presented to service a clear visual setpiece. It's best to absorb this game visually and not to try too hard to digest its meaning, which will likely disappoint you.

Software inc is one of those games you find in your que, and you think to yourself "I dont know if this looks i interesting"
Trust me it is.
Software inc is one of those hidden gems in steam you find when despretly looking for a game to play, i saw it on the store front one day and didnt even give it a second glance, then saw it in my que a week later. i gave it a shot and i've spent too much time on it to be right for a game in early access. This game is cheep, packed full of content supprisingly for a early access title and fairly detailed.
The low poly graphics make this game stand out among the other management type games on steam and give it a uniqe look. With character customization and building aspects, the game may not have the details of a triple A game, but the simplistic style will have you focusing on what acually matters, the management.
You create and manage software, as the title inplys you create a comanpy as well. You hire, fire and manage each employee including your own character on projects you want to create. you give the project a name, go through the 3 stages -> Pre Production(Design) -> Production(Development) -> Post Production(Support/Marketing) and pray that you allocated your team and time right to create a sucessfull project. If you do you create millions, if you dont, you go bankrupt, unless you are already a multi billionair taking advangte of the games mechanics
The game includes a stock market, a highly abusable(at the moment) system that allows you to invest stocks into any company on the market, thing is, you can abuse this system by looking for new companys that startup with an OS. they will always make millions and in year 1 without making anything, you're already a multi-millionair. But even with that the one thing that kept me engaged was the micro-mangament and the little details that kept me interested
Software can depend on other software, your OS can become big the next day because someone released a huge game for it and now you are making millions. You might be thinking "Well thats it? i make money to make money", its not that. the game keeps you engaged and on your toes most of the time when you are making that money. If you are like me you will be so focused on trying to get the perfect software, you lose track of time.
OVERALL:
This game is highly addicting, highly rewarding and generally fun. The building mechanic will take hours away from your life while managing your staff and prodcuts will cut your time even more. I highly recommend this game for anyone looking for a good managment game on the market. You will not be disapointed by the low price and fun gameplay

It's one of those love-hate games when you adore some aspects of it and cannot stand the other. It's also difficult to decide whether to recommend or not.
It has gorgeous environments, but horribly looking and poorly animated creatures.
It has a good level design, but too many issues with collisions not being where you suppose them to be or vice versa. Since it's a platformer, that's a big issue.
It has an interesting gameplay mechanics with the pulling glove, but cannot provide much more. Yes, there are rockets boots later on, but they don't really change the gameplay much.
It has an intuitive controls, but sometimes you cannot grab the object for some reason. The objects you can grab are marked with a bright symbol in the first levels, but later all not all of them are marked. This is especially frustrating on the last level, where you need to go via trial and error to find a correct path through the location. Why can I grab this stalactite and not the other one? They are looking the same!
In fact, the game has a lot of small irritating gameplay issues. Also it would be so easy to make the game more enjoyable: just add more checkpoints, light the correct path, show the distance to the objects so you know when you can grab them or not, etc. This wouldn't make the game casual, but would eliminate some of those trial and error moments.
Overall, not bad for an indie game, but the gameplay quickly becomes boring and clearly lacks more mechanics. Mostly because of this I decided not to recommend.

Few games have been able to capture a sense of ownership while at the same time suspending that ownership over a pit of loss like FTL does. The element of risk involved becomes very calculated as you play and explore the game, understanding its mechanics and just learning how to succeed.
Some runs will leave you feeling angry and questioning why you even liked the game in the first place. But that's okay, because you'll also have runs that will challenge you in ways that make you wonder why you would ever consider hating it.
That being said, it's important to note that this is absolutely an acquired taste. You will die. You will lose. You'll eventually win and it will feel amazing. But when you do lose, you start from scratch, carrying with you nothing but memories and the occasional unlocked ship.
Highly recommended, as long as you know what to expect from a roguelike.

Seconds to Square is simple in it's execution while maintaining the fun and a little bit of frustration.  Using either your right or left mouse buttons, you draw a white or black square.  White will speed you up and allow you to jump higher and further while the black square slows you down but will also protect you from environmental hazards.  See, simple!  Oh yeah - you have a time limit.  Good luck!
The game looks great with a minimalistic art style that really suits the fast paced nature of it.  Gameplay is quick and responsive.  Music is a bit soothing and relaxing - a must if your skill level is as poor as mine.
Only real complaint I have is that the main menu screen seems a bit sluggish.  I initially thought the Settings option wasn't operational because it took a few seconds to come up after clicking it.  But beyond that I haven't had any issues - especially for an Early Access title.
Overall this is an easy recommend.  It's fun, a small download and oh yeah! It's free!  No real excuse not to check it out if you're already here looking at it!

A delightful indie gem, Defender's Quest combines some of the funniest writing I've seen in a game with a terrific twist on tower defence.
The campaign is cleverly designed. Each battle has four difficulty levels. You can push through the storyline on a low level, and indeed you need to at the early stages. However, there is plenty of incentive to come back and try it again for special items, experience and rewards. Battles are short and varied so there is not really a sense of grinding; indeed, it is interesting to come back with new options through skills and classes.
There is plenty of scope for strategy in the battles. There are six different classes, each having different skills and attributes which can be levelled up. They can be boosted during the battle, and can be recalled and replaced.
There can be incredibly tense moments late in a battle when a powerful enemy is closing in and you have to frantically recall fighters to put them into better positions. The ability to pause or slow time means that success depends on your strategy, not your reflexes.
The variety of battle maps and enemies make for a different experience in each battle.
There are genuine laugh-out-loud moments throughout the campaign, which adds to the pleasurable experience of progressing through it.
The New Game+ is the finest example of this mode that I've ever seen. It's not just another run through the campaign at higher difficulty, it actually adds side quests, wonderfully-written journal entries and other bonus to make it well worth playing through again.
In short, I highly recommend this game. It's one of the best I've ever played.

As a hardcore rhythm game player, Before the Echo caught my attention soon enough but honestly I didn't know what to expect. The conclusion after beating everything is a fully recommendation of the game.
Before the Echo (also known as Sequence) is a rhythm game with RPG elements. The basic stuff  in summary (HP, Mana, EXP, weapons, accesories...). The main character, Ky, has somehow placed himself into a tower where he needs to fight mobs and bosses in order to escape.
The battle system consists in getting control of 3 labels of notes. They have different purposes and you need to know when to focus into one or another. I won't explain their features here since the game has tutorials for that.
PROS:
+ The artwork is cool. Backgrounds are good-looking, and so are characters and foes.
+ The soundtrack, as you might expect from a rhythm game, is pretty awesome. It also combines many music styles so if you're open minded with that stuff you'll probably enjoy it a lot.
+ 4 difficulties, from lame to more challenging.
+ The RPG system is pretty well included. Just as simple as it needs to be.
+ The storymode is surprisingly interesting. The characters' charisma helpsa lot here.
+ The dialogues. This is actually one of the most remarkable features. Dialogues in this game are VERY hilarious. Together with a pretty cool voice acting, dialogues will keep you super entertaining and will provide many, many laughs.
CONS:
- Despite having a cool artwork, there's not too much variety, specially from foes.
- At some points grinding/farming is mandatory.
- All achievements can be obtained no matter the difficulty you set, which makes them WAY less satisfying.
- No leaderboards.
- Steam version works like a Flash game (for instance, I couldn't make screenshots, nor broadcasts).
All in all, I've had a GREAT experience with this game. It has some minor flaws I could perfectly ignore, and every rhythm player should try this out. You'll surely find some good fun and discover a very consistent title despite its price (less than an euro during sales... WHAT?).
: 7.5/10

text: An rpg about Vampires makes twilight look like a piece of lint to a T-Rex  stomping on it.

Vampire: The Masquerade is a tabletop RPG game that was brought into the video gaming world with its first endeavor, "Redemption". After that, the creative and much more free roaming sequel, "Bloodlines" came out and basically shut down Troika games because of its bugs and glitches. However, the game itself, with its plot, choices, characters and overall lay out were good enough that fans have been releasing unofficial patches for the game in the decade since it was released. What does THAT tell you about the game? ;)
In Bloodlines, unlike Redemption, you get to choose your character by picking which gender you are and which vampire class. The vampire classes are an interesting assortment and essentially choose what your main skills and penalties turn out to be. If you're a Nosferatu, you're hideous and can roam about in public, but you're very intelligent and technical, if you're a Toreador, you're gorgeous and persuade/seduce almost anyone in the game, but you aren't very strong or intelligent and so on. Once you pick your class, you are thrust into a world of vampiric politics, gothic nightclubs and other fun stuff.
The fight mechanics are decent enough and the overall choices that you get make the game extremely enjoyable. The game has multiple endings and you essentially choose what kind of vampire you want to be (nice to people, recklessly homicidal to people, break all the rules, etc.) and what kind of vampire politics you want L.A. to turn into (ruled by the manipulative Vampire prince, ruled by the manipulative asian sorceress, ruled by you, or kill everyone and embrace vampiric anarchy). While the glitches are noticeable, even with any of the numerous fanmade uber-patches, the game is worth playing.

An excellent tower defense game that is traditional in all the ways I love but innovative where it counts. Instead of placing towers, you're placing party members. Like a traditional TD game, there are resource points you acquire within a round that you can spend on placing new towers (i.e. allies) or buffing the towers you've already placed. In Defender's Quest, this resource is called "PSI", which is essentially the "mana" of Azra (aka: you, the commander).  Howevever, Defender's Quest also gives you two other resources to spend BETWEEN rounds: gold and experience.
Experience is used to unlock abilities on an ally's skill tree, thereby making them available to use in battle. (Each skill is assigned a power level and is not available in battle until you buff this ally to that level using PSI points.)
Gold is used to hire new allies into the party or to purchase armor/weapon upgrades for individual allies, which immediately and permanently boosts their stats (i.e. unlike skill upgrades, these are conferred immediately at the start of battle---no PSI points required.)
Every level can be replayed as many times as you want to farm XP and gold, and every level has multiple difficulty settings that earn you better gold/XP rewards for beating them. (There is no penalty for running away.) Beating the highest difficulty on some levels earns you a legendary weapon or armor, far more powerful than anything you'll find in shops.
The only bad thing I could possibly say about the game is that the art in the cutscenes makes the game's aesthetic somewhat comparable to something you'd find on a flash portal. By flash portal standards, the artwork is amazing. By overall industry standards, the art seems a little amateur. The in-game art is pixely and SNES-tastic. I criticize only the cutscene art here. But in the end, it doesn't even really matter, because the cutscenes have no effect on gameplay, and you can even skip over them all if you like. The game itself is A+.
If you like Tower Defense, it's one of the better TD games in the Steam catalogue.

Despite only having logged an hour through steam, I've had KAG since beta. Now that my street cred is well established, onto the meat of it!
First off, yes, Terraria... We get it, you're able to distinguish a particular art style. Well done you.
Secondly, no, it's not Terraria. It's a completely different game.
Thirdly. So long as you don't have a terrible internet connection, this game is freakin fantastic.
Why you may ask? It's PvP focused precision combat with base building. I say precision combat because there can be some stunning trick shots made as an archer, some fantastic bomb jumping stunts as a knight, and collapsing wall sections as a builder at just the right time to squish your opponents.
As much as I love this game, I've given up on it due to a terrible New Zealand internet connection as the precise nature of the combat needs to be seen as it happens and not with a slight delay.
The base building is fun but is something that takes a while to master. Learning things like not making the section facing your enemy of your structure wooden or don't make traps/pitfalls that your own team falls into. But these things are relatively easy to pick up if you play as the other two classes for awhile first as you will constantly be assualting your enemy and seeing the mistakes they've made in their defenses.
The downside to this game is that it can be a bit repetetive. But if you've played any PvP game for any length of time then you'll easily keep coming back to this game as well.

King Arthur's Gold is Terraria online deathmatch. The gameplay rollicks on like a Roman civil war stand-off; a grand construction race to build smarter fortifications.
The class system is fairly bland and customization is purely aesthetic. Archer and Knight have uninteresting abilities, and the core mechanics of combat are too generic to make up for the lack of options. It is the Builder class that carries the depth of the game.
It's with the Builder that KAG offers a real opportunity for creative destruction that few other games offer. Unfortunately, that creativity is buried under a mound of busy-work. With the amount of time spent gathering, dying, and watching your buildings be destroyed you'll often find yourself less of a visionary architect, and more of an exasperated maintenance man.

King Arthurs Gold is a treasure in my usualy gaming rotation. When you get tired of playing FPS for the day and just want to build, slash, and dominate your way to the top, there's nothing quite like the team satisfaction of KAG.

This is a pretty good tough-as-nails retro platformer for people who are into hard games nowadays.
The gameplay is quite excellent, capturing the platforming style very well and adding some power-ups like wall jumping and double jumping into the mix, which in my opinion, gives the game a fresh little feel that isn't in platformers from the 80s and 90s.
The graphics and sound are also very reminiscent of a Commodore 64 game, straight down to the point where each room has names on the bottom of the screen, which is pretty decent for people who want to feel a sense of nostalgia.
The controls are also quite perfect and you'll most likely never find a single problem with them as they're pretty fluid and responsive.
So overall, if you want a extremely hard yet short and entertaining platformer game on the PC, then "You Have to Win the Game" is for you.

If you're looking at this during summer sales or any other discounts, wondering if the game still holds up, it really does.  You can really feel truely immersed while playing this.
Before I talk about how it plays, the game has two ways of being played.  You can play normal or harder difficulties, with or without Ranger Mode.  Ranger Mode removes most HUD, allowing for, in my opinion, THE BEST GAME IMMERSION I HAVE EVER EXPERIENCED.  If you're newer to the single player exploration types of games, Ranger Mode might feel off.  If you have a good sense of how to get through situations, it feels fantasic, both feeling like you're a part of the game, and
feeling accomplished at figuring out levels without being blaringly told what to do.
Main parts of gameplay:
1. Managing resources, your ammo count, gas mask filters, medical supplies, etc..  Discovering hidden caches full of special loot, and finding bodies of fallen soliders, with their own stories, and gear to be scavenged on them.  It's done in such a great way that it doesn't come off as tedious whatsoever, and the scavenging for supplies feels fun and rewarding.
2.  Stealthy or open combat.  When you're not exploring freely, gathering supplies, you're engaged in one of two types of combat: Completely stealthy, silenced, stabbing, using silenced, ranged guns or throwing knives, shooting out or extimguising nearby lights to conceal yourself better.  The second is being caught in large, open firefights, with large teams of soliders, gunning down mutants as they attack in hoardes, using rifles, shotguns, a multitude of explosives and quick movement to stay in one piece.
Either style of play feels fun, and the game generally doesn't hit that many boring parts.  The puzzles aren't overly complicated or obscure, but still take some thinking, and don't intervene with gameplay.
PERFORMANCE: Running a 960, 8GB RAM and an i7-6700, I never had any problems with lag or stutter, and ran 1920x1080, high settings, 4x AA, and never really dipped under 60FPS.
Overall, rock-solid 9.7 out of 10.  But only because there were some very minor texture bugs, or problems.

This review is written from an account of a player who uses the most recent Unofficial Patch by Wesp5, the Plus rendition. As I see it, the plethora of bugfixes and restored content make the game much more enjoyable than the latest official release. The patch, downloadable from the Patches Scrolls (google that :P ) is a must-have in my opinion.
As we're dealing with a game from... 2004, if memory serves... the graphics aren't top notch anymore and they never were, but they're realistic enough not to be a pain for the eyes. The Source Engine definitely helps with the realistic facial expressions and there's a lot of those. The music is a quite moody ambient-sounding set of tracks, however this changes when you enter the nightclubs - all the tracks used in those seem similar to one another, so similar they quickly bore. The sound effects - they are just there. Neither especially good or bad, just... there.
What the game shines in is the story. While fairly linear, it can be experienced in several different ways due to the number of different vampire clans available. The NPCs will react differently to a Ventrue than they do to a Malkavian, for obvious reasons - both clans have different personality traits. Ventrue are cunning in political nuances whereas Malkavian are insane, each of them. There are five different endings available too, so there's a lot of replay value.
Aside from the story, the game is a hybrid of RPG and FPS. The RPG aspects are focused on increasing your skills and traits in order to fare better in problem solutions of your choice, however you won't be able to avoid killing others in order to have your way and that's what the FPS aspect is for: guns, blades, combat disciplines - all this has but one goal. To kill. And depending on which side you pick, you'll get to kill some of the other side. The World of Darkness is a brutal place.
I could mention a whole lot of flaws - but the continuous support for the game - even if unofficial - and the amount of hours I spent on playing it even before I got it on Steam, all this speaks for itself. A 10/10 from me and a badass seal of approval.

The story is compelling, character a great, the choice you made have an impact one the game (more than i'm goud/evil), Plus with the hd patch you can play on a rock on resolution. This game goes head to head with deus ex in my book.

Worms World Party was released in 2001, two years after Worms Armageddon. It was referred to many as a big disappointment, because it hardly offered anything extra to the plate – Wormpot (where you can alter the game in various ways), some extra single play missions, a mission editor… and precious little else.
In Mid 2015 – Worms World Party Remastered was released on Steam. Once again, the new features were very minimal. It boasted higher resolution (which Worms Armageddon had YEARS ago), Steam Trading Cards, Achievements and a few other things that in my opinion, were not very noteworthy.
Thankfully I bought this on a sale at around £3, and that was only to revisit the single play missions. There was no way I was going to fork out £10.99 for this half-baked product.
PROS:
-	Achievements and Trading Cards, which is something I guess.
-	Wormpot offers a lot of diversity. You can have permanent Double Damage, Super Rope, or Unlimited Crate Shower           to name but a few selections.
-	A lot of Single Play Missions. Although some are pretty samey, some are really unique and actually quite fun to play.
-       The Mission Editor is also fun to use; good if you're the creative type and you know a group of friends who will play your missions.
CONS:
-	Let’s get the biggest problem of the game dealt with first. Online Multiplayer is virtually non-existent. Compare that to Worms Armageddon, where you usually see twenty plus people during the evening (UK), here, you are lucky to see one person at any time. This is a major issue, especially since multi-play is the absolute foundation of Worms.
-	Although Wormpot is a unique feature, about 75% of the options to choose from are just plain uninteresting and lazy. High powered Firearms, High Powered Animals, High Powered this, High Powered That. We’re not all kids that crave ‘big-boom’ weapons. It just shows a lack of originality.
-	The screen feels ‘choppy’ , and that’s with all the features cut down. Likely, this is something I encounter on my computer only, but when Worms Armageddon runs smoothly on the same resolution, why am I having issues here?
-	No features to unlock. It was a rewarding experience in Worms Armageddon, where you got an extra utility or an extra option to modify should you complete a mission. Here, everything is unlocked at the start – so it doesn’t feel all that satisfying when you do beat a hard challenge. Then again, there isn’t really a lot more features at the start anyway.
-	The Steam Achievements, again, are unimaginative. Complete all the missions, Complete Deathmatch, Drown 100 worms… yeah fair enough, but the majority are pretty lame and can honestly be accomplished by accident. Woo, I attacked the same worm with the bow and arrow twice. Wow! Have an achievement!
Overall, Worms World Party is the inferior younger brother to Worms Armageddon. Unless you can get it really cheap – and that’s really just for the single play missions – don’t waste your money here.

For starters, just to make things clear, this isn't a "remake". You know, like the old games getting remakes with modern graphics and possibly new features? No, no. This is not a remake, and people seem to be confusing it with one. This is a "remaster", which means you can just nicely run this game in 1080p on modern PCs without any pixelation or issues. There obviously isn't a lot to remaster in a flippin' Worms game, so the difference isn't huge, but the point is that it works! It doesn't crash, it doesn't bug out, it doesn't do weird things - it just works, and that's all I wanted. they also give you some remastered sounds as a bonus, but I just switched to the old ones to get my nostalgia fix (and because I think they still sound better than the new ones).
Now that we have that out of the way, the actual review:
It's a great game. It's basically Worms Armageddon with a few added features and most things unlocked from the start. (To be fair, I don't have the Steam version of Worms Armageddon, so I don't know how that looks like, but I at least assume they couldn't have changed much) It's honestly the golden era of Worms, and it never got even near the perfection of Armageddon-World Party ever again, sadly. So many hours spent in local multiplayer with my friend when we were young, getting gold medals in all the missions and challenges, achieving elite rank in the deathmatch, ahh. Worms is also where all the "party" games started, really. It's THE party game.
The only real issue could be the online multiplater because that, too, has not been changed from the original. And you probably know how that looked like in late 90s to early 2000s in some games... I'm not entirely sure if it even works.
If you have never played it and like Worms, what are you waiting for?
If you have played it before you know how great it is, so what are you waiting for?
If you are not familiar with Worms it's time to get familiar with this piece. What are you waiting for? (Also perhaps stop living under a rock)

There are so many options that it would be completely boring for me to list them all, so here are just a few:  Resolution (640x480 up to 1920x1024), Language (subtitles are the default), Full-screen, Quality, five different sliders for Sounds, etc.  You can play with the mouse and keyboard (key mapping is allowed) or with a controller, which is what I chose.
I could not play the game without it crashing when I was using a 32-bit system, but once I upgraded my Windows to 64-bit, it ran like a dream. (Happy day!!)  It will auto-save at certain points, but there is no manual save.
Controls are basic, with movement, camera (full 360 at your fingertips), a button to inspect/interact, one to crouch, one to zoom, and one to run.
There are 12 achievements that unlock simply by playing through the game, but there are also two secret achievements to be had.  One is rather easy to get, and the other is in three parts.  You could spend hours combing through the lush environment and still possibly miss part one, but oh -- what a beautiful place to get "lost" in~!
If you've seen anything about the game, you already know know gorgeous the graphics are.  There is a brightness slider if you're worried about not being able to see, but what I really would've liked to see is a contrast adjustment.  I love it the way it is, of course, but the artistic side of me would've liked to make the visuals even more rich by increasing the contrast... but I digress! ;)
Those who'd like to just immerse themselves in the world of Ethan Carter will want to simply explore and learn everything by trial and error, but for those of you who would like the basics of gameplay, I'll add them in a spoiler text here:
There's a fascinating dynamic that comes into play as you progress, requiring you to identify the sequence of events that took place.  This will come up in multiple areas, revealing more and more of the story as you go.  It can be surprising, even confusing at times, but everything ties together at the end.
Ethan Carter envelopes a realm full of beauty, wonder, and -- at times -- fear and unease.  The devs gave us a gift towards the end by allowing us instant transport to specific areas of the map so that we can continue to explore without having to spend 10 minutes or more just running to get back to where you want to go... Which is a good thing, because the game won't let you see the ending until you've discovered all of the story elements!
As for said ending, I really can't tell you anything without giving something away, and I wouldn't want to ruin it for you.  The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is something to be experienced for oneself, then talked about later.  I will say that I think that the second playthrough will be even more enjoyable than the first, now that I understand how to play.  Totally recommended for those who enjoy exploring and mysteries.

(Note: This review is for the Redux version of The Vanishing of Ethan Carter that was remastered for the Unreal Engine 4, but is otherwise identical to the original version.)
I'm just a (very) casual gamer and don't usually write reviews, but in the case of Ethan Carter I feel I'm compelled to.  It is by far the most beautiful, imaginative, immersive mystery game I have ever played, bar none.  Brimming with atmosphere, it is a joy to look at and roam in, ever so slightly unsettling, and features an intuitive, very clever gameplay concept that got me hooked straight away.
Ethan Carter's world is gorgeously rendered.  Its narrative is deliberately sparse in dialogue and devoid of the pseudo-occult mumbo-jumbo that you get with lots of other games, and, above all, it's entirely credible.  I'm quite the scaredy cat when it comes to mystery/horror games, but with the exception of one small creepy area, there are no scenes that are gratuitously scary.  Spine-tingling, yes, but never deliberately frightening.  Although set in a fictitious valley in the US, it has a remarkably 'European' feel to it, which will be instantly recognisable to anyone who has travelled across central and eastern Europe, and brings with it a fitting neo-gothic quality that serves the environment and narrative well.
It is amazing and very commendable that a relatively small game dev studio such as the 8-person operation that is The Astronauts have come up with a title that so perfectly combines the elements of a detective story, suspense and the power of imagination.  In doing so they have created a wondrous world of often faded beauty that forms part of the ever-present question: 'What is it all about?'
VERDICT: If you like a powerful narrative -or- if you're a bit of a dreamer -or- if Twin Peaks is your sort of thing -- you will enjoy The Vanishing of Ethan Carter.  And you'll understand why, in Ethan's world, it will always and forever be 7.04 o'clock.

One of my favorite cooperative twin stick shooters. Community is still active, is decent, and you can usually find a fun group who fit your play style. Edit:
Basically, there are four factions; bugs, cyborgs, Illuminati, and the humans. There is a galactic war of sorts and Helldivers are the human soldiers. This is YOU and up to three other comrades. You travel to different planets (swamp, snow, dessert, urban) and complete missions, or try to. Whoever is in charge of the "dive" (host), chooses the faction/location you are fighting, difficulty, and where each mission will start on each map. While completing missions, you are given the opportunity to collect "science". Ten science equals 1 coin. Coins are used to unlock weapon and equipment upgrades. Whether you complete missions or not, the most important part is to stay alive and to make it back to the ship. Some objectives are just not worth doing. Once a map is completed and a team is extracted; experience is gained, science added up to coins, and it all totals to some sort of gain towards the overall galactic war that never seems to end. After each dive you can spend coins for better equipment/weapons etc. Rinse and repeat... rinse and repeat. It is a lot of fun and the developers nailed it.
A few pointers for new "divers":
1. Try to stay with your team but watch fire lanes.
2. Take out patrols before they sound the alarm.
3. If the objective is going to get everyone killed, keep moving.
4. Two players with launchers and ammo can destroy a lot of stuff very quickly with buddy reloading. USE IT!
5. Wait for a good opportunity to call in equipment and such.

As a huge fan of Rhythm games and RPGs I thought that this game would be amazing, but I am extremely disappointed.
While I ultimately ended up playing on Spasmodic difficulty, and am capable of getting 100% on several songs when I 'practice' in the bonus mode, the RPG elements, coupled with the field switching mechanic makes many foes extremely challenging.
Speaking of RPG elements, there is absolutely no explanation of the actual mechanical effects of the offense and defense stats. It's logical to assume that defense decreases the damage you take from missed gems, which is in turn multiplied by the gem color, but no indication is given about how much defense reduces how much damage.
Coupled with the fact that you can't see actual concrete stats from enemies (only vague bars), and the RPG mechanics seem to be a gimick that was tacked on to a rhythm game to make it 'harder' without requiring them to add more songs or harder difficulties for the songs.
Ultimately, I'd rather play something like Stepmania on the harder difficulties for my Rhythm game fix, and then play an RPG like Dragon Age or one of the various Elder Scrolls.
I give this game a 2/5. I might have given it a 3/5 purely for the snarky dialogue during the cutscenes, but the audio quality is hit and miss. (You can tell that certain lines were recorded on different days when the ambient sound changes)

Before the Echo is an RPG where you have to play DDR every time you want to cast a spell, defend against an attack or restore your mana (so you can cast more spells). Combat can be quite frantic as you have to swap between the three aforementioned modes, and it becomes important to find gaps in an enemy's attack pattern to effectively go on the offense. Additionally all combat has a time limit: each monster has a track associated with it and you need to kill it before the song ends to gain any experience or drops.
It's a neat idea and can be quite fun, at least on normal since the DDR inputs for Hard are extremely challenging to anyone without a good sense of rhythm and coordination. A controller with a reliable D-pad is essential, and thankfully you can use a combination of the D-pad and ABXY for simultaneous direction inputs.
Unfortunately it is a grind-fest; you need to craft keys to progress from floor to floor, and to craft them requires items and experience which requires you to fight monsters over and over again. Sometimes you can fail crafting an item, but if you put more experience into the synthesis you will have a greater success rate. Most of your equipment requires crafting, and learning new spells means crafting the scroll then to learn it you have to use more experience and complete a challenge which if you fail doesn't reimburse the experience used.
Grinding often becomes something of a necessity in RPGs but with a game like this you can't just do it mindlessly because of the battle system in place. It probably doesn't help either if you're not fond of the music in the game because you're going to be hearing the same tracks over and over while you meticulously enter directional inputs and pray for the right drop this time.
For the majority of people Before the Echo will not be an enjoyable experience, but if you really love DDR (but are perhaps too corpulent or uncoordinated to deal with floor pads) and grindy RPGs this will kill two birds with one stone.

Before the Echo (formally sequence) is a game with many good ideas.  This is a shame, because it buries them in terrible design and writing.
Let's start with the good.  The basic gameplay of the game revolves around a rhythm based combat system. This is similar to DDR or Stepmania, but with three step charts (one for your attacks, one to defend, and one to recharge your mana).  This system is intuitive and rewards both musical ability as well as strategy (primarily for when you attack).  If this game was just a series of songs which had to be defeated using this system it would have been great.
Unfortunately the game has been lengthened with the most obnoxious forms of grind.  To get to the next boss fight and to proceed to the next area, you must craft a key.  To get the items for crafting the key you must fight the three monsters on your level.  They have a random chance of dropping various items, with some of the required items having a very low chance to drop.  And on top of this, crafting isn't guaranteed.  You can sacrifice your XP (and possibly lose levels) to increase the chance of success, but the success rate caps out at 95% so you can still fail.  If you do fail you lose everything and have to repeat your hunt for those items from scratch.
This means that the game very quickly forces you to repeat the same fight over and over and over again, long after it has ceased to be challenge anymore.  This completely killed any enjoyment I had for the game.  I have a feeling the developers added these grind elements to lengthen the amount of time that people would play the game, but it had the opposite effect for me.
While the grinding aspects are what kill this game, I should note that the writing is also horrible.  Absolutely everything in the game, from the dialogue of every single character and every single item description, is written in this ironic hipster tone.  This might have been amusing if it had been done in moderation, but as it is every bit of text in the game is trying to show you how funny it is, when very little is even amusing (unless you find lines like "I feel like my brain got stabbed by a hobo" to be hilarious).  It also kills your sense of immersion when absolutely every character is aware (and comments on the fact) that the game mechanics don't make sense and seem to be completely artificial.

It's an amazing game!  I was itching for a survival, looting, and weapon crafting type of game.  This was it.
PROS:
-Great Story.  If you're a fan of Resident Evil, it will sort of remind you of the early RE games with Raccoon City.
-On that note, if you're a fan, you'll enjoy listening to Roger Craig Smith basically using his Chris Redfield voice from REV1, RE5, and RE6.
-Addictive if you enjoy survival, looting, and crafting weapons.
-Parkour mixed in.
FUNNY:
-Crane snacking (for HP regen) will make you want to snack (due to the noises he makes).
NEUTRAL:
-Adjusting to first person parkour can be odd at first.  The last parkour series I played was Assassin's Creed and that was in 3rd person.  Parkour (especially climbing and getting down from high places) and get really clunky.  Expect to fall to your death a lot.
CONS:
-The story (although great) did feel really short.  It got a bit fogged out by all of the extra content like the side quests, challenges, and quarantine zones.
-There is no romance option (even though there is obviously one) and it doesn't happen due to plotholes.
-You don't hear from some major characters when you're near the ending (maybe you will in the Following).
-Looting can get old pretty quickly.  You can easily amass all of the crafting items you'll need for the whole game in a couple of hours.  But you'll basically only be looking for rare upgrades and hard/very hard chests/vehicles to unlock after that.
-One thing really frusterating was that during boss battles you lose all of your weapons and equipment.  It's annoying because you work so hard in the game and get them taken away when it matters most and then you just keep dying over and over with barely any way to defend yourself while losing survival points over and over.
-The parkour fever challenges are nearly impossible to complete.  One slip up and you're done.  A "medium" challenge can get really hard because there is barely enough time to finish one.  A difficulty should be based on time.  I only completed one of these and never bothered to waste time to complete more.

I'm a bit unfamilar with the "Tower of Defense" genre as a whole, so I picked this up on a whim for $2.49. Turns out that was a pretty damn sweet deal. Defender's Quest isn't overly complex, innovative, super-artistic or genre-defining. What it is, though, is easy to get into, sort of addicitve, and a lot of fun.
Honestly, the core mechanics are pretty simple - you have six character classes, each with slight customizability (basically skill trees and pallete swapping consist of the variations in-class), and each serve their own purpose. The challenges definitely lend themselves to exploiting this variation - you WILL not beat this game using just your archers, for example. The key strategical elements will be where along the paths you place your characters, how you choose to boost them during battle, and how to time the protagonist's abilities (a feature which helps engage a player and prevents one from just sitting back and watching the level unfold). Add in a mild RPG-twist with how you choose to level up skill sets, and you have a very simple concept turned into something that has multiple layers of combat. Good move on their part.
The story, while simple, is sufficient enough to make you want to keep going. Characters are all pretty eccentric for the most part, and the humor is just average. I'm okay with that, though, as when I bought a game that looked like it could be run on a flash-based website, I really expected a cliche-ridden excuse plot with bland characters. Kudos to the creators on that front.
The real downside of the game comes in the form of some rather noticeable forced level-grinding. The advanced and extreme challenges often change the way you play a level, but the general root of how you play it is still going to be there. Most average players (see: me) will have to repeat a level one or two times before confidently progressing on to the next challenge. This is extremely obvious in the otherwise-enteretaining new game+ as the enemy traits mean you have to work waaaay harder to beat the level.
Other than that though, this is a straight-forward game with a lot upside. I certainly wouldn't be disappointed if I'd dropped the regular price on it. Try it out.

The Vanishing of Ethan Carter is definitely a thought prevoking game, to say the least. It visually impresses and ensnares with a rather unique take on telling a story in a game. If you don't mind a lot of walking, and maybe even backtracking depending on how you play, the game can be quite enjoyable.
Visually the game is breath-taking and some screenshots don't really do it all the justice it deserves. From the very get go of the game you will be hit with beautifully encompasing vistas, forests and derelict towns.
The overal attention to design and look of enviroments in the game are really well thought out. You'll be able to feel every bit of tension or emotion emanating from everything from warm exteriors to dark ritualistic crypts.
Again the game almost overwhelmingly impresses with the audio throughout. The musical score is fitting and flows beautifully between enviroments. Voice acting is also some of the best I've heard; it all sounds natural, clean and no dialog is wasted.
Without going into any spoilers: go into this game expecting something different, but highly interesting. Your character is in this place looking for Ethan Carter and he's a detective, so it's natural for the story to follow a "piece it together" format.
The overal story is very morbid, this is made evident from the first few minutes (if not seconds) into the game. Throughout it is basically your job as the player to run around, or calmly meander, and piece together the overall happenings in this strange little valley  you've entered, by the use of your psychic powers.
This however can run against the games favour though, as it's rather core to the overal gameplay.
First off, just know that many of  gameplay mechanics are actually intricately tied to its story, as that's the games main selling point, its' story.
At the start the game could feel a bit overwhelming, as there is truly no hand-holding, it's up to you to figure stuff out. The game does do a great job at giving you lots of opportunities around the start to get use to or introduce you to those mechanics, hightening the chance for you to actually get the idea around them.
There is a lot of walking, but I feel like the addition of actuall content in between segments gives it enough weight to not be considered just another walking simulator. Even dullish walking between segments can very often be broken apart by our detective giving some very well recorded exposition.

The, "no hand-holding," can be very frustrating though, as there can quite often be no clear indication on where you're suppose to be going, or more importantly, what you're
suppose to be doing.
It could be inconsequencial, as there are only so many places you can actually walk around in.
The biggest issue is that if your unfortunate enough to miss certain "fragments" of the story on your way to the end, which is very possible, you will find yourself having to backtrack across the entire game world. This is actually a mechanic in game, as you will not be able to unlock the ending of the game (even if your standing awkwardly, literally right in front of it...staring at it) if you had missed any of the ethereal security-camera footage caches.
There are some horror elements to the game, but they definitely do not play an overwhelming role throughout. I would rate it more as a suspense/thriller. There are some puzzles, some running, but mostly just walking and thinking.
The game story is very gripping, interesting and something fairly fresh in the time it was released. It will capture your imagination and make you wonder about what truly happened in the place you're roaming around. There are elements from everything from the twisted forms of childrens imaginations to Lovecraftian horror and the repercussions that our actions may carry.
The gameplay is solid, with no bugs that I have experienced myself. The core gameplay will probably not appeal to everyone, it's a slow build up and in the simplest definition a puzzle game wrapped up in an amazing story, so don't buy this expecting a fast paced run through.
Otherwise, this game will really be a decent addition to you're steam library.

Wow, just wow. I can't express how fantastic this game turned out to be. It was not what I was expecting all while keeping up with my expectations, then shattering them. Though short, it is the perfect length for this kind of narrative. It pulls you in and keeps you in its grips.
The graphics: 10/10, some of the best I've seen. Not just how great they are but how they are composed within your FOV. It's almost like every angle of the world was meticulously crafted to keep you intrigued.
The story: 10/10. Go into it knowing nothing and you will come out with one of the most satisfying narrative experiences you have ever had. I'm not just talking about games here. Throughout all narrative mediums, this accels to the top with some of the best stories ever told.
The Characters: 8/10. I wanted more from them but at the same time the character you play as is phenomenal. The world unravels for you just as it does for him. His understanding of the events are real time with the player. By the end of the game, this is even more true. The other characters are just visages, some more interesting than others. I would have like to see more from them in terms of fleshing out Ethan's background. That is the only thing keeping me from going from an 8 to a 10. You might as well read this 8 as a 10 because it doesn't hinder your experience playing this game at all. Just something I would have liked to see fleshed out.
The Music: 10/10. Perfect. Just perfect. Experience it, you will see.
Overall: 10/10. I could go on all day about this game. I'm not kidding, I already have. It is that good. If you have the patience and the constitution to accept that you know nothing going into this game, you will have one of the most satisfying and fulfilling gaming/ narrative experiences you have ever had. It sticks with you and leaves you begging for another experience like it. Would play again and already have.

No offense, but when i first played; "You Have to Win the Game" it seemed pretty difficult playing, but then turned out to be a multi sidescroller game, and 2d platformer. It began slow, but as progressing, the game turned out fun. I remember one spot, a s I was playing, and said to myself: "Ha! bet they didn't think players could do this!", as i was jumping on walls dodging spikes, and doing loops, only to find a new, unexplored, area that was part of the game. After finding this, i went back through the whole 'map' like levels, and found more secret areas as the one I found before.
As progressing through the game, getting my boots first, I figured out that if I went back to ALMOST the beginning areas as before, I could reach those, "Not so easy to reach" areas with ease. Moving onto the room with the spider glove, it made the game even more fun just to keep on playing. I only wished there were more special abilities, or items the player could achieve in the game.
As a 'try-hard' gamer, I didn't want to go online to learn how to play, and am very proud of myself. But only to find that the game seems impossible... I walked to the very end of the game, knowing the 'secret word', and hopping through portals/mirrors to put the letters into the game code, only to find out that it didn't work. So, being very dissapointed in myself, I went online to find the answer, to see if I was even doing it correctly. I watched about a dozen videos, and still couldn't beat the game. To this very day, it is still a mystery, but I would give the game a 7.5 out of 10 for its awesome storyline, gameplay, checkpoints, and its classic 8-bit RETRO look. -Isaiah Hoop

Set in Russia after a neuclear event the surface is now too radiated to survive and mutated animals roam freely around Moscow. Artym must find a way to destroy the mutations before the metro lines become overrun. Venturing out into the city with only limited oxygen and ammo that also serves as currency is essential to humanities survival.
Gameplay wise Metro 2033 plays like most first person shooters with limited ammo counts. Keeping an eye on what type of ammo you are shooting as well as how much of it is a big part of the game, as well as finding it. The story is compelling and well structured into a memorable and easy to follow storyline. The interesting part of this game is the difficulty levels that the game offers. The standard formula for difficulty is to make the enemy shoot harder and have your health bar dropped. Metro uses the formula of making your bullets deadlier as well as the enemies, this can make for a different experience to what you will be used to.
Graphically redux showcases a massive improvement and overhaul to the original release. The developers have put a massive amount of effort into the remastering effects. It's becoming common for developers to half♥♥♥♥♥♥remastered releases but this one deserves praise for what they have ultimately achieved here.
8/10 Would get paid in ammo again.

First of all before starting this review, I admit I was worried about this port: there was a flood of complains back when this game got out on STEAM with many people complaining the game had many issues. Because of that I was with some doubts if I could get the game or not without fearing of having to ask for a refund. In the end I ended getting this as a gift and I decided to have a look if what people were saying is true. In the startup I did have two issues: the title screen and menu was a bit small with the clouds dragging on the black frame around it. Once I reached the Options screen, the screen went completely black, impossible to see anything. I had to open the task manager of Windows to exit the program. However, once I restarted the game those issues were gone. Since then I tested the game for several hours and I found NO issues anymore. Quick Match, Training, Missions, Deathmatch, Options and Online matches were working 100%. I dunno if I was either lucky or the developers launched patches in the meantime but by my experience with this port I can safely tell people that they can buy with trust.
As for the review, this is a sequel of the best Worms title up to date, Worms Armageddon, using the same game engine. This sequel not only counts with the most positive features of Armageddon but it includes many novelties like Wormapedia, Team Battlefields, Wormpot for random match rules, new missions and a MUCH more complete training campaign, allowing both unnexperienced and experienced players to learn the possibilities and tricks of the game and improve their skills.
The remastered version counts with new sound effects (that are optional to use or not) and a graphically improved menu.
As a personal suggestion, I would like to see the game supporting in future higher resolutions than just Full HD: Armageddon is capable of this.
To keep it short, Worms World Party is an obligatory title to Worms fans to expand even further from the Armageddon universe and to fans of fun and cartoony strategy games. 100% recommended!

For those who love videogames without the toxicity of strict competition (as it's trending nowadays) and manage to appreciate solo/co-op campaign games, I totally suggest this game.
In my opinion, Dying Light is the best survival zombie game that ever stepped on the market, being able to conciliate elements of free roaming, exploration, parkour and combat action with a wide and impressive loot & crafting system.
You can literally find weapons around: hammers, bats, blades and modify, upgrade them or dismantle them to recover some of the components to employ for something else, as you try to survive throughout a dynamic and dangerous world haunted by zombies.
The variety of tools and weapons is very large: medikits, molotovs, throwing knives, bows, guns, blades and so much more.
A very strong point of this title is also the experience and skill trees system that allows the player to literally evolve and unlock a set of new abilities that change and drastically improve gameplay quality.
There's a difference between day and night: in Dying Light you can find a night predators stalking the streets, creating tension and forcing to a more strategic approach as they widely diminish your chances of surviving but increase the reward in experience points.
About the game longevity, there's about 30hrs for the base game and 30hrs more for "The Following" dlc only including the main story quests.
Best thing is surely the multiplayer experience if you have friends to play with: the game allows you to do anything you can do in the single player campaign but with the company of up to 3 other friends.
This means that you can play the main story with your friends without receiving limitations or lack of main content!
In my selective opinion, this game is worth every cent.

The previous introduction to the story was copied and pasted from the game's wikipedia page since it compresses the story nicely. The introduction should also give you an idea about what you are doing in this game. You investigate the happenings of Red Creek Valley to hopefully find the missing boy, Ethan Carter. The gameplay itself is pretty straightforward. You have to find missing objects and return them to where they originally were to reveal visions from the past. These visions will tell you what happened at certain places. That is the gameplay in a nutshell and it is actually very relaxing. At least most of the time.
This is where the game really surprised me. The graphics and the soundtrack. The game has some unbelievably gorgeous sceneries and buildings that look very unique and realistic. You can't just walk past them without staring for a moment or two. The soundtrack contains some well made music that will have you relaxed and sometimes on the edge of your seat.

One of those games that can speak to you if you're open to that, or turn into a boring playthrough otherwise.

This charming mashup of the RPG and Tower Defense genres is a delight for any TD fan! While the TD genre is incredibly saturated with generic (and sometimes outright BAD games) this is an awesome example of how fun TD can be. Of course there are better TD games out there but the storyline and the retro feel to the graphics coupled with pretty good gameplay make this a Yes for the TD fan :)

I am a huge fan of Tower Defense games, but it's been a while since I've seen anything this fun. Getting the rhythm of the game is relatively easy, and the difficulty slowly grows with your characters, so it never feels too easy unless you've done some serious grinding in order to gear out your Heroes. The best part is the strategy, but the humour is definitely up there. If you like twisted humour, you will love this game. Slak and Wrenna are the absolute best when it comes to the jokes (though I wish Ice Mages were a bit more useful than just being a slow spam).

I love this little TD with all of it's little quirks. It's fun to upgrade all the gear even though repeating battles is necessary. It's nice to have a fun little game that you can pick up and have some fun drop it for weeks then come back for more.

The trailers and reviews look nice so I decided to pick this game up on sale. It became very boring within like 30 minutes. So it explains how to run, "super" jump if you will, and combine the two to make a far leap. Then gives you a glove like grappling hook. And then you just continuously run threw obstacle course like areas with pit falls that restart you back at the previous checkpoint when you slightly miss a grappling onto the next item and fall in water. The scenery makes it even harder to see the next point that you can grapple onto because it's so dark.
This game really didn't do it for me. I was surprised too because it has so many positive reviews. I got a refund for this one. In a nutshell, IMO the game is simply grappling obstacle after grappling obstacle, and then more grappling obstacles. "Oh you missed a grapple and fell into water? back to check point do it again, and again. Got it? Okay onto the next grappling obstacle......"

Great tower defence game!
